title: DJ UPDATE: Philippines Fires Warning Shot On Strengthening Peso
text:
--Philippine central bank intervenes as peso hits 4-year high

--Bank warns speculators it may curb NDFs

--Official moves may have only limited impact as investors flock to peso

(Combines previous stories, recasts throughout.) 


 
   By Martin Vaughan and Cris Larano 
 

The Philippine central bank signaled Wednesday it's leery of the peso's recent surge and may increase its efforts to curb the currency's rise.

The Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas sold pesos for dollars in the market, traders said, and the bank announced it will review rules on nondeliverable forward contracts, a tool traders use to speculate on the direction of emerging-market currencies.

Manila's authorities stepped in as the peso hit a four-year high, with the dollar falling to PHP41.60. The U.S. currency rebounded after the central bank announcement to PHP41.83 late in Asia trade. The bank's moves came before Standard & Poor's Ratings Services upgraded the government's debt by a notch to just below investment grade.

Central bank Gov. Amando Tetangco soft-pedaled the moves, saying the peso's recent action is in line with a broader pick-up in appetite for risky currencies.

"It's appreciating just like most (currencies) in the region are, although admittedly it has moved more than the others in recent days," Mr. Tetangco told Dow Jones Newswires in a text message. "We are monitoring price action and market behavior to determine (any) unusual activity."

The peso is up 5% against the dollar this year and his risen 4.5% since May 24 alone. That's in sharp contrast to most of its Asian peers, weighed by global risk aversion as the euro-zone debt crisis has roiled markets in recent months: Indonesian rupiah is down 3.0% this year, while the Malaysian ringgit and Thai baht are roughly flat.

Investors have been drawn to the peso for a number of reasons. The Philippine economy grew at a standout pace of 6.4% in the first quarter, and reforms by President Benigno Aquino III have narrowed the fiscal deficit. The peso's gains have been driven by foreign buying of Philippine shares, which increased 59% in the first half of the year.

Thomas Harr, Asia currency strategist at Standard Chartered, said the Philippines "is having a little bit of a moment similar to what Indonesia had between mid-2009 and mid-2011," when that country's assets, such as bonds and the rupiah, posted big gains on expectations of sovereign credit upgrades.

The Philippine central bank may struggle to curb the peso via NDF restrictions since it can only directly control what domestic banks do in this offshore market. "Any rule changes will be modest and limited and will have only a short-term impact on the peso," Mr. Harr said.

Mr. Tetangco said the central bank will review regulations on NDFs and "special deposit accounts"--fixed-term deposits by banks, trust entities and other financial institutions, used primarily to manage liquidity due to foreign exchange inflows--"because these two can be possible entry points for speculation."

Those statements are a "warning shot" to let markets know the central bank is watching, said Credit Suisse economist Santitarn Sathirathai.

But while the Philippine central bank was in the market Wednesday, it typically doesn't intervene as aggressively as its counterparts in such places as Indonesia, South Korea and Taiwan.

And the Philippine authorities aren't greatly concerned about supporting the country's exports, Mr. Santitarn said, because inflation remains low, keeping the peso competitive in inflation-adjusted terms.

Rather, he said, what worries the central bank is the exchange rate's impact on remittance flows from overseas workers. A growing segment of the population depends on those flows to purchase daily necessities, and a weakening dollar means the paychecks from overseas will translate into fewer pesos.

A Manila-based currency trader said the central bank may consider cutting interest rates to lessen the peso's attractiveness, especially if June inflation, out Thursday stays below the bank's 3%-5% target range.

title: DJ Fitch: Not Worried About Decline in Indonesia's  Forex  Reserves
text:
JAKARTA--Fitch Ratings Thursday cautioned that a fall in Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves highlights a longstanding weakness in the country's external finances, but said the drop doesn't change its outlook for the sovereign.

Bank Indonesia's forex reserves dropped almost $5 billion in May to $111.53 billion at the end of the month, undoing most of the gains made in April.

In a statement Fitch attributed the decrease to valuation effects and central bank intervention aimed at propping up the rupiah, Southeast Asia's worst-performing currency in 2012.

Fitch, which last December became the first of the three major credit rating firms to raise Indonesia's rating to investment grade, said that the fundamental strengths behind its rating for Indonesia remain. These include strong economic growth, declining public debt, and the long-term strengthening of external liquidity.

It said it is not yet "unduly concerned about the magnitude of the fall in reserves," but noted the potential risk of capital flight stemming from shocks to investor confidence.

"Indonesia's open capital account makes the risk of destabilizing short-term capital flows unavoidable. The need to further strengthen the external finances through foreign exchange reserve accumulation has therefore long been a factor in our ratings analysis," the agency wrote.

Bank Indonesia stepped up intervention efforts as the rupiah went on a dramatic slide in May, due in part to a lack of U.S. dollar liquidity as foreigners rushed to sell rupiah assets amid fears of a Greek exit from the euro zone.

Traders said the central bank sold some $2 billion of its reserves last week--its biggest intervention of the year--after trying to build up its reserves due to concerns about a worsening current account deficit.

Indonesia has recorded two straight quarters of current account deficit, and last week posted its first monthly trade deficit in almost two years.

Despite the fall in reserves, Bank Indonesia appears ready to continue its intervention. Deputy Governor Hartadi Sarwono on Thursday said again that BI would continue pumping dollars into the local currency market to reduce the rupiah's volatility.

While further intervention is likely to further erode the central bank's reserves, the level remains nearly double that four years ago, and enough to fund six months of imports and repayment of short-term offshore debt.

title: Bank Indonesia: To Continue Supporting Rupiah Government Bonds Via 'Measured' Purchases
text:
JAKARTA--Bank Indonesia will continue to support rupiah-denominated government bonds by making 'measured' purchases as heightened risk aversion prompts overseas investors to pull funds from emerging market assets, a senior official at the central bank said Wednesday.

BI has been buying government bonds partly to keep the rupiah stable, but it was less active in the bond market in May compared with during the previous bout of risk aversion in September, bond dealers said.

BI Director of Monetary Management Hendar said at a forum that the central bank is committed to supporting rupiah government bonds.

"Bank Indonesia will continue to intervene in the bond market in a measured manner," said Mr. Hendar, who, like many Indonesians, uses only one name.

The benchmark 10-year government bond yield rose 57 basis points in May, a month in which overseas investors sold a net 4.4 trillion rupiah ($466.4 million) worth of rupiah government bonds. At the same time, BI bought a net IDR7.7 trillion, less than the IDR13.0 trillion bought in September.

A Jakarta-based dealer said BI may have been less aggressive in its purchases to limit the cost of monetary operations.

Earlier Wednesday, BI Deputy Gov. Hartadi Sarwono said foreign currency reserves--the first line of defence against sudden fund outflows--fell to $111.53 billion by the end of May from $116.41 billion at the end of April.

title: UPDATE: Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor: To Keep Supplying Dollars to Prevent Steep Rupiah Fall
text:
-- Indonesia's central bank to continue intervention amid a foreign selloff of rupiah assets, says bank's deputy governor

-- Central bank to announce new measures to curb rupiah volatily, bank director says

(Adds context throughout, intervention update in 5th paragraph, central bank director's comments in 7th paragraph.)

By Joko Hariyanto

Special to Dow Jones Newswires

JAKARTA--Indonesia's central bank will continue to supply the local currency market with dollars to prevent the rupiah from falling excessively, following its strongest intervention of the year, while new measures to tame the rupiah's volatility could be introduced this week, central bank officials said Tuesday.

"The weakness of the rupiah and other regional currencies is because of the worsening situation in Europe, which has spread from Greece to other countries such as Spain," Bank Indonesia Deputy Gov. Hartadi Sarwono told Dow Jones Newswires in a text message.

"As long as [Europe's] problems remain unsolved, the dollar will remain strong," he said.

The central bank has been suspected of increasing intervention in the local currency market since last week, after the rupiah fell to its lowest level since December 2009. Traders said the week's total intervention likely topped $2 billion, the biggest this year.

Tuesday morning, after Mr. Sarwono's comments, the central bank was suspected of selling another $70 million to stem the rupiah's slide.

Bank Indonesia Director of Islamic Banking Edy Setiadi later told reporters in Singapore the bank may announce more measures to deal with the volatility in the nation's currency.

"There will be an announcement from the governor maybe this week," Mr. Setiadi said, adding Indonesia still suffers "from the turbulence from the European countries," so the priority is still there to temper the "volatility in the currency."

A growing current account deficit and a monthlong foreign selloff of rupiah assets have added pressure on the rupiah, Southeast Asia's worst-performing currency in 2012. The rupiah has fallen more than 4% on the year.

Part of the problem recently has been a lack of dollar liquidity, frustrating foreigners rushing to sell rupiah assets and return to safe havens amid the economic uncertainty in Europe.

Foreign investors, who hold roughly 60% of the local stock market, purchased a net 10 trillion rupiah ($1.1 billion) in stocks in the first quarter of the year but nearly erased those gains in May. A similar selloff occurred amid worries over Greece in the third quarter last year, but the losses proved temporary.

To boost dollar liquidity, the central bank said last week it would use its sizeable foreign-exchange reserves to prop up the rupiah and that it plans to introduce dollar-denominated term deposits within the next two weeks, to persuade banks in the country to keep their U.S. currency with Bank Indonesia instead of offshore. This is expected to boost its foreign-exchange reserves to boost its capacity for further intervention.

The central bank's reserves are relatively high in historical terms, topping $113 billion before the latest round of interventions last week.

--Sam Holmes and Ben Otto contributed to this article.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Ringgit touches 8-month low, growth worries weigh
text:
* Ringgit touches 8-month low; Taiwan dollar hits 4-month low

* Singapore dollar shows some resilience

* Dollar faces resistance vs Singapore dollar near 1.30

(Updates prices, adds comments)

By Masayuki Kitano

SINGAPORE, June 4 (Reuters) - The Malaysian ringgit hit an eight-month low and the Taiwan dollar touched a four-month trough on Monday on heightened worries about global growth after data last week showed surprisingly weak U.S. job growth in May.

Most emerging Asian currencies were weaker, although the Singapore dollar showed some resilience and pulled away from a five-month low set last week.

Emerging Asian currencies have slid over the past month on fears that Greece may exit the euro zone and worries that Spain may need external aid to shore up its ailing banking sector, and worries of a global economic slowdown have added to their woes.

The weak U.S. jobs data and the chaos in Europe have put "fear into the market", said a trader for a Malaysian bank in Kuala Lumpur. "Risk aversion is the main theme," he said, adding that some market players were looking to cover their short dollar positions.

The dollar rose to as high as 3.2050 versus the ringgit at one point, its highest since early October, according to Thomson Reuters data.

Dollar buying by hedge funds and interbank traders helped drag the ringgit lower, traders said.

Against the Taiwan dollar, the greenback climbed to its highest level since mid-January of 30.055.

The drop in the ringgit and Taiwan dollar came after data on Friday showed that U.S. employers added a paltry 69,000 jobs to their payrolls last month, the least since May of last year.

The weak reading has "very negative" implications for emerging Asian currencies, said Dariusz Kowalczyk, senior economist and strategist for Credit Agricole CIB in Hong Kong.

"Weakening of the U.S. consumer means less demand for Asian exports, which will weigh on external positions and growth," he said, adding that risks for emerging Asian currencies were tilted toward the downside in the near term, although the market may have already priced in a lot of bad news.

A recent Reuters survey underscored how market sentiment toward emerging Asian currencies has recently shifted. The poll on market positioning published on May 24 showed that market players turned bearish on currencies such as the Malaysian ringgit and the Taiwan dollar, and also increased their short positions in the South Korean won to the largest in more than three years.

The dollar may now be due for a pullback against emerging Asian currencies, said a trader for a major Japanese bank in Singapore.

"Personally, I feel the dollar/Asians (are) looking like a sell now," the trader said, adding that the market may have reached a point where the dollar has become overbought against emerging Asian currencies.

SINGAPORE DOLLAR

The dollar dipped 0.2 percent versus the Singapore dollar to 1.2906, retreating from Friday's peak of 1.2972, its highest level against the Singapore currency since early January.

The dollar faces resistance near 1.3000, which roughly coincides with the 76.4 percent retracement of the greenback's slide from October 2011 to April 2012.

INDONESIAN RUPIAH

The Indonesian rupiah, the second-worst performing emerging Asian currency this year behind the Indian rupee according to Thomson Reuters data of indicative prices, gained some support due to dollar-selling intervention by Indonesia's central bank, and traders were wary about the possibility of more intervention.

title: DJ Sharp Slowdown In Asia Manufacturing Sounds Ominous Warning
text:
-- China PMIs show slower manufacturing activity in May

-- Korea, Taiwan and Australia manufacturing slows or contracts

-- Exports fall in Korea, Indonesia; inflation benign

-- Data show the impact of crises in the West 


 
   By Michael S. Arnold 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones) Manufacturing activity in China and across a wide swath of Asia slowed in May, heightening fears that the turmoil in Western economies is dragging down one of the few remaining engines of global growth.

Two purchasing managers indexes for China fell in May. The official one, based on government data, showed manufacturing continuing to grow but by the barest of margins, falling to 50.4 in May from 53.3 in April. A figure above 50 indicates expansion.

A private index produced by HSBC and Markit showed Chinese manufacturing contracting ever more quickly, falling to 48.4 in May from 49.3 a month earlier.

"As risks of a hard landing have increased, Beijing should issue more policies to stabilize economic growth," said Li Huiyong, an economist at Shenyin & Wanguo Securities. "The quicker interest rates are cut, the better."

The data come as Europe's spiraling debt crisis and the sluggish U.S. recovery are washing up on Asian shores in the form of weaker demand for exports and capital flight from risk. Asian currencies such as the Indian rupee and Indonesian rupiah have plunged in recent weeks, forcing governments to intervene almost daily to support them and take steps to encourage investors to stay put.

Stock markets, which began the day weaker on global concerns about Europe, slipped further on the weak data, led by Taiwan, down 1.5% around 0330 GMT. Trading was cautious as the weekend approached and with European PMIs and U.S. nonfarm payroll data still on tap. Shanghai shares, though, were 0.5% higher on expectations that the sharp slowdown will prompt Beijing to take aggressive measures to shore up growth.

Asian currencies also extended their declines, with traders saying Bank Indonesia again intervened to defend the rupiah.

The stark exception in Asia, the yen, has served as a safe haven for risk-averse investors, boosting the Japanese currency to three-month highs against the dollar and undermining the key export sector. Japanese government officials ratcheted up their rhetoric Friday, vowing "decisive" action against "excessive" yen moves -- thinly veiled threats to intervene to weaken the yen for the first time since early November.

China's dour manufacturing readings were mirrored across Asia on Friday. A PMI for Australia fell deep into contractionary territory, down 1.5 points in May to 42.4. Indexes in South Korea and Taiwan remained barely positive but both showed growth slowing, with South Korea's HSBC PMI falling to 51.0 from 51.9, and Taiwan's to 50.5 from 51.2.

"Slower output growth shows that Korean manufacturers remain cautious, partly reflecting the recent escalation of external uncertainties," HSBC Economist Ronald Man said in a report on the data.

Korea's exports, considered a bellwether for the region, fell 0.4% in May from a year earlier for a third straight decline, a shock for an economy that depends on them and a surprise for the market, which had expected a 0.7% gain. Exports to Europe and the U.S. plunged.

Indonesia, where a large domestic market provides some protection from global ructions, also saw its exports plunge. They fell 3.46% on-year in April and 7.36% on-month for a trade deficit of $640 million, the first in nearly two years.

One bright spot was inflation, which has remained benign as economic growth slows. Inflation in Indonesia eased slightly to 4.45% on year in May from April's 4.5%. Consumer prices in South Korea rose 2.5%, well within the central bank's comfort zone.

title: UPDATE: Bank Indonesia Confident 'Large'  Forex  Reserves Can Defend Rupiah
text:
-- Bank Indonesia can draw on new dollar deposits to defend the rupiah

-- BI projects the dollar to average IDR9,100 to IDR9,300 in 2012 and 2013

-- BI expects capital inflows to rise in the second half

(Adds background on Indonesia's current account deficit in the sixth paragraph; latest dollar/rupiah rate in the eighth paragraph; and comments from the BI governor in the ninth through 13th paragraphs.)


 
   By Farida Husna 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia Gov. Darmin Nasution Thursday said he is confident the central bank will be able to defend the rupiah as it is armed with "large" foreign exchange reserves.

Its reserves totaled $113.1 billion as of Tuesday, equal to six months of imports and debt repayment.

Bank Indonesia Tuesday said it would offer U.S. dollar term deposits within the next two weeks, to encourage banks to keep their dollars at the central bank instead of offshore.

Nasution Thursday told reporters Bank Indonesia can use the dollars in the term deposits to intervene in the currency market if necessary, by selling them in the spot or swap markets.

Fear of Greece exiting the euro zone along with concern over Indonesia's widening current account deficit have sent the rupiah to its lowest level against the dollar since December 2009.

Indonesia booked a $2.9 billion current account deficit in the January-March quarter, widening from a $1.6 billion deficit in October-December due to robust imports of capital goods and petroleum products.

Dealers estimate the central bank to have sold close to $1 billion so far this week to defend the rupiah.

The dollar was at IDR9,550 at 0520 GMT, higher than IDR9,425 late Wednesday.

But during a parliamentary hearing Thursday Nasution said Bank Indonesia will be able to push the dollar lower to around IDR9,450 later in the day.

He said the rupiah will likely average IDR9,100 to IDR9,300 this year and next. The government assumed a 2012 average of IDR9,000 when it compiled its budget.

Nasution also said capital inflows will likely increase in the second half of the year because the global economic situation will likely improve.

"From a fundamental perspective, global economic improvement in the second half of the year will improve the performance of [our] exports and current account, which will attract more capital inflows than in the first half of the year," Nasution said.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Spain banks woes hit; rupiah, peso fall
text:
* Month-end corp dlr demand, foreign banks hit rupiah

* Philippine peso down on fixing-linked dlr bids, specs

* Baht at 4-mth low on gold importers; 31.92/dlr seen supportive

* S.Korean exporters relive won

(Adds details, updates prices)

By Jongwoo Cheon

SINGAPORE, May 30 (Reuters) - Emerging Asian currencies slipped on Wednesday as investors cut back on risky assets on escalating worries about Spain's banking sector, while Bank Indonesia's move to support the ailing rupiah along with intervention failed to arrest its slide.

Risk worries also restrained the peso's gains after Tuesday's rating outlook upgrade by Moody's Investors Service as interbank speculators continues to sell the currency and on fixing-related dollar demand.

"When we have such a strong USD thrust in the market, it is unclear where the bottom (for emerging Asian currencies) is," said Sacha Tihanyi, senior currency strategist at Scotia Capital in Hong Kong.

"Of course the worst case scenario can be compared with 2008-2009. If that is the benchmark then there is much scope yet for depreciation in Asia ex-Japan," Tihanyi added, referring to the period of global financial crisis.

A government source told Reuters on Tuesday that Spain would likely recapitalise Bankia, which asked for 19 billion euros on Friday, by issuing new debt and possibly drawing cash from the bank restructuring fund and Treasury reserves.

The 10-year Spanish government bond yield hit a six-month high on Tuesday, with the sell-off in the country's debt having driven up their risk premium over safe haven German Bunds to euro-era highs this week.

That pushed the euro to a two-year low and dented Asian shares on Wednesday. The Australian dollar fell after weaker-than-expected retail sales.

China is seen also taking cautious steps on stimulus to boost the world's second-largest economy.

Beijing needs to bolster investment to spur economic growth but it should shun aggressive fiscal stimulus, influential academics said in leading state-backed newspaper.

"Path of least resistance for USD/Asia FX we think is still up given that the risk appetite decline has grown pervasive," said Emmanuel Ng, foreign exchange strategist at OCBC Bank in Singapore.

Separately, the bank said in a note: "Alarm towards EM markets continues to mount with risk premiums blowing out and (we) expect potential USD strength to remain very much a dominant feature in the near-term."

RUPIAH

Dollar/rupiah leapt on month-end demand from Indonesian corporations and foreign banks' dollar bids, dealers said.

The pair's indicative price rose 1.8 percent to 9,550, but market prices were higher with some quotes above 9,600, according to dealers.

The central bank has been spotted selling the pair from 9,420 to 9,580 to select banks, dealers said. Bank Indonesia's intervention may calm the rupiah market, some dealers said.

"The central bank keeps supplying USD and it is estimated to inject $500 million-$600 million a day recently. Quite a bit of the USD demand has been met by now," said a Jakarta-based dealer.

"Demand by foreign banks is still there but it is slowing down a bit," the dealer added.

But investors did not expect an immediate remedy for the rupiah from the central bank's plan of dollar term deposits in short term.

Another trader in Jakarta said rates offered for the deposits must be higher than market rates to be effective.

On Tuesday, Bank Indonesia said the rates will be as competitive as market rates.

PHILIPPINE PESO

Dollar/peso rose on fixing-related demand from foreign banks and as interbank speculators bought the pair, dealers said.

On Tuesday, the pair slid to as low as 43.205 on stop-loss selling after Moody's upgraded Philippine sovereign rating outlook.

"The 43.205 was a bit excessive with global worries still present," said a European bank dealer in Manila.

The dealer expected dollar/peso to move between 43.300 and 43.500.

The pair is seen having technical resistance at 43.475, the tenkan line, as it ended below the line on Monday. Dollar/peso had been closing local trade above that since May 9.

BAHT

Dollar/baht hit its highest in more than four months on demand from gold related investors and interbank players, dealers said.

The pair rose to 31.815, the highest since Jan. 18. The pair may rise further, probably to 31.920, the high of Jan. 16, as worries about Spain's borrowing costs are likely to keep denting risk appetite.

But that level may be a strong technical resistance, analysts said.

If the resistance is cleared, dollar/baht may head to 32.11, the 38.2 percent Fibonacci retracement of its 2009-2010 slide.

WON

Dollar/won rose on persistent worries about the Spanish banking sector, but South Korean exporters limited its upside.

Exporters' dollar sales for month-end settlements prevented offshore funds and local interbank players from chasing up the pair.

"Despite a weaker euro and sluggish stocks, it is difficult to expect a big jump," said a senior foreign bank dealer in Seoul

He added exporters will be more aggressive above 1,180 and investors need to also be cautious over possible dollar-selling intervention by the foreign exchange authorities.

SINGAPORE DOLLAR

U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar edged up, but European investors and leveraged funds sold the pair on rallies.

Investors stayed also cautious over possible intervention by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to cap 1.2800.

But month-end demand from Singapore corporations and risk aversion continued to support the pair.

title: Indonesian Rupiah Hits 2-Year Low On Hedge-Fund Attack, Euro-Zone Fear
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah fell to its lowest level in two years Friday as short-term hedge funds attacked the currency and risk-averse foreign investors continued a month-long selloff in Indonesian stocks and bonds, adding to seasonal demand for dollars.

By Friday evening, U.S. dollar had risen to IDR9,350 from IDR9,280 late Thursday, even after the central bank was suspected of selling some $200 million to prop up the currency, the largest amount in perhaps two months, traders said.

The rupiah has been the worst-performing currency in Southeast Asia this year, falling 2.6% on the year and 1.2% so far in May.

"The rupiah weakening is now due to risk aversion over Greek fears, unlike in the first quarter when the weakness was driven by concerns over Indonesia's widening current account deficit," said Aldian Taloputra, economist at Mandiri Sekuritas.

"Bank Indonesia doesn't seem to want to buck the trend, as the rupiah weakness is due to global factors and isn't the only currency sliding against the dollar," he said, referring to the relatively small amount of dollars the central bank has sold recently in the spot market.

Two weeks ago, a Bank Indonesia deputy governor said the global forces behind the rupiah's fall meant there was little the central bank could do to strengthen the currency.

Traders on Friday said short-term hedge funds were making a speculative attack on the rupiah in the offshore-forwards market, which shook a sluggish market ahead of the long U.S. weekend. Thin liquidity exaggerated the effect, sparking a selloff in other Asian currencies that prompted the central banks of South Korea and India also to defend their currencies.

Bank Danamon's chief economist, Anton Gunawan, said problems in Europe have compounded the customary seasonal demand for dollars in May and June, which is due to offshore debt payments, import payments, profit taking in rupiah assets and holidays.

Bank Indonesia has been intervening for weeks by selling dollars, but only to select buyers--including some importers and banks with bond-related flows--and in smaller quantities than normal.

BI's relatively low level of dollar selling "leads to worries that if people want to buy dollars they won't get any. Consequently there's no credible rate in the spot market that they can use, so people use the NDF price as a reference for the spot transactions," Gunawan said.

NDF prices are typically IDR30-IDR50 higher than Bank Indonesia's spot rate, but were up to IDR400 higher on Friday, dealers said.

Foreigners have been net sellers of almost IDR6 trillion ($648 million) in the local stock market this month--including IDR0.9 trillion on Friday as the market fell 2.1%--after buying a net IDR10 trillion in the first quarter. Foreign holdings make up about 60% of the stock market.

Foreigners also have sold off some $450 million in Indonesian sovereign debt in May, effectively cancelling out April's net buys.

Saktiandi Supaat, head of FX research at Maybank in Singapore, predicted investors would return once global pessimism abated, perhaps after Greek elections in mid-June.

title: ANALYSIS-Investors like Indonesia, but take a rain check on rupiah
text:
SINGAPORE, May 3 (Reuters) - Investors in Indonesia are a facing a tricky manoeuvre balancing their bullishness on the economy with fears the currency is set to weaken this year, and are finding the best option is to cut exposure to rupiah-denominated assets.

Foreign investors have been cutting exposure to rupiah bonds and stocks for weeks, suspending a long spell of bullishness based on Indonesia's high yields, strong growth and its swift ascension into the investment grade club.

Fund managers have been distancing themselves from the rupiah market too, moving to neutral or even underweight positioning.

So when the same set of investors lapped up a $2.5 billion global dollar bond issued by Indonesia late in April, it was clear that their doubts and unease lay not with the fundamental attractiveness of Southeast Asia's largest economy, but rather with assets denominated in the local currency, the rupiah .

"This year won't be the year for Indonesia," said Arnout van Rijn, chief Asia-Pacific investment officer for Robeco.

Foreigners hold about a third of local bonds, which exposes the $84 billion market to a brutal sell-off should the global risk environment change. And the burden of servicing foreign creditors is burning a hole in Indonesia's external account, which is already hurting from slowing exports.

The central bank's somewhat unusual policies are part of the problem. It appears to have cut rates too much, oil prices are almost certain to push inflation higher, and no one's quite sure when Bank Indonesia will ease its tight grip on the rupiah .

"It seems to have become consensus now that Indonesia's policy is not heading in the right direction, but I don't think they are ready to retrace on any of their policies yet," said van Rijn.

"Until that policy changes, I don't think we will move from our underweight position."

Robeco, which has $2 billion under management in Asia, has been underweight Indonesian equities since the second half of 2011.

Mutual funds and other foreign players have pulled money from the Jakarta stock market in the past month, extending a trend seen in 2011 when their net investments dropped by almost half to about $1.3 billion.

Fund managers at Aberdeen Asset Management are neutral to slightly underweight Indonesian debt. Likewise, Schroders' fund manager Rajeev De Mello is staying away from both the rupiah and Indonesian government bonds for now.

Although an auction of 6 trillion rupiah ($650 million) of debt on Wednesday was well-received, foreign appetite has been gradually waning. Offshore investors have pared their holdings of rupiah debt down from as much as 35 percent of the market to 29 percent currently.

Bank Indonesia does not disclose the levels of foreign participation at its bond auctions. But responses at successive auctions have been lukewarm and bid-to-cover ratios have plunged. The government has astutely decided it will issue more global dollar bonds this year to meet its funding needs.

Rupiah debt yields have fallen, masking the declining interest, due to lower policy rates, rising money supply and the bids from benchmarked fund managers who are obliged to stay invested in Indonesia by their investment guidelines.

Ten-year bonds used to yield 9.3 percent early in 2011. Now they yield 5.9 percent. For any investor who feels the odds of the rupiah depreciating are relatively short, buying rupiah debt just doesn't make sense, simply because it can cost 5.6 percent to hedge the rupiah risk in offshore non-deliverable forwards.

TAKE NO RISKS

Although Indonesia did post its first current account deficit in four years in the final quarter of 2011, it was a modest 0.4 percent of GDP. Rising imports are not unexpected in an economy where growth is surpassing expectations and which is investing heavily in industrial capacity.

However, closer scrutiny shows bond coupon payments to foreigners, dividend payments to overseas equity investors and the servicing of rising amounts of cheap dollar loans are keeping Indonesia's external income account in a deep deficit.

So even those who see some short-term value in rupiah-denominated bonds are wary of standing on the wrong side of a market in which others are rapidly cutting positions and there is a view that the currency is set to weaken.

"The choice is to pick pennies in front of a steamroller or stay neutral," said one fixed income strategist who didn't want to be named.

CitiGroup economist Helmi Arman predicts the rupiah will drop to 9,370 by the end of 2012. It was trading around 9,200 per dollar on Thursday.

Morgan Stanleycurrency strategist Stewart Newnham expects the rupiah to decline to 9,550 by the third quarter because the income account will exert pressure on the balance of payments even if foreign holdings of bonds fall.

Export earnings aren't rising because the rupiah is too expensive. Bank Indonesia's heavy intervention has essentially kept it in a tight 8,800-9,200-per dollar range since October last year.

That policy, and a heavy pro-growth tilt, may prove to be counterproductive. As Bank Indonesia cut interest rates by a percentage point between September 2011 and February 2012, foreigners went from being overweight to underweight the bonds.

The more Bank Indonesia intervened to keep a tight rein on the rupiah, the more it exposed its concerns about potential capital outflows and that made investors edgy. Now they worry the rupiah market just isn't liquid or deep enough.

Those still invested are willing to give Bank Indonesia the benefit of doubt for now. Expectations for volatility and rupiah depreciation are modest, even if the widening current account gap reminds some of 2008 and the crisis in 1997/98, when the currency was attacked viciously by speculators.

"While top-line macro data appears strong, underneath the economy has begun to experience the same destabilizing financial engineering that preceded the 1998 Asian financial crisis," Sean Darby, chief equity strategist at Jefferies.

"A change in the terms-of-trade would have a far more disruptive effect on the economy than equity markets are discounting," Darby said in a recent note, adding he'd initiated cover on Indonesian equities with a bearish view.

(Additional reporting by Aditya Suharmoko in Jakarta; Editing by John Mair)

title: UPDATE 1-FULL TEXT-Indonesia c.bank holds rates steady
text:
JAKARTA, April 12 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank left its key interest rate unchanged at a record low of 5.75 percent on Thursday, as expected, as March inflation remained low and after parliament derailed a government plan to raise fuel prices this month.

 For more news on the rate decision, see 

 Following is the full text of the central bank statement:

 Bank Indonesia will continue strengthening monetary operations and macroprudential policies by consistently keeping interest rates with macroeconomic development going forward. By coordinating with the government through inflation management teams in the central and regional levels, Bank Indonesia is confident to bring 2013 inflation towards 4.5 plus minus 1 percent.

 The board of governors views that the global economy is still clouded by high uncertainty. While the U.S. economy has shown improvement, recovery in Europe is still hampered by the ongoing crisis resolution and there are indications of slowdown in China and India. A global economic slowdown is estimated to further reduce exports of emerging markets including Indonesia.

 Global inflationary pressures are still relatively low so developed economies still continue accommodative policies despite with limited room. But rising global commodity prices, particularly oil, have increased inflationary pressures that can push tighter monetary policy in emerging markets. Volatility of foreign capital inflows to emerging markets is estimated to continue.

 The board of governors estimate Indonesia's economic growth will still be relatively high amid risks of global economic slowdown and possible government policy on fuel prices. In the second quarter growth is estimated reaching 6.4%, slightly lower than the first quarter at 6.5%. Growth is estimated to reach 6.3-6.7% in 2012 and rise to 6.4-6.8% in 2013. Balance of risks for 2012 shows that growth tends to bias downwards because of global economic slowdown and possible fuel price policy by the government, if without stimulus particularly from the fiscal side.

 Indonesia's balance of payments in 2012 is estimated to record a lower surplus than the previous year. That is mainly due to a bigger current account deficit because of slowing exports. Capital and financial transaction is estimated to still record a quite high surplus supported by foreign direct and portfolio investments. Foreign exchange reserves until end-March were still quite big at $110.5 billion, equal with 6.1 months of imports and foreign debt payments.

 The rupiah in the first quarter weakened. Point-to-point it weakened 0.83% to 9,144 per U.S. dollar and in average 1.03% quarter-to-quarter to 9,066. The weakening was followed by rising volatility due compared to the previous quarter. Pressures to the rupiah were from foreign portfolio adjustments due to global sentiments and rising domestic inflation expectations, aside from rising forex demand for imports. Bank Indonesia's rupiah stabilisation by intervening in the forex market or buying government bonds in the secondary market made the rupiah movement still maintained.

 Inflation was still manageable although there are risks of rising inflationary pressures going forward. CPI inflation in the first quarter was at 0.88% quarter-to-quarter and 3.97% year-on-year, higher than the previous quarter. Going forward, Bank Indonesia will remain vigilant on the risks of rising inflation expectations particularly due to fuel price policy that could be pursued by the government.

 Banking system stability remained stable and followed by better intermediary functions in supporting economic financing. Loan growth as of end-February reached 24.2% year-on-year. Investment loans grew quite high at 33.2% and are expected to raise economic capacity. While capital working loans and consumer loans each grew by 23.4% and 19.6%.

 Going forward, the board of governors will learn the impact of possible government policy related to fuel prices and the risks of global economic slowdown to Indonesia. If the fuel price policy is pursued by the government, Bank Indonesia remains confident the impact to inflation will be temporary (one-time shock). However, Bank Indonesia will optimise various policies needed to minimise the temporary impact and manage inflationary pressures based on fundamentals to be as targeted.

 Bank Indonesia will strengthen the mixture of monetary and macroprudential policies that has been pursued. Interest rate responses are still aimed at managing inflationary pressures based on fundamentals according to future macroeconomic forecasts. Meanwhile to manage short-term and temporary inflationary pressures, the policies will be focused on strengthening monetary operations and managing excess liquidity. Coordination with the government will be intensified.     

(Editing by Kim Coghill)

Bank Indonesia said the reserves stood at $110.49 billion at the end of March compared with February's $112.22 billion.

title: UPDATE: Bank Indonesia Leaves Overnight Benchmark Rate At 5.75%; Could Mark End Of Easing
text:
-- Bank Indonesia keeps benchmark overnight rate at 5.75%

-- Decision could mark the end of recent easing campaign for this year

-- Bank Indonesia to control excess liquidity

(Recasts 2nd paragraph; adds Bank Indonesia comments in the 4th and 5th paragraphs, economists' comments in the 3rd, 10th, 11th, and 12th paragraphs, and market reaction in the 13th paragraph.)

By Farida Husna and I Made Sentana

Of Dow Jones Newswires

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia on Thursday kept its overnight benchmark rate unchanged at 5.75% in anticipation of rising inflationary pressures as the government is seeking to raise subsidized fuel prices next month.

The central bank's latest decision, which came even as annualized inflation unexpectedly slowed to 3.56% in February from 3.65% the month before, could signal the end of Bank Indonesia's recent easing campaign, at least for this year, as the central bank vowed to "optimize all monetary policies to mitigate the impact of the government's fuel price policy."

Societe Generale economist Wee-Khoon Chong said "Bank Indonesia has completed current easing cycle, and it is now in a fairly accommodative stance."

After the monthly rate-review meeting, central bank spokesman Difi Johansyah said Bank Indonesia will take the steps needed to head off rising inflation in the short term, including by stepping up its monetary operations to control excess liquidity.

He said the central bank will also continue to ward off a sharp fall in the rupiah by intervening in the foreign exchange market, and will buy rupiah-denominated government bonds in the event of massive sell-off by foreign investors.

The rupiah has been under pressure recently due to persistent demand from importers and outflows from the stock and government bond markets because of concerns Bank Indonesia's monetary policy may have been too loose after it surprised the market last month with a 25 basis point cut.

Meanwhile, the government is seeking approval from parliament to raise subsidized fuel prices by about a third from April in order to prevent its subsidy burden from ballooning due to the recent surge in global oil prices.

Bank Indonesia Deputy Gov. Hartadi Sarwono reiterated Wednesday that inflation may accelerate to 7% at the end of the year due to the government's fuel policy, overshooting its inflation target of 3.5%-5.5%.

Eleven of 13 economist polled by Dow Jones Newswires said they expected the central bank to keep the policy rate at an all-time low, after cutting it by a total of 100 basis points in the past five months.

"The rupiah will be helped by the decision to keep the BI rate unchanged," said Bank Internasional Indonesia economist Juniman.

He added Bank Indonesia should raise the rate by 25 basis points each in May and June if the parliament approves the government's plan to raise fuel prices.

OCBC economist Gundy Cahyadi said he expects Bank Indonesia to unwind the series of rate cuts it has made since last year, bringing the BI rate to 6.5% by year-end

The rupiah was at IDR9,125 to the dollar after the central bank's decision, little changed from before the announcement of its stance, but still up an intraday low of IDR9,170 due to a suspected Bank Indonesiaintervention. Meanwhile local stocks were 0.3% higher at 0657 GMT, while government rupiah bonds were generally steady.

title: INTERVIEW: IMF's Zavadjil: Indonesia Planned Fuel Price Hike 'Very Positive' Development
text:
-- IMF Jakarta representative Milan Zavadjil says Indonesia's planned fuel price hike is a "very positive" development

-- But he says Bank Indonesia should be ready to tighten monetary policy to prevent it pushing up other prices

-- He also says the central bank would likely tolerate a strong gain in the rupiah if global conditions improved

(Adds comments, context throughout.)

By Natasha Brereton-Fukui

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's planned increase in subsidized fuel prices is a "very positive" development, but its central bank should stand ready to tighten monetary policy to stop it pushing up other prices, Milan Zavadjil, the International Monetary Fund's senior representative in Jakarta, said in an interview Thursday.

In a speech, Zavadjil also stressed the need for flexible exchange rates and interest rates given the current uncertain environment, and said he thought Indonesia would tolerate strong appreciation in its currency, the rupiah, if global conditions improved.

Indonesia heavily subsidizes several fuel products to shield consumers from high oil prices. But that is costly, and its parliament is considering ways to adjust its fuel-price policy.

Zavadjil told Dow Jones Newswires the step could cause a "hiccup" in inflation, which could be "significantly" higher than the IMF's 2012 forecast of 5.8%, and damp private consumption, putting pressure on the fund's forecast of 6.1% growth this year.

But the country has a very strong pipeline of foreign direct investment and domestic projects, and the higher fuel prices shouldn't cause the economy to lose momentum, he said.

"From our perspective, it's a very positive development, because this subsidy spending is very large and very unproductive, and this (move) will over time create more space for spending on social issues and on infrastructure," Zavadjil said.

Still, the IMF official highlighted the need for Bank Indonesia to be as aggressive addressing inflationary pressures as it was toward signs of weakening. He noted that it had responded to fuel price hikes in 2005 and 2008, and stopped them pushing up core prices.

"I think BI needs to be ready to, again, tighten monetary conditions to prevent the spillover and the second-round effect of the fuel price hike," Zavadjil said in an interview on the sidelines of Bank of America-Merrill Lynch's Asean Stars Conference.

A 33% increase in fuel prices could add two to three percentage points to inflation, he said, but added that continuing favorable developments in food prices should give "room for maneuver."

Zavadjil said Bank Indonesia's currency intervention policy still seemed focused on limiting volatility, and in the past it had allowed the rupiah to adjust when confronted with strong pressures.

"I think if there's a turnaround in global sentiment and the rupiah started to appreciate, BI would be very happy with that and would tolerate a strong appreciation," he said.

-By Natasha Brereton-Fukui, Dow Jones Newswires, +65-6415-4044, natasha.brereton-fukui@dowjones.com

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's planned increase in subsidised fuel prices is a "very positive" development, but the country's central bank should stand ready to tighten monetary policy to prevent any inflationary spillovers, Milan Zavadjil, the International Monetary Fund's senior representative in Jakarta, said Thursday.

In an interview, Zavadjil said that while the step could cause a "hiccup" in inflation and damp private consumption "a little," posing some downward risks to growth in the short term, the country has a very strong pipeline of foreign direct investment and domestic projects, and the higher fuel prices shouldn't cause the economy to lose momentum.

In the medium term, Zavadjil said the move would free up more fiscal room for spending on infrastructure and social issues.

The IMF official also said the country's currency intervention policy still seemed focused on limiting volatility, despite its more modest presence in the foreign-exchange market recently.

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia to issue more bonds in the H1 2012
text:
(Updates with quotes, details)

JAKARTA, Dec 15 (Reuters) - Indonesia's finance ministry plans to accelerate the rate at which it issues bonds in 2012 due to concern over a global economic downturn and will issue 55-60 percent of its target in the first half of the year, the debt office said on Thursday.

The debt office earlier this month said it planned to issue 240.33 trillion rupiah ($26.45 billion) in government bonds next year to cover a budget deficit of 1.5 percent of the country's gross domestic product.

"We are considering (that the) market situation next year will not be as good as this year ... In the first semester we will issue more bonds and we don't have plans to issue foreign currency bonds in the domestic market," debt office head Rahmat Waluyanto told reporters.

The ministry plans to issue a global bond in the first quarter of next year, with a samurai bond in the first half and followed by a global sukuk at the end of the first half next year.

The ministry has said it will cap foreign issues at a maximum 18 percent of total bond issues next year.

Arga Samudro, a Jakarta-based analyst at Bahana Securities, said the government was confident its bond issues in the year's first half would succeed because it believes the global turmoil during that period would not be as bad as in 2008.

The bonds would attract foreign investors looking for high yields in emerging markets at a time of slow opportunities elsewhere, he said.

"Maybe the government sees there will still be strong demand, but if the turmoil is not too bearish. Investor appetite is still there," he said.

Indonesian markets have been volatile in recent weeks on investor worries over euro zone debt but the yield of the benchmark 10-year Indonesian government bond neared record lows due to recent government and central bank intervention and as Southeast Asia's largest economy shows resilience.

Indonesia's economy grew strong at 6.5 percent in the first nine months this year, showing few signs of being hurt by global woes, though foreign capital outflows have weakened its rupiah and analysts said it could suffer slower exports and direct investment flows next year.

($1 = 9,085 rupiah)

(Reporting by Adriana Nina Kusuma and Rieka Rahadiana; Editing by Matthew Bigg)

title: EM ASIA  FX -Short-covering supports Asia  FX , but poised for losing month
text:
* Macro names, specs cover short Asian FX positions

 * Indian rupee has slid 6.7 pct during November

 * Indonesian rupiah down 3.3 pct for the month

 * Won finds support from Asian c.bank demand to buy bonds 

(Adds details, updates prices)

 By Jongwoo Cheon

 SINGAPORE, Nov 30 (Reuters) - Emerging Asian currencies rose slightly on Wednesday on short-covering after European officials agreed to strengthen a bailout fund, but most regional units lost ground during November.

 The won found support from a central bank in central Asia, which dealers said had sold about $700 million in dollar/won on Tuesday to buy South Korean bonds. Some Asian central banks have bought bonds in Korea to diversify their foreign exchange reserves.

 Euro zone officials agreed on Tuesday on two ways to leverage the firepower of their bailout fund, the 440-billion-euro European Financial Stability Facility (EFSF), using both an insurance scheme and a co-investment programme. They also agreed to extend further aid payments to Greece and Ireland.   

 Hopes rose for more involvement from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) after Eurogroup President Jean-Claude Juncker said there was agreement to rapidly explore ways of boosting the IMF's resources through bilateral loans so it can match the leveraged EFSF's capabilities. 

 However, many investors looked to take profits from gains in emerging Asian currencies rather than to add more bets, due to  persistent scepticism about the euro zone's efforts. The caution put pressure on Asian stocks.

 "People are reducing long dollar/Asian currencies as they sense something is cooking in the euro zone," said a senior Asian bank dealer in Kuala Lumpur.

 "But the market has not gone short yet because once the euro breaks 1.3200, hell will break loose," he added.

 The euro, as of 0708 GMT, edged down 0.1 percent to $1.3300 for the day.

 Most emerging Asian currencies have fallen against the dollar this month, although they found relief from short-covering this week on hopes of progress in tackling the euro zone debt crisis.

 The Indian rupee , which last week hit a record low, has been the worst performer among the regional currencies. It has lost 6.7 percent against the dollar in November, according to Thomson Reuters data. 

 If the currency maintains the loss or falls more, that would be its biggest monthly fall in at least 16 years.

 The Indonesian rupiah has shed 3.3 percent versus the dollar this month, Thomson Reuters data showed, although dealers said the central bank has been intervening by selling dollars.

 Earlier, Bank Indonesia's governor said the central bank plans to intervene more heavily in the currency market and dealers spotted its dollar-selling. 

 Emerging Asian currencies are expected to stay weak next month, dealers and analysts said.

 "The EU agreement is definitely a welcome development in terms of EUR. However, it will be unable to lift general sentiment. I would think the minor risk-on sessions present better entries to short Asia ex-Japan currencies in the short-term," said Andy Ji, Asian currency strategist for Commonwealth Bank of Australia in Singapore.

 "We will have the usual USD strength in December. European bank recapitalization is likely to take two quarters judging by the experience in the last global crisis. While EUR/USD might get stuck in the range on these offsetting forces, these developments are certainly negative for Asia ex-Japan currencies."

 WON

 Dollar/won eased on supplies from custodian banks and South Korean exporters for month-end settlements.

 But the pair recovered most of its earlier slide as importers and some offshore funds bought it, prompting speculators to cover short positions.

 Investors were keeping an eye on flows linked to a sale of a stake in Kumho Petrochemical Co.

 IFR reported on Tuesday an undisclosed vendor has launched a block trade in Kumho to raise up to 418 billion won ($362.1 million). 

 An official at a bookrunner said foreign investors were estimated to have taken around half of the stake, which currency dealers say may result in dollar offers of about $200 million.

 RINGGIT

 Macro names and interbank speculators sold dollar/ringgit , but some players covered short positions with support seen at 3.1600.

 In the past, when the pair rose above that level, the dollar strengthened further.

 A Kuala Lumpur-based dealer said market players are reluctant to sell the pair more, given persistent worries about the euro zone.

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR

 U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar eased on selling from macro accounts and interbank speculators but recovered most of the slide.

 Investors covered short positions as the pair is seen facing support around 1.2900. 

 BAHT

 Dollar/baht fell on offshore banks' selling but its slide was limited, tracking other dollar/Asian currencies.

 The Bank of Thailand, as many expected, slashed interest rate by 25 basis points (bps) to cope with the floods and said it would ease policy again if the economy does not recover.

title: MONEY MARKETS-Funds dwindle in Asia as eurozone strains grow
text:
* Japan infuses dollar funds, Indonesia intervenes

* European banks' demand for ECB funds hit a two-year high

* Investors underweight towards Asian debt - StanChart

By Saikat Chatterjee

HONG KONG, Nov 30 (Reuters) - Rising strains in the euro zone have reduced the availability of dollar funds in Asian money markets, raising the risk of a selloff in vulnerable markets like Indonesia and South Korea.

Even though liquidity typically tends to recede from mid-December as banks reduce operations going into the year-end, traders were surprised that a noticeable drop in funding conditions began last week, underscoring fragile market sentiment.

While the funding fall hasn't led to a big selloff in Asian debt and FX yet, apart from the wobble in September, a further rise in dollar costs would force foreigners to start reducing their holdings in some of these markets.

"We are a bit surprised by the drop in interbank liquidity this week," said the head of short-term rates and money markets desk at a European Bank in Singapore.

"While most banks are comfortable holding funds this week and are loaning out money for short tenors, it does mean that raising funds is going to get a lot more difficult than we initially hoped for," he said.

The Bank of Japan supplied dollars in market operations for the fourth time this month on Tuesday - $100 million maturing in three months and $1 million maturing in a week.

The program had been untapped for more than a year because it usually costs more than borrowing dollars in the open market.

Signs of money market stress is popping up in some of the region's popular markets too. Indonesia's central bank intervened in the currency market on Tuesday by selling U.S. dollars to stabilise the local rupiah.

Such intervention is expected to rise as eurozone funding conditions get worse by the day.

Euro zone banks' demand for weekly funding from the ECB hit a new two-year high on Tuesday. A total of 192 banks took a combined 265.5 billion euros at the ECB's once-a-week handout of limit-free seven-day loans.

The amount tops the 247 billion that 178 banks took last week and comes at a time when indirect gauges of securing dollar funds, such as euro/dollar cross currency basis swaps, hover near October 2008 level highs.

On Wednesday, one-year rates which indicates the premium that borrowers have to shell out for swapping euro interest payments to get dollars, held at 108 basis points, its most expensive level since 115 bps in late 2008.

That is dictating investor positioning towards emerging markets.

After investor meetings in the U.K, strategists at Standard Chartered Bank said most of their investors have shifted towards an underweight duration in Indonesia from overweight.

In a research note on Tuesday, the bank said investors are generally underweight in Malaysia and Thailand as Asian bond yields are unattractively low.

In a sign of how vulnerable some of these markets may be, the bank said foreign holdings in Korea are concentrated at the front end of the curve while foreign holdings in Indonesia are more concentrated at the long end of the curve.

As the cost of borrowing dollars show no signs of easing, the pressure on some of these markets are rising.

Outright three-month dollars in Singapore fixed at 0.52556 percent, its highest level since July 2010 pointing to a higher LIBOR fix later in the day.

With December end LIBOR <0#ED:> indicated at 0.6075 percent, outright rates are set to rise more in coming days.

title: UPDATE: Bank  Indonesia  Gov: To Boost  Intervention  In  Currency  Market
text:
-- Bank Indonesia says it will step up defense of the rupiah.

-- Forex reserves fall further to $112 billion from $114 billion at the end of October.

-- Bank Indonesia revises down 2012 growth forecast to 6.3% from 6.7%.

(recasts the lead, and the 2nd paragraph; adds context in 4th-5th paragraphs, comments from deputy governor in 7th-9th paragraphs; suspected bank Indonesia's intervention in 7th paragraph; economists' comments in 6th, 10th, 12th and 13th paragraphs)


 
   By Farida Husna 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia Wednesday promised to step up intervention in the currency market to prevent the rupiah from falling sharply even as its foreign exchange reserves continued to fall in the face of ongoing capital outflows.

Bank Indonesia Gov. Darmin Nasution said besides selling more U.S. dollars in the currency market, the central bank may start to buy rupiah-denominated government bonds from foreign investors using dollars "if necessary."

By paying U.S. dollars instead of rupiah to foreign investors selling their government bond holdings, Bank Indonesia would help reduce demand for the U.S. unit in the currency market, Nasution added.

The Indonesian government's local currency bonds were in high demand in the past two years from foreign investors seeking higher yields than those in developed economies. These investors were attracted to Indonesia's stable political situation and robust economic growth, and in July they held as much as 35% of the government's outstanding rupiah bonds.

Foreign investors have since pared their holdings to 29% of the outstanding bonds, but economists warn the proportion is still high. They say it makes the rupiah vulnerable to sudden fund outflows when investors exit risky assets amid continued uncertainty about the European sovereign debt crisis.

Daiwa Securities said in a research report Wednesday that the rupiah is more vulnerable to sudden capital outflows than regional currencies, except the Hong Kong and Singapore dollars, as the country's short-term debt is equal to 36% of foreign exchange reserves.

Dealers suspected Bank Indonesia sold around $200 million of the U.S. currency at IDR9,190 after Nasution made the comments. The rupiah has lost 3.8% of its value to the dollar so far this month due to resurfacing concerns over the euro-zone debt problems.

Separately Deputy Governor Halim Alamsyah told reporters Bank Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves have fallen to around $112 billion, but they are still sufficient to cope with capital outflows.

The central bank said earlier this month its foreign exchange reserves were $114 billion as of Oct. 31., falling from its all-time high of $124.64 billion in August as the central bank tapped the reserves to slow the depreciation of the rupiah.

"Capital outflows amounted to $1.6 billion in November," Alamsyah told reporters.

Alamsyah also said the central bank revised down its forecast for 2012 economic growth to 6.3% from 6.7% previously due to the bleaker global outlook.

The lower growth forecast could prompt Bank Indonesia to keep its monetary stance accommodative to growth next year, economists said.

Bank Of America Merrill Lynch's economist Hak Bin Chua said Bank Indonesia will likely cut its benchmark overnight interest rate by 50 basis point in 2012 from 6.0% currently "if growth readings turn down."

title: INTERVIEW-UPDATE 1-Indonesia cbank says mkt turmoil complicates policy
text:
* Inflation in 2012 may be lower than 4.7 pct-cbank

* Cbank: exposure of Indonesian banks to Europe almost non-existent

* Cbank says forex reserves still adequate to stabilise rupiah

* Cbank sees rupiah tending to be stable in 2012

(Adds details)

By Aditya Suharmoko

JAKARTA, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank sees inflation below 4.7 percent next year, justifying its recent sharp rate cuts, but uncertainties in financial markets make further rate decisions "more complex", a senior Bank Indonesia official said on Thursday.

Indonesian markets have been volatile in recent weeks on investor worries over eurozone debt, though the exposure of Indonesian banks to Europe is almost non-existent, Perry Warjiyo, director of monetary research and policy at the bank, told Reuters.

"Volatility is higher because global uncertainties, especially Europe, are higher," said Warjiyo in an interview.

"Those are other factors that we have to include when designing our monetary and macroprudential policies. These have become more complex," he said, ahead of BI's board of governors meeting on Dec 8 to review its benchmark overnight rate.

The rupiah, which the central bank earlier this year was allowing to appreciate to dampen inflation, fell to a 17-month low of 9,215 per U.S. dollar on Thursday as most emerging Asian currencies slid after a weak German bond auction signalled wider fears on European debt.

Indonesia's central bank made a surprisingly large 50 basis points rate cut to a record low 6 percent earlier this month to mitigate the impact of a weakening global economy and keep the Group of 20 member on a strong growth path.

Some economists see a further 25 basis points rate cut in December, while others have said the November move was too aggressive given Southeast Asia's largest economy has so far shown few signs of weakening.

Warjiyo, a candidate for a BI deputy governor post that will be decided on Dec 7, said the 6 percent benchmark rate was still attractive to investors, after inflation in October fell to 4.42 percent, the lowest this year and nearing the floor of BI's 4 to 6 percent end-year target range.

Indonesia has been drawing investors in the past two years after the G20 economy showed resilience to the 2008 credit crisis and on prospects of ratings upgrades, but heavy exposure to foreign funds in the bond and stock market is a problem for policymakers worried about outflows hitting the currency.

Indonesia's central bank has been intervening to prop up a weakening rupiah, pushing its foreign exchange reserves down to $113.96 billion in October, about $10 billion lower than $124.64 billion in August.

Warjiyo said the currency would tend to be stable in 2012, with a strengthening trend, but not as strong as in the previous year, and the central bank had sufficient firepower to prop it up.

"We're still confident our forex reserves are still adequate as a cushion to face the impact of rising volatility from the global risks," said Warjiyo, 52, who earned his masters and doctorate degrees in international monetary economics from Iowa State University in the U.S.

BI Governor Darmin Nasution has said he expects Indonesian to get an investment grade rating by the first quarter of 2012, putting it at par with countries such as Brazil and China, boosting investment flows.

Warjiyo said Indonesian banks remained sturdy, but the central bank wanted lenders to lower the spread between lending and deposit rates to boost more loans in stimulating the domestic economy.

"The big messsage...is to push further measures so that what we have done can be more effective in supporting the real sector."

title: UPDATE 2-Indonesia cbank surprises by cutting rate 50 bps to 6 pct
text:
* Cbank says cut to ward off slowdown in Europe, China

* Cbank sees lower inflationary pressures

* Analysts say rate cut to push down short tenor yields

* Unexpected move weakens rupiah, trims fall by stocks

(Updates with details, comments)

By Aditya Suharmoko and Neil Chatterjee

JAKARTA, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank cut its benchmark overnight rate on Thursday by a surprisingly large 50 basis points to a record low of 6.00 percent, hoping to mitigate a weakening global economy and keep the G20 member on a strong growth path.

Thursday's unexpected slash followed last month's 25 basis point cut by Bank Indonesia, which made it one of the first and more aggressive central banks in Asia to switch to promoting growth from fighting inflation.

Moves by some emerging markets such as Indonesia and Brazil to loosen policy come as they seek to boost domestic growth because a slower global economy will shrink their exports to developed economies.

Brazil has also aggressively cut rates, reducing them 50 bps on Oct 19 to 11.50 percent after having made a cut of the same size on Aug. 31.

Thursday's rate decision was unexpected. None of 15 analysts polled by Reuters expected a 50 bps cut; nine forecast a 25 bps cut and six expected the central bank to hold the rate at 6.50 percent.

"It's too aggressive, I'm afraid they're being a bit rushed on the rate cut. Wasting it too early. The rate cut impact on the economy has a pretty long lag," said Winston Sual, fund manager at Panin Asset Management in Jakarta, which manages $1 billion in Indonesian stocks and bonds.

STILL-SOLID GDP GROWTH

In October, inflation slid to 4.42 percent, the lowest this year and nearing the floor of Bank Indonesia's 4 to 6 percent target range. That is why most analysts had anticipated a 0.25 percentage point cut on Thursday.

Though Indonesia's economy still posted solid annual growth of 6.5 percent in the third quarter on buoyant domestic spending and investment, the central bank expects GDP expansion to soften next year as exports drop. On Thursday, it said its GDP forecast for 2012 growth could slow to below 6.5 percent.

For this year, Bank Indonesia revised its GDP forecast to 6.5 percent from 6.6 percent. Bank Indonesia now expects inflation to ease to 4 percent by the end of this year.

"The board of governors will pursue an interest rate response and a mixture of other monetary and macroprudential policies to guard macroeconomic stability and mitigate the potential slowdown of Indonesia's economy," it said.

Bank Indonesia said Thursday's steeper-than-expected cut was also aimed at smoothening the structure of the bond market

"The BI rate cut is in line with lower inflationary pressures going forward, as well as a move at improving the term structure of short, medium and long-tenors," it said in a statement.

The government yield curve has flattened sharply in the past few weeks, as long-term term yields fell as capital inflows resumed after a brief selloff. A steep rate cut would bring the short-term yields down, steepening the yield curve, analysts said.

SPREAD HAS NARROWED

The spread between two-year and 10-year government yields has narrowed to about 101 basis points as of Wednesday from nearly 175 basis points in mid September.

"BI has hopes that the tenor structure won't be too high compared to other ASEAN countries," said Juniman, an analyst at BII. "Foreign investors will re-calculate their portfolios in Indonesia. They could leave Indonesia temporarily, and because of this the rupiah will be weakened further."

After the rate announcement, the rupiah extended earlier losses, dropping to 9,020 per dollar from 8,985 per dollar before the news. It later recouped some ground, but Thursday's loss cancelled out gains made earlier this year.

The Indonesian rupiah, which rose 4.6 percent last year, has been under pressure in recent weeks due to investor worries on the euro zone. Bank Indonesia has been intervening in the currency market to prop it up, causing the country's foreign exchange reserves to decline $10.7 billion in the past two months to $113.96 billion in October.

The central bank, which previously let the rupiah strengthen to curb imported inflation, has said it will guard the currency to support stable economic conditions.

Jakarta's benchmark stock index , which was off more than 2.5 percent before the rate decision in line with regional markets, rose after the news but ended the day down 1.9 percent.

Portfolio investors have been cautious recently, with the stock index seeing thin trading in recent weeks and having lost most of its gains earlier this year.

Foreign investors only bought a net 3.92 trillion rupiah of Indonesian government bonds after selling a net 29.29 trillion rupiah in September on euro worries. Their ownership slid to 30.9 percent as of Nov. 4, from above 35 percent in September, latest government data shows.

Indonesia's balance of payments in the third quarter showed a deficit of $3.96 billion due to capital outflows from nervous portfolio investors, but the current account surplus was steady at $0.2 billion from the previous quarter. ($1 = 8890 Rupiah)

(Additional reporting by Adriana Nina Kusuma, Janeman Latul and Olivia Rondonuwu; Editing by Richard Borsuk)

title: Bank  Indonesia  Official Hints Bank  Intervened  To Curb Rupiah Decline
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah's recent decline against the greenback is due to renewed global worries and not the currency's fundamentals, an official at the country's central bank said Thursday.

Along with other currencies in the region, the rupiah has been losing ground in recent days against the dollar amid risk aversion stemming from concerns over European debts.

"There's no [fundamental] reason for the rupiah to depreciate. This is due to sentiment and is temporary. But Bank Indonesia still needs to be in the market," Darsono, an official at the central bank's monetary research department, told reporters.

His comments hinted at market intervention by the monetary authority, but he didn't provide further details.

Dealers suspect the central bank of selling around $30 million at IDR8,995 earlier Thursday, to prevent the U.S. dollar-rupiah pair from breaching the psychologically important 9,000 level. At midday, the dollar was higher at IDR8,990, compared with IDR8,960 late in Asian trade Wednesday.

The rupiah will "remain solid in the longer term" and the country's fiscal situation is also healthy, Darsono, who only uses one name, said.

title: DJ FOCUS: Market Turmoil Shakes Image Of Indonesia As New Safe Haven
text:
--Recent market turmoil has shaken faith in Indonesia as a safe haven

--Indonesia suffering from general hesitation to invest in emerging markets during current turmoil

--Authorities have tools, funds available to boost market 


 
   By I Made Sentana 
   OF DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Capital outflows during August and September's market turmoil shaved 21% from Indonesia's main stock index and drove the rupiah to its weakest point in 15 months.

But the deeper damage could be more difficult to quantify: The sudden upheaval has shaken the notion that this emerging-market powerhouse is a new safe haven in turbulent times.

"Indonesia's relatively thin trading liquidity implies the country's bond and equity markets are exposed to large market volatility, implying the thesis of Indonesia as a 'safe haven' play may not be completely deep-rooted," Credit Suisse's analyst Teddy Oetomo wrote in a research note.

As recently as July, officials crowed as investors infatuated with Indonesia's growth story and improving fiscal position drove the JSX Index to a record high of 4,193 points (vs 3,701 currently), while foreign buying drove yields on rupiah-denominated government bonds to historical lows.

"Global investors are now avoiding (the U.S. and Europe) and instead they're going to Indonesia, one of the emerging countries with good fundamentals," Director General of State Debt Management Rahmat Waluyanto told Dow Jones Newswires in late July. "We call this the 'flight to quality' to Indonesia, and based on my observation in the domestic capital markets, (Indonesian) government bonds have become been a safe haven for investors."

How quickly things change. With markets spooked by Standard & Poor's downgrade of U.S. sovereign debt and Europe's debt crisis, $7 billion flowed out of Indonesia in August and September. Only about $900 million has returned in recent weeks despite an improvement in global market sentiment.

"With such uncertainty, hedge funds are less concerned with the specific fundamentals of a given market and more concerned with lowering their overall risk profile, especially in emerging markets like Indonesia," said Keith Ducker, San Francisco-based chief investment officer at dark pool operator Tora.

Analysts note the August and September outflows were less than half of the $15.2 billion in inflows to Indonesia in 2010, meaning there's still more money that could leave. Bank Indonesia's surprise rate cut Oct. 11 could further diminish the country's appeal to investors.

Even Jakarta's strengths have a downside: As a major exporter of coal and crude palm oil, "Indonesia would suffer from any further fall in commodity prices" as global growth slows, Citigroup global emerging markets strategist Geoffrey Dennis said.

Bank Indonesia officials say the central bank has enough tools, including frequent intervention in the currency market, to stabilize financial markets. Bank Indonesia also has around $114.5 billion in foreign exchange reserves it can use to stabilize asset prices, while the government has a IDR240 trillion fund to boost bond prices.

And at a sluggish moment globally, Indonesia's growth -- expected at 6.6% this year and 6.5% in 2012 -- sticks out.

"I think investors' confidence in us will not be easily shaken by any negative (global) sentiment," Waluyanto said in his July interview, "because if they pull out in big amounts, they don't know where else to invest their money."

-By I Made Sentana; Dow Jones Newswires; 62 21 39831277; i-made.sentana@dowjones.com
