Additional Information regarding the Notes

1. The EU has adopted a Directive regarding the taxation of savings income (the "Savings Directive"). The Savings Directive requires Member States (as defined below) to provide to the tax authorities of other Member States details of payments of interest and other similar income paid by a person to an individual in another Member State, except that Austria and Luxembourg will instead impose a withholding system for a transitional period unless during such period they elect otherwise.

The Bank undertakes that it will ensure that it maintains a paying agent in a country which is a member of the European Union (a "Member State") that will not be obliged to withhold or deduct tax pursuant to the Savings Directive.


   2.         United States Federal Tax Matters 

The following supplements the discussion under the "Tax Matters" section of the Prospectus regarding the U.S. federal income tax treatment of the Notes, and is subject to the limitations and exceptions set forth therein. Any tax disclosure in the Prospectus or this pricing supplement is of a general nature only, is not exhaustive of all possible tax considerations and is not intended to be, and should not be construed to be, legal, business or tax advice to any particular prospective investor. Each prospective investor should consult its own tax advisor as to the particular tax consequences to it of the acquisition, ownership, and disposition of the Notes, including the effects of applicable U.S. federal, state, and local tax laws and non-U.S. tax laws and possible changes in tax laws.

Due to a change in law since the date of the Prospectus, the second paragraph of "-Payments of Interest" under the "United States Holders" section should be updated to read as follows: "Interest paid by the Bank on the Notes constitutes income from sources outside the United States and will, depending on the circumstances, be "passive" or "general" income for purposes of computing the foreign tax credit."

Because the Notes are denominated in the Indonesian Rupiah, a United States holder of the Notes will generally be subject to special United States federal income tax rules governing foreign currency transactions, as described in the Prospectus in the last four paragraphs of "-Payments of Interest" under the "United States Holders" section. We believe that a United States holder will be required to determine amounts received with respect to a Note (including principal and interest) by reference to the U.S. dollar value of the Indonesian Rupiah amount of the payment, calculated at the currency exchange rate in effect on the date of payment. The U.S. dollar amount that is actually received by the United States holder may differ from the amount determined under the preceding sentence, since the U.S. dollar amount of the payment will be determined by reference to the IDR Rate as of the relevant Rate Fixing Date. Accordingly, a United States holder of the Notes may recognize United States source foreign currency gain or loss in an amount equal to such difference (in addition to any foreign currency gain or loss otherwise recognized upon the receipt of an interest payment or a sale or retirement of the Notes). The U.S. Internal Revenue Service could take the position, however, that the amounts received by a United States holder in respect of a Note should be equal to the U.S. dollar amount that is actually received by the United States holder. Prospective United States holders of the Notes should consult their tax advisors regarding these rules.

A United States holder of the Notes may elect to treat the excess of the Issue Price of the Notes over the principal amount of the Notes as amortizable bond premium. If a United States holder makes this election, such holder would reduce the amount required to be included in its income each year with respect to interest on the Notes by the amount of amortizable bond premium allocable to that year, based on the Notes' yield to maturity. Because the Notes are denominated in the Indonesian Rupiah, a United States holder would compute its amortizable bond premium in units of the Indonesian Rupiah, and the amortizable bond premium would reduce such holder's interest income in units of the Indonesian Rupiah. Gain or loss recognized that is attributable to changes in exchange rates between the time the United States holder's amortized bond premium offsets interest income and the time of the acquisition of the Notes is generally taxable as ordinary income or loss. If a United States holder makes an election to amortize bond premium, it would apply to all debt instruments, other than debt instruments the interest on which is excludible from gross income, that such United States holder holds at the beginning of the first taxable year to which the election applies or that such holder thereafter acquires. This election may not be revoked without the consent of the U.S. Internal Revenue Service.

Treasury Regulations Requiring Disclosure of Reportable Transactions.Treasury regulations require United States taxpayers to report certain transactions that give rise to a loss in excess of certain thresholds (a "Reportable Transaction"). Under these regulations, because the Notes are denominated in a foreign currency, a United States holder that recognizes a loss with respect to the Notes that is characterized as an ordinary loss due to changes in currency exchange rates (under any of the rules discussed under the "Tax Matters" section of the Prospectus) would be required to report the loss on IRS Form 8886 (Reportable Transaction Statement) if the loss exceeds the thresholds set forth in the regulations. For individuals and trusts, this loss threshold is $50,000 in any single taxable year. For other types of taxpayers and other types of losses, the thresholds are higher. Holders should consult with their tax advisors regarding any tax filing and reporting obligations that may apply in connection with acquiring, owning and disposing of notes.

Information with Respect to Foreign Financial Assets. Owners of "specified foreign financial assets" with an aggregate value in excess of $50,000 (and in some circumstances, a higher threshold) may be required to file an information report with respect to such assets with their tax returns. "Specified foreign financial assets" may include financial accounts maintained by foreign financial institutions, as well as the following, but only if they are held for investment and not held in accounts maintained by financial institutions: (i) stocks and securities issued by non-United States persons, (ii) financial instruments and contracts that have non-United States issuers or counterparties, and (iii) interests in foreign entities. Holders are urged to consult their tax advisors regarding the application of this reporting requirement to their ownership of the Notes. [ 25-02-15 0700GMT ]

Medicare Tax. A United States holder that is an individual or estate, or a trust that does not fall into a special class of trusts that is exempt from such tax, is subject to a 3.8% tax (the "Medicare tax") on the lesser of (1) the United States holder's "net investment income" (or "undistributed net investment income" in the case of an estate or trust) for the relevant taxable year and (2) the excess of the United States holder's modified adjusted gross income for the taxable year over a certain threshold (which in the case of individuals is between $125,000 and $250,000, depending on the individual's circumstances). A holder's net investment income generally includes its interest income and its net gains from the disposition of Notes, unless such interest income or net gains are derived in the ordinary course of the conduct of a trade or business (other than a trade or business that consists of certain passive or trading activities). United States holders that are individuals, estates or trusts are urged to consult their tax advisors regarding the applicability of the Medicare tax to their income and gains in respect of their investment in the Notes.


   3.         Additional Investment Considerations: 

The Notes offered by this Pricing Supplement are complex financial instruments and may not be suitable for certain investors. Investors intending to purchase the Notes should consult with their tax and financial advisors to ensure that the intended purchase meets the investment objective before making such purchase.

There are various risks associated with the Notes including, but not limited to, exchange rate risk, price risk and liquidity risk. Investors should consult with their own financial, legal and accounting advisors about the risks associated with an investment in these Notes, the appropriate tools to analyze that investment, and the suitability of the investment in each investor's particular circumstances. Holders of the Notes should also consult with their professional tax advisors regarding tax laws applicable to them.

Payment of each Interest Amount and the Redemption Amount will be based on the IDR Rate, which is a measure of the rate of exchange between the Indonesian Rupiah and the USD. Currency exchange rates are volatile and will affect the holder's return. In addition, the government of Indonesia can from time to time intervene in the foreign exchange market. These interventions or other governmental actions could adversely affect the value of the Notes, as well as the yield (in USD terms) on the Notes and the amount payable at maturity or upon acceleration. Even in the absence of governmental action directly affecting currency exchange rates, political or economic developments in Indonesia or elsewhere could lead to significant and sudden changes in the exchange rate between the Indonesian Rupiah and the USD.

The Indonesian Rupiah is an emerging market currency. Emerging market currencies may be subject to particularly substantial volatility, as well as to government actions including currency controls, devaluations and other matters which could materially and adversely affect the value of the Notes.

The methodologies for determining the IDR Rate may result in a Redemption Amount (or Early Redemption Amount, as the case may be) of the Notes, or an Interest Amount on the Notes, being significantly less than anticipated or less than what an alternative methodology for determining the IDR-USD exchange rate would yield.

title: Emerging-Market  Currencies  Tumble as Worries Over Greece, Ukraine Escalate
text:
Fears of a default in Greece and an escalating conflict in Ukraine spilled over into emerging markets as investors fled for safer assets, sending currencies in Asia and other developing countries tumbling.

Indonesia's rupiah sank as much as 1% while South Africa's rand hovered close to its weakest in over a decade and the Malaysian ringgit's slide gathered steam.

From a political gridlock in Europe over the restructuring of Greece's mountain of debt, to unsuccessful cease-fire talks aimed at ending the conflict in Ukraine and a renewed slide in oil prices overnight, pockets of risk for investors are growing with emerging market assets bearing the brunt.

"The markets are going to be sensitive for a prolonged period over time, " said Kenneth Akintewe, a portfolio manager at Aberdeen Asset Management in Singapore, which has $504.1 billion under management. "The strong dollar view is beginning to exert itself again, more strongly."

The U.S. economy is on its way to a recovery even as growth in other parts of the world slows and central banks are stepping in to competitively devalue their currencies. Moreover, the U.S. Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates, luring yield-hungry investors away from record low rates in the developing world and less risky assets elsewhere.

Bond markets are also tumbling, sending yields surging and pointing to investors also pulling out of these markets. Yields move inversely to prices.

For investors, the weakness in Asia's foreign-exchange markets, which have performed relatively well to their emerging market peers so far this year, is a surprise. As countries in Latin America and emerging Europe have grappled with domestic economic and political challenges, Asia has been resilient with signs of proactive new governments and central banks, and lower currency volatility.

Local currency bonds in Indonesia, Turkey, Thailand and the Philippines were top performers in 2014. Just weeks ago, yields on Indonesia's bonds fell to multiyear lows as foreign investors poured into local government bond auctions.

But the currency's sudden plunge Thursday had traders and dealers saying the central bank was intervening and had sold $50 million to $100 million.

A spokesman from Bank Indonesia said, "Bank Indonesia is always in the market and will intervene if necessary to prevent the rupiah from falling too sharply." He added that the currency's decline was exacerbated due to the dollar's strength and fears that Greece may pull out from the eurozone, expectations of a U.S. interest-rate increase and the Russia-Ukraine conflict.

He declined to confirm if Bank Indonesia had sold dollars Thursday.

Emerging markets have grappled with volatile portfolio and capital flows, as global investor sentiment waxes and wanes. Analysts from HSBC say this could lead to more currency weakness "that could spill over to other asset classes, possibly prompting less dovish or even hawkish monetary policy and eventually lower economic growth."

In Greece, the rescue deal expires at the end of the month and the government could run out of money in early March. With no agreement in sight with its creditors, analysts say Greece could exit the eurozone leading to widespread market turmoil, further dampening prospects of a European recovery. In Ukraine, world leaders are attempting to broker a cease-fire, and as of early Thursday there were only conflicting signs of progress.

-- to I-Made Sentana contributed to this article.

title: Bank Indonesia Likely Sold up to $100M to Stem USD/IDR Rise -- Market Talk
text:
0522 GMT [Dow Jones] Bank Indonesia was suspected to have sold dollars between $50 million and $100 million after the USD/IDR rose to 12,830 from 12,715 late Wednesday. Bank Indonesia spokesman Peter Jacob declined to confirm if the central bank intervened, but said "Bank Indonesia is always in the market and will intervene if necessary to prevent the rupiah from falling too sharply." Mr. Jacob added the pair's gain is due to the USD's strength across the board. Dealers said the USD's strength prompted foreigners to take profit on the government's rupiah bonds, sending the 10-year yield up by 20 basis point to 7.4%. Foreigners in January bought around $4 billion of the government's rupiah bond, government data shows. (i-made.sentana@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: DMF 
 

0516 GMT [Dow Jones] The market has let PCCW (0008.HK) know that it prefers yield over growth, as shares of the Hong Kong telecom operator fell after the company declared flat dividend growth. PCCW distributed only 72% of dividends it received from HKT (6823.HK) to its shareholders for 2014, a drop from 79% in the previous year. PCCW's 63% stake in HKT, which generates nearly all Ebitda for its parent, and the associated yield is the "primary reasons" for investors to own the stock, says Barclays. The company said it is actively looking for growth opportunities globally for its media and technology solutions businesses -- a move that could put its current yield at risk. Barclays and J.P. Morgan have both cut their dividend estimates for the stock. PCCW is down 4.7% to HK$5.05 Thursday. (jacky.wong@wsj.com; Twitter: @jackycwong) 


 
Editor: DAH 
 

0506 GMT [Dow Jones] The Australian dollar fell to a six-day low of 0.9647 against its Canadian counterpart Thursday, stalling near the 55-day moving average, as an intraday rebound in oil prices (Nymex crude was last up 62 cents at $49.46/bbl on Globex) boosted demand for the loonie, while worse-than-expected Australia January jobs data hit sentiment surrounding the Aussie. The AUD/CAD daily price chart is displaying a mixed technical picture with the MACD indicator bearish but the slow stochastic measure neutral. Further downside in the AUD/CAD cross may encounter support at 0.9582 (Feb. 3 reaction low). Spot AUD/CAD is at 0.9671. (jerry.tan@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: TFD 
 

0459 GMT [Dow Jones] Malaysia's surprising 5.8% on-year economic growth for the October-to-December quarter will likely prove short-lived as lower oil prices will be a major headwind for the economy this year, Capital Economics says. The economy grew 5.6% on-year during the third quarter. "Looking ahead, the economy faces a couple of challenges. While most economies in emerging Asia will benefit from the fall in oil prices, Malaysia is a key exception given its status as a big net energy exporter," Krystal Tan, an Asia economist, says in a note. "With energy-related revenues set to take a hit, the government will have to further cut back on its spending to prevent its fiscal deficit from ballooning." Capital Economics continue to expect Malaysia's GDP growth to slow at around 5.0% this year, which is broadly in line with its 10-year average and consensus expectations.(saurabh.chaturvedi@wsj.com; @journosaurabh) 


 
Editor: DMF 
 

0456 GMT [Dow Jones] South Korea's expected decline in exports will eventually outweigh its concerns over growing household debt. This could pave the way for a rate cut as early as April, says Nomura economist Kwon Young-sun. "This is because, given that exports remain the main growth engine for Korea, weaker exports should deteriorate corporate performance, which is negative for household income and job markets," Kwon says. Softer exports usually call for the Bank of Korea to ease its monetary policy while growing debt can justify a policy tightening to put a cap on credit. Nomura maintains that the BOK will lower its base rate twice in April and July to 1.50% to spur growth. The BOK is widely expected to stand pat on rates at its upcoming February 17 meeting. (kwanwoo.jun@wsj.com) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0452 GMT [Dow Jones] The Singapore dollar is lower at 88.24 against the yen Thursday versus its late Wednesday level of 88.47 as Singapore's FTSE Straits Times Index fell to a four-session low of 3,414.30, spurring fund outflows. The ST Index was recently down 0.8% at 3,416.89. In contrast, Japan's Nikkei Average was recently up 1.91% at 17,989. However, the SGD/JPY daily price chart is still positive-biased as the MACD and slow stochastic indicators are bullish; the five-day moving average is above the 15-day moving average and rising; the rate-of-change momentum indicator is advancing inside positive territory. Further downside in the SGD/JPY cross may encounter support at the middle 20-day Bollinger Band (now at 87.78). (jerry.tan@wsj.com)

0450 GMT [Dow Jones] Last Thursday, the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) issued guidelines on when it will require Indian banks to maintain a countercyclical capital buffer, an additional layer of loss-absorbing capital on top of banks' increased minimum capital requirements under Basel III. The RBI guidelines also detail how large the CCCB must be in India under different circumstances, and state that banks will be subject to restrictions on discretionary distributions such as dividend payments, share buybacks and staff bonuses if they do not meet the CCCB requirements. The guidelines are credit positive for Indian banks because they make clear that banks will be required to hold the additional capital amid periods of rapid credit growth. The RBI said it will require banks to hold the full 2.5% buffer when the gap between the credit to GDP ratio and the long-term trend exceeds 15 percentage points. The central bank will implement a CCCB of less than 2.5% when the gap is between three and 15 percentage points, with the size of the required CCCB increasing on a graduated scale. (kenan.machado@wsj.com)

0445 GMT [Dow Jones] Citi sees downsize risk for gold price ahead of possible rate hikes in the U.S. Emerging concerns over Europe "enabled gold to disengage from an inverse relationship with the U.S. dollar strength that had been prevalent since late 2012," it says. Yet the house notes better economic growth prospect in the U.S. has shifted expectation of rates hike to as early as June from September/fourth quarter in 2015. It forecasts gold price to decline by 2% to US$1,240/ounce in 2015 amid a stronger U.S. currency, and re-affirms its forecasts of an average gold forecast of $1,250/ounce in the first quarter, falling to an average of $1,230/ounce in the second quarter. 0441 GMT [Dow Jones] While unemployment spiked in January in Australia, the central bank is not likely to rush headlong into back-to-back rate cuts, says Tom Kennedy, economist at JP Morgan's Sydney office. He's tipping policymakers will hold fire until May when they will have a better idea about the state of the job market. Data have been volatile for sometime, Kennedy says. "Remember that we have been on a journey to a 6.4% jobless rate already in this cycle, a rise that subsequently was revised away," Kennedy says. (james.glynn@wsj.com; Twitter: @JamesGlynnWSJ)

0438 GMT [Dow Jones] The rebalancing of Australia's economy in the wake of a decade-long mining investment boom is going badly. New South Wales, the services engine of the economy Down Under, recorded a big jump in unemployment to 6.3%, its highest since mid-2009, or when the financial services hub was reeling from the global financial crisis and banks were laying off lots of staff. title: Bank Indonesia Steps Up Efforts to Defend Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA--Indonesia stepped up efforts on Tuesday to defend the rupiah as it continued to fall to levels unseen since the 1998 Asian financial crisis, underscoring the vulnerability of Southeast Asia's largest economy to fund outflows.

"We have been actively supplying [dollars] and buying government bonds," Senior Deputy Gov. Mirza Adityaswara said, adding that the rupiah has fallen below the 11,500-12,000 level that the central bank deems good for both exports and imports.

Central bankers refused to disclose the amount of U.S. dollars sold Tuesday, but Deputy Gov. Perry Warjiyo confirmed it increased its intervention. "We will continue to be in the market," Mr. Warjiyo told The Wall Street Journal.

Traders estimated the central bank likely sold around $500 million Tuesday. That would be about double the roughly $250 million it has sold daily on average since last week as global investors retreated from risky markets in expectation of a U.S. rate hike.

The rupiah fell to a new 16-year low of 12,900 to the dollar at one point early Tuesday from 12,700 late Monday, in line with the plunge in currencies of other countries whose finances likewise have been hurt by the decline in commodity prices.

Bank Indonesia's move seemed to help the rupiah--at least early on--as the dollar retreated to 12,690 in the late Asian session. But, economists said, the intervention alone may not be sufficient to shield the rupiah if a large portion of what economists estimate to be a $11.6 billion inflow to Indonesia so far this year reverses direction.

"Should the selloff continue due to deteriorating global risk sentiments, we wouldn't be surprised if this pushes the USD/IDR toward the 13,000-region and beyond in the near-term," Maybank said in a research note Tuesday, after Bank Indonesia's intervention.

The currency has slid throughout this year, but the fall accelerated on Monday.

President Joko Widodo last month raised fuel prices by more than 30%, a bold measure that gave a short-lived confidence to the market that the government is committed to economic reform. But longer-term concerns emerged.

Tumbling global oil prices, which should be a net positive for Indonesia, continued to drag commodity prices lower. Along with the country's fiscal and monetary tightness, this will likely keep growth below 6% in 2015, economists said. The price of coal, one of Indonesia's main exports, has fallen heavily this year.

Yet Indonesia remains an attractive investment destination for brave portfolio investors, with interesting stock-picking opportunities if they know where to look, said Bharat Joshi, fund manager for Aberdeen Asset Management in Jakarta. "Despite the many challenges, there are companies that pass our strict quality control tests and are well positioned to take advantage of the growing domestic consumption," Mr. Joshi said.

Jake Maxwell Watts in Singapore contributed to this article.

title: CORRECTED-Central banks  intervene  as Asia puts its strength to the test
text:
(Corrects to say traders say RBI has been intervening, RBI has not confirmed any intervention)               

* Asian central banks ramp up intervention amid EM sell-off               

* Selldown rekindles painful memories of Asian financial crisis               

* Analysts say this not a repeat of 97/98 but warn of more losses               

By Nicholas Owen and Nachum Kaplan               

JAKARTA/SINGAPORE Dec 16 (Reuters) - Asian central banks have ramped up their intervention in currency markets to stem the sell-off roiling emerging markets, testing the notion that the region is better placed to handle a market rout than during its 1997-1998 financial crisis.               

This battle between central banks and investors selling emerging market assets will likely intensify as analysts warn the region's currencies are set to slide further, pushed lower by falling commodity prices and the prospect of a U.S. rate hike.               

"Lower oil prices, weaker commodity currencies, lower material and oil service costs and increased efficiency are all reinforcing to the downside," wrote Goldman Sachs in a report.               

Bank Indonesia confirmed it sold dollars on Tuesday, with traders saying the Reserve Bank of India and Bank Negara Malaysia have been doing so as well in recent weeks.               

That comes as investors have dumped emerging market assets globally on tumbling oil prices and low growth prospects, with the Russian central bank's sharp hike in interest rates on Tuesday spooking markets further.               

The Indonesian rupiah hit its lowest level since 1998 for the second day running and the Indian rupee dropped to a 13 month low on Tuesday.               

Bank Indonesia said it intervened in the currency markets to reduce volatility rather than defend the currency while the Indonesian finance minister also said it would buy back government bonds in the secondary market if necessary to stem capital outflows.               

The Reserve Bank of India has also sold dollars to ease the severity of the rupee's fall, according to traders.               

"It is still not an alarming situation but we have to see how far the rupee drifts from current levels," a Indian central bank official told Reuters, adding they would only intervene "strongly" if there were large outflows.               

Bank Negara Malaysia declined to confirm intervention when asked by Reuters, while Bank of Thailand bank said there "was no need to act" and no abnormal outflows despite Thai stocks slumping to their lowest levels since June 2.                              

MORE FALLS AHEAD               

Analysts think further falls in currencies are likely when the expected rise in U.S. interest rate materialises.               

"The weakness of Asian currencies comes at a time when the Fed hasn't even increased interest rates yet," said Khoon Goh, a currency strategist at ANZ bank in Singapore.               

The Federal Reserve holds its policy meeting this week, concluding Wednesday, and any signal that rates could rise soon could spark further emerging market selling.               

However despite the risks, analysts point to big differences between Asia now and in 1997/98.               

Most emerging Asian currencies now float freely whereas they used to have pegged exchange rates.               

Central banks also have deeper foreign reserve and swap lines with other central banks that give them access to more dollars.               

"Part of the reason we saw a crisis in 1997 was that back then currencies were overvalued and a lot of the countries were running large current-account deficits," said ANZ's Goh.               

"This time around the currencies are not overvalued."               

Only Indonesia and India are running current account deficits while external debt is lower too.               

Within Southeast Asia today, Thailand is the most exposed with foreign liabilities equal to 39 percent of GDP, still well below the 60 percent seen in 1996.               

However there are risks beyond headline numbers. Indonesia's external debt is a modest 34.7 percent of GDP yet its shallow capital markets mean that it borrows about 38 percent of its local debt from foreigners, according to the finance ministry, highlighting the risk from a sovereign perspective.

   By I Made Sentana 
 

JAKARTA, Indonesia (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia has been "actively" present in the market in recent days to defend rupiah assets, central bankers said Tuesday.

"We have been actively supplying [dollars] and buying government bonds," Senior Deputy Gov. Mirza Adityasawara said, adding that the rupiah has fallen beyond the IDR11,500-IDR12,000 level that the central bank deems good for both exports and imports.

The local unit fell to a new 16-year low of IDR12,900 to the dollar early Tuesday from IDR12,700 late Monday. Traders said the central bank likely sold more than $200 million at IDR12,900.

"Now the rupiah is stabilizing around IDR12,700," Bank Indonesia Deputy Gov. Perry Warjiwo said at the same news conference.

Mr. Adistyawara said the central bank will continue to intervene in the currency and bond market "to help stabilize the economy."

Although Bank Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves fell to $111.14 billion as of Nov. 30, it is still at a "safe level" that gives BI enough ammunition to defend the local unit, he added.

Finance Minister Bambang Brojonegoro said at the news conference that the government is standing by to buy back its bonds if necessary to stabilize the bond market.

title: EM ASIA  FX -Rupiah hits 16-year low as Indonesian bonds retreat
text:
* Rupiah slides 1.6 percent, hits lowest since August 1998
    * Year-end dollar demand, worsening risk sentiment dents
rupiah
    * Focus also on possible rupiah selling by offshore
investors

 (Adds comments, updates levels)
    By Masayuki Kitano
    SINGAPORE, Dec 15 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah hit a
16-year low versus the dollar on Monday, dented by year-end
corporate demand for dollars and possible position squaring in
Indonesian bonds by overseas investors.
    The rupiah, like other Asian currencies, has faltered in
recent weeks as investors positioned for the U.S. Federal
Reserve to start raising interest rates next year on the back of
a gradual economic recovery in the United States.
    Its fall accelerated over the past two trading sessions,
with the currency hitting a low of 12,695 versus the dollar
  on Monday, its lowest level since August 1998,
according to Reuters data.
    Indonesia's central bank said on Monday it is intervening in
both the bond and foreign exchange markets to stabilise prices.
  
    The rupiah's weakness stood out on a mixed day overall for
emerging Asian currencies, with the South Korean won 
and Singapore dollar, edging higher while currencies
such as the Indian rupee retreated.
    Market participants said the rupiah was hit by worsening
global risk sentiment as well as year-end corporate demand for
the greenback. 
    "Ahead of the end of year, we are seeing some increased
onshore corporate demand for U.S. dollar, which is keeping
dollar/IDR quite bid," said Divya Devesh, FX strategist for
Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore.
    There was also focus on possible rupiah-selling linked to
overseas investor holdings of Indonesian bonds.
    "We have seen massive inflows into Indonesian bonds this
year, and there seems to be a minor selloff in bonds as well, so
people might be taking profit ahead of the year-end," said
Devesh.
    Indonesia's 10-year government bonds came under pressure on
Monday, with their yields rising 11.6 basis points to 8.203
percent, on track for the biggest one-day rise in
yields since late September.
    The rupiah's weakness in non-deliverable forwards (NDFs)
since around Friday suggests that overseas investors are behind
the currency's latest drop, said Satoshi Okagawa, senior global
markets analyst for Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation in
Singapore.
    "There are some visible signs of currency hedging against
rupiah weakness...by overseas investors," Okagawa said.
    The rupiah fell as low as 12,908 versus the dollar on
one-month NDFs, its lowest level since November
2008, according to Reuters data.

    PHILIPPINE PESO
    The peso edged lower versus the dollar but the
drop was limited, thanks to some support in the wake of its
sovereign rating upgrade last week.
    Last week, the peso had touched a 2-1/2 month high versus
the dollar at 44.470. That rise came after Moody's Investors
Service upgraded its rating on the Philippines by one notch to
Baa2 on Thursday, citing a decline in its debt burden and
structural improvements in fiscal management.

* Bank Indonesiaintervenes in currency, bond market               

* Increased dollar demand seen for year-end payments   (Recasts, adds details and comments)               

By Fransiska Nangoy and Masayuki Kitano               

JAKARTA/SINGAPORE, Dec 15 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah tumbled to its lowest level since August 1998 on Monday as declining risk appetites and increasing demand for dollars to settle year-end foreign loan payments put pressure on the country's currency, bonds and shares.               

Bank Indonesia said that it was acting in both the foreign exchange and bond markets to help stabilise prices, as emerging markets from Europe to Latin America suffer sharp outflows of capital.               

The rupiah fell to 12,695 rupiah before paring its losses to 12,665 per dollar. The currency was down 1.7 percent on the day - its biggest one-day drop in more than four months - and 4.3 percent this year.               

Analysts attributed the fall to a combination of factors including how the sharp drop in oil prices has increased pessimism about global growth, and a steady rise in the dollar on expectations the U.S. central bank will begin raising interest rates next year.               

"The U.S. continues to post positive economic data which in turn hit the rupiah," said Royke Tumilaar, head of treasury at Bank Mandiri.                              

'REALLY EXPOSED'               

"High foreign ownership in our capital markets makes us really exposed to a strengthening dollar," he added.               

The yield of the 10-year government bond rose to 8.203 percent from 8.087 percent on Friday. Traders said they believed state banks were buying bonds amid heavy foreign selling.               

At 0740 GMT,  the benchmark index for Indonesian shares was down 1.2 percent.               

Moves in rupiah's non-deliverable forwards suggest selling by overseas investors is behind the rupiah's latest drop, said Satoshi Okagawa, senior global markets analyst for Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation in Singapore.               

"There are some visible signs of currency hedging against rupiah weakness," Okagawa said.               

Divya Devesh, foreign exchange strategist for Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore, said that on top of weak risk appetites, year-end corporate demand for dollars plus profit-taking in Indonesian bonds may be weighing on the rupiah.                              

CHANGING FLOWS               

"We have seen massive inflows into Indonesian bonds this year, and there seems to be a minor selloff in bonds, so people might be taking profit ahead of the year-end," Devesh said.               

Wellian Wiranto, economist at Singapore's OCBC Bank, said  the rupiah "has been hit because of the relatively high degree of foreign ownership in its government bonds, which is not a plus point given the anticipation of broad strength in the US economy and dollar."               

Data from Indonesia's Finance Ministry shows an outflow of 11 trillion rupiah ($869.22 million) between Dec. 1 and Dec. 11, during which foreign ownership of total tradable bonds fell to 38.6 percent from a record high 39.5 percent.               

Indonesia's credit default swaps contacts were major underperformers on Monday. The 5-year contract  or the cost of insuring sovereign debt for 5 years rose 12 basis points (bps) to 167/177 basis points (bps) compared with the broad market index which widened by 6 bps.               

The rupiah's fall comes shortly after Bank Indonesia (BI) showed increasing concern about the level of foreign borrowing by Indonesian companies.               

In October, BI issued a regulation - to take effect on Jan. 1 - that private firms should hedge 20 percent of their dollar needs to repay offshore loans six months prior to maturity. The central bank has warned firms against unhedged loans.

title: Indonesia Shows Fatigue As India Continues to Captivate: Blame Inflation -- Barron's Blog
text:
Foreigners continue to pile into the Indian debt market although they have become more cautious towards Indonesia's government bonds, data provided by Nomura Securities show.

In November, India saw a strong inflow of 120 billion rupee into its debt markets. "Inflows in the quota allocated for investment by central banks and sovereign wealth funds in government bonds has remained strong (INR21bn vs INR30bn in October) and a further INR20bn in investment in December has pushed the u tilization for this quota to 91%," according to analysts Vivek Rajpal and Prashant Pande. Foreigners also showed interest in corporate debt, increasing their holdings by 119 billion rupee in November, up from INR113 billion in October.

Interest in Indonesia, however, started to show fatigue. After a record inflow of 21 trillion Indonesian rupiah into the local debt market in November, "there have already been outflows in December," wrote the Nomura analysts.

Inflationary expectation is the culprit. When a foreign investor buys into local debt, she is exposed to inflation as well as currency risks. While analysts expect Indonesia's inflation to hit 6.4% this year and 6.95% next, well above the central bank's 3-5% target, India's consumer price inflation slowed sharply in November to 4.4%.

The Indonesian rupiah fell to a 16-year low today as local companies bought the U.S. dollar before the year-end. The Financial Times report:

Analysts said that the rupiah was also under pressure because Indonesian companies were buying dollars at the year-end to make scheduled repayments on greenback loans.

"The impact on the bond and equity markets and the real economy will be negative," said Fauzi Ichsan, an economist at Standard Chartered in Indonesia. "The central bank has two choices: to intervene more aggressively in the foreign exchange market and shrink its reserves or to hike the FASBI rate [the overnight deposit rate]."

Mr Ichsan warned that if Bank Indonesia did not take action to support the rupiah, there was a risk of a downward spiral.

The Indonesia Jakarta Composite Index slumped 1.2%. By comparison, India's S&P BSE Sensex Index was only 0.1% lower.

Last week, the Bank of Indonesia kept its benchmark rates on hold but was ambiguous towards its future monetary policies. The rupiah fell 1.3% against the dollar while the rupee dropped 0.7%. The iShares MSCI Indonesia ETF ( EIDO) dropped 3.9%. The WisdomTree India Earnings Fund ( EPI) retreated 6.5%, mostly on equity losses. The iShares MSCI India ETF ( INDA) fell 6.5%.

title: Indonesia's c.bank says it is also acting in the bond market to stabilise bond price
text:
JAKARTA, Dec 15 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank said on Monday it is intervening in both the bond and foreign exchange markets to stabilise prices as the rupiah fell to its lowest level since 1998.

"Bank Indonesia has always been in forex market and today we are in the bond market as well to stabilise (bond prices)," Bank Indonesia's senior deputy governor, Mirza Adityaswara, told Reuters.

The yield on the 10-year government bond rose to 8.203 percent on Monday from 8.087 percent on Friday.

The rupiah touched a low of 12,695 per dollar, its lowest since August 1998, according to Reuters data on Monday. It is trading at 12,680 at 0525 GMT. (Reporting by Adriana Nina Kusuma; Writing by Gayatri Suroyo; Editing by Kim Coghill) 

Released: 2014-12-15T06:29:53.000Z

title: CORRECTED- Indonesia  c.bank says conducting "measured  intervention " as rupiah falls to lowest since 2008
text:
(Corrects headline and lead to say rupiah is lowest since 2008, not 1998)

JAKARTA, Dec 8 (Reuters) - Indonesia central bank said on Monday it is conducting "measured intervention" in foreign exchange markets, after the rupiah fell to its lowest level against the U.S. dollar since 2008.

"We don't do excessive intervention, (we do) measured intervention. We will find a new equilibrium," spokesman Peter Jacobs told Reuters.

"We are not letting the rupiah depreciate too much."

Spot rupiah earlier slid to 12,348 to the dollar, down nearly 0.5 percent on the day and taking its decline so far this year to 1.6 percent.

(Reporting By Adriana Nina Kusuma and Fransiska Nangoy; Editing by Kim Coghill)

title: India Rupee Down Vs USD But May Outperform Peers -HSBC -- Market Talk
text:
0528 GMT [Dow Jones] India's rupee falls to 61.54 from its Wednesday close of 61.28 versus the U.S. dollar due to a slight change in tone detected in the U.S. Federal Reserve's monetary policy statement released overnight. The greenback has risen across the board but by varying degrees on a more upbeat assessment of the U.S. job market by the Fed--which prompted traders to price in the possibility of a sooner interest rate rise. HSBC says in a research piece Thursday that the rupee may decline versus the U.S. dollar but may rise versus its peers due to several positive factors. Narrowing current account and budget deficits, together with controlled inflation and the rise of foreign investment inflows ought to benefit India's currency. India's second-quarter FDI of $8.2 billion was its biggest quarterly inflow since 2011. USD/INR is now 61.45 from its Wednesday close of 61.28. (ewen.chew@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: MNG 
 

0525 GMT [Dow Jones] The NZX-50 closes up 0.3% at 5370.18 led by a rise in Freightways (FRE.NZ) after the company released sharply higher 1Q earnings and said it expected FY15 earnings to be higher on year. Freightways ended the day 6.8% to NZ$5.50. This also supported Mainfreight (MFT.NZ), which ended the day 3.5% higher at NZ$15.90. Xero (XRO.NZ) remains under pressure on concerns about the company's U.S. growth prospects. Xero ended down 1.9% at NZ$15.85. (lucy.craymer@wsj.com;Twitter: @lucy_craymer) 


 
Editor: MNG 
 

0425 GMT [Dow Jones] Chinese smartphone maker Xiaomi continues to eat into Samsung and Apple's global market share, moving into the No. 3 position in the third quarter as it enters the list of top five vendors for the first time, according to research firm International Data Corporation, or IDC. Xiaomi had 5.3% of smartphone shipments in the third quarter, behind Samsung's 23.8% and Apple's 12%. IDC says Xiaomi's growth has been driven by its focus on China and adjacent markets but it remains to be seen whether the company can replicate its success at home overseas. (Gillian.wong@wsj.com @gillianwong) 


 
Editor: MNG 
 

0412 GMT [Dow Jones] China's official manufacturing purchasing managers' index likely held steady at 51.1 in October, according to the median forecast of eight economists surveyed by Dow Jones. "Although healthy export demand continues to support the manufacturing sector, cooling domestic demand remains a drag," says Julian Evan-Pritchard of Capital Economics. A preliminary reading of the competing HSBC manufacturing PMI, released last week, rose to 50.4 from September's (final) 50.2. The official PMI is due out at 0100 GMT on Saturday, followed by HSBC's final reading at 0145 on Monday. (richard.silk@dowjones.com) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0406 GMT [Dow Jones] Japan's Ministry of Finance sells 5.31 trillion yen of three-month Treasury discount bills with the lowest price of 100.0005, yielding -0.0018%; The MOF said it was the first ever for the highest yield to be negative at the auction. The average yield was also -0.0041%, marking the second consecutive negative rate following the previous auction last week. The Bank of Japan Governor Haruhiko Kuroda said Tuesday that negative yields in the short-term debt market reflected the central bank's aggressive asset buying and that they were not "a major problem." Lead December futures price was steady despite a weakening of the yen and higher stock prices. It was down only 0.01 at 146.52. (tatsuo.ito@wsj.comJ) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0328 GMT [Dow Jones] Bank Indonesia Governor Agus Martowardojo hints the central bank will likely continue to keep intervention in the foreign exchange market minimal and only will sell dollars if the USD/IDR rises too fast. "We will continue to reduce exchange rate volatility while still giving room for movement that reflects Indonesia's economic fundamentals," he tells business executives at a gathering. Bank Indonesia has rarely intervened in currency markets of late despite the fact that the rupiah has occasionally seen selling pressure. "Bank Indonesia likely wants to preserve its foreign exchange reserves to maintain market confidence that it has enough ammunition needed if massive capital outflows take place," a currency dealer says. (I-made.sentana@wsj.com) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0318 GMT [Dow Jones] Kenanga is keeping its Neutral call on the Malaysian plantations sector despite positive palm-oil forecasts from high profile analysts--James Fry, Thomas Mielke and Dorab Mistry at an industry event in Kuala Lumpur this week--who are predicting average CPO prices of MRY2,400/ton, 9% higher than current spot price at MYR2,195/ton. Kenanga analyst Alan Lim says even with Mr. Mistry's most bullish forecast of MYR2,500/ton by March 2015, the outlook for planters is neutral, as current share prices of the companies have already priced in recovery in CPO prices due to a lower inventory estimate by end-2015 and a decline in 4Q 2014 production. (huileng.tan@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: MNG 
 

0318 GMT [Dow Jones] The Nikkei is up 0.5% at 15636.60 midday, helped by the stronger dollar (now 108.97 yen) following the U.S. Fed's somewhat hawkish stance on monetary policy. Solid earnings results from bellwether companies are also helping to boost market confidence. "Buying has been mainly reflexive on the back of the stronger dollar, but there has not been an 'event trade' per se," says an equity trading director at a European brokerage. He notes that foreign hedge funds have increased their net long positions substantially after squaring some three trillion yen in short trades though the third week of October. Keyence (6861.TO) is up 5.6% at 50,270 yen after its first-half operating profits beat forecasts. Capcom (9697.TO) is up 4.9% at 1,704 yen after its second-quarter operating profits came in broadly on a par with consensus. Makita (6586.TO) is up 2.9% after raising its first half operating profit guidance. SoftBank (9984.TO) is up 1.9% at 7,650 yen following a slew of positive brokerage reports. (bradford.frischkorn@wsj.com) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0255 GMT [Dow Jones] Philippine's peso is weaker Thursday due to broad U.S. dollar strength, but could avoid depreciating further in the near term if USD/PHP ends the day below 44.85. Currently at 44.85 versus its Wednesday close of 44.72, the dollar is perched at the entrance to the daily Bollinger uptrend channel after a bout of overnight strength triggered by an unexpectedly upbeat assessment of the U.S. job market by the U.S. Federal Reserve. A Thursday close above 44.85 could give USD/PHP the impetus to keep climbing toward the round-figure trading barrier at 45.00. Analysts now think the Fed could raise interest rates earlier than the consensus forecast for the second-half of 2015. Later today, third-quarter U.S. gross domestic product data could motivate USD-bulls if the number comes in stronger than expectations for a 3.1% rise. (ewen.chew@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: CNG 
 

0248 GMT [Dow Jones] Japanese investment in foreign stocks remains strong with net purchases of Y197 billion in the week Oct. 19-25, stretching the streak of net buying to eight weeks in a row, according to Japan's MOF. The amount of Japanese net foreign stock buying over the past four weeks, including the latest data, comes to nearly Y1 trillion, accelerating the pace from the net purchases of more than Y2 trillion seen in the whole of the July-Sept quarter. Aggressive foreign stock buying by Japanese was one of the two drivers for the rally in USD/JPY in August and September along with expectations of rate rises in the U.S., says Tohru Sasaki, head of Japan Rates & Fixed Research at J.P. Morgan. "Now the FOMC last night may heighten the Fed's rate hike expectations further in coming days, whether Japanese will continue their foreign stock investments should be important to push up the USD/JPY further," he says. (hiroyuki.kachi@wsj.com) 


 
Editor: PJK 
 

0243 GMT [Dow Jones] The yuan falls after the central bank guides it weaker via daily fixing to track the dollar's broad gains overnight. The yuan is at 6.1138 to a dollar, compared with 6.1112 at Wednesday's close. The central parity is set at 6.1457 versus 6.1405 at Wednesday. "But the yuan's weakness is capped as the large Chinese banks are ready to sell the dollar at any time," says a Shanghai-based foreign bank trader. The yuan hit fresh seven-month highs in the past four sessions in a row. Offshore, one-year USD/CNY non-deliverable forwards are up at 6.2370/6.2385 from 6.2320/6.2360 late Wednesday. (wynne.wang@dowjones.com) 


 
Editor JSM 
 

0220 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/IDR rose to 12,180--implying a weaker rupiah versus the U.S. dollar--and stocks fell 0.5% as the market reacted to a surprisingly hawkish-sounding U.S. Federal Reserve. The Fed highlighted strong job growth in its post-FOMC statement, but also said that inflation likely remains muted. The change in its perception of the U.S. job market may signal that the Fed is stepping toward raising interest rates. This spooked greenback-shorts and sent USD/Asia broadly higher Thursday. USD/IDR could enter the Bollinger uptrend channel on a Thursday closing above 12,220--which may spur more U.S. dollar-buying. USD/IDR is now 12,150 from its last close of 12,075. (ewen.chew@wsj.com)

However, Credit Agricole says if the improved sentiment in the peripheral markets continues Spanish 10-year paper has already priced in an early concession ahead of next week's auction, and suggests going long the Spanish/Italian 10-year spread. 10-year bunds currently yield 3.05%, unchanged from Thursday. However, the bank says with the exception of EUR/CHF, where the risk is toward 1.31 and possibly 1.34, there is little evidence that the current move will be a long-term game changer. EUR/CHF now at 1.2894. (gary.stride@dowjones.com)

0939 GMT [Dow Jones] HUF weakens slightly, correcting from a recent peak on increased risk appetite, in turn the result of favorable bond auction results both in euro zone periphery countries and the region in recent days. EUR/HUF is 275.25 from 274.75 late Thursday. Takarekbank sees the EUR/HUF cross stable around 275. title: EM ASIA  FX -Rupiah stabilises; Taiwan dollar climbs
text:
* Rupiah stabilises on foreign fund inflows-trader

* Taiwan dollar hits 13-yr high

* Thai baht supported ahead of rate decision

SINGAPORE, Jan 12 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah was little changed versus the dollar on Wednesday, stabilising after a recent sell-off, and the Taiwan dollar hit a 13-year high, with both currencies supported by foreign fund inflows.

Traders said dollar-selling intervention by Indonesia's central bank also helped lend support to the rupiah, which has come under pressure this month as investors booked profits after a strong rally last year.

Foreign players were active sellers of the dollar against the rupiah in the spot market, said a trader for a European bank in Indonesia.

"Looks like some fresh inflows," the trader said, adding that offshore funds and real money investors seemed to be buying the rupiah.

The Taiwan dollar rose on the back of foreign fund inflows into the equity market, while the Thai baht rose ahead of a rate decision by its central bank.

TAIWAN DOLLAR

The Taiwan dollar hit a 13-year high against the dollar, as more foreign money flew into the stock market.

George Chou, deputy governor of Taiwan's central bank, told Reuters exporters should hedge against a Taiwan dollar appreciation, indicating the local currency may rise further.

"If the stock market keeps rising, the Taiwan dollar may go past T$29," said one trader at a local bank.

The Taiwan dollar hit a 13-year high T$29.056 to the dollar. After trimming some gains, the Taiwan dollar stood at T$29.100 compared to Tuesday's close of T$29.700.

INDONESIAN RUPIAH

Indonesia's central bank sold dollars against the rupiah early on Wednesday, and the dollar's broad weakness also lent support to the rupiah.

An equities rally helped to buoy the rupiah, with Indonesian shares surging 2.3 percent , rebounding from a three-month low struck the previous day.

The dollar was little changed against the rupiah at 9,045 .

The dollar edged up 0.4 percent against the rupiah in January as investors covered their short dollar positions to book profits in the wake of the dollar's 4.4 percent slide against the rupiah last year.

THAI BAHT

The baht rose against the dollar, supported by market expectations of the central bank raising interest rates later on Wednesday.

The dollar came under good selling pressure against the baht right away, in line with broad-based dollar-selling overseas. Macro funds were cited selling the dollar against the baht, with dollar selling interest seen both on- and offshore.

Most analysts polled by Reuters expect the Bank of Thailand to raise interest rates by 25 basis points to 2.25 percent at its policy decision due at 0730 GMT, with a few forecasting that rates will be held steady. [ID:nSGE70B00M]

But some market players are expecting a hike of 50 basis points on food inflation worries, dealers said.

In 4Q10, the CAD had the strongest correlation with crude oil prices among major currencies. The USD/CAD is at 0.9915, with near-term support pegged at 0.9895 (Friday's New York low), Nymex crude is at $89.59/bbl. (mark.cranfield@dowjones.com)

0129 GMT [Dow Jones] Philippine shares may drift lower after a weaker performance on Wall Street following the disappointing non-farm payrolls data and amid a dearth of domestic leads. The benchmark PSEi is likely to slide to a 4180 support after falling 0.3% to end at 4202.52 Friday; resistance is pegged at 4230. "The market will continue to consolidate, with a downward bias. There's no major market-moving news and even the U.S. (stock markets) ended flat," says Astro del Castillo, managing director at First Grade Holdings. (cris.larano@dowjones.com)

0121 GMT [Dow Jones] China shares are likely to rise slightly with support from likely continued buying interest in banks, which will offset possible weakness in property developers after the latest tightening measure in Chongqing. The Shanghai Composite Index is tipped to face resistance at 2850 after last ending up 0.5% at 2838.80. "The cheap bank sector may attract more buying interest after Friday's rise, while property developers are likely to open lower on the news of Chongqing's real-estate tax," says Huatai Securities analyst Zhou Lin; but adds the uptrend in property stocks remains intact due to "the low valuation of the sector and robust property sales." Note, Xinhua reports yesterday that China has decided to collect real-estate tax on high-end residential property in southwestern Chongqing city. Shenzhen Index ends down 0.8% to 1292.06 on Friday. (amy.li@dowjones.com)

0115 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/THB is higher at 30.37-30.39 from 30.34-30.36 late Friday in quiet trade. Concerns over euro-zone sovereign debt are lifting the pair, outweighing any falls in the USD on disappointing U.S. non-farm payroll data. "Between the U.S. dollar and the euro, players prefer the dollar (on hopes that the U.S. economy will recover faster than expected)," says a local dealer. He adds, investors will likely focus on the Bank of Thailand's policy rate decision on Wednesday. The dealer tips a 30.30-30.45 range for today. Ten of the 13 economists surveyed by Dow Jones tip the central bank to raise its policy rate by 25 basis points to 2.25% this week. (piyarat.setthasiriphaiboon@dowjones.com)

0113 GMT [Dow Jones] The HSI may stay in the 23,500-23,700 range as the modest decline in the DJIA on Friday is not expected to provide strong cues for the local market, says Conita Hung, head of research at Delta Asia Securities. "The local market is expected to witness some further consolidation in the near term, after its recent gains." The index ends down 0.4% at 23,686.63 Friday, snapping its 7-session winning streak (+5.2%). She expects HK property stocks to outperform, as the positive outlook of the sector remains intact, while some pressure in the mainland developers is expected, after Xinhua reports yesterday that China has decided to collect real-estate tax on high-end residential property in southwestern Chongqing city. (susanna.tai@dowjones.com)

0104 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/CNY is likely to fall as buying momentum slowed sharply late Friday after the dollar's recent gains. A Beijing-based trader at a local bank tips the pair to move in a 6.6200-6.6250 band for most of the session; the USD was at CNY6.6280 late Friday. Friday's weaker-than-expected U.S. payrolls data is also expected to hurt USD demand, the trader says. In addition, China is set to release its December trade data between 0100 GMT and 0200 GMT; though the trade surplus is widely expected to have narrowed last month, economists say the expected decline is unlikely to help alleviate tensions between China and the U.S. over the yuan exchange rate. (rose.yu@dowjones.com)

0101 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/PHP is expected to move higher as the EUR slides on renewed concerns over euro-zone debt. The USD/PHP is tipped to initially rise to 44.20 after settling late Friday at 44.15, with resistance at 44.30 and support at 44.00. But a local bank trader says, that gains maybe limited by the weaker-than-expected U.S. non-farm payrolls data. (cris.larano@dowjones.com)

0101 GMT [Dow Jones] Australia's November retail sales figures (+0.3% on-month) illustrate why the RBA will likely be on hold through 1H11, especially given the wet weather coupled with higher mortgage costs mean consumers will remain very cautious, says UBS Chief Economist Scott Haslem. "We expect only a modest improvement in retail spending near-term. Overall, today's data reinforce our non-consensus view that the RBA will be on hold for most, if not all, of the first half of 2011." UBS looks to July for the next central bank move. (enda.curran@dowjones.com)

0058 GMT [Dow Jones] Aussie retail sales will likely remain subdued in the near-term given that rising borrowing costs are hurting consumers, says Macquarie Economist Benjamin Dinte. "We expect activity to remain relatively subdued into early 2011." He adds, strong employment and wages growth is helping households, but the higher cost of living and mortgages will continue to keep sales tempered. Macquarie expects December's sales to have been pretty moderate overall. "It's seems to be a story of rising income being offset by rising costs." (enda.curran@dowjones.com)

0056 GMT [Dow Jones] The Kospi is 0.2% lower at 2082.40 in choppy trade. Analysts say the market has lost a bit of its strong upside momentum after last week's 1.7% rise, though the overall upward trend could persist for a while. "Technical pressure has mounted in the market as there has been no significant correction since the end of November," says Tong Yang Securities analyst Cho Byung-hyun; he tips a 2050-2100 range for this week. Other analysts tip 2077 as support for today. Heavyweight tech plays mixed, with LG Electronics (066570.SE) +3.1% at KRW117,000, on hopes for an earnings turnaround helped by improvement in TV, handset businesses, but Hynix Semiconductor (000660.SE) is down 1.0% at KRW25,850 on profit taking after its recent gains. (jieun.shin@dowjones.com) [ 01-09-11 2036ET ]

title: MARKET TALK: Treasurys Down Ahead Of Nonfarm Payrolls
text:
Contact us in London. +44-20-7842-9464 
Markettalk.eu@dowjones.com 
 

1014 GMT [Dow Jones] Treasurys are down in London ahead of the key nonfarm payrolls report at 1330 GMT. The strong ADP employment report on Wednesday bolstered expectations that the US economic recovery is gaining traction and prompted some economists to revise their forecasts. Nonfarm payrolls are now forecast to rise 150k in December, up from the initial estimate of 140k and a 39k rise in November. Additionally, Fed Chairman Bernanke will testify before the US Senate at 1430 GMT. The 2-year US Treasury note is slightly lower at 99-29/32, yielding 0.675%, 10-year down at 93-10+/32, yielding 3.427%, 30-year down at 95-08/32, yielding 4.541%, according to Tradeweb. March bunds down 0.09 at 125.64, March gilts down 0.12 at 118.21. (neelabh.chaturvedi@dowjones.com)

1014 GMT [Dow Jones] The weak euro, trading near a four-month low against the dollar early Friday, is likely to have a positive impact on the French trade deficit in early 2011, Asteres says. The French trade deficit was little changed at EUR3.87 billion in November 2010 compared with EUR3.71 billion in October. November exports rose 19% on year, while imports increased 15%. Asteres attributes the export increase to the sale of Airbus jets and a satellite and to a port blockade caused by strikes in October. (inti.landauro@dowjones.com)

1012 GMT [Dow Jones] Indonesia local government bonds continue to fall on a broad sell-off amid high inflation pressures, traders say. Two traders at a local securities firms say the falls may continue well into the middle of next week before selective bargain-hunting by investors emerges. The five-year yield is up at 6.78% from 6.69% Thursday, the 10-year yield is higher at 7.79% from 7.70%, the 15-year yield is at 8.40% from 8.32%, and the 20-year yield is at 9.17% compared with 9.04%. (andreasismar.sandiwan@dowjones.com)

1011 GMT [Dow Jones] CZK trades lower at 24.657-24.677 against the euro from 24.592 late Thursday as investors are closing short positions following a string of impressive Czech data releases this week, says a trader at Raiffeisenbank in Prague. "The good news is out and they can close positions; it's typical profit taking," the trader says. "In one month we could be lower, testing the 24.50 psychological level if German and Czech industry go well." (sean.carney@dowjones.com)

1007 GMT [Dow Jones] The Markit iTraxx corporate credit indexes are still little moved on the day as banks and sovereigns continue to suffer, says data-provider Markit. Notes both the Europe and Crossover indexes are nearly flat at 108/109bps and 429/433bps, respectively, with trading light ahead of key U.S. labor data due at 1330 GMT. However, says banks are wider after the European Commission's proposed framework for senior bank debt, and sovereigns are continuing to move out amid worries about impending government bond supply. Markit SovX Western Europe index is 5bps wider at 216/218bps. (art.patnaude@dowjones.com)

1005 GMT [Dow Jones] Thai shares end down 1.4% at 1036.45, snapping three straight sessions of gains in active trade. Most big caps retreat on consolidation mode. The SET Index is expected to continue to consolidate next week as the downside is weighed by expectations the Thai central bank will hike its benchmark rate Wednesday, says Asia Plus Securities' Therdsak Thaveethiratham. He adds, the selling force in certain tax benefit mutual funds due to be redeemed is likely to continue. He tips support at 1030 and resistance at 1050. Among the most active stocks, Siam Commercial Bank (SCB.TH) is down 2.8% at THB102.50, True Corp. (TRUE.TH) slides 8.7% to THB6.30, PTT (PTT.TH) falls 3.0% to THB322 and Thai Oil (TOP.TH) drops 3.3% at THB73.25. (piyarat.setthasiriphaiboon@dowjones.com)

1004 GMT [Dow Jones] Takarekbank expects Hungary's industrial output to have accelerated further in December after unexpectedly strong November growth data, released Friday. Adjusted November output is up 4.3% on the month and 14.5% higher on the year. Economist Gergely Suppan says it's likely December growth rose due to demand growth from German car manufacturers and a new tire plant owned by Hankook that began production at the end of November. Suppan expects strong industrial data to support Hungarian financial market assets given the implied improvement in economic prospects. (veronika.gulyas@dowjones.com)

1001 GMT [Dow Jones] The impact of the severe floods in Queensland is being felt beyond Australia's borders and the AUD, notes Barclays Capital. The bank says alternative suppliers of the affected commodities will benefit in terms of increased demand and higher prices and this is another reason to be short AUD/CAD, in addition to China's continued policy tightening. AUD/CAD now trades at 0.9923. (gary.stride@dowjones.com)

1000 GMT [Dow Jones] Norway's manufacturing output for November comes in at +0.9% on the month, reversing the previous month's dip, and the rise was higher than expected, says Handelsbanken. "If the December reading stays flat, the 4Q annualised growth in manufacturing production will be 3.1%, not much above Norges Bank's forecast," notes Handelsbanken, so this "shouldn't significantly alter Norges Bank's view of the manufacturing sector." (charles.duxbury@dowjones.com)

0944 GMT [Dow Jones] Indonesia shares end down 2.8% at 3631.453 in moderate volume as foreign funds trim their positions due to growing concern over the country's inflation. Investors are worried because rising food prices will add to Indonesia's inflationary pressures in January, traders say; they add, higher inflation could inspire the central bank to hike policy rate next month. Traders tip the main index to trade in a 3600-3670 range Monday. "Selling in most interest rate-sensitive and commodity stocks drove the main index lower despite sporadic bargain-buying by local funds," says a trader with Erdhika Securities. Among decliners: carmaker Astra (ASII.JK) is down 3.9% at IDR49,000, Bank Mandiri (BMRI.JK) is down 4.5% at IDR6,400, while Bank Rakyat (BBRI.JK) is down 5.3% at IDR9,800. Foreigners are net sellers of IDR1.5 trillion worth of shares. (edhi.pranasidhi@dowjones.com)

0943 GMT [Dow Jones] The Sensex is down 2.2% at 19,750.33 on growing concerns India's central bank may soon raise interest rates to tackle rising food inflation, say local dealers. Investors are deeply worried that "the RBI may raise policy rates by 50 bps (basis points) after market hours today and that is causing the sell-off," says a senior dealer. The RBI's next policy review is scheduled for January 25 but investors fear the central bank will move early to combat high food inflation, the dealers say. Among losers, Infosys Technologies (500209.BY) is down 2.8% at INR3,382.00, Reliance Industries (500325.BY) is 2.1% lower at INR1,061 and Housing Development Finance Corp.(500010.BY) is 3.0% lower at INR685.35. The Sensex is likely to find support at 19,680, according to Dow Jones technical analysis(sudeep.jain@dowjones.com)

0934 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/IDR is higher at 9,020 from 8,993 late Thursday, breaching the 9,000 resistance level, tracking the dollar's gains against several Asian currencies and as foreigners continue to cash in their gains from local stock and bond markets, traders say. "We don't see Bank Indonesia intervening today. They may see the rupiah slide as roughly in line with the region's," says a trader with a foreign bank, tipping the pair to trade in a 8,980-9,040 range next week. (andreasismar.sandiwan@dowjones.com) [ 01-07-11 0514ET ]

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia  Central Bank  moves to mop up excess liquidity
text:
* Dollar reserve requirements raised to 5 pct in March, 8 pct June

* Short term foreign borrowing by banks capped at 30 pct of capital

* Banks must disclose prime lending rates from March (Adds new details throughout)

By Aditya Suharmoko

JAKARTA, Dec 29 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank moved on Wednesday to mop up excessive liquidity and encourage more lending, announcing fresh measures that sought also to protect Southeast Asia's biggest economy against new inflationary pressures.

Bank Indonesia said the minimum dollar reserve requirement for commercial banks would be raised to 5 percent of total deposits from March 1 and to 8 percent on June 1, from the current 1 percent.

A rise to 5 percent in dollar reserve requirement -- which banks store at the central bank -- was expected to absorb $1.5-2.5 billion from the market, while the rise to 8 percent could absorb $3 billion, deputy bank governor Budi Mulya told a news conference.

Indonesian officials have tried channeling strong capital flows into the country towards longer-dated investments for fear a change in risk sentiment may trigger a "hot money" reversal, hurting the local currency and financial stability. [ID:nL3E6MN0OJ]

DARLING OF EMERGING MARKETS

Indonesia has been a darling of emerging market investors this year. The currency has risen nearly 3.5 percent and the stock market 40 percent -- driven by strong domestic consumption.

Foreigners have so far this year bought net 86.8 trillion rupiah ($9.6 billion) worth of Indonesian government bonds and 9.7 trillion rupiah of central bank SBI debt, latest Bank Indonesia data shows.

But Indonesia joins countries from South Korea to Brazil that have implemented stricter measures to protect their economies from a tide of capital, although Jakarta's steps have been more modest.

"The concern could stem from the fact that most foreign investors buying local assets exchange their dollar liquidity for rupiah via local commercial banks, which could lead to an alarming situation and create rupiah instability should there be a sudden and massive unwinding," Enrico Tanuwidjaja, an economist at OSK-DMG in Singapore, said of the new measures.

"I think Bank Indonesia is trying to ensure that local banks employ closer monitoring of their U.S. dollar banking books."

The central bank on Wednesday also capped banks' vostro accounts at a maximum 30 percent of capital beginning end January, with a three-month transition time. Vostro accounts are rupiah deposits in commercial banks held by foreigners and considered a form of short-term borrowing by the institution.

Inflation, the Achilles heel of Southeast Asia's largest economy, may yet prevent growth from reaching 6-6.5 percent as expected next year. Local food prices have been creeping up as heavy rains have affected commodities, while the partial end to a pump price subsidy on fuel and new taxes on vehicles will also be felt.

BENCHMARK RATE STABLE

Governor Darmin Nasution said on Wednesday that the central bank would keep its benchmark interest rate -- which has been at 6.5 percent for over a year -- consistent with the inflation target range of 4-6 percent in 2011, and 3.5-5.5 percent in 2012.

"Although we think that they will eventually raise interest rates in April 2011, there is a risk of them being reactive, instead of pre-emptive, in doing so," said Helmi Arman, an economist at Bank Danamon.

"Capital inflows have been a key concern among policy-makers. So far Bank Indonesia has taken liquidity management measures to mop up liquidity and sterilize their foreign exchange intervention."

On Wednesday Bank Indonesia also announced that commercial banks with assets of more than 10 trillion rupiah would be required to disclose their prime lending rates starting March 31.

The regulation may bring down rates and spur more lending to businesses which frequently complain about the high rates demanded by commercial banks, which currently hover around 14-15 percent.

Deputy governor Muliaman D. Hadad said banks would have to disclose their base lending rates for corporates, retails and consumers, both mortgage and non-mortgage.

This year's lending was estimated to grow by 22 percent, he said, and between 22-24 percent next year. ($1 = 9,017 rupiah) (Reporting by Adriana Nina Kusuma and Rieka Rahadiana; Editing by David Fox)
