text:
Contact us in Singapore. 65 64154 140; 
MarketTalk@dowjones.com 
 
 

0141 GMT [Dow Jones] If Indonesia puts into affect ban on motorcycles consuming subsidized gasoline, which country is considering, would definitely to help stoke inflation, although impact likely be moderate, analysts say. Move being considered to reduce subsidy costs. "It's being studied, and we must get approval from the parliament before we can implement it," Evita Legowo, director-general of oil and gas at the Energy and Mineral Resources Ministry, tells Dow Jones Newswires today; adds if approved, could implement policy as early as August. Still unclear if government would put plan into effect considering rejections from parliament, outcry from public over various options to reduce subsidy aired by government in recent years. (i-made.sentana@dowjones.com)

0138 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/TWD down at 32.219 vs 32.345 late yesterday on exporter selling above 32.200, tracking losses in USD vs Asians, says local bank trader. Tips pair in 32.170-32.300 band rest of morning. Notes "though local shares are slightly lower now, it seems like the Taiex may be headed for consolidation today and regional bourses also seem more stable," helping to add marginally to investor confidence. Expects trading volume to be smaller today as investors on sidelines waiting for further cues. (charmian.kok@dowjones.com)

0136 GMT [Dow Jones] Singapore stocks pull back slightly on Wall Street's decline, reluctance to buy with long weekend ahead. STI off 0.3% at 2687.06, with immediate support at year-to-date low of 2648 set earlier this week. Decliners outnumbering gainers by 2 to 1 in broad market, with most FTSE ST sub-indexes down. "Investors are unlikely to take on fresh positions," says NRA Capital. CIMB says headwinds inevitable in near term as investors keep tight watch on potential financial-market instability; "nevertheless, mid-term, our base case remains that European problems are unlikely to derail the global growth recovery and Asia's growth trajectory. With valuations undemanding and a cyclical recovery in place, we expect further market upside in 2H10." Among blue chips, notable decliners include yesterday's top performers; NOL (N03.SG) off 2.2% at S$1.76, SembMarine (S51.SG) off 1.6% at S$3.78. (frankie.ho@dowjones.com)

0133 GMT [Dow Jones] EUR/USD bounces back as short-term players buy, could rise as high as 1.2350 by end of global day "if no more bad news comes out" on euro-zone debt, financial market problems or on central bank EUR-selling, says senior FX dealer at major Japanese bank. Says after EUR/USD failed to break 4-year low hit last week at 1.2143, speculators in Asia bought pair back. Any breach of 1.2143 would expose 1.2133, half-way point between pair's all-time low, all-time high. "People are rather nervous about that half-way point, so there was enough relief from it holding above there to prompt some euro-buying this morning," trader says. But says EUR/USD outlook remains bleak for foreseeable future as "there are absolutely no reasons for macro-focused hedge funds and other investors who trade on economic fundamentals to buy the euro now."(andrew.monahan@dowjones.com)

0133 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/HKD continues to bounce back after sharp overnight fall, now at 7.7875 vs low of 7.7695 last night, though still below 7.8008 late yesterday. Brokers at U.K. bank expect HKD to remain on stronger side today, with pair to be capped at 7.7950 amid inflows related to upcoming IPOs, safe haven status of HK. They note market still looking at reasons into USD/HKD's major move last night, which partly due to major US$2 billion trade overnight by a German bank to sell USD, buy HKD, as well as several subsequent trades by other names to buy HKD, pushing pair even lower, with lack of market liquidity during overnight hours making moves more pronounced. They added there were no major news or underlying developments that triggered the HKD fluctuation. (jeffrey.ng@dowjones.com)

0132 GMT [Dow Jones] A Chinese fire sale of EUR holdings looks unlikely despite Financial Times report that China's SAFE met with foreign banks to discuss issue of European crisis and expressed concerns about Greece, Ireland, Italy, Portugal and Spain, Credit Agricole says. "Such news should not be exaggerated. We don't expect China to sell massively its European holdings, not only because of a lack of alternative, but also because it may become interesting to buy back EUR at some point in the future." Still, reckons China may sharpen focus going forward, aiming for top-quality European names, and be more reluctant to invest in lower-rated countries. Also says market reaction "suggests that the recent consolidation is fragile, and that both the market rebound and the EUR are still vulnerable to possible bad news emanating from Europe." EUR/USD last at 1.2212 vs 1.2193 late in NY trade. (david.roman@dowjones.com)

0129 GMT [Dow Jones] Korea treasury bonds, bond futures steady as investors trade cautiously due to increased volatility in local bond market of late, market participants say. "The market seems to be finding it hard to stabilize... while the longer-end bonds remain relatively weak," says local securities firm trader. Expects yield curve to steepen; short-term notes like monetary stabilization bonds, 3-year government bonds likely strong as rate hike concerns recede while bonds of 5-year tenor or longer expected to be weak. But "investors with either a long or a short position in bonds seem to have become increasingly risk-sensitive," leading to choppy trade. 3-year yield flat at 3.61%, tipped in wide 3.54%-3.68% range. 5-year yield +1 bp at 4.38%, June futures +2 ticks at 111.50. (min-jeong.lee@dowjones.com)

0126 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/IDR edges higher to 9,350 vs 9,320 late yesterday as U.S. stocks' slide overnight drove USD higher vs major rivals, dealers say; most deals so far between local participants, but foreigners also expected to buy pair later today. Pair tipped in 9,325-9,380 range, likely to trade closer to upper end of range, with players cautious on possible Bank Indonesia intervention if 9,400 region revisited. (i-made.sentana@dowjones.com)

0119 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/THB tad up at 32.55-32.56 vs 32.53 late yesterday in thin trade, with portfolio outflows following recent sharp falls in local shares supportive. "The baht in the near term is unlikely to turn significantly stronger as investors are still concerned over euro-zone's financial health," says Bangkok-based dealer; adds as such they're in risk-aversion mode. Notes BOT yesterday says 70%-80% of THB50.94 billion net selling by foreign investors so far in May has already left country. Pair tipped in 32.50-32.60 band. (oranan.paweewun@dowjones.com)

0112 GMT [Dow Jones] HSI may open lower, tracking Wall Street's decline; Conita Hung at Delta Asia thinks index may test psychological 19,000 as sentiment remains bearish due to lingering euro-zone credit concerns. "It's hard to expect a turnaround in trading sentiment, as euro-zone credit concerns are not expected to be cleared in the near term." Says HSI not yet bottomed out, reckons benchmark index likely to fall below its year-to-date trough of 18,974 near-term. Expects more volatility ahead of Friday's expiry of May futures. Companies with European exposure, such as HSBC (0005.HK), Esprit (0330.HK), likely to remain weak. HSI ends +1.1% at 19,196.45 Wednesday. (susanna.tai@dowjones.com)

0107 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/PHP may fall as EUR, most Asian currencies recover some ground vs greenback early in Asian trade. Still, market likely to be volatile, PHP's rise should be limited. Pair may slide to 46.60 vs 46.71 late Wednesday; support eyed at 46.50, resistance at 47.00. Manila-based currency trader says USD-demand not substantial but should be enough to temper PHP's gain. (cris.larano@dowjones.com)

0103 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/CNY likely to rise following EUR's sharp decline overnight; USD/CNY tipped to retest 6.8300 vs 6.8291 last close though central parity likely in range, expected to be set at 6.8281 vs 6.8280 yesterday as PBOC aims to keep CNY steady. Shanghai-based trader at local bank says traders likely to keep close eye on PBOC as central bank may support CNY either in automatic price matching system or spot market if pair rises sharply. He says USD/CNY ended lower Wednesday as large state-owned bank sold (USD) heavily late. Still, "it's difficult to say whether the bank did that on behalf of their corporate clients or the central bank," trader says. (joy.shaw@dowjones.com) [ 05-26-10 2141ET ]

title: MARKET TALK: IDR May Stay Solid Despite Risk Aversion - FX  ASIA
text:
0506 GMT [Dow Jones] IDR showing unusual resilience in face of latest risk scare, will likely outperform other Asian currencies thanks to solid outlook for local economy, central bank intervention that should limit any downside. USD/IDR down 0.7% YTD even as USD has made small gains vs most other Asians, which have been hit by concerns about economic fallout from Europe's debt crisis. Many analysts forecast USD may drop well below IDR9,000 before December vs IDR9,350 last. This reflects stark improvement in Indonesia's status among foreign investors, who sold IDR furiously in previous crises. Country's foreign exchange reserves +39% over last 12 months; central bank has been using that war chest to support IDR, including suspected $20 million intervention Tuesday. Another key to IDR's resilience is Indonesia's low exposure to euro zone-bound trade, as global markets fret over possible loss of demand due to unfolding sovereign debt crisis there.

Shanghai Composite Index last off 2.0% at 2619.05, may test support at 2,600 soon. Internet portal Sina.com reported yesterday Shanghai may include real-estate tax into rules that it's drafting to curb speculative investment in property market. "It's still unclear what the rules may be, but people believe that China will keep its tightening stance on the property market," says Zhang Yuheng at Capital Securities. Property developer China Vanke (000002.SZ) down 3.8% at CNY7.41, Poly Real Estate (600048.SH) down 4.7% at CNY11.58. Shenzhen Composite Index last down 1.5% at 1035.64. (rose.yu@dowjones.com)

0553 GMT [Dow Jones] EUR again starts falling on growing concerns that euro-zone's sovereign debt turmoil has started to undermine health of region's financial system, may extend declines to 1.2000 vs USD, 105.00 vs JPY in near term, says Masanobu Ishikawa, manager of foreign exchange at Tokyo Forex and Ueda Harlow. Notes many players have become worried over whether euro-zone's faltering financial system could drag down real economy in area; "it's extremely difficult to expect when the euro will hit bottom. Players remain very eager to sell the euro as economic conditions in Europe may worsen down the road." EUR/USD now at 1.2285 vs session high of 1.2372; EUR/JPY at 110.45 vs 111.62. Some traders say Europe investors just entering market, starting to sell EUR. (tomoyuki.tachikawa@dowjones.com)

0552 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/KRW off 1,277.0 high on another round of suspected USD selling intervention by central bank, according to 3-Seoul based traders; but pair still trading higher at 1,259.0 vs 1,214.5 late yesterday in Seoul on concerns over tensions between North, South Korea. "It's a crazy market that (I) haven't seen in a while," says local bank trader. Adds, pair still biased upward despite "the aggressive (dollar) selling intervention." Traders decline to provide near term USD/KRW. Pair has traded in wide 1,224-1,277 range so far today. (min-jeong.lee@dowjones.com)

0543 GMT 0000 GMT (Dow Jones) The Swiss National Bank's decision to decline to offer Swiss franc repos in recent days suggests it is unwilling to accept lower franc money market rates, says UBS. "We attribute the latest decline in franc interest rates and negative rates on the FX forward market to the excess liquidity in the local money market rather than anything else," says economist Reto Huenerwadel. "It's a fact, however, that over the last days the monetary conditions in Switzerland continued to loosen," he adds. (neil.maclucas@dowjones.com)

0543 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/CNY NDFs offshore extend gains on USD general strength vs major currencies; 1-year USD/CNY NDFs at 6.7560/6.7619 vs 6.7170/6.7220 late yesterday. Still, upside limited on lingering hopes China may allow CNY appreciation vs USD this year, says Hong Kong-based trader at Asian bank. "My personal feeling is that the one-year NDFs will be very toppish around 6.7700," trader says. (joy.shaw@dowjones.com)

0537 GMT [Dow Jones] For now, probably best to simply get out of way of rallying Aussie bond market, wait for another time to try a little profit-taking, says Stephen Nash, head of strategy for FIIG. Korean concerns helped lift bond prices today, with 3-years up 10 ticks at 95.32, and though those concerns could dissipate easily, risk-averse market sentiment won't. "We are in this period of assessing just how bad the European growth outlook will be. That's going to take some time and during this period, any bad news will be featured," says Nash. "Not to mention, in terms of the RBA, the case for tightening has simply gone away for the time being." (geoffrey.rogow@dowjones.com)

0535 GMT [Dow Jones] Thai shares down 2.1% at 728.97 midday in active trade, taking cue from regional slide following concerns over health of euro zone. Rebound after recent steep fall may emerge intrasession but unlikely to be strong enough to reverse benchmark to positive close, says Phillip Securities' Assistant VP Teerada Chanyingyong. Adds political situation still on radar as end of protests still leave consequent problems. Support put at 724, resistance at 742. Among top actives, PTT (PTT.TH) down 2.5% at THB236, Banpu (BANPU.TH) down 4.1% at THB564, PTT Aromatics & Refining (PTTAR.TH) down 3.6% at THB26.50, PTT Chemical (PTTCH.TH) down 6.0% at THB90.50. (piyarat.setthasiriphaiboon@dowjones.com)

0529 GMT [Dow Jones] China's move to hike investments in Syria masks challenges it is facing operating there. State-owned China Petrochemical Corp. (0386.HK) has struggled to maintain output from 2 Syrian fields acquired in $2 billion takeover of Tanganyika Oil in 2008. Fields produce heavy oil that is expensive to produce, difficult to refine. Royal Dutch Shell PLC (RDSB) said in April it was struggling to keep output from its fields in Syria's Dier-Ez-Zor area above 100,000 bbl this year. Last week, Shell sold 35% stake in Syrian oil unit to China National Petroleum Corp. But there is broader logic to China's Syrian investments, especially boost to its influence in Middle East, key strategic area. See "=CHINA ENERGY WATCH: Syria's Appeal Holds Despite Output Fall" (david.winning@dowjones.com)

0519 GMT [Dow Jones] Aluminum contango financing deals which allow speculators, market participants to make money by storing metals and profiting from difference between cash and futures price likely to persist, says Adrian Lismore, deputy head of commodities marketing at Societe Generale. "Some of these deals are now being rolled over," he says. Aluminum financing has kept estimated 75% of global aluminum inventories off the market, supporting prices since 2008 financial crisis. Some market participants fear price of aluminum could fall below cost of production if interest rates rise or market flips into backwardation for some reason, which could cause deals to unravel, pushing glut of supply into market. LME 3-month aluminum at $2,051/ton, down $33 with 621 lots traded so far. (james.campbell@dowjones.com)

0519 GMT [Dow Jones] S&P/ASX 200 down 2.4% at 4288.8, hits 2-day low of 4282.8, albeit on moderate volume. Index remains under pressure as offshore falls worsen, with Asian markets down 2%-3%, S&P 500 futures down 1.6% and AUD/USD down 0.9%. Markets are reacting negatively to tightening credit conditions, due to the European financial crisis, with 3-month Libor's rise to 10-month high causing widespread concern. "The markets are clearly very worried about credit conditions," says Patersons senior private client adviser Peter Morgan. "Company valuations are very attractive but a credit crunch can be diabolical and the fear factor is massive at the moment." Morgan says margin calls will be back on the agenda tomorrow if the S&P/ASX 200 closes below 4300.0 and Wall Street has another bad night. (david.rogers1@dowjones.com)

"Sentiment is very weak and many investors are worried because they think the bearish trend will continue for the rest of the month," says trader at Lautandhana Securities. Among decliners: gas and oil company Medco (MEDC.JK) down 6.5% at IDR2,500, car maker Astra (ASII.JK) down 3.6% at IDR36,550, Coal miner Bumi (BUMI.JK) down 2.2% at IDR1,740. title: INTERVIEW-Indonesia tinplate maker sees higher 2012 capacity
text:
* Output seen lower this year but capacity boost in 2012

* Euro zone debt to ease, tin at $18,000-$24,000/T range in 2012

* Indonesian rupiah below 9,000 best for foreign investors

By Michael Taylor

JAKARTA, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Output at Indonesia's only tinplate producer will slip almost 10 percent this year as improvement works begin this month, in a project that will help ramp up capacity for 2012 by nearly a quarter, a director at the firm said on Tuesday.

PT Pelat Timah Nusantara Tbk , also known as PT Latinusa Tbk, produced 110,000 tonnes of tinplate last year and this is forecast to fall to 100,000 tonnes in 2011, Hideyuki Iwasaki, deputy of finance director, told Reuters.

Full production capacity at its Cilegon facility is currently 130,000 tonnes a year, but an upgrade is due to start this month and be completed in December. These works will boost the annual capacity to 160,000 tonnes for 2012, Iwasaki added.

Established in 1982, domestically focused Latinusa was once part of PT Timah but became a subsidiary of the world's No.4 steelmaker, Nippon Steel in late 2009.

Latinusa produces tinplate in coil and sheet forms, used for manufacturing mostly food and milk cans.

State-owned Timah, the world's largest integrated tin miner, supplies around 60 tonnes of tin ingot to Latinusa each month, using annual contracts tied to LME prices, Iwasaki said.

But since Oct. 1, Indonesian tin smelters have put in place a self-imposed export ban, with the aim of pushing prices above $25,000 a tonne.

"We're OK, no problem," he said about the impact of the ban, adding that the Indonesian smelter's export ban only affected international shipments. "We are just a domestic consumer."

Yet he said that tin prices are still high despite having lost about a third since hitting records in April and give Chinese tin makers an edge over the company.

"Our competitors are tinplate makers in China," Iwasaki said. "Judging the current situation, we cannot make money if tin prices are hiked."

London Metal Exchange tin hit a record high above $33,000 a tonne in April, but like other base metals, has since slumped as the global economic and demand outlook became increasingly uncertain. Tin traded at $22,600 at 0927 GMT.

"Current prices are still too high," said Iwasaki. "Three years ago, prices were about $15,000. Hot money has entered the tin market and so prices rise."

"In 2011, our major target is how to improve our competitiveness against China," he said, adding that prices below $20,000 a tonne best reflected the current supply and demand fundamentals.

"The Chinese (tinplate) prices never follow the trajection of raw material prices," he added. "China prices are almost dumping."

A crackdown on illegal mining, tighter export rules, falling onshore reserves and rain that had hindered production in Indonesia, which supplies about 30 percent of the world's tin consumption, helped drive the tin rally earlier this year.

FIRM PRICE OUTLOOK

The outlook for benchmark tin prices is looking increasingly supportive, however, as euro zone debt worries ease and top refined exporter Indonesia, implements an export ban.

World equities clambered out of bear market territory on Monday after a pledge from German and French leaders to come up with a plan by the end of the month to tackle Greece's confidence-sapping debt woes.

"Financial conditions in Europe are getting... better and better," said Iwasaki. "Hopefully, conditions will get better and better... in my opinion $18,000-$24,000 is a range for 2012."

Aside from a small trial of exports to India, which began three years ago, Latinusa's customers are mostly Indonesia-based, with almost 70 percent in greater Jakarta and 22 percent in Surabaya.

About 30 percent of the company's sales are in U.S. dollars and the rest in Indonesian rupiah, to try to minimise foreign exchange rate fluctuations.

Indonesia's central bank has intervened heavily in the forex market to stabilise the rupiah, causing the country's forex reserves to fall.

"If they can keep the Indonesian rupiah against the U.S. dollar under 9,000, it is very good for us, especially for foreign investors to Indonesia," Iwasaki said.

($1 = 8892.500 Indonesian Rupiahs)

(Editing by Ramthan Hussain)

title: REFILE-UPDATE 2-Indonesia makes surprise rate cut to counter global risks
text:
(Fixes final bullet point)

* Bank Indonesia cuts rate by 25 bps to 6.5 pct

* Cbank gov says cut to anticipate global slowdown

* Exports seen slowing in 2012, gov says

* Cbank says it will keep guarding rupiah

By Aditya Suharmoko and Neil Chatterjee

JAKARTA, Oct 11 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank unexpectedly cut its benchmark policy rate on Tuesday, the first such move by a G20 member after Brazil, as Jakarta seeks to stimulate domestic demand and maintain investor confidence in Southeast Asia's biggest economy.

Despite few signs of actual cooling in a hot Indonesian consumer market, Bank Indonesia cut the rate by 25 basis points to a record low 6.50 percent, underscoring growing concern among policymakers that a global recession may be coming.

Bank Indonesia may also have started an easing cycle to keep international portfolio investors onboard, after a slide in its bonds and stocks in September on global risk aversion, as policymakers fear a repeat of destabilising selloffs.

"So far, the impact of the global economic turmoil is more felt in the financial markets, while the real sector is not yet impacted. However, a weakening global economy is estimated to impact the domestic economy in 2012," said Bank Indonesia in Tuesday's policy statement, adding this would lead it to pursue interest rate and other monetary policy responses.

"We are bringing the policy rate to a level that is more reasonable," Governor Darmin Nasution told reporters. "We saw the 6.75 percent rate as too high, unless we estimated inflation next year to be very high."

Just a month ago, many analysts expected Bank Indonesia -- which only raised rate once this year, in February -- to hike them once more by end-2011 to curb inflation. But then, as turmoil wracked financial markets while inflation eased, , central bank officials started talking about having "room" to cut rates.

So Bank Indonesia was seen as being among the first Asian central banks that would loosen policy. Still, a cut as early as now was not expected. In a Reuters poll last week, all 11 analysts forecast that BI would leave the rate at 6.75 percent on Tuesday, though three of the 11 forecast a cut to 6.50 percent by the year-end.

In September, annual inflation slowed to 4.61 percent due to easing food prices, and the central bank now sees it below 5 percent next year too, well within its policy target range.

As global funds saw Europe's debt crisis intensify, they pulled money out of Indonesian stocks and bonds, reinforcing Bank Indonesia's worries about the country's exposure to foreign funds and leading policymakers to keep asserting that the economy's domestic fundamentals are in good shape.

Indeed, industry data on Tuesday showed car sales in September surged 62 percent from a year earlier, while motorbike sales jumped 51 percent. Toyota last month announced plans for $337 million of investment in the country.

Yet foreign portfolio investors, who held 35.7 percent of total Indonesian government bonds in early September, dumped 37.13 trillion rupiah by Oct 5, reducing their ownership to 30.7 percent.

Tuesday's rate cut led the yield on benchmark 10-year Indonesian government bonds to edge lower to 6.4 percent on investor buying, from 6.5 percent before the central bank meeting.

INTERVENING HEAVILY

BI has more than doubled its foreign reserves since 2008 and intervened heavily in the past month to prop up the rupiah, causing the reserves to fall to $114.5 billion as of Sept. 30 from $124.6 billion a month earlier.

Still, the rupiah has slid 5 percent since the end of August, undermining BI's efforts to use a stronger currency to temper imported inflation and leaving reserves likely to fall further as Nasution said BI will continue guarding the rupiah.

"This is a brave decision. Two thumbs up. This is not expected by the market and it shows that Bank Indonesia is over confident with the currency. In the short term, the rupiah will depreciate...Bank Indonesia will need to do more intervention," said Juniman, economist at BII in Jakarta.

"Inflation is below 5 percent, that's why they cut the rate...In the medium and long term, the decision will give stimulus to domestic demand."

The rupiah was little changed after the rate decision, having earlier fallen about 0.6 percent against the dollar. Indonesian stocks also showed little initial reaction to the rate move, holding on to gains of more than 2 percent earlier in the session, buoyed by global markets.

" The key will be whether this move encourages equity inflows back into the economy on the basis that Asia is reflating," said Jonathan Cavenagh, FX strategist at Westpac in Singapore.

HIGHER LENDING AHEAD?

Indonesia's economy is expected to post solid 6.6 percent growth this year as exports remain strong in spite of a global slowdown. The country had annual growth of 6.5 percent in the first half on buoyant household consumption and investment.

Nasution said full-year loan growth was seen holding up at 24-25 percent, a figure bank executives expected to be boosted by its latest move and the possibility of a further cut.

"If inflation is manageable, the BI rate still has room to decline. The exchange rate is manageable and credit demand will be bigger," said Jahja Setiatmadja, CEO of Bank Central Asia

, Indonesia's biggest lender by market value.

A consumer confidence index rose in September as consumers saw lower financing costs and slower inflation in coming months

. Nasution said on Tuesday the central bank saw domestic consumption and investment staying strong in 2012, though exports were likely to slow on weaker global demand.

The country's export growth slowed in August, but at 37 percent from a year earlier would still be in the envy of many. The country is the leading exporter of thermal coal for power, palm oil and tin.

Economists say Indonesia is in better shape to face a global crisis than it was in 2008 and will likely expand above 6 percent next year even with an international slowdown.

"While this might be authorities' attempt at pre-emptively cushioning downside risks to growth, we still believe that the move was a tad premature given the need to support rupiah and contain volatility in the local markets. Strong loan growth and flush liquidity conditions could pose price risks going forward," said Radhika Rao, economist at Forecast in Singapore.

(Additional reporting by Adriana Nina Kusuma, Rieka Rahadiana and Fathiya Dahrul in JAKARTA,; Razak Ahmad in KUALA LUMPUR and Karen Lema in MANILA; Editing by Richard Borsuk)

title: DJ UPDATE: Asia Central Banks Tap  FX  Reserves To Support Their  Currencies
text:
-- Official reserves in Indonesia, Philippines, South Korea, Singapore fall in September

-- Central bank action to slow currencies' slide aimed at reassuring markets

-- Reserve levels remain ample to guard against future shocks

By Martin Vaughan

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Several Asian central banks dipped into their vast foreign exchange reserves in September to stem sharp declines in their currencies hit by global market turbulence driven by the euro-zone's debt crisis.

While Asian currencies have stabilized this week, the authorities still have ample firepower to support them if global appetite for risky assets takes another turn for the worse, analysts say.

The scale of the declines in reserves suggests most central banks were trying to smooth volatile movements in their currencies, rather than taking a no-holds-barred approach to defend specific levels.

"What they are doing is just trying to reassure markets: 'Just because we have a slip doesn't mean everyone has to pile out and put their money in dollars,'" said Robert Ryan, FX strategist at BNP Paribas. "They're saying, 'You don't need to run for the exits, we will be there.'"

Reserves held by Indonesia, Southeast Asia's biggest economy, fell by $10.1 billion to $114.5 billion as of Sept. 30 from a month earlier, Bank Indonesia said Friday, reflecting interventions to slow the rupiah's tumble as foreign investors pulled capital out of the country.

Foreigners cut their holdings of rupiah-denominated government bonds by 12% in September, a pace on par with a selloff in October 2008 at height of the global financial crisis, DBS says.

The Philippines' reserves declined by a more modest $301 million to $75.639 billion. Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas attributed the drop to debt payments made by the government and losses from a revaluation of the central bank's gold holdings. But the central bank has also been suspected by traders of intervening as recently as Tuesday to support the peso.

Singapore's reserves fell by $15.56 billion to $233.62 billion at the end of September. The reason for the decline was unclear, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore doesn't comment on reasons for changes in official reserves.

South Korea reported Wednesday its reserves fell by $8.8 billion to $303.3 billion at the end of September, the sharpest monthly fall since November 2008. Analysts attributed the drop to both won-supportive interventions and a fall in the euro, which hit the value of its euro-denominated assets in dollar terms.

Even after the declines in September, reserves remain more than ample to guard against shocks, economists said. Indonesian reserves are sufficient to cover 6.5 months of imports and government debt payments, said Bank Indonesia deputy governor Hartadi Sarwono.

Asian currencies swooned in September as foreign investors pared holdings in emerging markets and snapped up dollars on worries European banks were vulnerable and the global economy was tipping toward recession. Many have regained some ground this week as European officials have shown renewed resolve to support banks in the region and help Greece get its debt problem under control.

But analysts see room for the dollar to rise more in the short-term, as appetite for riskier currencies is vulnerable to negative signals from Europe and bad news out of the U.S., which some say could be headed for a recession.

Indonesia has been among the most aggressive in defending its currency.

"We think Indonesia's September foreign reserves data reveals an investor-friendly policy shift," ING chief Asia economist Tim Condon said. "Bank Indonesia will intervene heavily to prevent maxi-devaluations."

-By Martin Vaughan, Dow Jones Newswires; +65 6415 4033; martin.vaughan@dowjones.com

title: Indonesia  Forex  Reserves Fall To $114.5 Billion In Sept Vs $124.6 Billion In Aug
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves fell to $114.5 billion as of Sept. 30 from $124.6 billion a month earlier as the country's central bank intervened to halt the rupiah's decline, data from Bank Indonesia showed Friday.

Global investors have been trimming their holdings in riskier emerging markets assets due to combination of heightening risks of global economic slowdown and fears over euro zone debt, and like many other central banks in emerging Asia, Bank Indonesia has been spotted in the market trying to curb the volatility in the local currency.

Many analysts, however, say that Indonesia is better positioned to withstand any potential turbulence in the financial markets thanks to its much-improved reserves and its vast domestic markets, which would shield the local economy should a global downturn occur.

The last time global risk aversion affected the country's financial assets was during the panic following the collapse of major investment bank Lehman Brothers in late 2008. Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves stood at $50.6 Bln at the end of October 2008.

DBS said in a report this week that foreigners cut their holdings of rupiah-denominated government bonds by 12% in September from a month earlier, a pace similar to that seen in October 2008. However, this time around, the yield on 10-year government bonds only rose 12 basis points compared with a 410 basis points jump in October 2008 because local banks and Bank Indonesia were able to buy the bonds to help limit the price decline.

title: DJ  FX  ASIA: Asian  Currency  Bulls Temper Their Outlook With Caution
text:
-- Investors, speculators still long Asia FX, but holding back a while

-- More declines possible since Europe debt problem hasn't gone away

-- Singapore dollar, won may have been oversold in September

-- Asia FX declines mostly on hedging, not selling of underlying assets 


 
   By Martin Vaughan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Investors and speculators remain bullish on Asian currencies, despite the shellacking the region's markets have taken this month, but they are hesitating to resume their purchases as they watch to see how the euro-zone debt crisis plays out.

Some banks and fund managers say they are preparing to buy the Singapore dollar but are holding back for at least several weeks from buying other battered currencies, like the South Korean won, against the U.S. currency as the global turmoil continues to threaten Asian and other emerging-market investments.

"I cannot rule out another 5% to 10% weakening of the major Asian currencies in the next month or so," said Adam Gilmour, managing director and head of Asian corporate sales at Citibank. "But I have a very firm view on this--sell the dollar rally against Asia. When the dust settles, we'll see dollar/Asia go back to levels well below what we see now."

September's Asia-FX rout has been dramatic: As recently as early August, some central banks were intervening to slow their currencies' ascent; now many--Korea, Indonesia, Taiwan, Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines--have been in the market to defend them. The won has slid nearly 10% in September against the U.S. dollar and the Singapore dollar 7%, leading the region's decline and each shedding a year's worth of gains with a few weeks.

"We still want to be overweight on Asian currencies, but over the next two months things are going to move around a lot more," said Endre Pedersen, managing director at Manulife Asset Management. "We're running less risk exposure than in a more stable market."

An exception may be the Singapore dollar. The U.S. currency, which had sunk from January's high above S$1.55 to a record low below S$1.20 in August, has since rebounded to S$1.2971. That steep pullback in the Singapore dollar is making it look attractive to some.

"We had been short on the Sing dollar for quite some time, but at these levels we are looking for ways to get back in," Pedersen said.

The Philippine peso, by contrast, declined less than its regional peers, falling a comparatively small 3% this month. That is partly because foreign investors weren't as heavily positioned in the Philippines, and so there weren't as many trades to unwind. But it could also signal more room to catch up on the downside.

Much will depend on whether European policy makers can restore confidence that Greece won't suffer a disorderly default and that the region's banks can withstand any stresses. Market players say there hasn't yet been a broad sell-off in Asian emerging market debt--despite some commentators throwing the word "capitulation" around. Instead, the month's sharp declines in Asian currencies were driven by investors hedging the foreign-exchange risk on their long-Asia bets.

"There is almost no sign that real money has actually fled local markets," UBS economist Jonathan Anderson wrote in a note to clients. "Rather, as best we can tell the currency moves are due primarily to panicked hedging by foreign investors together with the normal unwinding of hedged trades on the back of it."

Foreign money has poured into emerging-market bonds and equities over the past two years, and the currency appreciation trend was so well established that investors didn't bother to hedge many of these positions, seeing it as a further boost to their returns.

"Most of them probably were entirely unhedged," said Ilan Solot, a strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman in London. "You give back a lot of carry trying to anticipate those kinds of risks." Investors seeking the high yields that emerging markets provide have been focused on maximizing those yields, and until the recent shocks have been hesitant to hedge them, he said.

But that also means there is much more downside for Asian currencies if global conditions worsen beyond current expectations and foreign investors start dumping assets in earnest.

Investors will also be watching central banks closely for policy cues. Monetary tightening helped fuel Asian currencies' long rally, and a shift to more accommodative policy to support growth could help them back down.

"If investors get the faintest whiff that an Asian central bank will ease, that's going to set alarms off," said Selena Ling, head strategist at OCBC Bank.

-By Martin Vaughan, Dow Jones Newswires; +65 6415 4033; martin.vaughan@dowjones.com

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia state insurers, banks told not to sell govt bonds
text:
(Adds details, quotes)

JAKARTA, Sept 28 (Reuters) - Indonesia's government made a rare plea on Wednesday to state-owned insurance firms and banks not to sell government bonds as authorities try to stabilise volatile markets in the face of foreign selling over euro zone worries.

Authorities also urged large state firms to coordinate before they buy U.S. dollars, a step to protect Indonesia's struggling rupiah currency which has fallen 4 percent against the dollar this month.

"State-owned insurance firms and banks have been urged not to sell government bonds when prices are volatile," Bambang Brodjonegoro, head of fiscal policy at the Ministry of Finance, told reporters on Wednesday.

Three years after the collapse of Wall Street giant Lehman Bros sparked a stampede out of higher risk assets and sent emerging economies reliant on foreign funding into shock, such fears have resurfaced in recent days amid heavy emerging equity and bond losses accompanied by sharp currency weakness.

The latest wave of foreign-led selling has been especially punishing on emerging-market darlings Indonesia, South Korea and Russia.

Foreign investors sold 14.05 trillion rupiah ($1.58 billion) of Indonesian government bonds from Sept. 16 to 26, reducing their ownership to 222.8 trillion rupiah, or 32 percent, of total outstanding bonds, the latest Finance Ministry data shows.

This compares to a record 251.23 trillion rupiah, or 35.7 percent, on Sept 9.

Indonesia's capital market regulator has also advised state-owned firms not to panic and sell stocks following volatility in Jakarta's benchmark stock index in recent days and heavy outflows of global capital.

Indonesia's central bank has intervened repeatedly in the foreign exchange market to prop up the rupiah and buy government bonds in the secondary market. It had 124.64 trillion rupiah in foreign exchange reserves as of the end of August.

Brodjonegoro also said the ministry had asked state firms to prepare funds to buy bonds if needed, under a scheme he called a bond stabilisation fund, to shore up the market.

But despite those headwinds, economists remain broadly upbeat about the outlook for Indonesia, Southeast Asia's biggest economy. The government expects economic growth of 6.5 percent this year, Foreign Minister Marty Natalegawa said on Tuesday, among the strongest in the region.

Brodjonegoro said the Finance Ministry now expects an inflation rate next year of 5 percent as the global economy slows. That compares with the central bank's forecast for annual inflation of 4.8-4.9 percent for 2011.

Headline inflation rose to 4.79 percent in August from 4.61 percent in July, while core inflation jumped to 5.15 percent in August from July's 4.55 percent, data on Sept. 5 showed.

Perry Warjiyo, the central bank's director of monetary policy and research, told reporters on Tuesday that Bank Indonesia may cut its benchmark reference rate to stimulate growth amid uncertainties in the global economy.

($1 = 8,905 rupiah)

(Reporting by Adriana Nina Kusuma and Fathiya Dahrul. Writing by Aditya Suharmoko. Editing by Jason Szep)

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia's c.bank signals may cut rates
text:
* C.bank repeats stands ready to cut rate to boost growth

 * C.bank says sees inflation easing to below 5 percent this year

 * C.bank says foreign reserves more than enough for intervention

(Adds details, qoutes)

 JAKARTA, Sept 27 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank signaled on Tuesday it may cut interest rates as Europe's debt crisis drives down the rupiah, stirs volatility in stock prices and takes a toll on Southeast Asia's biggest economy.

 It was the second time in a month Bank Indonesia suggested it was willing to cut its benchmark reference rate to stimulate growth amid uncertainties in the global economy.

 "Going forward, there is a room to lower the benchmark rate", the bank's director of monetary policy and research, Perry Warjiyo, told reporters. "Inflation pressure will continue to ease and this year it (CPI) will be below five percent."

 The central bank left its benchmark rate unchanged at 6.75 percent on Sept. 8 for a seventh straight month. But it  unexpectedly lowered the floor of its interbank overnight rates by half a percentage point to 150 basis points below the BI rate, which some analysts said was a form of policy easing.

 Warjiyo also said the central bank has more than enough foreign reserves to intervene and stabilise the rupiah, which has shed as much as 5.9 percent this month. 

 The central bank on Sept.22 for the first time bought government bonds in the secondary market and has been intervening in the foreign exchange market to prop up rupiah.

 The Indonesian currency hit a seven-year high at the end of August, taking bond yields to record lows and stocks

to record highs. But as the outlook for global growth has soured, local policymakers have sounded increasingly nervous

 about a reversal in sentiment. 

 The Jakarta Composite Index rebounded on Tuesday, rising 4 percent on the day, but it is down 10.5 percent this year after surging 46 percent last year, the biggest gain in Southeast Asia.   

(Reporting by Adriana Nina Kusuma. Writing by Janeman Latul. Editing by Jason Szep)

title: DJ IMF Sees Slight Moderation In Asia Growth, Risks From EU, US
text:
WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--The International Monetary Fund said Saturday economic growth in Asia for this year and next will be slightly weaker from its April projection, with downside risks increasing as a result of the euro-zone debt crisis and the slowdown in the U.S.

"In line with the weaker global outlook, growth in Asia is expected to be slightly lower in 2011-2012 than we projected in April, but the expansion should remain healthy as the fundamentals for domestic demand remain strong," said Anoop Singh, director of the IMF's Asia Pacific department.

He said he now expects growth at between 7.5% and 8% in the next one to two years for developing Asia compared with an 8.4% projection in April.

Downside risks have increased from the global uncertainty and in particular an "escalation of the euro-area financial turbulence or a renewed slowdown in the United States could have substantial trade and financial spillovers to Asia."

"The turbulence in the markets this week underscores that Asia has not decoupled from advanced economies and remains greatly exposed to risks of contagion," he added.

Deputy IMF Director for Asia Mahmood Pradhan said he supports recent intervention by Bank Indonesia in the foreign exchange market, but he is skeptical of intervention in the local bond market.

"Part of the intervention activity by Bank Indonesia is to maintain liquidity. One-way flows make the foreign exchange market very illiquid. So it intervenes not only to support the currency but also to maintain liquidity," he said.

Bank Indonesia said Thursday it sold dollars "in large amounts" to defend the rupiah and has also been buying rupiah-denominated government bonds to help stabilize the country's bond market from the turbulence in Europe and the U.S.

But Pradhan said the central bank should let yields rise and foreign investors should get used to it.

title: South Korea Caps Week Of Fierce Won Defense
text:
SEOUL (Dow Jones)--South Korea's currency authorities fired a late salvo of dollar selling Friday to cap a week in which they dumped around $7.5 billion to $10 billion to support the beleaguered Korean won, some of its most aggressive foreign-exchange intervention since the 2008 financial crisis.

The South Korean authorities have been among the most active in currency markets this week as central banks in emerging markets defend their currencies amid a general flight from risky assets. Authorities in India, Taiwan and Indonesia were also seen intervening Friday.

Traders say that the Bank of Korea, acting on behalf of Korea's finance ministry, intervened to sell dollars each day this week, and on most days more than once, in an effort to stem a sharp slide in the won. On Friday alone, the central bank sold around $4 billion, dragging the dollar down near the end of the trading day from a high of 1,196 won to close at 1,166 won. The dollar has risen 4.8% this week and 9.3% since the start of September.

Since the authorities won't provide details of foreign-exchange intervention, the amounts involved can't be confirmed. Based on accounts from traders, a similar scale of intervention hasn't been seen in the market since authorities defended the won during market turmoil in 2008.

Seoul's support for the won comes as South Korean markets have taken a hammering in recent weeks due to the continuing debt crisis in Europe and concerns about the health of the U.S. economy. South Korea's open, export-dependent economy means investors are often quick to exit Korean assets when there are worries about global growth. The main stock index closed down 5.7% Friday, the biggest single-day drop for a month, and is at its lowest level for over 14 months.

Local authorities have warned repeatedly in recent days that they are monitoring the currency market. Finance Minister Bahk Jae-wan said in an interview Thursday that the authorities are concerned about "excessive and unnecessary" volatility in the domestic currency market caused by capital flows.

Underscoring the level of concern, government officials met with executives at some of South Korea's biggest exporters on Friday, including Samsung Electronics Co. (005930.SE), to discuss the foreign-exchange market. The officials and companies wouldn't discuss details of the meeting, but analysts said the government likely asked the conglomerates to exchange their foreign-currency earnings for won to boost demand for the local currency.

"If the market knows there's real won demand [from exporters], they'll be more cautious about trading just in one direction," said Byeon Ji-young, an analyst at Woori Futures.

While a weaker won benefits the nation's big exporters, who account for around half of economic output, Korea is a heavy importer of basic commodities and won declines make those imports more expensive. Korea is currently grappling with inflation running well above the central bank's target levels.

Seoul has since mid-2010 taken some limited steps to stem flows of so-called hot money, including capping foreign-exchange forwards positions of banks operating onshore to limit speculation in the won. Local authorities say these measures have damped some of the whipsawing in local markets but they concede there's only so much that can be done unilaterally to limit the effects of global economic turmoil on Korea's markets.

Speaking Thursday in Washington, Finance Minister Bahk called on the Group of 20 nations to come up with near-term steps to stabilize global markets. The G-20 said there would be an "action plan" of coordinated short- and medium-term economic policies to be announced at the G-20 summit in Cannes in early November.

For currency traders in Seoul, the weekend brings a chance to recover from a hectic few days. "[I felt like I was] swept into a tsunami of [volatile] FX rates," said Han Sung-min, a currency dealer based in Seoul.

--By Jieun Shin and Min-Jeong Lee, Dow Jones Newswires; jieun.shin@dowjones.com [ 09-23-11 0711ET ]

title: UPDATE 1- Indonesia  cbank  intervenes  to prop up rupiah
text:
* Cbank buys nearly $200 mln debt, intervenes in FX mkt

* Cbank says country's fundamentals strong

* State pension fund says sell-off a buying opportunity

(Updates with details, fund manager comment)

By Adriana Nina Kusuma and Neil Chatterjee

JAKARTA, Sept 22 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank stepped in on Thursday to prop up the rupiah, intervening in the forex market and buying government bonds after selling by foreign investors drove the domestic currency sharply lower.

Bank Indonesia bought 1.74 trillion rupiah ($196 million) of long-dated, mostly 21-year government bonds as it sought to stabilise a selloff that also took gains in benchmark 10-year sovereign yields to 120 basis points in two weeks.

"Bank Indonesia is intervening in the forex market and buying government bonds in large amounts. The rupiah has returned to 8,750 per dollar," said Perry Warjiyo, Bank Indonesia's director for monetary policy and research.

The rupiah earlier on Thursday weakened as much as 2 percent to a low of 9,050 per dollar, before recovering following the central bank's intervention.

One-month dollar/rupiah non-deliverable forwards

jumped to a near 2-year high as offshore players kept buying dollars amid insufficient liquidity in onshore markets, dealers said.

NDF demand from offshore investors such as real money accounts, along with the bond outflows, put pressure on the spot rupiah.

The Indonesian currency had risen to a seven-year high by the end of August as investors poured into Southeast Asia's biggest economy to take bond yields to record lows and stocks to record highs.

But as the outlook for global growth has soured, local policymakers have sounded increasingly nervous about a reversal in sentiment.

FOREIGN EXPOSURE

Memories of the 1997/98 Asian financial crisis are still fresh, when a sudden withdrawal of foreign funds and high levels of foreign debt rocked the region, prompting the IMF to step in to help stabilise Asian currencies.

Bank Indonesia has made a series of moves this year to try to guard against a recurrence of such outflows that could destabilise its currency and economy, pushing investors towards government bonds by curtailing its popular short-dated SBI notes.

Earlier this month it said it will introduce a regulation requiring exporters to return export earnings parked overseas, in another effort to reduce dependence on foreign liquidity and boost the rupiah, but this will only take effect next year. It is also considering limiting firms' foreign debt exposure.

Despite these moves and the recovery in the rupiah, stocks slid 9 percent to wipe out this year's gains.

Policymakers are trying to prove the country is now more resilient to external shocks as they seek the approval of ratings agencies in the next year for an upgrade to an investment grade sovereign rating, which would lower government borrowing costs and spur fund investment interest.

The central bank has built up record foreign reserves, of $124.5 billion by mid-August, or over double the level in 2008, to give it plenty of ammunition to intervene.

"Our fundamentals are strong -- high growth, low inflation, surplus balance of payments," said Warjiyo, who last week said the central bank was ready to loosen monetary policy to counter the impact of the global slowdown.

Indonesia is exposed to the risk of fund outflows as 35 percent of total tradeable bonds as of mid-August were owned by foreign investors, and foreign ownership in stocks is even higher.

The country's biggest pension fund Jamsostek said the sell-off, an "expression of anger" by investors over U.S and European economic woes, was a buying opportunity.

"Jamsostek is in a buying position at the moment given the cheap valuation of stocks in banking and resources. I'm buying bonds and stocks now," said Elvyn Masassya, chief investment officer at the state fund, which manages more than $13 billion.

($1 = 8870 Rupiah)

title: WSJ: Emerging Markets Tumble World-Wide
text:
By  Tom Lauricella, Alex Frangos and  John Lyons 
  Of THE WALL STREET JOURNAL 
 

NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Investors turned tail on emerging markets, sending their stocks, bonds and currencies into steep declines, demonstrating that their relatively healthy economies are no match for the turmoil and uncertainty in the U.S. and Europe.

Across Asia, most major stock markets fell 2% to 3% Thursday. Indonesian stocks plunged almost 9%. In Latin America, Brazilian and Mexican shares stocks dropped almost 5%.

While foreign investors have been steadily pulling money out of emerging-market stocks since July, the recent rout has been more aggressive. It has also been driven by investors who focus on bonds denominated in local currency, rather than stocks.

The speed and scope of the declines serves as a reminder that emerging markets, while bigger and more active than in the past, can be still be treacherous and prone to sudden outflows of money, as happened during the peak of the financial crisis in 2008 and the Asian meltdown in 1998. As investors have turned away from riskier investments in general, emerging markets--where liquidity can quickly disappear--the result has been dramatic moves.

"These markets can be one-sided and they get one-sided fast," said Pablo Goldberg, head of global emerging-markets research at HSBC.

(This story and related background material will be available on The Wall Street Journal website, WSJ.com.)

In currency trading, Brazil's real--until recently one of the world's biggest gainers against the U.S. dollar--slid nearly 6% against the dollar before clawing back much of its losses after Brazil's central bank deployed $2.7 billion to support it.

"We are ready, absolutely ready," to meet the crisis, Brazil's President Dilma Rousseff said in New York. "We are a country with very low debt, we have our accounts in order, and we are a country with high reserves."

The currency was down 3% at 1.90 per dollar late in New York on Thursday. The real has now lost almost 9% in the past week and is down nearly 19% from its high against the dollar set in late July. Currencies in Mexico, Chile, Colombia and Peru also slid Thursday.

In Indonesia, the central bank stepped intervened in the bond market, buying its rupiah-denominated bonds to help support prices.

Despite the carnage, many investors remain optimistic about the medium- and longer-term prospects for many emerging market economies.

Unlike in their developed-market counterparts, many emerging-market central banks and governments are seen as having flexibility in their monetary and fiscal policy to soften the blow from a global economic slowdown.

Brazil's benchmark interest rate is one of the highest in the world at 12%, for example. Brazil cut the overnight lending rate by half a percentage point earlier this month, and more cuts are expected. Economists say central banks in other nations, such as Mexico, may also lower.

In addition, as was the case in 2008, the headwinds for emerging markets are coming from abroad. That, many investors believe, means that when markets calm, emerging markets should be in a better position to recover.

Emerging markets "are not the ones with the problems," said Sara Zervos, co-manager of the $14 billion Oppenheimer International Bond fund.

The International Monetary Fund, for example, is still predicting emerging market economies will grow by 6.1% in 2012, that's down just 0.3 percentage point from the June forecast. In contrast, the IMF lowered its forecasts for the world's developed economies by 0.7 percentage point to 1.9%.

Despite the longer-term optimism, emerging markets are being hit by a reversal of some of the huge amounts of investor money that had poured in over the past two years.

That is especially the case for bonds denominated in local currencies. For much of the history of developing economy bond markets, their debt has been denominated in dollars because investors were wary of taking on the risk of owning notoriously volatile emerging market currencies.

In recent years, however, as many emerging markets have successfully controlled inflation and improved their fiscal positions, their currencies have become less volatile and gained strength against the U.S. dollar. Investors looking to benefit from both rising values of emerging market currencies and their generally higher interest rates have poured $54 billion into local currency bond funds, according to EPFR.

Even as emerging-market stocks faltered in August, investors moved $2.6 billion into local currency bond funds, after a $3.4 billion July inflow that was the third-biggest monthly gain for the funds on record, according to EPFR.

Because a prime attraction of local currency bonds are the expected extra returns an investor can earn rising emerging-market currencies, most local bond investors left their positions unhedged against currency fluctuations.

But with the turmoil in Europe leading investors to buy the dollar as a safe haven, local currency bond investors have begun to sell those bonds outright or hedge their exposure to the currency using forward contracts.

Nicholas Chamie, global head of emerging markets research at RBC Capital Markets, said the exodus from the local currency said the timing of the selloff in emerging-market bonds, coming well after other riskier markets had started selling off in July, is typical.

"Emerging markets are less liquid and what you tend to see is the most liquid assets get sold first," he said. "Once the flow starts, the price action starts to gap and that's what we have started to see."

The yield on the benchmark Brazilian five-year note, for example, has jumped 0.75 percentage point to 12.20% from 11.45% since Sept. 12. That move over the past week and half reversed a rally that had taken place since mid-August.

Indonesia's bond market as well has been the poster child for the flows into emerging-market debt, where investors have been attracted to higher yields and strong economic fundamentals.

That is now reversing. Indonesia government figures show foreigners have sold nearly $2 billion from the $78 billion Indonesian bond market in the past 10 days. Foreigners owned 15% of Indonesia's bonds in early 2010, rising to 36% in August. It now stands at 33%, indicating a major pullback could still await.

An exodus out of a relatively small and illiquid market like Indonesia can mean oversized price drops as everyone sells at the same time. The drop in the rupiah against the dollar is forcing stock investors to quickly liquidate or hedge their positions in other ways, such as shorting commodities or other stock markets that run in tandem with Indonesia's.

"It's a small tunnel to get through," said Robert Levitt, founder of Levitt Capital Management, which oversees $500 million in private client assets, with some of that invested in Indonesia.

-By  Tom Lauricella, The Wall Street Journal; 212-416-2768 [ 09-22-11 1717ET ]

title: Bank  Indonesia  Official Confirms  Intervention  To Defend Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves fell to $122 billion as of Friday from $124.6 billion a week earlier due to intervention to defend the local unit and repayment of the government's offshore debt falling due during the period, deputy governor Hartadi Sarwono said Sunday.

"Negative sentiment over the global economy triggered by fears of worsening debt problems in Europe have triggered profit taking [on rupiah-related assets] by short-term investors," Sarwono told Dow Jones Newswires.

His comments confirmed speculation in the market that Bank Indonesia had sold dollars nearly every day last week as the local unit fell to its lowest level since March 14 with foreigners trimming their holdings in the local stocks, government bonds and Bank Indonesia money market securities.

Sarwono added that long-term "strategic investors, however, stay because of Indonesia's good prospects. We even detected some new strategic investors entered Indonesian markets."

The nation's central bank's deputy governor reaffirmed that Bank Indonesia will continue intervention if necessary either by selling dollars in the currency market or buying local government bonds using its rupiah or foreign exchange reserves.

He added that Bank Indonesia's action to defend the rupiah has restored investors' confidence and he believes the rupiah will resume its upward trend in the near future.

Bank Indonesia has been relying on the rupiah's appreciation to help curb inflation, and has been avoiding rate hikes on fears higher rates would further attract short-term capital.

Indonesia had experienced robust short-term fund inflows in the past two years attracted by relatively higher yields offered by rupiah assets and its sound economic fundamentals.

* Hedge funds, offshore players cited buying dollar/Asia

* Rupiah dips but stays above previous day's low

By Masayuki Kitano and Rick Lloyd

SINGAPORE, Sept 15 (Reuters) - The dollar rose broadly against emerging Asian currencies on Thursday, with the South Korean won hitting a six-month low on selling by offshore players and stop-loss offers.

The Indonesian rupiah stabilised somewhat after selling off sharply the previous day, when offshore real money investors were selling Indonesian government bonds. The rupiah fell but stayed above a trough hit on Wednesday.

Pressure on emerging Asian currencies persisted overall, with the Malaysian ringgit hitting a nine-month trough and the Philippine peso dipping to its lowest in six months.

"At this point we do not rule out further potential weakness for Asian currencies," said Emmanuel Ng, FX strategist at OCBC in Singapore.

Emerging Asian currencies have slid sharply this week as heightened jitters over the euro zone's sovereign debt crisis and the impact on the European banking sector, stoked risk aversion among investors.

Dollar buying by hedge funds and position unwinding by offshore investors have pummelled Asian currencies, which until recently, had remained relatively stable, stirring talk that they were increasingly being regarded as safe havens by investors.

"This was pretty much the last frontier, in terms of the... risk that was still on the table," said OCBC's Ng.

Hedge funds and offshore players were buying dollar again on Thursday, traders said.

Asian central banks, which spent an estimated $4 billion in dollar-selling intervention on Wednesday, were spotted selling dollars again on Thursday, with traders citing dollar-selling by the central banks of South Korea and Indonesia as well as the Philippines.

Jonathan Cavenagh, foreign exchange strategist for Westpac in Singapore, said dollar/Asia may start to see some consolidation in the near-term, but cautioned against jumping into short dollar/Asia positions at this point.

"The situation in Europe remains far from resolved and global growth is continuing to cool. The medium term outlook for Asian currencies remains upbeat but we suspect better entry levels for short USD/Asia positions will still present themselves over coming weeks," he said in a research note.

INDONESIAN RUPIAH

Dollar/rupiah stabilised somewhat after surging to its highest since late February of around 8,840 in the brokers' market on Wednesday. One trader said Thursday's high in dollar/rupiah was 8,800 .

Dollar-buying by offshore players was less active on Thursday than the previous day, traders said, adding that dollar-selling intervention by Indonesia's central bank helped temper the dollar's gains.

There was also talk of dollar-selling by leveraged names, while model funds were cited as dollar buyers.

Long-end Indonesian government bonds regained ground after the previous day's slide, with a dealer for a European bank in Singapore saying yields dropped roughly 15 to 20 basis points on the day .

The bond buying was led by onshore players, although there was some buying from offshore players as well, the dealer said.

KOREAN WON

Dollar selling against the won by onshore players initially weighed on the dollar, but momentum players and custodial names later bought dollar/won on dips.

Offshore players were among those cited as dollar buyers against the won, with traders saying offshore names were also spotted selling South Korean equities.

The dollar extended gains on stop-loss bids, hitting its highest in roughly six months of 1,119.9 , with an option barrier said to be lurking at 1,120.

Dollar-selling intervention by South Korea's central bank helped temper the dollar's gains against the won, traders said.

RINGGIT

Dollar/ringgit hit a fresh nine-month high of 3.1030

. Fast money and model accounts were cited as pushing dollar/ringgit higher. In addition, a Kuala Lumpur-based trader said onshore and offshore players were spotted selling Malaysian government securities and buying dollar/ringgit.

PHILIPPINE PESO

Dollar/peso hit a six-month high of 43.700 . It was supported by USD short-covering by real money investors, traders said, adding that the Philippine central bank conducted dollar-selling intervention to cap the dollar's rise.

HONG KONG DOLLAR

Hedge fund manager William Ackman, best known for selecting stocks, said he was buying the Hong Kong dollar, noting that it could become his biggest bet ever.

The manager of New York-based Pershing Square Capital Management, said he believes that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority will eventually allow the currency to appreciate dramatically against the U.S. dollar.

title: Emerging Market Debt,  Currencies  Echo Rebound In Risky Markets
text:
NEW YORK (Dow Jones)--Emerging-market currencies and credits took a bit of a break from their recent declines Thursday, as so-called risk assets recovered on news that five major central banks are working together to provide liquidity for crisis-embroiled European banks.

Latin American and Eastern European currencies were slightly stronger against the dollar and euro, while sovereign credit spreads tightened with U.S. Treasury yields rising. The joint announcement from the European Central Bank, the Federal Reserve, and three other key monetary authorities that they are going to coordinate efforts to provide euro-zone banks with dollar funding, lifted investors sentiment.

"People are feeling a little better about Europe from the ECB announcement, so emerging markets are largely up," said Win Thin, senior currency strategist at Brown Brothers Harriman. "But I'm still skeptical because not much about the underlying dynamic has changed."

The risk premium, or spread, on the J.P. Morgan Emerging Markets Bond Index Global was six basis points tighter to 385 basis points over Treasurys. In price terms, the index was down 0.23%.

Emerging-market currencies, which rallied early this year, have fallen sharply in recent days due to worries about global growth and contagion from the euro zone's debt problems. Now central banks in these countries are in the position of having to hold them up rather than find ways to weaken them, as was the case earlier in the year.

"By year-end, all these guys will probably be cutting rates," Thin said.

Chile's central bank rate decision is due later Thursday and it is widely expected to keep its target policy rate unchanged at 5.25%. Its spread on the Embig tightened five basis points to 1.59%, but fell a fraction in price terms.

The Bank of Indonesia was suspected of intervening to shore up its currency. Traders also said that the Philippines central bank appeared to have intervened to support its currency. Peru has been working on extending stimulus from the fiscal side and said Tuesday that it will adopt measures to speed public sector investments.

Indonesia may need to introduce fiscal stimulus next year to help shield its economy from a potential global economic slowdown, senior officials said Thursday. Finance Minister Agus Martowardojo told a parliamentary hearing that the country may need to issue a fiscal stimulus package in the first half of next year.

While growth across Asia appears relatively resilient, the outlook in emerging Europe appears to be headed for a slowdown given its ties to the beleaguered euro-zone bloc. The deteriorating sovereign debt problems there are expected to dent the export demand for goods produced by these highly open economies such as Hungary and the Czech Republic.

The Hungarian currency and credit markets have been coming under excruciating pressure in recent days as investors reel from new government proposals that could hit the country's banks. The forint has fallen particularly hard recently after Prime Minister Viktor Orban announced controversial plans Monday to help struggling households by locking in exchange rates on mortgages denominated in foreign currencies, particularly Swiss francs.

But the forint and Polish zloty recovered ground against the euro Thursday on the coordinated move by the central banks to provide dollar funding to European banks. That alleviates some pressure, for now, that has been mounting for euro-zone banks to raise short-term funding because investors fear their exposure to the region's debt crisis.

The zloty strengthened to PLN4.3284 per euro from PLN4.3809 to start the day, while the forint gained to HUF284.94 a euro from HUF287.06. Emerging Europe's region index on the Embig lost 0.08% in price, while its spread narrowed seven basis points to 3.45%.

title: Bank Indonesia Deputy Gov: Rupiah's Fall 'Playing Catch Up' With Regional  Currencies
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's central bank is not concerned about the rupiah's steep decline against the dollar Wednesday, Deputy Governor Hartadi Sarwono said, describing the decline as "playing catch up" with recent losses in other currencies in the region.

"The average of the rupiah's weakness in the past five days is comparable to that of regional currencies'... The rupiah's previous declines were not as deep as the others," Sarwono told Dow Jones Newswires on the sidelines of a central bank event, suggesting the monetary authority is not concerned about the drop.

The rupiah lost ground against the greenback Wednesday, with the dollar reaching an intraday peak of IDR8,820, the highest since March 14 and compared with IDR8,660 late Tuesday, as global risk aversion hit the country's assets. Yield on 10-year rupiah-denominated government bonds climbed to around 7.2% from 6.7% Tuesday, while the main stock index was down 1.8% at midday.

The dollar trimmed some of its gains and was quoted IDR8,730 at 0620 GMT, with traders saying the central bank likely sold dollars to stem the its rise.

"The most important thing is to ensure the market is not panicking...For today, it is unlikely for us to buy back government bonds as we have been intervening in the (spot currency) market," Sarwono added.

Bank Indonesia last month said it will buy back rupiah-denominated government bonds from investors, using its dollar reserves, if it is approached. The central bank will sell dollars and use the rupiah proceeds to fund the buyback, a move that could support the local currency and bond market in the event of a massive sell-off.

title: WSJ(8/24) Emerging Nations Seek To Bolster  Currencies
text:
(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL) 
   By Erin McCarthy 

Some emerging nations have stepped into the market this month to prevent steeper declines in their currencies.

The darkening economic outlook has turned the status quo for emerging-market currencies upside down. In recent weeks Turkey, South Korea and Indonesia have taken or forewarned of measures to curb their currencies' slides after global growth sent investors fleeing riskier assets, including equities and emerging-market currencies.

These central banks and others want to prevent their currencies from swinging sharply in either direction -- too steep a depreciation could scare off long-term foreign investment, while a too-strong currency hurts exports. But a global slowdown could simplify the bankers' task, as emerging nations may need to put in fewer controls to head off strength in their currencies if investment flows moderate.

"Most emerging markets still need external financing, and if they felt like that wall of money is suddenly withdrawing, they might loosen up in terms of their controls," said Sara Zervos, a senior portfolio manager at Oppenheimer Funds.

South Korean authorities earlier this month said they would step up monitoring of local financial markets, including conditions in the foreign-exchange market, amid heightened volatility. Currency dealers suspected Korea's central bank of selling dollars to support the won amid a plunge in the local stock market in early August. The won has weakened more than 2% this month against the dollar, though it still is up for the year.

Turkey's central bank cut rates and bought dollars earlier this year in order to weaken its currency. In recent weeks, the bank has canceled U.S. dollar-buying auctions and instead began auctions to sell dollars. The central bank kept its benchmark rate on hold Tuesday. The lira has fallen nearly 5% since Aug. 3 and is down about 15% this year.

Some Asian central banks, including Indonesia's, also have been playing a balancing act, though on a more subdued scale. This month, Bank Indonesia said it will buy back rupiah-denominated government bonds from investors if it is approached and said it will sell dollars and use the rupiah proceeds to fund the buybacks. Dealers also suspected Indonesia's central bank of intervening in the market by selling dollars earlier this month.

Analysts say the trend is still toward stronger emerging-market currencies as long as developing economies see robust growth. They add that any efforts by emerging-market central banks to fight depreciation are likely to be short-term, and more stable markets may erase the need to do so at all.
