4. Additional Investment Considerations:

The Notes offered by this Pricing Supplement are complex financial instruments and may not be suitable for certain investors. Investors intending to purchase the Notes should consult with their tax and financial advisors to ensure that the intended purchase meets the investment objective before making such purchase.

There are various risks associated with the Notes including, but not limited to, exchange rate risk, price risk and liquidity risk. Investors should consult with their own financial, legal and accounting advisors about the risks associated with an investment in these Notes, the appropriate tools to analyze that investment, and the suitability of the investment in each investor's particular circumstances. Holders of the Notes should also consult with their professional tax advisors regarding tax laws applicable to them.

The Bank will hedge its obligations under the Notes by entering into a swap transaction with an affiliate of the Lead Manager as swap counterparty. Assuming no change in market conditions or any other relevant factors, the price, if any, at which the Managers or another purchaser might be willing to purchase Notes in a secondary market transaction is expected to be lower, and could be substantially lower, than the original issue price of the Notes. This is due to a number of factors, including that (i) the potential profit to the secondary market purchaser of the Notes may be incorporated into any offered price and (ii) the cost of funding used to value the Notes in the secondary market is expected to be higher than our actual cost of funding incurred in connection with the issuance of the Notes. In addition, the original issue price of the Notes included, and secondary market prices are likely to exclude, the projected profit that our swap counterparty or its affiliates may realize in connection with this swap. Further, as a result of dealer discounts, mark-ups or other transaction costs, any of which may be significant, the original issue price may differ from values determined by pricing models used by our swap counterparty or other potential purchasers of the Notes in secondary market transactions.

Payment of each Interest Amount and the Redemption Amount will be based on the Applicable Rate, which is a measure of the rate of exchange between the Indonesian Rupiah and the USD. title: MARKET TALK: Indonesian Shares Down 1.5%; Support At 3520
text:
Contact us in Singapore. 65 64154 140; MarketTalk@dowjones.com 
 
 

0743 GMT [Dow Jones] Indonesian shares extend losses on worries earthquake in Japan may slow the global economic recovery, traders say. The benchmark index is down 1.5% at 3532.584 in moderate volume. They expect the main index to find support at 3520. "Foreign funds are dominating the selloff," says a trader with Reliance Securities. Foreigners are net sellers of IDR204 billion worth of local shares. Among decliners: heavyweight Telkom (TLKM.JK) is down 2.0% at IDR7,250, Bank Mandiri (BMRI.JK) is down 4.0% at IDR6,100, while BCA (BBCA.JK) is down 2.9% at IDR6,700. (edhi.pranasidhi@dowjones.com)

0742 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/TWD is higher at 29.6050 from 29.5060 late Thursday, following the rise in the USD/JPY after Japan was struck by an 8.9-magnitude earthquake, two local traders say. "The market was shocked by the news, those who hold lots of Asian currencies soon started to sell as they are worrying the disaster may impact Japan's economy," one of the traders says, adding investors are also concerned that foreign funds will flow to safer places outside Asia. Another trader says trading was volatile after the earthquake; the pair was pushed up immediately to above 29.600 from around 29.560. "Most people are watching news about the earthquake, some traders prefer to remain on the sidelines until the impact of the earthquake becomes clearer," another trader says, tipping resistance at 29.650. (fanny.liu@dowjones.com)

0741 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/IDR extends gains as players seek safe haven of U.S. greenback after earthquake in Japan. The pair is at 8,795 vs 8,790 earlier in the session and 8,785 in late Asian trade Thursday. "We have European debt problems, unrest in Saudi Arabia and now Japan's earthquake. But I expect Bank Indonesia to intervene so the pair won't breach IDR8,800 resistance," says a local dealer. (andreasismar.sandiwan@dowjones.com)

0740 GMT [Dow Jones] China onshore IRS are up on higher-than-expected February CPI and on PBOC Gov. Zhou Xiaochuan's remarks that real deposit rates are generally positive in the medium-term. 1-year IRS is up 2 bps at 3.42%-3.50%, 5-year IRS is up 4 bps at 4.05%-4.14% and the 1-to-5-year spread is 3 bps wider at 64 bps. But a Shanghai-based local bank trader says the upside for swaps are capped, as there may not be an immediate interest rate hike as expected as the PBOC Gov. Zhou Xiaochuan says the "real interest rate" may at times be negative in the short term. (wynne.wang@dowjones.com)

0739 GMT [Dow Jones] LME metals were looking fairly stable above Thursday's kerb levels but the 8.9-magnitude earthquake and subsequent tsunami in northern Japan has led to some knee-jerk selling, says Hong Kong based broker. "The volume is slowing down as everyone is watching their screens," he says. There is no visibility on prices for later with uncertainty over the earthquake and the Saudi Arabia political protests pushing traders to the sidelines, he says. LME 3-month copper is at $9,147.25/ton, down $42.75 with 4,283 lots done so far. (james.campbell@dowjones.com)

0738 GMT [Dow Jones] The Sensex is down 1.3% at 18,083.68, tracking falls in Asian markets after a powerful earthquake with a magnitude of 8.9 struck Japan. "This just adds to the negative global cues which have being weighing on the market. Investors are waiting to see how bad the damage is and whether companies with business interests in Japan will be affected," says a local analyst. JSW Steel (500228.BY), in which Japan's JFE Steel Corp. holds a 14.8% stake, is down 4.4% at INR897.75. Among the few Sensex gainers, Oil & Natural Gas Corp. (500312.BY) is up 2.1% at INR281.20. Sensex losses are led by Tata Consultancy Services (532540.BY) down 3.7% at INR1,067.15 and Housing Development Finance Corp. (500010.BY) is 2.5% lower at INR650.50. The Sensex is likely to find support at 17,950 and face resistance at 18,260, according to Dow Jones technical analysis. (sudeep.jain@dowjones.com)

0731 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/INR rises a tad and is hovering near the session's 45.26 high as local stocks slip deeper into negative territory after an 8.9-magnitude earthquake struck Japan, says a senior trader at a privately-run bank. The pair rises to 45.25 on the news of the earthquake from 45.19 before earthquake struck; the USD/INR was at 45.19 late Thursday. "Equities are on a down-swing and if the Sensex loses up to 500 points, which appears likely, the pair may test a resistance of 45.35 in the session as investors pull out from risk assets," he says. He tips the pair in 45.20-45.35 band. The Sensex is down 1.2%. (khushita.vasant@dowjones.com)

0727 GMT [Dow Jones] Northern Japan's 8.9-magnitude earthquake is not likely to have a large, long-term impact on the nation's economic growth, according to Andrew Freris, senior investment strategist for Asia at BNP Paribas. "Unless you are looking at something truly major, natural catastrophes generally have zero medium to long-term economic impact," he said. He cited the 2004 tsunami in Thailand, from which the country's economy bounced back quickly, and said even the devastating earthquake in Christchurch, New Zealand last week would take "perhaps a few basis points at most" off GDP. (martin.vaughan@dowjones.com)

0725 GMT [Dow Jones] China government bonds end flat, shrugging off February's higher-than-expected inflation, as sufficient liquidity in the money market is supporting bond prices, says a trader at Guotai Junan Securities. "Even if the central bank decides to lift the banks' reserve requirement ratio by 50 bps over the weekend, that won't have a significant impact on excess liquidity," he adds. The Shanghai Stock Exchange government bond index ends at 127.11, unchanged from Thursday's close; the interbank weighted average seven-day repurchase agreement, a benchmark gauge of short-term funding costs, is down 22 bps at 2.05%. The trader expects the bond index to consolidate in a 127.00-127.20 range next week.(ming.wang@dowjones.com)

0722 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/JPY is at 83.19 from about 82.80 before the Japan quake hit and 82.98 late Thursday in New York, after an 8.9 magnitude earthquake struck, causing damage in Tokyo, and sending a tsunami hurtling toward the country's northeastern coast. "It was mainly currency dealers not in Tokyo who sold the yen on the quake because some Tokyo dealers have evacuated. There are automated stop-loss (USD) buying orders at Y83.30 and if they are triggered, the dollar may rise to Y83.50. How far the yen will fall depends on the damage situation and if the damage turns out to be light, we (may) see the dollar (moving) back below Y83.00 again very soon. Market participants have calmed down by now," says Shinichi Hayashi, a senior dealer at Shinkin Central Bank. (takashi.mochizuki@dowjones.com)

0721 GMT [Dow Jones] The Kospi ends down 1.3% at 1955.54 as foreigners extend their selling streak to five sessions as escalating tensions in the Middle East and North Africa continue to hurt global risk sentiment; foreigners were net sellers of KRW507 billion worth of local stocks today. "The extent of the foreign selling seems to have passed its climax yesterday," when foreigners dumped KRW1.2 trillion worth in net, but it's unclear how soon their sentiment will recover, says a manager with a securities firm. Construction stocks fell sharply and tech shares were mostly lower amid persisting concerns over their 1Q earnings; Hyundai Engineering & Construction (000720.SE) ends down 2.0% at KRW77,200 and Samsung Engineering (028050.SE) ends 3.4% lower at KRW186,000, while Samsung Electronics (005930.SE) falls 0.5% to KRW862,000 and LG Electronics (066570.SE) ends 1.4% lower at KRW106,000. Key level (resistance) to watch next week is the 120-day moving average near 1970. (min-jeong.lee@dowjones.com)

0716 GMT [Dow Jones] Watch for tsunami impact outside of Japan, warns Pradeep Mohinani, credit analyst at Nomura. He says the tsunami watch in Hawaii suggests "this is going the other way as well", and wonders if it will spread to the west coast of the U.S.; commenting on investors' reaction, he said: "I don't think anyone's looking at their screens. Everyone is looking at their TVs." The monitoring agency has issued a tsunami watch for Indonesia, the Philippines, Papua New Guinea and Hawaii. The quake, originally reported at a magnitude of 7.9 but later upgraded to 8.9 apparently exceeding the 8.8 quake that struck off Chile in February 2010. Local television reported smoke rising from a Tokyo port building, and fire in the capital's waterfront Odaiba district. title: EM ASIA  FX -Rupiah at 4-yr high on c.bank; intervention  caps gains
text:
* Indonesia c.bank sees more room for rupiah's rise

* Intervention from Indonesia, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand spotted

* Won, Taiwan dlr at 2-wk high (Updates with text, prices)

By Jongwoo Cheon

SINGAPORE, March 4 (Reuters) - The rupiah hit a near four-year high against the dollar after the central bank signalled on Friday it was willing to use the currency's gains in its battle with inflation even though it was seen buying dollars in an effort to control the rupiah's rise.

The central bank kept its benchmark rate on hold at its policy meeting, but said that it would gradually lift borrowing costs in the future and that it saw room for the rupiah to strengthen further without hurting export competitiveness.

"The bank confirmed today that the currency strength is helping the inflation problem," said Christopher Gothard, chief currency strategist for Brown Brothers Harriman in Hong Kong.

"BI is still attempting to manage the rupiah's gains, with interventions designed more to slow the gain and make it more orderly, rather than stop it altogether," Gothard said.

Central banks in other Asian countries, such as Singapore, Philippines and Thailand, were also spotted buying dollars. Dealers said the interventions seemed designed to slow their currencies' gains rather than to weaken them because that would exacerbate inflation pressures.

RUPIAH

The Dollar slid by up to 0.3 percent against the rupiah to 8,780, the rupiah's strongest level since June 2007, from Thursday's close of 8,803.

Foreign investors continued to sell the pair, which has room to fall to 8,755, the low in June, but the central bank was on guard, dealers said.

Earlier, the central bank kept its overnight interest rate at 6.75 percent as forecast by a slender majority of economists, saying it would adjust the rate in stages if necessary and closely monitor rising core inflation.

"Today's decision implies BI will be more comfortable doing the tightening via FX. But slowly,, as they will continue to intervene," said a strategist of a U.S. Bank in Singapore.

TAIWAN DOLLAR

Dollar/Taiwan dollar slid to a two-week low as foreign investors sold the pair and on foreigners' continuous stock purchases.

Dollar/Taiwan dollar touched 29.310, the lowest since Feb 18.

WON

Dollar/won hit a near two-week low as continuous foreign purchases of Seoul stocks prompted stop-loss dollar sales.

The pair fell to as low as 1,114.1, the lowest since Feb. 21, but it found support from caution over dollar-buying intervention by South Korea's foreign exchange authorities and importers' demand around mid-1,110.

"They (the authorities) don't want it to go above 1,130, but they will buy dollars at 1,110 anyway even if the Bank of Korea raises interest rates," said a dealer in Singapore.

Foreign investors reported their biggest net buying of local stocks in two months.

PESO

Dollar/peso edged down on fixing demand and profit-taking from the peso's recent gains, but the Philippines's central bank was spotted buying dollars to check the peso's strength.

Bangko Sentral Pilipinas (BSP) was seen intervening at around 43.25-27, dealers said, even though it said higher February inflation supported its view that the scope for keeping rates steady has narrowed.

"All central banks in Asia, including the BSP, are facing the same dilemma -- how to check inflation and to support exports at the same time," says a senior European bank dealer in Singapore.

Philippine February inflation hit its highest since May, raising the likelihood the central bank will lift rates this month for the first time since the global financial crisis.

Dollar/peso may break through its support at 43.25, the low of on Feb 21 and the 61.8 percent of the November-January rise, if the central bank take actions to curb inflation.

A break of this support will see a decline to 42.90, the 76.4 percent of the rise. Strong resistance for pair is seen at 43.60 and 43.90.

A Shanghai-based local bank trader tips the pair to consolidate around Wednesday's fixing at 6.5736, saying, 'we expect the yuan to remain rangebound for the next two weeks while Beijing is pushing out the next five-year plan.' title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia eyes fuel subsidy cut delay, to let rupiah rise
text:
(Adds details)

JAKARTA, Feb 24 (Reuters) - Indonesia said on Thursday it is considering delaying a plan to limit the use of cheap subsidised fuels to next year as it seeks to avoid surging oil prices adding to inflation, despite a potential cost of over $600 million to the state budget.

Chief economics minister Hatta Rajasa said the government has no plans to hike subsidised fuel prices, a move that would boost inflation and likely to lead to protests. Vietnam on Thursday hiked gasoline and diesel prices by up to 24 percent.

Instead, Indonesia's central bank will let the rupiah currency strengthen to curb imported inflation, deputy governor Hartadi A. Sarwono said, as it is concerned about high oil prices following turmoil in the Middle East.

Indonesia's government had aimed to stop private cars in the capital Jakarta from using cheap subsidised fuel from end-March, before rolling the pan out across the country, but may delay the start, said Rajasa.

"The financial consequences would be to add 3-6 trillion rupiah of additional subsidies for one year," said finance minister Agus Martowardojo.

The comments come as London oil prices surged over $6 to $117 a barrel, and ahead of Indonesia's February's inflation data next Tuesday.

Some analysts see higher-than-expected inflation leading Bank Indonesia to hike rates by another 25 basis points when meeting on March 4 in an effort to stem price pressures, after January inflation reached a 21-month-high of 7 percent.

"We are concerned over imported inflation both from oil and food prices. We keep monitoring rising oil prices," Bank Indonesia's Sarwono told reporters.

Sarwono said Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves had reached a record $97 billion, a level nearly double two years ago and that gives the central bank more ammunition to intervene in the currency market.

Bank Indonesia hiked rates by 150 basis points in 2008 to counter growing inflation after the government was forced to hike subsidised fuel prices by almost 30 percent on average because of record oil prices.

Indonesia is the country in Southeast Asia that is the most exposed to a sharp rise in oil prices and policymakers will face a dilemma as tightening rates may slow growth, CIMB said in a report on Thursday.

"Some central banks are willing to tolerate a stronger currency as part of their efforts to bring inflation under control," said CIMB's Lee Heng Guie.

The rupiah has gained 1.5 percent this year, adding to near 5 percent gains last year.

The former OPEC oil producer is forced to import gasoline and diesel from the regional market since its ageing refineries do not produce enough fuel, but still maintains subsidised fuel.

Analysts say the government needs to use the money spent on subsidies to instead improve infrastructure, which would help draw further foreign direct investment and improve the chances of getting a coveted investment grade sovereign rating.

However, protests over price hikes were seen as a major factor in the ousting of Indonesia's autocratic President Suharto in 1998 and would hit the current administration's popularity. (Reporting by Adriana Nina Kusuma, Rieka Rahadiana and Aditya Suharmoko; Editing by Neil Chatterjee)

title: WSJ: Indonesia Raises Interest Rates Amid Inflation Concerns
text:
Indonesia's central bank lifted interest rates in the face of increasing inflation and investor agitation, highlighting the difficult position the world's emerging markets face in managing growth.

Southeast Asia's largest economy has boomed in recent years as political stability, low debt and economic overhauls have attracted a flood of foreign money. While that inflow makes inexpensive capital available for investment, it also complicates the country's economic management and illustrates the inherent dangers of capital flows on emerging economies generally.

Those dangers were on display in the lead-up to Friday's rate decision to raise its target rate to 6.75% from a record low 6.5%, the central bank's first move since August 2009. Foreign investors, spooked by rising inflation, sold $1 billion of Indonesian government bonds in a two-week period last month, sending bond-market interest rates sharply higher, the stock market down 11% at one point, and increased pressure on authorities to quell fears of an inflation spiral.

"Markets are waking up to the fact that the monetary authorities have this very delicate balancing act, and they could get it badly wrong," said Vijay Chander, fixed-income analyst at Standard Chartered in Hong Kong. "If they get behind curve on hiking rates, then inflation rips and rates are soaring out of control."

The influx of investor cash into emerging markets since the financial crisis ebbed has preoccupied policy makers from Brazil to South Korea. They worry ultra-low interest rates in the U.S., Europe and Japan will overwhelm their faster growing economies. Several nations and the International Monetary Fund have advocated the use of limited capital controls, or limits on money flows across borders. Indonesia, for example, last year imposed holding periods on some types of investments.

While inflows are generally seen as a positive sign for an economy, short-term investments can leave as quickly as they come in, whipsawing financial markets and causing wider economic damage.

Indonesia is one example. Global investors unsatisfied with the low interest rates in the developed world have bought $9.5 billion in Indonesian government bonds since the start of 2010. That has helped double the foreign-ownership share of Indonesian government to 30% from 15%.

Indonesia's ability to manage inflation and capital flows will have consequences for the country's ability to break into the top echelon of powerhouse emerging markets: Brazil, China, India and Russia. As a Group of 20 member, Indonesia's experience is likely to be closely watched by others.

Not wanting too much of that inflow, Indonesia has resisted raising interest rates, fearing higher rates would attract even more investors, putting pressure on its currency to rise. Last year, Indonesia intervened routinely in currency markets, selling rupiah for U.S. dollars to prevent its currency from rising too quickly and making its products less competitive, especially compared with China's. It has intervened so heavily, several analysts think the central bank will need an infusion of capital from the government to shore up the central bank's balance sheet.

The foreign capital built up in Indonesia's financial system has created a vulnerability. If that money flows out quickly, interest rates increase too rapidly for local banks and businesses to manage. And it puts pressure on the currency to weaken. A weaker currency exacerbates inflation by making imported goods, especially foods and energy products, even more expensive for local businesses and consumers.

Driven by rising food prices, Indonesia's inflation rate jumped in November and December to 7%, above the bank's target of 5% plus-or-minus one percentage point.

Bank Indonesia Gov. Darmin Nasution dismissed inflation concerns in an interview Monday. "We do not consider we are behind the curve yet," he said, noting much of the inflation pressure is in volatile food prices that he expects to wane. The central bank has said "macroprudential" tools such as raising banking reserve requirements and targeting specific asset prices was sufficient.

Investors have been less confident. In early January, money began pouring out of the country as investors worried the value of their investments would be eroded by inflation. Interest rates on 10-year government bonds went from 7.5% at the start of the year to as high as 10% on Jan. 21. They have since settled around 9%. Improved economic prospects in the U.S. and Europe have also caused investors to reorient their holdings toward developed markets and away from emerging markets.

The outflows put pressure on the Indonesian rupiah to weaken against the dollar, and sparked the central bank to draw on its $96 billion in foreign-currency reserves to prevent the rupiah from falling.

"They were able to keep the currency under control by intervening quite strongly," said Philippe Petit, who manages $17 billion in emerging-market bonds for Pictet Funds in Singapore. He thinks the selling is over for now. "The big investors haven't run," he said.

The mostly Muslim nation's strong domestic economy helped it weather the global downturn in trade and manufacturing. Moody's Investors Service upgraded Indonesia's debt rating at the start of January recognizing the progress the country has made since the Asian financial crisis in the late 1990s. Indonesia, with the world's fourth largest population--240 million people--grew a healthy 6% last year, but still lags behind the 10% growth in China and nearly 9% growth in India.

"Indonesia has a once-in-a-generation chance to substantially accelerate economic growth," said Manu Bhaskaran, partner in Singapore for Centennial Group, an economic research firm. "It would be a pity if all the good work done was negated because monetary policy was not tightened enough."

-By Alex Frangos, The Wall Street Journal; alex.frangos@wsj.com

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia cbank targets 9,000 rph/$ to stem inflation
text:
* Cbank dep gov says intervening in fx market

* Cbank using 9,000 rph per dollar for inflation target

* Analyst sees cbank using fx, other options than rates (Updates with quotes, analyst comment)

JAKARTA, Jan 27 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank is intervening in the foreign exchange market to stem inflation and is targeting 9,000 rupiah per dollar as a benchmark to achieve its inflation target, deputy governor Hartadi A. Sarwono said on Thursday.

A strengthening rupiah helped temper imported inflation last year but the currency has slipped in January amid a sell-off in Indonesian assets as investors are worried the central bank may be behind the curve in tackling inflation.

"If there is pressure in the rupiah, we enter the market. There, we have room to strengthen the rupiah to help stem inflation. The market reads this, that Bank Indonesia is concerned about inflation by intervening in the market," Sarwono told reporters.

Annual inflation reached a 20-month high of 6.96 percent in December, above the central bank's upper end-2010 target of 6 percent, and economists are calling for rate hikes by March or April to head off inflationary pressures.

The central bank, which next meets to decide policy on Feb 4, held rates at a record low 6.5 percent for all of last year.

The central bank now has greater reserves to draw on to stabilise the currency than in past bouts of foreign investor selling, since strong inflows last year pushed foreign exchange reserves to $96.2 billion by December, nearly double the level two years earlier.

The rupiah rose 0.12 percent to 9,022 against the dollar on Thursday, cutting losses for the year to 0.20 percent.

"If it weakens, there is a risk on the inflation target," said Eric A. Sugandi, an analyst at Standard Chartered, which forecasts the rupiah to reach 9,200 by the end of this quarter.

"This may signal that Bank Indonesia will let the rupiah strengthen to reduce pressures from imported inflation. They may prefer to use other options besides rates," he said.

The central bank has repeatedly said that it sees hiking interest rates as the last resort to curb inflation, though Sarwono told Reuters last month it would not hesitate to tighten policy if core inflation neared 5 percent.

"A rate hike is the last option. But the option is open if we need it," said Sarwono.

Full year 2011 core inflation is seen at 4-5 percent and headline inflation at 6.1-6.6 percent, said Bambang PS Brodjonegoro, head of fiscal policy at the finance ministry.

This was higher than a government budget target of 5.3 percent for headline inflation and above the central bank's end-2011 target of 4-6 percent. (Reporting by Adriana Nina Kusuma; Writing by Aditya Suharmoko; Editing by Neil Chatterjee)

title: MARKET TALK: China Home Prices To Rise At Slower Pace - Fitch
text:
Contact us in Singapore. 65 64154 140; 
MarketTalk@dowjones.com 
 
 

0227 GMT [Dow Jones] China's primary-market home prices will continue to rise this year but at a slower rate, Fitch Ratings says. "China's residential property sector will be supported by favorable near-term global and domestic macroeconomic conditions, underpinned by a persistent global liquidity glut and the potential appreciation of the Chinese yuan," says Ying Wang, a director at Fitch's Asia-Pacific Corporates. The average selling price of homes in tier 1 cities rose 20%-40% on-year, while the average selling price rose 6.0% nationwide in 2010, says Fitch. It adds that China's planned real estate tax will "only have a marginal impact on property prices and considers full-fledged property taxes on a national scale to be a remote possibility." Fitch says that its rated Chinese property developers have low refinancing risks since most have already refinanced their 2011 and 2012 bond maturities. While tightened bank lending will continue, mid-sized and large developers still have access to project loans, Fitch says. (esther.fung@dowjones.com)

0227 GMT [Dow Jones] Vietnam shares rise 1.4% to 519.22 led by financial stocks on a strong economic outlook, and also as investors buy on hopes for more solid 4Q earnings after blue chip stock FPT Corp (FPT.VH) says its net profit rose 18.8% on-year to VND1.263 trillion in 2010. "Sentiment continues to improve because the state media is still reporting a positive economic outlook for the country this year after the Party Congress recently appointed a new leadership," a Hanoi-based brokerage analyst says. (jean.yung@dowjones.com)

0210 GMT [Dow Jones] LME metals are up on some decent dip buying, after a second day of weakness in London. LME 3-month copper is at $9,405.75/ton, up $50.75 with 1,163 lots done and zinc is at $2,353/ton, up $23 with 970 lots done. Barclays Capital says that despite rising inventories and what is describes as a "lull" in the physical market, investors should look at the bigger picture and not lose faith in the medium-term bullish outlook. "This is an eerie replication of market conditions early last year and our warning to market participants is the same now as it was then: don't be fooled," it says in a report. "I expect that selling pressure today won't be as heavy as yesterday as many institutional investors will likely start to accumulate shares of companies that would report strong 2010 earnings," says a fund manager at a local state-owned company. Commodity-related stocks such as coal producer Bumi (BUMI.JK) and palm oil company Astra Agro (AALI.JK) may lead falls on lower oil prices, but Bank Negara (BBNI.JK) may rebound on bargain buying after Thursday's 3.7% fall. (edhi.pranasidhi@dowjones.com)

0208 GMT [Dow Jones] The USD/IDR is well bid on lingering concerns over domestic inflation risks; however, suspected intervention by Bank Indonesia is preventing the pair from rising sharply, dealers say. The pair is at 9,070, from 9,068 late yesterday; three dealers suspect the central bank to have sold around $10 million at IDR9,075 via state banks. "We are increasingly cautious about the direction of Indonesia's FX and debt markets as there is a risk that Bank Indonesia might fall behind the policy curve as inflationary pressure threatens to gain further traction," says Bank Of America Merrill Lynch. title: ASIA LOCAL BONDS-Yields rise as  currencies  sag
text:
* Indonesian, Philippine bond yields inch higher

* Thailand bond yields turn lower

By Saikat Chatterjee

HONG KONG, May 25 (Reuters) - Asian local currency bond yields rose on Tuesday as weakening currencies took some sheen off Asia's high-performing debt.

A strong rebound in growth in the continent's economies, rising currencies and low debt-to-GDP ratios have fuelled demand among global funds for Asian government debt in recent months.

But the euro zone's debt problems have triggered a wave of risk aversion in world markets leading to a marked slowdown in new capital inflows, which in turn has sapped the rally in emerging market currencies.

The ringgit <MYR=>, which is the star performer in Asia, up by more than 8 percent until the end of April, has seen its year-to-date gains cut sharply to a little above 2 percent.

Central banks in Indonesia and Philippines were seen intervening to support their currencies, both of which have fallen to their lowest in several months. [ID:nSGE64O03Q]

By early afternoon, the ten-year Indonesian bond yield <ID10YT=RR> was up six basis points at 9.03 percent, while the four-year bond yield in the Philippines <PHBD0567=> was two basis points higher at 5.94 percent, traders said.

"Risk aversion is still there and that has reduced the flows into local currency bonds," said Lum Choong Kuan, head of fixed income at CIMB Investment Bank. "Although there has been some selling in Thailand, we are still seeing a lot of demand for rupiah and ringgit assets."

Thomson Reuters data shows Indonesian local currency bonds in dollar terms have lost more than 2 percent in the past month cutting their year-to-date returns to 10 percent.

The latest EPFR data shows foreign fund inflows into emerging market bond funds have slowed to a trickle in recent weeks, a far cry from more than $1 billion per week seen in March.

In Thailand, however, yields fell as investors expected the central bank to keep rates on hold next week because of the negative impact of months of political unrest on its economy.

DBS expects the economy to contract 9 percent on a seasonally adjusted annualised rate in the second quarter after expanding at 15 percent in the March quarter because of the riots.

The five-year bond yield <TH5YT=RR> eased by six basis points to 3.11 percent, just shy of its lowest level since end April.

A two-month political standoff ended last week but economists said it could take months for the economy to get back to rates of growth seen in the March quarter. This puts any chances of a near-term rate hike in the freezer for now.

"While we believe the central bank is still keen to raise interest rates to a more neutral level, this will require a more stable political backdrop ... the situation remains fluid, but the possibility of fresh elections in the fourth quarter may allow them to begin tightening," Standard Chartered Bank said. (Editing by Chris Lewis & Jan Dahinten)

SINGAPORE, May 25 (Reuters) - The central banks of Indonesia and the Philippines intervened in currency markets on Tuesday to sell dollars to support their respective currencies, traders said.

title: FX  ASIA: As Asian Reserves Rise, Euro May Fall Into Disfavor
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asia's foreign exchange reserves rose 1.5% in April from March as continued intervention in foreign exchange markets offset a drop in the value of central banks' euro-denominated holdings.

That trend that may emerge as an additional negative for the euro if it forces some of the world's top reserve holders to review the preference they've shown for the European currency in recent years.

According to calculations by Dow Jones Newswires, reserves held by 11 key Asian central banks, not including China's, stood at US$2.810 trillion at the end of April, up from US$2.777 trillion at the end of March. That compares with a 0.3% increase posted in March from February.

China, which releases its data on a quarterly basis, reported US$2.447 trillion in reserves at the end of March.

Combined, Asian central bank holdings account for around two-thirds of the world's overall amount, and analysts believe some 20%-25% of that amount is in euros. That's likely below the international average of 27.4% as of last December, according to International Monetary Fund data, but Asia's percentage has grown steadily in recent years.

Worries about a possible reduction of central bank euro holdings hit the market earlier this year and are gaining pace as the euro loses ground against the dollar, eroding its status as the top alternative to the greenback. That's important because the latest data show that while market speculators (including hedge funds) are active euro sellers, observers believe most "real-money" managers like central banks and pension funds haven't yet joined the euro-bashing party.

In a recent report, Credit Suisse analysts said the euro-zone's structural problems and handling of the Greek debt crisis have "severely damaged" the notion--particularly among managers of central bank reserve funds--that euros can be held as a "safe alternative" to the dollar.

So far this year, the euro has lost 11% against the dollar; that includes a 1.6% drop in April and a 4.9% drop so far in May. But that may be just the beginning if Asian central banks start to unload euros.

In 2002, when the euro replaced individual euro-zone currencies, it accounted for only 23.8% of global reserves. It's up 50% against the dollar since, supported by the continued decrease in the dollar as a percentage of global reserves as central banks have diversified in favor of the euro.

Meanwhile, strong purchases of dollars in forex markets continued in many Asian countries in April. That matches the recent trend as central banks remain wary of allowing their local currencies to rise on the strength of sustained flows into fast-growing Asian markets.

Seven Asian central banks reported reserves at all-time highs, including Indonesia's, where reserves grew a whopping 9.5% on-month in April on the back of continued intervention. Bank Indonesia has been trying to contain the appreciation of the rupiah, one of Asia's best performers this year with a 3.9% gain against the dollar since January on top of a 12% rise in 2009.

Strong reserve increases in Singapore and South Korea also were likely driven by continued intervention in forex markets.

title: UPDATE 2-Indonesia, Manila prop up  FX  as emerging markets tumble
text:
JAKARTA, May 7 (Reuters) - Central banks in Indonesia and the Philippines intervened to shore up their sliding currencies on Friday as worries about Greece's debt crisis spurred investors to dump emerging market assets.

The high-yielding rupiah <IDR> has tumbled 3 percent against the dollar this week, among the worst hit in Asia, while the peso has skidded 2.7 percent as part of a broad sell-off in Asian currencies and a move into safer assets.

Though worries about Greece's problems spreading to the rest of Europe are likely to persist for some time, Indonesia's central bank said the country's solid fiscal and economic fundamentals would support for the rupiah in the long run.

"We don't see (the weakening rupiah) as too worrying because fundamentals are still good. This will just be temporary,"Darmin Nasution, Bank Indonesia's senior deputy governor, told reporters on Friday.

But he said the central bank has been closely following the rupiah's moves since earlier this week.

"The central bank is always in the market," he added.

In the Philippines, central bank Deputy Governor Diwa Guinigundo offered similar reassurances to nervous investors, saying the country can withstand shocks in financial markets as domestic consumption remains healthy and its foreign reserves are at a comfortable level.

"In case there is a double dip, we are well placed to absorb the shocks. On balance, we have what it takes to weather another crisis," Guinigundo told reporters.

The rupiah fell just over 1 percent on Friday to 9,300 per dollar, a two-month low, but later pared some of the losses on suspected cental bank intervention.

But the currency is still up 2 percent against the dollar so far this year. It had gained nearly 6 percent through April before Greece's debt crisis escalated and profit taking set in.

Investor sentiment toward Indonesian assets was also undermined by Finance Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati's decision on Wednesday to resign, as she played a key role in improving the economy.

Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist at BNP Paribas in Singapore, expects the rupiah to find support near 9,400/9,500.

"The rupiah has lost ground on unwinding of risk exposures, including liquidation of Indonesian bonds, on the global stock rout as well as the finance minister's resignation," she said.

"But the fundamentals for Indonesia remain positive and we expect the rupiah to be sought after again when the dust settles."

One of the central bank deputy governors, Budi Mulya, echoed Bank Indonesia's vigilance.

"Bank Indonesia (BI) will continue to ensure a stable rupiah that reflects its underlying fundamentals," Mulya said in a phone text message.

"At times of substantial capital inflow, BI safeguarded rupiah stability through its sterilisation, and that has built up foreign exchange reserves to more than $78 billion. Similarly, in the event of capital outflows, BI is also committed to safeguard the rupiah's stability."

The central bank also reiterated its commitment to ensure a free capital market and dispel concerns of any capital controls.

In the Phillipines, the central bank also sold dollars to slow the peso's decline, traders said.

The peso <PHP=> was down 0.9 percent at 45.78 per dollar despite the interventions.

Among other Asian currencies, the South Korean won <KRW=> fell 4.1 percent on the week, its biggest weekly fall since February 2009.

Foreign investors had flocked to emerging Asian assets earlier this year as the region's economic growth far eclipsed that of the West, but a spike in volatility in recent weeks has prompted some to scale back their positions and book profits. (Reporting Gde Anugrah Arka, Sonya Angraini and Kevin Yao; Writing by Yoko Nishikawa; Editing by Sara Webb & Kim Coghill)

title: UPDATE: Asian Shares Come Off Lows; Exporters Hurt Tokyo
text:
(Adds information, quotes, updates/adds market levels)

By Shri Navaratnam and Philip Vahn

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian shares recovered some ground Friday as investors were soothed by the realization that a trading glitch was partly behind Wall Street's slide overnight and began to bargain hunt.

However, concerns that Greece's debt problems could engulf the weaker European countries continued to linger.

In Tokyo, the market remained under pressure as the recent gains in the yen damped exporter stocks.

Jonathan Barrett, managing director at Commodity Broking Services in Sydney, referring to the early drop in Asian markets, said investors may have overreacted.

"People are factoring in a disaster scenario. If that contagion fear (of the Greece fiscal crisis spreading to other European countries) is real why did European markets only fall 1.0% to 1.5%?" he said.

In a note to clients UBS analysts said: "In our view, the lack of a clear 'end game' for sovereign risk in Europe means that despite recent sharp declines in markets, this is not a buying opportunity. Positions may still be unwound."

Japan's Nikkei 225 was down 2.7% while Australia's S&P/ASX 200 was down 0.8% at 4547 after hitting an eight-month of low 4427.30 earlier. South Korea's Kospi Composite fell 2.0%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index lost 0.8%, Taiwan's main index was off 0.4% and the Shanghai Composite index was down 0.3%.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average futures were up 65 points in screen trade.

The euro, which plumbed 14-month lows of $1.2510 against the U.S. dollar Thursday, recovered some ground in Asian trade although analysts expect more pain ahead for the single currency. The Korean won bounced back after hitting a three-month low against the U.S. dollar of KRW1,169.5 earlier. It was trading at KRW1,163.9.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average at one point on Thursday skidded as much as 9.2%, the biggest intraday drop in its history, before closing down 3.2%. The intraday dive appeared to be triggered in part by a breakdown of trading systems.

In Tokyo, Sony was down 5.3% while Panasonic lost 5.1%, Honda Motor was off 4.8% and Toyota Motor dropped 2.8%. Fast Retailing slipped 5.9% after saying late Thursday April same-store sales at its Uniqlo casual clothing chain fell 12.4% on-year.

Nintendo fell 10.0% after the video game giant said Thursday its net profit dropped to Y228.64 billion in the fiscal year ended March 31, from Y279.09 billion a year earlier; it also expects profit and sales to fall in the current year.

Metal plays were leading losses in China, hurt by sharp declines in metal prices in Asian trade. Baoshan Iron & Steel lost 4.0% and Yunnan Copper fell 4.0%.

Shanghai benchmark copper futures were trading 3.3% lower at CNY54,980 per metric ton. The red metal was also down 2.0% on the London Metals Exchange.

Financial stocks led the Australian market lower, with ANZ off 3.1% and Westpac down 3.5%. In the resources sector, BHP Billiton lost 1.3% and Rio Tinto was off 2.0%.

Financials were also weaker in Seoul. Shinhan Financial lost 3.7% while tech bellwether Samsung Electronics gave up 2.7%. Daewoo Shipbuilding slipped 2.5%, but was outperforming its peers after the Financial News reported it had won a $1.6 billion contract to build a floating production storage and offloading vessel.

In Hong Kong, Swire Pacific rose 2.4% after its property unit Swire Properties said Thursday it has shelved its US$3.09 billion Hong Kong initial public offering. Traders said the move was viewed positively, given prevailing weak property market conditions in the city state.

"Some investors were also concerned with the dilution effect of Swire Pacific's holding in its property unit's spinoff, which may also hurt investment value of Swire Pacific in the long-term," said First Shanghai's Linus Yip.

Elsewhere, Malaysian shares were 0.6% lower, Singapore's Straits Times Index fell 0.8%, India's Sensex was down 1.1% and New Zealand's NZX-50 was 1.5% lower.

In foreign exchange markets, the euro was at $1.2712, compared with $1.2599 late in New York, and was fetching Y117.55 against the yen, from Y113.26, but well below Y120.12 on Wednesday. The dollar was at Y92.51, from Y89.92.

Despite the steadier euro, "it only seems a matter of time before the key (1.2500) support level breaks" against the dollar, said Mark Smith, an economist at ANZ bank in Wellington.

"On the face of it, the overnight market reaction may have been overdone. But the question increasingly asked is where the mark-to-market losses on European debt will ultimately reside, and this is looking to be mostly in European financial institutions. We have now moved beyond a mere Greek debt crisis," Smith said.

Markets are also watching the outcome of Thursday's U.K. elections, with results so far showing the opposition Conservative Party leading the seats-count but could fall short of a majority, leading to a hung parliament. The British pound was at $1.4903, up from $1.4832 late in New York.

The sharp falls in Asian currencies prompted some central banks in the region to intervene in currency markets to slow the greenback's rise. The central banks of Indonesia and the Philippines intervened to support their currencies, local traders and dealers said.

Bank Indonesia sold some $150 million to support the rupiah, while the Philippine central bank sold $50 million to $100 million for pesos, market participants estimated.

Japanese government bond futures were sharply higher on stronger U.S. Treasurys. The lead contract was up 0.19 at 140.5 points after briefly tapping 140.10, the highest level since March 10.

Spot gold was at $1,199.00 per troy ounce, down $9.80 from the New York close.

Nymex June crude oil futures were down 41 cents at $76.70 a barrel on Globex, after falling 3.6% Thursday to the lowest close since mid-March.

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia delays Samurai bond issue in market selloff
text:
(Adds quotes, background)

JAKARTA, May 6 (Reuters) - Indonesia postponed a planned $1.1 billion Samurai bond to the second half of 2010 as bond yields rose and the rupiah fell on investor fears over debt woes in the euro zone and the Indonesian finance minister's resignation.

But a senior central banker reiterated the country's strong growth prospects and played down a selloff in the rupiah.

Investors sold Indonesian stocks, bonds and the rupiah on Wednesday and Thursday, prompting the debt office to announce it would postpone its samurai bond issue to the second half of this year to avoid paying a higher yield.

Rahmat Waluyanto, head of the finance ministry's debt office, said the country would delay its planned samurai bond issue to the second half of this year.

"The yield increased 30 bps in a half day (yesterday). That was a significant rise. It shows a change in investors' perception on risks associated with Indonesia," he said.

"We will change our strategy. We will reschedule. We will postpone (the samurai bond issue) until the second half (of the year)."

In March, the debt office said Indonesia planed to raise $1.1 billion via a single Samurai bond issue that could be launched by the end of April or in early May. [ID:nJAK366519]

Another official at the debt office said Indonesia has raised its total debt issuance target for this year to 178.1 trillion rupiah ($19.60 billion) from the previous target of 176.2 trillion rupiah. The debt office also expects to raise a minimum 8 trillion rupiah from a retail bond issue planned for early August, said Bhimantara Widyajala, director at the debt office.

Separately, the central bank's senior deputy governor said Indonesia's economy is expected to grow more than 5.7 percent in the second quarter from the same period a year ago and expand at an even faster pace in the third quarter.

"Economic growth in the second quarter will be better than the first quarter...and third quarter could be at around 6 percent," Darmin Nasution told reporters.

He played down worries over recent falls in the high-yielding rupiah <IDR=>, which lost over 1 percent earlier in the day, saying the currency's recent weakness was "normal".

"There is just a little weakness in the rupiah. We are still at a normal level and in the end the determining factor is the economic fundamentals. The impact on sentiment is only temporary."

His comments came after traders said Indonesia's central bank intervened in the currency market to support the weakening rupiah amid growing concerns that Greece's debt crisis is spreading to other euro-zone countries. [ID:nSGE645029]

Investor sentiment was also undermined by Finance Minister Indrawati's decision to quit on Wednesday, as she had played a key role in improving the economy, traders said.

As of 0400 GMT, the rupiah was near 9240 per dollar. (Reporting by Adriana Nina Kusuma and Dicky Kristanto, Writing by Yoko Nishikawa; Editing by Sara Webb)

Also, they seem to be selling on news," such as Moody's upgrade of Korea's sovereign ratings, positive earnings for global leading firms amid concerns recent stock gains have already priced in most of positive news, says Jun Gyun at Samsung Securities; but market mood remains positive, expects local stock market to recover, make gradual rise. Tips pair in 31.350-31.400 band rest of morning. "There's a chance the pair may rebound later in the session if stocks drop further and foreign investors start selling local shares." 0127 GMT [Dow Jones] Philippine shares likely to drift lower as investors continue to take profit ahead of the May 10 elections; benchmark PSEi tipped to slide toward 3250 support after closing 0.6% lower at 3278.84 yesterday, with index holding above 3300 resistance for most of trading session; "We saw profit-taking late yesterday and we might see follow-through selling early today. (cris.larano@dowjones.com)

0117 GMT [Dow Jones] Singapore government bond yields fall in line with Treasurys though domestic bonds likely to consolidate in Asian trade amid absence of immediate cues, trader says. However, notes some switching out of longer-dated bonds into new corporate issuance, which may continue near-term. Thursday, 2-year yields ended down 4 bps at 0.49%, 10-year yield down 5 bps at 2.74%. (samuel.holmes@dowjones.com)

Upbeat retail sales on Wednesday increase "bullish view on consumer spending. Higher-than-expected numbers may heighten optimism on the U.S. economy." Dow Jones poll tips consumer sentiment index at 75 in April vs 72.5 in March. Eyes also on U.S. housing starts due 1230 GMT; expected up 6.1% in March vs down 5.9% in February. Pegs support at 92.50 rest of day. (miho.nakauchi@dowjones.com)

0915 GMT [Dow Jones] China GDP stronger than expected but imminent tightening is unlikely, says Dong Tao, Credit Suisse 's chief regional economist, non-Japan Asia; has been "a bigger than expected moderation in inflation (while) Beijing said the high growth has been achieved mainly by the base effect and government stimulus. (Also), industrial investment is still missing and the export recovery is strong but remains fragile." Says inflation pressure may emerge in 2H10 to trigger a rate hike. (Rosalind.Mathieson@dowjones.com)

(kwan-por.lee@dowjones.com)

0912 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/IDR well supported at 9,000 on suspected Bank Indonesiaintervention, dealers say; central bank likely bought total $200 million between 9,000-9,010, helps lift pair from 9,000 intraday low to 9,008 now, but still tad below 9,010 late yesterday. "I think Bank Indonesia will continue to support the dollar at IDR9,000 Friday to slow down its recent rapid fall so as not to hurt Indonesian exports," a dealer says; 9,000-9,020 range tipped for tomorrow. (i-made.sentana@dowjones.com)

0904 GMT [Dow Jones] Data over the last few days has confirmed that the global recovery is continuing apace with inflation pressures remaining subdued. As BNP Paribas says, "global economies are developing within a risk supporting sweet spot, defined by strong economic growth rates combined with low inflation data." (nick.hastings@dowjones.com)

0902 GMT [Dow Jones] Bunds tick up as Greek bond yields surge, widening the spread Greece must pay investors to buy its debt instead of safe-haven bunds. There are concerns about possible delays to any aid plan for Greece, with the market also worried about potential debt troubles in other peripheral countries such as Portugal. June bunds are up 13bps at 123.27 and the benchmark 10-year bund is up at 101.11 to yield 3.116%. (neelabh.chaturvedi@dowjones.com)

0846 GMT [Dow Jones] Taiwan interbank overnight rate climbs higher to nearly 14-month high 0.165% vs 0.164% yesterday on cash demand from brokerage houses, but rise limited as foreign banks have excess cash on hand, says foreign bank trader. "The central bank didn't accept (large amount of) NCDs/CDs purchase from foreign banks these days," she says, noting central bank has actively drained excess liquidity by accepting more purchase of NCDs/CDs from banks in previous weeks. Tips rate biased up as central bank expected to hike short-term rates gradually in short term. (mason.wu@dowjones.com)

0843 GMT [Dow Jones] Sweden's spring budget has an overly optimistic view of overall economic trends and domestic consumption, says Swedbank. Swedbank adds that hopes for declining unemployment could prove to be premature, noting "the government could have stimulated the economy somewhat more last year to limit the downturn." The bank adds that much in the budget had been announced in advance. The yield on Sweden's two-year bond trades one basis point lower at 1.51%, while the 10-year bond yield trades one basis point higher at 3.21%. (karl.bruze@dowjones.com) [ 04-15-10 0518ET ]

title: *DJ Indonesia Unlikely To Limit Foreign Ownership Of Notes -  Central Bank  Official
text:
7 Apr 2010 05:55 EDT *DJ  Indonesia To Boost Corporate Bond Market To Tap Inflows - Central Banker

7 Apr 2010 05:55 EDT *DJ  Bank Indonesia Not Worried By Rupiah Level - Central Banker

7 Apr 2010 05:55 EDT *DJ  Indonesia Inflation Doesn't Warrant Rate Hikes Yet - Central Banker

7 Apr 2010 05:56 EDT *DJ  Indonesia Central Bank Official Was Speaking To Dow Jones Newswires

7 Apr 2010 05:56 EDT =DJ  INTERVIEW: Indonesia Unlikely To Limit Foreign Ownership Of Notes

By David Roman

Of Dow Jones Newswires

NHA TRANG, Vietnam (Dow Jones)--Indonesia is unlikely to set limits on the foreign ownership of central bank notes, and will instead boost the development of its corporate bond market to absorb surging fund inflows, a deputy governor of Bank Indonesia said Wednesday.

Indonesia's central bank has decided against imposing these limits on SBI notes, short-term instruments paying high interest rates that are used to soak up liquidity, following a recent study that found such measures would have negative effects on an economy that is still very much dependent on foreign financing, said Hartadi Sarwono.

He was speaking to Dow Jones Newswires on the sidelines of a meeting of top officials from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

"There is no problem with inflows, as long as we utilize them for the development of our domestic economy," he said.

Sarwono's comments follow recent speculation that Bank Indonesia was planning to curtail foreign ownership of SBIs at a time when the central bank is forced to step up expensive issuance to remove liquidity, given strong inflows into the country. Foreigners now own about 20% of SBIs, Sarwono said, the highest proportion ever, as Indonesia has become a preferred destination for global investors lured by economic growth rates that may approach double digits this year.

This has pushed the Indonesian rupiah to its highest level against the U.S. dollar since early 2008, despite continued Bank Indonesia intervention in foreign exchange markets that has resulted in a buildup of foreign reserves, currently at all-time high levels.

Sarwono said that Bank Indonesia believes the rupiah's current exchange rate is not a matter for concern, but further strength may erode the competitiveness of the country's exporters, especially if the gains are quick. He said there's a level for the dollar-rupiah rate that the bank considers dangerous for the economy, but he declined to provide a specific figure.

He said that Bank Indonesia plans to keep intervening in the forex markets to smooth out volatility, but it isn't looking to reverse trends.

On policy rates, Sarwono called current inflation levels "benign" and said they don't warrant a rate increase for the moment, but Bank Indonesia will keep a close eye on any inflation uptick, especially if the government goes ahead with plans to raise electricity and oil tariffs in the second half.

"The important thing for the market is to look at the inflation outlook," he added.

-By David Roman, Dow Jones Newswires, 65 9455 2447, david.roman@dowjones.com

(END) Dow Jones Newswires

title: *DJ Bank Indonesia Official: Year-End Inflation Likely 4.8%
text:
6 Apr 2010 02:05 EDT *DJ  Bank Indonesia Official: Won't Hike Rates If Not 'Really Necessary'

6 Apr 2010 02:08 EDT *DJ  Bank Indonesia: Not Targeting Certain Rupiah Level Against Dollar

6 Apr 2010 02:09 EDT *DJ  Bank Indonesia: Rupiah's Current Rise Due To Global Developments

6 Apr 2010 02:10 EDT *DJ  Bank Indonesia: Ready To Intervene In Currency Market If Necessary

6 Apr 2010 02:42 EDT DJ  Bank Indonesia Official: Rate Hike Only If "Really Necessary"

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia's acting governor reiterated that the central bank won't increase rates in the next few months unless it's "really necessary."

Darmin Nasution, who made the comment after the central bank decided Tuesday to keep its key rate unchanged at 6.5%, said inflation will likely reach 4.8% by year-end if the government doesn't raise administered energy prices.

Most recently, Indonesia's annual inflation eased to 3.43% in March from 3.81% in February due to lower basic food prices.

Meanwhile, Bank Indonesia predicted that the economy will grow 5.5%-6% this year, after expanding 4.5% last year.

The rupiah on Tuesday rose to its highest level against the dollar since August 2008, which Nasution attributed to global developments. He said Bank Indonesia was ready to intervene in the market if necessary to stop the rupiah's rise but that the central bank didn't have a specific target level for the local currency, as "the costs to set a certain level will be expensive."

Those remarks suggest Bank Indonesia may allow the rupiah to appreciate further, albeit gradually.

High-yield seekers have been buying Indonesian assets thanks to its improving economic fundamentals.

Taiwan CPI +1.27% in March on year, marking 3rd straight month of increase but slowing down from +2.35% in February, while WPI +6.61% as global commodities prices rose while TWD remained subdued vs USD. "But (domestic) demand remains moderate so there's likely no chance of a demand push that will cause the wholesale prices to filter into consumer prices," says Liao, expects central bank to continue monitoring inflation, unemployment, tips 25 bps hike in September. (alex.pevzner@dowjones.com)

0904 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/MYR down at 3.2100 late, 21-month low, but off intraday low of 3.2060, vs yesterday's 3.2260; dealer with local bank-backed brokerage says pair continues to trend lower with sellers of dollar active in market after Easter break. No sign of central bank intervention, means "smooth downward slide for the pair," says dealer. Adds, many brokers looking at revising targets for USD/MYR, some as low as 3.1000, on expectations Asia could outpace Europe, U.S. in economic recovery. "We expect the ringgit to continue to rise in the short term but there could be intermittent profit taking," dealer adds. Tips 3.2000-3.2200 range. (kwan-por.lee@dowjones.com)

0903 GMT [Dow Jones] Taiwan average interbank overnight rate unchanged at 0.150%, as central bank seems to have slowed down pace of draining excess funds recently, judging from fewer sales of short-term paper (NCDs/CDs) Thursday, Friday, says local bank trader. "The rising pace of the overnight rate will not be as fast as recent weeks, unless the central bank decides to drain excess funds actively" by selling larger-than-expected amounts of NCDs/CDs in short term, he says. Taiwan average interbank overnight rate rose to 14-month high 0.163% last week. (mason.wu@dowjones.com)

0858 GMT [Dow Jones] Hungarian forint is unchanged at 264.80 against the EUR in lackluster trade. Investors are reluctant to open new positions ahead of the upcoming parliamentary elections Sunday, Commerzbank says. Hungary's ability to maintain its commitment to prudent fiscal policy will remain investors' main concern, it adds. As the cross was unable last week to break the 265-267 range seen at end-February and early March, the HUF will continue to seek direction, Raiffeisen Bank says. (margit.feher@dowjones.com)

0856 GMT [Dow Jones] India government bonds slip tad from highs as market remains cautious ahead of fresh supply later this week, says trader with foreign bank; 6.35% 2020 bond at 90.23 vs 90.33 session high, 90.20 at Monday's close. "Until new supply hits the market, yields are not going to rise," says trader. Adds, onset of fresh supply may spark spike in yields as market grapples with absorbing government's borrowing programme. Tips yields on 10-year benchmark bond to test 8% next week. RBI will auction bonds of INR120 billion Friday.(khushita.vasant@dowjones.com)

0851 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/PHP lower late, under pressure from substantial inflows from overseas Filipino workers following Easter break; pair at 44.92, lowest since August 2008, from 45.01 late Monday. "This is still part of the inflows that we accumulated over the weekend," says local bank trader. Tips pair may head towards 45.15 resistance Wednesday, adding "market has been pretty oversold," citing substantial peso gains in recent sessions. Next support 44.80. (rhea.sandique-carlos@dowjones.com)

0843 GMT [Dow Jones] The rise in the annual rate of Swiss March inflation shows the strong CHF hasn't been able to damp imported price increases, says Vontobel. As expected, the Swiss CPI rose an annual 1.4%, largely driven by a 17% rise in energy and fuel costs, says economist Ralf Wiedenmann. (neil.maclucas@dowjones.com)

0840 GMT [Dow Jones] UBS recommends a short EUR/GBP position, expressed through options, as GBP has stabilized of late, and the expected announcement of the UK election date later Tuesday should remove some uncertainty on the UK front. "Paradoxically, the beginning of the election campaign may prove GBP positive," bank says. Meanwhile, sovereign debt concerns continue to weigh on EUR. Cross now trades at 0.8839 with GBP under broad pressure. (katie.martin@dowjones.com)

0838 GMT [Dow Jones] Price pressures in Switzerland remain moderate despite a quickening of consumer-price inflation in March, according to Credit Suisse. "However, given the increasing signs of a broad-based economic recovery and the Swiss National Bank's longer-term outlook for an inflation rate above the target band, we assume it will move to a less expansionary monetary policy in the months ahead," says CS economist Fabian Heller. (neil.maclucas@dowjones.com)

0823 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/TWD falls to 19-month low 31.695 late vs 31.759 yesterday, but off intraday low 31.651 as central bank suspected of buying USD to slow pair's drop, 2 traders at local banks say. Both traders estimate central bank may have bought over US$100 million Tuesday. "The intervention today is quite mild...(which means) the pair is likely to test next key support at 31.500 near term," says local bank trader, noting pair ended below key 31.700 mark in Taipei first time since Sep. 1 2008, level central bank suspected of firmly defending in past months. Pair weighed by foreign fund inflows as foreign investors buy net NT$18.62 billion Taiwan shares Tuesday. Tips pair in 31.630-31.700 band Wednesday. (mason.wu@dowjones.com)

0823 GMT [Dow Jones] The acceleration in March Swiss inflation reflects higher energy costs and isn't material on the medium-term monetary policy horizon, says ING. "As elsewhere in Europe, Swiss inflation is set to show some months of rates above 1%, but this should not last for long," says analyst Julien Manceaux. "We still believe the first Swiss National Bank rate hike will take place this year, but too strong a currency might alter this call," he notes. EUR/CHF was last at 1.43177 from a high of 1.4327. (neil.maclucas@dowjones.com) [ 04-06-10 0513ET ]

Every time they say the same thing, the market initially rallies and then that skepticism comes in." 3-year bonds recently at 94.73, flat after being up 7 ticks earlier. Topix at 1,050 correlates with 19X house's FY ending March 2011 expected EPS of Y55, and 16X its FY ending March 2012 expected EPS of Y65. "As this was widely expected, the dollar-yen's decline was just driven by the sell-on-the-fact after players bought the currency on a rumor," says Nomura Securities senior dealer Hiroshi Maeba. "Despite every indicator warning the central bank that prices will be a problem, the language coming out of both the RBI and the government remains biased towards caution so far," says trader. Notes, receiving interest strong so far in session particularly on less than 1-year swaps, but large British bank with note-issuing powers in Hong Kong seen bucking trend by stepping in to pay INR16 billion in 1-month OIS. (bijou.george@dowjones.com)

Adds March traditionally quiet trading month for gold, other metals; tips gold to stay in $1,100-$1,140 range. "There are still too many uncertainties in Europe that could lead to a risk reversal that could quickly end this rally within the range," says Tse. (elisabeth.behrmann@dowjones.com)

0422 GMT [Dow Jones] Vietnam shares end down 1.0% at 510.85, with corporate investors selling on worries about possibility of monetary policy adjustment after CPI released later this week or next. "They fear the central bank may tighten monetary policy as March's consumer price index is expected to be higher than in previous years," says Nguyen Viet Hung, chief analyst at SME Securities; adds, leveraged investors also selling to reduce risks. Among active shares, REE (REE.VH) +4.2% at VND50,000, Sacombank (STB.VH) down 0.9% at VND22,900, Saigon Securities (SSI.VH) down 1.1% at VND88,000. (trong-khanh.vu@dowjones.com)

Tips pair in 31.700-31.800 band in afternoon. (mason.wu@dowjones.com)

Instead of trying to push the yield curve lower, the BOJ decided to provide funds to more firms," says Barclays Capital chief Japan economist Kyohei Morita. title: EM ASIA  FX -Won dips on dlr strength; rupiah  intervention  seen
text:
* Won loses 1 percent, Goldman expects firmer won over time

* Indonesian c.bank seen intervening to support rupiah

* Most Asian currencies shackled in tight ranges

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, Feb 25 (Reuters) - The South Korean won fell 1 percent on Thursday, tracking the euro's weakness amid lingering investor concerns over debt problems in Europe, while the rupiah's decline again sparked official intervention.

Other Asian currencies mostly moved in thin ranges as sentiment was torn between the Fed's affirmation on low rates and persistent jitters over fiscal woes in Europe.

The euro slid to a one-year low of 120.60 yen <EURJPY=> and fell below $1.3470 <EUR=>, hurt by persistent worries about Greece's fiscal woes. [ID:nTOE61O03X]

Worries about a possible downgrade of Greece weighed. Standard & Poor's saying on Wednesday it may cut Greece's BBB+ rating by one or two notches within a month. [ID:nLDE61N2KL]

WON

The won <KRW=> shed nearly 1 percent to 1,164.6 per dollar, its lowest in two weeks.

The won has lost almost 4 percent since early January due to the dollar's resurgence and a sell-off of risky assets fanned by worries about European debt problems.

The won may be pressured in the near-term by South Korea's worsening balance of payments due to pent-up oil demand and other factors that led to a current account deficit in January, analysts at Goldman Sachs said.

South Korea reported the biggest monthly exports decline in January in a year, pushing the current account balance into deficit and providing new evidence that the economic revival is losing steam. [ID:nTOE61N090]

"Beyond the near term, the won is still supported by a positive outlook for capital inflows and ship and construction orders," Goldman analysts noted.

The bank kept its won forecasts at 1,150, 1,100 and 1,050 over 3, 6, and 12-month horizons, respectively.

Meanwhile, official dollar/won non-deliverable forwards <KRWNDFOR=> rose, tracking the weaker euro.

"One-month NDFs opened at 1,152.0 and then went as high as 1,159 when euro dropped below $1.35," said a trader in Singapore.

RUPIAH

The rupiah <IDR=> lost as much as 0.6 percent to 9,360 but later stabilised near 9,350 as traders suspected dollar-selling intervention by Bank Indonesia.

"The rupiah hit 9,360 before BI came in," said a trader in Jakarta.

A second trader said the central bank was providing dollar liquidity to meet corporate demand for monthly settlements.

Bank Indonesia has intervened many times in recent weeks to support the high-yielding rupiah, which is vulnerable to risk aversion. It has lost more than 2 percent since early January. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: MARKET TALK: USD/THB Steady; Verdict Of Thaksin's Case Eyed
text:
Contact us in Singapore. 65 64154 140; 
MarketTalk@dowjones.com 
 
 

0955 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/THB unchanged from 33.06-33.065 late yesterday. Pair drifts from 33.03 early low on buying by importers but upside limited by selling by exporters; foreign players mildly join selling force, says local dealer. "It's hard to predict what will happen. The market will probably be in idle mode while waiting for the (Thaksin asset case) verdict," he adds. Pair tipped 33.00-33.10 range. Supreme court will start reading its verdict in ousted-PM Thaksin's frozen asset case at 0630 GMT Friday. (PIY)

0953 GMT [Dow Jones] India's government must do away with dual imposition of Securities Transaction Tax, or STT, on investments into equity mutual funds in Friday's federal budget, says Dhirendra Kumar, chief executive of New-Delhi based Value Research, which provides fund analysis, industry data. "Investors pay STT on their investments into equity funds. However, when mutual funds invest that money in stocks, STT is again deducted from that money," adds Kumar. Says avoiding double taxation likely to attract more investments from retail customers, benefit industry in long run. India's mutual fund industry had total assets under management of INR7.59 trillion at end January, according to data from Association of Mutual Funds in India. (SHB)

0951 GMT [Dow Jones] Indonesia shares end down 1.2% at 2549.033 in moderate volume, weighed by weak IDR, falls in many Asian markets as concerns over Europe debt woes linger, traders say; expect shares to rebound Monday on bargain buying; tip resistance at 2570. Indonesian markets closed Friday for holiday. "Selling by foreign funds drove the main index lower despite sporadic buying by local institutional funds," says trader at Reliance Securities. Foreigners net sellers of IDR671 billion worth of shares. Astra (ASII.JK) down 1.5% at IDR36,250 on profit taking after gaining more than 4% in previous 5 sessions, Bank Mandiri (BMRI.JK) off 1.7% at IDR4,475, while Bank Rakyat (BBRI.JK) down 2.7% at IDR7,150. (EDH)

0947 GMT [Dow Jones] USD/IDR maintains gains at 9,355 late vs 9,340 late Wednesday on month-end demand, as well as short covering ahead of long weekend, dealers say. "There's no sign of Bank Indonesia intervention," dealer says; 9,325-9,375 tipped Monday; market closed Friday for public holiday. (IMS)

0941 GMT [Dow Jones] Sterling drops to the day's lows after data showed Business Investment in the UK fell at its sharpest annual rate in the data's 43 year history. GBP/USD hit a fresh month low of 1.5272 and EUR/GBP the day's high of 0.8830 for a half penny gain on the day. (GST)

0937 GMT [Dow Jones] The CBI distributive trade survey, out later than usual Thursday at 1245 GMT is of importance given that slowing consumer confidence has become evident in the major developed economies over the past few months, notes BNP Paribas. Any signs that the UK consumer is slowing will just add to sterling's problems, says the bank, and with GBP/USD already below support at 1.5365 a weak survey could tip it over the edge toward an initial target of 1.5065. GBP/USD now at 1.53. HSBC is looking for reported sales at -5 vs -8 in January. (GST)

title: EM ASIA  FX -Won, rupiah dip after Fed lifts discount rate
text:
* Won's implied vols edge up as spot slips

* Indonesian c.bank seen smoothing rupiah's fall

* Dollar/peso NDFs rise but lack momentum

By Kevin Yao

SINGAPORE, Feb 19 (Reuters) - The South Korean won led Asian currencies lower on Friday as the Federal Reserve's surprise discount rate rise spurred a dollar rally, prompting Indonesia's central bank to defend the currency for the second day.

The dollar hit a 8-month high against major currencies <.DXY> after the Federal Reserve said it would raise the discount rate to 0.75 percent from 0.50 percent, stoking expectations that it is moving towards normalising policy. [ID:nTOE61I03G]

Asian currencies have been undermined in recent weeks by the dollar's broad resurgence and capital outflows associated with the sell-off in riskier assets, and higher U.S. interest rates tend to encourage such outflows.

Markets in China and Taiwan remained shut for holidays.

WON

The won <KRW=> lost as much as 0.9 percent to 1,161.20 per dollar, but it later stabilised near 1,160.

Implied volatilities in the won <KRWVOL> edged up as the spot slipped, but investors appeared to be reluctant to snap up volatilities amid signs that the won was stabilising.

"We just see a bit of buying interest in the front-end with dollar/won spot moving higher," said an option trader in Singapore.

One-month vols rose to 12.64 percent from 12.49 percent late on Thursday.

The vols hit as high as 16.6 percent earlier this month as the won's steep decline caught investors off guard, but they have come off steadily as the spot rate recovered.

RUPIAH

The rupiah <IDR=> fell as much as 0.8 percent to 9,365 to the dollar, but it later cut losses as traders suspected dollar-selling intervention by the central bank.

"Bank Indonesia started selling dollars from 9,350 to 9,365," said a trader in Jakarta, adding that the rupiah could quickly fall to 9,400 if the central bank had not intervened.

A second trader said the central bank was aiming to check the rupiah's volatility amid broad dollar strength in recent sessions.

PESO

Dollar/peso non-deliverable forwards jumped across the curve in line with the dollar's broad rally, but the rise lacked momentum, traders said.

"We see higher bids at the opening but not much now," said a NDF trader in Manila.

One-month NDFs <PHP1MNDFOR=> hit as high 46.51 in early trade compared to 46.25 late on Thursday, while onshore forwards with the same tenor <PHP1M=> edged up to 46.42 from Thursday's 45.26.

That means offshore markets price in a bit more peso depreciation compared to onshore.

Meanwhile, spot peso <PHP=> fell 0.4 percent to 46.39 per dollar but traders expected it to get near-term support at 46.40. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: ASIA LOCAL BONDS-Philippine, Indonesia bond yields edge lower
text:
HONG KONG, Feb 18 (Reuters) - Philippine bond yields softened on Thursday on growing investor expectations that the government would borrow less from the local bond markets in coming months.

Manila will price up to 100 billion yen ($1.1 billion) of Samurai bonds next week and, with tax collections also recovering, the supply pipeline is expected to shrink keeping demand for bonds intact. [ID:nSGE61F0CX].

Benchmark five-year bonds <PH5YT=RR> were yielding 5.99 percent, a shade softer than the last close and traders said it could fall to between 5.8-5.9 percent in the coming weeks.

"Philippines in particular had made very good progress on fiscal consolidation prior to the crisis and we really need to see what the next administration does," Michael Hasenstab, a fund manager at Franklin Templeton who manages $60 billion in assets, told a Reuters chatroom. [ID:nTOE61H01L].

The Philippines, one of Asia's most active sovereign debt issuers, faces a budget shortfall of 293 billion pesos ($6.3 billion), or 3.5 percent of GDP, this year.

Latest data showed Manila had a record fiscal deficit of 298.5 billion pesos or 3.9 percent of GDP in 2009.[ID:nMNA002626]

It raised $1.5 billion from a global bond sale last month, the from Asia this year. It wants to raise a total of $2.5 billion from foreign debt markets this year to partly fund the budget deficit and repay debts.

Philippines goes for national elections in May.

INDONESIAN BOND YIELDS EASE

In Indonesia, bond yields eased after the central bank intervened to support its currency but volume was thin ahead of an auction next week.

The high-yielding rupiah <IDR=> fell as much as 0.7 percent in early deals before the central bank was seen intervening according to traders. [ID:nSGE61H04W].

Ten-year government bonds <ID10YT=RR> were now yielding 9.83 percent, two basis points below from Wednesday's close of 9.85 percent.

Foreign investors have continued to swarm to Indonesian bonds this year on top of aggressive buying last year. This month alone they have bought more than 4 trillion rupiah ($87 million) of bonds after buying $2.2 billion last year.

Templeton's Hasenstab said he was positive on the outlook for bonds as policymakers have proved very adept at managing the economy during, adding to the credibility of its macro policy.

"Clearly, as with any emerging market there are risks and we need to monitor developments closely, but any country that came through 2009 with positive growth deserves a degree of credit." ($1= 46.1 pesos, 9,300 rupiah) (Editing by Jan Dahinten)
