title: UPDATE: Bk Indonesia Surprises By Keeping Rates Steady
text:
(Updates with analysts' comments, closing rupiah price) 
 
   By I Made Sentana and Phelim Kyne 
   OF DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
   

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia's board of governors decided at a policy meeting Monday to leave the one-month benchmark rate unchanged at 12.75%, surprising traders and analysts, who had expected an interest-rate rise.  

The central bank cited a rising currency and stable inflation for the lack of action, which follows interest-rate increases at every prior policy meeting since last July.  

"The rate hasn't increased due to the latest developments in the economy where inflation is under control and the rupiah is on a rising trend," Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Aslim Tadjuddin later told reporters.  

"The decision not to hike the rate is expected to keep the macroeconomy stable and create a conducive climate for growth," he said.  

Still, the central bank will maintain its tight monetary policy, Tadjuddin said.  

Analysts had predicted that Bank Indonesia would raise rates following a 175-basis-point increase in its benchmark rate since November, to address lingering inflationary pressure powered by the government's move to, on average, more than double fuel prices last October.  

But a slowing in inflation in December likely emboldened the central bank to slightly loosen their recent tight monetary policy footing, said CIMB-GK Research Pte. Ltd. vice president of regional economics, Song Seng Wun.  

"The fact that the December consumer price index fell probably gave them a little bit more confidence (to temporarily halt rate hikes)," Song said.  

"They are also well aware that the spike in rates has affected the economy...so they're balancing what they have to do on the inflation-control front and what they need for the broader economy," he said.  

Indonesia's on-year inflation slowed to 17.11% in December from 18.38% in November. The country recorded 0.04% on-month deflation in December after 1.31% inflation in November.  

Inflationary Pressure, Rates To Steadily Decline  

Bank Indonesia officials have routinely warned that they will keep a tight grip on the monetary policy levers, and analysts had predicted that the benchmark rate could rise to around 14.0% by mid-2006.  

The government of President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono has cautioned that a combination of accelerated government spending, pending price hikes for public utilities and a 15.0% on-year salary increase for civil servants will continue to feed inflationary pressure in 2006.  

But December's data foreshadows an easing in inflation, which will prompt Bank Indonesia to scale back its tightening policy, Deutsche Bank said in a research note before the latest policy decision.  

"The inflation rate is likely to creep lower over the next two quarters, and then drop sharply in October as last year's fuel prices drop out of the calculation," the report said. "We expect Bank Indonesia will raise interest rates only a little over the next two quarters, perhaps keeping pace with the Fed, but then lower interest rates sharply in the fourth quarter."  

The end-2006 rate cut could "easily be much more" than 100 basis points, Deutsche Bank said.  

The central bank has been trying to carefully calibrate its anti-inflation rate hike policy so that it doesn't smother consumer consumption, which makes up around 70.0% of annual gross domestic product. The government has projected GDP expansion of 6.2% in 2006, outpacing the projected 6.0% rise in 2005.  

"They need to give the local economy a little bit of a break (in terms of lower rates) or that GDP target will be quite difficult to achieve," Song said.  

Central Bank Unlikely To Intervene In FX Market  

The decision to keep rates steady came as the U.S. dollar continued to slide against Indonesia's currency.  

The dollar closed Monday at IDR9,455, from IDR9,570 Friday and after touching an eight-month low of IDR9,430 in early trading.  

Central banks across Asia closely watched the dollar's continuing fall against a broad range of currencies and traders suspect a number have intervened to slow the greenback's fall.  

Bank Indonesia's Tadjuddin said the central bank reserves its right to intervene in the foreign currency markets, but he indicated that such action was unlikely in the short term.  

"In terms of keeping the foreign exchange market stable, intervention is always open...(but) what the ideal value of the rupiah is, we leave it to the market," he said.  

Tadjuddin attributed the rupiah's current strength to short-term foreign capital inflow on expectations that Indonesia's economy would continue to improve and he said the rupiah's rise against the dollar would help curb inflation.  

That view was echoed by Standard Chartered economist Fauzi Ichsan.  

Bank Indonesia's move to not hike rates Monday "won't hurt the rupiah", Ichsan said.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Up On Dlr Weakness, Stocks Rally
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended at a nearly eight-month high Monday due to the dollar's tumble against most regional currencies, and strong capital inflows to the stock market, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,455 versus IDR9,570 Friday. Monday's close is the dollar's lowest since May 23 when it ended at IDR9,445.  

The dollar lost ground against most Asian currencies Monday because of weaker-than expected U.S. jobs data.  

Dealers said the influx of capital to the Indonesian market, which yet rose to another record high Monday also helped the rupiah. The Jakarta Stock Exchange Composite Index rose 1.9% Monday to 1,245.054 points.  

The rupiah's nearly 4% gains so far this year and easing inflation in December prompted the central bank to keep its key one-month rate unchanged at 12.75% Monday. Many analysts had expected another 25-basis point hike.  

"The rate hasn't increased due to the latest developments in the economy where inflation is under control and the rupiah is on a rising trend," Bank Indonesia deputy governor Aslim Tadjuddin told reporters. "The decision not to hike the rate is expected to keep the macroeconomy stable and create a conducive climate for growth," he said.  

However, he added that the central bank will maintain its tight monetary policy. Many analysts are still expecting a gentle rate hike during the first half of the year.  

Dealers said the local foreign exchange market was widely unfazed by the central bank's decision to keep rates unchanged as the move is expected to further lift sentiment in the local stock and bond markets, which should then benefit the rupiah.  

"The contribution of the stock rise to the rupiah's recent gains is quite significant," said Fauzi Ichsan, an economist with Standard Chartered Bank in Jakarta.  

Still, some interbank players took profits against the rupiah, lifting the dollar from its intraday low of IDR9,430, dealers said.  

"I think they took profits first as a precaution just in case other players were upset with the central bank's policy too," a dealer with a local bank said.  

On the possibility of intervention to stem the rupiah's rise, Bank Indonesia's Tadjuddin didn't rule out such a move but said the bank leaves it to the market to determine the rupiah's "ideal value."  

Dealers said that the dollar-rupiah downtrend remains intact, but added that it will also depend on the outcome of U.S. trade data due Thursday.  

Dealers expect the dollar to trade between IDR9,400 and IDR9,500 Wednesday. The local currency market will be closed Tuesday for a Muslim holiday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Rupiah corrects after rally
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 12 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah fell more than a percent on Monday in what traders said was an overdue correction after last week's sharp gains that were driven by a surging stock market and a government reshuffle.  

 Other Asian currencies were flat to slightly weaker, in line with the Japanese yen <JPY=>, ahead of another expected U.S. rate rise on Tuesday, trade and inflation data from the United States and Japan's quarterly tankan business sentiment survey.  

 The rupiah <IDR=> fell to about 9,760/9,770 per dollar, down from Friday's 5-1/2-month peak of 9,625.  

 "The rupiah recovered too strongly last week. There was bound to be some reversal," said Vikas Suri, head of global markets at Standard Chartered Bank in Jakarta.  

 The rupiah gained more than 3 percent last week, which took its rise in the last 3 weeks to 5 percent, as foreigners poured money into Indonesian stocks and high-yielding bonds.  

 A rate rise last Tuesday and expectations that a team of economic ministers sworn in last week would push for faster reforms and toughen the fight against Indonesia's mounting inflation boosted market sentiment.  

 Suri said the rupiah would adopt a range of 9,700 to 9,800 per dollar while markets waited for the new economic team to deliver on their promised reforms.  

 Markets were also cheered last week by news that Indonesian state oil firm Pertamina and U.S. giant Exxon Mobil were close to resolving their dispute on who should operate the Cepu oil project on the island of Java, which would boost the country's oil output.  

 Analysts said the rupiah's rally last week, which nearly matched a rise in the key stock index <.JKSE>, had been too rapid.  

 Mirza Baig, Deutsche Bank's currency strategist, said he would be a cautious buyer of rupiah.  

 "Fundamentally, I am inclined to be a bear, but it is hard to ignore the constructive near-term story," he said.  

 "The JKSE is still doing well, and broader sentiment within Indonesia remains oddly positive despite the prospects of slower growth and higher inflation next year."  

 Besides, Bank Indonesia was unlikely to intervene much and would welcome some rupiah strength to help the economy contain inflation, Baig said.  

 CHINA SPECULATION  

 Elsewhere, the Philippine peso <PHP=>, Asia's best performer this year and one of last week's outperformers, shed more than a quarter of a percent from Friday's 2-½   year high of 53.38 per dollar.  

 China's markets shrugged of a rush of comments from the central bank. China's central bank chief Zhou Xiaochuan on Monday dismissed as nonsense speculation of a major shift in policy towards the yuan at the end of the year.

title: Bank Indonesia Gov: Ctrl Bk Not Behind Recent Rupiah Rise
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia hasn't intervened in the foreign-exchange market to help the rupiah's recent surge against the U.S. dollar, Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said Monday.  

"The central bank hasn't been boosting the rupiah's value and the unit's future movements depend on investor sentiment," Burhanuddin told reporters. "The market will determine (the rupiah's value)."  

The comments follow the rupiah's 3% rise against the dollar last week. On Friday, the dollar closed at IDR9,695, its lowest close since June 27.  

The dollar was at IDR9,730 at 0727 GMT Monday, down from an intraday high of IDR9,791  

Dealers attribute the rupiah's strength to buoyant sentiment linked to President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono's reshuffling of his economic team last week, and to dollar sales by investors to take advantage of higher domestic interest rates.  

Bank Indonesia has hiked its benchmark rate 175 basis points to 12.75% since Nov. 1 to cool inflation, which hit an annualized rate of 18.38% in November and 17.89% in October.  

The soaring inflation has been blamed on the government's raising fuel prices by more than double, on average, on Oct. 1.  

The higher interest rates have made rupiah-denominated investments, such as short-term fixed deposits, more attractive.  

But analysts warn that the rupiah's sudden strength exposes the volatility and lack of liquidity in Indonesia's foreign-exchange market.  

The rupiah's dramatic rise is "symptomatic of a dysfunctional foreign-exchange market that lacks liquidity and exacerbates volatility," JP Morgan said in a research note issued Monday.  

The rupiah "could just as easily swing violently back against the U.S. dollar due to the lack of liquidity," JP Morgan said.

text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended flat Tuesday as suspected Bank Indonesia dollar selling coupled with a hefty interest-rate hike helped the local unit recoupe its losses that were triggered earlier in the day by news of surging inflation in October, dealers said.  

The dollar closed unchanged at IDR10,115.  

Dealers said Bank Indonesia was suspected of selling dollars via state-banks when the greenback touched an intraday high of IDR10,200 earlier in the day, and again late in the late afternoon.

The local currency market will be closed Wednesday through Tuesday. The dollar may trade between IDR10,100 and IDR10,250 next week.

title: ANALYSIS-Bank Indonesia backs rupiah markets, as last resort
text:
(Adds ANALYSIS tag to headline)  

JAKARTA, Oct 18 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank has made itself available as the counterparty of last resort for investors seeking protection against a choppy rupiah, a move analysts say will make the currency market more liquid and more stable.  

But the terms that Bank Indonesia offers have so far tended to be more expensive than market rates, ensuring that banks will turn to it only during periods of high volatility.  

The rupiah <IDR=> was languishing near its weakest levels in four years in August when Bank Indonesia (BI) decided that, in addition to intervening in the spot market, it would conduct one- to seven-day currency swaps to regulate rupiah supply and demand.  

It followed that up on Oct. 3 with a hedging facility for investors to swap dollars into rupiah and back for three- to six-month periods.  

Similar practices had been in place before the Asian financial crisis of 1997/98, of which the rupiah was a big casualty.  

They are back now. As investors rushed for cover against a tumbling rupiah, BI felt the need to re-use swaps as a policy tool.  

Analysts lauded the move. By intervening through swaps -- a derivative that combines a spot and forward exchange of currencies -- the central bank will add volume to the forward rupiah market. At times, it can suck out excess rupiah funds that could be used for currency speculation.  

Its offer to be a counterparty to banks, with clients wanting to hedge rupiah assets, will bring investment flows that the country badly needs, they said.  

"For sure they will deter speculation and they will be providing liquidity," said a Jakarta-based bank treasurer.  

"But the pricing and conditions are such that this swap window will remain a facility that people will use in periods of extreme volatility."  

MARKET RUCTION  

In a typical transaction where a foreigner makes a fully hedged, six-month investment in Indonesia, the foreigner would sell dollars for rupiah to invest in rupiah assets. The investor would also buy six-month forward dollars for rupiah.  

If both transactions were to be done simultaneously, the investor could simply enter into a swap with a bank, which involves selling dollars for rupiah immediately in the spot leg and buying dollars for rupiah in the forward leg.  

After the events of recent months, the reason for the central bank's swap move is clear.  

Heavy imports of oil and investor demand for higher Indonesian yields drove the rupiah down to a four-year low of 11,750 per dollar on August 30, a 21 percent loss in 8 months. It has since recovered 16 percent.  

Demand for forward dollars surged in July and August and banks found it difficult to square their swap positions in the market. Local banks had more difficulty finding foreign counterparties because their credit ratings are mostly below investment grade.  

The central bank compounded the problem, analysts said. Seeking to defend the rupiah, in July it limited the access offshore players had to the forward rupiah market, making swap transactions more scarce.  

In early September, the premium on six-month dollars <IDRF=> shot up to an annualised 14 percent, from 6 percent at the end of July. The premium is now 10 percent, partly owing to higher official interest rates.  

Catherinawati Hadiman, corporate banking director at Indonesia's seventh-largest lender PT Bank Niaga, said the swap offers could attract more foreign currency inflows.  

"Hopefully this could help stabilise the rupiah."  

LAST OPTION

text:
Sep 01, 2005 (ODC via Comtex) --  

Yudhoyono said the government must finalize plans for direct cash subsidies to Indonesia's lower-income earners prior to a further fuel price increase. Yudhoyono's government already slashed fuel subsidies and hiked fuel prices by an average 29% on March 1.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Steady; Capital Inflows To Bond Mkt
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah rebounded from an intraday low to close flat Thursday as capital inflows into the local bond market triggered wider dollar-selling, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR10,225, little-changed from its close Wednesday at IDR10,250. The greenback touched an intraday high of IDR10,700 earlier as the markets were disappointed with the government's rupiah-support program unveiled Wednesday.  

Analysts said the program - which includes a planned reduction in fuel subsidy, reform on tax and investment regulations - lacks focus and doesn't set out a timetable for implementation.  

But the rupiah got a boost from London-based investors, who bought the government's rupiah bonds. Indonesian debt instruments took a beating recently due to rising interest rates and the rupiah's weakness.  

"We got some $20 million coming from these London-based investors," a dealer with a foreign bank said. "I think the total amount(including those received by other dealers)was around $100 million, not much, but enough to spark other players to sell the dollar."  

Dealers said the they didn't detect any direct intervention by Bank Indonesia in the market, but the nation's central bank might have sold dollars via state banks to help the rupiah.  

News that Indonesia had a higher-than expected trade surplus in July also spelt good news for the local currency, dealers said.  

The official Central Statistics Agency reported Thursday that Indonesia's trade surplus widened to $2.17 billion from $2.01 billion in June. The average forecast of four analysts polled by Dow Jones Newswires was for a surplus of $1.87 billion.  

Dealers expect the dollar to trade between IDR10,150 and IDR10,600 Monday. The local foreign exchange market will be closed Friday due to a public holiday.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Higher On  Central Bank 's Support
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah continued to recover Wednesday after the central bank intervened in the market to help the beleaguered currency, while the government was expected to announce complementary measures later in the day.  

Separately, Bank Indonesia chief Burhanuddin Abdullah said in Tokyo that the rupiah is undervalued by as much as 95%.  

The dollar closed at IDR10,200, lower than IDR10,525 Tuesday. The rupiah has now strengthened appreciably from IDR10,840 at the close Monday.  

To follow up a pledge made Tuesday, Bank Indonesia intervened in the local foreign exchange market Wednesday, using short-term swap instruments and selling dollars in the spot market, dealers said.  

The intervention with swap instruments pushed the overnight premium earlier in the day to around 20% from 8% Tuesday, making it more expensive for market participants to maintain long dollar positions, dealers said.  

"State banks, likely on behalf of Bank Indonesia, started to unload dollars in the spot market when the greenback was trading at IDR10,500," a dealer with a foreign bank said.  

Trading was calmer than Tuesday, with the market awaiting the government's measures to boost the rupiah.  

President Yudhoyono is expected to announce, among other things, a timetable for a further reduction of fuel subsidies, which have ballooned due to rising oil prices. Analysts have called on the government to reduce fuel subsidies to keep the state budget sustainable.  

Also Wednesday, Bank Indonesia senior deputy governor Miranda Gultom told Dow Jones Newswires that the central bank will review regulations that may be impeding capital inflows into Indonesia. She declined to provide further details.  

Meanwhile, the country's benchmark stock index rose 1%, helped by the rupiah's recovery. The stock market's gains, if sustained, would help ease pressure on the rupiah as investors will need to buy the local currency to settle their purchases.  

Dealers expect the dollar to trade between IDR10,000 and IDR10,500 Thursday.

title: Japan MOF:BOJ, Bk Indonesia Signed 2nd  FX  Swap Agreement
text:
TOKYO (Dow Jones)--The Bank of Japan and Bank Indonesia signed a second bilateral foreign exchange swap agreement Wednesday, Japan's Ministry of Finance said.  

The agreement will allow currency swaps of up to $6 billion between monetary authorities in the two countries. [ 31-08-05 0313GMT ]  

The latest agreement comes as Indonesian policy-makers announced a raft of measures to stem a recent and rapid decline in the rupiah due to record high oil prices and costly government subsidies on fuel prices.  

Bank Indonesia on Tuesday raised the target for benchmark one-month interest rates by 75 basis points to 9.5% and tightened the money supply by requiring banks to hold more money at the central bank.  

The rupiah has been steadily declining for much of this year and hit a four-year low of IDR11,900 to the dollar Tuesday before rebounding in response to Bank Indonesia's rate hike. At 0357 GMT, the rupiah was quoted at IDR10,410.  

State-owned oil company Pertamina (PTM.YY) needs as much as $1.8 billion a month to finance its oil imports, and that has gradually weighed on the rupiah, analysts said.  

The Indonesian government also devotes about a quarter of all government spending to fuel subsidies, which has rattled confidence in the rupiah as these subsidies seem unsustainable, analysts said.  

Indonesia has spent more than $5 billion of its foreign exchange reserves since April in repeated attempts to defend the rupiah by intervening in the currency markets.  

Earlier this month, Indonesia President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono projected that the country's foreign exchange reserves may fall to $27.1 billion by the end of next year from $32 billion.  

Japan and Indonesia's second currency swap arrangement doubles the amount of transfers under a previous agreement, which is in line with a pact by finance ministers from Japan, China, South Korea and the Association of Southeast Asian nations to significantly expand their existing $39.5 billion network of bilateral swaps in May.  

The second swap agreement between Japanese and Indonesian monetary authorities falls under the Chiang Mai Initiative, a series of currency swaps set up following the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis to help cash-strapped countries defend their currencies in times of crisis.  

-By Stanley White, Dow Jones Newswires; 813-5255-2929; stanley.white@dowjones.com

title: Bk Indonesia Raises Benchmark Rate 75 BPs To Help IDR -2-
text:
The nation's central bank also further hiked its one-week deposit rate by 100 basis points to 8.5% effective Wednesday. Bank Indonesia last week raised the rate by 25 basis points to 7.5%.  

The central bank raised the maximum rate for one-month guaranteed deposits to 10% for September from 8.45% currently and the one-month dollar deposit rate to 4.25% from 3%.  

The rate hikes are a follow-up to the central bank's increase earlier this month of the benchmark Bank Indonesia rate to 8.75% from 8.50%.  

The benchmark rate hike reflects the central bank's increasingly desperate efforts to stem an 11% surge in the U.S. dollar against the rupiah since January that has stymied all of Bank Indonesia's policy remedies to date.  

Those remedies have included repeated interventions to sell dollars in the market, which have bled Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves of more than $5 billion since April.  

The policy package is also a decisive response to heightening criticism from analysts that lax central bank monetary policy contributed to the rupiah's tumble.  

Analysts have called for aggressive interest rate hikes, cuts in budget-crippling fuel price subsidies and the removal of bureaucratic blockages to foreign investment inflows to provide meaningful relief for the rupiah.  

The central bank and Yudhoyono's government have been reluctant to raise interest rates too steeply or to cut fuel price subsidies due to fears that such measures could dampen economic growth and encourage public protests. The official economic growth projection for 2005 is 6.0%.  

Burhanuddin said commercial banks will also be required to increase their reserves with the central bank, with the additional amount to be tied to the ratio of their loans to deposits. This move is aimed at tightening market liquidity, he said.  

However, banks that have lent more than 90% of the deposits they received are exempt from the new policy.  

Banks with loan-to-deposit ratios between 75% and 90% must increase their reserves by 1%. Those with LDR of 60%-75% must increase their reserves by 2%; banks with LDR of 50%-60% must increase reserves by 3%; those with LDR of 40%-50% must up reserves by 4%; and those with LDR of less than 40% must increase reserves by 5%.  

Burhanuddin said the central bank will increase the returns given for the reserves of those banks with the 5% requirement to 5.5% from the current 3%.  

He said Bank Indonesia is also drafting additional measures to help the rupiah, which it will unveil in the near future.  

The measures will include providing swap facilities for companies that need to hedge their dollar exposure and intervening in the foreign exchange market via short-term swap instruments.  

The central bank will also adjust the maximum amount of foreign exchange net open positions that banks can have and tighten rules on foreign exchange margin trading, he said.  

Lastly, the central bank will intensify its monitoring of banks' foreign exchange trading, which are not based on underlying transactions.  

"With those measures, Bank Indonesia hopes that banks and society will support the efforts to create stability in the economy," Burhanuddin said.  

President Yudhoyono said later Tuesday in a televised speech that the government supports Bank Indonesia's rupiah package, adding that the government will introduce comprehensive measures to help the rupiah by Wednesday afternoon.  

-By I Made Sentana; Dow Jones Newswires; 62-21 39831277; I-Made.Sentana@dowjones.com

title: Dollar Rises Above IDR10,500 - Dealers
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The U.S. dollar broke the IDR10,500 mark in intraday trade at 0455 GMT Monday for the first time since Jan. 2, 2002, dealers said.  

"It (hit IDR10,500) in a very thin market when most dealers were away on lunch break," a dealer at a domestic commercial bank told Dow Jones Newswires.  

"The dollar was taken at IDR10,500 and is now being quoted around the 10,520 level."  

The greenback's latest record intraday high is likely to exacerbate market concerns about both the health of the rupiah and the severity of pending central bank and Indonesian government efforts to give the unit more traction against the greenback. [ 29-08-05 0511GMT ]  

The U.S. dollar has gained around 11% against the rupiah since January and was quoted as high as IDR10,475 Friday, its highest level since Jan. 2, 2002 before closing at IDR10,400. The close marked an acceleration from Thursday's IDR10,340.  

The greenback's surge has defied Bank Indonesia's foreign exchange market interventions, which have bled foreign reserves of more than $5 billion since April.  

On Friday, Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah vowed sterner policy measures to stem the rupiah's decline against the dollar including a new round of rate hikes. The central bank earlier this month increased its benchmark Bank Indonesia rate to 8.75% from 8.50% to help support the rupiah.  

The central bank last week also began offering commercial banks the opportunity to park funds at the central bank overnight at a fixed 7% interest. The central bank rolled out a new system earlier Monday allowing commercial banks to bid for rates of this overnight deposit facility that resulted in an average overnight deposit rate of 7.08%.  

Analysts have called for aggressive rate hikes above 10% and cuts in budget-crippling fuel price subsidies to decisively halt the rupiah's tumble against the U.S. dollar.  

But the central bank and government of President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono must balance the potential boost those policies might provide the rupiah with wider negative impact. Rate hikes could threaten projected economic growth of 6.0% in 2005 and fuel-price increases could spark potentially destabilizing public protests.  

The Jakarta Stock Exchange composite index was down 3.6% at the close of midday trading Monday due to factors including negative market sentiment over the potential growth-curbing impact of additional pending interest rate increases.  

"A substantial rise in interest rates would likely torpedo (Indonesia's) economy (and) the decline in private consumption because of energy subsidy removal would likewise torpedo the economy," a Morgan Stanley research note issued Monday cautioned.

title: Bank Indonesia Sells USD To Support Rupiah - Dealers
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia intervened again in currency markets Friday by selling dollars to try to boost a weakening rupiah, dealers told Dow Jones Newswires.  

Bank Indonesia sold dollars to defend the rupiah at IDR10,370 at 0305 GMT, dealers said.  

"Bank Indonesia is helping the rupiah somewhat (with dollar sales)," a dealer at a domestic commercial bank said. [ 26-08-05 0318GMT ]  

The intervention is the latest in a series of dollar selling by the central bank in the past week to slow the rupiah's decline. The dollar reached a new 43-month high of IDR10,425 midmorning Thursday. That compares with Wednesday's close of IDR10,340.  

The dollar eased to IDR10,408 at 0328 GMT Thursday.  

It may test IDR10,500 later on normal month-end corporate dollar purchases to fund overseas obligations, dealers said.  

Bank Indonesia officials have said repeatedly in recent weeks that the bank will intervene in currency markets "if necessary" to defend the rupiah.  

Those interventions have cost foreign exchange reserves of at least $5 billion since April and have been ineffective in reversing the rupiah's 8% on-year decline since January.  

Analysts have urged rupiah support policy measures, including aggressive interest rate hikes, cuts in fuel price subsidies and new foreign investment incentives to help increase foreign exchange inflows.  

Coordinating Minister for the Economy Aburizal Bakrie said late Thursday that there will be a fuel price hike by end-2005. This hike follows the average 29% increase in March 1.  

Dealers and analysts say the government is likely reluctant to increase interest rates in the near future as the move might derail an economic growth target of 6.0% for 2005. Bank Indonesia earlier this month raised the benchmark rate to 8.75% from 8.50%.  

Bank Indonesia apparently prefers to continue foreign currency market interventions along with possible further measures, including tightening commercial banks' net open forex positions and liquidity reductions by hiking rates of money market instruments, dealers said Friday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rupiah drops, others weaker on stocks
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 24 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah dropped nearly 2 percent on Wednesday to its weakest level in 3-½ years as foreigners selling Indonesian stocks and bonds added to pressure on the currency.  

Other Asian currencies also fell as the Japanese yen <JPY=> retreated about a yen to the weaker side of 110 per dollar, oil prices rose back above $66 a barrel and regional equity markets stumbled.  

The rupiah <IDR=> extended a two-week-long slide to hit 10,300 per dollar, its lowest since February 2002 and marking one of its biggest single-day drops since May last year.  

Relentless demand for dollars to pay for oil imports, debt repayments and speculation drove the currency down.  

Adding to the currency's woes, foreigners turned heavy sellers of Indonesian stocks <.JKSE> and bonds <0#IDBMK=> on Wednesday, traders said.  

The rupiah is Asia's worst-performing currency this year, having shed 5 percent this month and nearly 10 percent in 2005. The Jakarta stock index has fallen 14 percent this month.  

"It looks quite dicey. The BI has raised rates again but that does not seem to be helping the rupiah," said Thio Chin Loo, currency strategist with BNP Paribas.  

Bank Indonesia (BI) raised its 7-day intervention rate by a quarter point to 7.5 percent, but traders said interbank rates were much higher than the policy rate.  

INTERVENTION

Bank Indonesia has been intervening, both verbally and by supplying dollars this month.  

It raised the benchmark rate on one-month paper by a quarter point on August 9 to 8.75 percent, and has been offering short-term deposits to absorb funds, making it more expensive to sell the rupiah short onshore.  

On Monday, Bank Indonesia scrapped a repurchase facility that allowed banks to borrow funds against bonds from the central bank.  

Analysts say policy is not tight enough to shore up the currency and demand for dollars to pay for oil is rising. Oil was above $66 a barrel <CLc1> on Wednesday, just below a record high above $67 hit earlier this month.  

"The currency is structurally weak, partly from foreign debt repayments and partly from (oil) demand," said Craig Chan, a currency strategist with Royal Bank of Scotland in Hong Kong.  

Low real interest rates were another factor, Chan said. With inflation running close to 8 percent and a benchmark one-month rate at 8.75 percent, analysts say there is little incentive for investors to hold Indonesian assets.  

BAHT WEAKER  

The Thai baht <THB=> fell nearly half a percent to the weaker side of 41 a dollar, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> and the Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> also dropped nearly half a percent each.  

"We are seeing net foreign equity outflows, we are seeing equity indices coming off, dollar is on a bid tone and oil is remaining stubbornly high," Chan said.  

"So the demand for dollars from some of the oil importers is still there. In the near term, I continue to see a dollar-Asia bid."  

Chan said he expected the baht and the Taiwan dollar to be underperformers, partly because their trade accounts were deteriorating rapidly. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0818 GMT

The rupiah <IDR=> hit 10,225 per dollar, traders said, extending its decline this month to over 4 percent.  

"We are seeing a lot of onshore dollar demand and selling in the local stock and bond market," said one Jakarta-based trader.  

Traders said Bank Indonesia (BI) had been selling dollars through state-run banks to support the rupiah.  

"The currency is structurally weak, partly from foreign debt repayments and partly from (oil) demand," said Craig Chan, a currency strategist with Royal Bank of Scotland in Hong Kong.  

Low real interest rates were another factor, Chan said. With inflation running close to 8 percent and a benchmark one-month rate at 8.75 percent, analysts say there is little incentive for investors to hold Indonesian assets.  

Bank Indonesia has been intervening, both verbally and by supplying dollars this month.  

It raised the benchmark rate on one-month paper by a quarter point on August 9 to 8.75 percent, and has been offering short-term deposits to absorb funds, making it more expensive to sell the rupiah short onshore.

Analysts say policy is not tight enough to shore up the currency, and the demand for dollars to pay for oil is rising. Oil was above $66 a barrel <CLc1> on Wednesday, just below a record high over $67 hit earlier this month.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends At 42-Month Low; Ignores Rate Hike
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah tumbled sharply to end at a 42-month low Wednesday as cyclical month-end dollar demand from local companies, combined with weak domestic capital markets, heightened the pressure on the local unit, dealers said.  

The market ignored a 25-basis point hike of the central bank's one-week deposit rate as the currency market was mainly driven by supply and demand, dealers said.  

The increase in Bank Indonesia's deposit rate wasn't followed by a rise in the weighted average rate of one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia, or SBI notes, which was unchanged at 8.75% during a weekly auction.  

The dollar closed at IDR10,280 compared with IDR10,095 Tuesday. This is the dollar's highest close since Feb. 6, 2002, when it ended at IDR10,315.  

The greenback briefly touched an intraday high of IDR10,320 but suspected Bank Indonesia intervention pulled the unit below the IDR10,300 mark.  

Local companies and foreign investors bought dollars as there was no positive news for the rupiah, a dealer with a local bank said.  

Foreign investors continued selling Indonesian stocks and bonds Wednesday. The Jakarta Stock Exchange main index dropped 2.9% as foreign investors exited the local market following the rupiah's weakness.  

The yield of the government's rupiah five-year bonds rose to 14% from 13% Tuesday, dealers said.  

Dealers said the dollar may revisit the IDR10,300 level Thursday due to continued month-end demand from local companies.  

"It's hard to predict the resistance level for the dollar with technical charts as the market is driven by genuine demand," a dealer with a foreign bank said.  

Some dealers expect the dollar to rise to IDR10,400-IDR10,500 later this week.

title: Bank Indonesia Sells Dollars To Defend Rupiah: Dealers
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia sold dollars Wednesday to try to slow a continuous slide in the rupiah, dealers told Dow Jones Newswires.  

"The dollar came off its intraday high of IDR10,320 because Bank Indonesia intervened at that level," a dealer at a domestic commercial bank said.  

The IDR10,320 level marks the lowest point the rupiah has hit against the U.S. dollar since Feb. 7, 2002. The dollar hit an intraday high of IDR10,335 on that day.  

Dealers are currently quoting the dollar at IDR10,280-IDR10,300.  

Investors' "panic buying" of U.S. dollars prompted by the steady decline in the rupiah combined with corporate dollar purchases for overseas obligations are resisting Bank Indonesia's interventions to boost the local unit, dealers said.  

Dealers predict that the dollar may breach the IDR10,500 resistance in the near term unless the central bank and the government of President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono make politically painful policy choices.  

Those policies include loosening inward foreign exchange restrictions, raising the benchmark Bank Indonesia rate and slashing budget-crippling fuel price subsidies, analysts say.

title: Indonesia Min: IDR Slide Against USD "Still Manageable"
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The rupiah's continuing weakness against the U.S. dollar is "still manageable" in terms of its impact on the government's budgetary projections for this year, Minister of Finance Jusuf Anwar said Tuesday.  

The U.S. dollar's rise Friday to break IDR10,000 won't hurt Indonesia's macroeconomic fundamentals, Anwar indicated to reporters.  

"The IDR10,000 mark is not a psychologically important level, it isn't sacred," he said. "Although there will be an impact on the budget, it's still manageable."  

Anwar didn't elaborate. [ 23-08-05 0625GMT ]  

The rupiah may yet strengthen against the greenback, and the local currency is healthy compared with other regional currencies, Anwar said.  

His comments reflect government efforts to calm jittery markets as the dollar appears set to test IDR10,100 Tuesday after rising to a new 41-month high of IDR10,085 at the close of morning trade in the local market.  

The rupiah's fall defied suspected intervention in the market by Bank Indonesia, which dealers said sold dollars around O300 GMT.  

Government officials and analysts are unanimous that the rupiah's weakness against the greenback is due to external factors, including record-high global crude-oil prices.  

Indonesia's central bank officials have vowed to continue to intervene in the currency markets "if necessary" to defend the rupiah.  

But analysts warn that such intervention has bled Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves of more than $5 billion since April and has failed to reverse a more-than-5% tumble in the rupiah against the dollar since January.  

President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono last week projected that the country's foreign exchange reserves may fall to $27.1 billion by the end of next year from $32 billion now.  

Analysts say that Indonesia must take politically-risky policy measures, including raising interest rates and slashing budget-busting fuel-price subsidies to lend support to the rupiah.  

Earlier this month, the central bank raised the benchmark Bank Indonesia rate to 8.75% from 8.50%.  

Senior government officials have hinted that the government may increase fuel prices by early next year, having raised such rates by an average 29% on March 1.

title: Bank Indonesia Sells USD To Aid IDR At IDR10,075-Dealers
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia, the central bank, intervened Tuesday to slow the rupiah's slide against the U.S. dollar after a fresh 41-month low of IDR10,075 at around O300 GMT, dealers told Dow Jones Newswires.  

But they said the intervention wasn't helping much to calm a jittery market intent on selling rupiah to buy dollars.  

"Bank Indonesia has been intervening...but it's failing to help the rupiah rebound because of demand from both foreign and local companies for dollars," a dealer at a foreign bank in Jakarta said.  

Corporate dollar purchases were aimed to both service overseas debt as well as to hedge in case the rupiah continues to tumble against the greenback.  

Dealers were split on whether the rupiah will slide to below the IDR10,100 mark on Tuesday, but said that the unit will continue to lose traction against the U.S. currency in the short-term.  

The Indonesian rupiah closed at IDR10,030 Monday versus IDR10,000 Friday as foreign investors exited the stock market on worries over the recent weakness of the local unit.  

Indonesia's government and central bank have blamed the rupiah's weakness on external factors including record high global crude oil prices and a rising trend in U.S. Federal Reserve rates.

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia rupiah down, policy measures fail to help
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 23 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah slipped to a fresh 3-1/2-year trough on Tuesday, undermined by dollar demand from oil importers and a feeling among traders that authorities are not doing enough to defend the currency.  

The rupiah <IDR=> hit 10,055 per dollar, traders said, extending its decline this month to nearly 3 percent.  

Traders said Bank Indonesia (BI) had been selling dollars through state-run banks between 10,030 and 10,050.  

Indonesia's stock market <.JKSE> was also weak, with both currency and shares bucking the stronger trend in other parts of Asia.  

"The issue for Indonesia is clearly that of too little, too late," said Wong Keng Siong, economist with Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi.  

Bank Indonesia has been intervening verbally and physically in the markets this month.  

It raised the benchmark rate on one-month paper by a quarter point on August 9 to 8.75 percent, and has been offering short-term deposits to absorb funds, so that the onshore market will find it more expensive to sell the rupiah short.  

On Monday, Bank Indonesia scrapped a repurchase facility that allowed banks to borrow funds against bonds from the central bank.  

"Interest rates need to go up, but not at that kind of snail's pace," Wong said.  

With annual inflation running close to 8 percent, the benchmark rate should have been raised much earlier and to at least 10.5 percent to provide a decent real return on Indonesian assets, he said.  

"Higher oil prices have been partly responsible for the deterioration in the currency, but rising domestic inflation and low real rates of return on Indonesian deposits have been more important," analysts at UBS wrote.  

OIL SUBSIDY  

Analysts said another option for Indonesia would be to cut government subsidies on domestic fuel, lowering consumption and import demand for expensive oil.  

Global oil prices <CLV5> were near $66 a barrel on Tuesday, just off record highs over $67.  

Bank Indonesia said in early July that state-oil-firm Pertamina will receive dollars to pay for its oil imports from the government's account with the central bank, but the oil firm has been spotted buying dollars in the market.  

"The best hope for the rupiah is lower oil prices because interest rates are not going up nearly fast enough," ING's head of research, Tim Condon, wrote.  

Wong said the government's inaction on subsidies and reluctance to raise rates aggressively would weigh on the rupiah, and the central bank's $32.5 billion foreign currency reserves were insufficient to fight any major speculative attack.  

"We think that BI will ultimately be forced to lift rates much more aggressively in order to prevent much further weakness in the currency but will likely only do so grudgingly," UBS said.  

"The implications are that the rupiah is likely to continue steadily weakening in the short-term, punctuated by sporadic intervention by the central bank to prop up the currency."

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Stocks lend support, but rupiah weakens
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 22 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose on Monday, supported by rallying regional stock markets, a higher Japanese yen and a slight drop in global oil prices.  

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> was the exception to the trend. It hit a fresh 3-1/2-year trough and then recovered slightly after Bank Indonesia intervened to sell dollars, repeating a pattern seen last week.  

The Thai baht <THB=> was emerging Asia's biggest gainer of the day. It rallied nearly 0.7 percent to near 41 per dollar.  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> fell to 56 per dollar and recovered to end the day a quarter of a percent higher. The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> and the Korean won <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC> also gained about a quarter of a percent each.  

"The main driver today has been stronger equity markets in a few selected countries and the weak rupiah," said Ray Farris, markets strategist with Credit Suisse.  

Japan's Nikkei share average <.N225> ended at a four-year high on Monday, causing other regional stock markets <0#.INDEXA> to rally, brushing aside worries over dearer oil.  

Oil prices <CLc1> were slightly softer than the record highs over $67 a barrel hit this month, with U.S. September light crude futures trading just over $65.  

Farris said currency markets had priced in the current levels of oil prices.  

"If oil rises substantially from here, then that will be distinctly bearish for a lot of Asia, particularly the countries that are already running weaker current account positions, for instance Thailand, India, Taiwan," he said.  

Lehman Brothers said in a note the market was, quite needlessly, reluctant to buy the Asian currencies, fearing the impact of oil prices, deteriorating trade balances and the yen being overbought.  

"Net-net, the market is once again trying to talk itself out of buying Asian currencies, a cycle we have gotten used to in 2005," Lehman economists said in a note.  

"With Japanese markets finally waking up, regional growth still sound and inflation risks beginning to build, we are not going to follow suit - stay long yen, Singapore dollar and Taiwan dollar," they wrote.  

RUPIAH DIVERGES  

The rupiah hit 10,025 per dollar in morning deals, its weakest since March 2002, deepening its losses in the past 10 days to more than 2 percent.  

Indonesia's central bank was spotted selling dollars to stem the rupiah's decline. Bank Indonesia deputy governor Aslim Tadjuddin said the central bank would intervene if necessary to restrain rupiah volatility.  

The central bank also offered a 3-day deposit to mop up funds and scrapped its repurchase facility on Bank Indonesia bonds, both moves aimed at tightening short-term rates and making it more expensive to speculate against the rupiah.  

The rupiah is Asia's worst performer so far this year, with rising oil imports and foreign debt repayments weighing heavily on the currency. The Indonesian stock market <.JKSE> has lost 9 percent in the past 10 sessions.  

Bank Indonesia said in early July that Pertamina would get dollars to pay for its oil imports from the government's account with the central bank, but the oil firm has been spotted buying dollars in the market.  

Analysts said Pertamina had probably been forced to go to the market again for its dollar needs, after the central bank got worried about how fast its currency reserves were being depleted.  

An Indonesian business newspaper reported on Monday that Pertamina planned to raise at least $500 million through bonds next year to finance crude oil imports and strengthen its working capital.  

Anton Gunawan, an economist with Citigroup, said the fund raising would help the oil firm overcome its immediate cash shortfall, while alleviating pressure on the rupiah. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0838 GMT

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Down Despite Ctrl Bank Moves
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah closed below the key level of IDR10,000 to the U.S. dollar late Friday, despite repeated central bank intervention to defend the currency. Dealers expect the dollar to continue rising Monday as companies with dollar exposures get jittery and jump on the dollar-buying bandwagon.   

The dollar closed at IDR10,000, versus the previous close of IDR9,950, after going as high as IDR10,010 during the day. The close was the highest since March 8, 2002, when it ended at IDR10,015.   

Bank Indonesia aggressively sold dollars for the third straight day in a failed attempt to keep the unit below the threshold of IDR10,000. State banks also sold dollars, keeping the unit below IDR10,000 for a time, but market players eventually pushed it over the top after Bank Indonesia ended its daily trading activity.   

The central bank usually finishes dealing at 0900 GMT, but interbank players sometimes continue trading until there are no further quotations in the market.   

"Players continued buying dollars until the last minute since they expect more foreign investors to exchange their rupiah into dollars Monday," said a dealer with a foreign bank.   

Market participants were also expecting increased dollar demand Monday after the local stock market Friday fell 1.1%, the sixth consecutive day of losses.   

The Jakarta Stock Exchange's Composite Index fell 12.346 points to 1087.953 Friday, up from its intraday low of 1081.724 on expectations the falling rupiah might prompt an increase in the benchmark Bank Indonesia rate.   

The central bank increased the rate to 8.75% last week from 8.50% in a bid to curb inflation and support the rupiah.   

Earlier Friday, Economics Minister Aburizal Bakrie said central bank intervention would only be "temporarily" effective, and that pressure on the rupiah would continue if Indonesia doesn't reduce its fuel imports.   

Later, Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Aslim Tajuddin blamed the rupiah's fall on "external factors," including soaring global oil prices and the upward trend in U.S. interest rates.   

"Bank Indonesia is ready to intervene (to support the rupiah) if it is necessary and will continue to monitor fluctuations in the (currency) market," Aslim said. He also said intervention had managed to reduce volatility in the currency market.   

Aslim said Indonesia's macroeconomic fundamentals remain sound; but he said that for a stronger rupiah, the country needs more exports, an improved investment climate and reduced imports of consumer goods and fuel.   

An Asia-based syndicate banker with a large U.S. house said that if the rupiah stays weak or weakens further, investors will likely lose their appetite for Indonesian U.S.-dollar corporate bonds - both in the primary and secondary markets - as the issuers' burden of interest payments grows.   

At the same time, rupiah weakness could trigger hedge-fund buying in rupiah-denominated debt, as investors position themselves for a rupiah rebound, he said.   

Dealers said they expect the dollar to continue rising Monday, as companies begin to grow panicky and rush to buy dollars. Dealers said Bank Indonesia will likely try to calm the market by starting the week with aggressive dollar sales to bring it back below IDR10,000.   

"The first thing Bank Indonesia has to do Monday is push the greenback below IDR10,000 to give the impression that its rise to IDR10,000 was only a blip," said a dealer with a local bank. "Otherwise there will be panic dollar buying."   

But such efforts will likely to fail, said Citigroup economist Anton Gunawan.   

"They will try very hard to defend it, but the pressure is so high from dollar-buying by (state-owned oil firm) Pertamina and other corporates that we can still see (the exchange rate) go beyond IDR10,000," Gunawan said.   

The dollar could linger above IDR10,000 for a month, meeting strong resistance at the IDR10,200 mark, Gunawan said.   

To provide long-term support for the rupiah, Gunawan said, the government and the central bank need to raise the benchmark Bank Indonesia rate and cut fuel price subsidies, he said.   

ABN Amro Bank's regional head of sovereign and foreign exchange strategy warned that Bank Indonesia's dollar-selling to support the rupiah won't work, and is bleeding foreign exchange reserves to potentially dangerous levels.

title: Asia Benchmark Bonds Weaker, Oil Worries Take Shape
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Yield spreads on Asian U.S. dollar bonds widened slightly this week, with Indonesian credits by far the worst performers as investors turned bearish on the country's growth prospects in the face of rising oil prices.   

Looking ahead, analysts said that spreads could widen further if economic data show any signs that oil prices, which remain above $60 a barrel, are hurting economic activity and, more specifically, company profits.   

While oil companies clearly benefit from high oil prices, others for whom oil is a cost - such as airlines and power companies - could suffer.   

"September will be quite a critical month," said Dilip Shahani, head of fixed-income research at HSBC. "Once there's a suggestion of a global slowdown, there will be knock-on effects on assumptions for corporate earnings."   

Though analysts say a slowdown is unlikely to create outright defaults, declining company profitability would lead investors to demand a higher risk premium to hold corporate credit, pushing out spreads between yields on corporate debt and U.S. Treasurys.   

The widening in the broader market this week was modest. JPMorgan's Asia Credit Index composite rose only three basis points to 140 basis points.   

But the Indonesian component of the index widened 23 basis points in the week ending Thursday to a 290-basis-point spread over U.S. Treasurys. Over the same time period, the price of five-year Indonesian credit default swaps, which protect against an issuer's inability to pay, widened to 255-280 basis points from a bid price of 230 basis points.   

Elsewhere in the market, the usually heavily traded benchmark bonds from Hutchison Whampoa Ltd. (0013.HK) were quoted at 119-115 basis points over U.S. Treasurys midday Friday, wider than the 113-110 basis point spread quoted a week earlier.   

Bucking the trend were PCCW Ltd.'s (PCW) 2011 bonds for which the spread tightened toward the end of the week and quoted a basis point tighter Friday at 116-106 basis points from Thursday. The move followed PCCW's first-half earnings report, which showed a declining pace of market-share loss in its fixed-line division.   

"There's nothing to be really happy about (in the PCCW earnings), but it's not bad either," said Vijay Chander, senior credit analyst at BNP Paribas in Hong Kong. "PCCW still has some way to go before they become a growth company and can offer returns to shareholders."   


 
   High Oil Prices Trouble Indonesia 
    

Concerns about Indonesia stem mostly from the impact of rising oil prices, which are particularly harmful for developing economies as fuel isn't used as efficiently as in industrialized economies and they lack extensive buffers to cushion the shock.   

In Indonesia's case, the increased cost of importing oil has put downward pressure on the currency, forcing Bank Indonesia to spend foreign exchange reserves to stem the rupiah's fall. So far it hasn't had much success and many expect the dollar will push above the key psychological level of IDR10,000. In such an environment, investors are naturally nervous.   

Late Friday, the U.S. dollar was trading at IDR9,985 after Bank Indonesia intervened to support the rupiah, selling more of its dwindling supply of U.S. dollars between IDR9,985 and IDR9,990, according to traders.   

"In Indonesia, (oil is) a problem," said HSBC's Shahani. The rise in oil prices is likely neutral in the short term, but it raises the risk that government tax revenues fall as growth slows, he said.   

Indonesia's central bank is in a difficult position. If it hikes rates to maintain price stability and support the rupiah, it wins credibility at the expense of slower growth in the short term. If Bank Indonesia does nothing, the currency will likely continue to fall, lifting inflation and sapping growth.   

"At the moment, people are sitting on the fence," Shahani said. If Bank Indonesia does hike rates enough to get inflation under control, the local debt market could see a bull flattening as the market prices out some of the risk of holding longer-dated IDR-denominated bonds, he added.   

Most analysts expect the central bank's main interest rate to reach 9.75% by year end from 8.75% now.   

On the other hand, a persistently weaker rupiah would likely prompt some portfolio shift out of local debt and into Indonesian U.S. dollar bonds.   

"Paradoxically, people may buy (Indonesian) U.S. dollar bonds if the rupiah weakens," said BNP's Chander.

title: FX  ASIA:Reserves Not Enough To Support Indonesian Rupiah
text:
By Phelim Kyne and I Made Sentana 
     A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
    

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia should aggressively raise interest rates and remove obstacles to inward flows of capital to avert a hemorrhage in the country's foreign- exchange reserves, which have been deployed to support a weakening rupiah, analysts say.   

The prediction follows intervention by Indonesia's central bank for a second business day in a row Thursday to support the currency, which fell to a fresh 41-month (low against the U.S. dollar.   

Bank Indonesia sold dollars at IDR9,975, according to market participants to stop the greenback from surging above what dealers say is a key "psychological threshold" of IDR10,000.   

The intervention gave the rupiah some traction. The dollar closed at IDR9,950, down from both an intraday high of IDR9,975 and Tuesday's close of IDR9,920   

But intervention to support the currency has so far cost the central bank at least $5 billion since April and has failed to trim a more than 5% slide in the rupiah against the U.S. dollar since the beginning of the year.   

Some say the rupiah purchases aren't sustainable and a broader course of action is need to support the currency.   

Bank Indonesia's intervention poses a serious threat to the country's foreign-exchange reserves, said Irene Cheung, ABN Amro Bank's regional head of sovereign and foreign-exchange strategy.   

Despite the expense of supporting the currency, Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Aslim Tadjudin told Dow Jones Newswires that he hoped the dollar wouldn't hit the IDR10,000 mark and that the central bank will continue to intervene "if necessary" to defend the unit. He didn't elaborate further.   

Indonesia's 2006 budget, unveiled Monday, forecast an erosion in foreign exchange reserves to $27.1 billion by the end of next year from $37.4 billion in March. Currently, the reserves stand at $32.5 billion.   

"It appears that the central bank has resolved to cap the USD/IDR at below the 10,000 mark...(so) in our view the economy runs the risk of still slower growth and sharply lower foreign reserves," ABN AMRO's Cheung said in a research note.   

Cheung expects that the central bank will raise interest rates to support the currency and forecasts that the one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia rate or the benchmark Bank Indonesia rate will rise to as high as 9.75% in the next six months to bolster the rupiah.   

The central bank last week hiked the Bank Indonesia rate to 8.75% from 8.50%.   

Record-high global oil prices are in part to blame for the rupiah's fall and are playing havoc with Indonesia's macroeconomic stability. September Nymex global crude oil prices were up 35 cents to $63.60 at 0924 GMT Thursday.   


 
   USD/IDR10,000 Imminent Without Policy Initiatives 
    

Surging oil prices have fueled an acceleration in Indonesia's inflation to 7.84% on-year in July from 7.42% in June, which has weighed on the rupiah and slowed economic growth in the second quarter to 5.54% on-year from 6.19% on-year in the first three months of 2005.   

The rupiah has also suffered as the U.S. dollar has strengthened against major currencies cross Asia.   

"Bank Indonesia's intervention reduced the dollar's gains, but its upward trend remains intact," a dealer with a domestic commercial bank said.   

The dollar is likely to break the IDR10,000 mark by early September unless there is urgent monetary and macroeconomic policy moves to stem the rupiah's slide, said Standard Chartered economist Fauzi Ichsan.   

"The government and Bank Indonesia need to do the right thing by introducing the right policy package including hiking interest rates....to more than 10% to make it meaningful." Ichsan said.   

The government also needs to open Indonesia's choked inflows of dollars by reviving an official state firm privatization program, he said. The government should also fast-track other initiatives to increase investment injections into the economy, he added.   

Indonesia's official 2005 budget calls for revenue of IDR3.5 trillion from stake share sales this year, but analysts say the government has effectively sidelined the program.   

If those policies are put in place, the dollar could fall to IDR9,500 by the end of next year, slightly higher than an official budget projection of an average IDR9,400 for all of 2006, Ichsan said.   

The measures should include rigorous enforcement of a government regulation that requires exporters to repatriate foreign-exchange earnings, said Bank Mandiri's (BMRI.JK) chief economist, Martin Panggabean   

But enforcing compliance with that rule will be difficult, ABN Amro's Cheung suggested, and require sterner policy measures.   

"In this environment of a falling rupiah, exporters would even be more tempted to keep their dollar receipts overseas," she said.   


 
     Regional Currency Swap Deals Unlikely To Help 
    

Cheung instead urged a follow-up to a March 1 average 29% hike in fuel prices and an "appropriate adjustment" in the rupiah's value to protect the country's foreign exchange reserves. Cheung didn't elaborate on what the "appropriate" level should be.   

Failure to avert a decline in the rupiah to IDR10,000 against the greenback would create a dangerous "domino effect" of accelerating inflation and ever-higher interest rates that would choke economic growth, said Juniman a senior economist at Bank Internasional Indonesia (BNII.JK). He, like many Indonesians, has only one name,   

"It's an important psychological mark because when (the dollar/rupiah rate) hits 10,000, you can expect marked shrinkage in volume because the supply of dollars will dry up...(but) pressure on the rupiah will remain," Standard Chartered's Ichsan said.   

Indonesia is also unlikely to gain any assistance from currency-swap agreements between Association of Southeast Asian Nation members and Japan, China and South Korea.   

The group, known as Asean+3, in May agreed to increase the size of the program, under the Chiang Mai Initiative, which was set up following the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis to help cash-strapped countries defend their currencies in times of crisis.   

But Indonesia lacks the requisite International Monetary Fund program or equivalent that potential recipients of the Initiative require, Ichsan said. Indonesia last year ended participation in an IMF economic bailout program begun after the financial crisis.   

Still, the rupiah may yet strengthen as external factors that have so heavily weighted on the currency in recent months weaken, said BNP Paribas senior currency analyst Thio Chin Loo.   

"Oil prices have slowed quite sharply overnight and if that continues, it should alleviate some the pressure on the rupiah," Thio said. "If oil prices decline, the only remaining risk is a rising dollar, which could cause the rupiah to test IDR10,000 (against the dollar)."

title: DJ Indonesia Rupiah Ends Down Despite Ctrl Bank Moves
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah closed below the key level of IDR10,000 to the U.S. dollar late Friday, despite repeated central bank intervention to defend the currency. Dealers expect the dollar to continue rising Monday as companies with dollar exposures get jittery and jump on the dollar-buying bandwagon.   

The dollar closed at IDR10,000, versus the previous close of IDR9,950, after going as high as IDR10,010 during the day. The close was the highest since March 8, 2002, when it ended at IDR10,015.   

Bank Indonesia aggressively sold dollars for the third straight day in a failed attempt to keep the unit below the threshold of IDR10,000. State banks also sold dollars, keeping the unit below IDR10,000 for a time, but market players eventually pushed it over the top after Bank Indonesia ended its daily trading activity.   

The central bank usually finishes dealing at 0900 GMT, but interbank players sometimes continue trading until there are no further quotations in the market.   

'Players continued buying dollars until the last minute since they expect more foreign investors to exchange their rupiah into dollars Monday,' said a dealer with a foreign bank.   

Market participants were also expecting increased dollar demand Monday after the local stock market Friday fell 1.1%, the sixth consecutive day of losses.   

The Jakarta Stock Exchange's Composite Index fell 12.346 points to 1087.953 Friday, up from its intraday low of 1081.724 on expectations the falling rupiah might prompt an increase in the benchmark Bank Indonesia rate.   

The central bank increased the rate to 8.75% last week from 8.50% in a bid to curb inflation and support the rupiah.   

Earlier Friday, Economics Minister Aburizal Bakrie said central bank intervention would only be 'temporarily' effective, and that pressure on the rupiah would continue if Indonesia doesn't reduce its fuel imports.   

Later, Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Aslim Tajuddin blamed the rupiah's fall on 'external factors,' including soaring global oil prices and the upward trend in U.S. interest rates.   

'Bank Indonesia is ready to intervene (to support the rupiah) if it is necessary and will continue to monitor fluctuations in the (currency) market,' Aslim said. He also said intervention had managed to reduce volatility in the currency market.   

Aslim said Indonesia's macroeconomic fundamentals remain sound; but he said that for a stronger rupiah, the country needs more exports, an improved investment climate and reduced imports of consumer goods and fuel.   

An Asia-based syndicate banker with a large U.S. house said that if the rupiah stays weak or weakens further, investors will likely lose their appetite for Indonesian U.S.-dollar corporate bonds - both in the primary and secondary markets - as the issuers' burden of interest payments grows.   

At the same time, rupiah weakness could trigger hedge-fund buying in rupiah-denominated debt, as investors position themselves for a rupiah rebound, he said.   

Dealers said they expect the dollar to continue rising Monday, as companies begin to grow panicky and rush to buy dollars. Dealers said Bank Indonesia will likely try to calm the market by starting the week with aggressive dollar sales to bring it back below IDR10,000.   

'The first thing Bank Indonesia has to do Monday is push the greenback below IDR10,000 to give the impression that its rise to IDR10,000 was only a blip,' said a dealer with a local bank. 'Otherwise there will be panic dollar buying.'   

But such efforts will likely to fail, said Citigroup economist Anton Gunawan.   

'They will try very hard to defend it, but the pressure is so high from dollar-buying by (state-owned oil firm) Pertamina and other corporates that we can still see (the exchange rate) go beyond IDR10,000,' Gunawan said.   

The dollar could linger above IDR10,000 for a month, meeting strong resistance at the IDR10,200 mark, Gunawan said.   

To provide long-term support for the rupiah, Gunawan said, the government and the central bank need to raise the benchmark Bank Indonesia rate and cut fuel price subsidies, he said.   

ABN Amro Bank's regional head of sovereign and foreign exchange strategy warned that Bank Indonesia's dollar-selling to support the rupiah won't work, and is bleeding foreign exchange reserves to potentially dangerous levels.   

'If (Bank Indonesia) wants to just defend the currency, in the end they'll lose,' Irene Cheung said.   

The central bank should instead let the dollar rise to an 'appropriate value,' she said, without offering a specific projection.   

'If they allow the rupiah to adjust to a more appropriate level, it will mean less pain for the economy ... otherwise we're looking at foreign reserves sinking to $27.1 billion by the end of next year, which is dangerous for Indonesia's ratings.'

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Weaker as equity sell-off bites
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 19 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were knocked down against the dollar on Friday by a sell-off in stocks, with the Taiwan dollar at a seven-month trough and Indonesia's rupiah hitting a 3-½ year low near the pivotal 10,000 per dollar level.  

Equity markets weakened partly on persistent worries that high oil prices are squeezing company profits and consumer spending. This set the tone for regional currencies.  

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=TP> eased about a quarter of a percent from Thursday's close to 32.19 per U.S. dollar, its weakest level since mid-January.  

The South Korean won <KRW=><KRW=KTFC> eased as much as 0.7 percent to 1,025.8 per dollar, its lowest level in nearly three weeks, while the Singapore dollar <SGD=D4> fell more than half a percent to a three-week trough at 1.6710 per U.S. dollar.  

"The U.S. dollar should go up slowly because stock markets in Asia are not doing so well," said a Singapore-based trader.  

"The market has been short of dollars in the last couple of weeks, so there is a covering of positions."  

Foreign funds have been net sellers of Taiwan stocks all week. They sold a net 6.127 billion Taiwan dollars on Friday -- the heaviest selling so far this month. In South Korea, foreign investors continued to offload local stocks, taking their total net sales this week to around 334 billion won.  

AILING RUPIAH  

The rupiah <IDR=> touched a low of about 9,995 per dollar but recovered slightly after traders suspected the central bank was intervening to support the ailing currency.  

Indonesia's central bank said on Friday it will continue dollar-selling intervention to support the rupiah, which has shed almost seven percent against the dollar this year.  

Costly oil, which state oil firm Pertamina has been forced to import in increasing amounts to meet a domestic shortfall, and outflows of capital have been key reasons for the rupiah's slide.  

The latest sell-off comes as traders target the psychological 10,000 rupiah per dollar level, after the currency failed to hold onto important chart support in the 9,900 area earlier this week.  

"Until the central bank responds more vigorously with monetary policy, it will struggle to achieve its currency objectives," said HSBC currency strategist Richard Yetsenga.  

The interest rate on one-month central bank certificates <BISBI01> has risen by more than 130 basis points this year. Still, real interest rates are barely positive after taking into account annual inflation running close to 8 percent.  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> weakened about a fifth of a percent to a 1-½ week low of 56.05 per dollar, but pulled away from that level thanks to commercial demand for pesos and technical support, dealers said.  

Traders said optimism the Philippine Supreme Court would lift a freeze on a key sales tax, perhaps as soon as next week, prevented a bigger peso sell-off this week. The sales tax is the centrepiece of the government's economic reforms.  

The peso has shed about 0.7 percent against the dollar this week, while the rupiah has lost almost 2 percent and the Singapore and South Korean currencies have eased about 1 percent each.

title: UPDATE 1-Bank  Indonesia  to keep  intervening , govt has doubts
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 19 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank said on Friday it will continue dollar-selling intervention to support the ailing rupiah, even after the chief economic minister said it was not effective and called for fuel subsidy cuts instead.   

Pressured by rising oil costs, the rupiah <IDR=> has fallen almost 7 percent against the dollar this year, and on Friday it hit a 3-½ year low near the pivotal 10,000 per dollar level.   

"I saw that the intervention is still effective. There is no strong macro and fundamental reason for the rupiah to get weaker," Aslim Tadjuddin, a deputy governor of Bank Indonesia, told Reuters.   

"We are in the market. We always monitor the fluctuations in exchange rates and we are going to intervene if necessary," Tadjuddin said in a telephone interview.   

But Aburizal Bakrie, the government's chief economic minister, said earlier that it would be better in the long run if hefty domestic fuel subsidies were cut.   

"Intervention is only a temporary thing. The question is whether we should do all that? I think it is more important to reduce the subsidy," Bakrie told reporters.   

"With such huge fuel subsides, the rupiah will weaken. The situation is that we need to keep on supporting subsidies so we need to keep on buying dollars. If we keep on purchasing dollars, the dollar will become stronger," he added.   

The fuel subsidy and Indonesia's import system entail oil and energy product purchases that must be made in dollars by the state oil company, and which add to the government's already massive debt.   

OIL WOES   

Despite its membership of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries, Indonesia has become a net crude importer due to various problems causing a decline in production.   

President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono has warned that should world oil prices remain around current levels, fuel subsidies for 2005 could cost more than 140 trillion rupiah ($14.2 billion), nearly double the stated amount in the budget.   

Analysts and traders have said dollar buying of up to $1 billion each month by state oil company Pertamina to finance oil imports is putting a significant burden on the currency.   

The government and central bank have put in place several measures to defend the rupiah, including restricting Pertamina's dollar buying to appointed state banks.   

The central bank has also raised benchmark interest rates in to contain rising inflation and help the currency. The interest rate on one-month central bank certificates (SBI) <BISBI01> has risen by more than 130 basis points this year.   

At the last auction, the one-month SBI certificate yielded 8.75 percent, to be in line with the central bank's newly introduced reference interest rate.   

Some analysts say Indonesia needs to raise interest rates further and keep lowering domestic oil subsidies to halt the slide in the currency.
