title: Indonesian rupiah needs rate rise support-analysts
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 19 (Reuters) - Indonesia needs to raise interest rates further and keep lowering domestic oil subsidies to halt the slide in the rupiah, as its dollar-selling intervention is not achieving results, analysts said on Friday.   

The rupiah <IDR=> weakened to a 3-½ year low of 9,995 a dollar on Friday, close to the pivotal 10,000-per-dollar level. Losses in the past week have exceeded 2 percent, even after the central bank spent some of its foreign currency reserves trying to support the currency.   

Bank Indonesia has been intervening heavily this week. After confirming the intervention on Thursday, Bank Indonesia spokesman Halim Alamsyah said the central bank was open to other options to defend the currency.   

"That's a sign that the ammunition is running low without really producing the desired effect," said Tim Condon, head of research at ING in Singapore.   

"They fundamentally have a wrong policy mix, a rupiah-unfriendly policy mix," he said.   

The country's foreign exchange reserves stood at $32.5 billion on August 5 -- covering about 7 months of imports -- after it had spent $5 billion in 3 months supporting emerging Asia's worst performing currency this year.   

The mounting cost of oil, which state oil firm Pertamina has been forced to import in increasing amounts to meet a domestic shortfall, and outflows of capital have been primary reasons for the rupiah's slide.   

In early July, Bank Indonesia said Pertamina would get dollars to pay for its oil imports from the government's account with the central bank, hoping to ease pressure on the rupiah, but the oil firm has since been spotted buying dollars in the market.   

Analysts said Indonesia could cut subsidies on domestic fuel further, thereby encouraging consumers to become more efficient users of expensive oil and easing pressure on the budget. Indonesia's chief economic minister Aburizal Bakrie said on Friday the effectiveness of intervention was temporary and it was more important to reduce the subsidies.   

RATES   

Bank Indonesia adopted a more transparent inflation-targeting policy last month, changing its main policy tool to the rate on its one-month paper <ID1MSBI=BIIA>. It even surprised markets by raising that rate by a quarter point to 8.75 percent on August 9.   

Analysts said the central bank needs to do a lot more of policy tightening if it wants to conserve its dwindling reserves, with real interest rates barely positive after taking into account annual inflation running close to 8 percent.   

"Their option is really to switch to rate tightening and they are increasingly moving in that direction," said Claudio Piron, currency strategist with JPMorgan Chase.   

Indonesia tended to have a relatively higher pass-through of a weaker currency into inflation, and hence it was imperative Bank Indonesia prevent the rupiah from falling too much, he said.   

In June the central bank imposed restrictions on foreigners' holdings of rupiah onshore and access to hedging instruments.   

"The underlying situation is that there is heavy dollar demand and trying to deal with that through foreign exchange controls will not help," he said, referring to the possibility of other restrictions being imposed on rupiah trade.   

Piron said the relationship between rising oil prices and the depletion in Indonesia's currency reserves was strengthening, and every dollar rise in the Dubai crude <DUB-1M-A> corresponded to an almost $300 million fall in reserves.

title: FX  ASIA:Reserves Not Enough To Support Indonesian Rupiah
text:
By Phelim Kyne and I Made Sentana 
     A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
    

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia should aggressively raise interest rates and remove obstacles to inward flows of capital to avert a hemorrhage in the country's foreign- exchange reserves, which have been deployed to support a weakening rupiah, analysts say.   

The prediction follows intervention by Indonesia's central bank for a second business day in a row Thursday to support the currency, which fell to a fresh 41-month (low against the U.S. dollar.   

Bank Indonesia sold dollars at IDR9,975, according to market participants to stop the greenback from surging above what dealers say is a key "psychological threshold" of IDR10,000.   

The intervention gave the rupiah some traction. The dollar closed at IDR9,950, down from both an intraday high of IDR9,975 and Tuesday's close of IDR9,920   

But intervention to support the currency has so far cost the central bank at least $5 billion since April and has failed to trim a more than 5% slide in the rupiah against the U.S. dollar since the beginning of the year.   

Some say the rupiah purchases aren't sustainable and a broader course of action is need to support the currency.   

Bank Indonesia's intervention poses a serious threat to the country's foreign-exchange reserves, said Irene Cheung, ABN Amro Bank's regional head of sovereign and foreign-exchange strategy.   

Despite the expense of supporting the currency, Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Aslim Tadjudin told Dow Jones Newswires that he hoped the dollar wouldn't hit the IDR10,000 mark and that the central bank will continue to intervene "if necessary" to defend the unit. He didn't elaborate further.   

Indonesia's 2006 budget, unveiled Monday, forecast an erosion in foreign exchange reserves to $27.1 billion by the end of next year from $37.4 billion in March. Currently, the reserves stand at $32.5 billion.   

"It appears that the central bank has resolved to cap the USD/IDR at below the 10,000 mark...(so) in our view the economy runs the risk of still slower growth and sharply lower foreign reserves," ABN AMRO's Cheung said in a research note.   

Cheung expects that the central bank will raise interest rates to support the currency and forecasts that the one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia rate or the benchmark Bank Indonesia rate will rise to as high as 9.75% in the next six months to bolster the rupiah.   

The central bank last week hiked the Bank Indonesia rate to 8.75% from 8.50%.   

Record-high global oil prices are in part to blame for the rupiah's fall and are playing havoc with Indonesia's macroeconomic stability. September Nymex global crude oil prices were up 35 cents to $63.60 at 0924 GMT Thursday.   


 
   USD/IDR10,000 Imminent Without Policy Initiatives 
    

Surging oil prices have fueled an acceleration in Indonesia's inflation to 7.84% on-year in July from 7.42% in June, which has weighed on the rupiah and slowed economic growth in the second quarter to 5.54% on-year from 6.19% on-year in the first three months of 2005.   

The rupiah has also suffered as the U.S. dollar has strengthened against major currencies cross Asia.   

"Bank Indonesia's intervention reduced the dollar's gains, but its upward trend remains intact," a dealer with a domestic commercial bank said.   

The dollar is likely to break the IDR10,000 mark by early September unless there is urgent monetary and macroeconomic policy moves to stem the rupiah's slide, said Standard Chartered economist Fauzi Ichsan.   

"The government and Bank Indonesia need to do the right thing by introducing the right policy package including hiking interest rates....to more than 10% to make it meaningful." Ichsan said.   

The government also needs to open Indonesia's choked inflows of dollars by reviving an official state firm privatization program, he said. The government should also fast-track other initiatives to increase investment injections into the economy, he added.   

Indonesia's official 2005 budget calls for revenue of IDR3.5 trillion from stake share sales this year, but analysts say the government has effectively sidelined the program.   

If those policies are put in place, the dollar could fall to IDR9,500 by the end of next year, slightly higher than an official budget projection of an average IDR9,400 for all of 2006, Ichsan said.   

The measures should include rigorous enforcement of a government regulation that requires exporters to repatriate foreign-exchange earnings, said Bank Mandiri's (BMRI.JK) chief economist, Martin Panggabean   

But enforcing compliance with that rule will be difficult, ABN Amro's Cheung suggested, and require sterner policy measures.   

"In this environment of a falling rupiah, exporters would even be more tempted to keep their dollar receipts overseas," she said.   


 
     Regional Currency Swap Deals Unlikely To Help 
    

Cheung instead urged a follow-up to a March 1 average 29% hike in fuel prices and an "appropriate adjustment" in the rupiah's value to protect the country's foreign exchange reserves. Cheung didn't elaborate on what the "appropriate" level should be.   

Failure to avert a decline in the rupiah to IDR10,000 against the greenback would create a dangerous "domino effect" of accelerating inflation and ever-higher interest rates that would choke economic growth, said Juniman a senior economist at Bank Internasional Indonesia (BNII.JK). He, like many Indonesians, has only one name,   

"It's an important psychological mark because when (the dollar/rupiah rate) hits 10,000, you can expect marked shrinkage in volume because the supply of dollars will dry up...(but) pressure on the rupiah will remain," Standard Chartered's Ichsan said.   

Indonesia is also unlikely to gain any assistance from currency-swap agreements between Association of Southeast Asian Nation members and Japan, China and South Korea.   

The group, known as Asean+3, in May agreed to increase the size of the program, under the Chiang Mai Initiative, which was set up following the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis to help cash-strapped countries defend their currencies in times of crisis.   

But Indonesia lacks the requisite International Monetary Fund program or equivalent that potential recipients of the Initiative require, Ichsan said. Indonesia last year ended participation in an IMF economic bailout program begun after the financial crisis.   

Still, the rupiah may yet strengthen as external factors that have so heavily weighted on the currency in recent months weaken, said BNP Paribas senior currency analyst Thio Chin Loo.   

"Oil prices have slowed quite sharply overnight and if that continues, it should alleviate some the pressure on the rupiah," Thio said. "If oil prices decline, the only remaining risk is a rising dollar, which could cause the rupiah to test IDR10,000 (against the dollar)."

title: Bk  Indonesia  Dep: To  Intervene  In  FX  Mkt "If Necessary"
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia will intervene in the local foreign exchange market "if necessary", but it has no plan to introduce new regulations to defend the rupiah, Aslim Tadjudin, a deputy governor at the central bank, said Thursday.   

"We are monitoring the rupiah and there is no doubt that we are trying to defend the rupiah," Aslim told Dow Jones Newswires in a telephone interview.   

The rupiah fell to a fresh 41-month low of IDR9,935 to the U.S. dollar at 0212 GMT Thursday versus its previous close of IDR9,920 as high oil prices continued to hurt sentiment. Capital outflows from the local stock market, and dollar purchases by companies to hedge their offshore debts, also weighed. [ 18-08-05 0224GMT ]   

Aslim declined to say if the central bank had already sold dollars Thursday.   

"We have done a lot" in efforts to defend the rupiah, he said when asked if Bank Indonesia had any plan to introduce new regulations in the near future to help the currency.   

He referred to regulations which Bank Indonesia introduced in June to limit dollar-rupiah transactions by foreigners; the steps also limited PT Pertamina's dollar purchases in the market, and asked state companies to repatriate their export revenues.   

In addition, the central bank in late July raised the one-month dollar deposit rate that the government guarantees for August to 3% from 2.75% to discourage people from moving their dollars out of Indonesia.   

"The central bank will monitor the development of the Jakarta Interbank Offered Dollar Rate to decide whether it will raise the guarantee rate or not at the end of the month," Aslim said.   

He added that the central bank would also request banks in Jakarta to stop asking depositors to change their dollars into rupiah when they wanted to deposit dollars locally. Banks usually convert depositors' dollars into rupiah at less favorable exchange rates in such cases.   

"Banks here should stop doing that if they want to attract customers," Aslim said. He added that the central bank, however, would not issue a ruling on the matter as "it's a matter of business strategy."   

Aslim repeated that the main culprits for the rupiah's weakness were "external factors" such as high oil prices and the dollar's rise against the yen early Thursday.   

Some dealers said it was only a matter of time before the dollar reached IDR10,000.   

Aslim said he hoped the dollar wouldn't rise to that psychologically important level.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Mostly steady, rupiah hits 3-½ year low
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 18 (Reuters) - Indonesia's rupiah hit a fresh 3-½ year low on Thursday but recovered slightly after central bank intervention, while most Asian currencies were little moved against the dollar.   

A retreat in oil prices, which hit a record high of $67.10 last Friday, supported regional currencies, hurt this week by worries that firm oil prices would dent economic growth.   

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> <SGD=D4> and South Korean won <KRW=> <KRW=KTFC> pulled away from two-week lows hit against the dollar on Wednesday. The Thai baht <THB=> was up about a fifth of a percent at 41.19 per dollar -- above Wednesday's almost two-week trough at 41.33.   

The rupiah <IDR=> hogged the spotlight as it stepped closer to the key psychological level of 10,000 rupiah per dollar.   

Domestic demand for dollars pushed the rupiah to a 3-½ year low of about 9,980, before the central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market to support the battered currency.   

A Bank Indonesia spokesman confirmed the intervention.   

Seeking to support the rupiah, the central bank also said it would offer four-day instruments carrying an interest rate of 5.75 percent on Thursday to absorb excess rupiah liquidity.   

"Everyone is focusing on the 10,000 level, whether or not it goes and when," said Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore.   

"Intervention will be an obstacle to this in the short term. But more weakness is likely -- you have a balance of payments deterioration because Indonesia is a net oil importer, capital inflows are not picking up the slack, while interest rates are too low," Henderson said.   

The rupiah has lost more than 6 percent of its value since the start of the year, due mainly to rising inflation and soaring oil prices, which have increased dollar buying to finance oil imports. It has shed about 1.5 percent this week.   

RINGGIT WEAKER   

Malaysia's ringgit <MYR=> dipped to its weakest level since the currency was unpegged from the dollar a month ago, pressured by foreign investors selling local assets, traders said.   

They said the ringgit eased to a low of 3.7695 per dollar, taking it to its weakest level since July 22 -- the day after Malaysia abandoned the ringgit's peg to the U.S. currency.   

"Initially, when investors bought the ringgit at 3.8 they parked the money in ringgit assets, in bonds and equities," said one dealer in Kuala Lumpur.   

"When the currency tested the 3.7450 area it looked quite strong but didn't move further, so most investors sold their bonds and converted their ringgit back into dollars."   

Asian currencies were also likely to be held back by equity flows into Japan from the rest of Asia, dealers said.   

Foreign investors bought a net 721.9 billion yen ($6.58 billion) of Japanese stocks last week, up from 495 billion yen the previous week, official data from Japan showed on Thursday. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends At 41-Mo Low On High Oil Prices
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah closed at a 41-month low against the dollar Tuesday as high oil prices and capital outflows from the local stock market hurt the local unit, dealers said.   

The dollar closed at IDR9,920 versus Monday's close of IDR9,885. This was the greenback's highest close since March 19, 2002 when it closed at IDR9,980.   

It touched an intraday high of IDR9,925 earlier in the day, but suspected Bank Indonesia intervention capped the dollar's rise, dealers said.   

Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said Tuesday the central bank is always ready to help the rupiah, which is being hit by "external factors" such as rising oil prices in the global market and rising U.S. rates. Abdullah, however, didn't mention whether the central bank had sold dollars Tuesday as dealers suspected.   

"Rising oil prices still roiled sentiment on the rupiah," a dealer with a foreign bank said.   

Dealers said capital outflows from the Indonesian stock market also contributed to the rupiah's slide. The Jakarta Stock Exchange's main index fell 0.4% to a five-week low after a 3% drop Monday.   

Elsewhere in the money market, the weighted average rate of Bank Indonesia's on-month SBI notes rose to 8.75% in a weekly auction Tuesday from 8.71%. The SBI rate is now at the same level as the benchmark BI rate.   

Dealers said the central bank is under pressure to raise the benchmark rate again, likely next month, to help the rupiah and to cool inflation.   

Dealers expect the dollar to trade between IDR9,810 and IDR9,950 Thursday. The local currency market will be closed Wednesday for Indonesia's Independence Day.

title: INTERVIEW: Indonesia Fuel Subsidies Blowing Out Budget
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia must raise fuel prices by early 2006 in order to ease the pressure of fuel price subsidies on the cash-strapped government, Indonesia's Vice President Jusuf Kalla said recently.   

Record high global oil prices above $60 per barrel have created an unbearable subsidies burden for the government, Kalla told Dow Jones Newswires.   

"I think all of us understand that the price of oil is (around) $62 per barrel, which means our subsidies are too high right now," Kalla said.   

"We can't afford them and that's why we should increase (fuel) prices."   

The government will increase fuel prices "no later than early next year," he said, without elaborating. That suggests a retreat from statements Kalla made Wednesday indicating a fuel price increase before the end of 2005.   

Kalla's comments reflect how record-high global crude oil prices are forcing the government of President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono to consider the politically risky move of raising fuel prices less than a year after a highly unpopular average 29% fuel price increase on March 1.   

Fuel subsidies cost the government around $7.4 billion in 2004, or 3% of gross domestic product. Indonesia's Minister of Finance Jusuf Anwar said last month that fuel subsidies may rise to IDR123 trillion this year, well above the IDR78 trillion estimated in the official 2005 budget.   

Government assurances that it would keep price subsidies for kerosene, the fuel of Indonesia's poor, dissipated scattered public protests that greeted the March fuel price increase.   

But a second price hike may fan popular discontent with Yudhoyono's administration into large-scale and potentially destabilizing public protests that plagued the administration of his predecessor, Megawati Sukarnoputri.   

The size of the pending fuel price increase depends on factors such as fluctuations in the price of crude oil and the value of the rupiah against the U.S. dollar, Kalla said.   


 
   Cash Subsidies For Poor To Deter Protests 
    

The government also blunted criticism of the March fuel price increase by promising to direct the bulk of proceeds from the hike to fund social programs for the estimated 16.5% of Indonesia's people who live under the official poverty line. Indonesia's poverty line stands at around IDR130,000 per month for city dwellers and around IDR100,000 per month for rural residents.   

Kalla said that the government hopes to dampen the potential for such demonstrations of popular discontent with the pending fuel price increases through direct cash subsidies to the country's poor, prior to the increase.   

"Of course there (will be) protests," he said.   

"(But) local governments, our statistics office...are doing a census of poor people and then we'll directly subsidize the people and after that we'll increase the price of (fuel)," Kalla said.   

The government is also facing a cabinet shuffle before the end of 2005, Kalla said.   

The performance of individual ministers in their first year in office will be carefully evaluated and any possible cabinet post changes will likely occur in October, he said, without elaborating.   

Kalla said a pending peace deal between separatist insurgents and the Indonesian government in tsunami-devastated northwestern Aceh province will likely boost the exploration operations of U.S. petroleum giant ExxonMobil Corp. (XOM), which has oil and liquid natural gas operations in the troubled province.   

Representatives of the government and the Free Aceh Movement, or GAM, will sign an official truce on Aug. 15 in Helsinki, Finland.   

"Exxon of course can explore more (after the peace agreement) and if Exxon explores more, there are taxes and money for the government," Kalla said.   

Kalla indicated that he was uncertain whether the central bank's move Tuesday to raise the benchmark Bank Indonesia rate to 8.75% from 8.50% would achieve one of its desired effects of supporting the rupiah.   


 
   Inadequate Funds For Avian Flu Control 
    

The rupiah's health hinged on factors other than interest rates, including the relative strength of the U.S. dollar and Indonesia's export performance, Kalla said.   

The rupiah has lost around 5% of its value against the U.S. dollar since the beginning of the year and Bank Indonesia has sacrificed $5 billion, or 14% of total foreign exchange reserves, in interventions to support the currency.   

Kalla said Indonesia's government is unable to reallocate budgetary resources to bolster the Ministry of Agriculture's losing battle to combat H5N1 avian flu outbreaks among domestic poultry stocks.   

Minister of Agriculture Anton Apriyantono said last month his ministry can't undertake international-standard culling of poultry in H5N1 outbreak areas due to a lack of government funds to compensate farmers for their losses.   

International concerns about Indonesia as a potential weak link in the global effort to prevent or contain a possible future outbreak of a more deadly human variant of H5N1 have risen since the country reported its first three human fatalities from the illness last month.   

Avian flu has killed 61 people in Asia and devastated poultry stocks in the region since late 2003.   

"We haven't enough budget (funds) if we slaughter (poultry) according to a five-kilometer (affected) area parameter," Kalla said.   

Instead the government supports "selective" poultry culling in areas where H5N1 outbreaks occur, he said.

title: UPDATE: Indonesia Rate Hike Targets Inflation, Oil Price
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia, the central bank, said Tuesday it had hiked its benchmark Bank Indonesia rate to 8.75% from 8.50% to address inflationary pressure driven by rising oil prices.  

"Inflation expectations remain high in the wake of rising oil prices, which could increase (domestic) prices and weaken the rupiah," a Bank Indonesia statement issued late Tuesday said. "The increase in the Bank Indonesia rate is considered to be capable of supporting the continuity of the economic recovery."  

Oil prices have hovered around a record high $60 per barrel in recent months. The September Nymex crude oil price stands at $63.76 per barrel, down 18 cents versus Monday's floor close.  

Surging oil prices have accelerated inflationary pressure in Indonesia, Southeast Asia's sole member of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, as dwindling domestic output has forced the government to steadily increase the proportion of imported oil in its national energy mix.  

But state-owned oil firm Pertamina's (PTM.YY) voracious appetite for dollars to fund imports has contributed to a 5% erosion in the value of the rupiah against the greenback since the beginning of the year.  

Coordinating Minister of the Economy Aburizal Bakrie told reporters Tuesday that declining domestic output will make Indonesia a net crude oil importer for 2005.  

Analysts said the rate increase was overdue and linked to the toll taken on foreign exchange reserves by recent central bank interventions in the foreign currency market to stem a steady slide in the rupiah since the beginning of the year. The rupiah closed at IDR9,795 Tuesday, down from IDR9,772 on Monday.  

"Bank Indonesia has been intervening in the foreign exchange market to support the rupiah and couldn't continue to do that," Standard Chartered Bank economist Fauzi Ichsan told Dow Jones Newswires. "The alternative method to support the rupiah is raise short-term interest rates."  

Analysts Say Rate Hike Overdue  

The increase in the Bank Indonesia rate comes after criticism from analysts who have argued that the bank has hesitated to raise rates due to political rather than macroeconomic concerns.  

Analysts say the central bank has avoided aggressive interest rate increases to address inflation for fear of undermining the government's official gross domestic product growth target of 6.0% in 2005. That projection outpaces last year's 5.4% economic expansion.  

The rupiah has borne the brunt of that monetary policy choice, they say.  

Indonesia's currency has lost 5% of its value since the start of the year, despite the central bank running down its foreign reserves by $5 billion to defend the unit.  

The central bank has recently abandoned an original average IDR9,300 target for 2005 and Bakrie has predicted the unit will average IDR9,750 in the second half of 2005.  

The bank statement said the rate increase also aims to offset the "increased risk to macroeconomic stability" of other outside influences, including rising U.S. Federal Reserve rates and a weakening of major currencies against the U.S. dollar.  

The U.S. central bank's policy rate has risen 225 basis points to 3.25% since June 2004, while the dollar has strengthened markedly against regional currencies in recent weeks. Market participants anticipate that a U.S. Federal Reserve policy meeting later Tuesday may lead to a 25-basis-point increase in the Federal Funds target rate to 3.5%.  

Bank Indonesia's emphasis on the potential domestic economic impact of the rising Fed rate is a welcome proactive move, said Standard Chartered's Ichsan.  

"Many analysts are upwardly revising forecasts of U.S. interest rates to 4% by the end of the year...and think the Fed rate will rise to 4.5% next year," he said.  

This will also prompt Bank Indonesia to "make a move especially when it has been criticized for being behind the curve in raising interest rates," he said.

title: CENTRAL BANK  WATCH: Indonesia Rupiah Defense Ops Failing
text:
By Phelim Kyne 
     A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
   

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia's intervention campaign to stem a slide in the value of the rupiah to help fight inflationary pressures hasn't worked and is unsustainable, analysts say.  

The central bank should instead further tighten monetary policy to beat inflation and support the rupiah, they say.  

Indonesia's currency has lost 5% of its value since the start of the year despite the central bank running down its foreign reserves by $5 billion to defend the unit.  

The central bank has put on a brave face, saying that it has stabilized the currency.  

"We are quite confident that our actions have stabilized (the rupiah)," Bank Indonesia's economic research and monetary policy directorate head, Perry Warjiyo, said Friday.  

But the slide in the currency has delivered a black eye to the government of President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono by both skewering sunny official USD/IDR projections and fueling a hemorrhage in foreign exchange reserves.  

Bank Indonesia Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom said last month that the official USD/IDR target of an average of 9,300 for 2005 was unfeasible.  

Official pessimism about the rupiah deepened last week when Coordinating Minister for the Economy, Aburizal Bakrie, said the currency probably wouldn't rally against the dollar in the second half of 2005 and a USD/IDR average of 9,750 was likely in the same time period.  

The dollar was trading at IDR9,793 at 0445 GMT Tuesday, below a more-than-three-year high of IDR9,870 set on July 5 but well above IDR9,290 at the start of 2005.  

"The central bank has spent nearly USD5 billion - or 14% of its FX reserves - and increased interest rates by 110bps since April 2005 to support the rupiah," UBS said in a recent note. "Yet, the IDR has continued to weaken (and) though FX reserves at $32 billion currently are still adequate, FX interventions of such a scale are obviously not sustainable over the medium-term."  


 
     Interest Rate Hikes Advised 
   

Bank Indonesia has gradually raised its benchmark rate to 8.5% from a record low of 7.32% in May 2004 in response to rising inflationary momentum.  

But some say the central bank needs to be more aggressive.  

UBS predicts the rupiah will further slide to IDR10,000 against the dollar by the end of this year and hit IDR10,600 by the end of 2006 without more aggressive monetary tightening policies in the short term.  

The International Monetary Fund, which guided Indonesia's recovery from the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis, last month also suggested interest rate hikes to contain inflation.  

But such measures are unlikely in the short-to-medium term due to Bank Indonesia's monetary policy direction drift, said JP Morgan Chase economist Sin Ben Ong.  

"We tend to think that the rupiah (weakness) is symptomatic of a central bank that's too lax in running monetary policy," Ong said.  

Rather than risk the political fallout of raising interest rates to dampen the "mild overheating" in the Indonesian economy, Bank Indonesia is opting to address inflationary pressure through foreign exchange, Ong said.  

"The central bank is constrained by political considerations to raise interest rates...so it has intervened in foreign exchange markets," he said. "Bank Indonesia is concerned about (the rupiah's decline) because it has an immediate knock on effect on inflation in two-three months that lasts four to five months."  

Bank Indonesia is candid about the difficult monetary policy balancing act it's pursuing  

"What we are facing now is the dilemma of boosting macro-economic growth and maintaining macro-economic stability," Bank Indonesia's Warjiyo said last week.  


 
   Rupiah Strengthening Requires Investment Surge 
   

There's political wisdom in addressing inflation through foreign exchange rates. The alternative, aggressively raising interest rates, could sabotage an official economic target of 6% on-year growth for 2005.  

Inflationary pressure also increases the threat of noisy public protests about rising prices and potential social instability that dogged Yudhoyono's predecessor, Megawati Sukarnoputri.  

A 29% average hike in fuel prices in March prompted a surge in inflation to 8.12% year-on-year in April. Inflation has since eased to 7.84% on-year in July, but outpaces an upwardly revised inflation target of 7.5% for full-year 2005.  

While the central bank monetary policy juggles social and political stability concerns with macroeconomic realities, analysts suggest that only an injection of desperately-needed foreign investment will give the rupiah decisive traction against the greenback.  

Indonesia's economy needs investment dollars to correct an "imbalance in the system" that is weighing on the rupiah, said Irene Cheung, ABN Amro Bank's regional head of sovereign and foreign-exchange strategy. "I don't see in the near term any positive for the rupiah...(and) I'm concerned about the rupiah until (foreign investment) money starts coming into the country."  

Pallid investor sentiment fueled a 26% on-year decline in approved foreign direct investment to $10.3 billion in 2004.  

But Indonesia's official Investment Coordinating Board said last month that the country recorded a 70% on-year rise in actual FDI to $3.35 billion in the first six months of 2005. Indonesia's pledged FDI surged 71% to $5.93 billion in the same period.  

That data supports UBS' projection that FDI will provide needed support for the rupiah in the months ahead.  

"We remain confident that Indonesia will be able to attract FDI inflows and that residents will repatriate capital over the medium-term, thus providing support to the IDR," the UBS research note said.

title: Bk Indonesia: Has Stabilised Rupiah Exchange Rate
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Foreign-exchange intervention by Bank Indonesia has likely stabilized the local currency's exchange rate against the U.S. dollar, a central bank official said Friday.  

"We are quite confident that our actions have stabilized" the rupiah, said Perry Warjiyo, head of the economic research and monetary policy directorate at Bank Indonesia.  

He said the government's moves to impose capital controls are also likely supporting the rupiah.  

"Of course, we see blips" in the exchange rate, Warjiyo said at an economics forum in Singapore.  

The rupiah is down around 4% versus the U.S. dollar from the start of the year, but has gained gradually in recent weeks after reaching its weakest point this year on July 5.  

UBS estimates that intervention by Bank Indonesia since April cost the central bank almost $5 billion, or 14% of its total reserves.

title: Bk Indonesia: Can't Rely On Rate Hike To Cut Inflation
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's central bank couldn't rely on a possible interest-rate rise to stem rising inflation, a central bank official said Friday.  

He also said that Indonesia's economic growth rate remains below its potential and said that the central bank has intervened regularly to support the rupiah.  

"What we are facing now is the dilemma of boosting macro-economic growth and maintaining macro-economic stability," Perry Warjiyo, head of the economic research and monetary policy directorate at Bank Indonesia, said Friday. "Relying on increases in interest rates will not be enough."  

On the rupiah, Warjiyo said the central bank had intervened "regularly" to support the currency. But he also noted that the rupiah had lost 3% of its value against the U.S. dollar in the second quarter.  

The official didn't give any further detail on the timing of the intervention in his comments at an economics forum.  

At the start of August, the Indonesian central bank warned that the rupiah could weaken further as the Indonesian balance of payments pushes into deficit for the first time since 2001.  

The rupiah is down around 4% versus the U.S. dollar from the start of the year, but has gained gradually in recent weeks after reaching its weakest point this year on July 5.  

UBS estimates that intervention by Bank Indonesia since April cost the central bank almost $5 billion, or 14% of its total reserves.  

Increases in government-controlled prices have pushed up inflation, and the International Monetary Fund has said Bank Indonesia may need to raise its benchmark one-month rate, currently at 8.5%.  

-By Oliver Biggadike, Dow Jones Newswires; +65-6415-4044; oliver.biggadike@dowjones.com.  

-Edited by Iain McDonald [ 05-08-05 0926GMT ]  

Warjiyo said the best way to tackle rising prices is for the central bank to attack core inflation by increasing interest rates, while the government takes administrative measures to head off noncore inflation, which includes volatile food and energy prices.  

The central bank is coordinating with the government in this area, Warjiyo said; for example, the government has relaxed tariffs to ease import prices.  

Warjiyo estimates that Indonesia's core inflation in the second quarter was 6.8%, while headline inflation was 7.42%.  

-By Oliver Biggadike and Saeed Azhar, Dow Jones Newswires; +65-6415-4044; oliver.biggadike@dowjones.com or saeed.azhar@dowjones.com [ 05-08-05 1027GMT ]

"We are quite confident that our actions have stabilized" the rupiah, said Perry Warjiyo, head of the economic research and monetary policy directorate at Bank Indonesia.  

He said the government's moves to impose capital controls are also likely supporting the rupiah.  

"Of course, we see blips" in the exchange rate, Warjiyo said at an economics forum in Singapore.  

The rupiah is down around 4% versus the U.S. dollar from the start of the year, but has gained gradually in recent weeks after reaching its weakest point this year on July 5.  

UBS estimates that intervention by Bank Indonesia since April cost the central bank almost $5 billion, or 14% of its total reserves.

title: Bk Indonesia: Can't Rely On Rate Hike To Cut Inflation
text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's central bank couldn't rely on a possible interest-rate rise to stem rising inflation, a central bank official said Friday.  

He also said that Indonesia's economic growth rate remains below its potential and said that the central bank has intervened regularly to support the rupiah.  

"What we are facing now is the dilemma of boosting macro-economic growth and maintaining macro-economic stability," Perry Warjiyo, head of the economic research and monetary policy directorate at Bank Indonesia, said Friday. "Relying on increases in interest rates will not be enough."  

On the rupiah, Warjiyo said the central bank had intervened "regularly" to support the currency. But he also noted that the rupiah had lost 3% of its value against the U.S. dollar in the second quarter.  

The official didn't give any further detail on the timing of the intervention in his comments at an economics forum.  

At the start of August, the Indonesian central bank warned that the rupiah could weaken further as the Indonesian balance of payments pushes into deficit for the first time since 2001.  

The rupiah is down around 4% versus the U.S. dollar from the start of the year, but has gained gradually in recent weeks after reaching its weakest point this year on July 5.  

UBS estimates that intervention by Bank Indonesia since April cost the central bank almost $5 billion, or 14% of its total reserves.  

Increases in government-controlled prices have pushed up inflation, and the International Monetary Fund has said Bank Indonesia may need to raise its benchmark one-month rate, currently at 8.5%.  

-By Oliver Biggadike, Dow Jones Newswires; +65-6415-4044; oliver.biggadike@dowjones.com.  

-Edited by Iain McDonald [ 08-05-05 0526ET ]  

Warjiyo said the best way to tackle rising prices is for the central bank to attack core inflation by increasing interest rates, while the government takes administrative measures to head off noncore inflation, which includes volatile food and energy prices.  

The central bank is coordinating with the government in this area, Warjiyo said; for example, the government has relaxed tariffs to ease import prices.  

Warjiyo estimates that Indonesia's core inflation in the second quarter was 6.8%, while headline inflation was 7.42%.

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia key rate stays at 8.49 pct for third week
text:
(Adds details, comments)  

JAKARTA, July 27 (Reuters) - Indonesia kept key one-month interest rates unchanged at 8.49 percent for the third week in a row in an auction on Wednesday, just shy of the central bank's recently introduced 8.50 percent target.  

Traders said the result was a sign of Bank Indonesia's desire to underline the importance of the new policy target by keeping rates as close as possible to it.  

The market had forecast one-month central bank paper, or SBIs, would rise one basis point to match the target, known as the reference rate.  

"I think it sent a strong message to the market that the central bank wants the SBI rate to hover at around the reference rate despite the weak rupiah," a dealer at a large local bank said.  

"They can use other tools to strengthen the rupiah such as through foreign exchange intervention."  

Authorities steer SBIs, Indonesia's benchmark short-term debt, through weekly auctions.  

The country introduced a target for one-month SBIs in early July in a move to make monetary policy more transparent and increase confidence in the rupiah.  

The central bank took 38 trillion rupiah from the auction, against 39.4 trillion maturing Thursday.  

Dealers said that suggested short-term rates, including overnight rates, may remain low due to the expected ample liquidity in the banking system.  

The rupiah was quoted at around 9,814/34 per dollar on Wednesday, weaker than 9,808 on Tuesday.  

The currency has lost more than five percent against the dollar this year and is the third-worst performing Asian currency behind the Japanese yen and Thai baht.  

One-month SBI rates have risen more than 100 basis points this year as authorities have tried to support the currency.  

One big reason for rupiah weakness has been the surge in oil prices. Indonesian demand for oil means extra demand for dollars, and that has resulted in rupiah sales.

title: FACTBOX-Asian  currency  regimes
text:
SINGAPORE, July 22 (Reuters) - Asia's currency regimes grabbed the spotlight after China revalued the yuan against the U.S. dollar and said it would manage it against a basket of currencies, a move which sent regional currencies higher.  

Malaysia was quick to follow China's shift on Thursday evening, scrapping its seven-year-old peg and adopting a managed float. That leaves Hong Kong as the last major economy in Asia with a peg against the U.S. dollar.  

In general, Asian economies explicitly or implicitly shadow the U.S. dollar. But the regimes vary greatly -- the Singapore dollar is floated against basket of currencies while South Korea has an independently floating won.  

The following summary, drawn from official sources and investment bank reports, is based on the International Monetary Fund's definitions for fixed currency pegs, managed floats with varying degrees of fluctuations, and independent floats.  

FIXED PEG  

--------------  

HONG KONG DOLLAR <HKD=>  

Hong Kong adjusted its linked exchange rate system in May for the first time since 1998, moving its currency to a band between 7.75 and 7.85 to the U.S. dollar from a asymmetric peg that set a floor of 7.8 per U.S. dollar.  

The initial peg was part of a Currency Board Arrangement created on October 17, 1983, in response to a currency crisis. Under the board's rules, the Hong Kong dollar monetary base has to be matched by equivalent foreign currency reserves.  

MANAGED FLOATS:  

-------------------  

CHINESE YUAN OR RENMINBI <CNY=>  

After essentially pegging the yuan near 8.28 per dollar since the Asian crisis, China on Thursday revalued it to 8.11 and tied it to an undisclosed basket of currencies of trading partners.  

The yuan will be allowed to move 0.3 percent above or below the previous day's close against the U.S. dollar, and by 1.5 percent against other currencies.  

Theoretically, the trading band allows the currency to edge higher, but China has had such flexibility since 1994 but has not used it since 1996, instead holding the yuan almost still.  

China's central bank is still expected to intervene heavily, buying and selling yuan to maintain the new currency band.  

Prior to the Thursday's move, the yuan was kept in a 0.04 percent band centred on a rate of around 8.278 per dollar.  

China had followed a dual exchange rate since 1979 but unified those rates in 1994 to create a crawling yuan peg.  

The yuan appreciated from 8.7 per dollar to around 8.3 between 1994 and 1996, and continued to fluctuate around there until the Asian crisis, when Beijing rejected advice to devalue like its neighbours and virtually fixed the currency instead.  

MALAYSIAN RINGGIT <MYR=>  

Malaysia on Thursday dropped its seven-year-old peg of 3.8 to the U.S. dollar in favour of a managed float against an undisclosed basket of currencies, moving soon after China did.  

Malaysia has said the aim of its exchange rate policy is to maintain stability with currencies of major trading partners. The currency used to float until a flight of capital and a collapse in its value during the 1997/98 Asian financial crisis prompted authorities to impose capital controls and fix the ringgit.  

SINGAPORE DOLLAR <SGD=>  

Since 1981, the Monetary Authority of Singapore conducts monetary policy by steering the Singapore dollar in an undisclosed band against an undisclosed trade-weighted basket of currencies, rather than setting an interest rate as many central banks do.  

Economists say the regime is a combination of the band, basket and crawl foreign exchange systems.  

The MAS runs policy by letting the nominal effective exchange rate (NEER) appreciate or depreciate, either by shifting the mid-point of the band or adjusting its width. Economists say the U.S. dollar and dollar-bloc currencies make up the biggest proportion of the trade-weighted basket.  

Policy shifted from neutral to a tightening bias in April 2004 via a gradual appreciation of the mid-point of the NEER.  

The Sing dollar is freely convertible on the trade account and has very minimal restrictions on capital flows.  

INDIAN RUPEE <INR=>  

Economists say the Reserve Bank of India uses a monitoring band for the rupee, which allows it to float within a band determined by the currencies of India's top five trading partners, adjusted for inflation levels.  

Markets believe the width of the band is five percent on either side of this neutral real effective exchange rate (REER), and the RBI intervenes if the band is breached.  

The RBI regularly publishes data on the REER base period and neutral value, but with a lag.  

The current unified exchange rate was adopted in 1993 after a balance of payments crisis led to devaluations in 1991.  

The rupee is not fully convertible on the capital account. There are still some limits on residents borrowing overseas, on residents converting local assets into foreign currency and on the access foreigners have to Indian debt markets.  

THAI BAHT <THB=>  

Massive capital outflows forced Thailand to abandon the baht's peg against a basket of currencies on July 2, 1997, triggering a big devaluation against the dollar that marked the onset of the Asian financial crisis.  

Thailand adopted a managed float. Like other Asian central banks operating under similar regimes, the Bank of Thailand is averse to currency volatility and intervenes often in the market.  

Selective capital controls exist. There are strict limits on baht positions held by foreigners and offshore trading in baht is negligible.  

INDONESIAN RUPIAH <IDR=>  

Indonesia switched to a freely floating rupiah from a managed float in August 1997 during the Asian crisis. Several exchange controls remain.  

Indonesia's central bank regularly intervenes in the foreign exchange market to help the rupiah, which fell more than five percent against the dollar in the first half of 2005. To stabilise the currency, the central bank has also banned sales of rupiah securities by non-residents.  

INDEPENDENTLY FLOATING:  

------------------------  

KOREAN WON <KRW=> <KRW=KFTC>  

The won was floated in December 1997 and is one of Asia's most actively traded currencies.  

The Bank of Korea runs an inflation-targeting policy, but the government dictates currency policy and keeps a watchful eye on the won's competitiveness. This occasionally leads to strains between the central bank and the finance ministry.  

Foreigners have greater access to South Korean capital markets than to most others in emerging Asia, yet there are some restrictions on offshore won trading and on local banks' positions in won.  

The won non-deliverable forward (NDF) market that has developed as a consequence is among the most liquid in Asia.  

The yen-won is a popular cross rate, traded in the belief that Seoul likes to keep the won competitive versus the yen because of the overlap between South Korean and Japanese exports.  

PHILIPPINE PESO <PHP=>  

The peso is allowed to trade in a wider band than most other Asian currencies and is prone to volatile swings in response to political developments. It is also sensitive to data on the Philippines' large fiscal deficit and on remittances from overseas Filipinos, a major source of foreign exchange.  

The central bank, with limited official reserves, intervenes occasionally. It also adjusts reserve requirements, and the rate at which they are remunerated, to help smooth the currency.

title: Bank Indonesia Chief Says Rupiah Woes To Ease By End '05
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's central bank will tackle the current "volatility" in the value of the rupiah and help boost the currency to 9,300 against the U.S. dollar by the end of the year, its governor said Wednesday.  

"In recent months the volatility (in the value) of the rupiah has been higher than usual," Bank Indonesia's Burhanuddin Abdullah told reporters. "We will try to ease that volatility using many policies...(and) if necessary we will intervene (in the currency market)."  

Bank Indonesia data indicate the rupiah has lost 4.32% in value against the dollar in the past two months.  

Burhanuddin'sassertion seems to counter a statement by the central bank's Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom, who had said Monday that it is unlikely that the rupiah would go back to the level of IDR9,300 by the end of the year.  

The dollar closed at a more-than-three-year high of IDR9,870 on July 5 due to state-owned petroleum firm Pertamina's massive dollar purchases to fund imports at a time when global oil prices hover around $60 a barrel.  

The rupiah has since rebounded on the back of a government plan to take Pertamina out of the currency market by directly selling the company dollars through the central bank. At GMT 0547 Wednesday, the dollar was trading at IDR9,771.  

The Pertamina dollar-supply plan is part of a series of rupiah- defense measures the government has announced in recent weeks, including tighter foreign exchange rules that will take effect Thursday.  

The new rules include a cut in the size of foreign exchange derivative transactions with foreign counterparts against the rupiah to a maximum of $1 million from $3 million earlier.  

The regulations also limit dollar purchases in outright forward transactions and swaps to a total of $1 million. Such transactions weren't previously subject to any cap.  

-By Jakarta Bureau, Dow Jones Newswires; 62 21 3983 1277; dj.jakarta@dowjones.com

title: Indonesia  Rupiah Ends Up On Ctrl Bk  Intervention
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended up Friday as suspected /central bank intervention helped to bolster the currency against the dollar, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR 9,790, slightly down from IDR9,795 on Thursday. The dollar hit a high of IDR9,833 in intraday trade.  

"The market was a little bit off today as Bank Indonesia kept intervening at the IDR9,830 mark," a dealer from a foreign bank said.  

"I think there was also a trend of players who'd overbought dollars selling back into the market."  

Friday's closing rupiah result also reflects the impact of the government's move late Tuesday to directly supply state-owned petroleum firm Pertamina with dollars through the central bank.  

Dealers have attributed Pertamina's voracious dollar appetite to fund oil imports amid record-high global oil prices for a seven-day slide in the rupiah's value that didn't stop until Wednesday. Dealers and economists say Pertamina normally accounts for up to 25% of dollar demand in the local currency market.  

Central bank and senior government officials have said that the rupiah will meet an official projected average value of IDR9,300 against the dollar in 2005. But dealers say that a market tracking a strong dollar against regional currencies and continuing domestic corporate demand for dollars will weigh on the rupiah.  

The dollar will likely trade between IDR9,770 to IDR9,800 on Monday, dealers said.

title: ANALYSIS-Indonesia's inflation targeting hostage to rupiah
text:
SINGAPORE, July 7 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank has embarked on a policy of transparent interest-rate and inflation targeting, a laudable effort in the eyes of financial markets but one that economists say will prove challenging.  

The jury is still out on whether Bank Indonesia's new policy tools will lead to more stable growth and prices, given that it has to juggle the management of a volatile rupiah with calls from Indonesia's coalition government for lower interest rates.  

For the first time this month, the central bank has announced a target for the yield on one-month certificates, aimed at hitting an explicit target for inflation.  

That was a marked shift from its policy of the last six years of steering yields through market intervention and trying to hold down inflation through managing base money -- a policy widely seen as opaque and hard to convey to the public.  

But success hinges on the currency, since the rupiah's value influences the price of everything from the huge amounts of oil Indonesia imports to the commodities it exports. And the rupiah's fortunes are linked to the government's economic reforms and the ability to attract foreign investment.  

"It is a step in the right direction, but a plan alone is not going to make much of a difference," said Fauzi Ichsan, Standard Chartered Bank's Jakarta-based economist.  

Targeting interest rates was necessary, since higher rates would support the rupiah, but not sufficient, Ichsan said.  

"Because, as the rupiah keeps tanking, you need stronger and stronger measures. It has to be introduced in conjunction with other policy measures to stem capital outflow and increase capital inflow."  

The Indonesian economy is growing comfortably at an annual rate of about 6 percent, but the rupiah <IDR=> has fallen 6 percent this year, adding to the problems of imported inflation at a time of record high oil prices.  

On Thursday it was at 9,830 per dollar, just above a three-year low of 9,900 hit earlier this week.  

Bank Indonesia is formally independent. Indonesian law states its mission is "to achieve and maintain rupiah stability", so it could give priority to the currency and become lax on inflation.  

Sanjeev Sanyal, an economist with Deutsche Bank, said Bank Indonesia knew inflation targeting in Indonesia involved a lot of exchange rate management and that it was raising interest rates to support the rupiah.  

But according to Ramkishen Rajan, a professor at Singapore's LKY School of Public Policy, such multiple objectives can frustrate central banks' efforts to communicate monetary policy in a straightforward manner.  

CREDIBILITY  

Some 41 countries target inflation, using interest rates and other tools to keep price rises to an advertised level.  

Indonesia adopted the policy after agreeing to an International Monetary Fund programme during the 1997/98 Asian financial crisis. Until this month, policy was conducted by steering base money -- cash in circulation in the economy plus bank reserves.  

Bank Indonesia managed to get annual consumer price inflation down from double-digit rates in 2002 but it remains volatile.  

It hit a two-year high of 8.8 percent in March, after the government cut fuel subsidies to ease pressure on the state budget, but had fallen to 7.42 percent by June.  

The yield on one-month central bank certificates (SBIs) <ID1MSBI=BIIA>, which is the new policy benchmark, has risen to 8.44 percent from 7.4 percent at the start of the year but is still five points below levels at the end of 2002. On Tuesday, Bank Indonesia announced a target for consumer price inflation of 7 percent by the end of 2005 and a one-month bond yield of 8.5 percent for the next three months.  

One big problem for many Asian central banks is political interference, since exchange rate policy is often the domain of the political leadership.  

For instance, the Bank of Korea has to balance its policy around the government's intervention to keep the won competitive. In Indonesia, Ichsan said, lawmakers do not want rates to rise too fast and they have been slow in clearing the red tape and rigid labour laws that put off foreign investors.  

In the end, a central bank has to build up credibility, said Huw McKay, regional economist with Westpac Bank in Sydney.  

"You can announce a target. But if your market does not respect your ability to achieve that target, expectations will be unchanged," he said.  

"Basically, you have to deliver on an inflation target for a sustained period of time, up to a decade, before the market begins implicitly trusting you. And the Indonesian economy hasn't performed in a fashion that has enabled the central bank to gain credibility."

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Up On  Central Bank  Support Measures
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones Newswires)--The Indonesian rupiah ended higher Wednesday after hitting a more than three-year low Tuesday, as market sentiment rebounded on new central bank measures to support the currency.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,790, down from IDR9,870 Tuesday. Wednesday's result marked the first time in seven sessions that the rupiah gained against the dollar.  

Dealers said a government plan unveiled late Tuesday for Bank Indonesia to directly supply U.S. dollars to the state-owned petroleum firm Pertamina (PTM.YY) brought the dollar down to its opening level of IDR9,830 and limited its peak to IDR9,880 during Wednesday trading.  

The plan is aimed at easing the impact on the rupiah of Pertamina's massive appetite for dollars to fund oil imports.  

Analysts have attributed the rupiah's recent decline to Pertamina's dollar purchases as the currency strengthens globally and oil prices hit record highs. The benchmark August price for crude oil rose 31 U.S. cents to $59.90 per barrel Wednesday.  

The off-market dollar supply mechanism for Pertamina will reduce total dollar market volume by almost 25%, Standard Chartered economist Fauzi Ichsan told Dow Jones Newswires.  

But dealers cautioned that the rupiah remained vulnerable to long-term dollar demand by local companies, including Pertamina.  

"The central bank's plan was effective...but at the end of the day, corporates still need to buy dollars," a dealer at a foreign bank said.  

The dollar will likely trade in a range of IDR9,700 to IDR9,900 Thursday, dealers said. Bank Indonesia is likely to intervene with dollar sales through state-owned banks to ensure the rupiah doesn't fall below IDR9,900.  

-By Phelim Kyne; Dow Jones Newswires' Jakarta Bureau; 62 21 3983 1277; phelim.kyne@dowjones.com  

-Edited by Paul Baylis [ 06-07-05 1110GMT ]

title: Indonesia  Rupiah Ends Up On Talk Of Ctrl Bk  Intervention
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones Newswires)--The Indonesian rupiah rose Wednesday due to likely market intervention by the country's central bank and the U.S. dollar's weakness against other currencies, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,648, down from its close Tuesday at IDR9,665.  

The rupiah also benefited from an easing in dollar demand from local corporates, dealers said. Much of that demand was on behalf of state oil importer Pertamina, which is scrambling to comply with a government directive to increase its fuel reserves to cover consumption for 20 days from a current level of 12 days.  

"Basically, today was a quiet trading day compared to yesterday's volatility, but again the dollar demand for local corporates is still healthy for the same reason of importing oil," a dealer said.  

"Also, we see some dollar-selling by state banks, probably on behalf of the central bank as part of its regulatory role in preventing the dollar from rising too fast (against the rupiah)."  

The dollar's weakness against other major currencies also helped the rupiah. The dollar fell to HK$7.7706 Wednesday from HK$7.7743 Tuesday due to renewed speculation about a possible revaluation of the Chinese yuan. Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. dollar closed at NT$31.355, down from NT$31.390 Tuesday.  

Indonesia's looming implementation of tighter forex trading rules has also severely trimmed speculative trading in the rupiah, traders said.  

Bank Indonesia will implement next month regulations that will restrict the amount of dollars banks can borrow from offshore counterparts without underlying transactions at $1 million. Previously, there was no cap on the amount.  

Central bank officials have said that the move is aimed at reducing the amount of speculative offshore money coming into Indonesia, which can destabilize the exchange rate.  

"Domestic flow is the main driver (of dollar demand)," a dealer said. "Since the regulations came out, I think speculative flows have very much reduced."  

Dealers expect the dollar to trade between IDR9,630 and IDR9,680 Thursday.

title: RPT-Indonesian rupiah near 8-week low on oil,  FX  rules
text:
(Repeats to fix headline)  

SINGAPORE, June 21 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah traded on Tuesday near an eight-week low hit overnight as record high oil prices and central bank measures to curb offshore speculation led local oil importers and offshore investors to buy dollars.  

The rupiah <IDR=> traded near 9,660 per dollar, its lowest level since April 27. The currency had hit a three-year low of 9,800 on April 26.  

U.S. benchmark light crude oil futures <CLc1> jumped to a record $59.52 per barrel on Monday raising import costs of Indonesia's main fuel importer, PT Pertamina, which seeks to boost imports to replenish inventory after solving a cash-crunch.  

"Asian currencies which are particularly vulnerable to high oil prices are the baht and the rupiah," Irene Cheung, head of Asian currency strategy at ABN AMRO Bank, said in a note.  

The baht <THB=> traded as low as 41.155 per dollar on Tuesday, near its 7-1/2-month low of 41.17 hit on Friday. The baht and the rupiah are Asia's worst performing currencies this year, after the Japanese yen <JPY=>.  

Indonesian state oil-and-gas company, Pertamina, said on Monday it was seeking a loan of between $500 million and $700 million to finance oil product imports.  

The company plans to increase its fuel stocks to equal 20 days of demand, from the current 17.5 days, Pertamina President Director Widya Purnama told reporters.  

Cheung said the rupiah has also seen selling pressure since the central bank announced plans last week to tighten foreign exchange trading, including limiting certain derivative deals, from July 14 to stabilise the the currency.  

Bank Indonesia, the central bank, also banned buying of rupiah-denominated securities issued by non-residents.  

"No doubt Bank Indonesia will continue to resist with both intervention and rate hikes of various sorts but a creeping increase in the (dollar-rupiah) pair is most likely," IDEAglobal Ltd. said in a note.

text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah closed lower Monday on broad bullish sentiment toward the dollar globally, but suspected Bank Indonesia intervention helped the local unit recoup some of its losses, dealers said.

title: Indonesia  Rupiah Ends Up On Bank  Indonesia 's  Intervention
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah closed higher Friday, thanks to Bank Indonesia's steadfastness in defending the local unit, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,590, down from its close Thursday at IDR9,610.  

The greenback rose to an intraday high of IDR9,655 due to a combination of its global bullishness and local security concerns after the Australian government warned of possible terrorist attacks.  

"We continue to receive a stream of credible reporting suggesting that terrorists are in very advanced stages of planning attacks in Indonesia," Australia's Department of Foreign Affairs said in a warning posted on the department Web site. "Attacks could occur at any time, anywhere in Indonesia and could be directed at any locations known to be frequented by foreigners."  

Dealers said that Bank Indonesia unwound dollars to push the greenback lower.

He, however, said that intervention is only a temporary measure, urging the government to boost efforts to make the country a net oil exporter again. He blamed the rupiah's weakness on partly the high oil import bills.  

Dealers said the dollar may try to test IDR9,600 against next week as its global bullishness still looks intact.

A corrected story follows.  

JAKARTA, June 8 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank governor said on Wednesday that intervention in the foreign exchange market to help the rupiah currency <IDR=> was a temporary solution.  

"Intervention is only for a short term. We cannot stay like this. We need to keep the economy in balance to solve this problem," Burhanuddin Abdullah said at an Indonesian Chamber of Commerce meeting.  

Abdullah added that becoming a net oil exporter once again would be an important goal in trying to maintain balance in the economy.  

"An increase in the oil price should benefit the Indonesian economy if we are a net exporter. That's what we should achieve. Without it we will be very vulnerable".  

Despite being the only Asian member of Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries, Indonesia has been a net oil importer during recent periods.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Flat On Alleged Central Bk Moves
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah closed steady Monday thanks to reported intervention by Bank Indonesia to prevent the dollar's rebound versus major rivals from spilling over to the local foreign exchange market, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,480, unchanged from its close Friday.  

Dealers said the greenback rose to an intraday high of IDR9,510 earlier in the day, which triggered alleged dollar selling by the nation's central bank.

title: Indonesia  rph up on  intervention , lower dlr demand.
text:
JAKARTA, May 2 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah strengthened slightly on Monday partly on an easing of dollar demand from local corporates and a suspected small amount of central bank intervention in the thin market.  

The rupiah was quoted at 9,530/9,540 per dollar at 0520 GMT, up from 9,585 late on Friday, when it fell as much as 0.6 percent despite a sharp rise in other Asian currencies on heightened speculation that China would revalue the yuan soon.  

"The central bank is likely to have intervened, that has helped the rupiah to strengthen. Apart from that, Pertamina is not seen buying dollars in the market today," said a dealer with a private bank in Jakarta.  

Last week the Indonesian authorities announced various money market measures to soak up excess rupiah in the system, promised higher interest rates and raised guaranteed deposit rates sharply.  

But the boost from these efforts proved limited and the rupiah headed lower after recovering by 3 percent between April 26 and 28.  

Analysts have said the rupiah would probably remain under pressure as long as state oil firm Pertamina continues to buy dollars from the market to import oil and unless investors regain their confidence in Indonesia's monetary policy and economic growth prospects.

title: Indonesia  Rupiah Ends Up On Reported Ctlr Bk  Intervention
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah closed slightly higher Friday as Bank Indonesia reportedly unloaded dollars to prop up the local unit, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,560, down from its close Thursday at IDR9,570. The dollar was well-bid earlier in the day as several offshore market participants who had short-sold the unit bought back the currency to lock in profits. But the central bank persistently sold dollars via state banks, dealers said.  

"Some Singaporean-based players cut their dollar-long positions shortly before trading closed on concerns that Bank Indonesia may intervene Monday when the players are away on holiday," a dealer said.  

Businesses will be closed in Singapore Monday.  

The market seemed to welcome Bank Indonesia's move to raise the maximum interest rates on dollar deposits covered by the government's blanket guarantee by 135 basis points to 2%, effective Sunday.  

An official with the central bank told Dow Jones Newswires Friday that the move is aimed at persuading people to keep their dollar deposits domestically instead of moving their funds out of the country to get higher returns.  

This is eventually expected to help ease the pressure on the rupiah, which this week fell to its lowest level against the U.S. dollar in more than three years.  

Dealers expect the dollar to trade between IDR9,530 and IDR9,600 Monday, with trading volume expected to be thinner due to the holiday in Singapore.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rupiah jumps on govt moves, peso up on China.
text:
By Yoo Choonsik
    SINGAPORE, April 27 (Reuters) - Indonesian efforts to shore
up the rupiah drove the currency more than 1 percent higher on
Wednesday, while a weak Philippine peso found support from
Chinese investment and lending plans.
    The peso was quoted at 54.36 per dollar late on Wednesday,
against 54.35 on Tuesday, having slipped as low as 54.60
earlier.
    However, it climbed from the intraday lows after China's
president, Hu Jintao, agreed China would invest and loan $1.6
billion to fund infrastructure and mining projects in the
Philippines.
    The South Korean won ended domestic trade 0.1 percent
lower, marking its first drop in eight sessions. The Singapore
and Taiwan dollar were slightly weaker as the U.S. dollar rose
following strong data on new home sales.
    The rupiah gained as much as 1.1 percent to 9,585 per
dollar, bouncing from three-year lows generated by concern
Indonesia's monetary policy was too loose.
  


    The currency has lost 3.4 percent so far this year making
it Asia's weakest actively traded currency after the Japanese
yen.
    Some analysts doubted the rupiah had secured a turnaround,
pointing to high oil prices, investor concern over economic
prospects and signs investors are moving out of emerging market
debt as U.S. interest rates rise.
    "I would say it will provide some relief, but ultimately
(the rupiah) will still be subject to a combination of
factors," said Philip Wee, a currency strategist with DBS Bank.
    This week, Indonesian officials have promised higher
interest rates. Indonesia introduced a new short-term money
market operation and promised more frequent auctions of debt to
absorb excess rupiah.
    Officials also considered on Wednesday measures to allow
state oil firm Pertamina to buy dollars from the central bank
instead of from the market to pay for oil imports.
    But late in the day State Enterprises Minister Sugiharto,
who oversees Pertamina, said the company would continue to buy
dollars from the market, purchases dealers have cited as
weakening the rupiah.
 
    Sugiharto said Pertamina needed about $50 million each day,
suggesting its monthly demand could amount to some $1 billion.
   Indonesian President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono ordered
officials to seek ways to stabilise rupiah and dealers also
cited some dollar-selling intervention by authorities.
    "Though the BI (Bank Indonesia) remains on guard to prevent
  

the dollar/rupiah from hitting 10,000, much will still depend  

on the development of oil prices and dollar movements," Chin  

Loo Thio, a senior currency analyst with BNP Paribas, said in a  

research report.

title: Indonesia  Rupiah Ends Higher On Ctrl Bk  Intervention
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah extended its recovery by another 1.2% Wednesday as Bank Indonesia reportedly sold dollars and sent auditors to foreign banks' dealing rooms in Jakarta to deter currency speculation, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,573, down from its close Tuesday at IDR9,688. The rupiah had risen 0.6% Tuesday.  

Dealers said that the nation's central bank aggressively unloaded dollars via brokers to prop up the rupiah. The central bank couldn't be reached for comment, but its officials have said recently that the bank would intervene to defend the rupiah when necessary.  

Dealers said that Bank Indonesia also dispatched its auditors to look at foreign banks' transaction activity.  

"Suddenly, we saw a dollar selloff today from foreign banks, who likely unloaded their dollar long positions after central banks sent their auditors to those banks," a dealer with a local bank said.  

Foreign banks are the main players in Jakarta's interbank foreign exchange market.  

Dealers said that dollar demand from local companies also abated as they chose to wait on the sidelines, likely hoping to buy the greenback at lower levels.  

The market welcomed President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono's call earlier Wednesday for his ministers to coordinate closely with the central bank to boost the rupiah's value, which recently fell to over-three-year lows.  

"It shows that the president is in charge on this (rupiah weakness) problem," a dealer with a local bank said.  

Dealers expect the dollar to continue sliding Thursday. They, however, forecast a wide IDR9,500-IDR9,750 range as the market remains unstable.
