title: WSJA: Asian Shares Drop,  Currencies  Sharply Lower
text:
OF THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA 
 

HONG KONG (Dow Jones)--Asian stocks were sold off heavily Thursday, knocking many of the region's currencies sharply lower and prompting governments to intervene.

Markets in Tokyo, Hong Kong and South Korea fell in response to a broad selloff overnight in the U.S. Tokyo's benchmark index fell 6.9%, while Hong Kong and Seoul were down 4% and 6.7% respectively. Australia's major benchmark dropped 4.2% and Shanghai fell 1.7%. Mumbai and Singapore were down 4.1% and 2.8% late Thursday. Jakarta was down 2.8% late.

The selling continued in Europe, where the DJ Stoxx 600 index was 3% lower. U.S. stock futures were down 1% to 1.5% in screen trade.

The stock hits reflect fears of deflation in the U.S., a major market for Asia-made goods, and the impact of a slowdown on commodity-rich nations like Australia and Indonesia.

That has led to a flight to safer investments typically denominated in U.S. dollars and the Japanese yen, taking money out of Asian markets and contributing to a drop in local currencies.

"It's part of the wholesale destruction of wealth across the planet," said Patrick Bennett, a strategist with Societe Generale in Hong Kong. "With asset and equity prices tumbling, investors are being encouraged to cut exposure completely."

Weaker currencies can boost big exporting nations because it makes their goods cheaper to sell in other markets. But declining currencies also hit countries with extensive foreign borrowing needs, can drive up inflation by making imports more expensive and can scare off foreign investment.

Among the hardest hit, Indonesia's rupiah and South Korea's won fell to their lowest level against the U.S. dollar since the Asian financial crisis a decade ago.

Thailand's baht fell to its weakest level since March 2007, while Taiwan's dollar hit a three-week low and the New Zealand and Australian dollars also weakened further.

The central banks of South Korea, Malaysia, the Philippines, Indonesia, Singapore and India intervened to defend their currencies, local traders said. Australia's central bank issued data that showed it plowed A$3.15 billion into currency markets last month to defend the Australian dollar against a sharp decline.

Japan and Hong Kong have defied the trend, the former because its currency is seen as a safe haven and the latter because it is pegged to the value of the appreciating U.S. dollar. The Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the city's de facto central bank, put roughly HK$15 billion into the market Thursday to bring the currency's value within its trading band with the U.S. dollar.

Economists cautioned that the current environment hasn't reached the point of the Asian currency crisis, when domestic funds followed foreign investors as they ran for the exits. Most governments have moved to back bank deposits to reassure consumers. Regional financial institutions have cleaner balance sheets than a decade ago, and bad loans have so far had only a minor effect on regional banks.

Still, continuing hits to currencies continue could erode consumer confidence, leading locals to consider moving their money elsewhere. "The impact on confidence could become a much bigger problem," said Sim Moh Siong, an economist at Citigroup in Singapore. "If this goes beyond how much money foreigners remove from Asia, the situation could broaden out."

In Tokyo, the Nikkei Stock Average of 225 companies ended down 6.9% at 7703.04. Shares of major banks and brokerages were hammered, with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group tumbling 10% to Y281,500 and Nomura Holdings ending down 11% at Y666.

Shares of nonlife insurers dropped after sector companies reported dismal fiscal first half results Wednesday and sharply reduced their earnings forecasts for the full fiscal year ending March.

Although most of the bad news had already been factored in by investors, forecast revisions confirmed the grim outlook. Tokio Marine Holdings went limit-down at Y2,220, and Mitsui Sumitomo Insurance Group Holdings also went limit-down at Y2,035.

Real estate stocks also sank, dogged by credit concerns, with Mitsui Fudosan skidding 14% to Y1,070, and Mitsubishi Estate falling 13% to Y1,077.

In Seoul, the Korea Composite Stock Price Index, or Kospi, finished down 68.13 points, or 6.7%, at 948.69, based on skepticism over conditions in the U.S., particularly among financials.

Shinhan Financial Group declined 9.7% to KRW26,400, and KB Financial Group plunged by the daily limit of 15% to KRW24,550. Among builders, Hyundai Engineering & Construction and GS Engineering & Construction both dropped by the daily 15% limit to KRW42,100 and KRW45,200, respectively.

In Shanghai, the benchmark Shanghai Composite Index, which tracks both A and B shares, ended down 1.7%, or 33.71 points, at 1983.76. Railway companies and insurance companies fell on profit-taking.

China Railway Group Ltd. dropped 4.1% to CNY5.82 after gaining 4.7% Wednesday, while China Life Insurance Co. fell 4.0% to CNY20.24 after rising 6.1% in the previous session.

-By Carlos Tejada, The Wall Street Journal; carlos. tejada@wsj.com

(Takashi Mochizuki and Takashi Nakamichi in Tokyo and Rosalind Mathieson in Singapore also contributed to this article.) [ 20-11-08 0946GMT ]

title: 4th UPDATE: Asian Shares Slump On US Woes; Nikkei Falls 6.9%
text:
(Adds information, quotes, updates/adds market levels)

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian share markets fell Thursday - some of them to multiyear lows - after a late-day slump on Wall Street, with the health of the banking and auto sectors still cause for much concern.

"We haven't seen bargain hunting because nobody knows whether anything is a bargain anymore - value is disappearing overnight," said Najeeb Jarhom, senior vice president of research at AmFraser in Singapore.

Falls accelerated as the day wore on: Australia's S&P/ASX 200 ended down 4.2% at its lowest level since early 2004, with Japan's Nikkei shedding 6.9%, hurt in part by a surprise trade deficit in October; Korea's Kospi ended with a 6.7% decline with Taiwan's market down 4.5% at a more than six-year trough.

Margin lenders "are flat out with their margin calls," said Chris Blair, head of retail at Patersons Securities in Sydney; analysts elsewhere noted some redemption activity, though others said the continued slide in markets might prove attractive for braver, longer-term investors.

Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was recently down 6.2% with India's Sensex off 5.1%.

Light trading volume showed the level of caution among investors; "the market continues to trade on fear. Fundamentals are going to take a back seat for a while. It's like (watching) a terminal patient," said broker David Price of Forsyth Barr in New Zealand.

Japan's yen was notably higher with central banks intervening in several markets in Asia to keep a lid on the U.S. dollar; risk aversion was showing up in wider credit spreads while crude oil futures came in for some selling on demand-related concerns.

U.S. stock futures were down 1%-1.5% in screen trade and European spreadbetting firms were calling stocks there to fall; CMC Markets tipped London's FTSE-100 to drop 93 points.

Asia's declines came after the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed under 8000 for the first time in more than five-and-a-half years as investors worried about the future of U.S. auto makers and banks; it declined 5.1% while the Nasdaq Composite dropped 6.5%.

There were ongoing concerns about the U.S. economy with poor data Wednesday on the housing market and gloomy minutes from the recent meeting of the Federal Open Markets Committee.

Some were starting to talk about the risk of a global deflationary spiral: "Faced with this prospect, central banks (in Asia, ex Japan) are loosening monetary conditions and will continue to do so well into 2009," said analysts at Standard Chartered.

Technology stocks suffered with the Semiconductor Industry Association forecasting global chip sales for 2009 to decline 5.6%; Hynix Semi shed 15% in Seoul with Powerchip Semi down 6.9% in Taiwan and Elpida Memory off 3.7% in Tokyo.

"As dramatic declines in consumer and industrial confidence began developing in late summer, order cancellations began to grow and in many cases, slowing orders degenerated into a complete stop in orders as players across the supply chain moved to extremely cautious positions," said iSuppli senior vice president, market intelligence services, Dale Ford.

Shipping stocks were hit with Divay Goel, director and head of operations for Drewry Maritime Services, telling Dow Jones Newswires Wednesday he expected around 20% of orders for building new dry bulk shipping vessels may be canceled in 2009; Korea's Hyundai Heavy Industries sank 14.4%.

Japan's main index traded under 8000 for the first time since Oct. 29; banks were hit with Sumitomo Mitsui Financial tumbling 10% and Nomura Holdings 11% while insurer Tokio Marine Holdings shed 15% after reporting poor first half results and terminating its plan for a share buyback.

Miners and financials fell in Australia with BHP Billiton down 9.1% and Rio Tinto down 13%; ANZ Bank lost 5.9% with Commonwealth Bank 5.2%.

Hong Kong property stocks were hit with that subindex down 7% and Cheung Kong down 5.9%; HSBC fell 4.2% on worries about the outlook for business in Europe and the U.S.

The Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.6% after a 6.1% rally Wednesday; Singapore's Straits Times Index was down 4.1% with Malaysia's main index falling 2.0%, Indonesian shares 3.5% and Thai shares 4.0%.

New Zealand's NZX-50 closed with a 2.3% fall to its lowest level since June 2004, while Philippine shares ended down 3.5% decline.

In currency markets, the U.S. dollar fell to Y95.15 with the euro at Y118.80; the euro was around $1.2490 while the Australian dollar slipped back to US$0.6346.

Asian currencies were active: The U.S. dollar rose above S$1.53 against the Singapore dollar and against the Korean won it hit its highest level since March 1998, while it reached a 2008 high against the Malaysian ringgit; against the Thai baht, it touched its best level since March 2007.

The Philippine central bank was suspected of selling U.S. dollars to support the peso, with intervention also spotted in Indonesia, Korea and India; in Hong Kong, authorities again sold Hong Kong dollars to preserve the currency peg.

"Though valuations might look cheap for some currencies, this is typically not the time that investors take on more risk. Given how brutal this year has proved for many investors, we sense this adage may hold particularly true this year," said analysts at Morgan Stanley.

Japanese government bonds rose with futures adding 0.49 to 139.32; credit default swaps widened with the iTraxx Japan Series 10 index at 330 basis points from 290 basis points Wednesday.

Toyota CDS were at 170 basis points, from 135 basis points on Nov. 18 and 55 basis points on Oct. 2; "pretty wide, huh? Toyota used to trade almost the same level as sovereign" CDS, said a credit trader at a Western bank in Tokyo, adding "autos are just taking it on the chin - everyone's keeping an eye on what's happening with the Big Three in Detroit."

The cost of protection in Asia ex-Japan widened, too, with the five-year iTraxx investment grade index quoted at 425-470 basis points versus a 420 basis-point midspread close Wednesday.

U.S. Treasurys nudged up in Tokyo after strong U.S. gains with the 10-year note up 7/32 at 103 14/32, yielding 3.342%; players were betting on a further Fed rate cut in December.

Spot gold was at $735.20, up 30 cents from New York; front-month Nymex crude was down 93 cents at $52.69 a barrel on Globex - a 22-month low - after declining 77 cents in New York.

title: Emerging  FX -Rupee at record low, rupiah falls to Aug 1998 trough
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah fell to its lowest levels since the Asian financial crisis and the Indian rupee hit a record low on Thursday, driven by investors' growing fears of a global recession and capital flight from those countries.

 At the same time, the Hong Kong central bank was forced to pump funds into the market to stop its currency from breaching the upper limit of its 7.75-7.85 band against the U.S. dollar.

 Investors exiting carry trades and risky markets have been pumping money into the safety of the pegged Hong Kong dollar.

 The rupiah <IDR=> hit 12,400 per dollar, an August 1998 trough, in trading marked by illiquidity and verbal and dollar-selling interventions by the central bank, Bank Indonesia.

 "BI is not happy whenever we buy dollars. They are making calls almost every single hour asking us about our foreign exchange positions," one trader at a foreign bank in Jakarta said, declining to be identified. "That's why there are few deals done."

 The currency has fallen 16.5 percent against the dollar in the last three weeks, pressured by worries over the huge foreign holdings of its debt market and corporates' ability to service their large overseas borrowings.

 Asian stock markets fell sharply on Thursday, with investors' even gloomier about global growth after the U.S. Federal Reserve warned of protracted weakness in the economy and hopes for a bailout for the troubled U.S. automakers dimmed.

 "The market is still in risk reduction mode apparently," said Han-Sia Yeo, a strategist at Bank Of America

 "But the (dollar) buying pressure is not as intense as in October or May periods. The worst period is probably over, but liquidity will be quite bad for the balance of the year."

 "It's going to difficult to expect investors to put on risk in a significant manner ahead of year end," he said.

 The rupee <INR=IN> fell to a record low of 50.6 per dollar, after which the central bank was suspected of selling dollars through state-run banks.

 The Korean won <KRW=> fell 3.4 percent, closing at its weakest in nearly 11 years. [nSEO339969].

title: Emerging  FX -Rupiah at 7-year low, won at 3-wk trough
text:
TAIPEI, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> hit a fresh 7-year low against the dollar on Tuesday, once again at the fore of declines in Asian currencies spurred by falling stock markets and increasing evidence pointing to a global recession.

The rupiah fell 2.9 percent to 12,050 to the U.S. dollar, with some dealers expecting the currency to weaken towards 12,100 in the coming week due to market worries over foreign fund outflows from the country's financial market.

The South Korean won <KRW=> fell to a three-week closing low, while the Taiwan dollar <TWD=> declined to a two-week intraday trough as more key economies, such as Japan and the euro zone, slipped into a recession.

"It's mainly the bearish global market hitting the rupiah. Stocks all around are falling and market sentiment is quite weak," a dealer in Indonesia said.

"Indonesia's GDP figures pressured the rupiah, but the overall impact was limited," the dealer said.

Indonesia's central bank has been intervening in markets to defend its falling currency, which has fallen 21 percent this year. On Tuesday, the central bank said it will not let the rupiah hit irrational levels.

On Monday, Indonesia, southeast Asia's biggest economy, reported third quarter growth of 6.1 percent, easing from the second quarter, mainly because exports slowed.

"We think financial turmoil associated with the rupiah's weakness will slow fourth quarter growth," ING said in a report.

Economies in emerging Asia, such as South Korea and Taiwan, are largely powered by exports and a global downturn will likely sap demand for the region's produce, such as electronics gadgets, cars and textiles.

Japan's recession could be longer than previously expected and governments around the world are doing everything to try and boost domestic consumption, with Taiwan offering to dole out shopping vouchers to its citizens.

The Korean won <KRW=> ended 2.7 percent lower at 1,447.9/9.1 per dollar, the Taiwan dollar hit a three-week intraday low of 33.290, while the Singapore dollar lost 0.2 percent to trade at 1.5261, hovering at an over one-year low.

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia cbank: won't allow 'irrational' rupiah level
text:
(Adds quotes, details)

JAKARTA, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank will not let the rupiah <IDR=> hit "irrational" levels, Bank Indonesia's governor said on Tuesday, following a further depreciation of the currency.

Boediono's comments came after the rupiah hit a fresh 7-year low against the dollar on Tuesday, once again at the fore of declines in Asian currencies spurred by falling stock markets and increasing evidence pointing to a global recession.

"We will steer it towards a good and realistic level. We will not let the market make our exchange rate irrational," Boediono said. He did not elaborate further.

The rupiah briefly fell 2.9 percent to 12,050 to the dollar, with some dealers expecting the currency to weaken towards 12,100 in the coming week due to market worries over foreign fund outflows from the country's financial market.

Indonesia imports a significant amount of basic necessities especially food. Failure to stabilise the rupiah, which has fallen 21 percent this year, could push up the cost of imported foods and put pressure on the country's balance of payments.

Bank Indonesia has been intervening in markets to defend its falling currency and it has also introduced a new measure on buying foreign exchange.

title: UPDATE:Bank  Indonesia  Reiterates Open Capital Account Policy
text:
(Adds background on intervention, loan boost to foreign reserves)

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian central bank Friday reiterated that it has no plan to resort to capital controls following its announcement Wednesday limiting purchases of foreign currencies without underlying transactions.

"We are still committed to an open capital-account regime," Bank Indonesia Governor Boediono said in a press conference.

Boediono said that the central bank will continue to be in the market to reduce exchange rate volatility. He, however, said that the central bank "won't operate against the market."

"We will work along with the market movement in order to lessen volatility," he said.

Dealers said that Bank Indonesia has recently reduced intervening in the foreign exchange market after spending nearly $7 billion last month to support the rupiah, which has fallen 20% against the dollar since the beginning of the year.

Boediono said that the government will take a $2 billion offshore loan in December that will boost the country's foreign exchange reserves, which stood at $50.6 billion as of end-October.

title: Indonesian rupiah tumbles, CDS spikes on  FX  rule
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah shed another 3.8 percent of its value against the dollar on Thursday after a new rule on foreign currency outflows raised worries that the authorities are bracing for a steep fall in the currency.

The rupiah hit 11,950 per dollar, its weakest since April 2001, at which level state banks were seen selling dollars. Traders suspected the intervention was on behalf of the central bank.

Bank Indonesia said on Wednesday that purchases of foreign exchange in Indonesia above an equivalent of $100,000 per month must be supported by underlying transactions.[ID:nJAK262096]

"It's only documentation requirement," said Enrico Tanuwidjaja, a strategist at OCBC Bank.

But traders said the measure, while aimed at curbing naked speculation on the rupiah, revealed authorities' concern over the currency and therefore spurred more rupiah selling.

"Investors' take on the move is still not very positive with widening CDS this morning," Tanuwidjaja said.

SINGAPORE, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies slid against the dollar on Monday as investors dumped assets amid heightened fears of a global downturn, forcing central banks in Indonesia and the Philippines to intervene.

The high-yielding Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> bore the brunt of the selling, briefly hitting as low as 10,800 per dollar but later steadied near 10,600 thanks to official intervention.

The rupiah's drop of around 3.5 percent on Monday took its cumulative decline so far this year to 11 percent.

"They (the central bank) are selling the dollar at various levels from 10,300," said a trader in Jakarta.

A second trader said state banks were selling dollars at 10,600.

The Philippine peso <PHP=> lost 0.8 percent to 49.385 per dollar, its weakest since December 2006, despite dollar-selling intervention by the central bank to set a floor for the unit.

Some traders said they expected the peso to test the 49.50 level in the near term unless the central bank intervened more aggressively.

The Philippine stock index <.PSI> tumbled 10 percent on Monday, triggering an automatic suspension of trading.

The MSCI index of Asian stocks outside Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> fell for a fourth consecutive session, losing 4 percent as of 0520 GMT, marking its lowest since June 2004.

Meanwhile, the South Korean won <KRW=> dropped as low as 1,447.9 per dollar as investors shrugged off the central bank's 


move to slash its key interest rate by 75 basis points -- the
biggest rate cut ever -- to calm the jittery market.


Analysts at Goldman Sachs said the won, which has lost 35 percent against the dollar so far this year, would face further selling pressure in the near term amid the global market turmoil.

"However, we continue to believe that the won/dollar has overshot on the downside and expect the won to strengthen beyond the near term," they said in a note.

The Japanese yen climbed towards a 13-year peak against the dollar <JPY=> and an all-time high against the Australian dollar <AUDJPY=R>, as a slide in Tokyo shares overshadowed a G7 warning about excessive yen volatility.

The Group of Seven big industrialised economices said on Monday that a rapid rise in the Japanese yen was bad for both markets and the economy and that it would watch developments accordingly.

title: Emerging  FX -Asians plumb multi-year lows on growth fears
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 23 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah hit its lowest level in nearly three years as Asian currencies fell to new multi-year lows on Thursday, hit by investor fears over global growth and persistent selling of risky assets.

 A day after Hungary raised rates by a hefty 3 percentage points to defend its currency, risk aversion was elevated in Asia with stock markets in Korea, Indonesia and the Philippines falling between 4 and 7 percent.

 The rupiah <IDR=> hit its lowest in nearly 3 years at 9,950 a dollar, the Philippine peso weakened to its weakest since early 2007 at 49 per dollar while the Malaysian ringgit fell to 3.5771, a nearly 2-year trough.

 The broad selling in emerging markets seemed to have sucked Asia in deep, even though it is backed by better fundamentals, such as ample reserves and growth estimates in higher single digits even in dismal global circumstances.

 "The nasty part is that deleveraging/balance sheet hole-plugging can produce indiscriminate selling, so Asia can be swept up even though its fundamentals are better," said Sean Callow, a strategist at Westpac Bank

 Central banks in India, Indonesia, Korea and the Philippines have been intervening to slow their currencies' decline and some of them were suspected of being in the market on Thursday.

 Analysts reckon policy makers are however merely smoothing the currency depreciation, and are tolerant of the weakness at a time when the risks of recession in Asia's main export markets are as high as that of heavy capital outflows triggered by the credit crisis.

 "Adding liquidity to increasingly thin and volatile markets is a valid policy decision, and note that FX reserves of most economies are ample," Patrick Bennett a strategist at Societe Generale said in a note.

 "We would only become concerned with a central bank attempting to defend a particular level, or one which was clearly acting contrary to economic fundamentals."  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR  Change on the day at 0526 GMT

title: 4th UPDATE: Asian Shares Drop On US Econ Woes; Shippers Sink
text:
(Adds information, quotes, updates levels)

SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Asian share markets skidded Thursday with financial and shipping stocks under water as concerns mounted about the global economy amid signs consumer spending was flagging heading into the end-year holiday season.

Japan's Nikkei 225 led the way after large gains earlier this week, ending down 11.4% for its largest one-day percentage drop since October 1987.

Australia's S&P/ASX 200 shed 6.8% with Korea's Kospi Composite ending down 9.4% in its largest one-day percentage fall since September 2001.

"A day is a long time in financial markets, let alone a week. The unwinding of most of the early-week gains on many bourses suggests there is still a large segment of the market standing ready to sell into bounces," said the analysis team at Westpac Institutional Bank.

"Certainly no-one can have confidence that we are near the end of the wave of mutual fund and hedge fund redemptions."

European spreadbetting firms were tipping stocks there to open lower with BGC Partners forecasting London's FTSE-100 down 214 points.

But in a slightly unusual dislocation, riskier currencies like the Australian dollar made a cautious recovery against the U.S. dollar and the Japanese yen; some said that was a sign of the return of the market focus to the negatives stacking up against the U.S. economy.

"What is hammering home is that people are getting beyond the financial crisis and seeing implications for the broader economy. Growth is looking pretty dismal," said Bank of New Zealand Currency Strategist Danica Hampton in Wellington.

Reflecting those concerns, base metal and crude oil prices dropped in Asia, with LME copper down 5%. Overnight, mining giant Rio Tinto said it would reassess expansion spending plans and curtail production of aluminum.

Shipping stocks around Asia fell on a slump in the Baltic Dry Index, a benchmark for rates on the bulk shipping sector; the index sank 10.7% to 1615 Wednesday in what freight derivatives broker FIS called a "day of disbelief," and was down more than 86% from its peak in May.

"I feel like we are in a deep sea with nothing we can do for now," said Taurus Investment & Securities analyst Oh Tae-Dong.

Traders were on the lookout for redemption selling, with talk of mutual funds offloading shares in the U.S. overnight.

But, for now, volume was on the light side. "We haven't seen panic selling. The mood is very, very cautious," said First NZ Capital broker James Snell.

U.S. stock futures were down 1.5%-2% in screen trade; Ebay Inc. fell 5.6% after-hours as it cut its fourth-quarter revenue outlook and earnings projections to below what analysts were expecting; also, its Chief Executive John Donahoe said the company expected a "very challenging" fourth quarter holiday season.

Earnings reports are due out later in the U.S. from such key names as Merrill Lynch and Advanced Micro Devices.

The moves in Asia followed the S&P 500's biggest percentage loss since Oct. 19, 1987; the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 7.9% after September U.S. retail sales fell the most in three years.

Japan's Nikkei 225 was hurt by declines in financial stocks, plus commodity-linked plays and those with exposure to consumer sentiment and/or a stronger yen; Sony fell 12.9% with Inpex Holdings down 14.2%, while Elpida Memory dived 16.9% to a limit-low and year-low of Y983.

The Topix index of all the Tokyo Stock Exchange First Section issues fell 90.99 points, or 9.5%, to 864.52, while December Nikkei 225 futures ended down 1240 points, or 13%, at 8250 on the Osaka Securities Exchange.

In Australia the share index ended near its lowest level since May 2005, as commodity price weakness hurt mining stocks; BHP Billiton fell 13.1% and Rio Tinto 15.9% while Woodside shed 5.5%.

New Zealand's market ended down 4.8% at its lowest level since September 2004; bellwether Telecom sank 8.6% to its lowest level since its 1991 listing, after cutting its profit forecasts.

Korea suffered its biggest point fall in the index's history as foreigners dumped shares worth KRW635.4 billion; KB Financial Group fell the daily limit of 15% with Shinhan Financial Group down 11.2%.

Steelmaker Posco also fell its 15% daily limit while the world's largest shipbuilder by orders, Hyundai Heavy Industries, was down the 15% limit, too, as were Hanjin Shipping and Korea Line.

Hong Kong shipping stocks were hurting the market there with the Hang Seng Index down 8.4%; China Shipping Development was down 25.1% at HK$5.89, China Cosco off 16.1% and Pacific Basin down 6.1%.

India's Sensex was 7% lower after briefly touching a 2008 trough; there wasn't much support from late Wednesday's news of another cash requirement ratio cut from the central bank.

Taiwan shares ended down 3.3% with volume slowing to a four-year low.

Philippine shares finished with a fall 5.2% with Singapore's Straits Times Index recently off 7.3% and the Shanghai Composite Index down 3%; Thai shares were lower by 4.7% and Indonesia 4.6%.

Among currencies, the U.S. dollar was around Y100.17 after falling to Y99.28 and the euro at Y134.12 after touching Y133.39, though against the dollar it had fallen to $1.3380.

The Australian dollar was back near US$0.6675, from an early fall to US$0.6521, and was showing some resilience against the yen too, as was the New Zealand dollar.

"Investor fears are increasingly focusing on threats to the real economy and in the wake of the soft U.S. retail data released overnight and some further easing of dollar funding pressures, the U.S. dollar is losing some of its recent shine," said Societe Generalecurrency strategist Patrick Bennett.

But Asian currencies remained weak: The U.S. dollar rose sharply against the Korean won and hit an 18-month high against the Philippine peso; central bank intervention sell dollars was suspected in India, Indonesia and the Philippines.

U.S. Treasurys were boosted by a flight to safety with the 10-year note up 17/32 at 100 15/32, yielding 3.940% and the two-year up 5/32 at 100 27/32, to yield 1.551%.

Lead 10-year Japanese government bond futures were helped by a solid auction of five-year notes with the contract at 134.91, up 0.11.

Credit default spreads blew wider with the Markit iTraxx Asia ex-Japan high-yield index quoted at 890-930 basis points, from 790-820 basis points Wednesday; the investment-grade index was 320-325 basis points, versus 260-265.

LME 3-month copper was down 4% at $4,700 a metric ton with notable falls too in zinc and nickel.

"It's not wise in the current environment to stick one's head out. I expect more downward pressure on metals prices across the board," said Barclays Capital analyst Yingxi Yu; "the whole complex will be under pressure as long as the financial situation doesn't get better and there's more confidence in the economy."

Spot gold was lower, down $6.10 at $842 a troy ounce, hurt by the commodity-wide pullback which also curbed silver and platinum.

Front-month Nymex crude was down $2.14 on Globex at $72.40 per barrel, after falling $4.09 in New York; it briefly touched its lowest level since last August, at $72.31.

The fall in oil was reducing gold's appeal as an inflation hedge.

title: Indonesia unveils more crisis measures, IMF positive
text:
JAKARTA, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Indonesia is well placed to weather a global economic crisis, an IMF official said on Wednesday, as Southeast Asia's top economy unveiled more measures to shore up confidence in its capital and currency markets.

Investor confidence took a dive last week and stocks in Jakarta plunged, prompting the closure of the stock exchange for three days and pressing policy-makers to quickly push through several measures in order to avoid a replay of the crisis that battered Indonesia's economy a decade ago.

The rupiah <IDR=> and the stock market <.JKSE>, which reopened on Monday, have been more stable this week, alongside a global rebound in market sentiment.

"The fundamentals are very strong and it's in good shape to weather this turmoil," said Milan Zavadjil, the International Monetary Fund's senior representative in Indonesia.

The IMF led a $43 billion rescue package for Indonesia a decade ago after it was hit by the Asian financial crisis.

He said that growth in Indonesia was much more reliant on domestic consumption and it was not as exposed to potential slowdowns in exports to markets such as the United States and Europe, in contrast to Singapore and the Philippines.

"Consumption currently has a lot of momentum and it's not suddenly going to stop dead," he told a panel discussion on the global crisis, adding that Indonesia's "fiscal position is sound" and that it had relatively low government debt levels.

Indonesia's economy grew 6.3 percent last year, the fastest pace in over a decade, aided by exports of commodities including palm oil, rubber, gas, and a steady drop in interest rates.

Analysts, however, expect global demand for key exports of commodities and mining products to be hit by the credit crisis.

GUARANTEES

Zavadjil said that while Indonesia was exposed to a drop in commodity prices, export volumes were unlikely to fall, noting that a lot of exports go to China where growth should hold up better.

Indonesia's parliamentary budget commission on Wednesday approved an economic growth forecast of 6 percent for 2009.

Along with the authorities halting stock trading last week, Indonesia's central bank is thought to have intervened to prop up the rupiah, particularly when it neared 10,000/dollar on Friday.

Indonesia moved on Monday to raise its guarantees on bank deposits to 2 billion rupiah ($203,000), up from 100 million rupiah previously, following similar steps taken by governments across the world that were aimed at tackling the biggest financial crisis since the Great Depression.

Indonesia's maximum guaranteed rupiah deposit rates were rasied this week by 75 basis points to 10 percent, part of efforts to bolster confidence in the rupiah and after a sharp increase in the amount of deposits it guarantees. Firdaus Djaelani, the head of state-owned deposit insurance corporation LPS said in a telephone text message late on Tuesday night that the agency had kept its guaranteed dollar deposit rates unchanged at 3.5 percent. Both were effective Oct. 14. As in other economies, Indonesian's interbank money market had been hit by the global credit crisis. But unlike some others, the liquidity squeeze in the domestic money market had also been made worse due to lower deposit growth relative to loan growth.

The Indonesia Stock Exchange may also increase the upside limit for share trading to 20-25 percent from 10 percent currently, President Director Erry Firmansyah said on Wednesday, but will keep its 10 percent downside limit in place. (Additional reporting by Andreas Ismar; Editing by Sara Webb)

title: USD Ends At IDR9,935; Dollar Off Intraday High Of IDR10,000
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah weakened sharply against the dollar Friday, falling amid thin trade to close at its weakest since December 2005.

The dollar traded at IDR9,935 at the close of local trading after hitting an intraday high of IDR10,000. The dollar had closed Thursday at IDR9,655.

It was the weakest level for the rupiah since Dec. 2, 2005, when the dollar fetched IDR9,990.

Currency dealers said the rupiah weakened due to panic-buying of dollars as a safe haven amid the current uncertainty over local stocks.

The Indonesia Stock Exchange remained closed Friday, its third day of suspension after a trading halt was declared halfway through the morning session Wednesday.

Dealers said that had the bourse opened as planned for Friday's afternoon trading session, both the rupiah and domestic stocks would probably have fallen more.

The exchange's composite index fell more than 21% this week prior to the trading halt. A 25-basis-point hike in the Bank Indonesia policy rate Tuesday also hurt growth expectations and increased bearishness on the bourse.

Dealers said that dollar/rupiah non-deliverable forward contracts rose sharply. The one-week offshore NDFs reached IDR10,025in early trading Friday, they said, compared with IDR9,950.

The spot market weakened more slowly, probably due to heavy central bank intervention. Bank Indonesia likely sold as much as $400 million Friday and around $2.5 billion in the foreign exchange market so far this week, traders said.

"We cannot see (the market fundamentals) too clearly as (today) the market has been very thin," a dealer at a major foreign bank said. "It seemed to take (the dollar) no effort to get from IDR9,900 to IDR10,000" as liquidity was so tight.

The dollar may rise more Monday when the stock market re-opens. Dealers said, however, that the weekend break will likely prompt investors to re-assess fundamentals, which might mean that shares likely won't tank further.

They said the dollar should find resistance at IDR10,000 and be supported at IDR9,850.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia slides as stocks pounded, won trades wildly

SINGAPORE, Oct 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were battered on Friday as investors dumped stocks amid the financial turmoil despite a round of global interest rate cuts, prompting dollar-selling intervention in South Korea, Indonesia and India.

 The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> fell as far as 9,750 per dollar, down about 1.6 percent from Thursday's close, as trader cited dollar-selling intervention by the central bank to support the local currency.

 "The action keeps players sidelined," said a trader in Jakarta.

 The South Korean won <KRW=> moved wildly, gaining over 12 percent to 1,224.9 per dollar at one point after falling sharply earlier, as the authorities were seen selling dollars to defend the won, which has lost 27 percent against the dollar this year.

 A wave of selling pounded Asian shares amid growing fears of the financial turmoil, with the MSCI index of Asia-Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> falling 7.7 percent to its lowest since January 2005.

 The Indian rupee <INR=IN> hit a record low at 49.25 per dollar, as the central bank said it would cut bank's cash reserve requirements to 7.5 percent to ease a liquidity crunch. [ID:nBOM357479]

 Meanwhile, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell to 1.4865 per U.S dollar, giving up its early gains as investors turned bearish on data showing the economy is in recession.

 "It's due to the GDP figure," said a trader in Singapore.

 The Sing dollar briefly rose to 1.4724 immediately after the central bank announced an easing in monetary policy.

 Some traders said suspected official intervention helped the local unit.

 Singapore's central bank, which sets policy by managing the Singapore dollar in a secret trade-weighted band against a basket of currencies, eased monetary policy for the first time in five years after its economy sank into recession [ID:nSIN389047]

 The central bank said on Friday it was shifting policy from a gradual appreciation bias to a neutral zero-appreciation bias for the trade-weighted currency, in response to slowing growth and expected easing in inflation.

 The central bank maintained the width of the secretive band.

title: WRAPUP 1-Asian governments act to prop up stocks,  currencies
text:
* Asian governments step in, tighten stock selling rules

* Indonesia prohibits short selling in October

* Thai, Philippine central banks intervene in currencies

By Rafael Nam

HONG KONG, Sept 30 (Reuters) - Asian governments from South Korea to Indonesia stepped in swiftly on Tuesday to try to prop up markets reeling from an overnight plunge in the United States after U.S. lawmakers rejected a $700 billion plan rescue plan for the financial industry.

Throughout the region, finance authorities and central banks spoke up to defend the soundness of their economies and acted by tightening stock-selling rules and buying tumbling currencies hurt by the flight of money from emerging markets.

In Taiwan, the president, vice premier, central bank and financial regulator made moves and comments to ease jittery markets.

"Taiwan's economic fundamentals are still good," President Ma Ying-jeou said in a speech at a local event. "We have the means to weather this global financial crisis."

India's finance minister, Palaniappan Chidambaram, stepped in to assure investors that market regulations would be tightened if needed.

"There is nothing to worry about. The regulations that are in place are adequate. If the regulations are to be tweaked, we will do so," he told reporters.

Malaysian Deputy Prime Minister Najib Razak said the government was maintaining its growth forecast of 5.5-5.8 percent for the year, adding the country was on track with opening its markets despite the Wall Street collapse.

Among Asia's financial market watchdogs, Taiwan's top financial regulator placed tighter limits on the short-selling of stocks, while Hong Kong's Securities and Futures Commission warned it would not tolerate abusive practices and could impose market-wide controls.

OUTRIGHT BANS

Other governments moved to outright bans.

Indonesia's stock exchange said it would prohibit short selling of stocks in October, and South Korea said it would do so for the time being while at the same time increasing the amount of shares firms are allowed to buy back.

The restrictions or outright bans on short selling follow similar actions by U.S. and European regulators this month, and come as Asian stocks head in September for their biggest monthly slide since the financial crisis a decade ago.

The failure on Monday of Washington's biggest and most comprehensive bid to keep financial sector shockwaves from tearing up the real economy handed the U.S. S&P 500 stock index its biggest decline since October 1987 and the Dow Jones industrial average its biggest points fall on record.

Asian stocks suffered heavily in September, victims of a sell-first-and-ask-later mentality among global investors. With risk aversion widespread, emerging market holdings have been among the first to be sold, analysts have said.

The MSCI index if Asia-Pacific stocks outside Japan is down about 16 percent in September, similar to the slide seen in the same month eight years ago and potentially its largest decline since October 1997.

"Despite the fact that the U.S. is at the centre of the crisis, every time the crisis escalates, capital leaves emerging Asia," said Citigroup analysts in a note to clients on Tuesday.

"This is probably a result of flight to quality. But it also provides strong evidence (that) refute the so-called decoupling thesis," they added.

The tighter rules on short-selling, combined with expectations that U.S. lawmakers will eventually approve a rescue plan helped many Asian stock markets pull back from their day's lows, but analysts expect broad risk reduction to continue as investors pull money out of the region.

CURRENCIES UNDER FIRE

Asian currencies have also come under fire this month.

The South Korean won dropped 1.5 percent on Tuesday, bringing its loss for September to 9.8 percent, its biggest monthly percentage loss since December 1997. Its loss for the year so far is well over 20 percent.

The falls on Tuesday came despite some talk over dollar-selling intervention by the foreign exchange authorities and even after the Finance Minister said the country would spend part of its foreign exchange reserves to stabilise markets if necessary.

South Korean authorities have spent more than $30 billion this year to try to underpin the won.

Other governments also moved to support their ailing currencies. The Philippine central bank sold dollars on Tuesday to prop up the peso, while the Bank of Thailand intervened on the baht to keep its moves in line with other Asian currencies though it did not specify which action had been taken. title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia c.bank deputy says "no liquidity problem"
text:
(Adds quotes, background, comments on intervention)

JAKARTA, Sept 17 (Reuters) - An Indonesian deputy central bank governor said on Wednesday "there is no liquidity problem" in the banking sector, a day after Bank Indonesia reduced its overnight repo rate to help commercial banks cope with a liquidity squeeze.

Even before the latest wave of credit turmoil struck global markets, Indonesian money market had been squeezed by foreign investors' selling local bonds and gradual policy tightening by the central bank in its battle to contain double-digit inflation.

Rapid growth in loans in step with a still fast expanding Indonesian economy, outstripping growth in bank deposits, also contributed to the tight liquidity.

"In regards to liquidity conditions in the banking sector, there is no problem," deputy governor Budi Rochadi told reporters.

"Of course liquidity is an important issue to meet needs (for cash) for the Eid al-Fitr celebrations," Rochadi said, adding that "in regards to liquidity, we will make it easier for banks to meet their liquidity needs including through repo."

Rochadi was referring to the Eid celebration to mark the end of the Muslim fasting month of Ramadan, which this year falls in early October. Demand for cash usually rises ahead of the celebrations as families head to their home towns to visit relatives.

The central bank on Tuesday cut its overnight repo rate, the rate at which it lends to commercial banks, by 200 basis point to 10.25 percent and raised the rate it pays on overnight deposits -- also known as the Fasbi rate -- by 100 basis points to 8.25 percent.

Bank Indonesia also offered to pay more on deposits that banks place with it, offering local lenders extra help at a time when markets have been rattled by the collapse of U.S. investment bank Lehman Brothers, the takeover of crisis-hit Merrill Lynch and funding troubles at insurer American International Group.

Separately, another deputy governor, Hartadi Sarwono, said on Wednesday that Bank Indonesia had intervened in the foreign exchange market, selling dollars to support the rupiah currency <IDR=>, in recent days.

He also said that the central bank was considering revising its reserve requirement ruling for commercial banks under which the requirement would no longer be linked to banks' loan ratios but to the possible use of debt paper by commercial banks in meeting the requirement.

"It is no longer relevant for the current minimum reserve requirements to be linked to the LDR (loan to deposit ratios)," Sarwono told reporters.

"Now the (annual) loan growth is over 35 percent, so we will try to revoke this ruling. There is possibility the minimum reserve requirements will no longer be related with LDR but with debt paper."

title: 2nd UPDATE: PBOC Cuts Rates; Policy Shift To Aid China Econ
text:
(Adds analysis, details of actions by other central banks.)


 
   By Terence Poon and Victoria Ruan 
   Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
 

BEIJING (Dow Jones)--China's central bank cut interest rates for the first time in six years Monday, abruptly reversing course and signaling Beijing may step in with more measures to support an economy hurt by the global slowdown.

The People's Bank of China's announced the rate cut just hours after turmoil engulfed the U.S. financial sector, with Lehman Brothers Holdings Inc. seeking bankruptcy protection from creditors and Merrill Lynch & Co. agreeing to be rescued by Bank of America.

The PBOC's policy easing caught many analysts off guard, though most said it likely wasn't directly driven by the dramatic news on Wall Street. China's "government is more concerned than we thought about the prospects of growth," said Standard Chartered economist Stephen Green.

The central bank cut its benchmark lending rate effective Tuesday and reduced the portion of reserves that smaller financial companies must set aside, particularly those in areas that were hit hard by a devastating earthquake in May.

As China's inflation has steadily slowed, the PBOC had recently been hinting that it would fine-tune its two-year-old tightening policy. But few expected such a dramatic easing so suddenly.

Monday's measures are intended to "solve the prominent economic problems" and to "maintain and sustain steady growth of the economy," the central bank said on its Web site. The PBOC said the moves are in line with second-half economic tasks set by top policymakers at a key meeting in late July.

The cuts in lending rates and the reserve ratio are the latest moves by Beijing to support growth, ending a round of policy tightening that started in April 2006. Beijing had previously been focused on taming inflation and curbing economic overheating, but consumer-price rises have been moderating and officials have increasingly turned their focus to sustaining economic growth.

The PBOC cut the one-year yuan lending rate by 27 basis points to 7.20%, the first cut since February 2002, and cut the required reserve ratio for smaller banks by 100 basis points from Sept. 25, the first cut since mid-2006.

Analysts expect Chinese shares to rally when they reopen from a three-day holiday weekend Tuesday, but any gains could be hard to sustain amid persistent concerns about the health of the domestic economy.

"The central bank's move will likely prompt the index to open higher and then head south again because I think investors already have lots of bad news to digest," said Xu Yinhui, analyst at Guotai Junan Securities.

Bond yields and money market interest rates are expected to fall, though one Shanghai-based dealer at a foreign bank predicted the yuan could rise slightly.

Analysts said more pro-growth policies, such as lifting the ceiling on bank lending and introducing fresh fiscal stimulus, are likely. Standard Chartered's Green said Beijing is "just around the corner" from ending its ceiling on bank lending and the chances of fiscal policy stimulus "just went up a lot."

Since the late-July meeting, the central bank has lifted this year's lending quota, widely seen as Beijing's most effective tool for slowing credit and investment growth. China has also since raised the export-tax rebate on certain textile products.

The PBOC Monday left the one-year deposit rate unchanged. This could help maintain consumption at a time when China's exporters are hurting from a slowdown in advanced economies that could get worse as Wall Street's troubles mount.

Before the latest announcement, the central bank had raised the benchmark one-year lending rate eight times since April 2006, and the one-year deposit rate seven times since August 2006. China had raised the reserve requirement ratio to 17.5% for most commercial banks from 14.5% at the start of the year. The government has been raising the reserve ratio since mid-2006 to drain liquidity as its huge foreign-exchange reserves continue to grow.

Other central banks in Asia could come under increased pressure to follow China's lead and cut the cost of borrowing as the U.S. economy, a key destination for Asia's exports, shows more signs of trouble.

While many central bankers have been focused on fighting inflation with tighter policy, worries about growth are coming increasingly to the fore and some could conclude that rates have gone as high as they need to.

Although many of Asia's biggest markets were closed Monday for a holiday, central bankers and regulators across the region were closely watching the unfolding events on Wall Street.

The PBOC "might have long been prepared" for Monday's moves, but Lehman's troubles "might have encouraged them to move faster," said China International Capital Corp. analyst Xu Jian.

Financial authorities elsewhere in the region also took action Monday.

The Reserve Bank of Australia injected A$1.3 billion into the financial system to ensure ongoing access to cash while South Korea's Financial Services Commission said the authorities would provide foreign currency liquidity, as necessary.

India's central bank apparently stepped into the currency market Monday, selling dollars to prop up the rupee, traders said. Bank Indonesia said it will continue to intervene where necessary and "stands ready" to stabilize the Jakarta's markets. It said Monday it would cut the amount of bonds it issues this year as part of that.

Bank of Thailand Deputy Gov. Bandid Nijathaworn warned that the fallout in the U.S. banking sector would prompt investors to move funds out of Asia to inject liquidity into U.S. assets.

"We'll have to closely monitor the capital-outflow situation. The (outflow) trend has been continuing for sometime," Bandid told reporters. "The capital movement will affect liquidity in the domestic financial market."

-By Terence Poon and Victoria Ruan; Dow Jones Newswires; 8610 6588-5848; victoria.ruan@dowjones.com

-Denis McMahon also contributed to this story. [ 15-09-08 1252GMT ]

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia c.bank sees cautious response to  currency
text:
(Recasts with c.bank gov remarks, adds details, quotes)

JAKARTA, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank governor said on Friday the authority would continue to be in the market to ensure stability for the rupiah <IDR=> but policy responses would be cautious. The rupiah fell on Friday to a seven-month low and has weakened since earlier August -- a trend that has accelerated in the past week -- raising speculation that the central bank may have to keep monetary policy tighter for longer.

The rupiah fell on Friday to 9,465 per dollar, its lowest level since January.

The currency had been hit in recent days as investors worried about a withdrawal of foreign money from the high-yielding bond market after seeing the deterioration in the country's trade account.

Global risk aversion has also flared again this week, which often means that emerging markets take a hit as investors pare back their riskier holdings.

The rupiah recorded its biggest one-day fall in 15 months on Sept. 5, which dealers said had prompted Bank Indonesia (BI) to intervene.

"We will always be in the market," the central bank governor, Boediono, replied when asked about the rupiah's weakness.

He has said in the past the phrase does not necessarily mean currency intervention. It could also refer to market monitoring, he has said.

"We certainly have to respond to these changes in a fundamental way, meaning we will respond to changes which are fundamental, not changes that are temporary," Boediono told reporters.

"I think our response should not be excessive, whether in regards to interest rates or exchange rates."

However, Vice-president Jusuf Kalla said the fall in the currency should not be cause for concern. The currency's level was still in line with budget projections and a weaker rupiah would support exports.

Indonesia's major exports include palm oil, cocoa and rubber.

"Of course, for importers and consumers (the rupiah fall) is not good, but it is good for exporters," the former businessman from the country's commodities producing island of Sulawesi told reporters.

"The state budget targets (the rupiah) at around the current levels, between 9,400-9,500 (per dollar). So we do not need to worry with (the rupiah) at the current levels."

The stock market has also fallen sharply. The Indonesia Composite Index <.JJSE> has fallen more than 11 percent this week, its deepest weekly fall since August 2007. title: SE Asian Stocks-S'pore off 2-yr lows, Jakarta down on  FX  fears
text:
*Singapore bounces off two-year lows as property stocks rise

 *Jakarta falls to 18-mth low on fears of weak rupiah

 *Bank stocks pare gains after rising on hopes of Lehman sale

 By Koh Gui Qing

 SINGAPORE, Sept 12 (Reuters) - Singapore shares <.FTSTI> rose 1.16 percent, off near two-year lows on Friday, as investors bought battered property stocks like CapitaLand , but a weak rupiah pushed Indonesian stocks <.JKSE> to a near 18-month low.

 Singapore's Straits Times Index ended at 2,570.67 points, and Indonesian stocks dropped 3.5 percent to a level last seen in March 2007.

 Elsewhere, Thai stocks <.SETI> rose 1.17 percent by 0951 GMT, Philippine shares <.PSI> fell 0.99 percent, and Vietnam stocks <.VNI> dropped 4.2 percent.

 In Singapore, some analysts said recent share price weakness in Southeast Asia's top developer CapitaLand  reflected investor fears over a weakening property market in China and its impact on the firm's Chinese investments.

CapitaLand shares have tumbled 50 percent since hitting a record level in October, and are down 32 percent for the year.

 "Some residential property developers have reportedly slashed prices to generate sales," said Wilson Liew, a Kim Eng analyst. "CapitaLand could face short-term price pressures."

 Liew has a "hold" rating for CapitaLand, with a price target of S$4.48, a 4.4 percent upside to Friday's closing price.

CapitaLand ended 2.9 percent higher. Other property stocks in Singapore rose too -- City Developments  climbed 1.4 percent and Hongkong Land  gained 2.8 percent.

 DBS Group , the region's largest bank, ended down 0.4 percent after rising 0.9 percent in early trade on Friday as investors bought bank stocks on hopes of a possible takeover of Lehman Brothers .

 In Jakarta, investors dumped stocks on fears the weakening Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> signalled a worsening economic outlook as the country's current account deteriorated.

 One analyst said some investors were worried Indonesia's central bank and government would not intervene to support the currency. Jusuf Kalla, Indonesia's vice-president, said on Friday the rupiah's fall was good for the country's exports.

 The rupiah hit a 3-½   week low on Tuesday at 9,370 rupiah to a dollar. It weakened 0.3 percent on Friday and was last traded at 9,450.

 Heriyanto Irawan, a Deutsche Bank analyst, said in a note to clients on Friday that the healthy Indonesian economy should support the rupiah in the longer term.

 However, a current account deficit, weak commodity prices and fears a soft rupiah would fuel inflation might pressure the currency in the short run.

 Telkom Indonesia , the country's largest telecoms firm, fell 4.9 percent.

PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia Tbk  Indonesia's fourth-largest bank, was down 6.5 percent, and PT Astra International , the country's largest automotive distributor, dropped 10.1 percent.  (Editing by Jennifer Tan)

title: UPDATE:Bk Indonesia:To Maintain Continual Presence In  FX  Mkt
text:
(Adds quotes from central bank governor; vice president's comment)

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia maintains a constant presence in the foreign exchange market and will respond to any market moves driven by fundamentals, central bank governor Boediono told reporters Friday.

However, the central bank avoids responding to market movements it deems temporary, and measures its responses to avoid excessive intervention, Boediono told reporters.

Also Friday, Vice President Jusuf Kalla told reporters that the possibility of the dollar reaching IDR9,500 is "not a concern."

"We can still overcome (that level of rupiah weakness)," Kalla said. "It will of course cause losses for importers, but on the other hand, it benefits exporters, so it isn't a problem. This is a temporary up-and-down move."

Boediono said the authorities "must respond to all movements of the markets that have fundamental characteristics, but not to those that are temporary."

"We must be on guard (to ensure) our response does not have a 'rhythm' that is excessive, whether it is in (the form of changes to) interest rates or foreign exchange" intervention, he said.

Boediono made the remarks after the dollar strengthened to around IDR9,460, its highest level since Jan. 23, when it reached IDR9,475 in intraday trading.

He didn't say whether he thought the rupiah's weakness Friday was driven by fundamentals, but reiterated official remarks earlier this week that Indonesia's economic fundamentals are sound.

"Our fundamentals are fine and I am very certain that we can calmly overcome" the weakening in the local currency and overall weakening in world financial markets. "All countries now must align their (policies) with the changes that have taken place in the global market."

Boediono didn't say whether Bank Indonesia had sold dollars to intervene in the foreign exchange market Friday.

Dealers say the central bank has sold several hundred million dollars in recent days to shore up the local currency.

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia raises rph deposit rate, holds dlr rate
text:
(Adds quotes, details)

JAKARTA, Sept 11 (Reuters) - Indonesia's deposit insurance agency said it would raise its guaranteed rupiah deposit rate with effect from Monday, but analysts said the new rate was lower than expected, and failed to provide support for the rupiah.

The rupiah <IDR=> fell more than 1 percent to 9,475 per dollar on Thursday, its weakest since late January, as troubles in the U.S. financial sector reduced appetite for riskier assets. Traders said Bank Indonesia had intervened, selling dollars.

Firdaus Djaelani, head of the state-owned deposit insurance corporation (known as LPS), said the agency had raised its rupiah guaranteed bank deposit rate by 50 basis points to 9.25 percent for the period Sept. 15, 2008 to Jan. 14, 2009.

The agency kept the maximum dollar guaranteed bank deposit rate at 3.50 percent. Analysts said that would make it less attractive for holders of rupiah to switch into dollars, a move aimed at reducing selling pressure on the Indonesian currency.

The maximum guaranteed bank deposit rates are usually closely watched by commercial banks because they affect the commercial banks' deposit and lending rates, and therefore affect their profitability.

"We're anticipating inflationary pressure...many have predicted inflation will remain in double digits until year-end, so we're anticipating that," Djaelani told Reuters by telephone when asked about the reasons behind the deposit rate hike.

Indonesia's inflation rate inched lower to 11.85 percent in August on the back of lower oil prices, but food prices and transportation fees typically rise during the Muslim fasting month of Ramadan, which this year started on September 1.

Bank Indonesia forecast inflation at 11.5-12.5 percent this year before easing to 6.5-7.5 percent at the end of 2009.

The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate, known as the BI rate <BIPG>, by 25 basis points to 9.25 percent last week, the fifth time this year, to curb inflation.

Analysts had expected the deposit agency to raise the maximum deposit rates by more than 50 basis points in order to encourage investors to park their funds in rupiah.

"In my view (the hike) should have been bigger," said Anton Gunawan, economist at Bank Danamon.

Some commercial banks now offer deposit rates of around 12 percent, much higher than the guaranteed rates, as banks are competing for depositors' funds amid tight market liquidity following monetary tightening by the central bank. title: UPDATE:Indonesia 2Q Curr Acct In Deficit;First In Nearly 3 Yrs
text:
(Recasts lead, adds further details, rupiah's levels and analysts' comments)

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia recorded a current account deficit in the second quarter, its first in almost three years, but analysts are confident that the country's economic fundamentals remain sound.

The country posted a $1.5 billion deficit in its current account in the second quarter, swinging from a $2.3 billion surplus in the first quarter, Bank Indonesia said in a statement Friday. The current account deficit was the first since the third quarter of 2005 when the country recorded a $1.2 billion deficit.

Bank Danamon Chief Economist Anton Gunawan maintained his forecast that the country will record a current account surplus for the entire year. He said a sharp fall in global oil prices recently will likely help improve Indonesia's current account balance. The country has been a net oil importer since 2003.

Indonesia's balance of payment was in a $1.3 billion surplus in the second quarter, up from $1.0 billion in the January-March period, the central bank said.

The balance of payment surplus was due to a $3.7 billion surplus in the capital and financial account, reversing from a $337 million deficit in the first quarter, it added.

The surplus in the capital and financial account was due to capital inflows related to portfolio investment, corporate offshore borrowings and foreign direct investment, the central bank said.

The capital inflows were due to an increase in economic activities, an improving investment climate, attractive interest differentials, economic stability, and a positive response from investors on the government's move to hike retail fuel prices in May, it added.

Several economists had already expected Indonesia to record a current account deficit in the second quarter due to the 51% on-year rise in imports outpacing export growth of 28% during the period.

The current account deficit may undermine the rupiah in the present environment, said Lehman Brothers Friday, referring to the current selloff in the currencies of emerging markets.

Indeed, the rupiah closed at IDR9,395 against the dollar Friday, down from IDR9,250 Thursday. The rupiah's intraday fall Friday to IDR9390 prompted Bank Indonesia to intervene but its move failed to reverse the local currency's decline, dealers said.

Lehman Brothers, however, said that it remains broadly confident with the underlying Indonesian story.

"Bank Indonesia has proven perhaps the most determined central bank in Asia, issuing a series of hikes and hawkish policy statements, backed by a relatively strong performing local economy," it said.

In addition, Bank Indonesia continues to protect the rupiah with consistent intervention in the foreign exchange market, it noted.

Bank Indonesia said earlier Friday that its foreign exchange reserves fell to $58.36 billion as of Aug. 29 from $60.56 billion July 31 due to a number of its interventions to help bolster the local currency and partial repayment of the government's offshore debt.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia slides, c.banks step in to prop  currencies
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 2 (Reuters) - Asian currencies extended losses against a broadly stronger U.S. dollar on Tuesday, prompting central banks in Thailand, Malaysia, Indonesia, India and the Philippines to defend their struggling currencies.

 Thailand's deepening political turmoil put additional pressure on the Thai baht <THB=TH>, which fell 0.6 percent to a one-year low at 34.49 per dollar, as traders cited dollar-selling intervention by the central bank to support the local currency.

 The baht <THB=W> dipped to 34.52 in offshore trading.

 Thai Prime Minister Samak Sundaravej declared a state of emergency in Bangkok on Tuesday and gave the army control of public order after overnight clashes between pro- and anti-government protesters.

 "This will definitely rub investors the wrong way, and we are likely to see pressure on Thai assets and a weaker Thai baht - the offshore baht markets have already given a good indication of what can be expected," said Vishnu Varathan, economist at Forecast in Singapore.

 The onshore baht was likely to fall below 34.50 per dollar soon before getting some technical support at 34.75, he added.

 The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> fell 0.7 percent to as low as 3.4260 per dollar, its weakest level in a year, and traders suspected the central was intervening to prop up the ringgit.

 Official intervention was also spotted in Indonesia, where the rupiah <IDR=> fell to a two-week low at 9,196 per dollar.

 "It's not large. I think they realise that there is no point intervening aggressively in a dollar bull market," said a Jakarta-based trader.

 STRONGER DOLLAR

 The dollar hit a 10-month high against a basket of major currencies <.DXY>, boosted by a sharp drop in oil prices on expectations that Hurricane Gustav's damage to U.S. energy facilities may be smaller than feared.

 The dollar's rally also weighed on other Asian currencies, with the Indian rupee <INR=IN> falling to 44.47 per dollar as the central bank was seen selling dollars to stem the rupee's slide.

 Such dollar-selling intervention, which has become routine in recent months, helped the Philippine peso <PHP=> stabilise at 46.60 per dollar, its weakest level in almost a year.

 "The market is definitely and decisively for the dollar, so there is nothing they (central bank) can do, but they are still intervening just like all the other central banks," said a trader in Manila.

 The South Korean won <KRW=> hit a fresh four-year low at 1,133.9 per dollar, down nearly 1.6 percent from the domestic close on Monday, when the currency tumbled 3 percent.

 A wave of capital outflows fuelled by concerns about the fallout of the global credit crisis and high oil prices have hit Asian currencies, pushing most of them into the red this year.

title: Emerging  FX -Growth worries deepen, push ringgit to 2008 low
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Deepening worries about global growth hurt Asian currencies on Monday, particularly those of trade-dependent countries, with the Malaysian ringgit diving to its lowest in 2008 and the Singapore dollar to a five-month low.

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> fell to a one-month low while the Philippine peso <PHP=> hit a two-week low of 44.485 per dollar as the latter's broad strength overshadowed the fall in the price of oil <CLc1>, which is one of Asia's biggest imports.

The dollar struck a six-month high against a basket of currencies <.DXY> as fund managers and investors unwound holdings of commodities and high-yielding currencies.

Growth concerns were pushed to the fore by last week's remarks from the European Central Bank acknowledging that euro zone economies were slowing more than expected, and by suggestions the Australian authorities could be cutting rates.

Market participants seemed to be growing confident that the U.S. dollar's 6-1/2-year decline had ended, said Sean Callow, a Westpac Bank strategist.

"If this is true then the assumption that dollar/Asia must fall is being thrown into the dustbin," he said, adding that explained the profit-taking on Asian currency holdings.

"Westpac does not agree that dollar has formed a cycle low but right now that's where a good amount of money is being placed," he said.

The ringgit <MYR=> hit 3.3255 per dollar, its weakest this year, and the Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell to the weaker side of 1.41 per U.S. dollar briefly after the government lowered its growth forecast for the economy.

"The dollar buying seems a bit overdone, but the dollar is still rallying against the majors," said a trader in Kuala Lumpur.

Central banks in Taiwan, Indonesia and South Korea were suspected of having intervened to defend their falling currencies.

Jonathan Ravelas, chief market strategist at Banco De Oro Universal Bank in the Philippines, said the peso had also reacted to the dollar's broad strength.

"We are looking for a rally towards 44.50-45.00 levels in the near-term, following a near-term bottom at last week's low at 43.76," Ravelas said.

Analysts at JPMorgan Chase said market positions were exacerbating the Asian currency selling, owing to stop losses being triggered on long positions in the regionals.

"The low yielding currencies from open economies most leveraged to global growth are taking the brunt of the impact, while less cyclical FX that also benefit from the oil price decline are being impacted the least," they said in a note to clients.

"With positions still relatively flat and growth concerns rising, near-term momentum remain for these moves," they said.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia rangebound; c.banks shore up won, rupiah
text:
SINGAPORE, July 8 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies moved in tight ranges on Tuesday with investor sentiment torn between falling oil prices and renewed credit fears, while authorities in South Korea and Indonesia intervened to prop up their currencies.

 The won <KRW=> hit a two-week high at 1,025.3 per dollar, up 1.7 percent from Monday's domestic close of 1,042.9, as dealers said authorities sold up to $2 billion to boost the local unit.

 Meanwhile, traders also cited dollar-intervention by Indonesia's central bank to try to support the rupiah <IDR=>.

 "Bank Indonesia is still on the offer side," said a trader in Jakarta. "It seems that they are trying to push the dollar below 9,200."

 A second trader said the central bank's intervention was aimed at keeping the rupiah in tight ranges.

 The intervention pushed the rupiah <IDR=> as high as 9,190 per dollar before it edged back to around 9,205.

 The currency has gained about 1 percent against the dollar in the past month, benefiting from the central bank's three successive interest rate rises since early May, which took the benchmark rate to 8.75 percent, among the highest in Asia.

 Standard Chartered expects the Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> to trade near 9,200 per dollar at the end of September before rising to 9,150 by the end of 2008, analysts at the bank said in a note, raising their forecast from 9,250 and 9,200, respectively.

 "Bank Indonesia is committed to raise interest rates gradually which should mitigate capital outflows," the analysts said, adding that the rupiah could hit 9,100 by end-March 2009 and 9,000 by end-June.

 Several authorities in Asia have been intervening regularly in recent months to support their currencies as part of efforts to cushion rising import prices from the likes of surging oil.

 WEAKER PESO

 The Philippine peso <PHP=> pulled back to 45.88 per dollar, down a third of a percent from Monday's close to its weakness level since September, after briefly hitting as high as 45.63.

 Traders said buying interest in the peso was undermined by concerns about high oil prices and the global credit crisis.

 "The bullish sentiment (on the dollar versus the peso) is still intact, it seems a test of the 46 level is just around the corner," said a trader in Manila.

 A second trader added: "Oil prices are still above $140 and (domestic) inflation is getting higher and higher."

 Oil prices <CLc1> held largely steady on Tuesday after dropping close to $4 on Monday, backing off last week's record high of $145.85.

 On Monday, a Lehman Brothers report said a pending accounting change could force Fannie Mae  and Freddie Mac , the top U.S. mortgage funders, to raise a combined $75 billion in capital at a tough time. [ID:nN07435475]

 Elsewhere, the Pakistani rupee was 2.9 percent weaker at a record low of 73 to the dollar <PKR=PK> because of worries about inflation, widening current and budget account deficits and security, dealers said.

 The rupee had closed at 71.00/05 to the dollar on Monday.

 The rupee has lost more than 18 percent against the dollar this year as annual inflation accelerated to a three-decade high of 19.27 percent in May and fiscal and current account deficits widened.  CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR
