title: WRAPUP 3-Asia cbanks prop up  currencies  over inflation worries
text:
* Central banks in South Korea, Taiwan, the Philippines and Indonesia sell dollars to support their currencies.

 * Central banks are concerned about the inflationary impact of rising oil prices.

 * Most of the currencies are seen remaining under pressure despite the interventions.  (Updates with third intervention in Korea)

 By Cheon Jong-woo and Melissa Chia

 SEOUL/SINGAPORE, May 27 (Reuters) - Asian central banks moved to prop up falling currencies on Tuesday to help prevent surging oil prices from stoking inflation in economies bracing for a global slowdown.

 Central banks in Indonesia, the Philippines, South Korea and Taiwan were spotted selling dollars to support their currencies under pressure from inflation fears and wobbly stock markets, currency traders said.

 Asian central banks have traditionally intervened to prevent the currency appreciation which would hurt exports, the main driver of growth for most of the region's economies.

 But the focus of policy in some countries is now shifting to containing inflation with oil prices at record highs above $130 a barrel driving up costs across the economy and fuelling demands for higher wages.

 "In choosing between a stronger currency and potentially higher rates it would seem authorities believe higher rates would be more detrimental for growth prospects," said Magnus Prim, chief Asia strategist at SEB in Singapore.

 A strong domestic currency makes imports cheaper, helping limit the inflationary impact of soaring energy costs.

 "This may become a common pattern in Asia," said another analyst in Singapore. "Central banks would need to draw down their reserves, given the turn from trade surpluses to trade deficits and much more sparse capital inflows," said the analyst who declined to be named.

 In South Korea, where the central bank is under political pressure to cut interest rates, authorities intervened three times in one day to support the won, Asia's second worst performing currency this year after the Pakistan rupee.

 Five currency dealers in Seoul said the Bank of Korea had sold as much as $800 million to support the won for the second time in a week. They reported two more interventions later in the day, estimating a total of nearly $2 billion had been spent.

 GROWTH DOWN, PRICES UP

 The won, which has fallen 9.8 percent this year, has been under pressure from a soaring oil import bill, foreign selling of local stocks and a government plan to control overseas borrowing as the country braces for its first current account deficit since the Asian financial crisis 11 years ago.

 The central bank said this month South Korea economic growth would likely slow to around 4.5 percent this year from 5.0 percent in 2007. The bank kept rates steady this month because inflation is running at a four-year high of 4.1 percent, above its target of between 2.5 percent and 3.5 percent, partly due to rising import costs.

 But minutes from the Bank of Korea's meeting showed two of the central bank's six board members wanted rates to be cut, and that the central bank believed a weak won has more negative than positive effects on the economy.

 "The won fell as oil prices jumped but we are worried that the won's fall might be excessive," Choi Jong-ku, head of the South Korean finance ministry's international bureau, told Reuters.

 The won rallied on his remarks and hit a session peak after the second intervention, but analysts said they expected more weakness in the Korean currency and other currencies supported by central banks on Tuesday.

 "Intervention doesn't have a long term impact," said Han-Sia Yeo, strategist, Bank of America in Singapore.

 Three Manila-based traders said the Philippine central bank sold dollars around 43.70 per dollar, although the peso <PHP=> still fell to a low of 43.73, its weakest since November. One trader estimated the central bank had sold around $200 million.

 The Philippine economy is feeling the heat of rising import costs and weakening demand for exports as the U.S. credit crisis and housing slump weigh on the global economy.

 Imports of oil products jumped 87 percent in March while electronics exports fell almost 17 percent. The peso, Asia's top performer in 2007, has fallen 5.5 percent this year against the dollar.

 Bank Indonesia was also suspected of selling dollars between 9,365 and 9,380 rupiah per dollar, two traders in Jakarta said. A trader in Singapore also said Indonesia's central bank had intervened. Most central banks in the region usually do not comment on currency interventions.

 The rupiah <IDR=> has fallen 1.3 percent in the past month against the dollar despite its high yield, shunned by investors who fear that the central bank may not raise rates aggressively enough to temper inflationary pressures.

 The country raised its subsidised fuel prices by almost 30 percent on Saturday, making it likely that inflation which is at a 19-month high near 9 percent will soon hit double-digits.

 Traders in Taiwan said the central bank had intervened to support the currency <TWD=TP>, which fell for a third consecutive session as foreigners turned net sellers of Taiwan stocks.

 But portfolio outflows were the only factor weighing against a currency backed by Taiwan's huge current account surplus, a central bank that is tightening policy and an administration that promises better ties with China.

 Taiwan is also abolishing price controls on petrol and diesel from June.  (Additional reporting by Kevin Yao in Singapore; Writing by Vidya Ranganathan; Editing by Tomasz Janowski)

title: Indonesia rupiah pricing in risk of policy let-down
text:
SINGAPORE, May 14 (Reuters) - A simultaneous bearish move in Indonesian yields and rupiah forwards indicates market participants are betting interest rates will rise but not fast enough to prevent inflation from undermining the currency.

Offshore investors now expect the rupiah <IDR=> to hit 9,850 per dollar within a year, nearly 6 percent weaker than current spot levels at 9,825.

Inter-bank one-year rates <JIBOR=BIIA> are just above 9 percent, pricing in at least 75 basis points more of rate rises by Bank Indonesia over the next 12 months.

At the same time, the offshore non-deliverable forward curve <IDRNDFOR=> is at its steepest in more than two years. Spreads between 3-month and one-year dollar/rupiah levels are at 460 points.

That, analysts say, shows that while Bank Indonesia's intervention could keep the rupiah tightly bound in the short term, it may be unable to contain longer-term downward pressures on the currency from rising inflation and portfolio outflows.

"The market is hoping for the best but is attaching a risk premium to the rupiah," said Claudio Piron, JPMorgan Chase's currency strategist.

Bank Indonesia raised rates last week after inflation hit a 19-month high and long after analysts had warned it was behind the curve and sacrificing an inflation-fighting policy mandate in pursuit of growth.

INFLATION WORRY

Indonesia's annual inflation, already near 9 percent, is expected to hit double-digit levels if the government follows through on a plan to raise domestically controlled fuel prices.

The 25 basis-point rate rise on May 6 raised expectations the central bank will strive to keep prices stable.

But market participants, familiar with the street protests and the rupiah's tumble that followed a fuel price rise in 2005, are nonetheless worried the central bank may be reluctant to do enough to keep inflation under control.

Those worries have translated into a higher longer-term implied volatility on rupiah <IDRVOL> and a weaker rupiah in the offshore forwards.

"It comes down to central bank credibility, and the anticipated sequence of events," said one Hong Kong-based analyst.

"If you think that Bank Indonesia will fall behind the curve, and the rupiah will sell off, then Bank Indonesia will tighten as a reaction to that sell-off, then you can be bearish both rates and currency."

Apart from a possible foot-dragging central bank, other factors could weigh on the rupiah.

Indonesia has among the highest pass-throughs in the region from currency to inflation, making it imperative that Bank Indonesia defends the currency if it wants to rein in prices.

JPMorgan's Piron estimates that even with foreign exchange reserves of $58 billion, Bank Indonesia can cover only 7 months of imports, roughly the same average monthly reserves-to-import ratio that it had in 2005.

"It appears that Bank Indonesia looks better placed and highly motivated to defend its FX stability relative to some of its regional peers," Piron said in a note.

"This is not to say that the rupiah is without risk or that the market is oblivious." (Editing by Neil Fullick) ((vidya.ranganathan@reuters.com; +65-68703090; Reuters Messaging: vidya.ranganathan.reuters.com@reuters.net))

title: UPDATE:Bank  Indonesia :To Tame CPI With Rate Hikes, Intervention
text:
(Adds background and analysts' rate predictions)

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia officials Wednesday hinted of the central bank's readiness to further hike its benchmark one-month interest rate and possibly intervene in the currency market to combat inflation, a day after it raised the benchmark rate by 25 basis points.

"What we do to tame inflation include raising the interest rate, stabilizing the currency and optimizing money market operations," Bank Indonesia's Deputy Governor Budi Mulya told reporters on the sidelines of a banking event.

"The rupiah's stability is important (in containing inflation), as if it (the rupiah) is not under control, what we do on interest rate will be useless," Mulya added.

But when asked if Bank Indonesia will increase the key interest rate for sure, he said the central bank will decide during monthly rate meetings.

Meanwhile, Bank Indonesia's Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Goeltom told reporters at the same event that she predicts inflation to be above 9% at the end of the year, way above the top end of the central bank's inflation target of 6%.

The comments came after the central bank's quicker-than-expected reversal in its recent rate easing cycle that started in May 2006 and had resulted in total cuts of 475 basis points up till December 2007. Since then, the central had held the key rate unchanged at 8.00% until it raised the rate to 8.25% Tuesday.

The central bank, which has previously been viewed as being reluctant to adopt monetary tightening on worries that such a policy will hurt economic growth, now seems to recognize the need to move preemptively to check rising inflation expectations, analysts said.

Further rate hikes - while not expected to bring the rate to above the inflation level - may be considered as inflation may rise further soon as the government plans to hike subsidized fuel prices by as much as 30%, probably early June, they added.

Most analysts predict that the Indonesian central bank will raise its benchmark rate to between 8.75% and 9% by the end of the year. But Goldman Sachs forecast more aggressive hikes of 75-100 basis points in addition to the 25-basis-point hike Tuesday.

Expecting a total of 75 basis points of hikes over the next three months, Standard Chartered has forecast for Bank Indonesia to deliver a 25-basis-point hike each when it meets June 5, July 3, and August 5.

Bank Danamon predicts the central bank will hike its rate to 8.75% in June after the fuel price hike is implemented, before raising the rate further to 9% later this year.

Goldman Sachs has, however, suggested that Bank Indonesia should take a more aggressive stance.

"Although growth is likely to moderate this year, inflation is the more pressing issue at hand," it said in a research note Tuesday.

It added that there are also upside risks to its interest rate forecast in the event investors exit Indonesian assets as higher inflation threatens stability. Consequently, this could force Bank Indonesia to push rates higher to stem capital outflows.

-By Farida Husna and I Made Sentana; Dow Jones Newswires; 62-21 39831277; I-Made.Sentana@dowjones.com [ 07-05-08 0749GMT ]

title: 2nd UPDATE: Boediono Named As Next Bank Indonesia Governor
text:
(Adds Boediono comments on inflation, quotes from parliamentarian, background.) 
    

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--A commission of the Indonesian parliament Monday named senior economic minister Boediono as the country's next central bank governor, an appointment that is set to restore confidence in a corruption-tainted Bank Indonesia, and bolster investor confidence in the Southeast Asian nation.   

"Some heavy challenges will face Boediono in synchronizing monetary policy with the fiscal authorities, and in tackling the difficulties with our national economy which is under strong pressures both from internal and global (factors)," said Awal Kusumah, head of Parliamentary Commission 11, which reviewed potential appointees to the central bank governor position.   

The appointment is subject to a plenary hearing April 9, which will be presided over by house speaker Agus Laksono, Kusumah told reporters after a day-long hearing.   

In previous appointments of Bank Indonesia governors, the plenary hearing has been little more than a formalizing of the parliamentary commission's candidate.   

Boediono, who like many Indonesians is known by only one name, will be sworn in as the next central bank chief on May 17 when the incumbent, Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah, finishes his five-year term.   

Abdullah opted not to seek re-election after the Anti-Corruption Body in February named him as a suspect in a corruption investigation that has embroiled several other senior central bank officials. Abdullah has denied any wrongdoing.   

"The markets really respect Boediono," said Standard Chartered Economist Fauzi Ichsan. "He is the most qualified person (to head Bank Indonesia)."   

President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono last week proposed Boediono - who has an extensive track record in managing the economy - after parliament last month rejected two candidates for what they said was a lack of relevant experience.   

Boediono, a graduate of the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton School, was a director at the central bank in the mid to late 1990s. His latter experience could smooth decision making at the central bank, current governor Abdullah said.   

In pre-appointment hearings to parliament Monday, Boediono vowed to improve morale at the central bank and to work hard to combat inflation which threatens to breach Bank Indonesia's target this year.   

"The current inflation targeting system that Bank Indonesia uses now could be perfected," Boediono said without elaborating.   

He said that the key for the achievement of the inflation target is "the credibility of the target itself, measures taken to achieve it and the institutional credibility of Bank Indonesia itself."   

Like many countries around the world, Indonesia is facing mounting inflationary pressures stemming from soaring global food and energy prices. Bank Indonesia has admitted that could mean inflation heading a little beyond its 6.5% target for the year but many analysts believe that is overly optimistic.   

Just last month, the consumer price index spiked to 8.2% on year, the fastest rise in prices for 18 months. But the central bank has been reluctant to raise its 8.0% interest rates, arguing that external, not internal, conditions were behind the high inflation rate.   

Analysts said Boediono might not alter that stance any time soon.   

"Balancing the pressures of higher inflation and a potential global slowdown, he will find it appropriate to take a wait-and-see approach on interest rates," said David Cohen, chief economist at Singapore-based Action Economics. Bank Indonesia next meets to discuss interest rates on May 8.   

But he forecast Bank Indonesia will continue regular intervention in the foreign exchange market to support the rupiah against the U.S. dollar.   

Besides tackling inflation, Boediono also said Monday that Bank Indonesia needs to form a task force to improve budgetary decision making to prevent a recurrence of the corruption allegations now surrounding several central bank officials.   

The allegations concern alleged illegal transfer of funds from a Bank Indonesia foundation to several former members of parliament.   

Boediono said that he has never illegally taken "even one cent of the public's money," and said he aims to stamp out the culture of corruption that remains so prevalent in Indonesia that even a central bank governor became a graft suspect.   

"Throughout the length of my career, and God-willing until I die, I hope I can continue to maintain this characteristic" of being immune to corruption, Boediono said.   

Boediono's departure to the central bank leaves an opening at the head of President Yudhoyono's economic team at a time of persistent turbulence in world financial markets and economies.   

Indonesia's government has been criticized of late for a lack of policies to deal with a rising budget deficit, inflated by ballooning energy subsidies.   

Boediono also said that the rupiah is currently satisfactorily stable against the dollar, and said that over the coming years Indonesia should be able to achieve an inflation rate more closely in line with regional peers.   

He said that "in the next few years," he hopes Indonesia will lower inflation to around 3% to 4%.   

-By I Made Sentana, Linda Silaen and Reuben Carder; Dow Jones Newswires; 62-21 39831277; I-Made.Sentana@dowjones.com, Reuben.Carder@dowjones.com [ 07-04-08 1259GMT ]

title: UPDATE:Bank Indonesia: To Act "At Any Time" If CPI Soars
text:
(Adds background)   

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian central bank is ready to respond to rising inflationary pressures "at any time" if necessary, its senior deputy governor told reporters Monday, suggesting that Bank Indonesia may soon turn hawkish in its policy outlook.   

"If (near-term) inflation continues to increase, Bank Indonesia has to respond to it at any time," Bank Indonesia Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Goletom said.   

She didn't state clearly whether the central bank will raise its key interest rate - now at 8% - to contain rising inflation.   

Last week, the central bank kept the rate unchanged for a fourth straight month after on-year inflation spiked to 8.2% in March, its highest level in 18 months.   

Her comment suggests that the central bank wouldn't rule out future rate hikes if inflationary pressures don't abate over the next few months.   

Bank Indonesia so far has been hesitant to raise rates, arguing that the country's high inflation environment is mainly due to rising commodity and energy prices globally and not because of its loose monetary stance.   

It also feared that any rate hike will further damp Indonesia's economic outlook for this year, as underlined by several official forecasts made in the past week.   

Bank Indonesia earlier Monday predicted that economic growth will likely slow to 6.2% this year from 6.3% last year. The World Bank and the Asian Development Bank have made similar downward revisions to their 2008 gross domestic product growth forecasts for Indonesia to 6.0% from 6.4% previously.   

Analysts expect Bank Indonesia to continue intervening in the foreign exchange market to support the rupiah, hence reducing the impact of imported inflation.   

-By Farida Husna; Dow Jones Newswires; 62 21 3983 1277; edhi.pranasidhi@dowjones.com [ 07-04-08 0629GMT ]

title: Indonesian Shares Fall 4.5%; Inflation Concerns Mount
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's share market has fallen sharply Thursday as investors grow concerned that rising inflation will start to take a bite out of economic growth.   

The share declines have been exacerbated by margin calls with the market now down a total of 8.8% over three days.   

Jakarta's benchmark share index was recently 4.5% lower at 2,237.92 with trading volume on the heavy side at a value of IDR3.5 trillion.   

Mandiri Sekuritas expects the JSX index to find some support at 2200, though its head of research, Ari Pitoyo, said any break below this level could push the index towards the 1700 to 1800 range.   

Foreign investors have been selling, concerned about the inflation outlook after data earlier in the week showed a spike in price pressures. There are worries that Jakarta lacks the policy options for dealing decisively with inflation, especially with the rupiah falling and a widening budget deficit. "Our macroeconomic fundamentals look weaker with inflation rising," said Andreas Yasakasih, a fund manager at PT Ciptadana Asset Management.   

Investors likely to have been hit by margin calls include those holding shares of Bumi Resources (BUMI.JK); its shares were down 6.5% after it booked only $473 million in gains from the sale of coal assets in 2007, less than the expected $553 million.   

Bumi shares were also lower because investors had been looking to raise cash in order to subscribe to a rights share offer at  Bakrie & Brothers (BNBR.JK), which will use the proceeds to buy Bumi stock and that of other affiliates.   

Heavyweight  PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia (TLKM.JK) meanwhile was down 3.6%, with  Astra International (ASII.JK) 7.7% lower on concerns higher inflation will hurt car and motorcycle demand.   

The consumer price index in March rose 0.95% on month and 8.17% on year, well above expectations in a Dow Jones Newswires poll for a rise of 0.31% on month and 7.46% on year.   

The data follow above-target numbers for January and February and economists say this suggests the government may have a hard time meeting its full-year inflation target of 4% to 6.5%.   

A Dow Jones Newswires poll of 12 economists shows the general expectation for the central bank to keep interest rates on hold at its meeting Thursday, with the benchmark one-month rate now at 8%.   

Standard Chartered bank added "in the aftermath of the meeting, Bank Indonesia may signal that near term rate cuts are off the table."   

Indeed, given inflationary pressures, there will be growing expectations that the central bank will eventually be forced to raise rates, it said.   

The rupiah meanwhile has weakened further, hurt by fund outflows from stocks and the bond market. Recently, the U.S. dollar was trading around IDR9,230 compared to IDR9,215 Wednesday.   

"We have many orders from our foreign clients investing in the stock and bond markets to buy the dollar," said one currency dealer, who added Bank Indonesia was expected to intervene if the rupiah fell further.   

Traders expect the dollar to trade in a IDR9,225-IDR9,240 range for the rest of the session.

title: UPDATE: Bank Indonesia Leaves 1-Month Rate Unchanged At 8%
text:
(Adds central bank quotes and comments on the outlook for interest rates and the rupiah, and analysts' comments)   

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia left its benchmark one-month interest rate unchanged at 8% Tuesday due to concerns about rising inflationary pressures, but it said there is still room for cuts later this year.   

"According to Bank Indonesia's evaluation, inflationary pressures in 2008 will be quite strong," Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said at a press conference after a monthly board of governors' meeting.   

Economists say rising oil and commodity prices globally and the rupiah's recent weakness are likely to drive prices of goods higher in the coming months.   

Bank Indonesia is targeting an inflation rate between 4% and 6% this year, down from 6.59% in 2007.   

Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Goeltom said that "looking at the current situation, we still see room for rate cuts in the future. But (we) can't say yet when they will happen as we must see monthly developments in the economy."   

Most analysts expect the one-month rate to remain at 8% until the end of the first half of the year at least, but views on the outlook for interest rates later in the year are mixed.   

HSBC said the central bank could be forced to raise the official rate by 150 basis points this year to rein in inflation, and such increases would be very negative for the local stock market.   

Bank Indonesia has cut rates a total 475 basis points in an easing cycle that began in May 2006. The rate cuts have helped to spur commercial bank lending, which rose 23% on year during the first 11 months of 2007.   

Meanwhile, Governor Abdullah said Tuesday that the rupiah was less sensitive to global oil price movements last year than in previous years. He didn't elaborate, but oil price increases have had less effect on confidence since the government cut local price subsidies in October 2005.   

The average exchange rate of the U.S. dollar last year was IDR9,140, versus IDR9,197 in 2006, even though global oil prices continued to rise, Abdullah said.   

Bank Indonesia will intervene in the foreign exchange market if the rupiah comes under selling pressure, he said.   

The rupiah was rising in the first half of the year, but it has tended to weaken since risk aversion rose following the U.S. subprime mortgage crisis. At 0740 GMT, the dollar was quoted at IDR9,452, little changed from Monday's close of IDR9447.   

-By Farida Husna and I Made Sentana; Dow Jones Newswires; 62-21 39831277; I-Made.Sentana@dowjones.com [ 08-01-08 0747GMT ]

title: 2nd UPDATE: Oil Prices To Dent Indonesia Growth, Deficit
text:
(Adds comments from ministers, background.)   

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's economy will likely grow 6.2% this year, missing the government's official growth target of 6.3% due to the sharp rise in global oil prices, Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said Tuesday.   

Abdullah said economic growth of 6.2% for 2007 would be "still okay" but the comments suggest higher energy costs are taking a toll on the Southeast Asian nation, a net importer of oil.   

The government maintains subsidies on domestic fuel sales to shield consumers from volatility in global energy markets. The cost of that effort will swell with higher oil prices, Finance Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati told reporters Tuesday at a joint briefing with Abdullah.   

Indonesia next year will likely pay IDR179.4 trillion from the state budget in such subsidies, more than double the IDR85.4 trillion allocation it had previously planned, as the higher oil prices mean it will need to outlay more in subsidies, Mulyani said.   

The increased outlays won't do much damage to the government's budget. With global benchmark oil price around $100 a barrel, Indonesia's deficit would shrink to 1.3% this year from 1.5% originally forecast, as the country will receive higher profits from oil exports, Mulyani said.   

But high oil prices will likely continue weighing on rupiah against the U.S. dollar, Abdullah said.   

The dollar was at IDR9,395 at the close of Indonesian trading at 0900GMT Tuesday. By contrast, the U.S. currency was trading below IDR9,100 in mid-October.   

The dollar will likely trade around IDR9,400 until the end of the year, Abdullah predicted. But he didn't say what effect the lower rupiah might have on economic growth.   

"The devaluing of the rupiah is affected by several factors - among others, the rise in the price of oil and subprime (problems) have made investors reposition their portfolios. So this is still a movement that is normal. We know that heading toward the end of the year (investors) are always taking profit and buying (dollars) to pay debts," Abdullah said.   

He didn't comment on possible Bank Indonesia intervention in the currency market to defend the rupiah.   

The central bank recently sold dollars via state banks when the dollar reached IDR9,430, and currency dealers say they expect the authorities to keep defending the currency around that level.   

Meanwhile, in order to mitigate impact on the budget from the higher fuel subsidies, the government will strive to speed up its conversion of household heating fuel to liquid petroleum gas from kerosene, Mines and Energy Minister Yusgiantoro Purnomo told reporters at the same briefing.   

The government has been offering various incentives, including giving away free LPG-burning stoves to some low income households, to encourage Indonesians to switch over to the more efficient fuel for cooking and heating. That has reduced the amount of kerosene used and eased the subsidy burden on the budget while helping ease inflation.   

-By Jakarta bureau, Dow Jones Newswires; 62 21 3983 1277; Reuben.Carder@dowjones.com [ 27-11-07 1251GMT ]

text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 19 (Reuters) - The Singapore dollar and Philippine peso rose on Monday against a tumbling U.S. dollar but other Asian currencies had difficulty appreciating as regional stock markets fell and concerns over credit markets intensified.   

The U.S. dollar fell against the yen <JPY=> and hit a 12-year low against the Swiss franc <CHF=>, battered by weak industrial production data on Friday and worries about credit-related losses at financial institutions.   

Traders said some of the selling pressure on the dollar arose after a source familiar with Saudi Arabian currency policy told Reuters the world's largest oil exporter could consider revaluing its dollar-pegged currency. [ID:nL19685742]   

The credit market concerns weighed on investor sentiment and appetite for risk and led to weakness in Asian stock markets <0#.INDEXA>.   

MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> fell slightly on Monday. Last week, it dropped 3.4 percent, marking its third consecutive week of losses.   

The Singapore dollar <SGD=> barely gained 0.3 percent, even after the government raised its economic growth forecast for 2008 and forecast higher inflation rates. [ID:nSIN258187]. The currency rose to 1.4459 per U.S. dollar and then retreated to 1.4483.   

"You'd have thought the market would have reacted a bit more positively to that," said  Merrill Lynch strategist Simon Flint.   

"But people are using the Singapore dollar as the most liquid proxy for their risk aversion fears and growth fears," he said, adding investors held sizeable short dollar position but were also looking to reduce or hedge some of their risk in other markets.   

"We're bearish on the dollar. What's going on in the Middle East is quite meaningful," Flint said.   

He said he expected an eventual appreciation in the Singapore dollar.   

"The Asian decoupling story is very much alive and the Monetary Authority of Singapore has got quite an aggressive and forward-looking appreciation stance," he said.   

The high-yielding Philippine peso <PHP=> rose as far as 43.19 per dollar, up 0.8 percent from Friday's close. Other Asian currencies barely moved.   

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> was steady around 9,320 per dollar, while the Indian rupee <INR=IN> kept to a tight range around 39.3 per dollar.   

Indonesia's central bank intervened on Friday to prop up the rupiah <IDR=> currency and is prepared to take more action if necessary, deputy governor Hartadi Sarwono told Reuters on Monday.   

Sarwono also repeated that the fall in the rupiah, Asia's worst-performing currency against the dollar so far this year, was likely to be temporary.

title: UPDATE 1- Indonesia central bank intervened  on Friday-deputy
text:
(Adds details, quotes)   

JAKARTA, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank intervened on Friday to prop up the rupiah <IDR=> currency and is prepared to take more action if necessary, deputy governor Hartadi Sarwono told Reuters on Monday.   

Sarwono also repeated that falls in the rupiah, Asia's worst performing currency this year, were likely to be temporary.   

The rupiah rose as far as 9,278 per dollar on Monday, up almost 0.5 percent from late Asian trade on Friday, as investor sentiment stabilised after last week's sharp sell-off due to concerns about the health of the U.S. economy.   

Asked to confirm market speculations that the central bank had intervened on Friday, Sarwono said : "Yes we did. There had been some sort of panic in the market. Even though the amount was small, it has had an impact."   

The high-yielding rupiah recovered to 9,320 per dollar in late trade on Friday after falling to as low as 9,405 earlier in the day, after Sarwono promised to support the ailing currency.   

The rupiah has fallen about 3 percent versus the dollar so far this year.   

Asked whether the central bank will intervene further to strengthen the rupiah, Sarwono said : "We will continue to take the necessary steps in regards to monetary policy and foreign exchange. This is a matter of (market) sentiment."   

"Everything is going to be fine. I think by doing that, it will have a positive impact to prevent panic," Sarwono said, referring to intervention to prevent sharp fluctuations in the foreign exchange market.   

He declined to elaborate.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia falls on weaker stocks, rupiah recovers
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 16 (Reuters) - Weak regional stocks weighed on Asian currencies on Friday amid worries about the health of the world's largest economy, while the Indonesian rupiah recovered after the central bank pledged to limit its falls.   

 The high-yielding Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> recovered to 9,320 per dollar from as low as 9,405, after deputy central bank governor Hartadi Sarwono promised to support the ailing currency.   

 "People are selling the dollar now as they are worried that Bank of Indonesia will intervene," said a trader in Jarkata.   

 A second trader said more investors followed through in the later session to take profit from the dollar's recent gains.   

 "I think the rupiah should settle around 9,250-9,350 near term," said the trader.   

 Sarwono told Reuters that the bank would intervene, if necessary, to stabilise the rupiah, which slid below the 9,400 level for the first time in two months and was at one point down about 1 percent from late Asian trade on Thursday.   

 The rupiah, the worst performing currency in Asia, has fallen about 4 percent versus the dollar so far this year.   

 MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> fell about 2.4 percent on Friday, extending its losses.   

 The Philippine peso <PHP=>, another high-yielder, fell as far as 43.50 per dollar, down 0.6 percent from Thursday's close.   

 "Basically investors are trimming their long positions," said a trader in Manila.   

 The peso remains the region's top performer with gains of almost 13 percent versus the dollar so far this year.   

 The Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> hit 3.3895 per dollar at one point, down about 0.7 percent from late Asian trade on Thursday.   

 Meanwhile, the Singapore dollar <SGD=> fell as far as 1.4546 per U.S. dollar, down about half of a percent.   

 CORRECTION   

 Most Asian currencies have been retreating in recent sessions amid renewed jitters about the U.S. housing sector, but optimism about sustained capital inflows continued to underpin sentiment.   

 "There has been a bit of risk aversion in play. But I'm pretty confident that Asian currencies will strengthen back again, this is just a correction," said Suresh Ramanathan, currency strategist at CIMB.   

 "Asia is pretty much insulated from subprime, plus the fact that Asian currencies have stronger underlying demand," he said.   

 The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> was little changed near 7.4235 per dollar, as strong investment data fuelled expectations that the central bank would have to raise interest rates again.   

 Investors now look to the pace of yuan appreciation, which has quickened in recent weeks amid signs that policy makers are keen to fight inflation, to support Asian currencies.   

 Hong Liang, China economist at  Goldman Sachs, said in a note that the investment bank expects the yuan to rise to 7.28 per dollar in three months, to 7.11 in six months and 6.78 in 12 months.   

 "We believe that the chances are rising that policy makers will re-think the currency issue in the face of rising domestic inflation, renewed weakness in the dollar, mounting international pressures, and most of all, a dismal score card of trying to rebalance the economy without tackling the root cause of such imbalances in the past four years," she said. The rupiah, Asia's worst performing currency this year, has been hit hard in recent weeks as investors continued to shun high-yielding but riskier emerging market assets, such as the rupiah, because of concern about U.S. credit market problems.   

The rupiah was quoted at around 9,435 per dollar at 0340 GMT on Wednesday, little changed from its levels late on Tuesday. It has lost almost 5 percent against the dollar this year.   

"We have intervened ... in a bid to stabilise (the rupiah). I think the possibility is that a new equilibrium will be reached in the coming weeks. I think it will continue to be at around 9,000 levels," Abdullah said.   

The governor made the remarks to reporters after attending a swearing-in ceremony at a central bank office in Denpasar in the resort island of Bali.   

The central bank has said it is comfortable with the rupiah in a range of between 8,500-9,500 per dollar.

title: Emerging  FX -Asia's high-yielders rally, mood still cautious
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 22 (Reuters) - The high-yielding Indonesian rupiah and Philippine peso rose on Wednesday in cautious trade amid growing hopes the Federal Reserve will cut its main interest rate to calm turbulent markets.   

The peso went as far as 46.50 per dollar, up almost 0.9 percent from Tuesday's close.   

The rupiah <IDR=> gained 0.6 percent to 9,380 per dollar, while the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> followed by rising half of a percent to about 3.48 per dollar.   

"We're finally seeing the short-term relief. I think there was some lag effect on the dollar/peso side and the pressure in the offshore market seems to be easing as well," said a trader in Manila.   

Bank Indonesia chief Burhanuddin Abdullah said that the central bank had intervened to support the rupiah and expected the currency to stabilise at around 9,000 in coming weeks.   

Analysts said investors remained edgy after last week's heavy battering, but prospects of a near-term U.S. rate cut offered support to share and currency markets.   

"Cautious tone remains. It's range trading with some dollar/Asia downside bias on equity market stability," said Han Sia Yeo, currency strategist at  Bank of America.

"However, with market positioned for a Fed cut near-term, risk is on the upside for dollar/Asia for now," he said.   

A senior U.S. lawmaker said on Tuesday Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke assured him the central bank would use "all available tools" to calm financial markets, which investors took as a signal the Fed could cut rates at its Sept. 18 meeting.   

In a sign of improved sentiment MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> rose 1.4 percent, But Richmond Federal Reserve Bank President Jeffrey Lacker poured some cold water on rate cut hopes, saying market turmoil only warranted a change in rates if it affected the outlook for inflation or growth.   

NO YUAN SURPRISE   

The Chinese yuan <CNY=CFXS> fell 0.16 percent to 7.6031 per dollar -- still off its six-week low of 7.6099 hit on Friday -- after the central bank raised interest rates for the fourth time this year in its campaign to curb rising inflation.   

Most analysts expect Chinese leaders to stick to their long-standing policy of letting the yuan appreciate only gradually in the run-up to a Communist Party congress later this year.   

"Although a stronger yuan will be able to offset higher price trends, major reform is unlikely ahead of sensitive political events this autumn,"  UBS analysts said in a research note.   

The Japanese yen, which has moved in the opposite direction to most emerging Asian currencies in recent weeks, held gains against the dollar <JPY=> as investors continued to cut risky positions.   

The Philippine peso <PHP=>, South Korean won <KRW=> and Indian rupee <INR=IN> were the most negatively correlated to the yen's recent swings, DBS analysts said in a research note.   

The Taiwan dollar <TWD=> and Singapore dollar, which were little changed in afternoon trade, were least responsive to the yen's changes as investors used them as an alternative funding currencies for carry trades, they said. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR Change on the day at 0730 GMT

title: Emerging  FX -Asia rebounds on Fed move, but caution remains
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 20 (Reuters) - Asian currencies bounced back on Monday as regional stocks rallied after the U.S. Federal Reserve cut its discount rate in a surprise move on Friday, but the spectre of a credit market squeeze still weighed on sentiment.   

The Korean won <KRW=> steadied near 943 per dollar after hitting 939.9, which was up about 1 percent from late Asian trade on Friday.   

The high-yielding Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> rose as far as 9,380 per dollar, up nearly 1 percent, although it remains the worst performer in Asia this year with a loss of 4.2 percent versus the dollar.   

A Jakarta-based trader doubted that the rupiah would sustain its rally in the near term, given continuuing jitters about the U.S. subprime market crisis.   

"The subprime issue is still not finished -- there is still some doubt about it. If the subprime woes turn up again, I'm afraid the rupiah will go down again," he said.   

But Indonesia's central bank would want to stop the rupiah falling below the 9,500 level, traders said.   

Last week, central banks in Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines were reported to have intervened to support their currencies as investors fled risk amid credit market turmoil.   

MSCI's measure of Asia Pacific stocks excluding Japan <.MIAPJ0000PUS> jumped 5.5 percent following a rebound in U.S. stocks on Friday after the Fed cut its discount rate.   

Leading the pack, Indonesian stocks <.JKSE> jumped 6.6 percent, while South Korean shares <.SK11> surged 5.7 percent.   

NOT OUT OF THE WOODS   

Rising local stocks helped drive the Singapore dollar <SGD=> as far as 1.5240 per U.S. dollar, up almost 0.9 percent from late Asian trade on Friday and its strongest in nearly a week.   

Elsewhere, the Thai baht <THB=THB> rose as high as 34.30 per dollar, up more than 0.8 percent, while the Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> gained about 0.6 percent to 3.491 to the dollar.   

Philippine markets were closed for a public holiday.   

Many analysts remained cautious as fears of a global credit squeeze persisted, even though the Fed's statement accompanying its discount rate cut fuelled expectations that it could be moving towards lowering its benchmark fed funds rate target.   

Thomas Harr, a currency strategist at Standard Chartered Bank, said he would refrain from telling his clients to buy into Asian currencies for now, despite the recovery in Asian stocks.   

"I think what we are seeing today is obviously a little bit of recovery, which is natural given that the Fed at least did something by cutting the discount rate on Friday," he said.   

"But the feeling in the market is that this may not improve liquidity that much. It's not clear that we are out of the woods yet and we expect the market to be choppy in the coming days." The Japanese yen, which has moved in the opposite direction to most emerging Asian currencies in recent sessions as investors unwound carry trades, eased against the dollar <JPY=> after pulling back from a 14-month high on Friday. title: Emerging  FX -Asia slides to new lows as investors flee risk
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 16 (Reuters) - Asian currencies tumbled to fresh lows on Thursday as regional stocks collapsed and investors cut their exposure to riskier assets due to worries about credit market risk, forcing central banks to continue supporting them.   

 The South Korean won <KRW=> took the biggest hit, dropping 1.5 percent to a 3-month low near 947 per dollar.   

 Other high-yielders such as the Philippine peso <PHP=>, Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> and Indian rupee <INR=IN> also shed up to nearly 1 percent each.   

 Central banks in Singapore, Malaysia, the Philippines and Indonesia were suspected of selling dollars to slow the declines in their currencies, but the bearishness seemed deeply entrenched as bad news continued to hit credit markets.   

 "It's a crazy market here. Prices jump 100 pips in two minutes!" said one trader in Kuala Lumpur.   

 "I am going to stay long dollars because surely there will be more subprime news every day," he said.   

 The latest market scare was set off by worries that  Countrywide Financial , the largest U.S. mortgage lender, could face bankruptcy if liquidity worsens. [ID:nN15253338].   

 Australian Mortgage lender RAMS Home Loans Group Ltd.  slumped after it said it had failed to roll over short-term loans due to a lack of liquidity in the U.S. commercial paper market. [ID:nSYD33571].   

 Some Asian stock markets <0#.INDEXA> saw the biggest losses since the Sept. 2001 attacks on the United States.   

 Central banks around the region assured markets of support. Australia's central bank also pumped in a larger than usual amount into its money markets.   

 The Japanese yen jumped to a five-month high against the dollar <JPY=> and euro <EURJPY=> as investors unwound carry-trade positions funded by the low-yielding yen.   

 Traders in Asia said the Malaysian central bank could have sold up to $700 million as the ringgit <MYR=> hit a March trough of 3.5070 per dollar.   

 Bank Indonesia's dollar selling managed to put a floor on the rupiah around 9,482 per dollar and even nudge the rupiah higher to near 9,450.   

 "Imported inflation is a key consideration for Bank Indonesia,"  UBS analysts said in a note.   

 Bank Indonesia might intensify its dollar-selling intervention as the rupiah approaches 9,500, particularly because the central bank has said in the past the acceptable range for the currency is between 8,500 and 9,500 per dollar,  UBS said.   

 "We expect Bank Indonesia to put up a fight at 9,500, although the generalised rampage into the dollar fuelled by ongoing credit woes may give the central bank an excuse to tolerate a higher dollar/rupiah if the defence of 9,500 fails,"  UBS said. title: UPDATE 1- Indonesia  c.bank says to  intervene  in  FX  if needed
text:
(Adds details, quotes)   

JAKARTA, Aug 16 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank will intervene in the foreign exchange market if necessary to defend the rupiah <IDR=>, Bank Indonesia (BI) Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah told reporters on Thursday.   

Despite the rupiah's recent fall, Abdullah said the currency was still within its comfort range of 8,500-9,500 per dollar and that the bank would maintain its monetary policy, under which interest rates have gradually been cut in the past two years.   

Traders in Jakarta said Bank Indonesia sold dollars on Thursday to help smooth a decline in the high-yielding rupiah, which fell to 9,480 per dollar at one point, down two-thirds of a percent on the day and its weakest level since June 2006.   

It has fallen about 5.1 percent versus the dollar this year, making it the worst-performing currency in Asia, as investors cut their exposure to high-yielding but riskier assets due to worries about credit markets.   

"We will continue to smooth out volatility and we will intervene. We will continue to be in the market," Abdullah told reporters.   

Economists said a sharp drop in the rupiah could push up inflation since prices in Indonesia were highly sensitive to currency swings.   

Asked whether the central bank would change its monetary stance due to the volatile markets, Abdullah said: "Inflation will still be within target, therefore there is no need to change."   

In a speech to parliament on Thursday, President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono forecast year-end inflation of 6.5 percent in 2007 against the central bank's forecast of 5-7 percent.   

Analysts say the volatile global markets were a big factor behind the central bank's decision to keep its benchmark interest rates <BIPG> unchanged this month.   

Bank Indonesia (BI) had cut its benchmark rate to 8.25 percent in July, the lowest since the rate was launched in July 2005, after a steady drop in inflation. It has cut the rate 13 times from a high of 12.75 percent in April last year.

title: UPDATE 1-FACTBOX-How central banks have acted to inject funds
text:
(Updates with no action from Fed)   

FRANKFURT, Aug 14 (Reuters) - Global central banks are withdrawing much of the extra cash they have injected into banking systems to calm panicky credit since last Thursday.   

Below is a list of central bank actions since the credit markets upheaval turned nasty last week.   

EUROPEAN CENTRAL BANK

Aug 9 - 94.8 billion euros ($129.8 billion) in a one-day tender on Thursday, the largest amount ever.   

Aug 10 - 61.05 billion euros ($83.61 billion) in a three-day tender on Friday to cover the weekend,   

Aug 13 - 47.67 billion euros ($65.29 billion) in one-day money on Monday   

Aug 14 - 7.7 billion in one-day money on Tuesday. The ECB also added an extra 73.5 billion euros in one-week money more than its estimated liquidity needs for banks during its main refinancing operation.   

Trichet also issued a statement on Tuesday calling for investors to stay composed composure in face of market volatility and a repricing of risk.   

The ECB's injections exceed those that it flooded into markets immediately after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks on the United States. At that time, 69.3 billion euro in overnight money was allocated on Sept. 12, 2001, followed by 40.5 billion euros the next day.   

U.S. FEDERAL RESERVE   

Aug 9 - $24 billion during its regular market operations, only slightly above the usual allocation.   

Aug 10 - Added $38 billion through three separate repurchase agreements, its biggest single-day cash injection since Sept. 19, 2001. The repos brought down the federal funds rate, the cost of overnight loans between banks, to the Fed's target rate of 5.25 percent.   

Aug 13 - Added $2 billion of temporary reserves to the banking system through overnight repurchasing agreements.   

Aug 14 - The Fed took the unusual step of refraining from an open market operation at 9:30 a.m. (1330 GMT), when daily operations are usually conducted. In an earlier statement, the Fed said it was evaluating whether or not to conduct an operation at that time and said it stood ready to conduct additional operations later in the day as needed.   

BANK OF JAPAN   

Aug 10 - Added 1.0 trillion yen ($8.45 billion) at its regular money market operation on Friday after a slight rise in the benchmark overnight call rate, the highest amount in about six weeks. Traders said the amount was at the higher end of market expectations, but was not a major surprise.   

Aug 13 - Added 600 billion yen ($5.1 billion) into the banking system in a one-week operation.   

Aug 14 - Drained 1.6 trillion yen ($13.6 billion) in two operations.   

BANK OF ENGLAND   

The Bank of England said banks hit by tough credit conditions could use its emergency lending facility, which is routinely available and priced at 100 basis points above the bank's 5.75 percent policy rate.   

BANK OF CANADA   

Aug 9 - Injected C$1.64 billion ($1.55 billion) on Thursday, saying it was in contact with other central banks on the global situation and stood ready to add money as needed.   

Aug 10 - Injected a total of C$1.685 billion ($1.605 billion)   

Aug 13 - Injected C$670 million.   

THE RESERVE BANK OF AUSTRALIA   

Aug 10 - The RBA added more than twice the usual amount of money into the banking system, injecting A$4.95 billion ($4.19 billion).   

Aug 14 - The RBA added A$2.6 billion ($2.2 billion) in its regular morning money market operation, slightly higher than average.   

SWISS NATIONAL BANK   

Aug 9/10 - The SNB offered banks money at a below-market rate of 2.6 percent on Thursday and Friday, adding a total of 3.1 billion Swiss francs ($2.57 billion) <CHF=>. It since has started to drain the extra liquidity.   

Aug 13/14 - Traders said the SNB drained liquidity as overnight rates remained low after the previous week's liquidity-providing actions.

Traders said the Asian central banks intervened in foreign exchange markets on Friday to support their currencies by selling U.S. dollars. title: Indonesian rupiah steady but lags regional  FX  rally
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 13 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah stabilised against the dollar on Monday after its heavy fall in previous sessions, but it lagged a rally in other Asian currencies on the view that it is still a risky asset.   

The rupiah <IDR=> stayed around 9,345 per dollar, down 3.2 percent in just over two weeks and close to Friday's one-year trough of 9,365.   

Other Asian currencies such as the Philippine peso <PHP=> and Korean won <KRW=> rallied as investors tentatively bought some Asian currencies after central banks over the world pumped money into troubled credit markets.   

The rupiah, Asia's highest-yielding currency, is the worst performing currency in Asia this year.   

"It looks like it has stabilised this morning," said a trader in Jakarta.   

"I think the market is a bit worried. But Bank Indonesia said they will try hard to defend the rupiah from here, so the market is content about that."   

He added that he felt the markets were trying to play it safe and that the rupiah remained risky.

text:

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia will make "all-out efforts" to help local financial markets weather the impact of the U.S. subprime market woes, Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Aslim Tadjuddin said Friday.   

This would include intervening in the currency market, he indicated.   

"Our foreign exchange reserves are strong enough to maintain calm in the market," Tadjuddin said.   

The reserves are currently at $52.4 billion, he said.   

The reserves stood at $51.88 billion as of July 31, but Tadjuddin didn't explain what drove them higher amid fund outflows from the local financial markets.   

He said that the impact of the U.S. subprime market on Indonesia has so far been limited to only the financial markets.   

"Our economic fundamentals are quite strong," he said. "There's nothing to worry about."   

Bank Indonesia Tuesday said that Indonesian banks don't have any exposure to U.S. subprime assets as they aren't allowed to invest in overseas papers.   

Bank Indonesia still believes that the government's target for the dollar-rupiah average exchange rate of IDR9,100 for this year is achievable, Tadjuddin said.   

The dollar was trading at IDR9,330 at 0425 GMT, up from its close Thursday at IDR9,305.   

The rupiah has fallen to a one-year low against the dollar as foreign investors are trimming their holdings in local stocks, government bonds and the central bank's Sertifikat Bank Indonesia papers.   

Bank Indonesia on Tuesday decided to keep its one-month key rate at 8.25% in light of the current turbulence in global financial markets.

title: UPDATE:Bank Indonesia Dep Governor:IDR Weakness Is Temporary
text:
(Adds further comments from the central bank official, background on interest rates.) 
    

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The rupiah's recent slide against the U.S. dollar is temporary and reflects a trend of weakening in emerging market currencies rather than cracks in Indonesia's economic fundamentals, but Bank Indonesia stands "very ready" to intervene to prevent excess rupiah volatility, a senior central bank official said Monday.   

Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Aslim Tadjuddin said he was "certain" that the rupiah's weakness won't prevent Indonesia's ability to reach its 2007 inflation target of 5-7%, and predicted that the country's strong domestic fundamentals will likely boost the rupiah again soon, perhaps as early as next week.   

"This movement (in the rupiah) I am sure is temporary, and investors' perceptions (of Indonesia) will improve again. I see that overall the rupiah is on a strengthening trend because our economic conditions are good," he told reporters.   

Bank Indonesia is "very ready" to intervene in the domestic currency market to prevent excess rupiah volatility, he said.   

The dollar was trading at IDR9,347 as of 0541 GMT Monday, up sharply from IDR9,075 a week ago.   

"The current weakness of the rupiah is temporary in nature. It is due to global and external factors, primarily in America," Tadjuddin said.   

Tadjuddin didn't elaborate further, but the comments reflect an effort by Indonesian authorities to calm investors nerves, which have been rattled by turmoil in the U.S. subprime mortgage market and ensuing slump in global stocks. Assets and currencies of emerging economies such as Indonesia's have been among the hardest hit by the spike in risk aversion that has swept over global markets in recent weeks, analysts and traders say.   

Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves are currently around $52 billion, the highest level in the country's history. That means Bank Indonesia "has sufficient (reserves) to make intervention safe," Tadjuddin said.   

But he said that the central bank isn't targeting a specific range for the rupiah against the dollar.   

A decision expected Tuesday on interest rates "depends more on internal factors" than on global currency fluctuations, Tadjuddin said.   

"We know our macroeconomic conditions are very strong, although we will still also look at external factors" when deciding whether or not to cut borrowing costs, he said.   

The central bank's board of governors are slated to meet Tuesday to determine whether the benchmark interest rate will be changed this month. The one-month policy rate currently stands at 8.25%. Bank Indonesia has slashed the benchmark rate by 450 basis points since headline inflation began to ease in May last year.   

However analysts have said the central bank may stand pat on rates this month due to the local currency's weakness and higher on-year headline inflation in July.

title: Emerging  FX -Rupiah leads stellar gains in Asia
text:
SINGAPORE, May 7 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah rose more than 1 percent to a one-year high versus the dollar on Monday, leading a strong rally across Asian currencies as the dollar took a blow from weak U.S. jobs data at the end of last week.   

Comments in the past few days from some Asian officials suggesting they were not too worried about strength in local currencies fuelled the rally.   

Both the Indian rupee <INR=IN> and Malaysian ringgit <MYR=> hit nine-year peaks, while the Philippine peso <PHP=> rose to a six-year high and the South Korean won <KRW=> climbed 0.6 percent to its highest in more than 4-½ months.   

The rupiah <IDR=> outperformed its Asian peers, building on sharp gains on Friday. It rose as far as 8,855 per dollar, its strongest level since mid-May 2006.   

It had lagged gains in its Asian peers, but market focus has now returned to the currency on renewed interest in carry trades, talk of another cut in Indonesian interest rates and signs that Jakarta will not stand in the way of rupiah strength.   

In the past three sessions, the rupiah has shot up 2 percent, triggering a jump in rupiah implied volatility <IDRVOL>, a measure of expectations about the size of future market moves.   

"The currency to focus on at the moment is the rupiah," said Callum Henderson, head of currency strategy at Standard Chartered Bank. "It has been the laggard in regional gains. Also, the message from the central bank appears to be that there will not be so much intervention."   

Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Aslim Tadjuddin said on Friday the central bank would allow markets to determine the rupiah rate, even if the currency strengthened beyond 9,000 per dollar. The rupiah broke through that level shortly after his comments.   

A Jakarta trader said the central bank had been spotted in the market on Monday buying dollars for rupiah to smooth a volatile market but said the intervention appeared small.   

"They are still there, but only buying dollars in small amounts," he said. "There are strong flows from offshore into the bonds and interest rates market."   

Indonesian President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono is expected to announce a cabinet reshuffle later on Monday, but this is not seen having a significant impact on the rupiah.[ID:nJAK215355]   

Regional currencies were also bolstered by strong gains in local shares -- Taiwan's stock index <.TWII> hit a 6-½ year high, while shares in Singapore <.STI> and Korea <.KS11> rose to record peaks.   

LAISSEZ FAIRE   

Weekend comments from Asian officials at an Asian Development Bank meeting in Japan also helped drive regional currency gains.   

The strength of Malaysia's currency is not affecting its exports because they are fundamentally competitive, the country's Second Finance Minister Nor Mohamed Yakcop said on Sunday.   

Philippine central bank Governor Amando Tetangco indicated on Sunday that the strong peso was not a concern as it reflected the nation's improved economic performance and helped tame inflation.   

The ringgit rose to a nine-year high at about 3.4135 per dollar, while the peso gained almost a quarter of a percent to a six-year peak around 47.35 per dollar.   

"We expect strong inflows from remittances and follow through selling of the dollar after the payrolls data, are behind the peso move," said a trader in Manila. "The Tetangco comments should also boost the peso today."   

The U.S. economy added a lower-than-expected 88,000 jobs in April, data showed on Friday, reinforcing expectations the Federal Reserve will cut interest rates later this year. The Fed is expected to hold the federal funds rate steady at 5.25 percent when it meets on May 9.

title: Emerging  FX -Rupiah leads weak Asia on equity falls
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 28 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah led the decline in Asian currencies on Wednesday as regional stock markets fell and investors unwound yen-funded carry trades following a steep sell-off in global stock markets.   

Traders said the Indonesian and Philippine central banks sold the dollar for their local currencies as the rupiah and peso led a broad decline in most Asian currencies.   

The rupiah <IDR=> recovered from a three-month low of 9,195 per dollar, but was still down about 0.8 percent at 9,150 per dollar. The peso <PHP=> was near 48.50 per dollar, down a quarter of a percent and just off three-week lows.   

The South Korean won <KRW=> fell a third of a percent to 941.6 per dollar, while the Singapore dollar <SGD=> also dipped nearly 0.3 percent to around 1.53 per U.S. dollar.   

Analysts remained bullish about the underlying strength of Asian currencies in general, citing the region's solid economic growth and hefty balance-of-payment surpluses.   

"I think what we see right now in the market is just a reaction to what happened yesterday, so you see people starting to get a bit risk averse again," said Magnus Prim, chief Asia currency strategist at SEB.   

"But I see the fundamentals are still pretty good and the falls should prove to be a short-term correction," he said.   

The yen <JPY=> fell against the dollar, taking a breather after surging to 10-week highs in the previous session as investors unwound risky trades on fears of rising volatility.   

A tumble in global stock prices including the biggest daily fall in Chinese stocks in a decade, soft U.S. economic data and growing tensions with Iran jolted investors from complacency and prompted them to cut exposure to risk.   

The Chicago Board Options Exchange Volatility Index, or VIX <.VIX>, rose 70 percent on Tuesday in another sign of investor jitters. The VIX typically rises as investors become anxious about the stock market and tends to fall when fear subsides.   

Asian equity markets <.MSCIAPJ> were weaker on Wednesday, but Chinese stocks <.SSEC> rose about 4 percent on Wednesday after falling nearly 9 percent on Tuesday.   

China's yuan <CNY=CFXS> hit a new intraday post-revaluation high of 7.7378 per dollar, extending the previous day's gains.   

RUPIAH, PESO FACE BIGGER PRESSURE   

Aslim Tadjuddin, a deputy Indonesian central bank governor, said that the bank views a sharp fall in the rupiah as temporary and will do "everything necessary" to defend the currency.   

But traders said the central banks would not over-react.   

"They just want to smooth the movement, nothing more than that," said a trader in Singapore, referring to the suspected intervention in Indonesia and the Philippines.   

JPMorgan analysts Claudio Piron and Yen Ping Ho said in a research note that the rupiah, the peso and the Indian rupee would face greater pressure as investors had borrowed the cheaper yen to build long positions in the units.   

"While we struggle to identify fundamental changes in the external backdrop that warrants a fundamental reversal of the carry backdrop, we acknowledge that the technical environment of market caution, heavy long risky asset positions and tight valuations mean pressures could remain for some time."   

The Thai baht, which has been caught in a two-tier market since the government imposed currency controls in December, gained about 0.3 percent to 35.43 per dollar onshore <THB=>.   

But it was volatile in offshore trading <THB=W>, moving between 33.05 and 34.10 per dollar.

title: WSJA(12/29)  Indonesia  Stands Pat: Won't  Intervene  On Rupiah
text:
WSJA(12/29) Indonesia Stands Pat: Won't Intervene On Rupiah  

(From THE WALL STREET JOURNAL ASIA) By Tom Wright  

JAKARTA, Indonesia -- The Indonesian government doesn't believe its currency is overvalued and has no intention of intervening in financial markets as Thai authorities did to cool inflows of foreign capital into stocks, bonds and other assets, Finance Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati said Thursday.  

'The [competitiveness] of the economy should not rely on exchange-rate policy,' she said in an interview. 'We are not manipulating the level [of the rupiah] -- we maintain policy consistency. This is what investors want to hear from us.'  

Jakarta's improved economic management has put Indonesia back on investors' radar screens, economists say. In late 2005, the government slashed costly fuel subsidies, which were weighing on state finances, and increased prices at the pump. The ensuing inflationary pressure was quickly nipped in the bud by the central bank, which recently was able to begin lowering interest rates.  

The government expects inflation-adjusted economic growth of 6.3% in 2007 -- up from 5.5% in 2006 -- as lower interest rates lift consumer spending, according to Ms. Sri Mulyani. The economy relies heavily on Indonesia's huge domestic market to fuel growth, making local companies less dependent on exchange-rate policy than the region's more export-oriented corporations. Moreover, Indonesia's export growth is driven by oil, gas and other commodities that have done well this year due to strong global prices. That has pushed up the value of exports in rupiah terms, despite the currency's appreciation against the dollar.  

Ms. Sri Mulyani said government spending on infrastructure projects such as roads and airports also is likely to fuel growth in the new year. In 2005, the government only spent about half of its budgeted capital expenditure; this year, the government expects to use about 85% of its capital expenditure budget, she said.  

Indonesia's economic gains and improved outlook have sparked increased international investor interest in its stock market. With plenty of liquidity in the global financial system looking for strong returns, speculative money flows have created a 'herd instinct' toward Indonesia that has driven the Jakarta Stock Exchange's benchmark index up more than 50% this year and fueled a rally in bond prices, Ms. Sri Mulyani said.  

A similar influx of short-term foreign money into stocks, bonds and commercial paper helped prompt Thailand to impose controversial capital controls on Dec. 18 in an attempt to stop a rapid appreciation in the value of the baht against the dollar. The policy triggered a sharp sell-off in the Thai stock market and forced the government to roll back provisions that made investing in the country's shares unattractive.  

Although Ms. Sri Mulyani didn't directly criticize Thailand's capital controls, she played down the effectiveness of such measures to boost export competitiveness, which was one of Thailand's goals. In particular, Thailand was concerned about declining export competitiveness with China, which has only allowed a small strengthening of its currency.  

Ms. Sri Mulyani declined to blame Beijing's yuan policy for increased pressure on the currencies of other Asian economies. But she indicated that China should consider allowing the yuan to strengthen to avoid overheating in its own economy. 'They themselves need to adjust their own policy for their own good,' she said.  

The finance minister stressed that Indonesia wouldn't adopt measures to control short-term foreign investments. She argued that Indonesia's economic situation is different from that of Thailand. The rupiah has appreciated about 7% against the dollar this year, less than half the increase in the value of the baht. And Indonesia's propensity to suffer from bouts of inflationary pressure will also act as a natural brake on rapid currency appreciation in the future, she said.  

Indeed, Ms. Sri Mulyani suggested Indonesian stocks are still undervalued, despite the market's recent gains, because of a perception of political risk that Indonesia has been unable to fully shake since the fall of former President Suharto in 1998. 'Indonesia has been suffering from a discount factor for quite some time,' she said.  

The minister also said the increase in the value of stocks and other financial assets wasn't translating into more direct investment in business activities, which is crucial to alleviate Indonesia's growing unemployment problem. Jakarta needs to do more to overhaul labor, tax and investment reform laws that are deterring foreign companies from investing in the manufacturing sector, she said.  

Indonesia's current economic growth rate is short of the 7% the World Bank estimates is necessary to create enough jobs for the two million Indonesians entering the work force each year. About a third of the 120 million-strong work force is either unemployed or underemployed, according to some estimates.  

'We definitely need to create more employment and that can only happen if we put more investment in manufacturing,' Ms. Sri Mulyani said.  

One key reform -- an effort to push through a new tax law that treats foreign and local businesses on an equal footing -- is bogged down in Parliament. Nevertheless, Ms. Sri Mulyani said her ministry was making progress creating special tax departments, where officials are paid higher salaries in a bid to help stamp out corruption. The ministry also is planning to crack down on Indonesians who evade taxes. 'I'm going to find any law which can punish them,' she said.

title: Bank Indonesia:USD/IDR May Sink Below 9,000 Level In '07
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The U.S. dollar may sink to below the IDR9,000 level in 2007 due to Indonesia's increasingly positive macroeconomic fundamentals, a senior Bank Indonesia official said Friday.  

But the dollar is unlikely to tumble as low as the IDR8,000 level, Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Aslim Tadjuddin told reporters.  

"The rupiah is affected by our fundamental (macroeconomic) factors so the better our fundamentals, the better the rupiah (against the greenback)," Tadjuddin said  

Tadjuddin said that Bank Indonesia doesn't want the rupiah to "over-strengthen" because it would undermine the competitiveness of Indonesia's exports, without elaborating on possible central bank intervention to stall the rupiah's rise.  

The dollar was at IDR9,077 at 0630 GMT. [ 22-12-06 0631GMT ]  

The comments echo Bank Indonesia's forecast Monday that the dollar would likely trade in a band of IDR9,000-9,500 in 2007.  

Indonesia's improving macroeconomic outlook includes declining inflation and an ongoing easing in monetary policy.  

The government of President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono has projected economic growth of 6.3% in 2007 compared with 5.8% in 2006. The economy expanded 5.6% last year.  

Tadjuddin said he was confident that a central bank target of around $45 billion in foreign currency reserves by end-2007 was achievable due to Indonesia's robust trade performance.  

Indonesia's reserves stood at $41.5 billion at end-November from $39.9 billion a month earlier, Bank Indonesia spokesman Budi Mulia said earlier this month.

title: Bank Indonesia: Thai Baht Moves May Have Regional Impact
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The stability of the Indonesian rupiah isn't under any immediate threat from the type of speculative activity that recently sent the Thai baht to a nine-year high against the U.S. dollar, a senior Bank Indonesia official said Tuesday.  

"We have sufficient regulations to curb any speculative moves...and more-than-sufficient foreign exchange reserves (to defend the rupiah)," Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Aslim Tadjuddin told reporters.  

But Tadjuddin said Bank Indonesia is "always in the market" and would intervene if necessary to protect the rupiah from currency speculators.  

At 0730 GMT, the dollar was trading at IDR9,178, down from an intraday high of IDR9,203, but considerably higher than Monday's close of IDR9,084. [ 19-12-06 0737GMT ]  

The situation in Thailand was "nothing to worry about" for the rupiah due to existing laws that curb currency speculation activities, Tadjuddin said.  

Bank Indonesia also has around $41 billion in foreign reserves it can deploy to protect the local unit, he said.  

Tadjuddin said Indonesia's regulations, including a 2005 rule that restricts rupiah transactions and foreign currency lending, meant the central bank "needn't follow suit" and emulate the Bank of Thailand's capital control measures.  

"The (existing) regulation is sufficient to prevent the market from speculative trading," he said.  

The Bank of Thailand from Tuesday has imposed new foreign exchange controls to prevent the baht from appreciating sharply after speculative inflows pushed the unit to a nine-year high.  

Tadjuddin said the recent spike in the value of the baht against the dollar and the Bank of Thailand's moves would likely have only a temporary regional impact.  

Normal regional foreign exchange conditions would likely resume "after the market knows what's happening in Thailand," he said.  

-By Farida Husna contributing to Dow Jones Newswires; 62 21 3983 1277; phelim.kyne@dowjones.com [ 19-12-06 0815GMT ]

title: Bk Indonesia:"Not Overly Concerned" About Thai Baht Rise
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia is so far "not overly concerned" about potential spillover effects from the recent surge in the value of the Thai baht and the Bank of Thailand's measures to clamp down on speculative inflows, a senior central bank official said Tuesday.  

The central bank will only intervene to support the rupiah if there is "huge pressure" on the local unit, Bank Indonesia Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom said.  

"In an open economy and with an open capital account policy, we have to observe the market reaction to the Bank of Thailand announcement," Gultom said.  

"Up to now, it's clear that we have confidence that the...(domestic foreign exchange) structure is still healthy," Gultom said.  

The dollar was trading at IDR9,124 at 0445 GMT, down from an interday high of IDR9,128, but considerably higher than the Monday closing of IDR9,084. [ 19-12-06 0452GMT ]  

Gultom's comments reflect how Asian central bankers remain painfully cognizant of the lessons of the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis when massive, sudden movements in speculative inflows caused regional currencies to plummet against the U.S. dollar.  

The Bank of Thailand from Tuesday has imposed new foreign exchange controls to prevent the baht from appreciating sharply after speculative inflows pushed the unit to a nine-year high.  

Indonesia is particularly sensitive to the impact of speculative capital after emerging market risk aversion in May prompted a sudden short-term reversal in inflows estimated at $1 billion per month. That reversal caused the rupiah to tumble 5.5% against the dollar that month before rebounding.  

Dealers said Indonesian state banks began selling dollars early Tuesday in a move that appeared to be aimed at counteracting dollar purchases by market participants spooked by the sharp movement in the Thai baht.  

The dollar selling appeared to reflect an official desire to keep the rupiah relatively stable against the dollar in the symbolically important year-end period, dealers said.  

Bank Indonesia has a policy of not commenting on its interventions in the local currency market.  

Gultom indicated that it was still too soon to adequately evaluate the wider regional impact of recent events in Thailand.  

The central bank is confident that an improvement in Indonesia's investment environment will convert an increasing proportion of speculative inflows into long-term foreign direct investment next year, Gultom said.  

Gultom said that conversion of that speculative capital into meaningful FDI will require the central bank and the Indonesian government to ensure that "all (investment) projects in the pipeline waiting for finance" are available for investors.  

"We think we are sure of the likelihood of some of the inflows being converted into FDI in 2007," she said.  

The Indonesian government unveiled in November 10 "model" infrastructure projects valued at $4.4 billion designed to entice investors to commit to long-term investment in the country.  

-By Phelim Kyne; Dow Jones Newswires; 62 21 3983 1277; phelim.kyne@dowjones.com

title: Bk Indonesia: Dollar Likely At IDR9,000-IDR9,500 In 2007
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The U.S. dollar will likely move between IDR9,000 and IDR9,500 in 2007, with an average exchange rate of IDR9,300, Bank Indonesia said Monday.  

The nation's central bank didn't give further details to back its prognosis on the rupiah.  

The market will likely take the forecast as an indication of the range Bank Indonesia is comfortable with and may intervene if the currency pair trades outside that band.  

At 0220 GMT, the dollar was trading at IDR9,106. [ 11-12-06 0223GMT ]  

A Bank Indonesia handout distributed in a seminar on Shariah banking reiterated the central bank's forecast of 6.1% economic growth next year, slightly below the government's 6.3% target.  

The central bank also said it expects inflation next year at 6.5%.  

"Further rate cuts in 2007 will hinge on inflation and macroeconomic stability," it said.  

The central bank last week cut its benchmark rate by 50 basis points to 9.75% as inflation continues to ease.  

-By Farida Husna; Dow Jones Newswires; 62-21 39831277; I-Made.Sentana@dowjones.com [ 11-12-06 0241GMT ]
