title: Bank Indonesia: USD Likely Below IDR9,000 By End '06
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The U.S. dollar may drop below IDR9,000 by the end of 2006, Bank Indonesia's deputy governor said Friday.  

"I believe there is room in that direction, as our exports have been good enough, and we hope to control inflation," Aslim Tadjuddin told reporters.  

Tadjuddin said inflation would likely remain in check throughout August. While he didn't specify a projection for inflation figure, he indicated it would likely be near July's level.  

"Last month, inflation was 0.45% (on month), and hopefully we can control inflation this month also," he said. [ 25-08-06 0637GMT ]  

Tadjuddin's comments suggest that Bank Indonesia may be rethinking its traditional de facto policy of intervention at perceived "psychologically important" levels in order to maintain the country's export competitiveness.  

Bank Indonesia's policy is to allow the market to determine the rupiah's movements but hedges that position by reserving the right to intervene to prevent "volatility" in the currency market.  

"Even though in the last few days (the rupiah) has weakened, that is a temporary shift in line with the movements of global and regional (currencies)," he said.  

"So I predict that the rupiah will continue to trend upwards from its current position."  

The dollar was at IDR9,144 at 0712 GMT, up from an intraday low of IDR9,123.  

Tadjuddin's stance is likely to draw fire from Vice President Jusuf Kalla, who has repeatedly expressed his preference for the dollar to trade around IDR9,500 to help boost exports.  

Tadjuddin said that the central bank's successful efforts to control inflation had created "substantial room" for future cuts in the benchmark Bank Indonesia one-month rate.  

Bank Indonesia cut its benchmark rate by 50 basis points to 11.75% earlier this month, the third and steepest such decline since monetary policy easing began in May.  

Analysts expect the benchmark Bank Indonesia rate to fall to around 11% by the end of this year, in tandem with an expected decline in on-year inflation to around 8% in the same period. Indonesia's on-year inflation in July was 15.15%.  

Bank Indonesia's Board of Governors will decide next on possible benchmark rate movements at a monthly meeting on Sept. 5.  

-By Reuben Carder; Dow Jones Newswires; 62 21 3983 1277; reuben.carder@dowjones.com [ 25-08-06 0749GMT ]

title: Bk Indonesia Gov: USD Seen At Around IDR9,000 To End '06
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Macroeconomic conditions provide the central bank "room" to cut its benchmark one-month rate again next month, Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said Friday. "There is room (for a September rate cut)," Abdullah told reporters. He said the bank would monitor softening on-year inflation movements before making any monetary policy decisions.  

But Abdullah shied away from predicting a repeat of the 50-basis point cut in the benchmark rate that the bank announced last week.  

"We have to be very careful (about the pace of monetary easing)," he said. [ 11-08-06 0652GMT ]  

Adbullah's comments, which echo those Thursday by Bank Indonesia Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom about the likelihood of additional benchmark rate cuts, will heighten market anticipation of further monetary loosening next month.  

The central bank's decision last week to bring the rate down to 11.75% from 12.25% was the third and deepest interest rate cut since Bank Indonesia initiated monetary policy easing in May.  

Analysts expect the benchmark Bank Indonesia one-month rate to reach 11.00% by end-2006 in line with a decline in on-year inflation to around 8.0% in the same period.  

Abdullah also indicated that Bank Indonesia will aim to keep the U.S. dollar from falling below the IDR9,000 mark.  

"It seems the rupiah will be around 9,000 up to the end of the year, I think the trend is like that," he said.  

That statement is in line with central bank policy to avoid references to currency market intervention, but supports the government's aim to keep Indonesia's exports competitive.  

At 0725 GMT, the dollar was at IDR9,085, up from an intraday trading low of IDR9,045.  

-By Farida Husna, Dow Jones Newswires; 62 21 3983 1277; phelim.kyne@dowjones.com

DJ IMF: Lower Interest Rates Would Support Indonesian Econ  

WASHINGTON (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian government has room to ease interest rates and increase public spending to support the economy, the International Monetary Fund said Monday.  

Indonesia's key challenge is raising economic growth rates to reduce unemployment and alleviate poverty, the IMF said in its latest annual review of the Indonesian economy. Though the IMF forecasts gross domestic product will pick up in the second half this year, the multilateral lender noted downside risks from any renewed financial market turmoil for developing countries and high oil prices.  

The IMF predicted Indonesia's economy will expand 5.2% for the year 2006.  

'There is scope for fiscal policy to support activity in 2006, while firmly pursuing fiscal prudence,' the IMF said in a press summary of the review. The IMF urged the government to quickly implement a package of tax reforms that would make the tax system more efficient, and improve investor confidence.  

Monetary policy, too, could provide more support for the economy, as long as the timing and pace of any interest rate reductions takes into account the stability of global financial markets, the IMF said.  

The fund said the value of the Indonesian rupiah seems 'broadly in line with fundamentals' after some real appreciation recently. Recent intervention by the central bank to build foreign exchange reserves was 'appropriate' but the IMF said intervention should remain limited to smoothing volatility.  

The IMF urged Indonesia to push ahead with privatization of state-owned banks that don't have a specific public policy objective. Overall, performance by Indonesian banks has been steadily improving, the IMF said.  

'In the meantime, governance could be improved by allowing private shareholders to participate in their management,' the fund said. -By Elizabeth Price, Dow Jones Newswires; 202-862-9255; Elizabeth.Price@dowjones.com

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Down; Tight Liquidity Limits Fall
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah closed lower Friday as rising oil prices dragged most Asian currencies lower, dealers said.  

But tight rupiah supply in the interbank money market and central bank intervention helped the local unit claw back some of the losses, dealers added.  

"The rupiah was not spared by the weakness of other regional currencies," a dealer with a foreign bank said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,180, up from its close Thursday at IDR9,103, after rising to an intraday high of IDR9,253 earlier in the day.  

Dealers said a huge corporate tax payment due Friday drained rupiah liquidity from the market, which in turn pushed the overnight interbank rupiah lending rate to 15% from 8%. The rising interbank overnight rate eventually sparked players to trim their dollar-long positions, dealers said.  

Bank Indonesia admitted it intervened in the market Friday to help the rupiah, and promised more intervention in the future if necessary.  

Bank Indonesia expects the dollar to be stable around IDR9,200, Deputy Governor Aslim Tadjuddin told reporters Friday.  

Dealers said the dollar still looks well-bid Monday on uncertainties over oil prices globally. They expect the greenback to trade between IDR9,125 and IDR9,250 Monday.  

-By I Made Sentana; Dow Jones Newswires; 62-21 39831277; I-Made.Sentana@dowjones.com

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Higher as stocks, Fed, lift sentiment
text:
SINGAPORE, June 16 (Reuters) - Asian currencies rose on Friday, bouncing back from this week's multi-month lows thanks to a broad rebound in equities, upbeat U.S. economic data and a rise in the yuan to a post-revaluation high against the dollar.  

Dealers said remarks on inflation from Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke on Thursday appeared less hawkish than comments made a week ago, helping trigger stock market gains.  

Bernanke said the Fed's inflation-fighting credibility had limited the degree to which lofty energy costs have bled into other prices paid by American consumers.  

Data on Thursday showing solid U.S. regional manufacturing activity also eased concerns about a slowdown in growth, helping boost sentiment in fragile currency markets.  

"What we're seeing is anxiety about the U.S. is diminishing for now and the Asian currencies should strengthen," said Tim Condon, head of research at ING in Singapore.  

The South Korean won <KRW=> rose as much as 0.6 percent to 953.9 per dollar as local shares notched up their biggest one-day percentage gain in more than 1-½ years.  

The Taiwan dollar, which hit a 5-month low at about 32.75 per dollar on Wednesday, hit a one-week peak at 32.40, while the Singapore dollar <SGD=> rose as high as 1.5862 -- rebounding almost one percent from a low of 1.5999 per dollar hit this week.  

The Philippine peso <PHP=> also touched a one-week high at 52.98 per dollar.  

"We are going into a consolidation phase and a dollar-selling trend is unlikely to start so soon as the market continues to focus on inflation and imbalances in the global economy," said Philip Wee, a currency strategist at DBS Bank in Singapore.  

The rally in Asian currencies was aided by the yuan <CNY=CFXS>, which hit 7.9970 per dollar -- the highest level since its revaluation in July last year.  

Dealers say a pick up in yuan gains this week suggest China is using the exchange rate in its battle to slow the economy.  

RUPIAH, RINGGIT FIRM  

The Indonesian rupiah <IDR=> firmed as much as 1 percent to 9,289 per dollar, the highest level in more than a week and comfortably stronger than Wednesday's 5-month low at 9,560.  

Dealers said there had been no signs of central bank intervention to boost the rupiah after Bank Indonesia governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said on Thursday the central bank was "in the market" to help the currency.  

A trader said there had been signals from foreign banks of renewed investor interest in Indonesian assets such as bonds.  

"The yields are just too attractive," he said.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Higher On Regional  Currency  Rebound
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended higher Thursday on the back of a regional currency rebound against the U.S. dollar, dealers said.  

The rupiah gained against the greenback due to large-scale dollar sales in the local currency market by offshore investors including Singapore-based foreign investment banks, according to a dealer at a foreign bank.  

"We also saw some dollar selling by state banks, likely on behalf of Bank Indonesia," the dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,385 compared to IDR9,478 on Wednesday. That reflects a strengthening in the rupiah since the dollar's more-than-six-month high Tuesday of IDR9,505 powered by foreign investors' concerns about a widely anticipated U.S. Federal Reserve Rate hike on June 29.  

Bank Indonesia's apparent intervention to protect the rupiah comes as no surprise to the market.  

Central bank governor Burhanuddin Abdullah told reporters Thursday that his staff was closely monitoring currency markets and would intervene to protect the rupiah from any serious volatility against the dollar.  

"We are in the market," Abdullah said.  

"We do intervene...in times when the rupiah is stronger and when the rupiah weakens."  

Dealers indicated that such intervention may continue to be necessary in the days ahead to counter the impact of jittery foreign investors warily awaiting the Fed decision later this month.  

"If nothing happens in New York tonight, the dollar should remain around the IDR9,350 level on Friday," the dealer said.  

"But if something bad happens in New York time tonight, we will easily hit IDR9,500 (tomorrow)," he added.

title: INTERVIEW: IMF Says Indonesia Addressing Mkt Volatility
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's policy-makers are taking adequate measures to protect the economy from recent shocks that reversed strong gains in the Jakarta bourse and the rupiah against the U.S. dollar, a senior International Monetary Fund official said.  

The government of President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono is implementing policies that should help cushion the economy from external turbulence, Milan Zavadjil, assistant director in the IMF's Asia and Pacific department, told Dow Jones Newswires recently.  

That confidence contributed to the IMF's decision last week to upgrade its projection for Indonesia's 2006 economic growth to 5.2% from 5.0%. The government forecasts a more robust 6.2% growth this year, outpacing last year's 5.6% expansion.  

"The impact of the last few days hasn't been (due to) Indonesia-specific factors...This sort of volatility is a concern for everybody," Zavadjil said.  

"But in principle, what we think is the government is addressing it through improvement in (Indonesia's economic) fundamentals."  

Those fundamentals include reductions in the external debt-to-GDP and public debt-to-GDP ratios, he said. The government aims to reduce its public debt-to-GDP level to around 30% by 2009 from a current level of 40%.  

Worries over rising U.S. inflation and interest rates over the past week have sent ripples through global markets, including Indonesia.  

The Jakarta Stock Exchange Composite Index fell 11% over the previous three sessions but rebounded Tuesday, ending up 1.3% at 1326.260 on bargain hunting in bank blue chips.  

The Indonesia rupiah also ended higher Tuesday as some foreign companies in Indonesia sold dollars, triggering market participants to liquidate their dollar-long positions.  

The dollar finished at IDR9,260, down from Monday's close of IDR9,300 but still above its May 17 closing low of IDR8,910.  

Analysts have blamed the Jakarta bourse's recent slide on a sudden reversal in short-term speculative inflows, or "hot money," which have flooded Indonesia since the beginning of the year due to the country's bullish economic prospects.  


 
     IMF Says Foreign Reserves Counter Hot Money Threat 
   

That outlook prompted monthly hot money inflows of up to $1 billion, Coordinating Minister for the Economy Boediono said last month.  

Zavadjil said Indonesia's steadily increasing foreign currency reserves help mitigate the potential threat of a massive reversal in fund flows.  

Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves rose to $42.81 billion as of April 28 from $40.08 billion as of March 29.  

"In fact reserves have risen by more than inflows," Zavadjil said.  

"So the (hot) money has come in, but (Bank Indonesia) can intervene (to support the rupiah) when it goes out."  

The IMF also supports Bank Indonesia's move earlier this month to initiate a long-awaited loosening in monetary policy by cutting its benchmark one-month rate by 25 basis points to 12.50%.  

Analysts expect the Bank Indonesia benchmark rate to ease to 10.00%-11.00% by end-2006 in tandem with a projected decline in on-year inflation to around 8.00%.  

"We support the way Bank Indonesia is bringing down interest rates in a gradual manner," Zavadjil said.  

"They're doing the right thing to insulate themselves as much as possible against this (global economic) volatility."  

That volatility hadn't shaken the central bank's resolve to continue monetary loosening, Bank Indonesia Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom indicated Monday.  

"We didn't say that we will (definitely) cut rates, but there's room (to do so)," Gultom told reporters.  

But Zavadjil cautioned that Bank Indonesia must balance its desire to cut rates to stimulate domestic consumption with the need to be vigilant of external macroeconomic influences that might derail economic growth.  

"A lot of things are happening (so) Bank Indonesia really has to be on its toes," he said, without elaborating.  

-By Phelim Kyne; Dow Jones Newswires; 62 21 3983 1277; phelim.kyne@dowjones.com

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends 1.1% Down On Dollar's Regional Rise
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah lost a further 1.1% to the dollar Monday amid the U.S. unit's strong rally against the yen and other regional currencies, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,300, versus its close Friday at IDR9,200.  

"The dollar-rupiah is tracking the dollar's rise to above Y112," a dealer with a foreign bank said.  

Dealers said that Bank Indonesia was suspected of intervening via state banks to slow the dollar's rise. They said that the central bank likely sold dollars between IDR9,325 and IDR9,350.  

The stock market, meanwhile, ended 6% lower at 1,309.045 points as foreign investors exited the Indonesian market amid weakness on regional bourses, dealers said.  

The selloffs in the stock market may further drive the greenback higher during the rest of the week as foreign investors will likely use their rupiah to buy the dollar.  

"There is a big potential for the dollar to rise to IDR9,500 over the next three days if the regional stock markets don't recover," a dealer said.  

Dealers said that Vice President Jusuf Kalla's statement Friday that IDR9,200-IDR9,500 is the "normal" range for the dollar may embolden market participants to test IDR9,500 in the coming days.  

Dealers set IDR9,200 and IDR9,500 as the possible range for the dollar Tuesday, but still expect Bank Indonesia to intervene to prevent the greenback from breaking the psychologically important level.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends 5% Dn At 2-Mo Low On Fund Outflows
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The rupiah fell nearly 5% Monday to end at a two-month low against the dollar as hedge funds exited Indonesia as part of their risk aversion strategy on emerging markets, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,160, up from its close Friday at IDR8,735. Monday's close is the greenback's highest closing level since March 14, when it ended at 9,165.  

Dealers said dollar outflows came mostly from the stock market, which fell 6.3% Monday, the largest single drop ever.  

Inflows of speculative funds seeking high yields had been cited as the main force that brought the rupiah to its four-year high recently.  

Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanduddin Abdullah said that the central bank intervened Monday to curb the dollar's rise, and vowed to do it again to bring the U.S. currency to its "appropriate level" of IDR8,750.  

He said that the rupiah fell as hedge funds exited emerging markets after some of them suffered losses in Brazil and Turkey recently.  

Dealers said Bank Indonesia had failed to contained the dollar's rise as the amount of dollars it sold in the market was likely marginal.  

"Bank Indonesia's intervention failed to curb the dollar's rise," a dealer with a foreign bank said. "Given the speed of the dollar's rise today, IDR9,500 doesn't seem to be very far away."  

Still, Finance Minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati told parliament Monday that the dollar will likely remain below IDR9,000 until the end of the year. Mulyani didn't give any reason.  

Dealers said that news of Indonesia's slowing economic growth in the first quarter was well expected, but added to the dampened sentiment.  

The Central Statistics Agency said that Southeast Asia's largest economy expanded 4.59% on year in the first quarter, slowing from 4.90% on year in the fourth quarter of 2005. It is a tad lower than the average forecast of economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires of 4.61%.  

Dealers expect the dollar to test IDR9,200 upside resistance Tuesday, with IDR8,990 seen as solid support for the U.S. currency.  

If IDR9,200 is broken, dealers expect the dollar to scale higher toward IDR9,400, Tuesday.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Lower As State Banks Buy Dollars
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended slightly lower Thursday on dollar bids from state banks, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR8,735, up from its previous close of IDR8,726.  

Dealers said state banks bought the greenback at levels between IDR8,720 and IDR8,730, likely on behalf of the central bank.  

"I think Bank Indonesia was behind the state banks," a dealer with a foreign bank said.

title: Indonesia Mar CPI +0.03% On Mo Vs +0.31% Consensus
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's consumer price index rose 15.74% on-year last month amid declining food prices during the seasonal harvest, the official Central Statistics Agency said Monday.  

On month, the inflation rate was 0.03%. In February, on-year inflation was 17.92% while the on-month reading was 0.58%  

Core inflation - which excludes prices that are controlled by the government, such as energy and food - was 9.64% on year.  

March inflation was below the average forecast of 16.18% by five regional analysts polled by Dow Jones Newswires. They expected on-month inflation at 0.31%. [ 03-04-06 0657GMT ]  

March's on-month inflation was the lowest such increase in two years, Central Statistics Agency Chairman Choiril Maksum told reporters at a press briefing.  

The March inflation result "was caused by the decreasing price of rice, as the harvest season has begun," Maksum said. "If we can maintain the (same) level of inflation as in March, on-year inflation by the end of the year should be good."  

Maksum didn't provide any specific forecasts for on-year inflation. He urged the government to ensure that food supply and distribution systems are functioning well to reduce potential new sources of inflation.  

The March CPI data appeared to reflect official projections that the stubbornly persistent inflationary trend will ease toward the single-digit level on year by the end of 2006. Bank Indonesia has forecast on-year inflation of around 8.0% by end-December.  

Inflation peaked at 18.38% on year in November due to the government's move to effectively raise fuel prices by more than double on Oct. 1.  

The government decided last month to shelve a politically unpopular plan to also raise electricity tariffs this year, in order to avoid a renewed surge in inflationary pressure.  

The March CPI data will likely fuel expectations that Bank Indonesia will soon start planning cuts in the one-month benchmark rate if easing inflationary pressure rolls into April.  

"Although this isn't the under the authority of (the Central Statistics Agency), I think the central bank should ease monetary tightening," Maksum said.  

However, Bank Indonesia's Board of Governors is expected to keep the benchmark lending rate unchanged at 12.75% when it holds its monthly monetary policy meeting Thursday.  

Analysts predict the central bank will cut rates beginning sometime in the second half of 2006.  

"We remain of the view that the next interest rate move by Bank Indonesia is down, not up, with the inflation data affecting the timing and amount of BI's moves, but not the direction," an ING-Barings research note issued Friday said.  

But Bank Indonesia Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom said last month that the bank's tightening posture remains intact due to concerns about potential inflation-spiking "external influences," including a possible increase in the price of crude oil on the global market.  

That position has cheered analysts who've urged Bank Indonesia to maintain the tightening posture to avoid spooking offshore speculative investors who have poured into Indonesia's markets this year due to bullish sentiment about the country's economic prospects.  

Those inflows of have resulted in the dollar easing to IDR9,040, as of 0824 GMT Monday, from its end-2005 value of IDR9,835 and from a four-year high of IDR11,900 in August 2005.

   By I Made Sentana and Phelim Kyne 
   OF DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 
   

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The pace of Indonesia's inflation eased in March, which will likely encourage the country's central bank to maintain its current tight monetary policy with a view to cutting rates later this year.  

The country's consumer price index rose 15.74% from a year earlier and 0.03% from the previous month, as rice prices declined during the seasonal harvest, official Central Statistics Agency Chairman Choiril Maksum told reporters Monday.  

Those results compare with a consensus forecast from economists polled by Dow Jones Newswires for inflation of 16.18% on the year and 0.31% on the month.  

The figures also indicate a slowing from 17.92% and 0.58% on the year and month, respectively, in February.  

Core inflation, which excludes prices that are controlled by the government such as energy and food, declined to 9.64% year-on-year in March from 10.20% in February.  

"The issue is when they'll start cutting rates...and the most judicious thing to do would be to wait until third-quarter (2006)," said Sailesh Jha, CSFB's senior economist for Southeast Asia and India.  

"I think it will be a progression...to about 10.25% by year-end."  

Bank Indonesia's one-month benchmark rate has stood at 12.75% since December, as the central bank tries to cool an inflationary surge which peaked in November, at 18.38% year-on-year, after the government effectively more than doubled fuel prices on Oct. 1.  

The tight monetary policy has put Bank Indonesia on track to achieving its target of year-on-year inflation around 8.00% by the end of 2006. The central bank is trying to control inflation to help the government reach its target for 6.2% economic growth in 2006.  

Minister of Finance Sri Mulyani Indrawati said last week she expects the economy to expand a more conservative 5.9% in 2006, which would still outpace last year's 5.6% growth rate.  

Massive inflows from foreign investors bullish on Indonesia's economic prospects have also helped reduce inflation. Those inflows have resulted in the rupiah rising to IDR9,030 to the dollar at 0900 GMT Monday from its four-year low of IDR11,900/dollar in August, and IDR9,835/dollar at the end of last year.  

The March CPI data "...gives Bank Indonesia flexibility" in deciding when to start cutting rates, Action Economics economist David Cohen said.  

Bank Indonesia's Board of Governors will review monetary policy at its monthly meeting Thursday.  


 
     Possible Inflationary Spikes Loom 
   

Analysts said Bank Indonesia will hold off on any immediate cut in benchmark interest rates due to the potential for further spikes in inflation.  

Bank Indonesia must allow for the possible impact of government increases in industrial fuel prices and deteriorating road infrastructure which could drive up basic food costs, Citigroup economist Anton Gunawan said.  

"I don't think Bank Indonesia will want to cut interest rates very soon...probably August at the earliest," he said.  

Bank Indonesia Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom said last month that the bank's tightening posture remains intact due to concerns about potential "external influences" that could drive inflation, including a possible increase in the price of crude oil on the global market.  

Meanwhile, Indonesia recorded a fairly robust trade performance in February, with the trade surplus rising to $2.84 billion from $2.4 billion a year earlier.  

However, the February result was below a Dow Jones Newswires consensus forecast by economists for a $3.07 billion trade surplus.  

Indonesia's exports eased to $7.35 billion in February from $7.51 billion in January. Imports rose to $4.51 billion from $4.27 billion in the same period.  

A $376.2 million deficit in oil trade in February indicated that Indonesia, the sole Southeast Asian member of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, is missing out on the benefits of high global crude oil prices.  

Still, CSFB's Jha said that the Indonesia's trade performance in February was "fairly solid" and that Bank Indonesia isn't likely to intervene against the recent strengthening in the rupiah against the U.S. currency.  

"I don't think Bank Indonesia will be overly worried that the (rise) in the (rupiah) is hurting exports," he said.

title: Indonesian Rupiah Ends Higher On Offshore Invest Inflows
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended at a more-than-15-month high Tuesday, powered by offshore investors buying into Indonesia's equities market, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,114, down from Monday's close of IDR9,140 and marking the lowest end-of-day result for the U.S. unit since the IDR9,097 level reached on Dec. 7, 2004.  

"Offshore inflows for equities and other offshore investment money just keeps coming into the country," a dealer said.  

"I think the trend is still pretty bullish for the rupiah."  

The Jakarta Stock Exchange Composite Index edged down 0.2% Tuesday, but that followed three days of gains that ended with a 1.8% rise Monday to a record close of 1330.113 points.  

Foreign investors have been piling into Indonesia's equities markets due to increasingly upbeat sentiment about the country's economic outlook.  

The government has targeted economic growth of 6.2% in 2006, which would outpace the 5.6% increase in 2005.  

High expectations that President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono's economic cabinet team will make significant progress this year in reducing regulatory and bureaucratic obstacles to investment growth are fueling investor sentiment, analysts say.  

Dealers said the greenback will strengthen against the rupiah in the days ahead as local corporates make routine end-month dollar purchases to service foreign debt obligations.  

But subtle intervention by Bank Indonesia through state-owned banks will likely keep the greenback from falling below the IDR9,000 level this week, dealers say.  

Bank Indonesia officials routinely express their support for market forces determining the value of the rupiah against the dollar, but hedge those comments by adding that the central bank reserves the right to prevent potentially disruptive movements in the currency's value.  

"We'll probably see Bank Indonesia selling dollars through state banks to smooth out the recent rise," a dealer said, without elaborating.  

Dealers expect the greenback will trade in a IDR9,090 to IDR9,115 band Wednesday.  

-By Phelim Kyne; Dow Jones Newswires; 62 21 3983 1277; phelim.kyne@dowjones.com

title: Indonesian rupiah stays near 1-yr high on inflows
text:
SINGAPORE, March 2 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah was trading on Thursday just shy of a one-year peak hit on Wednesday, with sentiment boosted by the response to a sovereign bond issue but the upside capped by fear of central bank intervention.  

The rupiah <IDR=> was quoted at 9,185/9,190 per dollar, just off Wednesday's high of 9,150, having gained more than 1.8 percent in a week.  

Traders in Jakarta said increasing interest from foreign investors in high-yielding rupiah assets was supporting the currency.  

But a Singapore-based trader said the central bank, Bank Indonesia, had been seen intervening around the 9,200 level this week to rein in the rupiah, which had made the market wary.  

"Emerging market carry is broadly doing well. The Turkish lira, Brazilian real and South African rand are looking bid, so there's plenty of appetite for carry," said Mirza Baig, Deutsche Bank's currency strategist.  

A twin sovereign dollar bond offering from Indonesia had attracted $8 billion of subscriptions so far, market sources told Reuters on Thursday. Pricing is expected later in the day.  

Indonesia has not fixed how much it plans to raise from the bond sale, but the response is more than 5 times initial market expectations for the size of the offering.  

Baig said sentiment on the rupiah had improved on the news, particularly on expectations some of the proceeds may be converted into rupiah.

title: Traders:USD Falls Below IDR9,400; 1st Time Since Mar 23
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)-The U.S. dollar fell below the IDR9,400 mark in early trading Thursday for the first time since March 23, 2005, traders told Dow Jones Newswires.  

The dollar was being taken at IDR9,395 at 0155 GMT traders said, the lowest point since it fell to IDR9,378 in intraday trading March 23 before rebounding above the IDR9,400 mark the following day.  

Traders say the rupiah's strength is underpinned by a combination of strong offshore currency inflows into Indonesia's stock market and a surge in regional currencies against the dollar. [ 12-01-06 0210GMT ]  

The Jakarta Stock Exchange Composite Index ended up 1.3%, or 16.229 points, at a new closing high of 1261.283 Wednesday, surpassing the previous record of 1245.054 Monday. Indonesia was closed Tuesday for a holiday.  

Dealers said expectations of a steady interest-rate environment after the central bank left its benchmark Bank Indonesia rate unchanged Monday at 12.75% triggered buying, offsetting sporadic profit-taking by local retail funds.  

The index is likely to rise higher Thursday on the rupiah's surge against the dollar and gains in other Asian equities markets, dealers said.  

Central bank intervention to stem the rupiah's rise is highly unlikely, dealers and currency analysts said.  

Bank Indonesia perceives the rupiah's strength as a useful tool in curbing inflation, which hit 17.11% in 2005.  

Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Aslim Tadjuddin said Monday the central bank reserved its right to intervene in foreign-exchange markets, but insisted that "we leave to the market" the value of the rupiah.  

"There is no need for Bank Indonesia to intervene as (the dollar slide) is due to market forces," a currency dealer at a foreign bank in Jakarta said.  

That view was echoed by the secretary of the Indonesian Forex Dealer Association, Panji Irawan.  

"We have seen the dollar at IDR8,300, and at that level our exports were still competitive," Panji said.  

Bank Indonesia intervention at this point would likely be fruitless, BNP Paribas senior currency analyst Thio Chin Loo said. "Most people agree there's no point in intervention...it would be like trying to catch a falling knife or fighting against a huge flock of birds flying the same way."  

A "feel-good factor" toward Asian markets and currencies, combined with concerns about U.S. macroeconomic data and signals that the U.S. Federal Reserve is about to stop hiking rates, are underpinning the dollar's slide, Thio said.  

"This is still a dollar story ... people are jumping on the (dollar sale) bandwagon and momentum is strong," Thio said.  

-By I Made Sentana and Phelim Kyne; Dow Jones Newswires; 62 21 3983 1277; phelim.kyne@dowjones.com

title: Indonesia's Pres Urges Govt Action To Stabilize Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesian President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono called on his government Wednesday to cooperate with central bank efforts to stabilize the rupiah after the currency hit a more-than-three-year low of IDR9,810 Tuesday against the U.S. dollar.  

"The president today instructed the vice president and ministers to take necessary actions to stabilize the rupiah to ensure it remains at a reasonable level, to communicate effectively and work closely with the monetary authority so that its actions will be fruitful," a statement issued by the president's office said, without elaborating.  

In the statement, Yudhoyono also urged his government to reassure the public that Indonesia's finances, including foreign exchange reserves, remain "strong" and that the rupiah is at a "reasonable value." [ 27-04-05 0236GMT ]  

Indonesia recorded a $1.37 billion increase in its foreign exchange reserves to $37.32 billion as of April 21 from a week earlier.  

Yudhoyono's statement marks the first time an Indonesian president has issued a public appeal for solidarity in the face of currency fluctuations since the dying days of the regime of former dictator Suharto during the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis.  

"The government calls on the public to remain calm...the economy is growing well and the political situation remains stable," the statement said.  

The statement reflects government efforts to head off any possible public panic over the slide in the value of the rupiah that might result in mass dollar purchases.  

Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah responded to the sliding rupiah Tuesday by announcing a currency support plan that includes a pending interest rate hike of 15 to 20 basis points, the use of forward transactions to protect the rupiah and a move to "monitor" state-owned Pertamina's (PTM.YY) dollar purchases.  

The market rallied on the news and that, in tandem with Bank Indonesia's move to intervene by unloading what traders suspect was up to $150 million on the market, prompted a rebound in the rupiah's value with the U.S. dollar closing at IDR9,688 Tuesday.  

Bank Indonesia intervened again Wednesday morning to support the rupiah, pushing the dollar to IDR9,665 at 0127 GMT.  

But analysts have cautioned that official efforts to stem the rupiah slide against the U.S. dollar won't address the currency's basic problem of rising oil prices, which are powering massive dollar purchases by domestic state firms.

title: DJ  Indonesia  Rupiah Ends Higher On Ctrl Bk  Intervention
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah extended its recovery by another 1.2% Wednesday as Bank Indonesia reportedly sold dollars and sent auditors to foreign banks' dealing rooms in Jakarta to deter currency speculation, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,573, down from its close Tuesday at IDR9,688. The rupiah had risen 0.6% Tuesday.  

Dealers said that the nation's central bank aggressively unloaded dollars via brokers to prop up the rupiah. The central bank couldn't be reached for comment, but its officials have said recently that the bank would intervene to defend the rupiah when necessary.  

Dealers said that Bank Indonesia also dispatched its auditors to look at foreign banks' transaction activity.  

'Suddenly, we saw a dollar selloff today from foreign banks, who likely unloaded their dollar long positions after central banks sent their auditors to those banks,' a dealer with a local bank said.  

Foreign banks are the main players in Jakarta's interbank foreign exchange market.  

Dealers said that dollar demand from local companies also abated as they chose to wait on the sidelines, likely hoping to buy the greenback at lower levels.  

The market welcomed President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono's call earlier Wednesday for his ministers to coordinate closely with the central bank to boost the rupiah's value, which recently fell to over-three-year lows.  

'It shows that the president is in charge on this (rupiah weakness) problem,' a dealer with a local bank said.  

Dealers expect the dollar to continue sliding Thursday. They, however, forecast a wide IDR9,500-IDR9,750 range as the market remains unstable. -By I Made Sentana; Dow Jones Newswires; 62-21 39831277; I-Made.Sentana@dowjones.com

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia c.bank soaks up cash to help rupiah.
text:
JAKARTA, April 26 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank launched a three-day intervention tool on Tuesday and said it could raise interest rates in an effort to soak up excess rupiah in the banking system as the currency fell to three-year lows.  

The new deposit facility, which Bank Indonesia called a fine tuning instrument, offered banks a rate of 3.625 percent. It attracted 1.69 trillion rupiah ($174.7 million) from the market.  

"The auction has helped push up rates. The overnight rate is now being offered at above four percent. It was below that before the announcement," a bank dealer said.  

The central bank is under pressure to support the battered rupiah currency, which hit a three-year low of 9,800 per dollar on Tuesday.  

Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said on Tuesday the central banks was studying the possibility of raising the reserve requirements for commercial banks to help the rupiah.  

He also said the central bank would lift the interest rates on its short-term debt certificates.  

"We plan to absorb liquidity by raising interest rates, possibly by 15-20 basis points," he told reporters, without giving a specific timeframe.  

The rupiah has weakened on expectations that rising world oil prices will lead to increased demand for dollars to pay for oil imports. The dollar buying leads to excess rupiah in the money market, which the central bank is trying to absorb to stop the currency falling and counter inflation risks.  

Worries over the rupiah hurt sentiment at an auction of two-year bonds on Tuesday, the proceeds of which would be used to help finance budget deficit.  

The government raised a targeted three trillion rupiah from the monthly auction at an average yield of 9.77 percent, well above a forecast of 9.54 percent from a Reuters survey.  

A central bank official told Reuters that under the new three day facility banks would deposit money at Bank Indonesia. The central bank did not exchange any assets for the cash, so it was not a repurchase agreement or an issue of debt paper, the official said.  

The three-day facility adds to the central bank's relatively limited number of tools to absorb liquidity. They include a seven-day intervention facility, plus one-month and three-month central bank certificates (SBIs).  

The central bank has used its seven-day intervention facility daily of late, and offer its three-day instrument only when it is deemed necessary.  

The interest rate on the three-day facility may vary regularly, unlike the seven-day rate which is changed only occasionally, a central bank official said.  

The central bank raised the seven-day rate by 25 basis points to 7.25 percent earlier this month, after annual inflation hit a 27-month high of 8.8 percent in March.

title: FX  Asia: Bk Indonesia Rate Hike Unlikely To Boost Rupiah
text:
By Phelim Kyne 
   A Dow Jones Newswires Column 
   

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia's plan to hike interest rates to support the tumbling value of the rupiah against the U.S. dollar will boost market sentiment but won't address the currency's core problem of rising oil prices, which are fueling massive dollar purchases by domestic state firms, analysts said.  

Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah Tuesday unveiled a rupiah defense plan that includes a pending increase in the benchmark Sertifikat Bank Indonesia, or SBI rate, of 15 to 20 basis points, the use of forward transactions to protect the currency and a move to "monitor" state-owned Pertamina (PTM.YY)'s dollar purchases.  

That news and Bank Indonesia intervention helped spur a rebound in the rupiah's value with the U.S. dollar closing at IDR9,688 Tuesday, down from a-more-than three-year high of IDR9,810 earlier in the day and Monday's close of IDR9,750.  

The central bank's moves are welcome, but they won't put much of a dent in the voracious domestic appetite for dollars powered by high oil prices, said JP Morgan Chase Bank's Asian foreign exchange strategist, Claudio Piron.  

"The risk is we may see (the dollar) touch IDR10,000 by year's end," Piron said. "The central bank can watch Pertamina, but understand that Pertamina has a budgeted rate of $24 a barrel and outside that they have to go to the market to buy dollars (to purchase supply)."  

At 1025 GMT, the front-month June Brent contract on London's International Petroleum Exchange was down 41 cents at $53.99 a barrel in electronic trading, but above an intraday low of $53.88/bbl. Front month Nymex crude was trading 66 cents lower at $53.91/bbl.  

Piron said that Bank Indonesia had been "resting on its laurels a bit" in responding to the recent rupiah decline, but that movements in the currency reflect a healthy managed currency and shouldn't be cause for market gloom.  

"Generally speaking, the currency is responding to the macroeconomic environment...but (Bank Indonesia) has to get (support measures) just right because sentiment is fragile and if they overstep they may panic the market," he said.  

A weaker rupiah threatens the financial performance of local firms, which have substantial dollar debt, and could hurt Indonesia's most prolonged period of economic growth since the Asian financial crisis of 1997-98. Indonesia's government of President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono has projected an average annual rise in gross domestic product of 6.6% from 2004 to 2009, outpacing 5.1% GDP growth last year.  

The rupiah's decline has also prompted the central bank to consider introducing a new generation of money market management tools, including a currency swap instrument, to reduce U.S.-dollar buying by state-owned firms. Bank Indonesia's Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom told Dow Jones Newswires that the bank's board of governors would discuss the currency swap tool in a meeting Tuesday, without elaborating.  


 
    Interest-Rate Rise May Not Help Rupiah Long Term 
   

The psychological impact of Bank Indonesia's moves to support the rupiah will likely help keep the U.S. dollar at IDR9,500 to IDR9,600 for the next few weeks, but projections beyond that period remain "quite hazy," said ABN Amro Bank Asian sovereign and foreign exchange strategist, Emmanuel Ng.  

Ng said that raising interest rates to absorb excess liquidity won't influence domestic companies' purchases of dollars to pay foreign currency debts.  

"I think the market will have a positive spin on (the rupiah support measures) because it shows that Bank Indonesia is being proactive," he said.  

"But raising interest rates will only have transitory impact," Ng said. Monitoring "Pertamina and the use of forward transactions would have the most impact because those two measures would actually address the real dollar (transactions)."  

That view was echoed by Citibank economist Anton Gunawan, who said the current circumstances behind the decline in the rupiah mirrored those in May to July 2004.  

Bank Indonesia helped stem the rupiah's slide against the dollar at that time by trimming the estimated $30 million that Pertamina spends daily on oil supplies. It did that by limiting those purchases to state-owned bank transactions closely monitored by the central bank.  

Gunawan said the central bank's efforts to bolster the value of the rupiah against the dollar may get a boost from a massive U.S. currency injection from an unlikely source: U.S. cigarette manufacturer Philip Morris.  

Philip Morris, a unit of the world's biggest tobacco company Altria Group Inc. (MO), said last month that it will pay $2 billion to buy a 40% stake in Jakarta-listed PT Hanjaya Mandal Sampoerna (HMSP.SK) from a group of major shareholders. Sampoerna is Indonesia's third-largest cigarette maker by sales.  

Philip Morris will make a general offer for the rest of Sampoerna which, if fully accepted, will lift the value of the total acquisition to $5.2 billion, including around $160 million in debt.  

The rupiah may benefit from an influx of U.S. dollars timed to meet an end-May payment deadline for a portion of the Sampoerna acquisition, Gunawan said.  

"(Philip Morris) has already brought in about a billion, probably...and if they bring some more money in then the rupiah value can go to IDR9,400 to IDR9,500, he said.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Up On  Central Bank  Moves
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesia rupiah recovered from volatile trading Tuesday after Bank Indonesia unloaded U.S. currency in the spot market and stated plans to stop the dollar's rally, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,688, down from its close Monday at IDR9,750. But the greenback touched a fresh three-year high of IDR9,810 earlier Tuesday as panic-stricken local companies continue to hedge offshore obligations.  

Dealers estimated that Bank Indonesia sold around $150 million in the spot market, which helped the rupiah recover.  

Bank Indonesia's Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said the central bank will take a raft of measures to support the rupiah, including raising its benchmark Sertifikat Bank Indonesia, or SBI, interest rate by 15 to 20 basis points. The rate on the one-month SBI now stands at 7.7%. The rupiah's decline has also prompted the central bank to consider rolling out newer, more sophisticated money-market management tools, including a currency swap instrument, to reduce U.S.-dollar buying by state-owned companies, Bank Indonesia Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom said. She didn't provide a timetable for such a move.  

The bank's plan includes a temporary decrease in commercial banks' net open position to 20% of equity capital from 30%, effective immediately. The central bank is also considering increasing banks' reserve requirement ratios as an added measure to absorb excess liquidity in the financial system. Commercial banks currently must maintain a minimum reserve ratio of 5%.  

Bank Indonesia will also intervene in the market via forward transactions to defend the value of the rupiah against the U.S. dollar, Burhanuddin said.  

The central bank will take a much more proactive stance against state-owned firms whose dollar purchases have been linked to the decline in the value of the rupiah against the U.S. dollar, the governor indicated.  

Burhanuddin was quoted Tuesday by Bisnis Indonesia as naming state-run oil company Pertamina and electricity company Perusahaan Listrik Negara as examples of state-owned firms currently securing large quantities of U.S. dollars to pay foreign-currency-denominated bills that come due up to six months in the future.  

Dealers said that demand for the dollar may resurface Wednesday as the end of the month is drawing nearer. They expect the dollar to trade between IDR9,650 and IDR9,750, with Bank Indonesia expected to enter the market again.

title: Bk Indonesia Chief: Rate Hike Planned To Defend Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said Tuesday the central bank will raise its benchmark Sertifikat Bank Indonesia, or SBI, interest rate by 15 to 20 basis points to defend the local currency following a recent slide in its value against the U.S. dollar.  

The planned increase in the SBI rate will help the rupiah by draining excess liquidity out of the system, Burhanuddin told reporters, without elaborating on a timetable for the rate hike.  

The next auction of SBI notes, the central bank's money market papers, is scheduled for next Wednesday.  

The rate on the one-month SBI stands at 7.7%. [ 26-04-05 0711GMT ]  

The central bank plan spurred a rebound in the value of the rupiah against the U.S. dollar to IDR9,678 at 0728 GMT from a more than three-year low of IDR9,810 at 0435 GMT, dealers told Dow Jones Newswires.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,750 Monday.  

Dealers have blamed the slide in the value of the rupiah against the dollar on local firms' purchased of the U.S. currency to hedge offshore obligations.  

A weaker rupiah threatens the financial performance of local firms which have substantial dollar debt, which in turn could hurt the nation's economy. The Indonesian government and private companies have around $130 billion in foreign debt.  

The rupiah's fall has also prompted the central bank to consider rolling out newer, more sophisticated money market management tools, including a currency swap instrument, to reduce U.S.-dollar buying by state-owned companies, Bank Indonesia's Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom said. He didn't provide a timetable for such a move.  

Governor Burhanuddin indicated that the planned interest rate increase is justified to boost the value of the rupiah against the U.S. dollar.  

The central bank intervened by selling dollars Tuesday morning to stem the local currency's slide.  

"At a 9,600-level effective exchange rate, the rupiah is undervalued by 9% against the U.S. dollar," Burhanuddin said.  

He said the pending rate hike is part of a four-point central bank plan to stabilize the rupiah's value.  

That plan includes a temporary decrease in commercial banks' net open position to 20% of equity capital from 30%, effective immediately. title: =DJ  FX  Asia: Bk Indonesia Rate Hike Unlikely To Boost Rupiah
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column  

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia's plan to hike interest rates to support the tumbling value of the rupiah against the U.S. dollar will boost market sentiment but won't address the currency's core problem of rising oil prices, which are fueling massive dollar purchases by domestic state firms, analysts said.  

Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah Tuesday unveiled a rupiah defense plan that includes a pending increase in the benchmark Sertifikat Bank Indonesia, or SBI rate, of 15 to 20 basis points, the use of forward transactions to protect the currency and a move to 'monitor' state-owned Pertamina (PTM.YY)'s dollar purchases.  

That news and Bank Indonesia intervention helped spur a rebound in the rupiah's value with the U.S. dollar closing at IDR9,688 Tuesday, down from a-more-than three-year high of IDR9,810 earlier in the day and Monday's close of IDR9,750.  

The central bank's moves are welcome, but they won't put much of a dent in the voracious domestic appetite for dollars powered by high oil prices, said JP Morgan Chase Bank's Asian foreign exchange strategist, Claudio Piron.  

'The risk is we may see (the dollar) touch IDR10,000 by year's end,' Piron said. 'The central bank can watch Pertamina, but understand that Pertamina has a budgeted rate of $24 a barrel and outside that they have to go to the market to buy dollars (to purchase supply).'  

At 1025 GMT, the front-month June Brent contract on London's International Petroleum Exchange was down 41 cents at $53.99 a barrel in electronic trading, but above an intraday low of $53.88/bbl. Front month Nymex crude was trading 66 cents lower at $53.91/bbl.  

Piron said that Bank Indonesia had been 'resting on its laurels a bit' in responding to the recent rupiah decline, but that movements in the currency reflect a healthy managed currency and shouldn't be cause for market gloom.  

'Generally speaking, the currency is responding to the macroeconomic environment...but (Bank Indonesia) has to get (support measures) just right because sentiment is fragile and if they overstep they may panic the market,' he said.  

A weaker rupiah threatens the financial performance of local firms, which have substantial dollar debt, and could hurt Indonesia's most prolonged period of economic growth since the Asian financial crisis of 1997-98. Indonesia's government of President Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono has projected an average annual rise in gross domestic product of 6.6% from 2004 to 2009, outpacing 5.1% GDP growth last year.  

The rupiah's decline has also prompted the central bank to consider introducing a new generation of money market management tools, including a currency swap instrument, to reduce U.S.-dollar buying by state-owned firms. Bank Indonesia's Senior Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom told Dow Jones Newswires that the bank's board of governors would discuss the currency swap tool in a meeting Tuesday, without elaborating.  

Interest-Rate Rise May Not Help Rupiah Long Term  

The psychological impact of Bank Indonesia's moves to support the rupiah will likely help keep the U.S. dollar at IDR9,500 to IDR9,600 for the next few weeks, but projections beyond that period remain 'quite hazy,' said ABN Amro Bank Asian sovereign and foreign exchange strategist, Emmanuel Ng.  

Ng said that raising interest rates to absorb excess liquidity won't influence domestic companies' purchases of dollars to pay foreign currency debts.  

'I think the market will have a positive spin on (the rupiah support measures) because it shows that Bank Indonesia is being proactive,' he said.  

'But raising interest rates will only have transitory impact,' Ng said. Monitoring 'Pertamina and the use of forward transactions would have the most impact because those two measures would actually address the real dollar (transactions).'  

That view was echoed by Citibank economist Anton Gunawan, who said the current circumstances behind the decline in the rupiah mirrored those in May to July 2004.  

Bank Indonesia helped stem the rupiah's slide against the dollar at that time by trimming the estimated $30 million that Pertamina spends daily on oil supplies. It did that by limiting those purchases to state-owned bank transactions closely monitored by the central bank.  

Gunawan said the central bank's efforts to bolster the value of the rupiah against the dollar may get a boost from a massive U.S. currency injection from an unlikely source: U.S. cigarette manufacturer Philip Morris.  

Philip Morris, a unit of the world's biggest tobacco company Altria Group Inc. (MO), said last month that it will pay $2 billion to buy a 40% stake in Jakarta-listed PT Hanjaya Mandal Sampoerna (HMSP.SK) from a group of major shareholders. Sampoerna is Indonesia's third-largest cigarette maker by sales.  

Philip Morris will make a general offer for the rest of Sampoerna which, if fully accepted, will lift the value of the total acquisition to $5.2 billion, including around $160 million in debt.  

The rupiah may benefit from an influx of U.S. dollars timed to meet an end-May payment deadline for a portion of the Sampoerna acquisition, Gunawan said.  

'(Philip Morris) has already brought in about a billion, probably...and if they bring some more money in then the rupiah value can go to IDR9,400 to IDR9,500, he said.  

-By Phelim Kyne of Dow Jones Newswires' Jakarta Bureau; 62 21 3983 1277; phelim.kyne@dowjones.com

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Flat; Exporters Sell Dollars
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah closed steady Tuesday as exporters unloaded dollars, helping to offset demand from local importers, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,575, unchanged from its close Monday.  

Dealers said exporters sold the dollar to take advantage of its recent gains against the rupiah.  

"Exporters were probably happy with the rupiah's current levels to exchange their dollars to local money," a dealer with a foreign bank said.  

Importers - notably the oil company Pertamina - however, continued to collect greenbacks to settle their trade bills, dealers said.  

Bank Indonesia was not thought to have intervened in the market Tuesday, probably because the rupiah was stable.  

The nation's central bank has said recently it would unload the U.S. currency to reduce volatility in the foreign exchange market.  

The pressure on the rupiah also abated slightly as capital outflows from the Indonesian stock market seemed to stop, dealers said. The Jakarta Stock Exchange's main index rose 0.2% Tuesday, recovering from a 3.3% loss Monday.  

Dealers expect the dollar to trade between IDR9,550 and IDR9,590 Wednesday.

title: UPDATE 2-Indonesia raises key rate on inflation worries.
text:
JAKARTA, April 4 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank, worried by rising inflation, on Monday raised a key interest rate by a quarter percentage point and said it was ready to act again.  

Bank Indonesia increased its benchmark seven-day intervention rate to 7.25 percent on Monday, the first change since it was introduced in June 2004. The central bank previously used an overnight rate, which it stopped using in January.  

Jakarta stocks shrugged off the largely expected rate rise, with analysts seeing limited impact on corporate earnings, while the rupiah and local bonds continued their downtrends.  

"We are monitoring market conditions. We will again raise it if needed," central bank deputy governor Maulana Ibrahim told reporters at an economic seminar in the central Java town of Yogyakarta.  

Annual inflation climbed to 8.8 percent in March, the highest rate in more than two years, according to data on Friday. A sharp increase in fuel prices was the main culprit.  

The 7-day intervention rate, also known as the Fasbi, is used by the central bank to manage the amount of funds in the money market.  

Analysts said the rate rise was likely to be followed by bigger rate increases on benchmark one-month and three-month central bank paper (SBI), and they expected SBI rates to hover at around 8.0 to 8.5 percent at most by year end.  

The rate on one-month SBIs has crept higher at auctions to 7.44 percent in March from 7.40 percent in October. Three-month SBIs have held at around 7.3 percent since October.  

LIMITED IMPACT  

Monday's rate hike "is not going to hit corporate earnings. Debt-to-equity ratio of Indonesian corporates is quite low, they are not highly indebted," said a senior research analyst at a large foreign fund management firm in Jakarta.  

He said the debt ratio at some firms was around 30 percent following a restructuring drive after the Asian financial crisis of 1997/1998.  

Jakarta stocks did not seem too perturbed by the rate rise, ending 0.47 percent higher at 1,100.20 points on Monday.  

However, the rate rise did not support the rupiah much. It lost a quarter percent to 9,480 against the dollar. The rupiah is the second-worst-performing Asian currency this year after the yen, partly due to domestic inflationary pressures.  

Government bond prices weakened slightly, extending a recent downward trend, with the rate rise further dampening sentiment already hurt by the spike in inflation, analysts said.  

Total outstanding Fasbi facilities currently stand at 74 trillion rupiah ($7.8 billion), against a more normal figure of 5-10 trillion rupiah.  

The Fasbi amount has jumped sharply as investors took advantage of the facility last week when SBIs matured and there was no auction of new SBI paper, a central bank official said.  

But the amount will likely return to its normal level after an SBI auction on Wednesday, he said.  

Total outstanding SBIs, widely held by investors, particularly commercial banks, stand at around 57 trillion rupiah. ($1=9,480 rupiah).

text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended slightly higher Wednesday on profit-taking in the dollar following the recent rise in the U.S. unit and Bank Indonesia's suspected intervention, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR9,510, down from Tuesday's close of IDR9,525. The greenback touched an intraday high of IDR9,535.

Dealers expect the dollar could fall below IDR9,500 Thursday, but that will depend on the dollar's movement against its major rivals later Wednesday. The greenback could be anywhere between IDR9,470 and IDR9,525 Thursday, they said.

Abdullah reiterated the bank may raise interest rates by higher absorption of funds during its monetary operations including through the twice-monthly auction of the benchmark one-month and three-month central bank papers (SBIs).

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Lower As Local Cos Buy Back Dollar
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended lower Thursday as local corporates bought the U.S. dollar after its fall Wednesday, dealers said.  

The dollar finished at IDR9,270, up from its close Wednesday at IDR9,260. The U.S. unit hit an intraday low of IDR9,230.  

"There were fresh bids from local players to buy back the dollar at the 9,230 level," said a trader with a foreign bank.  

Traders say the overall mood was cautious with many holding back their orders to buy the U.S. unit amid worries that Bank Indonesia might intervene further in the market to defend the rupiah.  

Wednesday, traders suspected the central bank sold dollars to stop the U.S. currency from rising above IDR9,400, which would have been a six-month high.  

Analysts say Bank Indonesia needs to stop the rupiah from falling further to help curb imported inflation. If it does so, the central bank doesn't have to raise interest rates - which could hurt the economy.  

"The dollar regained ground due to healthy bids from local importers...," another trader with a state-owned bank said Thursday. Moreover, the central bank is suspected to have sold only modest amounts of the greenback Wednesday, the trader said.  

Demand for the dollar is usually robust toward the year-end as local companies repay maturing offshore debts. Local companies are saddled with around $60 billion in offshore borrowings.  

Dealers expect the U.S. currency to trade between IDR9,250 and IDR9,325 Friday.

title: INTERVIEW-Indonesia c.banker says Asian  FX  to adjust slowly.
text:
BERLIN, Nov 21 (Reuters) - A senior Indonesian central bank official said on Sunday a Group of 20 call for exchange rate flexibility would lead to higher Asian currencies, but the adjustment would be a slow one.  

Speaking to Reuters on the sidelines of a G20 meeting in Berlin, Halim Alamsyah, director of Economic Research and Monetary Policy at Bank Indonesia, also said Indonesia was happy with the current level of the rupiah while he warned the budget deficit target might not be achievable this year.  

G20 finance ministers and central bankers, closing a two-day summit, urged Asian economies to move towards "greater exchange rate flexibility".  

When asked whether flexibility in exchange rates would lead to higher exchange rates in Asian currencies, Alamsyah said "it's looking like that way. Large movements in major currencies will have a big impact on the Asian economies. I don't think the alignment of Asian currencies will be abrupt."  

"We don't want to see the dollar sliding too much, of course, but if the market mechanism is in place and if it is supported by the necessary adjustment within each country including the U.S., I think it will be okay," he said in an interview.  

The dollar hit a nine-year low against a basket of currencies last week, extending its recent sharp losses on concerns about the U.S. current account deficit.  

The G20 call on flexibility appeared to be a reference to China, which came under international pressure to revalue its pegged yuan higher to help correct global imbalances.  

"I think there was a general feeling in the meeting that the global imbalance is not only between China and the U.S. or between Europe and the U.S. But it is the general concern of G20 members and will be discussed at the next meeting," he said.  

"We have to rely on market mechanisms to remedy the global imbalances, but at the same time we are also looking to adopt a kind of self-initiative response - not only China but each relevant countries should make some adjustment."  

HAPPY WITH RUPIAH In the case of Indonesia, Alamsyah said possible depreciation of the rupiah - which is trading between 8,900 and 9,100 per dollar this month - could have a negative impact.  

"The depreciation of the rupiah and also in some Asian currencies will not have an expansionary impact on the economy. Instead, it may cause a contractionary impact," he said.  

He said Indonesia - which intervenes on a regular basis in the foreign exchange market - was comfortable with the current level of the rupiah.  

Alamsyah said: "We are not focusing on the foreign exchange rate at a certain level. We try to reduce volatility because it creates uncertainty. This approach is being carried out by many Asian countries."  

"The current level of the rupiah, around 9,000, is okay for the purpose of promoting exports and maintaining public expectations on inflation and also for exports and the sustainability of our fiscal situation. We are quite happy."  

He also warned the government's budget deficit target might not be achievable. Indonesia has a budget deficit aim this year of 1.3 percent to gross domestic product. But this could be in jeopardy because of lower government revenue.  

"It may increase a bit this year to 1.5 percent but next year there is general agreement within our government that it should be and can be reduced to one percent," he said.  

For economic growth, it has targets of five percent this year and 5.5 percent next year.  

"GDP targets are realistic and achievable of course. The most dynamic component of our economy is the investment ratio. The ratio this year will be around 20-21 percent and next year will be around 22-23 percent. That would be enough to drive the economy towards 5.5 percent (growth) next year," he said.  

"We have achieved macro economic stability with less inflation. Now we need investment from abroad as well as domestically... Seven percent annual growth is possible going forward if we increase the investment ratio to 27-28 percent within the next five years."

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Won weaker as oil stays firm, yen lifts others.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Sept 29 (Reuters) - The Korean won slipped in
offshore markets on Wednesday, catching up with the rest of the
region after high oil prices exerted downward pressure on Asian
stocks and currencies.
    The benchmark global oil price stayed around $50 a barrel,
just short of Tuesday's record high, but, despite the threat of
those high energy costs hurting growth and earnings in Asia,
the trend in regional currencies was mixed.
 
    The yen was off Tuesday's six-week lows and that helped the
Sing dollar and Thai baht post small gains.
    Some of the positions were driven by expectations ahead of
Japan's quarterly tankan corporate sentiment survey due on
Friday and a Group of Seven meeting that begins on Oct. 1.
    The yen has been sold recently because of worries that an
improvement in Japanese business sentiment might have stalled,
but it was bought back on Wednesday.
    The Indonesian rupiah was slightly higher at 9,205/9,210 a
dollar.
  


    But, when Taiwan's markets opened after Tuesday's holiday,
the Taiwan dollar fell to a one-month trough of 34.10 and
Taiwan stocks to a three-week low.
    Korean markets were closed for a third day for the full
  

moon festival and the won was unmoved in onshore trade.  

Offshore markets initially pushed it to 1,157 a dollar, its  

lowest in a month and down from Friday's levels around 1,149.  

It later rallied to 1,153.   


 
    "It's a holiday in Korea and the tendency of offshore
markets is to overshoot," said one Singapore-based trader.
    "The street is looking at 10.4 on yen-won and so they are
pushing the won lower."
    Markets believe the South Korean authorities are anxious to
maintain the won's competitiveness versus the yen in export
markets.
    This week, with Korean markets closed and the yen weakened,
  

the cross rate hit 10.28 won per yen, the won's highest against  

the yen since October 2003. That cross moved back to 10.4 on  

Wednesday.   


 
    Traders said the yen was probably heavily oversold and some
people were buying the won to bet on a yen rally.
    While high oil prices remained a concern, traders said
currencies in the region found some respite on Wednesday as oil
stabilised near its peaks.
    The baht trimmed some of its losses after falling on
  

Tuesday, when Thailand said it had its first known probable  

case of one human infecting another with bird flu. It hit a  

three-week low of 41.61 on Tuesday but was higher at 41.55 on  

Wednesday.   


 
    The Philippine peso came further off Tuesday's low of
56.45, closing at 56.315.
    It hit the record low of 56.45 for the third time since

central bank had sold dollars. The central bank denied  

intervening.  

In Indonesia, operators were divided between buying the  

rupiah to prepare for gains once Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono is  

officially sworn in as president and announces his cabinet and  

the likely impact on growth from Indonesia's position as a  

temporary oil importer.

title: =DJ  CENTRAL BANK  WATCH: Bank Indonesia Faces Policy Dilemma
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column  

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia is facing an interest rate dilemma.  

Rising global rates, growing inflationary pressure at home and the rupiah's 8% depreciation since the start of 2004 are adding to pressure for higher rates, economists said.  

But the central bank has so far resisted calls for a hike, arguing it needs to keep rates low to help the government achieve a 4.8% economic growth target this year.  

'A sharp rate hike will have a (negative) impact on the economy, including our stock market,' Bank Indonesia's deputy Governor Aslim Tadjuddin said defending the central banks stance. 'The current interest level is satisfactory. I don't see any urgency to raise it further.'  

The weighted average rate of the widely watched one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia or SBI note is currently at 7.39%. The Indonesian financial markets looks at the one-month SBI as the benchmark although Bank Indonesia's official policy rate is the overnight Fasilitas Bank Indonesia, or FASBI, now at 7%.  

Evidence is growing, however, that investors don't see it that way. Many economists think the rupiah could fall further this year as funds move their money out of Indonesian assets to take advantage of climbing rates elsewhere.  

The U.S. Federal Reserve is widely expected to increase its federal funds rate again next week, which is further pressuring Indonesia to act, economists said.  

'Bank Indonesia's current monetary policy is not sustainable,' said Sin Beng Ong, an economist with J.P. Morgan Chase Bank.  

The dollar could rise to 9,700 rupiah by the end of 2004, J.P. Morgan forecasts, up sharply from IDR9,115 in Thursday morning trading.  

Currency weakness would increase Indonesia's foreign debt load, and add to inflationary pressure which, although still manageable, has been growing this year.  

So why is the central bank so reluctant to act?  

Apart from the growth argument, many economists think that political pressures have something to do with it.  

Indonesians will vote Monday in the country's first ever direct presidential elections, and rate hikes never go down well in an election year.  

Rising unemployment and a stagnant business environment are major reasons voters appear to be turning their backs on President Megawati Sukarnoputri. The latest polls show her losing next week by a wide margin to retired general Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono.  

Will Have To Raise Rate Sooner Or Later  

The conclusion of the elections, which began with a first-round of voting in July, could help lift investor sentiment, some economists said.  

Election uncertainty has helped add to pressure on the rupiah, but this could lift next week, and take some pressure off the central bank in the short term.  

'Bank Indonesia can say that these are transitory factors, and there's no real need to shift monetary policy too much in this environment,' said Song Seng Wun, an economist with G.K. Goh in Singapore.  

Still, most economists say the central bank will sooner or later have to raise rates to keep pace with the global tightening cycle which is underway.  

The one-month SBI rate fell to an all-time low of 7.32% in May after more than two years of soft monetary policy. Rates climbed skyward after the 1997-98 Asian crisis to defend the rupiah, but began falling in 2002 once the currency and inflationary pressures were contained.  

Signs that inflation could be returning have pushed the central bank to allow rates to climb up moderately since the May low. The benchmark one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia note is now yielding 7.39% from 7.32% in May.  

But with consumer prices growing 6.7% in August and the government revising up its 2004 inflation target to 7% from 6.5%, economists said that such rate hikes won't likely be enough to keep the real interest rate attractive to investors and support the rupiah.  

Higher rates are also needed to absorb about IDR10-IDR20 trillion in excess liquidity which daily circulates through Indonesia's monetary system, adding to inflationary pressure. Bank lending to companies remains low, leaving spare cash sloshing around, and adding to speculative pressure on the rupiah.  

'If you look at the amount of the excess liquidity, the pressure to increase interest rates is strong enough,' said Juniman, an economist with PT Bank Internasional Indonesia. He expects the one-month SBI rate to rise to 7.5% by the end of the year.  

Armed with $34 billion in foreign exchange reserves, Bank Indonesia will likely prefer intervention in the foreign exchange market should the rupiah come under pressure again rather than raising interest rates sharply, Juniman added.  

Bank Indonesia's Aslim said the bank will continue to use non-interest rate methods to reduce speculation. These include a regulation implemented in July which forces commercial banks to place a larger amount of their spare cash on deposit with the central bank.
