Currency weakness would increase Indonesia's foreign debt load, and add to inflationary pressure which, although still manageable, has been growing this year.  

So why is the central bank so reluctant to act?  

Apart from the growth argument, many economists think that political pressures have something to do with it.  

Indonesians will vote Monday in the country's first ever direct presidential elections, and rate hikes never go down well in an election year.  

Rising unemployment and a stagnant business environment are major reasons voters appear to be turning their backs on President Megawati Sukarnoputri. The latest polls show her losing next week by a wide margin to retired general Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono.  


 
   Will Have To Raise Rate Sooner Or Later 
   

The conclusion of the elections, which began with a first-round of voting in July, could help lift investor sentiment, some economists said.  

Election uncertainty has helped add to pressure on the rupiah, but this could lift next week, and take some pressure off the central bank in the short term.  

"Bank Indonesia can say that these are transitory factors, and there's no real need to shift monetary policy too much in this environment," said Song Seng Wun, an economist with G.K. Goh in Singapore.  

Still, most economists say the central bank will sooner or later have to raise rates to keep pace with the global tightening cycle which is underway.  

The one-month SBI rate fell to an all-time low of 7.32% in May after more than two years of soft monetary policy. Rates climbed skyward after the 1997-98 Asian crisis to defend the rupiah, but began falling in 2002 once the currency and inflationary pressures were contained.  

Signs that inflation could be returning have pushed the central bank to allow rates to climb up moderately since the May low. The benchmark one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia note is now yielding 7.39% from 7.32% in May.  

But with consumer prices growing 6.7% in August and the government revising up its 2004 inflation target to 7% from 6.5%, economists said that such rate hikes won't likely be enough to keep the real interest rate attractive to investors and support the rupiah.  

Higher rates are also needed to absorb about IDR10-IDR20 trillion in excess liquidity which daily circulates through Indonesia's monetary system, adding to inflationary pressure. Bank lending to companies remains low, leaving spare cash sloshing around, and adding to speculative pressure on the rupiah.  

"If you look at the amount of the excess liquidity, the pressure to increase interest rates is strong enough," said Juniman, an economist with PT Bank Internasional Indonesia. He expects the one-month SBI rate to rise to 7.5% by the end of the year.  

Armed with $34 billion in foreign exchange reserves, Bank Indonesia will likely prefer intervention in the foreign exchange market should the rupiah come under pressure again rather than raising interest rates sharply, Juniman added.  

Bank Indonesia's Aslim said the bank will continue to use non-interest rate methods to reduce speculation. These include a regulation implemented in July which forces commercial banks to place a larger amount of their spare cash on deposit with the central bank.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends At 8-Wk Low On Corporate Dlr Demand
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah closed at an eight-week low Friday on rising dollar demand from local companies to pay offshore obligations at the end of the month.  

The dollar closed at 9,320 rupiah, up from its close of IDR9,290 Thursday and its highest closing level since June 30, when it ended at IDR9,395.  

A correction in the dollar against most Asian currencies, however, slowed down its rise versus the rupiah, dealers said.  

"Most offshore players sold the dollar on rises," said a dealer with a foreign bank.  

Dealers said there was no sign of Bank Indonesia's intervention in the market Friday to help the rupiah. The central bank was suspected of selling the greenback Thursday via state banks.  

Dealers expect the dollar to trade in a higher range Monday between IDR9,290 and IDR9,350 as more local companies are likely to buy dollars for month-end debt repayments.  

Dealers also expect local companies to accumulate dollars in the near term as the political temperature rises ahead of the presidential runoff Sept. 20.

title: UPDATE 1-Bank Indonesia says no plan to raise FASBI.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 19 (Reuters) - The Indonesian central bank has no plan in place to raise its money market intervention rate, known as FASBI, a senior bank official said on Thursday.   

When asked by reporters if the central bank plans to raise FASBI rates, Hartadi Sarwono, a deputy governor of the bank said: "up until now we don't have such a plan."   

Bank Indonesia has overnight and seven-day intervention instruments for the money market.   

Last month Aslim Tadjuddin, another deputy governor of the bank, told Reuters the market should refer to the FASBI rates as a signal of future rate direction.   

There has been speculation among market players the central bank would increase domestic interest rates due to higher inflationary pressure and a weakening rupiah currency.   

Indonesia's inflation in the year to July was 7.2 percent, exceeding the recently revised finance ministry forecast of seven percent as well as the government budget assumption of 6.5 percent.   

The rupiah currency has lost more than 10 percent of its value so far this year.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rate cut unsettles won.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Aug 12 (Reuters) - The South Korean won was
unsettled by a surprise rate cut from the Bank of Korea on
Thursday, which heightened worries about the economy while
boosting the domestic stock market.
 
    Other Asian currencies were moved little on Thursday,
mimicking a stable yen and euro.
    The won fell to 1,165 a dollar after the central bank
caught markets off guard by cutting the overnight call rate
target by 25 basis points to a record low of 3.5 percent.
    It rallied slowly back to early levels around 1,157, even
as markets debated the impact of the rate cut on the currency.
    The Bank of Korea said boosting domestic demand was a
priority and higher oil prices were hurting growth.
    "On first impulse, the market had to sell the won. This
seems to have signalled the economy is in bad shape," said one
currency strategist in Singapore.
    Still, strategists differed on whether South Korea would
  

simultaneously encourage won gains to ward off pressures on the  

trade account and inflation from higher oil prices, or whether  

the Bank of Korea (BOK) had signalled growth would take  

priority.   


 
    U.S. oil prices held near $45 a barrel, this week's record
highs, and Korea is the world's fourth-largest importer of oil.
    "The BOK seemed to admit that oil price rises were
  

disinflationary in the medium term. Later comments about export  

growth likely to slow down to single digits suggest that they  

are more worried about growth than inflation," Bhanu Baweja of  

UBS said.  

While the authorities would not allow the won to depreciate  

too much against the dollar, they would also probably prevent  

the won from gaining against the yen and Sing dollar, he said.   


 
    The yen-won cross was higher, with a yen yielding 10.47
won, against 10.35 on Tuesday.
    But Korean stocks rose 1.8 percent on Thursday, and have
  

been benefitting from heavy foreign portfolio investment flows  

this month. Analysts said that would prop up the won despite a  

shrinking yield.  

"Funds flows have been more dominated by portfolio  

investment in equity as opposed to carry trade," Sun-Bae Kim of  

Goldman Sachs wrote in a note.   


 
    "On balance, an easier monetary policy stance may well
prove won bullish by encouraging more equity portfolio inflow."
    REST OF ASIA
    Elsewhere, the U.S. dollar stabilised after Tuesday's rise
in U.S. rates, helping the yen recover some ground.
    The Singapore dollar was slightly higher and trading closer
to 1.71 per dollar, compared with the previous day's lows near
1.7170.
    The Taiwan dollar was a shade higher within its narrow
ranges just on the weaker side of 34 per dollar.
    The Thai baht was trading just shy of 41.57 per dollar, a
one-year low it struck in offshore deals.
    The Philippine peso rose to 55.58, its highest since June,
while the Indonesian rupiah failed to benefit from the yen's
rise and remained near the week's lows around 9,270 a dollar.
    The rupiah has been volatile this week amid suspicion Bank
  

Indonesia has been intervening in its defence. Traders say the  

approaching presidential election in September, declining real  

interest rates and the abundance of domestic cash are leading  

to outflows from Indonesia.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Small losses after U.S. rate rise.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, Aug 11 (Reuters) - Asian currencies suffered
modest losses on Wednesday after the United States raised
rates, although they lagged the yen and benefited from the
market's apparent unwillingness to buy the U.S. dollar
aggressively.
    Traders said recent weakness in U.S. economic data,
particularly jobs, continued to weigh on the dollar. Regionals
also found support in the view that Asian authorities would
defend their currencies to ease the pressure from oil prices.
    As expected, the U.S. Fed raised rates by 25 basis points
to 1.5 percent on Tuesday, following a similar quarter point
rise on June 30. The Fed said the economy had been hit by
higher energy costs but was poised for faster growth.
    Crude oil prices        hit fresh highs over $45 a barrel
on Tuesday, complicating the outlook for global growth and
currencies.
  


    "To the extent that global conditions for growth
deteriorate via higher oil prices, that should be bearish
dollar," said Ray Farris, markets strategist with CSFB in
Singapore.
    But higher oil prices would also be a negative factor for
the currencies of the heavy oil-importing Asian economies, the
only difference being that authorities in Asia often used
currencies as policy tools, he said.
    "Higher oil prices mean higher inflation in a region that
already has higher inflation, so it is difficult to allow
currencies to depreciate and import further inflation."
 
    The Japanese yen        fell more than 0.6 percent from
Tuesday's levels and was quoted near 111.30/40 a dollar.
    Barring the usually volatile Indonesian rupiah, most Asian
currencies had minimal losses.
    The rupiah        was back at Monday's one-month lows near
  

9,270 a dollar despite a suspicion the central bank had  

intervened to defend the currency on Tuesday and Bank  

Indonesia's stating it would keep domestic cash conditions  

tight.   


 
    The Thai baht        fell to 41.50, testing an 11-month low
hit late in July.
    The Singapore dollar        erased gains it made on Tuesday
on the back of unexpectedly strong GDP data. It fell over a
quarter of a percent to 1.7160/70 a dollar.
    The Korean won                   and Taiwan dollar
fell slightly, but found support in rallying stock markets and
the Fed's optimism on the economy.
    "If the global outlook for growth begins to deteriorate, it
will be unpalatable for Asia to appreciate currencies and it
will be unpalatable to increase interest rates," Farris said.
    That meant Asian currencies would not be allowed to
  

depreciate, nor would any appreciation that hurt export  

competitiveness be tolerated until the growth outlook improved,  

Farris said.  

BUY VOLATILITY  

Merrill Lynch strategist Vincent Low said in a note the  

stability in Asian currencies would not be sustained and  

markets should brace for volatility.  

"Either U.S. dollar-Asia eventually breaks lower as policy is  

tightened or breaks higher as investors take a view that policy  

is behind the curve and rising inflation translates to capital  

outflows and weakening currencies," Low said.  

There was the danger of emerging Asia mimicking the  

Japanese yen's moves against the U.S. dollar, and it was a  

mistake for non-Japan Asia to import the policy of the country  

with the lowest inflation, he said.  

With the risk of currencies moving out of their ranges and  

quite sharply in either direction, investors could hedge  

themselves by buying cheap volatility, he said. Implied  

volatility on one-year Korean won is around 7.5  

percent, the lowest since February 2003.  

"Owning volatility is one way to express this view without  

taking a directional bet on FX," Low said.

By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, July 29 (Reuters) - A suspicion that Asian
central banks, many of which are believed to have sold dollars
this week, were intervening in the markets on Thursday limited
losses in regional currencies despite a weaker Japanese yen.
    Most of the regionals fell in offshore deals after U.S.
economic optimism boosted the dollar and pushed the yen
to fresh six-week lows.
 
    Their recovery in early Asian trading suggested the central
banks were once again defending their currencies, dealers said.
    They said central banks in Taiwan, Singapore, India and
  

Indonesia appeared to have been intervening because local  

banks, which are thought to act on their behalf, had supplied  

dollars.

Singapore-based trader.
    The Singapore dollar        dropped to near 1.73 in

    The Taiwan dollar          hit a fresh eight-month low of

    The Thai baht        briefly touched a new low since August
2003 near 41.50 before paring losses.
    Traders said the upcoming Thai holiday on Monday was
  

causing markets to offload dollars, even though the Bank of  

Thailand's Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula showed no discomfort  

with a weaker currency in remarks made on Wednesday.   


 
    Pridiyathorn said the weak baht would not hurt the economy
and was on account of the U.S. dollar's broader gains.
    The Korean won                   found support at 1,170 in

    "It also stacks up well from a central bank policy

title: Asian central banks step in as  currencies  trip up.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, July 28 (Reuters) - Asian central banks appear
to be intervening in foreign exchange markets this week after a
three-month lull, but this time they have been buying their
currencies against a resurgent U.S. dollar, traders say.
    Central banks in India, Singapore, Taiwan, Thailand and
Indonesia are all suspected to have intervened as some of their
currencies hit lows for the year against the dollar this week.
    That represents a change in tack after the heavy
dollar-buying intervention they conducted through all of 2003
and the first few months of 2004, boosting their combined
foreign reserves to over $2 trillion.
 
    Traders cited dollar-selling intervention in India, where
the rupee hit a fresh one-year low of 46.35/40 on Wednesday.
    The Taiwan dollar has shed about 1.5 percent in less than
   

three weeks and on Wednesday hit 33.23, its lowest in eight   

months. Traders in Singapore said they had heard that the   

central bank offered U.S. dollars in onshore markets above   

34.20.   

Expectations of higher yields in a rebounding U.S. economy,   

weakness in technology stocks and diminishing interest in the   

once-popular Chinese yuan revaluation trade seemed to be   

driving foreign funds out of Asia, analysts said.   

But they felt that policy makers might be reacting too   

quickly, given they had been battling strength in their   

currencies for a couple of years, until April.    


 
    "Some of them are hypersensitive at this moment in time,"
said Claudio Piron, a strategist with Standard Chartered Bank.
    "And it seems to be a combination of where the currencies

are in historical terms, where they are in their trade-weighted   

baskets and also in terms of managing inflationary   

expectations."   

POLICY DILEMMA   

Piron said the Thai baht's two percent slide in two weeks   

had taken it to its lowest levels historically in   

trade-weighted terms. The baht hit 41.45, its weakest since   

August 2003, on Wednesday.   

Although Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula   

said the weak baht would not hurt the economy, traders   

suspected the authorities would sell dollars if there were   

further losses.   

Similarly, analysts said it was reasonable for the Monetary   

Authority of Singapore (MAS) to worry if the Sing dollar moved   

too far to the weaker side of the trade-weighted band it is   

managed in, particularly after the central bank announced in   

April it wanted to tighten policy by guiding the currency

higher.   

Local banks in Singapore were seen buying their currency

this week, spurring suspicion they were acting on behalf of the   

MAS.    


 
    South Korean markets have been baffled by conflicting
statements from policy makers.
    More than any country in the region, South Korea is faced
   

with the dilemma of whether to continue with a policy of   

boosting exports through a cheap currency, despite the risk of   

higher imported inflation from rising oil and commodity prices.   

"In Korea, they are getting a bit more sensitive in terms   

of price expectations and some of the inflationary pressure,"   

Piron said. "Some of the growth picture has started to fade,   

but they don't want price inflation to also deteriorate."   

Nonetheless, analysts said inflation was still benign in   

Asia and central banks might be acting to curb market   

volatility rather than signalling a shift in policy.

title: Emerging Asia  FX - Intervention  fears limit losses.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, July 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies fell on
Tuesday, some to new lows for the year, as foreign investors
kept up their liquidation of Asian assets though the fear of
intervention by local central banks lent some support.
    The Singapore dollar        fell as far as 1.7235 before
returning to the firmer side of 1.72 on heavy sales of U.S.
dollars by local banks that markets suspected were acting on
behalf of the Monetary Authority of Singapore.
    The Indonesian rupiah        hit a three-week low of 9,150
per dollar before rebounding as Bank Indonesia said it had not
intervened but would do so if the currency became too volatile.
 
    The Philippine peso        rose slightly from an early
level of 56.135, its lowest in a week.
    The U.S. dollar gave up some of the gains it made against
  

the yen and European majors as markets waited for U.S. GDP and  

consumer confidence data to confirm Federal Reserve Chairman  

Alan Greenspan's bullish testimony on the U.S. economy last  

week. That too provided the region some relief.  

"Inasmuch as Asian central banks are concerned about export  

competitiveness implied by softness in equities worldwide, they  

are unlikely to tolerate excessive currency weakness either,  

due to supply-side inflation pressures," Philip Wee, a  

strategist with DBS Bank, said in a note to clients.  

"We don't expect runaway depreciation in Asian currencies."  

Still, traders said the early losses showed foreigners were  

still pulling their money out of Asian stocks and  

currencies, partly because of rising yields in the United  

States and because of waning expectations of a revaluation of  

the tightly controlled Chinese yuan .  

The Taiwan dollar slipped to 34.16, a fresh low  

for 2004, and the Thai baht fell to 41.25 a dollar, its  

lowest since August 2003.  

Wee said the baht was the most vulnerable because Thailand  

ranked second in the region in its exposure to the risks of  

oil, the yen and stocks. The Taiwan dollar was sensitive to  

movements in its stock market, he said.  

Asian markets have also been pressured by the fall in the  

prices of U.S. technology stocks. The technology-packed Nasdaq  

Composite Index posted its lowest close since last  

October and the Philadelphia Stock Exchange's semiconductor  

index fell to an 11-month low on Monday.   


 
    UBS published data showing the Asia-Pacific region lost a
net $346 million of foreign money in the week to July 23.
    South Korea's stocks have declined 20 percent while

title: Indonesian Rupiah Ends Steady, Tracking USD/JPY Movement
text:

title: Indonesian Rupiah Ends Lower; Corp Dlr Demand Resurfaces
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended lower Thursday as local companies bought the dollar following its rise against the yen, dealers said.  

The dollar's rebound against the Japanese currency dashed hopes of a further dollar slide against the rupiah in the short run, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at 9,385 rupiah, up from its close at IDR9,285 Wednesday. The dollar rose to an intraday high of IDR9,420 after the dollar rebounded above Y110 in early Asian trading. But it failed to maintain the gain against the yen, and that also dragged it from its high against the rupiah.  

Local companies in the past three days were mostly absent from the market, waiting to buy the U.S. unit at lower levels to hedge foreign debt payments on concerns over political fighting ahead of next month's presidential election.  

Dealers said foreign players also bought back the dollar to cover their dollar-short positions.  

The central bank wasn't spotted in the market to help the rupiah Thursday, dealers said.  

"I didn't hear any talk of Bank Indonesia intervention," a dealer said.  

The central bank has been active recently in the market to defend the rupiah. But it said Wednesday that the rupiah's recent weakness to a 26-month low isn't yet expected to have significant negative impact on the economy.  

Some analysts said the rupiah weakness may help the country's struggling exports.  

Dealers said corporate dollar demand will continue to persist Friday, which will likely push the greenback as high as IDR9,425, with support predicted at IDR9,350.  

-By I Made Sentana, Dow Jones Newswires; 62-21 39831277; I-Made.Sentana@dowjones.com

title: Indonesian Rupiah Ends Up On Dlr Pft-Taking, Ctrl Bk Move
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah closed higher Monday as foreign market participants took profit against the dollar and Bank Indonesia allegedly intervened to help the local unit, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at 9,340 rupiah, down from its close Friday at IDR9,465.  

Dealers said foreign players took profit against the U.S. currency after its slide against the yen to around Y110 spurred dollar-selling across Asia.  

Taking advantage of the dollar profit-taking, Bank Indonesia allegedly sold the unit through state banks, dealers said.  

The nation's central bank has repeatedly said it would continue to intervene to help the rupiah, which last week fell to a 26-month low of IDR9,590 to the dollar.  

Ebbing demand from local companies also paved the way for the dollar's slide, dealers said. They added that the usual large dollar buyers, such as state-owned oil and gas company Pertamina, were not heard bidding for the U.S. currency Monday.  

Local companies were the main dollar buyers recently as they were hedging their offshore debts amid concerns of rising political tension ahead of the presidential election July 5.  

Choosing a president, in the country's first direct election for the post, could take up much of the rest of the year - creating a long period of uncertainty, dealers said.  

Dealers, however, said that ebbing dollar demand could be just because local companies are waiting to buy the dollar at lower levels.  

"Dollar demand from local companies may resurface near IDR9,300," a dealer with a foreign bank said.  

Dealers expect the dollar to trade between IDR9,310 and IDR9,360 Tuesday.  

-By I Made Sentana,Dow Jones Newswires; 6221-3983-1277; I-Made.Sentana@dowjones.com

title: Bk  Indonesia  Dep Gov: Still  Intervening  To Help Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia, the country's central bank, said Wednesday it was continuing to intervene to support the rupiah but ruled out hiking interest rates.  

The currency fell to a 26-month low in early trade against the U.S. dollar.  

"We will continue to be active in the market, and will intervene if it's necessary," Aslim Tadjuddin, a Bank Indonesia deputy governor, told Dow Jones Newswires. [ 02-06-04 0231GMT ]  

The central bank has been selling dollars over the past couple of weeks to slow the rupiah's decline, but to little avail. The currency has fallen 9% since the start of May, and is trading at IDR9,485 to the dollar early Wednesday, weaker than IDR9,380 at Tuesday's close.  

Investors are concerned over Indonesia's presidential elections July 5, which many believe could lead to a long period of political fighting. Campaigning for the elections began Tuesday, sparking a new round of dollar buying.  

"Of course elections are a factor," Aslim said.  

Fears of rising global interest rates, especially a U.S. rate hike, have also increased the risk of investing in emerging markets such as Indonesia, analysts say. Higher rates increase the cost of borrowing, and make emerging markets less attractive.  

Analysts say Bank Indonesia needs to increase interest rates to help support the rupiah, and nip growing inflationary pressure in the bud.  

But the central bank is concerned "increasing interest rates could hurt demand," Aslim said. Indonesia's annual 5% economic growth depends largely on consumer spending at a time when investment remains weak.  

Local companies have been buying dollars strongly amid concerns the U.S unit could fall further, making foreign debt and imports more costly.  

Foreign investors that poured money into Indonesian stocks and bonds last year have also been pulling out their money. Foreigners pulled out about IDR2 trillion from the government bond market in April and May, Aslim said.  

-By Dow Jones Newswires; 6221 3983 1277; tom.wright@dowjones.com  

-Edited by Brett Miller [ 02-06-04 0258GMT ]

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends At New 19-Mo Low On Corp Dlr Demand
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended at a fresh 19-month low Thursday as local companies continued to buy dollars on fears the local currency could fall further.  

The dollar ended at 9,290 rupiah, up from IDR9,275 at Wednesday's close, its highest finish since Oct. 14, 2002.  

The charts suggest the dollar is likely to climb over the coming weeks toward its October 2002 high of IDR9,425.  

Concerns the rupiah will fall further is pushing local companies to buy dollars now to make foreign debt repayments and fund import bills.  

Dollar-selling by state-owned banks Thursday did little to aid the rupiah, traders said. Indonesia's central bank has warned it will intervene but wasn't active Thursday, they added.  

Emerging markets everywhere are feeling the pinch as global capital flows head back to the U.S. in expectation of an imminent interest rate hike there.  

Indonesia is faring especially badly as political and economic concerns add to reasons for investors to shift their money elsewhere. The rupiah currency is trading at 19-month lows and has lost more value than other Asian currencies in recent weeks.  

The country's voters returned a fractured parliament last month, and political fighting looks set to continue as presidential elections begin in July.  

Growing concerns over anemic investment are also causing jitters that Indonesia's economic growth is trailing that of its Asian neighbors.  

The dollar is likely to test resistance at IDR9,310 Friday, traders said.  

-By Tom Wright, Dow Jones Newswires; 6221-3983-1277; tom.wright@dowjones.com

title: Bk  Indonesia  To Continue  Intervening  To Help Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia said Tuesday it will continue to sell dollars in the currency market to help the beleaguered rupiah.  

"We will continue to take necessary actions," Aslim Tadjuddin, a central bank deputy governor told Dow Jones Newswires. "If it's necessary, we will intervene in the market."  

He said the rupiah's recent fall is mainly due to expectations of a U.S. rate hike, which has spurred investors to move their funds to dollar assets.  

At 0252 GMT, the rupiah traded at IDR9,230 to the dollar, its lowest level since Nov. 4, 2002. This means the rupiah has lost 8.8% against the U.S. currency since the beginning of the year.  

Dealers said Bank Indonesia was suspected to have sold dollars early Tuesday to curb the U.S. unit's rise.  

The rupiah's weakness may fuel inflationary pressures in Indonesia as the country imports some food products. This could pressure the central bank to raise interest rates, some analysts said.  

But Aslim said he expects inflation to remain under control this year as he believes the large U.S. trade deficit would weaken the dollar in the near future. "The dollar's current strength won't last long," he said.  

He also said Bank Indonesia has no plans to raise interest rates. The benchmark weighted average rate of the central bank's one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia notes was unchanged at 7.32% in a biweekly auction last week.

title: Indonesian Rupiah Ends Sharply Lower As Yen Slumps Vs Dlr
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended sharply lower Monday as the dollar surged against the yen on expectations for an early interest rate hike in the U.S., dealers said.  

The dollar finished at 8,950 rupiah, its highest close since March 24. It ended at IDR8,735 Friday.  

Dealers said reports that Bank Indonesia would intervene in the market to help the rupiah failed to lift the local currency.  

Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Aslim Tadjudin warned Monday that the central bank may intervene in the currency market, if needed, to curb excessive volatility.  

"Bank Indonesia is ready to do something," he told reporters when asked if the central bank would intervene.  

Aslim attributed the rupiah's weakness partly to the dollar's gains versus other major currencies on expectations the U.S. economy is gathering pace.  

U.S. employment data issued Friday showed 288,000 jobs were created in April, outstripping market expectations for 150,000 new jobs. The stronger-than-expected data fueled expectations that Federal Reserve policy-makers will start raising rates early this summer.  

Dealers said a recent fall in the Indonesian equity market has also damped rupiah sentiment.  

On Monday, the Jakarta Stock Exchange's main index slipped 4.9% to 707.218 points, down for the eight consecutive session.  

Some analysts predicted the dollar may rise to around IDR9,000 on political concerns in the run-up to the presidential elections in July.  

Dealers said they expect the dollar to retain its upside bias against the rupiah Tuesday, and that it will likely continue to track its performance against the yen.

text:
JAKARTA, May 10 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank said on Monday it will supply more dollars into the foreign exchange market if necessary to help defend the rupiah, which lost around 1.5 percent during the day.   

When asked about the bank's response to the rupiah's sharp fall, central bank deputy governor Aslim Tadjuddin told reporters: "An exchange rate is a function of supply and demand."   

He said that there was a lack of dollar supply in the market. "Bank Indonesia must add (dollar supply) if needed. The role of the central bank is to increase supply in the market."

title: Bank Indonesia Says To Keep Rates Around Current Levels
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia said Friday that it will maintain interest rates around current levels to achieve an inflation target of between 5% and 6% this year.  

The weighted average of Bank Indonesia's 1-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia (SBI) notes fell to 7.32% in an auction Wednesday from 7.33% two weeks earlier, and the 3-month SBI rate dropped to 7.24% from 7.25%.  

The central bank said that although on-year inflation in April picked up to 5.92% from 5.11% in March, price increase this year are expected to remain within its target range.  

"In the next months, Bank Indonesia will maintain its cautious monetary policies in order to achieve its medium and long-term inflation target," the central bank said in a press release after a monthly board of governors' meeting late Thursday.  

It added that it will "closely watch" the possibility of an increase in the U.S. federal funds rate, which could put pressure on the rupiah.  

Meanwhile, to maintain rupiah stability, Bank Indonesia will continue intervention, and intensify monitoring of banks actively involved in the currency market.  

The rupiah has recently been under pressure due to the dollar's rise against the yen, and rising concerns over securities ahead of July presidential elections.  

It has traded at IDR8,720 to the dollar early Friday, or around 3.4% lower than its level at the end of last year at IDR8,420.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Steady On Alleged Bk Indonesia Move
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended steady Friday as alleged intervention by Bank Indonesia managed to curb the dollar's rise sparked by a sharp drop in the local stock market, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at IDR8,700, unchanged from its close Thursday, after trading between IDR8,680 and IDR8,710 intraday.  

Dealers said offshore investors bought dollars as they unloaded Indonesian stocks as part of a trend to exit regional capital markets on worries about the future of the Chinese economy.  

The local stock market dropped 2.3% to 783.413 points.  

Bank Indonesia is suspected to have sold dollars when the greenback was trading around IDR8,700.  

Bank Indonesia's Deputy Governor Aslim Tadjuddin said the central bank is always ready to intervene to help the rupiah if necessary. He, however, didn't specifically confirm that it sold dollars Friday.  

Aslim said the rupiah's recent slide is due to external factors, mainly the dollar's rise against the yen, and not due to domestic factors.  

Dealers said market participants also bought the U.S. currency due to the long weekend. The local currency market will be closed Monday because of a Muslim holiday. Market participants usually prefer to hold dollars during a long market closure.  

Dealers said the dollar-rupiah will track the dollar-yen movement when it resumes trading next week. They expect the dollar to trade between IDR8,675 and IDR8,725 Tuesday.

The dollar closed unchanged at IDR8,650. The U.S. currency touched an intraday high of IDR8,660 earlier in the day tracking the dollar's ascent to above Y109.  

But Bank Indonesia's intervention helped the rupiah recoup its losses.

Dealers said the market takes this level as a virtual trading band tolerated by the central bank.  

However, demand for the dollar remained robust as many local companies usually need the dollar by month-end to pay off maturing offshore debts.  

"Demand from local companies provided a strong support to the dollar near IDR8,650 today," a dealer said.  

Dealers said the dollar's strength and demand from local companies is expected to maintain an upward bias toward the greenback in the near term, although they expect Bank Indonesia to remain in the market.  

Dealers expect the dollar to trade between IDR8,630 and IDR8,670 Friday.  

The market is also warily watching political developments as some analysts said the retired Gen. Wiranto has a good chance of being elected president in the July poll.  

Indonesia could face international isolation if Wiranto wins as he was implicated in the killing of over 1,500 East Timorese when the former Portuguese colony chose to break away from Indonesia in 1999.

text:

The dollar closed at 8,590 rupiah, up from its close Friday at IDR8,560. The local foreign exchange market was closed Monday for a public holiday.  

No one was injured in the explosion, which came days after Washington warned Islamic militants may be planning fresh attacks in the world's most populous Muslim nation.  

Police said the explosion was an accident that occurred when eight men and a woman were learning to make bomb.  

Still, dealers said the incident could signal an increased likelihood of terrorist attacks in the run-up to parliamentary elections early next month.  

Dollar demand from local companies to pay maturing offshore debts also pushed the U.S. unit higher. Dealers said Bank Mandiri and Bank Internasional Indonesia were among the most active dollar buyers, likely for the purpose of rolling over their dollar-denominated bonds maturing later this month.  

Dealers expect the dollar to test higher ranges Wednesday as local companies are expected to continue buying the currency. But fear of central bank intervention is expected to cap the dollar's rise at IDR8,600, they said.  

Bank Indonesia has said it will intervene in the market, selling dollars to prevent the local unit from falling sharply.

title: Jakarta stocks may rise on speaker court ruling.
text:
JAKARTA, Feb 13 (Reuters) - Indonesian shares may rise on Friday after a ruling was issued in a high-profile graft case, ending uncertainty, and as fears over possible wide-spread unrest from the issue appeared unjustified.   

"We see the market testing 772 levels today. Yesterday the markets were hesitant while waiting for the Supreme Court ruling. Now I think the market could be positive," said Fitri Murniawati, an analyst at BNI Securities.   

After the market closed on Thursday the Supreme Court overturned a graft conviction of parliament speaker Akbar Tandjung, keeping him in place as a political powerhouse and potential presidential candidate.   

Analysts had said investors were concerned protesters outside the court building would spark wide-scale violence following the ruling, but that failed to materialise.   

Another supporting factor for the market would be cuts in Indonesia's interest rates this week.   

Bank Indonesia reduced its overnight intervention rate on Thursday by 25 basis points to 7.50 percent after the benchmark rate, the central bank's one month certificate, fell by 11 basis points to 7.66 percent at Wednesday's auction.   

"The market had not priced in the interest rate decline, I think that factor could come into play today," Murniawati added.   

Several analysts said the cut would have a positive impact on banking shares.   

Shares of PT Indonesian Satellite Corp Tbk (ISAT.JK), the country's second largest telecommunication firm, may extend gains this session as analysts said the fair valuation of the stock was around 20,000 rupiah ($2.38) each, following various positive news items on the company.   

Indosat has posted a gain of almost 20 percent since announcing its plan for a stock split at a ratio of one to five earlier this month. But some dealers said investors might be tempted to lock in their gains.   

MARKET LEVELS   

The Jakarta Composite Index finished down 0.48 percent at 766.083 points on Thursday.   

In New York, markets were down with the Dow Jones Industrial Average off 0.41 percent to 10,694.07 points and the Nasdaq Composite falling 0.77 percent to 2,073.61 points.   

The rupiah currency was being quoted at 8,415/8,420 to the dollar early on Friday, slightly lower than late Thursday's level.

title: Jakarta stocks may rise on rate cuts, bank shares.
text:
JAKARTA, Feb 12 (Reuters) - Jakarta stocks may trade higher on Thursday following a series of cuts in the country's interest rates, which some analysts said could positively affect the banking sector.    

Gains in the Tokyo market and some other bourses in the region could also help sentiment.    

"The banking sector will be positive today, although the increase would not be solely due to the rate cuts, but also because of the divestment news," said Arwani Pranadjaya, technical analysts at Mandiri Sekuritas.    

Indonesia's central bank has cut its rupiah overnight intervention rate, also known as FASBI, to 7.50 percent from 7.75 percent after a steeper-than-expected decrease on the rate of the central bank's one-month certificate to 7.66 percent a day earlier.    

An Indonesian parliamentary commission agreed on Wednesday to the sale of a 71 percent stake of mid-size PT Bank Permata Tbk (BNLI.JK), valued around $730 million, and minority holdings in four other banks.    

Permata shares rose 12.5 percent following the news but Pranadjaya doubted the share could book further gains in the short run.    

The share price of PT Bank Danamon Tbk (BDMN.JK), the country's fifth largest, are expected to rise as the bank plans to announce what are expected to be good 2003 financial results later this month.    

A Reuters estimate produced an average of around 1.3 trillion rupiah ($159 million) for the bank's net profit, or some 41 percent higher than the previous year's figure.    

MARKET LEVELS    

The Jakarta Composite Index ended 0.39 percent higher at 769.793 points on Wednesday.    

In New York, markets ended higher with the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumping 1.17 percent to 10,737.7 points and the Nasdaq Composite edged up 0.69 percent to 2,089.66 points.    

The rupiah currency was being quoted at 8,402/8,407 to the dollar, stronger than late Wednesday's value.

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia c.bank cuts rph overnight rate by 25 bps.
text:
JAKARTA, Feb 12 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank has cut its rupiah overnight intervention rate, also known as FASBI, to 7.50 percent from 7.75 percent with immediate effect, a central bank official said on Thursday.   

Under the central bank's rule the new rate would be applicable to the morning session while the afternoon session rate would be 3.75 percent from 3.875 percent previously.   

The cut came after a steeper-than-expected decrease in the interest rate on the central bank's one-month certificate (SBI), which fell by 11 basis points to 7.66 percent on Wednesday, amid expectations of a decline in the FASBI rate.   

Some money market dealers had expected Bank Indonesia to cut the overnight rate by 25 basis points, amid benign inflation, a steady rupiah currency and a lot of extra cash in the money market.

title: Indonesian Rupiah Ends Lower On Dlr Demand From Importers
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended lower Thursday as local importers bought the dollar to finance extra food imports ahead of a national holiday, dealers said.  

The dollar closed at 8,525 rupiah, up from its close at IDR8,480 Wednesday.  

Dealers said the state-owned food logistic company, Bulog, was suspected as the main dollar buyer Thursday, most likely to fund increased food imports ahead of a Muslim holiday later this month.  

Dollar demand from importers sparked some banks to cover their dollar-short positions, thereby pushing the dollar higher, a move that was exaggerated by thin volume, dealers said.  

"Other players jumped into the market, cutting their dollar-short positions at losses after they saw the dollar rise above IDR8,500," said a dealer with a European bank in Jakarta. "This further pushed the dollar even higher."  

Dealers expect the dollar to maintain its strength Friday, likely rising to IDR8,550 as market participants are expected to continue covering their dollar-short positions.  

Still, they don't rule out the possibility of the U.S. currency gaining toward IDR8,600 if the central bank fails to intervene in the market.  

Bank Indonesia, the nation's central bank, usually sells the dollar in the spot market to defend the local unit.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Down Late; Peso At 2-Mo Low
text:
MANILA (Dow Jones)--The Philippine peso ended at a two-month low on continued security and political concerns Friday, while other Asian currencies were also mostly weaker against the dollar.  

Short-dollar covering following a recent sell-off, and importer demand drove dealings across the region, but trading was muted by holidays in Asia, including Singapore and Malaysia.  

The dollar ended at 55.330 pesos, its highest level since closing at PHP55.450 on Aug. 26, and was up from PHP55.240 Thursday. Volume declined to $145.2 million from $236.5 million Thursday.  

Central bank deputy governor Amando Tetangco said the dollar's recent rally is partly due to corporate demand, particularly from firms covering their month-end debt payments and import requirements.  

"The political noise isn't helping. It has been a cautious market," said Tetangco, who noted that banks were also buying dollars ahead of the May 2004 presidential elections. There are concerns of political and security instability in the months leading to the polls.  

There have been renewed security concerns following reports that 30 members of the terror Jemaah Islamiyah group remain in the country.  

Senior Philippine officials have been trying to calm the markets, and central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura added his voice Friday, saying the peso should recover from its recent weakness toward the year end when remittances from overseas Filipino workers during Christmas should help support the local currency.  

He also warned that "we are closely watching the market. If we need to go in, we will, but so far there's no need to do that."  

However, traders believe the central bank could still sell dollars. "It all depends on how you define intervention," said a Manila trader. "There's nothing that stops the central bank from influencing the exchange rate," he added.  


 
   Bank Indonesia Said Didn't Intervene To Help Rupiah 
   

Indonesia's central bank also said Friday it won't intervene to support the rupiah, which has weakened due mainly to dollar demand from corporates for month-end debt repayments.  

"The rupiah still trades within a fair range," Anwar Nasution, a central bank deputy governor, told reporters.  

The dollar ended at 8,490 rupiah, higher than IDR8,475 Thursday.  

Apart from growing demand from local corporates, recent losses in the local equity market also pressured the rupiah.  

"Some foreign investors sold shares and bought dollars," said a Jakarta trader.  

The Korean won, meanwhile, fell over the day with market participants suspecting the government hand in the decline, weakening the won to boost exports and support the flagging economy.  

But South Korean Minister of Finance and Economy Kim Jin-Pyo stressed Friday that government interventions in the foreign exchange market have been aimed only at preventing speculation.  

The market shrugged off Kim Jin-Pyo's comments Friday, noting they were somewhat contradictory to earlier remarks that the government will continue to sell won as needed to prevent undue gains, traders said.  

The dollar climbed to 1,186.8 won before settling at KRW1,185.7 won, preferring to track the gains in non-deliverable forwards and its advance against the yen. The U.S. unit closed at KRW1,184.4 Thursday.  

Elsewhere, the New Taiwan dollar was weaker on importers' requirements, with interbank players mostly quiet, keeping trades relatively light. The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.020, up from NT$33.975 a day earlier.  

Bucking the regional trend was the Thai baht, which gained some ground Friday after a local holiday Thursday. The dollar was trading at 39.815 baht against Wednesday's close of THB39.97. Dollar demand from importers though limited the local unit's gains.  

The Bank of Thailand Friday said that recent limits imposed on outstanding balances of nonresident accounts with local financial institutions to curb speculation in the foreign exchange market had been effective.  

The dollar has hovered around THB40 in recent days, recovering from a 40-month low of THB38.95 early October on account of the central bank's measures.  

The Singapore dollar also strengthened in offshore trading, with onshore markets closed for a public holiday. The U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7414 in late Asian trading, compared with S$1.7418 a day earlier.

title: UPDATE 1- Indonesia  c.bank to  intervene  if rupiah weakens more.
text:
JAKARTA, Oct 14 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank said on Tuesday it will intervene in the market if the rupiah currency continues to weaken.   

"Today the rupiah got weaker by 0.83 percent... If this continues, we will intervene only to smooth it out, to prevent a sharp fluctuation," Central Bank Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah told Reuters by telephone.   

Abdullah also said that Bank Indonesia did not have a target for the rupiah exchange rate but would help it find a "comfortable" level so export and import activity would be uninterrupted.   

He said Bank Indonesia needed to slow down the decline in the key interest rate on its one-month debt papers.   

"From the central bank's board of governors meeting today, we believe that there is no change in our policy stance. We have to be more cautious on the declining trend of the SBI. It seems slowing down the SBI rate decline is a must," he said.   

The one-month central bank certificate (SBI) has declined by 440 basis points so far this year.   

Benign inflation and a relatively stronger and stable rupiah this year had helped the central bank to maintain its policy of lowering interest rates.   

On the overnight rate, known as FASBI, Abdullah said that the bank would keep its options open, adding that it was just one instrument to control liquidity in the market without increasing the burden of both commercial banks and the central bank.   

Currently the FASBI stands at 8.5 percent for the morning session.   

The rupiah currency was at 8,435/8,445 to the dollar at 1253 GMT.

title: Indonesian Rupiah Ends Higher With Region, S&P Upgrade
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah ended stronger Wednesday in line with other Asian currencies and after Standard & Poor's upgraded the country's sovereign rating by one notch.  

The dollar ended Asian trading at 8,365 rupiah, down from IDR8,395 at Tuesday's close.  

The yen's strength against the dollar lent a positive tone to trading in other Asian currencies Wednesday, and this filtered through to the rupiah, dealers said. Despite heavy dollar buying by Asian central banks, aimed at limiting gains in their currencies, most Asian units ended higher.  

Traders said Indonesia's central bank didn't intervene as the government has said it's happy with a dollar trading range of between IDR8,200 and IDR8,700. If the dollar falls through the support at the lower end of this range, however, they expect the central bank to sell rupiah to maintain the country's export competitiveness.  

S&P's move Wednesday to raise Indonesia's foreign-currency rating to B from B-minus also helped boost the rupiah, traders said. It was the ratings agency's second upgrade for Indonesia this year, and shows growing confidence in the country's ability to continue managing its finances prudently without the International Monetary Fund next year, analysts said.  

Dealers expect the U.S. unit to trade between IDR8,300 and IDR8,400 Thursday.  

Expected capital inflows to purchase state-owned assets are also underpinning the rupiah.  

Next week, the government will launch an international roadshow to promote its upcoming initial public offering of a 30% stake in state-owned PT Bank Rakyat Indonesia. Pre-marketing for the issue has shown strong foreign demand for the IPO, the underwriters say.  

The Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency is also planning to sell a majority stake in PT Bank Internasional Indonesia later this year. But IBRA said late Tuesday it was willing to cancel the sale of PT Bank Lippo, which is also on the auction block, because so far no credible bidder had shown interest in the sale.  

-By Tom Wright, Dow Jones Newswires; 6221 3983 1277; tom.wright@dowjones.com

title: Bk Indonesia: Rupiah Comfort Zone IDR8,200-IDR8,700/Dlr
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's central bank will be happy to see the dollar trading between IDR8,200 and IDR8,700 for the rest of the year, its Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah said Thursday.  

"The rupiah comfort zone is between IDR8,200 and IDR8,700," Burhanuddin told reporters. "Bank Indonesia won't take any action if the rupiah fluctuates within the range."  

This is the first time in recent months when officials from the nation's central bank have mentioned a desirable trading level for the local unit  

The dollar was trading at IDR8,365 at 0710 GMT, down from its close Wednesday at IDR8,385.  

Bank Indonesia floated the rupiah in late 1997 as the Asian financial crisis hit Indonesia, but it does intervene in the spot market to defend the currency as and when it feels necessary.  

Bank Indonesia's Burhanuddin said he expects the benchmark weighted-average rate on the Sertifikat Bank Indonesia notes, or SBI, to be between 8.5% and 9% by the end of the year, compared with 8.59% now.  

His forecast is in line with most economists' forecasts amid the softer inflation outlook this year.  

Some economists even expect the SBI rate to fall to 8% on the assumption inflation will fall to 6% in 2003 from above 10% last year.  

On-year inflation fell to 6.2% in September from 6.38% in August.  

Another highlight for the economy is that Moody's Investors Service Tuesday upgraded Indonesia's sovereign rating by one notch to B2, saying falling public debt, and rising foreign reserves, mean the country is unlikely to default on its foreign borrowings.

title: UPDATE 1-Bank  Indonesia  says no rph  intervention  right now.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 29 (Reuters) - Bank Indonesia said on Friday it would not intervene in the foreign exchange market right now to prop up the rupiah, under selling pressure over the past few days, saying the currency remains largely stable. 

 When asked by reporters whether the central bank would intervene right now, central bank deputy governor Aslim Tadjuddin said: "There is no need to do so. It is still stable. There is no such need." 

 His comments came as the rupiah  on Friday continued to be pressured by month-end imports and market expectations falling interest rates may erode its attractiveness to investors. 

 The rupiah was quoted at around 8,550 against the dollar in afternoon trade on Friday, down from some 8,505 in late trade the previous day. 

 Despite falls in recent days, the rupiah remained among the best performing currencies in the region, gaining some 4.7 percent against the dollar so far this year. 

 The central bank cut its overnight rupiah intervention rate (FASBI), a key policy tool, by 50 basis points to 8.5 percent on Friday, the seventh time since May. 

 The FASBI has been cut seven times since the beginning of May, reducing the rate by a total of 275 basis points. The latest cut comes after the country's benchmark rate (SBI) fell below the intervention rate earlier this month.

title: Indonesia  Rupiah Ends Up As Ctrl Bk Warns Of  Intervention
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah rebounded against the dollar in volatile trading Wednesday after the central bank warned it would intervene to defend the local currency, if necessary, amid continued concerns stemming from Tuesday's bomb blast in Jakarta. 

 The dollar ended at 8,600 rupiah, down from its previous close of IDR8,665 but still above Monday's closing level of IDR8,490. 

 The dollar shot up to an intraday high of IDR8,710 in thin trading early in the session on follow-through buying from Tuesday. 

 But the dollar came off its intraday high, falling to an intraday low of IDR8,550 before the lunch break after Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Aslim Tajudin said the central bank is committed to guarding the rupiah and expects the local unit to recover soon. 

 Dealers, however, said Bank Indonesia didn't appear to be selling dollars. 

 Elsewhere, the Indonesian stocks rebounded 1.2% to 494.436 points on bargain hunting in blue chip shares after falling 3% Tuesday. 

 Some analysts said that the blast outside the Jakarta Marriott Hotel, which killed at least 10 people and injured around 150 others, will damp confidence in the Indonesian economy, at least in the short term. 

 The slump in direct foreign investment, which started during the 1997-98 Asian financial crisis, will remain protracted because of the latest bombing, said Anton Gunawan, a Jakarta-based economist with Citigroup. 

 Dealers said sentiment on the rupiah remains bearish as the latest blast shows the difficulties President Megawati Sukarnoputri's government is facing in its efforts to fight terrorism. 

 Dealers said that the market remains jittery as the first verdict on a key suspect involved in the Bali bombing will be delivered Thursday. 

 The police have said there are similarities between the Bali bombing and Tuesday's attack, although it hasn't been confirmed that both attacks were carried out by the Jemaah Islamiyah terrorist group. 

 The rupiah is expected to remain volatile Thursday with the dollar expected to trade between IDR8,550 and IDR8,700, traders said.

title: Bk  Indonesia  Deputy Gov: To  Intervene  To Guard Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's central bank said Wednesday it will intervene to support the rupiah after a bomb killed at least 14 people in a downtown Jakarta hotel. 

 The bomb blast Tuesday sent the rupiah and stocks tumbling on fears that Islamic militant groups are stepping up attacks on President Megawati Sukarnoputri's government. 

 "Bank Indonesia is committed to defend the rupiah. We will intervene if necessary," Aslim Tajudin, a deputy governor, told Dow Jones Newswires. He added the rupiah should recover soon. 

 At 0220 GMT, the dollar was at 8,665 rupiah, up from IDR8,480 before the bomb. 

 Indonesia has foreign reserves of more than $33 billion, meaning it can easily move the currency, which isn't widely traded by foreign investors. 

 But the rupiah is likely to remain under pressure in the short term as players fear further terrorist attacks ahead of the verdict in the trial of a key suspect in last year's Bali bombing, which killed more than 200 mainly Western tourists. The court will hand down its verdict Thursday on Amrozi bin Nurhasyim, a ringleader of the attack who faces the death penalty.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rupiah, Sing hit by blast - Seoul buys won.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Aug 5 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah fell
nearly two percent on Tuesday to a one-week low, rocked by the
bombing of the Marriott Hotel in central Jakarta, which also
triggered knee-jerk selling of the Singapore dollar.
 
    Meanwhile, U.S. dollar purchases by authorities in South
Korean pulled the won to a one-month low.
    The rupiah slipped to 8,650 per dollar, from late Monday's
8,490, in response to the blast which killed six people and
wounded dozens.
    Dealers said initial response was muted as the incident


 happened during the local market's lunch break. Later, local 

 brokers quoted the rupiah in a wide 8,560/8670 range, 

 indicating few people were willing to trade. 

 A dealer at a foreign bank in Jakarta said most players 

 were still reluctant to aggressively sell the rupiah fearing 

 that might provoke an aggressive central bank response. 


 
    "There was some speculation of central bank bids so the
market is very cautious," one dealer said.
    The rupiah had hit a three-month low of 8,725 last month,
as mainly foreign players unwound long rupiah carry trades.
That provoked heavy intervention by the Bank Indonesia.
    Bhanu Baweja, UBS currency strategist in Singapore, said



the risks of investing in Indonesia were well known, and so



markets were not likely to be too unsettled for an extended



period.



 
    "Most of the people who are in Indonesia really do know the
security risk that goes along with investing in this place."
    The rupiah's fall accentuated losses in the Singapore
dollar , and pulled it to a three-month low of 1.7661 per
dollar.
    It was quickly pushed back to levels on the stronger side



of the technically crucial 1.7650, a level the market had



breached but failed to close above on June 30, July 18 and last



Friday.



 
    The downside was limited by data showing an expansion in
the manufacturing sector for the second straight month in July.
    WON HITS 1-MONTH LOWS
    The South Korean won                  was sold down to



1,189.0 per U.S. dollar, its weakest since July 2, after



dealers said they spotted dollar purchases from the finance



ministry apparently aimed at soaking up equity-related dollar



inflows.



James Malcolm, currency strategist at JP Morgan Chase in



Singapore, said South Korean authorities had been buying



dollars since Friday and that given the yen's weakness on



Tuesday those purchases might have picked up.



Despite the won's losses, it stayed on the strong side of



10 on the yen-won cross , where it has been since



mid-July.



"We are still in an environment where central banks in Asia



are reluctant to see their currencies appreciate," Malcolm



said.



 
    An over three percent rise in Taiwan's foreign exchange
reserves to $182 billion backed those views.
    Dealers in Singapore said the central bank has absorbed



most foreign inflows to keep the Taiwan dollar  locked



in a narrow 34.30-34.50 per U.S. dollar range since it hit a



10-month high of 34.25 in July.



The Philippine peso  kept in sight of Monday's local



close of 54.80, amid speculation the central bank has raised



its monitoring of dollar purchases by banks.



 
    The peso fell to four-month lows just shy of the 55 per
dollar level last week after a failed mutiny on July 27.

title: Indonesian stocks, rupiah dive after Jakarta blast.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 5 (Reuters) - Indonesian share prices and the rupiah currency plunged on Tuesday after a huge explosion in a luxury hotel in Jakarta's business district that killed at least eight people. 

 The main stock market index fell almost five percent to its lowest since May 27 after the explosion in the basement of the Marriott Hotel reinforced worries about the law and order situation in the world's most populous Muslim nation. The market later recovered some of the losses. 

 No one has claimed responsibility for the blast, which wounded at least 83 people seriously. 

 "Stocks fell because of the explosion. I heard it is very damaging. It raises fresh concerns over the security condition," said a local dealer. 

 At 0800 GMT, the index was down 2.74 percent. 

 The rupiah also weakened, with quotes down around two percent on the day to 8,670 per dollar - although the fall was limited by the likelihood of central bank intervention. 

 "Major banks are not moving as they fear the central bank may soon come in," one currency dealer in Jakarta said. 

 The rupiah avoided a three month low of 8,725 per dollar hit in late July, and still remains the strongest Asian currency against the U.S. dollar this year. 

 The blast coincided with high-profile trials in Indonesia of suspected Islamic militants on bomb-related charges - including influential Muslim cleric Abu Bakar Bashir, accused of leading the Jemmah Islamiah group which has been blamed for a series of attacks on Western targets in the country. 

 A court in Bali was expected to deliver its first verdict on Thursday in the trials of those charged with planting a bomb that killed over 200 people on the resort island in October last year. 

 Bhanu Baweja, UBS currency strategist in Singapore, said the risks of investing in Indonesia were well known, and so markets were not likely to be too unsettled for an extended period. 

 "Most of the people who are in Indonesia really do know the security risk that goes along with investing in this place," he said. 

 "I think security risk is probably on the rise slightly, but you haven't seen the international investor come into Indonesia in a very big way in any case." 

 When the rupiah slumped in July as investors switched out of Indonesia's high-yielding debt and into equity markets elsewhere, the losses were stemmed by Bank Indonesia intervention. 

 Last week, central bank governor Burhanuddin Abdullah told Reuters he expected the rupiah to trade between 8,200 and 8,600 per dollar for the rest of the year. 

 Asked about the amount of foreign funds flowing into Indonesia, he said: "In the past two months around $4 billion came in - around $2 billion in the form of FDI, around $1 billion into the stock market or portfolio investment and $1 billion in the money market, i.e. hot money."

title: Rupiah quoted 2 pct lower at 8,670/dlr after blast.

SINGAPORE, Aug 5 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah  was quoted down two percent at 8,670 per U.S. dollar on Tuesday after an explosion at the Marriott Hotel in central Jakarta that police said had killed five people and seriously wounded five. 

 Initial reaction to the unexplained blast was muted because it happened during the local market's lunch break, with the rupiah easing to around 8,510 from 8,490 per dollar. Quotes on the rupiah were lowered as the local market reopened. 

 "The market has opened and brokers are quoting rupiah at 8,570/8,670," said a dealer at a European bank in Jakarta. 

 Another dealer at a foreign bank said there were few takers in the market of the offered rates as players are reluctant to aggressively sell the rupiah fearing that might provoke an equally aggressive central bank response.

    The peso touched 54.60 per dollar minutes after the open of
local trade, having closed at 54.01 on Friday.
    It pared its losses to around 54.25, a move dealers said



was prompted by the fear of central bank intervention, but



further weakness was expected as investors reassessed their

    "People would want to see where central bank draws the line
in the sand," said a dealer at a local bank in Manila.
    Rovic De Guzman, head of trading at the Union Bank of the
Philippines in Manila, said the 54.60 level might hold for some
time, but the future direction for peso was down.
    "There was no bloodshed in the incident so it will help,
but the fact that it happened will have its impact on
investors."
    On the weekend, hundreds of soldiers took over and wired a



premier shopping and apartment complex in Manila with



explosives, accusing the government of corruption and collusion



with Muslim rebels. They surrendered on Sunday after hours of



negotiations.



Dealers said people were waiting to see what President



Gloria Macapagal Arroyo had to say in an address to the nation



due later in the afternoon.



Rating agency Standard & Poor's said on Monday it was



sticking to its BB-rating and stable outlook for the



Philippines.



"Judging by the public information the political issues are



relatively minor in the medium to long-term," Takahira Ogawa,



S&P's director for Asia-Pacific sovereign ratings, told



Reuters.



YEN HELPS



Elsewhere, a steadier yen  and month-end settlement



of export deals helped other Asian currencies retain a firm



bias.



The Singapore dollar  rose to 1.7460 per U.S. dollar



ahead of June manufacturing data at 0500 GMT. The data is



expected to show a pick-up from May when SARS hit ouput.



The Thai baht  rose to 41.88 per dollar, from late



Friday's 41.96, with dollar sales by exporters adding distance



to one-month lows on the weaker side of 42 hit last week after



the central bank relaxed some foreign exchange controls.



The Indonesian rupiah  was also recovering from



three-month lows it had hit last week, mainly prompted by



unwinding of carry trades.



 
    The rupiah rose to around 8,490 per dollar, from Thursday's
three-month low of 8,725.

a floor under the currency has prompted players to trim long
dollar positions, although market sentiment was still fragile.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rupiah falls sharply to 11-week low.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, July 23 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah lost
almost two percent on Wednesday as it fell to 11-week lows,
with suspected central bank intervention unable to counter the
pressure from foreign investors withdrawing their funds.
    The mood was apprehensive even in the rest of Asia as
traders watched funds move out of high-yielding currencies into
growth plays, as a result of which the currencies of leveraged
economies such as Singapore and Taiwan found support.
    Additionally, local factors held sway after authorities in
Singapore intervened to calm a runaway rise in bond yields and
Korean policymakers tried to talk down the won.
    "Confidence in global reflation is beginning to jeopardise
capital flows into the high-yielding markets, as previously
popular global carry trades are coming unstuck," said James
Malcolm of JP Morgan in a note to clients.



    The rupiah        fell to 8,640 in morning deals, its
lowest low since May 5, on Wednesday -- the second anniversary
of Megawati Sukarnoputri's taking over as Indonesia's
President.
    The rupiah's slide had probably been triggered by the news
that BP Plc (BP.L) and global mining giant Rio Tinto
 (RIO.L) (RIO.AX) were selling their stake in Indonesia's PT
Kaltim Prima Coal to a local firm, traders said
 
    "Some of the hot money that entered Indonesia is getting
out," said Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist with UBS.
    "And the BP deal highlights the problems in Aceh, and the
difficulty Indonesia is likely to have in attracting foreign
investment," he said.
    With interest rates falling rapidly and investors flocking
to the more technology-dominated stock markets in the region,
foreign investment was bound to leave Indonesia, he said.
    JP Morgan's Malcolm said Jakarta's markets had been
complacent about the local risks of political stability and
success in sales of bad loans during the past 18 months.
    Slowing growth, the possibility reforms will be put on the



backburner heading into parliamentary elections in 2004, and



the uncertainty over financing as the country opts out of a IMF



loan programme could all weigh on the rupiah, he said.



Meanwhile, a Indonesian central bank official said the



market could determine the rupiah's level and there was no need



to intervene continuously - although traders said they thought



Bank Indonesia had been active on both Tuesday and Wednesday.



PESO WEAKENS



Elsewhere, a top finance ministry official in Korea said



the won's             strength was not justified, given



the weak economy.



 
    The Philippine peso        was initially steady, but
slipped in later trades to 53.95, a four-month low.
    The rest of the regionals were stuck in ranges, like the



Japanese yen which barely reacted to reports of the deaths of



former Iraqi leader Sadddam Hussein's sons and the resultant



bullishness on the U.S. dollar.



The Sing dollar  moved in a 1.7560-1.7590 band, and



some traders said market nerves had calmed after suspected bond



purchases by the Monetary Authority of Singapore on Tuesday, to



contain the volatility that pushed 10-year yields to a



nine-month high of 3.45 percent.



The Taiwan dollar  was steady, but poised to rally



when the central bank was prepared to let it appreciate,



Malcolm said.



"The US dollar/Taiwan dollar has one of the highest



correlations to global growth of all the U.S. dollar crosses we



track globally, so we expect the Taiwan dollar to benefit



disproportionately in a recovery scenario," Malcolm said in a



note.

title: UPDATE 2- Indonesia  c.bank  intervening  to prop up rupiah.
text:
JAKARTA, July 23 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank scrambled to put a floor under the shaky rupiah currency on Wednesday after it hit an 11-week low against the dollar, but said it still had room to cautiously lower interest rates. 

 When asked if the bank was intervening, senior deputy governor Anwar Nasution told Reuters: "I cannot say exactly when or how much but I can assure you we are in the market." 

 He earlier told reporters that the foreign exchange market should determine the rate of the currency and that there was little point to continuous intervention - a comment which helped drag the unit down. 

 The rupiah fell to 8,640 in morning deals, its lowest since May 5, but later recovered and at 0510 GMT was being quoted at 8,495/8,515. 

 Separately, the bank's governor, Burhanuddin Abdullah, told Reuters that the rupiah's fall was temporary and that interest rates could still head lower despite the rupiah's fall. 

 The weaker rupiah has raised concern over how much more inflation would ease in Indonesia, which still has one of the highest rates in Asia, and whether the central bank would have to curtail its policy of gradually lowering interest rates. 

 "We think it is something temporary. We will guard the rupiah exchange rate in the market so the movement will not disturb the economy," Abdullah said, adding intervention was one option. 

 "Generally the policy will remain that there is still room to lower interest rates," he said. 

 The currency, under pressure since late last week, has been relatively stable and strong in recent months mainly due to short-term capital inflows. 

 Asked why the currency had depreciated so rapidly, Nasution said: "Some companies saw the appreciation of the rupiah as an opportunity to re-pay their debts so they started buying U.S. dollars." 

 "The other reason might be demand from PLN and Pertamina," he said, referring to the state electricity utility and the national oil company, respectively. 

 Even at the current rates, the rupiah is stronger than the 9,000 average exchange rate assumed under the 2003 state budget. 

 In an interview with Reuters earlier this month, Nasution estimated the rupiah could strengthen to 8,000 per dollar in the third quarter but cautioned that those short-term inflows could also destabilise it.

title: Bk  Indonesia  Gov Admits Ctrl Bk  Intervened  To Help IDR
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah admitted the central bank has intervened in the foreign exchange market Wednesday to support the rupiah. He said it will continue to take action to reduce volatility if necessary. 

 But he declined to provide the amount of dollars the central bank has sold to help the local unit, which fell to a fresh three-month low of IDR8,650 against the dollar earlier Wednesday as foreign investors took profit on the rupiah and local bonds. 

 "We will stay in the market from time to time," he told reporters. 

 Burhanuddin's statement contradicted early Wednesday remarks by his senior deputy Anwar Nasution, who said the central bank won't sell the dollar in the market. 

 Burhanuddin said he expects the rupiah's weakness is "temporary," and a factor that isn't expected to obstruct the central bank's policy for easing rates. 

 Bank Indonesia has cut its benchmark one-month interest rate from around 13% late last year to 9.21% currently amid easing inflation and the rupiah's appreciation. 

 The rate cuts are expected to cut the bailout costs of local banks and spur economic growth.

title: Bk  Indonesia  Deputy Gov: Won't  Intervene  To Help Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia won't intervene to support the rupiah, which fell to a fresh three-month low Wednesday as foreign investors took profit on the currency and local bonds, Senior Deputy Governor Anwar Nasution said. 

 "I don't think so," he said, when asked if the central bank will intervene in the currency market. "We adopt a floating exchange rate policy and let the market decide." 

 His remarks contradict earlier comments by dealers, who suspect Bank Indonesia has been intervening in the market since Monday to slow down the dollar's rise. 

 The rupiah fell to IDR8,540 to the dollar early Wednesday from its close Tuesday at IDR8,425 as foreign investors continued to take profit on the Indonesian unit and rupiah-denominated assets in the run-up to the annual session of the nation's highest legislative body, the MPR, early next month. 

 Although the session is expected to be peaceful, political temperatures are expected to rise, providing an excuse for market players to sell the rupiah and buy back the dollar.

title: UPDATE 1-Bank Indonesia cuts overnight rate to 9.00 pct.
text:
JAKARTA, July 10 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank decreased its rupiah overnight intervention rate, known as the FASBI, on Thursday following a further decline on the benchmark interest rate (SBI) in its weekly auction. 

 The FASBI rate was cut to 9.00 percent from 9.75 percent, a central bank official told Reuters. That was in line with some analysts' expectations. 

 The central bank said earlier this week that the inflation rate, already at three-year lows, would stay restrained in the third quarter and the rupiah currency would tend to strengthen in the second half. 

 The central bank's comments combined with the fall in FASBI could open possibilities for further rate cuts ahead. 

 Under the central bank's policy, the new rate would be applicable for the morning session while the afternoon rate would be 4.50 percent, down from the previous 4.875 percent.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Sing dollar at month low, peso slips.

still don't look particularly strong and therefore policymakers
are going to remain wary, especially as we enter the season of

two."
