title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed On Equity Flows, Intervention  Fear
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies put up a mixed showing Thursday supported by strong equity inflows, but with the central bankintervention theme a strong deterrent to attempts to take the units too high. 

 The Singapore dollar, the Philippine peso and the Indonesian rupiah slipped, while the South Korean won, the Thai baht and the New Taiwan dollar were modestly higher. 

 Analysts said central banks in the region are loathe to allow their currencies to appreciate too fast for fear of losing export competitiveness at a time of uncertainty for the global economy. 

 "Across the board, central banks are still not sufficiently confident of a turnaround (in the economies), at least until the end of the year," said Chong Hui Chin, a currency strategist at J.P. Morgan Chase Bank. 

 The Singapore dollar fell to a one-month low during the session, but managed to trim losses. Late in the local session, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7380, up from S$1.7365 late Wednesday. 

 A trader at a European bank in Singapore said there were a lot of U.S. names buying the currency pair, continuing a trend seen in the last few days. 

 There's been talk in the market in recent days that the Monetary Authority of Singapore has been supporting the U.S. dollar, which has damped any enthusiasm to push up the local unit. 

 Talk of such intervention seems to be supported by the recent foreign reserves data, which showed a sharp rise in reserves last month, analysts said. 

 The trader said he believes the government wants to weaken the Singapore dollar to make it more competitive against countries like neighboring Malaysia, whose currency, the ringgit, is pegged to the U.S. dollar. 

 The Philippine peso was weighed down by a ratings downgrade from Fitch Ratings, and also as banks bought dollars ahead of a long weekend. However, strong equity inflows into the local stock market put a floor under the peso. 

 The dollar closed at 53.610 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP53.535 Wednesday. 

 Fitch lowered the long-term foreign currency rating on the Philippines by a notch to "BB". The move had to a large extent been anticipated as it was reported in a local newspaper in the previous session. 

 Chong of J.P. Morgan Chase Bank, said foreign equity inflows into the Philippine stock market are now more than five times the average in the last 12 months, and such strong flows should help slow the dollar's gains. 

 The key stock index rose 1.9% Thursday to end at its highest close since July 1, 2002. Philippine markets are closed for a holiday Friday. 

 Against the Indonesian rupiah, the dollar was quoted around IDR8,251 late in Asia, up from IDR8,230 Thursday. 

 Market players continued to take profit on the rupiah, which has rallied sharply in recent weeks, amid concerns the central bank might intervene to stem the rise. 

 Chong said the rupiah is expensive and on a purchasing power parity basis, its fair value should be closer to 10,000 to the dollar. 

 Still, she said continued interest in the high-yielding currency and the momentum of good news in the country should help the rupiah rise to 7,500 by September, although it should then go on to lose ground by year end. 

 Meanwhile, Bank Indonesia Thursday cut its overnight money market intervention rate for the second time this month on easing inflation to help spur economic growth. 

 The South Korean won edged up despite official jawboning, although overall activity was quiet as traders believe the government had already intervened in the previous session to support the dollar at KRW1,190. 

 Exporters, foreigners and players fixing non-deliverable forwards positions all sold the dollar, which closed at KRW1,193.2, down from KRW1,195.4 Wednesday. 

 Earlier, Kwon Tae-shin, deputy minister for international affairs at the Ministry of Finance and Economy, said the government will step in for a "smoothing operation" anytime when the dollar/won rate fails to reflect the economy's fundamentals, according to Yonhap Infomax. He repeated the same message in the afternoon. 

 Meanwhile, the central bank decided at its monthly monetary policy meeting to keep its overnight call rate target unchanged at 4%, a decision that was widely expected by markets. 

 The New Taiwan dollar was boosted by foreign equity inflows following news that Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. would be included in the Philadelphia Stock Exchange's Philly chip index, one of the most widely watched semiconductor indexes in the world. 

 The U.S. unit ended at NT$34.667, down from Wednesday's NT$34.682. 

 The key local stock index rose 1.5% to end at its highest level in more than four months Thursday. Foreign investors net bought nearly NT$3 billion of local shares, which helped underpin the local dollar's gains, dealers said. 

 The Thai baht recovered from an early drop to move to a stronger footing. Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around 41.72 baht, down from THB41.79 Wednesday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late;Peso Down On Monetary Easing
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were a mixed bag late Thursday, caught between strong stock market performance and concern that central banks might intervene to curb local currency strength. 

 The Philippine peso ended lower after the central bank effectively eased monetary policy in a move that was widely expected. 

Indonesia's central bank also cut its overnight money market intervention rate Thursday, its sixth such reduction so far this year. The Indonesian rupiah closed lower after a choppy session. 

 The South Korean won was little changed. The Singapore dollar, Thai baht and New Taiwan dollar were firmer. 

 The tone of the broad market during the day was biased toward a softer U.S. currency due to the flow of foreign funds into regional equity markets, said a trader at a U.S. bank. 

 "Dollar/Asians are on a soft-ish bias. Basically, (Asian currencies) are trading on a strong stock market performance as capital flows come into the region," he said. 

 There was also a lot of play on euro crosses as market players sold the common currency ahead of a widely anticipated rate cut by the European Central Bank later Thursday, he added. 

 Bank of America, in a research note, said a combination of currency appreciation and easing bias in interest rate policy globally is allowing Asian central banks room to maneuver monetary policy to stimulate domestic demand. 

 "Low interest rates and abundant liquidity is giving support to regional stock markets - in turn aiding further currency appreciation. Regional central banks tread the fine line of allowing appreciation as a result of greater foreign capital inflows, and resisting any damage to their export competitiveness," Bank of America said. 

 The dollar ended at 53.330 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP53.270 Wednesday, but off the intraday high of PHP53.415. 

 Traders said many banks took a long dollar position because of a narrowing of the differential between U.S. and local interest rates from the easing of local monetary policy, traders said. 

 The central bank effected monetary easing by reinstating the tiered interest rate system on its overnight borrowing rates. The system, which pays lower rates for funds in excess of PHP5 billion, was scrapped in March to quell speculative demand for the dollar, which at that time was trading at PHP55. 

 "Some banks covered their short positions on the dollar because of the central bank's move," said a trader with a local bank. Some banks also bought dollars for corporate clients. 

 However, Central Bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said the peso's fall was triggered by the weakness in regional currencies, and not by the return of the tiered system. 

 Meantime, a combination of profit taking and dollar demand from local importers pulled the rupiah lower after a volatile session, traders said. 

 The dollar closed local trading at 8,225 rupiah, up from IDR8,165 Wednesday. 

 Dealers said market players took profit on the rupiah after it earlier rose to a 34-month intraday high of 8,140 to the dollar. 

 Earlier Thursday, Bank Indonesia cut its overnight money market intervention rate to 10.25% from 10.50%. 

 Governor Burhanuddin Abdullah told Parliament that domestic interest rates will fall further amid a benign inflation outlook. 

 The South Korean won finished almost unchanged in quiet pre-holiday trade. Local financial markets will be shut Friday for a public holiday. 

 The dollar closed at 1,200.3 won, from KRW1,200.6 Wednesday. 

 The market is wary of testing the dollar below KRW1,200 after banks bought the U.S. currency under that level Wednesday. Many suspect the buying was done on behalf of the central bank. 

 "The market was restrained on the downside by the BOK (Bank of Korea) and on the upside by dollar selling by exporters and for stock settlements," said a dealer. "Traders are losing interest in trading." 

 Foreign investors bought Korean shares for a seventh session, ending as net buyers of KRW187.4 billion of shares Thursday. 

 The New Taiwan dollar also finished higher on the back of a strong stock market, as well as on the yen's gains versus the U.S. unit, traders said. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.665, down from NT$34.687 Tuesday, marking its strongest close since May 21. Local markets were closed for a holiday Wednesday. 

 Pent-up demand for U.S. dollars after the holiday, however, helped pull the U.S. currency off its session lows, traders said. 

 The Singapore dollar was modestly stronger late in Asia, although it came off highs as the yen retreated slightly against the U.S. dollar, dealers said. 

 Late in the local session, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7233, compared with S$1.7248 late Wednesday in Asia. 

 Aside from brief spurts of activity, trade in the local currency market remained quiet. 

 "Everyone's lost interest to trade. It's been very quiet for the past two days, aside from some cross-related trade," a foreign bank dealer said. 

 "Everybody's watching the ECB (European Central Bank) today for direction," he added. 

 As against the Thai baht, the dollar was quoted around 41.60 late in Asia, down from THB41.68 Wednesday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Dn Late On Yen; New Dlr Buying Interest
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies fell Thursday as the dollar strengthened against the yen, which briefly weakened to a near-four week low as market players unwound short-dollar positions. 

 "We are seeing new interest in buying dollars," against global majors, and a similar trend was also apparent against regional units, a trader at a European bank said. 

 But whether that pattern can be sustained is moot, analysts and traders said. Although economies in the region are seeing a slowdown in growth, and the trend appears to be increasingly for further monetary easing, the U.S. economic outlook remains cloudy. 

 "Just as the upside (for Asian currencies) is contained by central bank intervention, the downside is contained," by relatively stronger fundamentals in Asia, said Vincent Low, head of foreign exchange and bond strategy for Asia at Merrill Lynch. 

 "My sense of it is, people still want to consider reloading longs on some Asian currencies," he added. 

 The Thai baht and the Indonesian rupiah, for instance, have been attracting strong buying interest in recent days; the former supported by robust domestic demand, and the latter by its high yields. 

 Their losses have hence been limited even as the dollar strengthens. 

 By contrast, currencies of countries like Singapore, which is heavily dependent on external demand, are more vulnerable to any dollar correction, Low said. 

 As against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7362 late in the local session, up from S$1.7274 late Wednesday. 

 The U.S. dollar was at 41.86 versus the Thai baht late in Asia, from THB41.69 previously. 

 The dollar was quoted around 8,350 against the Indonesian rupiah, up from IDR8,220 late Wednesday, due to month-end demand from local companies to repay offshore debt ahead of a long weekend, dealers said. 

 Thursday was the last day for companies to buy dollars as local markets will be closed Friday for a public holiday 

 Market players also trimmed short-dollar positions following the U.S. currency's rebound against major rivals and other Asian units. 

 A cut in Bank Indonesia's policy rate failed to move the market as it was widely expected, dealers said. 

 Bank Indonesia cut the overnight money market intervention rate by 25 basis points to 10.50% amid easing inflation. This is the second rate cut this month and the fifth this year. 

 In Taiwan, the U.S. unit closed at 34.772 against the New Taiwan dollar, up from NT$34.730 Wednesday, tracking its rise against the yen and the South Korean won, as well as other regional currencies. Japan and South Korea are two of Taiwan's top export competitors. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around Y118.87, up from Y118.65 overnight in New York, and Y117.10 late Wednesday in Tokyo. 

 The South Korean won was weighed down by the weak yen, and also Minister of Finance and Economy Kim Jin Pyo's remarks that the government will conduct smoothing operations in the foreign exchange market to curb speculation. 

 Exporters selling dollars to balance their books at the end of the month saved the won from steeper losses, dealers said. The dollar finished at 1,207.0 won, up from KRW1,200.4 Wednesday. 

 "Recently the government strongly showed its intention to support the market," said Gin Lee, head of fixed income at Credit Agricole Indosuez. "The Korean economy is getting worse and worse. The Korean won cannot be stronger considering the economy." 

 South Korea's weak industrial output data for April, released earlier Thursday, paint a grim picture of the economy with all key components pointing to a further economic slowdown in coming months as capital investment shrinks and consumption cools further. 

 April industrial production rose 1.8% on year, slowing from a 5.0% rise in March. It was the weakest growth since September 2002, and was worse than the average 3.4% rise predicted in a Dow Jones Newswires poll. 

 The Philippine peso closed at a two-month low on the back of the yen-led decline in regional currencies and thinning remittance inflows from Filipinos working abroad, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at its intraday high of 53.350 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, its highest since April 1, and up from PHP53.100 Wednesday. 

 Traders said first-quarter gross domestic product growth data, released earlier Thursday, didn't have an impact on the market as players focused on the surging dollar against the yen. 

 Philippine GDP rose 4.5% on year in the January-March period, at the higher end of the government 4%-4.5% projection, and accelerating from 3.8% in the year-earlier quarter. But it was lower than the 5.8% rise in the last quarter of 2002. 

 A local bank trader said the central bank was suspected to have bought dollars to boost foreign exchange reserves ahead of payment of maturing debt in October. 

 The central bank couldn't immediately be reached for comment. 

 Traders said there was also some corporate demand for dollars to cover month-end requirements.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Up At 32-Mo High On Ratings Upgrade
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah ended at a 32-month high against the dollar Monday as Standard and Poor's Ratings Service upgraded its long-term foreign currency rating on Indonesia, further bolstering already bullish sentiment for the country, dealers said. 

 S&P raised the rating to B Minus from CCC Plus, reflecting the diminished likelihood that government will seek additional debt restructuring, a situation made possible by its improving fiscal and external positions. 

 The dollar closed at 8,430 rupiah, down from Friday's close at IDR8,555. 

 Sentiment for the rupiah turned positive in April as the much-feared violent protests against the Iraqi war in the world's most populous Muslim country didn't happen. Foreign investors started to park their funds in Indonesia's capital markets as the war in Iraq approached its end last month, slowly driving the rupiah higher from levels around IDR9,000. 

 Meanwhile, Indonesian stocks have risen around 23% during the same period as foreign investors snapped up undervalued blue-chip stocks. 

 Bank Indonesia's deputy governor Miranda Gultom said Monday that the central bank isn't concerned about the dollar's fall to below IDR8,500 as exporters can still be competitive at that level. She also said the benchmark one-month rate of Bank Indonesia's Sertifikat Bank Indonesia notes may fall to 10.5% by the end of the year from 10.91% currently if "conditions keep improving." 

 "Her comment is an endorsement for the market's intention to drive the dollar to near IDR8,000," said a dealer with a foreign bank. 

 But some dealers were still concerned the rupiah's sharp rise could trigger Bank Indonesia intervention. 

 The rupiah's appreciation has helped reduce inflation to 7.54% on year in April, and consumer prices are likely to continue falling in the coming months, which will pave the way for further interest rate cuts. Cutting rates is expected to spur economic growth as well as help reduce the costs of bailing out the country's banking system. 

 President Megawati Sukarnoputri's rise to power in July 2001 has improved political stability in the country, and that has over time helped to improve investor sentiment. 

 Also, the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency's plan to sell a 51% stake in nationalized PT Bank Danamon Indonesia to Singapore's Temasek Holdings and Deutsche Bank, following its sale of PT Bank Central Asia and PT Bank Niaga last year, showed that the government is serious about implementing economic reform programs. 

 But analysts warn that the rupiah's strength is mostly underpinned by short-term capital inflows, which could easily exit the country. 

 Long-term foreign direct investment, which is the true measure of foreign investors' confidence in the country, remains scanty as the government has been slow in reforming its weak and corrupt legal system. 

 Still, dealers said there's still a lot of upward momentum in the rupiah, and the dollar Tuesday is expected to head lower toward IDR8,300.

text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, May 9 (Reuters) - Asian currencies remained
strong against the U.S. dollar on Friday, kept off this week's
highs by the fear of intervention, but the region weakened
against the surging euro .
 As the euro hit four-year highs on the dollar and matched its
life-high against the yen , the Singapore dollar was
at its lowest against the euro since it was launched in January
1999, and the cross  was heading towards 2.0.
    Against the U.S. dollar, the Singapore dollar       , Thai
baht  and the Taiwan dollar were off two-month highs. The
South Korean won  also eased from a two-month high as
markets in Seoul resumed trade after a holiday.
    Even the high yielding Philippine peso        wiped out its
gains for the week as it fell from an eight month high. The
Indonesian rupiah  also tripped off an 11-month peak.



    Wariness of intervention pulled the yen back from 10-month
highs near 116 yen to around 117 yen on Friday, which also
weighed on regionals as Japan is a major trade partner for
Asia.
    Japanese Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa said yen has
risen too much, but declined to comment if Japan had
intervened.
    Dealers believe most Asian central banks had been buying
dollars in recent sessions to protect export competitiveness,
and this had also triggered profit-taking.
    "Central banks are watchful. They are still assessing the
impact of SARS on their economies. So they are maintaining some
caution," said Thio Chin Loo, senior currency analyst at BNP
Paribas in Singapore.
 
    Still, she said the outlook for Asian currencies was
brighter than that of the yen.
    "The dollar's downward trend against Asian currencies has
restarted, but they are not likely to rally at the same speed

    The Singapore dollar eased to around 1.7420 per U.S.

    The peso eased to around 52.40 per dollar, a day after it
hit 51.88, its strongest since September 13 last year.
    Dealers in Manila said while remittances from overseas
workers would offer support, most players were looking to book
profits before taking fresh positions.
    The peso is still about five percent higher from its lows



above 55 per dollar in March. Its high yields have proved



attractive to investors, overshadowing their worries about



ratings downgrades and the large budget deficit.



The Indonesian rupiah , the leading Asian gainer so



far this year, pulled back to around 8,600 per dollar from



Thursday's 11-month high of 8,495.

title: Indonesian Rupiah Ends Up On Fresh Foreign Buying
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah ended slightly higher against the dollar Friday as foreign investors continued to buy the local unit to invest in the country's capital markets, dealers said. 

 The dollar finished at 8,545 rupiah, slightly down from Thursday's close at IDR8,555. 

 The dollar's fall Friday was a bit of a surprise for most dealers, who had expected follow-through profit-taking on the rupiah ahead of the weekend following its recent strong rally. 

 "This signifies the market is still very bullish on the rupiah," said a dealer with a foreign bank. 

 He pointed out that the sale of Bank Danamon 51% stake to Singapore's Temasek and Deustche Bank has helped boost market confidence that the government is serious in implementing economic reform programs. 

 The government's efforts to revamp the economy have seen some results: high inflation is easing, and that gives the central bank room to cut interest rates further. 

 Bank Indonesia Friday cut the overnight money market intervention rate by 25 basis points to 10.75%. It was the fourth rate cut so far this year. 

 Lower interest rates are expected to spur economic growth, and also to relieve the bad debt problem in the country, which in the long turn will encourage banks to start lending afresh to companies. 

 Dealers expect the dollar to trade lower toward IDR8,490 Monday. Resistance for the U.S. currency is expected at IDR8,600.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Flows dominate, rupiah surges.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, May 5 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah surged
to its highest level in over 10 months in holiday-thinned Asian
trading on Monday, driven by heavy flows believed to be
offshore investments related to the country's asset sales.
 
    Holidays in Japan, China, Korea and Thailand kept trade
thin.
    The Singapore dollar rose to a one-month high near 1.7635


 as a few foreign banks vigorously sold their holdings of U.S. 

 dollars, disregarding a steady Japanese yen and media talk of 

 the government introducing yen-weakening policies. 

 The Philippine peso found renewed strength in data showing 

 strong export growth as Manila markets opened after a Labour 

 Day holiday weekend, but it closed off highs. The peso hit a 

 high of 52.235, a level last seen two weeks back. 

 The rupiah struck 8,618, last traded at the end of June 

 2002. A trader in Jakarta said it was likely offshore players 

 had brought into the country funds meant for investing in the 

 Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency's (IBRA) sale of a 

 majority stake in Bank Danamon. 

 Monday was the deadline for final bids. IBRA had earlier 

 said there were three bidders - a consortium led by 

 Singapore's Temasek Holdings, a group led by Bhakti Capital 

 Indonesia and including Bank Mega, and another group including 

 Bank Artha Graha. 


 
    Traders said there were few signs the central bank had
intervened to contain the rupiah's rise.
    "Inflation has come lower, so they can allow the rupiah to



appreciate in nominal terms," said Bhanu Baweja, currency


strategist with UBS Warburg. Baweja said the central Bank

Indonesia might have been intervening.



The rupiah has gained 6.1 percent in 1-= months, and in



April Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves increased by one



billion dollars to $33.6 billion, after rising by $4.7 billion



in the 12 months before that.



SARS DATA BOOSTS SING DOLLAR



Traders said aggressive position-squaring propped up the



Singapore dollar and drove it to a one-month high after some



players considered it excessively weak given the slowly



improving outlook on the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome



(SARS) epidemic.



"I imagine that a good chunk of that is position-squaring,



because SARS news has been better for the past week or so,"



said James Malcolm, currency strategist at JP Morgan.



"We'd continue to recommend selling U.S. dollars. The



mid-point of our band doesn't come in until 1.7300, so we have



a long way to go before we're back at the mid-point," he said,



referring to the undisclosed trade-weighted band authorities



manage the Sing dollar in.



There were no fresh cases of SARS in Singapore and new



cases dropped in Hong Kong. Worldwide, deaths from the virus



rose to over 460 people, and the number infected climbed to



almost 7,000.



Meanwhile, amid expectations the U.S. Federal Reserve would



leave rates unchanged at its meeting this week, analysts



expected the rally in high-yielding currencies, such as some



Latin Americans, the South African rand, Australian dollar and



Indonesian rupiah, would continue but with less momentum.



JP Morgan's Malcolm warned local markets could be a bit



nervous after the light sell-off seen in other emerging markets



last week. The Brazilian real and South African rand were sold



last week after some rather steep rallies.



 
    But a spillover of that kind of profit-taking was unlikely,
he said.
    "Those markets have been very heavily bought in the past



couple of weeks. And, those are not the sensitivities or



overhangs we have in Asia at the moment, so the impetus for



profit-taking in Asia is much more modest."



The Taiwan dollar stuck to a very thin range around 34.80,



with neighbours Japan and Korea shut for holidays.

title: Bk Indonesia Gov Not Worried Over Rupiah's Sharp Rise
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia isn't worried over the rupiah's recent sharp rise against the dollar and will leave it up to the market to determine an appropriate level for the local currency, the bank's governor Sjahril Sabirin said Monday. 

 The central bank governor added that the rupiah's recent strength is due to improving market sentiment toward Indonesian investments. 

 The rupiah rose to new 10-month high of 8,675 to the dollar Monday. 

 Worries over the possibility of a violent backlash over the U.S.-led war in Iraq sent the local currency lower to 9,095 earlier this month. 

 But anti-war protests went off peacefully, which encouraged foreign investors to buy Indonesian portfolios that are offering favorable returns. 

 Some analysts have expressed concern that the rupiah's sharp rise may hurt Indonesian exports, which are already facing weakening demand from the country's main export destinations, such as the U.S. and Japan. 

 Some dealers have said Bank Indonesia may intervene to stem the rupiah's rise as it is trading outside the IDR8,800-IDR9,200 range that the central bank had forecast for this year. 

 Sjahril said that the central bank will leave the rupiah's exchange rate to market forces, as long as it isn't "too volatile." 

 Looking ahead, Sjahril said that he expected market sentiment toward the rupiah to remain positive, but didn't elaborate. 

 -By Farida Husna; Dow Jones Newswires; 62-21 39831277; djn.jakarta@dowjones.com.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Up in volatile, war-driven trade.
text:
By Vidya Ranganathan
    SINGAPORE, April 8 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were mostly
higher late on Tuesday after a volatile session driven
primarily by news from the Iraq war and worries over the spread
of SARS.
    The Singapore dollar       , Thai baht        and Taiwan
dollar  were choppy, following the lead of the Japanese
yen , amid reports the U.S. military had bombed a target
in Baghdad where Iraqi President Saddam Hussein may have been.
    Asian currencies also grappled with anxiety over the Severe
Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) virus, which has claimed over
100 human lives and has infected over 2,700 people.
    "In the near-term, the market will continue to trade on how
the war is shaping up in Iraq," DBS Bank economist Lee Boon
Keng said in a commentary.
    "And we expect the victory dance to stay for a little
longer.



 Hence, the dollar will stay relatively well-bid, and
bonds will continue to face downside pressure."
 
    The Singapore dollar spent most of the day around 1.78 per
dollar, clear of Monday's five-month lows near 1.7850.
    Still, markets worried about the prime minister's remark
that the SARS could cut growth in China, Hong Kong and
Singapore by as much as one percent.
    Speculation was also rife over whether the Monetary



Authority of Singapore would tolerate a Singapore dollar



outside the weaker end of the undisclosed trade-weighted band



it is managed in.



 
    "There is a possibility they will consider these kind of
measures," said Thio Chin Loo, strategist with BNP Paribas.
    "Given there is also volatility with this war, the
justification for a wider band is there."

local markets resumed after a holiday.
    One-year forwards on the Hong Kong dollar peg



hugged 200 points, coming off an early high of 210 basis

SARS could put pressure on Hong Kong's economy, its reserves



and hence the HK dollar peg.



"Asian currencies may not react very positively to the end



of the war because there still are a few risk factors such as



North Korea and SARS that loom over this region," UBS Warburg's

    The Philippine peso        opened steady, and then extended
its three-week uptrend to close at a 3-=   month high of 52.88,



indifferent not just to the regional swings but also to news



that the government had overshot its first quarter budget



deficit target by 10 percent.



The Indonesian rupiah  was surprisingly strong even



after the central bank cut rates. Bank Indonesia cut its



overnight intervention rate by 25 basis points to 11.25 percent



on Monday.



The Korean won             and Taiwan dollar mimicked



the early gains in the yen, but markets were suspicious of the

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late;Choppy Trade On War News
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mostly firmer late Tuesday in a choppy session marked by reports on developments in the war in Iraq and speculation about the fate of Iraqi President Saddam Hussein. 

 Regional currencies started the day on a stronger footing following overnight profit-taking on the dollar following recent gains. 

 But some weakness began to emerge following a wave of dollar buying in the Asian morning on talk that Saddam may have been killed in a bomb strike on a building in Iraq. 

 The speculation was fueled by reports that U.S. forces bombed a "leadership target" in Baghdad. 

 The target was believed to be one or more of the top government or military leaders in Saddam Hussein's regime, according to military officials. 

 The attack, and the ensuring rumors about Saddam's fate, pushed the dollar briefly to an intraday high around Y120.16, up from Y119.86 overnight in New York. 

 "There was quite a lot of dollar buying as the market reacted to the news," a trader at a European bank said, noting that this caused "the weakening trend of regional currencies to reassert itself." 

 This was compounded by concerns over the economic impact of the deadly severe acute respiratory syndrome, or SARS, outbreak, he said. 

 But the dollar buying wasn't sustained and as of 0830 GMT, the dollar had dropped back to around Y119.65. 

 "The dollar came into the Asian session a little bit 'positive news weary'. That set the tone for the Asian session. Within that, there was a burst of dollar buying but it wasn't really sustained," said David Simmonds, senior emerging markets strategist for Asia at Royal Bank of Scotland. 

 The Singapore dollar was off session highs as concerns about the economic fallout of the SARS outbreak continued to plague the market, dealers said. 

 Near the end of local trading, the dollar was quoted at S$1.7810, down from S$1.7849 late in Asia Monday, but off the intraday trough of S$1.7780. 

 Singapore has been one of the countries most affected by SARS. Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong said over the weekend that the government's forecast for a 2%-5% economic growth for 2003 would have to be revised downward as the viral outbreak takes its toll on the local travel and hospitality sectors. 

 The city state's advance gross domestic product estimates for the first quarter will be released Thursday, and market watchers say the government may also come up with a more up-to-date forecast for the full year. 

 The Philippine peso closed at a five-month high after the long weekend, bolstered by expectations of a quick conclusion to the war in Iraq, traders said. 

 Some remittance inflows amid a lack of corporate demand for dollars also strengthened the peso, some traders said. 

 The dollar finished at its intraday trough of 52.880 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System - its lowest close since Nov. 7, 2002 - and down from PHP53.250 Friday. Local financial markets were closed for a public holiday Monday. 

 "Everyone was worried about the Iraq crisis. The nearing conclusion of this crisis is causing the peso to reverse its downtrend," said Jose Emmanuel Hilado, a member of the Open Market Committee of the Bankers Association of the Philippines, which owns and operates the Philippine Dealing System. 

 The South Korean won firmed in tandem with the yen with the dollar closing at KRW1,253.5, down from KRW1,257.6 Monday. 

 The U.S. unit has been sandwiched between KRW1,250 and KRW1,260 for more than a week as fears of intervention capped its upside while offshore buying provided support. 

 Offshore players are poised to buy dollars on dips on expectations that with a quick end to the war in Iraq, the U.S. would next focus its attention on the nuclear standoff with the communist North, a move that would undermine the won. 

 "Because of North Korea risk, offshore players are all looking to buy (dollars) on dips," said one dealer. 

 The New Taiwan dollar also took its cue from the yen, with the U.S. unit ending at NT$34.818, down from NT$34.844 Monday. 

 The Thai baht shrugged off early losses after the long weekend and was quoted around 43.05 to the dollar late in Asia, from THB43.09 Friday. Local financial markets were shut for a holiday Monday. 

 The dollar spent much of the Asian session locked between THB43.12 and THB43.15, an offshore dealer in Singapore said. 

 Meantime, Thailand's Finance Ministry expects the economic fallout from the SARS outbreak to trim the country's gross domestic product growth by 0.3-0.5 percentage point this year, a source at the ministry's Fiscal Policy Office said earlier Tuesday. 

 The ministry's most up-to-date forecast is for the economy to expand 5.1% in 2003. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was also firmer with the dollar quoted around IDR8,877 late in Asia, from IDR8,885 Monday. 

 There was some suspicion earlier that the central bank intervened to accelerate the dollar's slide. 

 "Bank Indonesia likely wants to see what support level for the pair the market wants," a dealer said, but noted there was limited downside as the dollar is near the psychologically important IDR8,850 level. 

 -By Nirmala Menon, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4046; nirmala.menon@dowjones.com

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late As Dlr Trims Gains Vs Yen
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies pulled out of early troughs and were mixed late Monday as the dollar trimmed gains against the yen. 

 The South Korean won, Singapore dollar and Philippine peso were weaker, the Indonesian rupiah was firmer, and the New Taiwan dollar and Thai baht were little changed. 

 The dollar came off a three-month high of Y121.88 reached in New York Friday on signs the war in Iraq may not be progressing as smoothly as expected. 

 Going into the second day of the war Friday, market players had been expecting "that the war could finish fast. That's why they bought dollars," a trader at a European bank said. 

 But following weekend reports of fierce Iraqi resistance and the capture of some U.S. troops, "people are feeling a little bit different now," though they still expect the U.S. to prevail, the trader added. 

 As the dollar gave up some of Friday's sharp gains against the yen, market players took the opportunity to also book profits from its rise against Asian units. 

 UBS Warburg said in a research note that developments on the war front over the weekend, and signs that Saddam Hussein is alive "have all worked to erode the war buoyancy of markets that was so much in evidence on Friday. 

 There was speculation that Saddam was killed during the initial strikes on Iraq when the U.S. launched military action during the Asian morning Thursday. 

 "Most importantly, there is no sign as yet that pro-Saddam forces will simply fold, or that Iraq's general population are treating the allied forces as liberators, both factors seen as vital ingredients for a quick and easy war," UBS Warburg said. 

 Saddam addressed his nation late Monday in Asia, vowing that "victory will be ours soon," 

 He hailed Iraqi "bravery" and said Iraqi fighters were "causing the enemy to suffer and to lose every day." 

 "As time goes by, they will lose more and they will not be able to escape lightly from their predicament," he said. "We will make it as painful as we can." 

 The South Korean won was slightly lower as concerns over a protracted war in Iraq had a greater negative impact on the local currency than on the dollar, which ended at 1,251.0 won, up from KRW1,247.4 Friday. 

 The U.S. unit briefly spiked to a high of KRW1,255.2 in the morning session before falling back to touch a low of KRW1,248.0 on selling by offshore players and local exporters, dealers said. 

 Dollar buying by oil refineries helped support the currency in the afternoon, though trading came to a near standstill ahead of the Iraqi President's speech. 

 "Trading was almost on hold toward the end, as all wanted to get a clue from Saddam Hussein's speech," said a dealer at Kookmin Bank. 

 As against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. unit was quoted at S$1.7678 near the end of local trading hours, off a session high of S$1.7710, but still modestly up from S$1.7655 late Friday in Asia. 

 The dollar finished at 54.500 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP54.450 Friday, after trading between PHP54.410 and PHP54.510. 

 The New Taiwan dollar was nearly flat as U.S. dollar selling by exporters offset purchases by oil importers and day traders, dealers said. 

 The U.S. unit closed at NT$34.788 after trading between NT$34.720 and NT$34.850. It ended Friday at NT$34.791. 

 Taiwan's central bank bought U.S. dollars to make sure the local dollar didn't strengthen too much, a dealer at a foreign bank in Taiwan said. 

 Meantime, dealers also suspected Indonesia's central bank of intervening to prop up the rupiah, which earlier fell as low as 8,995 to the dollar following weekend warnings by the U.S. and U.K. that terrorists may launch an attack on their citizens in the country. 

 The dollar closed at IDR8,955, down from IDR8,965 Friday. 

 Dealers said Bank Indonesia was heard offering the dollar when the U.S. currency moved close to the psychologically important IDR9,000 level. 

 The government is aiming for an average dollar exchange rate of IDR9,000 this year. 

 Elsewhere, Thailand's central bank governor Pridiyathorn Devakula Monday reiterated that he was comfortable with the current baht movements, though he wasn't complacent about it. 

 "Fluctuations of half a percent against major currencies aren't a concern," Pridiyathorn told reporters. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around THB42.95, off an early high of THB43.05. The dollar was buying THB42.98 late Friday in Asia. 

 -By Nirmala Menon, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4046; nirmala.menon@dowjones.com

title: Indonesia  Rupiah Ends Up; Talks Of Ctrl Bk  Intervention
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah ended slightly higher against the dollar Monday on talks of intervention by the central bank to prop up the local unit, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at IDR8,955, down from its close Friday at IDR8,965. The dollar rose to its intraday high of IDR8,995 earlier Monday on warnings by the U.S. and U.K. over the weekend that terrorists may launch an attack on their citizens in Indonesia due to the war in Iraq. 

 Dealers said Bank Indonesia was heard offering the dollar when the U.S. currency moved close to the psychologically important IDR9,000 level. 

 The government is aiming for an average dollar exchange rate of IDR9,000 this year. 

 Besides suspected Bank Indonesia intervention, the dollar also gave up its early gains because anti-Western protests in the world's most populous Muslim country have remained orderly so far. 

 "There are far bigger protests in other parts of the world, so I don't think protests here will necessarily irk the market," said a dealer with a foreign bank in Jakarta. 

 Most market participants, however, still chose to stay on the sidelines as it remains unclear how long the Iraq war will last. 

 Dealers expect the dollar to trade between IDR8,900 and IDR9,000 Tuesday.

 However, so far the protests have remained peaceful, which is a good signal for the local currency. 

 In a verbal intervention to help the rupiah, Bank Indonesia Governor Sjahril Sabirin said Friday that the nation's central bank would continue its market intervention policy to help the rupiah if necessary.

title: Indonesia 's Ctrl Bk Gov: To  Intervene  To Protect Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's central bank said Friday it stands ready to intervene in the foreign exchange market to support the rupiah during the U.S.-led strike on Iraq. 

 Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves of $32 billion mean the country has adequate funds to stage a defense of the rupiah if necessary, central bank governor, Sjahril Sabirin, told reporters. 

 "We will continue to rely on intervention and money market operations to help the rupiah," Sjahril said. He gave no details on whether the bank has already been active this week. 

 The dollar is trading at 9,030 rupiah midday Friday, flat on Thursday's close. But the U.S. currency has moved higher in recent days on fears of anti-U.S. protests in Jakarta. 

 Demonstrators are expected to amass outside the U.S. embassy in Jakarta later Friday after weekly communal prayers. Indonesia is the world's most populous Muslim nation, and a large number of its people are against the war in Iraq.

 The dollar closed at 8,965 rupiah, up from its close Friday at IDR8,915 as the market anticipated widespread anti-West protests in Indonesia, the world's most populous Muslim country, if Iraq is attacked.

title: Bank Indonesia Says To Continue Cutting Rates Gradually
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's central bank said Tuesday that it will continue to cut interest rates gradually as inflationary pressure continues to ease and with the rupiah likely to remain stable versus the dollar. 

 "The monetary policy will continue to be able to accommodate a gradual and cautious rate cut," Bank Indonesia said in a statement following a monthly meeting of its board of governors late Monday. 

 Bank Indonesia Friday cut its key money market rate, the overnight intervention rate, to 11.500% from 12.125%. 

 The rate cut followed a fall in inflation to 7.34% on year in February from 8.74% in January. 

 Indonesia's government has been pressing for lower rates to help spur economic growth at a time when unemployment is rising and threatening social unrest. 

 The local currency has been stable as capital inflows linked to government asset sales has helped mitigate the damaging impact of fears over an Iraq war. 

 The dollar was trading at 8,885 rupiah at 0136 GMT, unchanged from its close Monday.

title: Most Asian  Currencies  Down Late; But Dlr Still Vulnerable

Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The dollar opened the new year on a firm note against most of its Asian counterparts, but longer-term prospects for the currency remained clouded by a possible war in Iraq, and concerns about the health of U.S. economy. 

 Helped by its relatively strong performance against the yen, the dollar notched gains against all Asian currencies, except the Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah. 

 Much of the dollar's support came from players covering their short positions in the currency after its recent steep declines in the region, analysts said. 

 The dollar had been "looking oversold," said Jimmy Koh, currency strategist at United Overseas Bank in Singapore. 

 "There was some pullback in dollar selling, but the fundamentals are still there for a weaker currency going forward," he said. 

 The dollar is likely to remain under pressure until at least the end of January when United Nations weapons inspectors are scheduled to deliver their report on Iraq's compliance with U.N. resolutions regarding disarmament, according to Koh. 

 Market participants will also be looking to upcoming economic data to see whether recent signs of weakness in the U.S. economy are temporary, or spell more trouble ahead, he said. 

 And even if the dollar manages to clear those obstacles, it will still face potentially crippling effects of the mammoth U.S. current account deficit, which is approaching 5% of gross domestic product, Koh added. 

 The dollar managed to grind its way back above the Y119 level for the first time in three sessions, hitting an intraday high of Y119.41. More verbal threats from Ministry of Finance officials about possible intervention to cap the yen's gains helped keep a floor under the dollar. 

 By the end of Asian trading the dollar had slipped back to Y119.05, still above Y118.70 in New York late Tuesday. Major global currency markets were closed Wednesday for the New Year holiday. 

 Importers were doing most of the dollar buying against the South Korean won, dealers said. 

 The dollar finished at 1,192.9l, above Tuesday's close at KRW1,186.5. 

 Dealing rooms were sparsely staffed after the New Year holiday and thin trading conditions exaggerated the won's moves. 

 The Singapore dollar weakened after the Monetary Authority of Singapore announced that it would maintain its neutral policy stance toward the currency. 

 The MAS also disclosed that the Singapore dollar had been trading for some time in the stronger half of the MAS' undisclosed target band for the currency, which was taken to mean the defacto central bank may not tolerate further gains, dealers said. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7432, up from S$1.7378 Tuesday. 

 Also, some dealers took advantage of the recent broad U.S. dollar weakness to reestablish long U.S. dollar positions, with the aim of taking profit later. 

 In Taipei, commercial demand from importers and interbank short-covering supported the U.S. dollar against the New Taiwan dollar. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.791, near its intraday high of NT$34.792, and up from NT$34.753 late Tuesday. 

 The Taiwan currency often tracks the yen, due to the close trade ties between Taiwan and Japan, and because Taiwan and Japan compete in several export categories. 

 Hedging by Philippine companies and thinning remittance inflows from Filipinos working overseas weighed on the peso. 

 The dollar closed at PHP53.470 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP53.300 Friday, the last time the peso was traded. 

 Traders said the demand for dollars rose as oil companies and other importers braced for a a weaker peso going forward. 

 Sentiment toward the currency has slipped in part due to a series of bomb attacks and an ambush that killed 30 people and injured dozens in the southern Philippines in the last two weeks. 

 The Indonesian rupiah ended higher against the dollar in volatile trading Thursday thanks to alleged intervention by the nation's central bank, dealers said. 

 Suspected intervention by the Bank of Indonesia kept the local currency well bid, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at 8,915 rupiah, down from IDR8,950 late Tuesday in thin offshore trade. Local financial markets were closed Tuesday in advance of New Year's Day. 

 Dealers said Bank Indonesia was suspected of intervening in the market after the dollar rose to an intraday high of IDR8,995 on the back of demand from local companies. 

 Against the baht, the dollar was quoted at THB43.110 in late Asian trading, down from THB43.130 late Tuesday. Financial markets in Bangkok were closed Tuesday, but the baht saw limited activity in offshore trading.

title: Indonesian rupiah confounds doomsayers.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 15 (Reuters) - Indonesia has been on the ropes this year as its economy struggled, its credit ratings fell to default levels, privatisation made a bumpy start, and the October bombings in Bali dented hopes of foreign investment inflows. 

 Yet the Indonesian rupiah has emerged as the best performing Asian currency of 2002 by a large margin. 

 In fact, a 17 percent gain year-to-date against the dollar, has made the rupiah second only to the South African rand's 34 percent rise in emerging market currencies. 

 "In 2002, in terms of Asian currencies, there was really only one place to be and that was in rupiah," said David Simmonds, emerging markets strategist at Royal Bank of Scotland in Singapore. 

 On Friday, the rupiah traded near a three-month high of 8,850 per dollar, supported by the expected sale of a key stake in state telecom firm PT Indosat, Indonesia's leading overseas call operator. 

 The IMF injected more confidence by approving a delayed $365 million loan early this month and last week ratings agency Fitch affirmed, rather than downgraded, the country's credit ratings, citing the government's quick response to the Bali bombings and its commitment to economic reform. 

 HIGH YIELD HELPED 

 Analysts say while Indonesia's economic conditions remain precarious and political stability is fragile, the currency could repeat its 2002 performance next year. 

 Cliff Tan, director of Asian research at Salomon Smith Barney in Singapore, said while a healthy recovery would need interest rates and inflation to come down from around 13 percent and 10 percent respectively, Indonesia's better-than-expected fiscal performance, steady state asset sales and progress on security issues would support the economy and the rupiah. 

 "It is not inconceivable that once again the rupiah would be the best performer next year, and even against a tepid recovery, Indonesia's economy may look better by next year-end than it does today," he said. Economists polled by Reuters in October lowered their 2002 growth forecast to 3.5 percent and for next year to 3.8 percent. 

 At the height of the Asian financial crisis in 1997/1998 the rupiah dropped to record lows of almost 17,000 to the dollar. It was shaken again in 2001, knocked to more than 12,000 per dollar on fears capital controls might be imposed. 

 But 2002 saw some unexpected positives. 

 Balance of payments pressure eased as Indonesia worked out debt restructuring deals with bilateral and private creditors. The deal pulled its credit ratings back above default grade, although they are still below investment grade. 

 More dollars flowed into the country from the sale of state assets making the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency a regular player in the forex market, Jakarta dealers say. For details on FDI inflows to Asia, click on 

 But more importantly, says Philip Wee, market strategist at DBS Bank in Singapore, the growing interest rate differential between the rupiah and the dollar provided a pillar of support. 

 "Because of the high yield, net exporters kept supplying the market with dollars," he said. 

 With Indonesia's real interest rates around three percent and U.S. rates at four-decade lows, much of Indonesia's $2 billion a month trade surplus was kept in the country. 

 RESILIENT INVESTORS 

 Much of the rupiah's strength this year has come from the resilience of domestic investors, who faced their toughest test after the Bali bombings, in which almost 200 people, mostly foreign tourists, were killed. 

 The rupiah slumped to six-month lows around 9,400 per dollar after the bombings, which raised security fears, in a country hardened to civil strife in recent years, to new highs. 

 Aggressive intervention by the central Bank Indonesia pushed the rupiah back towards 9,000, but analysts said the intervention was successful only because domestic investors did not respond to Bali as negatively as had been expected. 

 "The fact that local investors choose not to pull out as forcefully as expected made the central bank's job relatively easy," said James Malcolm, currency strategist at JP Morgan Chase. 

 Salomon's Tan said Jakarta's progress on investigations into the bomb attacks has also surprised most of its critics. 

 "In public, we have seen a noticeable step-up in official commitment to anti-terrorism efforts from the highest levels of government, and closer observers tell us that on the ground such efforts are driven more by national intelligence services than by their overseas critics," Tan said.

 Some foreign banks also sold dollars, likely on behalf of investors that were buying assets held by the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency and needed the local currency for payment, they added.

title: Indonesia's c.bank says Bali probe spurs rupiah.
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 19 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank said the strengthening of the rupiah against the dollar on Tuesday to a more than two-month high was primarily due to police progress in the Bali bombing investigation. 

 The currency - which sank to a five-and-a-half month low of 9,350 per dollar after the October 12 blasts on Indonesia's premier tourist island - was quoted at 8,985/8,995 per dollar around midday on Tuesday, its highest level since September 13. 

 "Progress in the Bali case, that's the main thing to do with the rupiah's strengthening," Central Bank Deputy Governor Miranda Goeltom told Reuters. 

 But one head of treasury at a foreign bank in Jakarta doubted the Bali probe was having much impact and said Bank Indonesia had been intervening heavily in the market, as recently as last week, to hold the unit around the 9,000 level. 

 "Most players are sitting here being a bit cynical about the bali bombing investigation," said the foreign bank source, who declined to be identified. 

 "Bank Indonesia has been in the market in the last couple of weeks and quite heavily - around $20-$30 million - not every day, just now and then," he added. 

 The government has proposed revising down the average rupiah rate for the 2003 budget to 9,000/dlr from a previous forecast of 8,700/dlr in the wake of the blasts, which killed nearly 200 mainly foreign tourists. 

 Despite the recent falls and the rupiah's failure to recover to anywhere near pre crisis levels, it is still the region's best performing currency, up more than 15 percent on the year. 

 Indonesian police investigating the Bali bombings have made significant progress in the past two weeks, beginning with the arrest of key suspect Amrozi, who confessed to his involvement, and the naming of six others as official suspects. 

 Goeltom said the rupiah was also benefitting from the overall strengthening of regional currencies against the U.S. dollar and the central bank's tight monetary policy. She declined to say whether the bank was intervening. 

 The foreign bank source said he felt there was some potential upside in the currency, maybe to 8,850/dlr, but said any gains would likely be fragile, especially in light of continued security threats. 

 "There are more threats out there and still very high risk and for that very reason, I would be cautious of the rupiah and I think at these levels and below, multinationals especially will start picking up dollars again just to hedge themselves," he said. 

 The Australian and U.S. embassies in Jakarta on Friday issued notices saying they had received "credible information" about the possible targeting of international schools associated or identified with Western interests. 

 That warning prompted several major international schools in the capital to close. They remained shut on Tuesday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Easier bias, peso at 14-month low.
text:
By Ovais Subhani
    SINGAPORE, Oct 18 (Reuters) - Security concerns and
economic worries pushed the Philippine peso to a fresh 14-month
low on Friday, as most Asian currencies treaded narrow ranges
with a weaker bias.
    The peso fell to 53.29 per dollar, a low since August 2001,
on early news of a grenade explosion in Manila's main financial
district, a day after a deadly bombing in southern Philippines.
    Also discouraging was data showing a trade deficit of $174
million in August after three months of surpluses, backing the
view that exports were losing momentum.
 
    Philippine central bank Deputy Governor Amando Tetangco
said the bank would intervene if necessary to ensure stability.
    "We are monitoring market movements. We have a flexible
exchange rate policy but we will take measures if necessary to
maintain orderly market conditions," Tetangco told reporters.
    Dealers in Manila said talk of the central bank checking


 rates with local banks offered some support. However, as there

 just above 53.24 kept the peso under pressure in late trade. 


 
    James Malcolm, currency strategist at JP Morgan Chase in
Singapore, said the oversold peso's downside was limited.
    "Offshore investors are long dollars and importers are well



hedged," he said, adding rising remittances from overseas



workers ahead of Christmas would also provide some near term



support.



BAHT STEADY



Rumours about central bank activity kept the Thai baht in a



tight range around 43.75, as dollar purchases from foreign



names absorbed sales, mainly from exporters and other local



players selling some dollar holdings built earlier in the week.



Dealers in Bangkok said amid lack of fresh local leads, the

Singapore dollar before pushing the baht further down.



They said no activity from the central bank was spotted,



but players were cautious on rumours the Bank of Thailand was



in the offshore market late Thursday to buy dollars at around

9,000.



Dealers in Jakarta said there was little price action in

title: Emerging Asia  FX -Rupiah leads rebound, funds sell dlr.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 16 (Reuters) - A sharp rebound in the Indonesian rupiah, after its heavy losses following the Bali bombings, and heavy profit-booking by U.S. investment houses sparked a rally in Asian regionals on Wednesday. 

 The currencies were also helped by a five percent rally in U.S. stocks, taking gains in the last four sessions to over 13 percent, that boosted regional share markets, although disappointing results from Intel Corp limited gains. 

 Traders said a firmer yen after the U.S. dollar's failure to hold its gains above 125 yen, a high since June, was an added plus. The yen was around 124.25 per dollar in late trade. 

 "Rallying stocks and the firmer yen is underpinning a broad-based Asian currency recovery with several markets showing signs of major reversal," Lehman Brothers strategist Ron Leven said in his market commentary. 

 As some of the bearishness related to regional security and economic risks ebbed, the rupiah rallied to 9,200 per dollar, regaining half the losses incurred after the bombings. 

 Some state banks were reported to have sold dollars, suspected to be on behalf of the central Bank Indonesia, which had intervened on Monday and Tuesday to prop up the rupiah at six-month low around 9,400. 

 "Similar to the September 11 attacks, many agreed that business activities and consumers spending would not be adversely affected as long as the Bali blast is an isolated incident," Jimmy Koh, economist at United Overseas Bank, said. 

 "Indeed, most Asian equities chose to ignore the weekend bombing focusing instead on the outperforming U.S. equities." 

 "Overall, other than the short-term financial markets implications, the real sector impact is likely to be contained for now, although there will definitely be an increase in regional risk aversion," Koh said. 

 Foreign fund inflows helped the Taiwan dollar bounce from an 11-month low of 35.268 and close at a two-week high of 34.97. 

 The Sing dollar, helped by the rupiah, strengthened to around 1.7950/60, where it traded last Friday, after hitting a five-month low of 1.8079 in offshore trade on Tuesday. The rupiah is thought to be significant in the trade-weighted basket that authorities use to manage the Singapore dollar. 

 Traders said heavy position liquidation by U.S.-based investment houses helped drive the rebound in the Sing dollar and the Thai baht. 

 SLUGGISH BAHT, RELUCTANT PESO 

 The baht made a slow start, but soon caught up with other regionals. The baht rallied past 44 per dollar from a 10-month low of 44.26 per dollar in offshore trade. 

 A 1.4 percent gain in Thai stocks and an upgrade of some bank ratings by Fitch also buoyed the baht in later deals. 

 "The baht is firm but lagging and we are thinking of getting long again via options," Leven's report said, adding the implied volatility had not moved from around seven percent for months. 

 The Korean won also erased losses sustained since the Bali blasts, and surged from five-month lows at 1,267 amid talk of foreign direct investment flows. 

 The Philippine peso came off this week's lows of 53.12, also a low since August last year, following its regional counterparts and reassured by comments from central bank deputy governor Amando Tetangco on Tuesday. 

 Tetangco said the government was expecting substantial remittances from overseas workers in the fourth quarter. He also advised against speculation and requesting those with remittances to convert those into pesos. 

 But traders said worries about the fiscal deficit had resurfaced. Media reports quoted a government official saying the deficit could surge to 180 billion pesos ($3.4 billion) in 2002.

title: ASIA DEBT: Indonesia Dlr Bonds Swoon After Bali Blast
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The fallout from the weekend bombings in Bali reverberated through Indonesia's debt market Tuesday, hammering dollar-denominated bonds especially hard. 

 The bomb blast shattered what little was left of investor confidence in Indonesia, and it further dimmed the nation's economic outlook, with the tourism industry expected to feel the brunt of the terrorist attack. 

 "The near-term implications on the economy will likely be harsh, as the latest incident puts to an end the hitherto improving trend in underlying macro fundamentals," J.P. Morgan Chase Bank said in a report. 

 The U.S. investment bank's estimates point to a possible loss of up to $2.7 billion in tourism earnings over the next 12 months - accounting for 1.3% of the country's annual gross domestic product and nearly half of the projected current account surplus. 

 The government's policy response will be crucial in reviving confidence among international investors, analysts said. 

 The Indonesian government has blamed al-Qaida for the attacks that ripped through nightclubs on the Indonesian resort island on Saturday night, killing almost 200 people and injuring many more. 

 Standard & Poor's Ratings Services warned late Monday the bomb blast "could adversely affect Indonesia's economy," although the international ratings agency maintained the sovereign long-term foreign currency rating at CCC-plus, with a stable outlook. 

 Indonesia's bonds were marked lower Tuesday as bond market participants from Hong Kong and Tokyo returned from their three-day weekend. Still, the bonds were barely traded. 

 "Dealers are marking them lower because they're not sure where the customers want to buy," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 The extent of the fall in prices was especially stark in the bids that were quoted in the market, as those with any interest in buying bided their time, waiting for lower levels. Earlier Tuesday, the offer spreads on Indonesian corporate credits widened some 50-60 basis points, while bids blew out even more by 100-120 basis points. 

 Indonesian bond prices consequently fell by two or three points compared with Friday's levels. 

 The Indonesian sovereign 7.75% bond due 2006 was quoted at 103-104. 

 Among Indonesian corporate credits, the more liquid Indofood 10.375% paper was quoted at 101-102. 

 "We think that net selling from foreign investors is likely, though we expect local players to step up on selective names, given that local liquidity remains strong and supply pipeline from Indonesia issuers would appear more unlikely now," UBS Warburg said in a report. 

 J.P. Morgan Chase reiterated its investment stance on Indonesia: "steer clear of Indonesia's sovereign debt given its unattractive risk-reward tradeoff." 

 At the heart of the debt market's concerns is the potentially damaging impact a weaker rupiah could have on the country's debt burden. 

 The bombings in Bali roiled Indonesian financial markets, sending the Indonesian currency reeling by more than 4% to a fresh six-month low of 9,400 rupiah to the dollar earlier Tuesday. The dollar had been quoted around IDR9,005 as of late Friday. 

 Although Indonesia's central bank has apparently intervened to slow the rupiah's slide, analysts expect the local currency to weaken further. 

 A weaker rupiah would make it harder to service Indonesia's $131.2 billion in foreign debt, of which some $71 billion is government debt and about $60 billion is private, analysts said. 

 Even after having undergone restructuring, many companies still haven't converted their outstanding dollar debt to rupiah, analysts said. 

 "For a company that has a lot of forex exposure, they're more vulnerable," said Prasoon Dayal, a Hong Kong-based credit analyst at J.P. Morgan. A weaker rupiah would increase their costs, hurting their bottom line. 

 "On the pure revenue side, I would imagine less companies will be directly affected," given that domestic demand will likely remain buoyant, said Dayal. 

 Indonesian corporations that will be hurt by the Bali aftermath include those that need to raise equity in order to recapitalize their balance sheet. Also, companies with a significant amount of foreign-currency debt relative to cash flow, short-term refinancing needs or foreign exchange-sensitivity to cash flow will be vulnerable, UBS Warburg said. 

 The fundamental impact on companies like cellular operator Telkomsel, Satelindo, Freeport Indonesia, Medco Energi and APP Group would be neutral, according to analysts at UBS Warburg. These companies have either sufficient financial cushions or revenues denominated in dollars, they added. 

 The impact on Indofood Sukses Makmur would be moderately negative, according to the investment bank. 

 "While revenues should be resilient, we expect profit margins to come under pressure from the weaker rupiah," said UBS Warburg. 

 Some 88% of the food company's revenue is denominated in rupiah, while 60% of production and distribution costs are denominated in U.S. dollars. 

 The impact on cement makers Indocement Tunggal Prakarsa and Semen Cibinong will be moderately negative as domestic demand for cement will likely decline, UBS Warburg said. 

 Both companies also have mainly dollar-denominated debt, though backing from their respective foreign parent companies and a favorable debt amortization profile should mitigate the fallout from the Bali blast, the bank added. 

 Car maker Astra International will be particularly vulnerable to the fallout from Bali because of its dollar debt and its ongoing debt restructuring. Most of the component cost of the automobiles and motorcycles the company manufactures are denominated in dollars, so the fundamental impact would be negative, UBS Warburg noted. 

 But Dayal at J.P. Morgan is more sanguine about the prospects for these Indonesian companies notwithstanding the potential Bali aftermath. 


The rupiah has been relatively resilient for most of the year, making
it easier for companies to service debts, so a brief pullback in the
currency isn't likely to create a huge problem, he said. The rupiah has
been the world's third strongest currency so far this year, having
appreciated some 11.5% against the dollar since the end of 2001.

title: Bk  Indonesia Intervenes  To Help IDR Off 6-Mo Low-Dealers
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's central bank intervened early Tuesday to help the rupiah off its six-month lows, dealers said. 

 The dollar rose to IDR9,400 in the opening minutes of trade Tuesday due to security concerns after the weekend Bali bombings, up from IDR9,340 at Monday's close. 

 Bank Indonesia, the central bank, sold dollars through the market, which has helped bring the U.S. currency back down to IDR9,375, dealers said. 

 Bank Indonesia had said Monday it will intervene to stop the local currency from losing too much ground after the bombing, which killed almost 200 people, most of whom were Western tourists. 

 The dollar hasn't traded as high as IDR9,400 since April this year. 

 Traders are waiting to see whether the central bank will be able to stop the dollar from further strengthening. 

 Market participants expect dollar resistance at IDR9,450 Tuesday.

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Heavy losses after Bali blasts.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 14 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah's plunge to a 5-= month low after weekend bomb blasts in Bali raised concerns over security and risk-aversion in Asia, forcing other regional currencies to fresh lows on Monday. 

 The rupiah fell to 9,350 per dollar, down 3.6 percent on the day, a level last seen in April, only recovering after central bankintervention around 9,300. Indonesia's stock market had fallen 10 percent by late afternoon. 

 Traders anxiously bought up the dollar against the Philippine peso , which was seen as vulnerable to security threats and was placed on high alert following the blasts, and the Singapore dollar , seen exposed if foreign businesses shift out of Asia. 

 Moreover, there was disheartening data from the United States on Friday showing retail sales fell more than anticipated and consumer sentiment hit a nine-year low. 

 "While Asian countries' current account surpluses have kept their asset markets and currencies fairly buffered from risk-aversion flows and from contagion from Latin America's woes year-to-date, fears of heightened security risk are likely to weigh on regionals," UBS Warburg said in a market commentary. 

 By afternoon, regional currencies were marginally off their lows but substantially weaker than Friday's finish, while stock markets in Thailand and Philippines ended down, as traders assessed the impact of the blasts. 

 No one has claimed responsibility for the bombs late Saturday night in Bali. The explosions ripped through packed nightclubs popular with foreign tourists and killed at least 183 people. 

 Traders also felt market reaction had been subdued, with trade thinned by holidays in Japan and Hong Kong. The U.S. bond market is also shut on Monday. 

 MULTI-MONTH LOWS 

 The Thai baht tested early February lows at 44.02 per dollar and the central bank denied market talk that it had intervened to prop up the currency. 

 The peso extended 14-month lows and slipped past 53 to 53.05, ending close to those lows. 

 The Taiwan dollar slide past Friday's close at a 15-year low of 35.157 and hit a low of 35.21. 

 Global growth concerns and a drop in the Korean consumer outlook to a nine-month low weighed on the won , although stock purchases by foreign investors buoyed the currency to a firmer close. 

 The Singapore dollar bounced off a five-month low of 1.8025 and clambered back towards 1.79 as other regionals recovered. 

 A JP Morgan note said any weakness in the rupiah could have a heavy impact on the Sing dollar, given the rupiah was a key component of the trade-weighted index against which Singapore is believed to manage its exchange rate. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR AT 0900 GMT Change on the day

title: Dollar Ends Firm Against Yen, Euro and Pound in Subdued Trading
text:
Dow Jones Newsiwres 

 NEW YORK -- The dollar put in a mixed performance Monday -- edging moderately higher against the yen and modestly lower against the Swiss franc -- following the weekend bombing on the Indonesian Island of Bali, though more localized currencies including the Australian and New Zealand dollars did see some selling pressure. 

 Late Monday in New York, the dollar was trading at 124.26 yen, up from 124.03 yen late Friday in New York. The euro was worth around 98.67 U.S. cents, unchanged from late Friday in New York. Against the Swiss franc, the dollar was worth about 1.4810 Swiss francs, down from 1.4831 francs Friday in New York. Sterling was changing hands at $1.5572, down from $1.5614 late Friday in New York. 

 Aside from slight weakness against the classic safe-haven currency -- the Swiss franc -- perhaps the most remarkable currency reaction to Saturday's blasts was the fact that the dollar barely reacted at all. 

 Even with the hike in risk aversion following the Bali attack -- which President Bush said appeared to be linked to al Qaeda -- the greenback strengthened against the yen and the pound and held its ground against the euro. 

 No doubt partly accounting for the dollar's resilience were the extremely thin trading conditions in foreign-exchange markets, as many financial professionals were out of the office with holidays in Canada, the U.S. and Japan. But analysts said the dollar's lack of movement also stemmed from a sense that other terrorist events had to a certain extent, been expected. 

 "The dollar has already priced in a lot risk of this kind of thing," said a currency analyst at UBS Warburg, who asked not to be named. "That supports the view that [the Bali bombing] is not being seen as a sign of heightened global risk." 

 The dollar was also likely reverting to its traditional role as a magnet for investors in times of global turmoil. 

 With sliding stock markets around the world and the growing threat of a U.S.-led war on Iraq, investors were increasingly risk averse ahead of the Bali explosion in any case. This has kept the ripple effects from the devastating bomb attack largely within the region. 

 The Indonesian rupiah crumbled to its weakest level in almost six months, while the attack also sent shock waves through regional currency markets and knocked more than 10% off Jakarta stocks. The blast also initially supported gold and oil prices. The rupiah, which is barely traded in New York, was quoted at 9,330 Indonesian rupiah late in the day, up from 9,010 rupiah Friday, but off an intraday peak of 9,350 rupiah after Bank Indonesia, the central bank, intervened to stem the rupiah's slide. 

 Explosions ripped through a nightclub district in southern Bali Saturday night, leaving at least 188 dead and hundreds more injured. Investors' rattled nerves over the blast dragged down currencies and stock markets in Asia, as well as shares in Europe. That tension carried over initially also into Wall Street in early trade, although the broad market indexes managed to end the day in positive territory. 

 Analysts said the attack could pose longer-term threats to the Australian and New Zealand currencies, potentially hampering tourism and export demand. Australia, because of its proximity to Indonesia and the large number of Australians among the casualties, is particularly vulnerable, some said. "It will have some effect on the [Australian] economy," said Tim Stewart, chief currency strategist for Morgan Stanley in New York. "Certainly you would expect a knock on consumer confidence." 

 The Australian dollar was trading at 54.64 U.S. cents late Monday, down from 54.95 cents late Friday. The New Zealand dollar was worth 47.86 U.S. cents, down from 48.10 cents late Friday. 

 Elsewhere, the other key focus for foreign-exchange markets was Brazil, after the central bank called an extraordinary meeting and hiked interest rates by three percentage points, in a move that analysts said seemed designed to shore up the real after the currency fell to an all-time low around 4.104 Brazilian reals last week. 

 "Ultimately this is a stopgap measure" to help tide the real over until the new presidential administration takes office in Brazil next year, said Steven Leach, emerging markets strategist at Citibank in New York. 

 Nonetheless, the real failed to take heart from the rate hike, ending the day weaker as analysts questioned the implications of the surprise rate hike, both for Brazil's debt servicing costs and for the real economy. Late Monday, the currency was quoted at 3.860 Brazilian reals to the dollar, weaker than 3.820 reals late Friday. 

 "This interest rate hike is unlikely to do much [that's] constructive, apart from lingering the growth slowdown," said Yianos Kontopoulos, global head of currency strategy at Merrill Lynch in New York. "I don't understand why they needed to do it now as opposed to a week from now. I wouldn't even understand it then." 

 The central bank's decision came nine days before a regularly scheduled meeting, leaving market participants confused as to why it had rushed the rate hike now, particularly given the real's apparent lack of sensitivity to interest rates. "The currency is suffering from a confidence issue and 300 basis points will have no meaning here," said Douglas Smith, chief economist for the Americas at Standard Chartered in New York. "The bias for the real to weaken will be unaffected," by the rate hike. 

 Analysts said the central bank's decision now further complicates the prospects of government-backed hopeful Jose Serra in a second-round presidential vote on Oct. 27. Serra is already trailing in a distant second place in opinion polls to Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva of the left-leaning Workers' Party.
