title: Asian  Currencies  Down Late;Rupiah At 5-Mo Low On Bombing
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah crumbled to a five-month low Monday after the weekend's fatal bomb attacks in Bali, which sent shock waves through regional currency markets and roiled the local stock market. 

 The incident, which killed at least 188 people, heightened risk aversion in Asia and drove the Singapore dollar, the Thai baht and the Philippine peso to levels unseen in several months. 

 The dollar closed at 9,330 rupiah, up from IDR9,010 Friday, but off an intraday peak of IDR9,350 after Bank Indonesia, the central bank, intervened to stem the rupiah's slide. 

Indonesia's key stock index plunged 10.4% to 337.475, its lowest since April 1998, though other markets were mixed. Singapore shares climbed 0.4%, Korean shares jumped 4.6%, and Taiwan's stock index rose 1.6%, but Thailand's key stock index fell nearly 2%, Malaysian stocks lost 1.2%, and Philippine shares fell 0.4%. 

 Bank Indonesia said it will continue to monitor the rupiah and will act if necessary to keep its level stable. 

 But the central bank may be hard-pressed to defend the currency amid mounting security concerns. 

 The bombings added to fears voiced by the U.S. government recently that Indonesia - known for its relatively weak law enforcement - has become a base for international terrorism with links to al-Qaida. 

 Ratings agency Standard & Poor's said the bomb blasts could hurt tourism, a major revenue earner for Indonesia. The agency said the government will have to walk a fine line to win both domestic and international support to regain confidence in the country and its government. 

 Analysts see further downside to the rupiah going forward as jitters over global terrorism prompt investors to shun this region. 

 Chong Hui Chin, currency strategist at J.P. Morgan Chase Bank, said the incident "reinforces our view that things are not going to look up (for Indonesia) in the next three months." 

 The U.S. investment bank, which had previously been upbeat about Indonesia, last week revised its dollar/rupiah target to 10,000 by year end, from 8,700 previously. 

 Bank of America said any attempts by the government to clamp down on terror groups could induce a further backlash from them and dramatically increase domestic security risks. 

 "The perception of such risks is likely to damage Indonesia's capability to attract much needed foreign capital and hurt its already fragile economy," the bank said in a note. 

 In the Philippines, the incident in Bali spooked a market that was already jittery after a bomb blast killed six people in the southern Mindanao island Friday, traders said. 

 The dollar pierced the key 53-peso resistance to end at 53.030 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, its highest close since Aug. 8, 2001, and up from PHP52.750 Friday. 

 Some traders suspected the central bank sold dollars at PHP52.990 and PHP53.030 earlier in the session to prevent the currency from staging a convincing break of the PHP53-level. 

 Meanwhile, the U.S. currency bounced off early highs against the Singapore dollar and was quoted around S$1.7986 late in Asia, from S$1.7934 Friday. 

 Earlier, the dollar jumped to S$1.8022, its highest since late-May 

 In Thailand, early demand for dollars dragged the baht to its lowest since end-January, though this was tempered after exporters sold the U.S. unit when it reached its intraday peak of 44.03 baht. 

 But later in the day, dollar buying by local oil companies and importers pushed the dollar up again to close the Asian session at 44.02 baht, up from THB43.875 Friday. 

 There was no sign of the central bank intervening during the day as the baht's weakness was minimal compared with other currencies, traders said. 

Central bank Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said the baht's movement was minimal and in line with other regional currencies. 

 He said the central bank is monitoring the currency's movements, but thinks the effects from the Bali bombings will be limited. 

 Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said the attacks may have an indirect impact on Thailand's tourism industry. 

 Previous security incidents in Indonesia and Philippines have resulted in tourists diverting their travel plans to Thailand, which has a reputation for greater stability and less strife. 

 Elsewhere, the New Taiwan Dollar extended losses to close at a fresh low since January 1987 as importers and interbank players bought U.S. currency. 

 Traders said market players are concerned the Bali bomb blasts will add further gloom to the already murky outlook for the region's economy. 

 But volume was thin with market players mostly sidelined as the Japan and Hong Kong markets were closed for holidays. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$35.168, up from NT$35.157. Friday, but off an intraday high of NT$35.21 as offshore non-deliverable forward players took profit on the dollar after modest foreign equity inflows. 

 The South Korean won was relatively steady with trade at a trickle since Tokyo markets were shut for a holiday and U.S. markets will be closed later in the global day. 

 The dollar ended at 1,259.3 won, slightly down from KRW1,259.5 Friday. 

 The rally on the local bourse helped calm sentiment toward the won, which was pressured in recent days by plunging share prices, said Oh Suktae, economist at Citibank/Salomon Smith Barney.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends At 5-Mo Low Vs Dlr On Bali Bombings
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah took a severe drumming against the dollar Monday, closing at a five-month low in a volatile session after the weekend terrorist attacks on the island of Bali. 

 The dollar rose to an intraday high of 9,350 rupiah earlier in the day but slipped back slightly to close at a five-month high of IDR9,330 as the central bank intervened. That was 3.4% higher than its close Friday at IDR9,010. 

 The Saturday night attack on a nightclub packed with Western tourists on Bali has further undermined investor confidence toward Indonesia, analysts said. 

 The attacks could adversely affect Indonesia's economy and influence the politics of the country, Standard & Poor's Corp. said in a press release Monday. 

 "The government's response to the fatal bombing, which killed more than 180 people, has implications for policy direction, and potentially the result of elections due next year. To a more limited extent, the incident could have fiscal and economic implications," it added. 

 The dollar came off its intraday high after Bank Indonesia intervened in the market to sell the dollar. Confirming its intervention, the central bank said in a statement it will continue to monitor the rupiah and will act if necessary to keep its level stable. 

 It didn't mention how much it sold in the local foreign currency market, but dealers reckoned it sold between $15 million and $20 million. Dealers also alleged that the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency joined forces with Bank Indonesia to help the local unit. 

 Dealers said they expect the dollar to test IDR9,400 resistance Tuesday as foreign investors are expected to buy the dollar in the coming days after they unloaded Indonesian stocks Monday. 

 The Indonesian stock market main index fell 38.991 points, or 10.36%, to close at a four-year low of 337.475. 

 Bank Indonesia is expected to try to defend the rupiah again. But dealers doubt if it will be successful given the extent of the blow on the Indonesian economy from the attacks. 

 Many currency strategists predict the dollar to close around IDR10,000 by the end of the year.

title: Bali Blasts Deal Blow To Confidence In Southeast Asia
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The deadly weekend bombings in Bali have dealt a major blow not only to Indonesia's economy but to efforts across southeast Asia to win back investor confidence after economic setbacks in the past five years. 

 Businessmen and analysts worry that the massive car bomb which tore apart a nightclub on the Indonesian resort island Saturday night, killing at least 188 people and injuring hundreds more, indicates Indonesia has become a base for international terrorism with links to al-Qaida. 

 If so, that could mean further such attacks in coming months, not only in Indonesia but in the Philippines, which is fighting a Muslim secessionist movement, or Malaysia and Singapore, which have had to act against terrorist groups since last year's September 11 attacks in the U.S. 

 "This just puts an exclamation point on the concept that southeast Asia is a hotbed of international terrorism," said Dick Baker, Indonesia specialist at the East-West Center in Honolulu. 

 Although nobody had claimed responsibility for the attacks by Monday, the Bali bombings significantly expanded the violence in Indonesia beyond previous attacks, which were carried out mainly by separatist movements, Baker added. 

 "This has all the earmarks of an international terrorist attack," he said. 

 If the idea of southeast Asia as a terrorist danger spot becomes entrenched among U.S., European and Japanese investors, analysts said, capital flows into southeast Asia will shrink further, some institutions may pull long-term money out, and trade and tourism could suffer serious damage. 

 "This comes at a very bad time for everyone," said Paul Schymyck, regional economist at IDEAglobal in Singapore. "With a possible double-dip recession coming in the U.S., this is the last thing you need." 

 Indonesian markets plunged Monday in response to the bombings. The Jakarta stock index lost 10% to its lowest levels since April 2001, while the rupiah tumbled from Friday's close of 9,010 against the dollar to 9,350, before intervention by Indonesia's central bank cut its losses. 

 Traders said the rupiah could drop as low as 10,000 by the end of this year if security fears persisted, and in Jakarta on Monday such fears were widespread, especially after the U.S. embassy said it was sending non-essential staff out of the country. 

 Indonesian officials warned foreign energy firms could be the next targets. "There is information that the energy sector will be targeted by terrorists," Indonesia's senior security minister, Susilo Bambang Yudhoyono, told reporters, pledging to step up protection of such investments. 

 Markets Outside Indonesia Quite Calm 

 Elsewhere in the region, however, markets were much calmer. Although the Singapore dollar sank to a four-month low of 1.8030 against the U.S. dollar in the opening minutes of trade from Friday's 1.7835 close, it had come well off that low by afternoon. 

 The Philippine peso and Thai baht also fell, and the Australian dollar slipped amid concern that the terrorists could be targeting Australian citizens; many of the victims in Bali were Australian tourists. But these currencies didn't drop as much as the Singapore dollar, and currencies in northern Asia were stable. 

 In Asian stock markets, there was selling of individual stocks with large business interests in Indonesia or exposure to southeast Asian tourism, particularly airlines. Australia's Qantas lost 2.5%, and Singapore Airlines had dropped 2.9% by late afternoon. 

 But outside Jakarta, stock markets weren't sold across the board, and several actually rose on the back of Wall Street's strong rebond on Friday. Sydney's S&P/ASX 200 rose 1.2% and Singapore's main index was up 0.6% in late trade; "temporarily funds exiting Indonesia are seeing Singapore as a safer place," a foreign broking house trader said. 

 Asian U.S. dollar bond spreads widened slightly in response to the Bali attacks but trade was thin, partly because of Monday's closure of Hong Kong, Tokyo and the U.S. Treasurys market for holidays. 

 HSBC economist John Edwards said the uncertainty created by the Bali bombings had probably eradicated any remaining chance of Australia's central bank raising rates at its next board meeting on November 5. But he added that the central bank likely retained its tightening bias, given economic factors such as Australia's housing boom. 

 Fund manager William Pitman at Henderson Global Investors, which has about US$2 billion invested in Asia, said it was too soon to think there would be an exodus of foreign money from southeast Asia. 

 "It really depends whether (terrorism) is perceived to be more of an endemic problem, which it has probably not proved to be yet," he said, adding that ultimately, economics would drive the stock markets. 

 Economies Vulnerable To Confidence Shocks 

 But the region's economies are vulnerable to any confidence shock, analysts noted. Singapore last week reported growth in the third quarter that was well below expectations. The Philippine economy is coming under increasing pressure from its growing budget deficit, and Malaysia's export sector is threatened by a possible slowdown in the event of a U.S. invasion of Iraq. 

 Foreign companies, which are already directing a larger portion of their overseas investment to China, may now have one more reason to avoid southeast Asia. 

 "The bomb blasts illustrate the risks involved in many countries in Asia, particularly southeast Asia," said Steve Brice, chief economist at Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. 

 The Bali attacks may reinforce the perception that China and northeast Asian economies such as South Korea and Taiwan are better placed in terms of their risk-return profile than southeast Asia, he said. 

 Singapore, a traditional safe haven in Southeast Asia, "may now appear more vulnerable", Brice added. 

 Song Seng Wun, regional economist at securities house G.K. Goh in Singapore, said the Bali attacks were unlikely to have any long-term impact on Asian economies unless they were followed by more terrorist incidents. 

 But if there is a string of further attacks, there will be negative implications across a range of commercial activities, in tourism, the services sector, the travel industry and domestic consumption, he said. 

 As it is, the Bali tragedy may mean an expected lift in regional economies in the fourth quarter of this year could be less than originally expected, even though economic indicators will have support from their low bases during the post-September 11 period last year. 

 -By Alan Yonan Jr., Dow Jones Newswires; 65 6415 4045; alan.yonan@dowjones.com

title: Asian  Currencies  At Multi-Mo Lows After Bali Bomb Blasts
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- -The weekend's fatal bomb blast in Bali dragged the Indonesian rupiah to its lowest level in five months and roiled the stock market Monday, sending shock waves through regional currency markets. 

 The Singapore dollar tumbled to near five-month lows, the Thai baht dived to an eight-month trough and the Philippine peso crashed to a 14-month low. 

 Traders said what appeared to be intervention by Indonesia's central bank helped limit the dollar's rise in that market, but it was likely to be little more than a temporary respite, as jitters over global terrorism prompt investors to shun this region. 

 Around 0520 GMT, the dollar was quoted around 9,263 rupiah, up from IDR9,010 at the Asian close Friday, but off its intraday peak of IDR9,335, which was its highest level since early-May. 

 The Jakarta Stock Exchange Composite index was down 9.1% to 342.122. 

 At the same time, the dollar was quoted around S$1.7990, up from S$1.7935 late Friday, and at PHP52.95, up from its PHP52.75 close Friday. 

 Regional stock markets were faring better, with Singapore's STI up 0.8% at 1385 and Taiwan's benchmark index up more than 1% at 3910.98. 

 Stock markets in Malaysia and Thailand were both slightly lower, while Korea's KOSPI index was up nearly 5% at 615.60. 

 Hong Kong and Tokyo financial markets were closed for holidays. 

 Saturday's car-bomb attack on a popular nightspot in Bali, which killed at least 188, marks the first large-scale terrorist attack directed at foreigners in Indonesia. Two other bombs went off almost simultaneously, one at a U.S. consular office in Bali and the other near the Philippine consulate on Sulawesi island, but there were no casualties in those attacks. 

 Although no group immediately claimed responsibility for the attacks, the bombings added to fears voiced by the U.S. government recently that Indonesia - known for its relatively weak law enforcement - has become a base for international terrorism with links to al-Qaida. 

 Analysts say the weekend's events support their views that there's little to be positive about Indonesia going forward. 

 Just last week, J.P. Morgan Chase Bank, which had previously been upbeat about the country, sent out notes to clients advising them to cut rupiah positions. 

 Chong Hui Chin, a currency strategist at the bank, said J.P. Morgan has also revised its dollar/rupiah target to 10,000 by year end, from 8,700 previously. 

 That revision was made just before the weekend's events, and it "reinforces out view that things are not going to look up (for Indonesia) in the next three months," she said. 

 Irene Cheung, sovereign and forex strategist at ABN Amro Bank in Singapore, said the blasts were a wake up call to regional governments, and may prompt more cooperation among the countries in handling the threat. 

 But in the near term, it adds to the broad market uncertainty and will likely keep investors sidelined on Asia, she said. 

 The terrorist attacks are expected to have a negative impact on travel in the region. Japan's Foreign Ministry was quick to issue a warning for Japanese nationals in Indonesia to stay away from crowded places as much as possible. 

 In Thailand, Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra said the attacks in Bali may have an indirect impact on Thailand's tourism industry, but it remains to be seen to what extent there would be a reduction in travel overall. 

 He said the baht should continue to move in line with other regional currencies. 

 "The baht doesn't need to weaken more or even as much as the rest of the regional currencies because we aren't suffering any (direct) impact," Thaksin told reporters. 

 "The baht must move in line with the region. If the baht weakens or strengthens in line with the region it is no problem for us," he said. 

 The dollar was trading just under THB44 at midday, off an early eight-month high of THB44.03 but up from THB43.875 at the Asian close Friday. 

 The Taiwan dollar extended losses from Friday's weakest closing since January 1987, though this was offset by some central bank intervention, traders said. 

 At midday, the dollar was traded at NT$35.171, up from NT$35.157 Friday, but off a high of NT$35.210 earlier. 

 The Korean won was relatively stable, with the dollar quoted at KRW1,258.5, down slightly from KRW1,259.5 Friday. 

 -By Nirmala Menon, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4046; nirmala.menon@dowjones.com

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Late On Yen, Oil, US Ports Closure
text:
Of Dow Jones Newswires 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Several Asian currencies hurtled to multiple-month lows Monday, driven by a sagging yen and falling equity markets, with Japan's Nikkei 225 Stock Average hitting a new 19-year trough. 

 Higher oil prices on news of an explosion on a French oil tanker off eastern Yemen early Sunday and the continued closure of U.S. West Coast ports due to a labor dispute took further toll on regional currencies. 

 The ports shutdown, which comes in the run-up to the critical Christmas shopping season, could hurt Asian exports as these ports are the main entry points to key U.S. markets. 

 It adds to existing uncertainty about global economic growth, especially that of the U.S., where latest data continues to send mixed signals, analysts said. 

 "There's so much of uncertainties plaguing the markets at the moment. There's a whole list of risks," said Claudio Piron, Singapore-based head of foreign exchange strategy at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 The South Korean won closed at its weakest level against the dollar since May 24, reflecting the yen's drop and the sharp fall on the local bourse, where the key index plunged 3.6%. 

 The dollar, which was also buoyed by offshore buying, closed at 1,240.9 won, up from KRW1,232.4 Friday. 

 "Participants continued to buy dollars on jitters over the stock market's weakness and the dollar/yen's rise," said A.R. Park, a dealer at Shinhan Bank. "They are buying dollars or delaying their dollar sales on anticipation of further gains in the U.S. currency." 

 Uncertainties over the global economy and the possibility of a war in Iraq have caused players to hold on to or buy dollars recently, traders said. 

 The Philippine peso extended last week's losses to close at yet another 14-month low, but central bank Deputy Governor Amando Tetangco reiterated that the currency's weakness is likely only temporary. 

 He told Dow Jones Newswires that the peso has been pressured by general weakness in regional currencies, and also dollar short-covering by banks. 

 He said the peso is expected to be lifted toward year-end by seasonally stronger remittances from Filipinos working abroad. 

 Tetangco said the central bank hasn't been selling dollars to support the peso, but is monitoring the foreign exchange market to prevent any excess volatility. 

 The dollar ended at its session peak of 52.900 pesos, up from PHP52.725 Friday, and its highest close since Aug. 9, 2001. 

 Some traders said demand for dollars was mainly coming from oil companies bracing for higher crude prices globally. 

 Declining stocks and weak regional currencies dragged the New Taiwan dollar to a seven-month closing low. 

 Taiwan's main stock index fell 3.5% to a fresh 11-month low, prompting traders to switch from the local dollar to the U.S. currency. 

 The dollar ended at NT$35.069, its highest close since March 5 and up from NT$34.994 Friday. It traded between NT$35.046 and NT$35.089 intraday. 

 The Thai baht tumbled to a six-month low despite two apparent interventions by the central bank, traders said. 

 The dollar hovered at around 43.54 baht at the Asian open before a run up fueled by offshore players' adjustments to keep the local unit in line with regional currencies, and also demand from local oil importers. 

 Oil importers bought dollars as global oil prices rose following the oil tanker explosion off the coast of Yemen. 

 "The dollar's steep rise against the yen also convinced offshore players to buy the greenback. Most of the active players were European banks," a local bank trader said. 

 "A Japanese bank in Singapore, which usually acts on behalf of BOT (Bank of Thailand), bought the baht two times at THB43.62 and THB43.72. But the orders were too weak to make much difference," the trader added. 

 The dollar hit a six-month peak of THB43.80 before closing the Asian session a tad lower at THB43.78, but up sharply from THB43.51 Friday. 

 Elsewhere, the Singapore currency fell as the weaker yen triggered sporadic bouts of aggressive U.S. dollar buying. 

 Market participants also started to take a more cautious tone against the local dollar ahead of advance estimates of third-quarter gross domestic product data Thursday. 

 The U.S. dollar opened the Asian session at around S$1.7825, and then rose sharply to breach the psychological S$1.7900 resistance level, sparked by its gains against the yen. 

 The jump caught some market participants holding short U.S.-dollar positions, sparking further buying to drive it to a session high of S$1.7916. 

 But volume was thin and liquidity tight, with only a few dominant interbank market participants trading actively in the market. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around S$1.7902, from S$1.7804 late Friday. 

 In Indonesia, the central bank was again suspected of intervening to hold the Indonesian rupiah steady after the long weekend, traders said. 

 Bank Indonesia is believed to have been in the market almost daily since late last month. The central bank doesn't comment on specific interventions. 

 Overall trading was thin as the market still lacked fresh incentives, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 9,015 rupiah, unchanged from Thursday, after trading between IDR9,012 and IDR9,020. The markets were closed for a public holiday Friday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Up Late On Yen, Dlr Sales By Exporters
text:
Of Dow Jones Newswires 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were lifted along with the yen late Monday after the dollar slid following the ouster of Japan's top banking regulator who was known to oppose a publicly funded cleanup of banks' bad loans 

 The Korean won and the New Taiwan dollar also gained from end-of-month dollar sales by exporters. 

 The U.S. currency shed more than a yen and a half in Asia on heavy selling by U.S. and European funds that correctly bet top bank regulator Hakuo Yanagisawa would be removed in a Cabinet reshuffle. 

 In a surprise move, he was replaced with Heizo Takenaka, one of the most vocal proponents of a stepped-up bank cleanup. 

 Coupled with dollar sales by exporters, the U.S. unit sank to an 11-day low of Y121.12 in Asia. 

 Claudio Piron, Singapore-based head of foreign exchange strategy at Standard Chartered Bank, said market players may also be betting Japan would take other surprise action going forward, which would be positive for the yen. 

 By extension, that would mean more upside for regional currencies, especially the Singapore dollar and the Korean won which most closely track the yen, he said. 

 The dollar ended nearly flat at 1,227.8 won from KRW1,227.9 Friday as the South Korean unit recouped early losses in the wake of the yen's strength. 

 The session was initially marked by strong demand for dollars due to large-scale short-covering by banks, which took the U.S. unit to a day's high of KRW1,233.0. 

 But the dollar's subsequent decline against the yen, coupled with end-of-month sales of the U.S. currency by local exporters helped the won recover, traders said. 

 In Singapore, market participants took their cue from the yen's firm tone to unwind long dollar positions. 

 The dollar sellers were mainly U.S. and Japanese investment houses that had built up long positions since Friday, traders said. 

 The market players had to cut these positions to minimize losses following the sharp fall on Wall Street Friday, they added. 

 But trading was thin amid continued uncertainty over the U.S. economy, the city state's biggest export market. 

 Against the Singapore dollar, the U.S. unit was quoted around S$1.7778 late in Asia, from S$1.7782 Friday. 

 Meanwhile, Taiwan exporters also sold the U.S. unit for local dollars to pay salaries or cover other expenses, traders said. 

 That, together with the yen's strength, helped the New Taiwan dollar recover from early losses that were caused partly by the exit of foreign equity funds and the yen's initial weakness. 

 The U.S. dollar ended at NT$34.918, slightly down from Friday's NT$34.921. 

 Intraday, the dollar reached a peak of NT$34.980, and hit a trough at NT$34.913. 

 The island's central bank, which regularly intervenes in the market to prevent any sharp movement of the currency, was largely quiet Monday, traders said. 

 The Philippine peso was also buoyed by the yen-led rise of regional currencies although trading volume was almost flat, indicating mild activity. 

 But activity in the black market was reportedly strong. One bank trader said the dollar was traded between PHP52.55 and PHP52.63 in the parallel market. 

 Some dollar buyers may have opted to go there to skip documentation required by banks and the central bank, another bank trader said. 

 On the Philippine Dealing System however, the dollar closed at PHP52.400, slightly down from PHP52.460 Friday, after moving between PHP52.385 and PHP52.450. 

 Trading volume was hardly changed at $83.7 million, from S$83.1 million previously. 

 In Indonesia, the central bank was again suspected of intervening to support the rupiah, helping to counter further negative news which took the dollar to its intraday high of IDR9,017 early in the session. 

 News that soldiers had opened fire on police on the island of Sumatra, leaving four police dead, helped keep the dollar well bought, traders said. 

 But Bank Indonesia, the central bank, was reported to sell about $5 million through state banks, with thin volumes aiding in pushing the dollar lower. 

 The dollar ended at its intraday low of IDR9,000, from IDR9,015 Friday. 

 Elsewhere, the dollar was also weaker against the Thai baht, in line with the regional trend. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around THB43.40, from THB43.43 late Friday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Late On Yen, HK$ Peg Speculation
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- A weak yen and renewed speculation of a delinking of the Hong Kong dollar from the U.S. unit drove Asian currencies lower Friday, with the Philippine peso closing at its lowest in over a year. 

 The first ever undersubscription of a 10-year Japanese government bond auction highlighted uncertainty about Japan's economic policy and weighed on the yen, which broadly sets the trend for regional currencies. 

 Analysts said the dollar is also plagued with its own problems, given weak economic data from the U.S., falling stock prices and continued fears of a war with Iraq. 

 So, the broader picture lies in "trying to work out which of the major currencies to dislike the least," commented David Simmonds, senior emerging markets strategist for Asia at The Royal Bank of Scotland. 

 Although the yen's movements against the dollar was the main driving force in regional markets, revival of talk that the Hong Kong authorities may abandon the local dollar's 7.8 peg to the U.S. unit created a buzz in the early in the trading session. 

 The speculation, which sent premiums on one-year Hong Kong dollar forwards soaring, was fanned by a Hong Kong news report on lawmaker Emily Lau's request for a study of the peg. 

 The Singapore dollar and the Thai baht faced mild selling pressure on the speculation, which was largely dismissed by analysts and traders. 

 However, "most investors are holding on to the dollar amid the uncertainties," a trader said. 

 The Hong Kong Monetary Authority later issued a statement saying the government "has clearly stated that it has no plan to change the linked exchange rate system," while Lau told Dow Jones Newswires that she was appalled by the furor and was ready to support abandoning the proposed study. 

 Late in Asia, the U.S. dollar was quoted around $1.7796 against the Singapore unit, from $1.7693 late Thursday. 

 Activity was moderate as market participants remain uncertain about the U.S. dollar's near-term direction on lingering concerns of a possible war between the U.S. and Iraq, traders said. 

 In the Philippines, the dollar ended at 52.475 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System - its highest finish since Aug. 9, 2001 - from PHP52.285 Thursday. 

 Volume jumped to $118 million from $76 million. 

 Despite an initial dip to PHP52.35 in early trading, the dollar climbed steadily for the rest of the day, hitting an intraday high of PHP52.49. 

 "The peso simply tracked the depreciating yen," said a trader at a local bank. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency ended at 34.772, up from NT$34.620 at the previous session close, after trading between NT$34.670 and NT$34.780 intraday. 

 Traders said the local dollar tracked the yen, as it often does due to close trade ties between Japan and Taiwan, and also because they have similar export markets. 

 A rise in equity-related outflows, which increased demand for the U.S. currency, also weighed on the local dollar, a dealer said. The Weighted Price Index of the Taiwan Stock Exchange fell 1.4% to a fresh 2002 low of 4429.25 points Friday. 

 However, traders said the central bank intervened to shore up the local unit by selling U.S. dollars at around NT$34.75. 

 In Indonesia, traders said the country's central bank also intervened to support the rupiah, which fell as low as 9,040 after Thursday's sharp decline on the stock market. 

 The dollar closed Asian trading at IDR9,030 up from IDR9,005 Thursday. 

 The central bank has a policy of intervening but never confirms specific actions. Recently, it said it's happy with the dollar trading below IDR9,000. 

 All eyes are now on the likelihood of a U.S. led war on Iraq, which is widely seen as a danger for security in Indonesia, the world's most populous Muslim country. The U.S. claims a number of militant groups with al-Qaida links are operating in the country. 

 As a result, even though higher oil prices in the event of war means better export earnings for Indonesia, it could also put off investors from returning to the country. Indonesia is Asia's only member of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries. 

 The dollar also climbed against the Thai baht in line with the regional trend, closing the Asian session at THB43.32 baht, up from THB43.02 Thursday. 

 South Korea's financial markets were closed Friday for Chuseok, or the local Thanksgiving holiday. 

 -By Nirmala Menon, Dow Jones Newswires; 65-6415-4046; nirmala.menon@dowjones.com

title: Indonesia c.bank says closely watching rupiah.
text:
JAKARTA, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank said it is closely watching the rupiah currency which fell to one-month lows on Monday amid weak regional currencies, but traders said so far Bank Indonesia had stopped short of intervening. 

 The rupiah was quoted at 9,050/9,060 against the dollar by 0815 GMT and despite its recent falls the local unit is still the best performing currency in the region this year, gaining some 15 percent. 

 "It's not just the rupiah, other regional currencies are also weaker because of the uncertainty in the Middle east and outlook on the global economy. We will be closely watching the rupiah, any options are open," deputy governor Miranda Goeltom told reporters. 

 Analysts have said the rupiah's firmness in recent weeks - it hit 8,750 in early August and last week bounced off 8,800 - masked its vulnerability to a likely U.S.-led attack on Iraq. 

 The rupiah has been propped up by expectations of foreign investment inflows into the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency's bank privatisation programme. 

 Commented Sameer Goel, a strategist with Bank of America: "The risk-reward profile is against the rupiah at the moment because the market is not pricing in the prospect of a U.S. invasion on Iraq." 

 But Goel said Indonesia, being an oil exporter, would benefit from any spike in global oil prices spurred by an invasion of Iraq, although political sentiment might be adversely affected. 

 "The benefit from oil exports will be mitigated to some extent by the impact on the budget since oil in Indonesia is subsidised," he added. 

 Goel said slower growth in other parts of the world because of higher oil prices would also hurt the export-oriented country.

title: Asian  Currencies  Dn Late On Dlr Demand, Econ Concerns
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies slid against the U.S. dollar late Friday as market players covered short-dollar positions ahead of the weekend. 

 Traders reported demand for dollars from oil companies hedging against higher oil prices. Concerns about foreign equity outflows from the region also weighed on regional currencies. 

 Worries about the pace of economic recovery in the region were reignited after disappointing data from the U.S., and rather downbeat remarks on the economy from Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan. 

 But continued uncertainty about a U.S. led war against Iraq, and its impact on oil prices means market players will be more inclined to hold dollars, traders said. 

 "There's a bit of risk premium building in," noted Bhanu Baweja, currency strategist at UBS Warburg in Singapore. 

 The Thai baht and the Singapore dollar were among the biggest casualties Friday. 

 Demand for dollars from oil companies, and short-covering by market players holding dollar/baht options dragged down the baht, a senior trader at a Singapore-based Asian bank said. 

 Oil prices have risen in recent days following mounting tensions between the U.S. and Iraq. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around 42.695 baht, from 42.522 Thursday. 

 Meanwhile, U.S. dollar purchases by foreign funds pulled down the local dollar as low as S$1.7656 - a level last seen on Aug. 10 - during the Asian session. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted at SS$1.7645, from $S1.7592 previously. 

 Growing concerns that a prolonged war with Iraq would hurt the economy also weighed on the local dollar, traders said. 

 Security Fears Weigh On Rupiah 

 The U.S. unit rose against the Philippine peso as banks covered short dollar positions, and oil companies bought dollars to hedge import requirements amid mounting U.S. tensions with Iraq, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at 52.230 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System, up from PHP51.970 Thursday. This was the dollar's strongest finish since Aug. 26. 

Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said the peso's weakness was driven by both external and domestic factors. 

 "Part of it is the possible war in Iraq," he said, adding that the latest kidnapping case in Manila, the country's capital, is also weighing on the peso. 

 He was referring to the kidnapping of the son and daughter of a Philippine congressman earlier Friday. 

 Traders said demand for dollars also increased as some companies raised in advance their dollar requirements for the end of the quarter. 

 In South Korea, dollar sales by exporters, and the yen's firmer tone overnight caused the U.S. unit to slip below 1,200 earlier in the day. 

 But a flurry of dollar buying by onshore players later in the session sent the U.S. currency higher, forcing many interbank players to cover their short-dollar positions. 

 The dollar ended at KRW1,203.8, up from KRW1,201.4 Thursday, after trading in a tight range between KRW1,198.5 and KRW1,204.5 during the day. 

 "We expect no big movements in the dollar in global markets, which means the trading range could be even narrower" next week, possibly between KRW1,195 and KRW1,205, said Oh Suktae, an economist at Citibank. 

 Elsewhere, Indonesian companies bought the U.S. currency to hedge their dollar exposure amid concerns over tensions between the U.S. and Iraq. 

 The market remained on tenterhooks as the U.S. kept its embassy closed in Jakarta Friday for the fourth day due to security threats from unidentified groups thought to be linked to al-Qaida. 

 The market is also concerned U.S. companies in Indonesia may face attacks from militant Muslim groups if the U.S. attacks Iraq, traders said. 

 The central bank was believed to have sold the dollar in the market earlier in the day to defend the rupiah, but the amount wasn't enough to curb the U.S. unit's rise. 

 Bank Indonesia has said it will intervene if necessary to support the rupiah but it doesn't confirm specific interventions. 

 The dollar closed at 8,965 rupiah, up from IDR8,915 Thursday. 

 In Taiwan, a late spate of U.S. dollar buying by importers kept the U.S. currency steady against the local dollar, which had earlier tracked the yen's firmer tone. 

 The New Taiwan dollar often tracks the yen because Taiwan and Japan compete in some export categories. Taiwan also imports large amounts of goods from Japan. 

 The Taipei stock market's 1.5% decline also hurt sentiment toward the local dollar, traders said. 

 The dollar closed at NT$34.410, unchanged from Thursday.

Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said the peso's weakness was driven by both external and domestic factors. 

 "Part of it is the possible war in Iraq," he said, adding that the latest kidnapping case in Manila, the country's capital, is also weighing on the peso. 

 He was referring to the kidnapping of the son and daughter of a Philippine congressman earlier Friday. 

 Traders said demand for dollars also increased as some companies raised in advance their dollar requirements for the end of the quarter. 

 In South Korea, dollar sales by exporters, and the yen's firmer tone overnight caused the U.S. unit to slip below 1,200 earlier in the day. 

 But a flurry of dollar buying by onshore players later in the session sent the U.S. currency higher, forcing many interbank players to cover their short-dollar positions. 

 The dollar ended at KRW1,203.8, up from KRW1,201.4 Thursday, after trading in a tight range between KRW1,198.5 and KRW1,204.5 during the day. 

 "We expect no big movements in the dollar in global markets, which means the trading range could be even narrower" next week, possibly between KRW1,195 and KRW1,205, said Oh Suktae, an economist at Citibank. 

 Elsewhere, Indonesian companies bought the U.S. currency to hedge their dollar exposure amid concerns over tensions between the U.S. and Iraq. 

 The market remained on tenterhooks as the U.S. kept its embassy closed in Jakarta Friday for the fourth day due to security threats from unidentified groups thought to be linked to al-Qaida. 

 The market is also concerned U.S. companies in Indonesia may face attacks from militant Muslim groups if the U.S. attacks Iraq, traders said. 

 The central bank was believed to have sold the dollar in the market earlier in the day to defend the rupiah, but the amount wasn't enough to curb the U.S. unit's rise. 

 Bank Indonesia has said it will intervene if necessary to support the rupiah but it doesn't confirm specific interventions. 

 The dollar closed at 8,965 rupiah, up from IDR8,915 Thursday. 

 In Taiwan, a late spate of U.S. dollar buying by importers kept the U.S. currency steady against the local dollar, which had earlier tracked the yen's firmer tone. 

 The New Taiwan dollar often tracks the yen because Taiwan and Japan compete in some export categories. Taiwan also imports large amounts of goods from Japan. 

 The Taipei stock market's 1.5% decline also hurt sentiment toward the local dollar, traders said.

title: Asian  Currencies  Down Late On Yen, Risk Aversion
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- A softer yen drove Asian currencies broadly lower Wednesday, with the New Taiwan dollar falling to its weakest level since late May. 

 However, regional currencies managed to claw out of their intraday troughs as profit-taking on the dollar helped trim losses. 

 Volumes were thin as market players opted to wait out the first anniversary of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in the U.S. 

 Risk aversion was the main theme amid growing prospects of a U.S.-led war on Iraq and the attendant spike in oil prices, with market players unwilling to be caught short of dollars. 

 "There has been some risk aversion that has favored a strong dollar. The headline risks are quite high on the fundamental side. The biggest headline risk is the potential conflict in Iraq," said Vincent Low, Singapore-based head of foreign exchange/bond strategy for Asia at Merrill Lynch. 

 Economic concerns remained a key concern as higher oil prices, if sustained, will dent economic recovery in an export-dependent region, which is already trying to deal with the prospects of slower growth in the U.S. 

 A UBS Warburg report rated the Philippine peso, the Korean won and the Thai baht as the most vulnerable among Asian currencies to a sustained rise in oil prices 

 With uncertainties both on the geopolitical and economic front, market players were unwilling to take strong positions, traders said. 

 "It's (trading) mostly done for small amounts, to square off positions," with the dollar's gains capped by profit-taking, said a senior regional trader at an Asian bank in Singapore. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the U.S. currency ended at NT$34.395 - its highest since May 24 - from NT$34.303 Tuesday, but off an intraday high of NT$34.403. 

 A dealer said central bank intervention helped support the local dollar, which took its cue from the yen; the central bank sold between US$150 million and US$200 million to help support the local unit. 

 The New Taiwan dollar often tracks the yen because Taiwan and Japan compete in some export categories. Taiwan also imports large amounts of goods from Japan. 

 Trading was light, with dealings valued at US$371 million, down from US$486 million previously. 

 Talk of central bank intervention also helped pull the dollar back from intraday highs against the Indonesian rupiah, traders said. 

 Bank Indonesia has a policy of intervening in the market but never comments on specific actions. 

 The dollar ended at IDR8,890, up from IDR8,865 the previous day, but off the day's high of IDR8,905. 

 The rupiah didn't react to a statement from Bank Indonesia's board of governors that it hopes to keep cutting rates due to benign inflation, and a stronger rupiah, as market sentiment is barely affected by rate policy. 

 Indonesian authorities are hoping lower rates will spur growth. Finance Minister Boediono said the country was likely to meet its near 4% economic growth target this year. But experts, including the World Bank, warn Indonesia needs at least 6% growth to create enough work for new job seekers each year. 

 In South Korea, the dollar closed at 1,202.5 won, down from KRW1,198.4 Tuesday but off an intraday high of KRW1,204.0. 

 Like recent sessions, importers and exporters were the main market participants. Importers were buying dollars on dips and exporters were selling them on upticks, dealers said. 

 "Recently, the market cannot find any specific momentum or any direction," said Dong-Ki Jang, chief dealer of foreign exchange and derivatives at Shinhan Bank. "I expect rangebound trading will continue for the moment - at least until the end of the month." 

 The dollar climbed against the Thai baht, but failed to break through the day's high of THB42.50 due to substantial exporter selling orders around that level. 

 The dollar finished at 42.465 baht at the Asian close, up from THB42.41 Tuesday. 

 The U.S. unit was also up against the Singapore dollar, but off earlier highs as market participants took profits. 

 Late in Asia, the dollar was quoted around S$1.7551 from S$1.7527 in the previous session. The pair traded between S$1.7555 and S$1.7580 in Asia. 

 The Philippine peso initially tracked the yen but later bucked the regional trend to close slightly firmer. 

 Traders said a lack of corporate demand for dollars allowed the peso to gain ground. 

 The dollar closed at 51.910 pesos on the Philippine Dealing System from PHP51.960 Tuesday, after moving between PHP51.900 and PHP52.080 intraday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Dn On Taiwan-China, US Economy
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 KUALA LUMPUR -(Dow Jones)- Mounting China-Taiwan tensions and concerns over a double dip recession in the U.S. pulled most Asian currencies lower Monday. 

 The Taiwan markets were the hardest hit, with stocks down almost 6% and the local currency skirting a key support level against the U.S. dollar, following weekend remarks by Taiwan's President Chen Shui-bian that were interpreted as being pro-independence. 

 However, it was concerns over a double dip recession in the U.S., which gathered momentum after last week's disappointing overall growth, a weak job market and flat manufacturing activity, which pressured other Asian currencies, market participants said. 

 In his strongest comments since taking office, Chen said over the weekend that Taiwan and China are both countries - a view that is anathema to Chinese leaders who believe the island belongs to China. A civil war split the two sides 53 years ago, and Beijing says the island must unify eventually or face war. 

 Chen also said Taiwan's laws should be amended to allow a national referendum on the island's fate. 

 Beijing has never renounced the use of force to reunify the island under mainland control, and has repeatedly warned that a declaration of independence by the island will prompt a military response. 

 Chen's comments drew an angry response Monday from China, with its top Taiwan affairs spokesman Li Weiyi saying cross-strait relations have been seriously damaged, and that Chen was leading the island to "disaster." 

 Damage control by Taiwan's top China policy maker Tsai Ing-wen, and intervention by Taiwan's central bank failed to calm nerves as investors sold off the New Taiwan dollar and cashed out of equities. 

 "It's (regional currencies are weak because of) Taiwan, and basically taking the cue from the dollar/yen (which rose late in the Asian trading day). It's pretty much a knee-jerk reaction," said Philip Wee, market strategist at Singapore's DBS Bank. "The currencies in the region are just going to be reactive to developments in the U.S. and things in the region," he added. 

 Despite the late rise, the broad picture for the U.S. dollar is still bearish, currency strategists said. 

 "Most of the data is pointing to much softer global recovery led by the U.S. A bad U.S. is not good news for Asia," Wee at DBS said. 

 The New Taiwan dollar came close to crashing through a key support level at NT$34.00 to the U.S. dollar, but aggressive intervention by Taiwan's central bank helped shore up the local unit. 

 The dollar closed at NT$33.825, up from NT$33.723 Friday, after trading in a range of NT$33.723 and NT$33.980 through the day. Trading was heavy, with volumes rising to US$880.5 million, compared with US$653 million Friday. Traders estimated the central bank bought more than $200 million of the New Taiwan dollar to prop up market confidence. 

 Still, "compared with the stock market, the forex market is relatively calm as institutional investors are the major players here," and they're not bailing out en masse, said a foreign bank trader. 

 Meanwhile, the South Korean won finished markedly lower as foreigners offloaded local shares for a fourth straight session, and as the yen retreated against the dollar. 

 The greenback ended at 1,198.0 won, up from Friday's close of KRW1,184.5, after trading between KRW1,180.5 and KRW1,199.0. 

 The won initially opened stronger thanks to a slight gain by the yen, but soon succumbed to selling pressure as foreigners sold off their equity holdings. Korean shares ended 3.6% lower over the day. 

 Dealers said more participants are now long on the dollar, suggesting that most expect the U.S. currency to gain further Tuesday and possibly the rest of the week. The dollar will likely continue to be supported by foreigners' selling of Korean shares. 

 "People think it (the dollar) will go to KRW1,200 in the mid term. Below KRW1,187 is not expected because the dollar is very well-bid," said a dealer. 

 The U.S. currency may even test KRW1,200 as early as Tuesday, said dealers. 

 The greenback was also buoyed against the Philippine peso as companies seek dollars for import and debt payment requirements, and on expectations the central bank may cut overnight rates soon following a set of weak inflation data for July. 

 However, central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura appeared to rule out an immediate rate cut. 

 "They are probably out of their minds," he said of banks bidding up the dollar in anticipation of a narrowing of the gap between local and U.S. interest rates. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at 51.510 peso, from 51.300 Friday. 

 The greenback also strengthened against the Thai baht, which weakened in tandem with the regional currencies and on strong importer buying of dollars. 

 Traders said that fears of Thai central bank intervention ensured the THB42.30 resistance level held. The U.S. dollar was quoted at 42.15 baht in late Asian trading, from THB42.105 Friday. 

 The greenback had a choppy ride against the Singapore dollar as gains from short-covering were eroded by selling on a cautious outlook for the world's largest economy. 

 Still a trader at an Asian bank said, "although the sentiment remains bad toward the U.S. dollar, as a base currency, it still attracts bargain hunting." 

 The tumble in the Taiwanese equities and currency markets Monday amid heightened tensions between the island and China also reinforced the U.S. dollar's image as a safe haven, he said. 

 There are signs some U.S. investment houses have been buying back their own currency to shift asset portfolios back into the U.S., he said. 

 The market also shrugged off a slight improvement in Singapore's Purchasing Managers' Index for July, saying the month-on-month growth is too small to be relevant. 

 The PMI rose to 52.3% in July from 52.1% in June on the back of increases in orders and manufacturing output. 

 An index reading above 50% indicates the manufacturing sector is expanding whereas a reading below 50% indicates a contraction. The PMI is an advance indicator of trends in manufacturing activity. 

 The greenback was quoted at S$1.7558 in late Asian trading, from $1.7559 Friday. 

 The U.S. dollar closed flat at 9,080 rupiah as suspected intervention by Bank Indonesia shielded the local unit from the waves of dollar buying across the region.

suspected dollar selling by the central bank. But it rebounded steadily
during the course of the day as market participants bought the greenback
in line with its rally against other Asian currencies.

title: Indonesia  Rupiah Ends Higher After Ctrl Bk  Intervention
text:

 The dollar ended at IDR9,085, lower than IDR9,140 at Thursday's close. 

 "The central bank was in the market," a local trader said. 

 The central bank doesn't comment on specific actions in the foreign exchange markets. 

 The action involved selling about $20 million in the spot market, traders said. 

 Indonesia's central bank said Friday it expects interest rates to fall further this year due to benign inflation. 

 Bank Indonesia also thinks the rupiah will continue to climb against the dollar toward the end of the year, Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom told reporters. 

 "Looking forward, Bank Indonesia still expects inflation to fall. So we see an opportunity to cut interest rates further," Gultom said. 

 The government is easing its monetary policy to help spur economic growth. The country of 220 million people expects gross domestic product to jump about 5% this year, but this isn't enough to create new work for the thousands of new jobseekers every year. 

 Political stability under President Megawati Sukarnoputri during her first year in power has helped stabilize the rupiah, and reduce inflation pressures on the economy. The dollar was trading at IDR9,085 in late trade Friday, up about 12% since the start of the year. 

 The central bank cut its overnight intervention rate - the rate offered to banks that park their rupiah-denominated funds with the central bank - by 50 basis points Friday to 13.625%. The rate is a signal of the country's monetary policy intentions. 

 The rate cuts came after the government announced Thursday that annual inflation had fallen to 10.05% in July from 11.48% in June.

title: UPDATE 1- Indonesia  c.bank  intervenes  to help rupiah-dealers.
text:
JAKARTA, July 12 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank intervened in the foreign exchange market on Friday morning to bolster the rupiah, which had sagged in the past two to three weeks, dealers said. 

 One bank treasurer said the central bank sold around $50 million, while another said it was a "substantial" amount. 

 By 0734 GMT the rupiah was being quoted at 9,040/9,070 from a low of 9,170 earlier in the day. 

 The reported intervention came before central bank governor Sjahril Sabirin said the rupiah would strengthen against the U.S. dollar on Friday afternoon. He did not give a reason but said the central bank would intervene in the market if necessary. 

 "It's the most we've ever seen - they did upwards of $50 million," the first bank treasurer said. 

 "They're very keen to protect this 9,200 level so they might well come in with another $50 million plus this afternoon." 

 Dealers estimated average daily turnover on the USD/rupiah market at around $200 million during the past month. They pinned the recent weakening of the rupiah partly on demand for dollars to repay foreign debts and importers covering payments. 

 The central bank said its policy was not to comment on speculation of intervention. 

 "Bank Indonesia's role is to prevent (excessive) volatility in the rupiah," a central bank director, Made Sukada, said. 

 Earlier, bank governor Sabirin said: 

 "The rupiah is likely to strengthen again this afternoon. We will intervene if necessary. The important thing is market sentiment on the rupiah is improving," Sabirin told reporters. 

 Sabirin said the bank would not raise its benchmark interest rates to support the currency, which has weakened in the past two to three weeks from around 8,600 to the dollar. 

 Underscoring its concern over the rupiah's recent downtrend, the central bank last week called in all foreign and major local bank treasurers and asked them to exercise caution in trading activities, the first treasurer said. 

 "They're very worried about the 9,200 level. It's a technical level - if it breaks that, you open up the 9,500 area," he said. 

 "Personally, I think they're being a bit paranoid and are overreacting." 

 The 2002 state budget targets a rupiah rate of 9,000.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Up Late As US Dlr Takes Battering
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 KUALA LUMPUR -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies were higher Monday with several shooting to new multi-month highs Monday as confidence in the U.S. dollar was hammered by a new string of accounting revelations from U.S. companies, and after Japanese Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa's bearish remarks over the weekend. 

 The decline in the U.S. dollar reversed last week's gains and surprised many analysts and traders who had expected Wall Street's strong showing Friday to support the greenback. 

 The sharp gains in Asian currencies drew the ire of several central banks which made the obligatory warnings or intervened. However, as in recent days, their efforts failed to break the dollar's fall. 

 Only the Indonesian rupiah weakened against the U.S. dollar as central bank purchases of the local currency couldn't offset corporate purchases of dollars to pay for imports. The Korean won and the Thai baht both ended at multi-month highs, while the Philippine peso, Singapore dollar and New Taiwan dollar closed higher against the U.S. unit. 

 "People pretty much jumped on the sell dollar bandwagon," said Thio Chin Loo, senior currency analyst at BNP Paribas in Singapore, adding that Shiokawa's remarks over the weekend "isn't good for the (dollar's) outlook." 

 At a weekend meeting of European and Asian finance chiefs in Copenhagen, Shiokawa said officials in various countries believed the dollar was in a downtrend, and could fall to its post-Sept. 11 low of Y115.80. 

 Although Shiokawa's comments weren't a major surprise, "he basically just added more fuel," said Philip Wee, market strategist at Singapore's DBS Bank. 

 As at 0515 GMT, the dollar was quoted at Y119.13 yen, well below Y120.43 late Friday in Tokyo, and Y120.24 in New York. 

 The greenback was dealt a further blow by more accounting-related controversies at big U.S. companies, analysts and traders said. 

 Drug giant Merck & Co. (MRK) said it recorded $12.4 billion in revenue from its pharmacy benefits unit over the past three years that it never actually collected. However, Merck said its revenue-recognition policy conforms to generally accepted accounting principles and that it wouldn't affect its net income. 

 That news came soon after energy firms Reliant Resources and Reliant Energy late Friday announced they had amended their revenues downward by more than a combined $15 billion. 

 Analysts said the spate of accounting controversies has further overshadowed the dollar's already week outlook. 

 "A lot hinges on the headline news on these issues. For now, the risk is to the downside on the U.S. dollar," said Thio. 

 In Asian trading, the Singapore dollar rose in tandem with the yen, and ahead of the release of advance estimates of second-quarter gross domestic product data Wednesday. 

 The data are widely expected to show the city state has emerged from its long recession. A Dow Jones Newswires poll of 11 economists forecasts an average 2.8% on year rise in the city-state's GDP, after contracting for four straight quarters. 

 Singapore's GDP shrank 2% in 2001, its worst performance since independence in 1965. 

 Late Monday, the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7625, from S$1.7721 late Friday. 

 "Everyone's long on dollars and will look to sell on any rallies from here," a dealer at a European bank said. 

 Against the baht, the dollar crashed to a 22-month low and was quoted at THB41.435 late Monday from THB41.645 before. 

 Stop-loss selling by both exporters and offshore players in afternoon trade coupled with the yen's appreciation pulled the U.S. unit to its Monday low, said a dealer at a foreign bank. 

 Support for the pair is around THB41.35-41.40, with resistance coming at THB41.55, market observers said. 

 A lack of corporate demand for dollars coupled with the greenback's general weakness helped boost the Philipine peso. The dollar ended at PHP50.470, from PHP50.595 Friday. Traders expect the dollar to test support at PHP50.30 in the next few days. 

 Meanwhile, the Korean won rode on the yen's rise to a 19-month high against the dollar. The dollar ended at KRW1,191.4 from KRW1,204.9 Friday. 

 Dealers said that any U.S. dollar bids during the trading session came predominantly from state-run banks, with the majority of market players offloading the dollar. 

 The won strengthened despite another government warning intended to dull the bullish won sentiment. Kwon Tae-shin, director general at the Ministry of Finance and Economy's international bureau, said early Monday market players' "excessive expectations of further won gains based on the yen's recent movements" are undesirable, and that the government will take "active" steps to stabilize the foreign exchange market. 

 The dollar popped up KRW2 immediately after Kwon's remarks, but quickly returned to its downward trajectory since players believe there's little the government can do to stem the dollar's fall given the worldwide trend. 

 As is usual when the local market is moving contrary to what the authorities want, the Bank of Korea checked banks' market positions. One dealer felt the central banks' phone calls were intended to keep banks from shorting the dollar Monday, but another said the checks weren't intended to influence market positions. 

 Against the New Taiwan dollar, the greenback closed at NT33.513, from NT33.580 Friday, even though the central bank reportedly intervened to buy U.S. dollars intermittently. 

 But the Indonesian rupiah bucked the regional trend and weakened, despite intervention by Bank Indonesia. 

 Traders said demand from importers surged, likely against any rising political uncertainty ahead of the annual session of the country's highest legislative body next month, and after weekend violence in troubled Aceh province. 

 State oil company Pertamina was suspected of buying U.S. dollars earlier in the day to finance the import of fuels. 


Late Monday, the dollar was quoted at IDR8,900, from IDR8,850 late
Friday.

title: China seen expanding  FX  swap network by end-2002.
text:
COPENHAGEN, July 6 (Reuters) - China plans to sign bilateral swap agreements with the Philippines and Malaysia by the end of this year, extending an Asian-wide currency safety net designed to prevent future financial crisis, a senior Japanese Finance Ministry official said on Saturday. 

 These deals are part of the Chiang Mai Initiative (CMI), which aims to forge closer ties by creating a network of central bank currency swaps among the 10-strong Association of South East Asian Nations plus Japan, China and South Korea (ASEAN+3). 

 The swap pacts make foreign exchange reserves available at short notice to a country which faces a rapid deterioration in its balance of payments and whose currency comes under speculative attack, like the Thai baht in 1997. 

 "China has started its negotiation with the Philippines two to three weeks ago. China is also about to begin its negotiation with Malaysia," the official told Reuters on the sidelines of the Asia-Europe meeting (ASEM) in Copenhagen. 

 "I think China wants to seal deals with Malaysia and the Philippines by the end of this year. Korea is also very close to signing deals with Malaysia." 

 Japan, a driving force behind the CMI, already has bilateral swap agreements with South Korea ($2 billion), Thailand ($3 billion), the Philippines ($3 billion) and Malaysia ($1 billion). 

 The Japanese government is also in negotiations with Indonesia and Singapore about swap agreements. 

 "We are in a final arrangement with Indonesia and Singapore and we plan to sign the deal as soon as possible," the official said. 

 "The size of the deal with Indonesia would be similar to those we have signed already, which were worth around $3 billion although it might change in the future." 

 China and South Korea signed a $2 billion agreement in June. 

 The official said Korea has recently signed a deal with Thailand worth $1 billion. 

 Japan has a yen-yuan swap agreement with China worth $3 billion, signed in March, although the deal is seen as primarily symbolic because neither Japan nor China are likely to face liquidity or balance of payments in the short term. 

 Japan and China are the world's two biggest holders of external reserves. Japan's foreign reserves, the world's biggest, stood at $446.198 billion at end-June. China has more than $200 billion in foreign reserves. 

 Japan has only one other yen-denominated currency swap line, with the European Central Bank, but that facility is mainly for currencyintervention purposes and was used in September 2000 when the ECB and the BOJ intervened to prop up the euro. 

 ASEAN groups Brunei, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

 Some analysts remain bullish toward the rupiah in the medium term due to the government's plans to sell IDR150 trillion in non-performing loans by mid August. Money is expected to come in to Indonesia from Singapore and other financial centers to buy the loans and boost the local currency. 

 But others point to continued problems with the country's legal system, which is viewed as the most corrupt in the region, as deterring foreign investors. Foreign direct investment fell 59% in the first five months of this year compared with the same period of 2001. 

 Indonesian companies are also likely to repay about $5 billion in the last three quarters of 2002 to overseas creditors, again putting pressure on the local unit, the rupiah's detractors say.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Late; Dlr Buoyed By Gain Vs Yen
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 

 SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The dollar was steady to firmer against most Asian currencies Wednesday, drawing some support from its gains against the yen. 

 The yen's slippage was partly due to capital outflows from Japan associated with purchases of foreign securities by Japanese investors, analysts said. 

 The dollar, which fell to a six-month low against the yen late last month, stabilized over the past week following a series of foreign exchange market interventions by Japanese monetary authorities to cap the yen's rise. 

 That stability has provided some assurance to Japanese investors looking to move their money offshore, analysts said. 

 The dollar traded as high as 128.60 yen during Asian hours before giving up some of its gains later in the session. Near the end of Asian trading the dollar was quoted at Y125.50, up from Y125.23 late Tuesday in New York. 

 The South Korean won was the main casualty of the weaker yen, falling against the dollar for the fourth time in five sessions. The Thai baht also retreated, while the New Taiwan dollar and Singapore dollar were little changed. The Indonesian rupiah strengthened after the government promised the International Monetary Fund that it would get tough with former bank owners that are refusing to pay billions of dollars they owe the state. 

 The won's slippage was welcome news for South Korean monetary authorities, who have repeatedly expressed concerns about the impact of the currency's strength on the country's export competitiveness. The won hit an 18-month high against the dollar last week. 

 The dollar closed at 1,233.6 won Wednesday, up from KRW1,225.5 late Tuesday. 

 The state-run Korea Development Bank took advantage of the dollar's momentum, buying the U.S. currency late in the afternoon to push it even higher, dealers said. 

 South Korean monetary authorities are most concerned about the won's competitiveness against the yen because of the overlap in exports between the two countries, said Andy Xie, an economist at Morgan Stanley. 

 "Obviously, Korea has an exchange rate based on its value against the Japanese yen. It is an effective policy to manage export growth and balance of payments for Korea," Xie said. 

 Expectations that the IMF would soon disburse more funds for Indonesia, and suspected central bank intervention for the second day in a row, underpinned the rupiah. 

 Late in Asia the dollar was quoted at 8,700 rupiah, down from IDR8,765, late Tuesday. 

 Dealers said they suspected Bank Indonesia sold up to $5 million via state banks to bolster the local currency after selling an estimated $3 million to $5 million Tuesday. 

 In addition, the government said it has signed a new letter of intent with the IMF outlining economic reforms it plans to undertake as part of its loan program with the multilateral lender. 

 The IMF is expected to decide by the end of June on the disbursement of the next $340 million loan installment of a $5 billion program. 

 In Taipei, central bank intervention helped offset U.S. dollar selling by interbank dealers. 

 The U.S. dollar closed at NT$34.116, compared with NT$34.117 Tuesday. 

 The U.S. dollar rose to an intraday high of NT$34.175 in early trading following its strong performance overnight against the yen. 

 However, interbank dealers, who generally hold the view that the U.S. currency is overvalued, sold the U.S. dollar in the afternoon and pushed it to a low of NT$34.104. The central bank then entered the market and bought the U.S. dollar to lift it before the close. 

 The Singapore dollar recovered from a slow start to finish virtually unchanged against its U.S. counterpart. 

 Near the end of Asian trading the U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7875, compared with S$1.7873 late Tuesday. 

 The U.S. dollar traded as high as $1.7945 in the first hours of trading on spill-over strength related to its gains against the yen before losing steam later in the session. 

 The Thai baht weakened in line with the yen, but equity-related inflows helped limit the baht's losses.

title: Emerging Asia  FX  - Down on yen losses, c.bank fears.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 5 (Reuters) - Asian currencies backtracked 

 on some of their recent gains on Wednesday following the yen 

  which stayed depressed after last night's intervention

 by the Bank of Japan in favour of the dollar. 

     That was BOJ's fourth intervention in recent days although 

 it failed to convince the market that it would continue to 

 stand in the way of any yen appreciation from here, but did 

 manage to keep a lid on short dollar positions. 

     The intervention also made players in regional currencies

 wary of similar actions by their central banks. 

     Taking advantage of that wariness, officials in Seoul 

 stepped up their verbal intervention to pull the Korean won 

 -2 off its recent multi-month highs against the dollar. 

     Japan is both a major trading market and competitor for 

 most other Asian countries, so regional policy makers tend to 

 use dollar/yen as a measure of their competitiveness. 

     But in the case of Korea they also keep an eye on the 

 yen/won cross , which has appreciated from levels 

 above 10 won in mid-April to around 9.7 won in recent sessions. 

     WON TALKED DOWN 

     Both the central bank and officials of the Ministry of

Finance were in the market to talk the won down, pulling it to 

 a session low of 1,225 per dollar, against a five-and-a-half 

 month high of 1,219.9 hit on Tuesday. 

     The won ended onshore trade at 1,224.3, versus Tuesday's 

 close of 1,220.10. 

     Dealers in Singapore said the market gave little response 

 to a widely expected central bank decision to leave the key 

 overnight call rate target unchanged at 4.25 percent. 

     The market also failed to react to central bank chief Park 

 Seung's statement that he saw economy growing by six to seven 

 percent, against last year's three percent and an earlier 

 forecast of 5.7 percent. 

 But what the market heard loud and clear was his statement 

 that the won's rise, near six percent so far this year, would 

 hurt export competitiveness and monetary authorities were ready 

 to take action if necessary. 

 Later Kim Yong-duk, responsible for the Finance Ministry's 

foreign exchange operations, said it was about time to take 

 action to tame the won's steep rise. 

 BI DENIES INTERVENTION

Central bank comments were also the main focus in Indonesia

 where the rupiah slid to a near two-week low of 8,975, 

 as players bailed out of short dollar positions, uncertain 

 about the the bank's position on the currency and depressed by 

 recent delays in the sale of state assets. 

 The central bank came out to deny rumours it was buying 

 dollars to cap the rupiah's recent gains and said 8,500-8,600 

 was an appropriate range for the currency. 

 On Tuesday, the rupiah touched a high of 8,440, its highest 

 since August 21, before the central bank warned the forex

 market not to overreact on currency strength which could lead 

 to excessive swings and affect economic recovery. 

 The momentum of the rupiah's fall eased a bit, pushing the 

 rupiah back to 8,900, and was further helped by the benchmark 

 one-month SBI interest rate that fell in the weekly auction to 

 15.17 percent from 15.51 percent in the previous auction. 

 PESO, SGD & BAHT 

 Inflation data in Philippines had little impact on the peso 

 , which eased to 50.80 from Tuesday's close of 50.43, 

 mainly on political worries after the defection of Senator John 

 Osmena to the opposition, tilting the balance in the Senate 

 against President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo. 

     Philippines inflation in May rose by an expected 3.6 

 percent and was unchanged from April. 


    The Singapore dollar        eased to a one-week low of



1.7955 per dollar, from late Tuesday's 1.7825, weighed down by



the yen's losses against the dollar.



    The Thai baht        also tracked the regional mood and



slipped to bump against one-week lows at 42.535 before bouncing



back to 42.49, still down from late Tuesday's 42.29.



    Dealers said slowing equity and export-related inflows also



weighed on the baht.
