title: UPDATE 2-Rupiah bounces as Bank Indonesia steps in.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 12 (Reuters) - The bruised rupiah clawed back above the 11,000 mark as players rushed to unload the dollar after Bank Indonesia stepped in with verbal and actual intervention. 

 The rupiah bounced to 10,500 from around 11,200 just minutes after Bank Indonesia senior deputy governor Miranda Goeltom said the bank would do its best to support the currency. 

 "Bank Indonesia will continue to do its best. We have enough funds to help the rupiah ... we will continue to do it (intervention)," Goeltom told Reuters in Jakarta. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said the central bank offered between $5-$10 million in the market in the afternoon after selling around $2 million to no avail in the morning. 

 The rupiah floundered past 11,200 per dollar earlier on Monday on mounting concerns over Indonesia's political and economic woes, with analysts predicting a further drop. 

 Goeltom's remark contradicted earlier comments by deputy governor Anwar Nasution who said the central bank had limited ability to defend the currency. His statement sent the rupiah reeling to its worst level since September 24, 1998. 

 Dealers said doubts over President Abdurrahman Wahid's leadership and his ability to handle economic and ethnic problems had spurred dollar demand. 

 News that thousands of anti and pro-government protesters had poured on to the streets of Jakarta also unnerved the market. 

 Bank Indonesia and state banks were the only sellers of dollars in a thin market as most exporters held on to their dollar earnings and Indonesian companies and banks sold rupiah. 

 MORE DECLINES 

 In a straw poll on Monday, most analysts surveyed by Reuters said barring capital controls and a significant turnaround in the political situation, the rupiah could head toward 12,000-15,000 by the end of June. 

 "If the rupiah continues to go at its current pace, I think the government would come up with fresh measures ... i.e. one form of capital control or another. In that case, it could pick up to around 10,000," said Andrew Fung, head of Asia-Pacific treasury research at Rabobank. 

 "Barring that, there is a possibility that it could go to 13,000. I still think the rupiah should trade above 10,000, but sentiment is driving market dynamics at this point," he said. 

 Another analyst at a foreign bank in Singapore said if things continued as they were, the rupiah could falter to anywhere between 12,500-15,000. 

 The currency hit an all-time low of about 17,000 in June, 1998. 

 "The two things that I'm looking at are the situation with the IMF and the situation with Wahid ... Even if things are patched up with the IMF, things still will look shaky if Wahid hasn't stepped down by June," the analyst said. 

 Most analysts believe the IMF will not pull out of Indonesia and is soon likely to disburse long-delayed loan payments. 

 But they expected the Fund to stick to its guns on the four key issues related to the sale of state shares in two major banks, amendments to the central bank law, borrowing by regions and corporate debt restructuring.

title: Rupiah Up To 10,500/Dlr On Bk  Indonesia Intervention
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's central bank intervened directly in the foreign exchange market in thin lunchtime trade Monday, helping to pull the rupiah back from 30-month lows, traders said. 

 Bank Indonesia sold around a $5 million while most traders were at lunch, adding to a similar amount of direct intervention in the morning. 

 The dollar selling pushed the rupiah back to IDR10,500 versus a IDR11,500 high in morning trade on political concerns. 

 Still, the intervention is unlikely to lead to a sustained rally in the rupiah, which remains under pressure as thousands of student protesters Monday call for President Abdurrahman Wahid to resign. 

 Earlier, deputy central bank governor Anwar Nasution admitted that intervention is unlikely to help support the rupiah, and urged politicians to stop bickering. 

 Many lawmakers want Wahid to resign, and blame him for the country's myriad of economic and social problems.

title: Bk  Indonesia  Dep Gov:  Intervention  Capability Limited
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's central bank admitted Monday its ability to support the ailing rupiah through intervention in the foreign exchange market is limited as the currency's fall is mainly due to political instability. 

 "The weakness is mostly because of political factors, so political parties should stop bickering," Deputy Governor Anwar Nasution told reporters. 

 Bank Indonesia's foreign reserves - currently at $29 billion on a gross basis - aren't large enough to defend the rupiah, he added. 

 The rupiah touched 30-month lows Monday, falling through the IDR11,000 support to the dollar as students took to the streets to call for President Abdurrahman Wahid's ouster. 

 Around 0358 GMT (10:58 p.m. EST Sunday), the dollar was traded at IDR11,100. 

 Earlier Monday, the central bank sold at least $5 million directly to help the rupiah. It sold around $50 million directly Friday, but this hasn't helped the rupiah.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends 4% Down But Off 30-Mo Lows
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah closed nearly 4% lower Monday from Friday as political unrest continued fueling active dollar buying, dealers said. 

 The local currency, however, ended the session off the 30-month low of IDR11,500 it fell to earlier in the day due to intervention by Bank Indonesia in the foreign exchange market. 

 Dealers said they believed the central bank spent between $50 million and $60 million to defend the rupiah Monday, either by selling dollars indirectly through state banks or directly in the foreign currency market. 

 The dollar closed at IDR10,500 Monday, up from its close at IDR10,100 Friday. 

 Dealers said the market got nervous as thousands of students protested outside the presidential palace demanding President Abdurrahman Wahid's resignation and the cancelation of a proposal to increase fuel prices April 1. 

 Despite the protest, Wahid told a news conference that he won't resign. The government, however, decided to delay the planned fuel price increase until October at the earliest. It will only increase fuel prices for large industrial users, it added. 

 The market welcomed the government's decision to delay the fuel price increase as such a move is expected to reduce social unrest. 

 "It's the best political decision to make regarding the current unstable social-political conditions," said a dealer with a foreign bank. 

 Besides intervention in the foreign exchange market, Bank Indonesia also raised its overnight money market rate by 50 basis points to 12.125%. Such a move would encourage banks to park their rupiah with the central bank instead of use them to buy dollars. 

 Many banks, however, held onto their rupiah as they expect active dollar buying in the spot market will boost demand for the rupiah in the interbank money market in coming days, thus enabling them to earn even higher returns. 

 Elsewhere, the rupiah's plunge dragged Indonesian share prices 4.2% lower Monday. 

 Despite the rupiah rebounding off IDR11,500, dealers say the bullish sentiment toward the dollar is still intact as the country's political problems persist. 

 The market also knows that Bank Indonesia's ability to intervene is limited as the central bank has only gross foreign exchange reserves around $29 billion, dealers said. 

 Senior Deputy Governor Anwar Nasution admitted Monday that Bank Indonesia's capability to help the rupiah is limited as the rupiah's weakness is due mainly to political factors. 

 Senior Economic Minister Rizal Ramli also said that the government isn't considering capital controls to help the rupiah. 

 Barring new political developments, dealers expect the dollar to trade in a wide range of between IDR10,200 and IDR11,000 Tuesday.

title: Singapore MAS Reaffirms Modest, Gradual SGD Rise Policy
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Monetary Authority of Singapore's policy stance of a gradual and modest appreciation of the Singapore dollar remains unchanged, a spokeswoman told Dow Jones Newswires Monday. 

 The local currency fell sharply Monday, mirroring the fall of the Indonesian rupiah and the yen. Around 0942 GMT (4:42 a.m. EST), the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7617, up from S$1.7571 late Friday in Asia. 

 The U.S. dollar rose to an intraday high of S$1.7622 - its highest since November last year - as the Indonesian and Japanese currencies fell amid growing political uncertainty in Indonesia and Japan. 

 The central bank spokeswoman also declined to offer specific comments on the level of the Singapore dollar Monday. 

 With the MAS making no effort to defend the local currency, banks, investors and local companies continued to buy U.S. dollars at levels above S$1.7610 even after the U.S. currency fell below IDR11,000 on intervention by Bank Indonesia and retreated from its high against the yen, dealers said. 

 In a move that surprised most analysts, the MAS in February affirmed its policy of allowing a "gradual, modest appreciation" of the Singapore dollar. 

 The MAS manages the Singapore dollar exchange rate against a trade-weighted basket of currencies of the country's major trading partners and competitors. It maintains the trade-weighted exchange rate within an undisclosed band.

title: Singapore Dlr Dn Late On Rupiah, Yen Fall;Expected Weaker
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- The Singapore dollar tracked the rupiah and yen lower Monday, and remained pressured by demand for U.S. dollars from companies and banks even after the Indonesian and Japanese currencies bounced off their intraday lows. 

 Around 0807 GMT, the U.S. dollar was trading at S$1.7617, up from S$1.7571 late Friday in Asia. Against the rupiah and the yen, it was at IDR10,650 and Y120.40, respectively, compared with IDR11,500 and Y120.66 earlier Monday. 

 The U.S. dollar rose to an intraday high of S$1.7622 as the Indonesian and Japanese currencies fell amid growing political uncertainty in Indonesia and Japan. 

 With the Monetary Authority of Singapore making no effort to defend the local currency, banks, investors and local companies continued to buy U.S. dollars at levels above S$1.7610 even after the U.S. currency retreated below IDR11,000 on intervention by Bank Indonesia, and retreated from its high against the yen, dealers said. 

 "A large government-linked bank was the main buyer of U.S. dollars when it moved above S$1.76, and almost everybody continued to buy (U.S. dollars) because the market is very bearish on regional currencies," a dealer said. 

 "The fact that (the U.S. dollar) won't go below S$1.7610 shows there is very strong demand, and I won't be surprised if it goes up to S$1.7650 today (Monday)," he added. 

 However, a chief dealer at another bank said that market participants will likely hesitate to bid the U.S. dollar above the S$1.7620-30 range on fears of intervention by the MAS. 

 Dealers said any retreat from the U.S. dollar's current level against the Singapore currency will likely cause the U.S. currency to be bought on dips by banks and companies that are keen to create a long position in it. 

 The U.S. dollar is expected to trade in a S$1.7580-S$1.7650 range overnight.

title: WSJ.COM WRAP: Indonesian Rupiah Plunges Amid Protests
text:
A WSJ.COM News Roundup 

 JAKARTA, Indonesia -(Dow Jones)- The ailing rupiah continued its freefall by closing nearly 4% lower Monday compared with Friday as political unrest fueled active dollar buying. 

 The dollar closed at 10,500 rupiah Monday, up from its close at 10,100 rupiah Friday. 

 The local currency, however, ended the session off the 30-month low of 11,500 rupiah it fell to earlier in the day due to intervention by Bank Indonesia in the foreign-exchange market. Traders said they believed the central bank spent between $50 million and $60 million to defend the rupiah Monday, either by selling dollars indirectly through state banks or directly in the foreign-currency market. 

 Still, the intervention is unlikely to lead to a sustained rally in the rupiah, which remains under pressure as thousands of student protesters Monday called for President Abdurrahman Wahid to resign. 

 The dollar last traded at this level in September 1998 at the height of the Asian financial crisis. Senior Economics Minister Rizal Ramli said that the government would not resort to capital controls despite the rupiah's plunge. "We aren't considering any sort of capital controls," Mr. Rizal said. 

 Meanwhile, Indonesia's central bank admitted its ability to support the ailing currency through intervention in the foreign-exchange market is limited because the plunge is mainly due to political instability. 

 At the heart of the problem is Mr. Wahid. Last week, the embattled Muslim cleric came under increased fire for remaining on an overseas excursion while ethnic conflict in the region of Kalimantan left more than 400 people dead. Mr. Wahid already is facing impeachment proceedings launched by Parliament in February over his alleged involvement in two corruption scandals. 

 Despite growing displeasure with his rule, however, the political uncertainty plaguing Indonesia is unlikely to end soon. Even Amien Rais, speaker of the country's highest legislative body and one of Mr. Wahid's fiercest critics, said last week that the impeachment proceedings will likely take several more months. 

 "The weakness is mostly because of political factors, so political parties should stop bickering," Deputy Governor Anwar Nasution told reporters. 

 The fall of the rupiah to levels not seen in more than two years underscores how seriously Indonesia lags behind other Asian countries in emerging from a region-wide financial crisis that began in 1997. While South Korea and Thailand, for example, can likely raise capital in international markets, Jakarta talks of issuing bonds backed not by the state but by receipts on natural-gas sales. South Korea at least made efforts to follow International Monetary Fund-favored reforms and push corporate restructuring, but Jakarta has been in almost a constant state of bickering with the IMF and has barely gotten corporate reform off the ground. 

 The tense relationship with the IMF is hurting investor confidence. The agency has been withholding a $400 million installment of its $5 billion support program to Jakarta since December because of disagreements on reform measures, and the standoff could sour Indonesia's Paris Club creditors and jeopardize an agreement reached last year to restructure $5.8 billion of foreign debt. 

 Bank Indonesia's foreign reserves -- currently at $29 billion on a gross basis -- aren't large enough to defend the rupiah, Mr. Nasution said. 

 Normally, the central bank intervenes indirectly through state banks. However, the central bank sold around $50 million directly Friday, but this hasn't helped the rupiah. Selling dollars directly to commercial banks is meant to give a signal to the market the central bank is ready to defend the rupiah. 

 Protesters Assemble at Wahid Palace 

 More than 10,000 demonstrators gathered in front of Mr. Wahid's white-column residence. Thousands more rallied at campuses across the capital and staged street marches. Scores of riot police and soldiers guarded the palace and kept the students apart from a small group of Wahid supporters. 

 Organizers of Monday's protests originally had called for a national strike. The capital was quiet, however, and many offices and stores were open as usual. 

 Following the student rally, the cabinet announced that the government has decided not to increase the price of "fuel for the people," including kerosene and leaded gasoline, but will consider raising it on Oct. 1 after consulting the House of Representatives. 

 "The government, however, has decided to increase fuel prices for industrial sectors by 50% and for foreign ships by 100% on April 1," Minister of Energy and Mineral Resources Purnomo Yusgiantoro told reporters. 

 Ordinary people usually use kerosene to cook, while public transportation uses leaded gasoline. The fuel-price increase is a sensitive issue that could lead to mass rioting. In 1998, it was regarded as a factor in the fall of Suharto. The government earlier planned to increase fuel prices by an average 20% on April 1 as recommended by the IMF. Without the increase, the government will have to cover a shortfall of 4.3 trillion rupiah in the budget. 

 Mr. Wahid later reiterated at a press conference that he wouldn't resign. "I will not resign," Mr. Wahid said. "The country will fall apart if I resign," he added. Mr. Wahid said he has urged his more popular vice president, Megawati Sukarnoputri, to take a more active role in government. 

 Under a power-sharing agreement last year, Ms. Megawati was supposed to take over the day-to-day running of the government. But members of her Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle, or PDI-P, say the president has failed to hand over any meaningful power to their leader. 

 The pressure on Mr. Wahid rose in recent weeks following the slaughter of more than 450 migrant settlers at the hands of indigenous Dayak tribesmen in the province of Central Kalimantan. 

 In another restive province, Aceh, officials said Monday that separatist rebels attacked an oil depot owned by the state Pertamina petroleum company, blowing up several drums of oil but causing no injuries. Insurgents also killed two people in nearby Pidie, police said. 

 Over the weekend, Exxon Mobil's Indonesian subsidiary announced it had cut oil production in the region due to escalating fighting. But Mr. Yusgiantoro said the government will help guard ExxonMobil's facilities there. 

 The Jakarta Stock Exchange composite index fell 17.495, or 4.2%, to close at 396.611 Monday, off an intraday low of 391. 

 -- Wall Street Journal staff reporter Michael Schuman contributed to this article.

title: B. Indonesia  says reserves enough for  intervention .
text:
JAKARTA, March 9 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank said on Friday it had enough reserves to intervene in the currency market to prop up the plunging rupiah and that there was no need to impose capital controls. 

 "It's enough to intervene," Bank Indonesia Governor Sjahril Sabirin told reporters when asked whether the central bank had enough reserves to defend the rupiah. 

 "(Intervention can be done) directly. It's standard procedure," he said when asked whether the central bank had directly intervened in the market on Friday as the currency fell to 29-month lows. 

 The bank would also leave any decision on interest rates to the market, he added.

title: Emerging  FX -Rupiah flounders as others stand firm.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 9 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah slammed into 29-month lows on Friday, while other regional currencies were tethered to a steadier yen. 

 But their prospects were not looking very sunny, as the yen stumbled over the Japanese government's emergency economic package in late Asian trade. 

 Local corporate demand for dollars finally pushed the rupiah over the 10,000 mark, which it last saw on October 7, 1998, according to Reuters Graphics data. 

 Direct intervention by Bank Indonesia and dollar selling by state banks failed to bolster the rupiah. Heavily indebted Indonesian companies have been snapping up dollars in recent sessions as the first quarter end nears and amid the country's deepening political and economic crisis. 

 In the meantime, regional currencies enjoyed a reprieve for most of the session as yen bears took a break ahead of the announcement of the emergency economic package. 

 The yen has suffered this week at the hands of a market confused by sometimes conflicting statements from various government officials. 

 Its stuttering movements have dominated activity in regional markets, and left most Asian currencies in weaker ranges. 

 With the yen very much in the hot seat, the euro was steady, helped by the relatively brighter outlook for Europe's economy compared with the U.S. and Japan's. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah dropped past 10,000, succumbing to mounting pressure from local corporate demand for dollars despite Bank Indonesia's efforts to rein it in. 

 Bank Indonesia later said direct intervention was "standard procedure," adding that the bank had enough reserves to defend the rupiah and there was no need to impose capital controls. 

 However, a prominent local banker called on the government to force Indonesian exporters to repatriate their earnings. Gunarni Soewaoro, the head of the local bank association Perbanas, said such an idea would be more palatable given the gridlock between Indonesia and its chief donor the IMF. 

 Local companies who are seeking to fulfil dollar requirements by the end of the first quarter have fueled the dollar buying spree, as the market remained on edge over Indonesia's economic and political woes. 

 Dealers said the main concern was the stalled talks between the IMF and Jakarta, which have helding up a $400 million loan disbursement. Jakarta said on Friday it hoped to resolve its differences with the IMF this month. 

 KOREAN WON -2 The won gained as the firmer yen spurred unwinding of long dollar positions, but dealers dismissed it as merely a short-term reprieve given persistent worries about Japan's outlook. 

 Further foreign fund sales of local shares also limited the won's upside prospects, but dealers said a reluctance to take aggressive positions before the release of U.S. jobs data later in the day dampened overall trading interest. 

 The won was expected to face near term resistance around 1,260, which marks the 38 percent retracement of the dollar's February 21-March 8 rise. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht shifted to the middle of its recent range of around 43.30-43.70 as the market rooted around for fresh factors. 

 For the past several sessions, the baht has been caught tracking the yen's moves. But with little activity in the yen for most of the session, the baht was stuck in a holding pattern. 

 Dealers in Bangkok and Singapore said activity was dull amid a general feeling the market was long of dollars. 

 However, many players were still reluctant to unwind their long dollar positions, hoping for another push towards 43.70 if the yen should fall past 120 again. 

 The government had yet to announce the pricing formula for its planned asset managememt company. Government officials and bankers were meeting to discuss details of the plan. 

 Thailand's finance minsitry also said it would issue 94 billion baht worth of government and Financial Institutions Development Fund bonds between April and June, and 20 billion baht worth of savings bonds, to help plug the budget deficit. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso weakened slightly in a somewhat delayed reaction to the unsteadiness of regional currencies. 

 Dealers in Manila said trading was uneventful with dollar sales from local exporters quickly matched by bids from interbank players mindful of a dimming peso outlook. 

 Looking ahead, dealers said they were bracing for the local import season, which starts in April. They added the sagging sentiment towards regional currencies in the midst of the global economic slowdown did not bode well for the peso. 

 However, French-based investment bank BNP Paribas said on Friday it felt the impact of the U.S. economic slowdown on Asia was overstated, and predicted the Philippines would weather the downturn well. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar was off its low as fears of potential central bank intervention prompted some players to sell the U.S. dollar near 1.7600. 

 The troubled rupiah and expectations of high demand for the dollar in the wake of fresh mergers and acquisition activity should continue to weigh on the local currency, dealers said. 

 "People in the market believe the Singtel and Optus deal is a done deal. But I think the company must have covered most if not all of its dollar demand to buy Optus," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 "News of PSA aiming to buy a Belgian company also added to the downward pressure," he said. 

 Singapore port operator PSA Corp said on Friday it intended to buy at least 51 percent of Hesse Noord Natie (HNN), a newly merged Belgian port management company. 

 HNN has been valued at between 580 million and 650 million euros ($541 million and $606 million). 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar ended easier, slipping past the 32.40 per dollar level as local shares slipped for the second day and the currency market fretted over the yen's dim outlook. 

 The benchmark TAIEX was hit by sales of heavyweight tech stocks after the Nasdaq's 2.48 percent fall and Intel's third straight sales warning. 

 Dealers said the central bank had intervened to lift the Taiwan dollar off early lows of 32.418, but they expected a range of 32.40-32.50 for next week.

title: Bank  Indonesia intervenes  directly to buy rupiah.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 9 (Reuters) - Bank Indonesia intervened directly in local currency markets on Friday, selling an estimated $20 million to defend the rupiah around the 9,920/30 level, dealers in Jakarta said. 

 "We saw Bank Indonesia intervening directly in the market this morning at 9,920/30," said a dealer at a foreign bank in Jakarta. 

 "There's genuine demand for dollars out there, and Bank Indonesia is the only supplier of dollars in the market. There are no other suppliers," he added. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said several state banks were also spotted in the market selling dollars. State banks have tended to sell dollars on behalf of the central bank in recent sessions. 

 The rupiah was quoted at 9,935/45 to the dollar at 0211 GMT, against levels of about 9,925 late on Thursday. 

 Heavily indebted local companies have been buying dollars in order to repay or service foreign debt. 

 Dealers have noted that buying has picked up steam in recent sessions as the end of the first quarter approaches and amid growing worries over Indonesia's shaky political and economic outlook.

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesia rupiah hits 29-month low.
text:
SINGAPORE, March 9 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah hit 29-month lows on Friday as local companies sought dollars for debt servicing needs amid growing gloom about the country's political and economic picture. 

 Jakarta dealers said the rupiah traded at a low of 10,040 to the dollar in late afternoon trade shortly after hitting 10,000 for the first time since October 7, 1998, according to Reuters Graphics data. 

 Dealers said state banks were seen selling dollars in local currency markets all morning as the rupiah extended its slide. 

 Bank Indonesia was also seen intervening directly early in the day, selling an estimated $20 million at 9,920/30, they said. 

 BANK INDONESIA INTERVENES

Central Bank governor Sjahril Sabirin later said direct foreign exchange intervention was "standard procedure". 

 He said the bank had enough reserves to defend the rupiah and that there was no need to impose capital controls. 

 Indonesia's gross foreign reserves stood at $29.09 billion as of February 19, down from $29.11 billion the previous week. 

 Despite the central bank's defence, dealers in Jakarta said the rupiah could slip further. "If the demand is still there, we could touch 10,050," said a dealer at a foreign bank in Jakarta. 

 In the meantime, the offshore rupiah non-deliverable forward market was anxiously monitoring the spot market. 

 "It's not good that 10,000 was broken without much of a fight," said an NDF dealer at a foreign bank in Singapore. 

 At 0659 GMT, the one-month rupiah NDF was quoted by Prebon Yamane at 10,400/10,500. The six-month was at 11,400/11,600. 

 GLOOM GROWS 

 The rupiah has come under growing pressure recently as heavily indebted companies buy dollars to make end-quarter payments on foreign loans. 

 Mounting pessimism about President Abdurrahman Wahid's shaky leadership and a long-running spat with the International Monetary Fund, which could jeopardise a $5.8 billion debt rescheduling deal with the Paris Club of official creditors, have also weighed on the currency. 

 The IMF delayed a $400 million loan to Indonesia in December, amid concerns about the central bank's independence and worries that new regional autonomy laws would lead to fiscal laxity. 

 On Friday, a prominent Indonesian banker urged the government to force exporters to repatriate their earnings. 

 "There has to be...(forced export earnings repatriation) to help the economy," Gunarni Soeworo, head of the local influential association of local banks Perbanas, told Reuters. 

 "Under normal conditions there is no need to do so, but we cannot expect this to happen (voluntarily) in the current situation," he said.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends At 29-Mo Low On Politics,
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah plunged to a 29-month low Friday as rising domestic political conflicts and moves by international ratings agencies continued to fuel dollar buying, dealers said. 

 Standard & Poor's Thursday cut its outlook on the country's sovereign debt to negative from stable. Earlier in the week Moody's Investors Service cut its outlook on Indonesia's sovereign rating to stable from positive. The cuts confirmed the market's already bearish sentiment on the rupiah. 

 Despite Bank Indonesia intervention, amid strong demand for the U.S. currency, the dollar easily broke through the psychologically important level of IDR10,000 Friday. After rising to IDR10,140, the dollar ended at IDR10,090 compared to its close at IDR9,930 Thursday. 

 Dealers said Bank Indonesia likely spent around $60 million Friday to defend the rupiah - directly and through indirect interventions by state banks. 

 "The dollar's rise seemed to be unstoppable as everyone was buying the dollar," said a dealer with a local bank. "People were worried that the political conflict has reached the grass-root level." 

 Dealers said the market ignored Bank Indonesia Governor Sjahril Sabirin's warning that the central bank is ready to intervene to help the dollar. 

 "With gross foreign exchange reserve of around $29 billion, the market knows that Bank Indonesia's pockets aren't deep," said a dealer. 

 The dollar's sharp increase pushed the one-month interbank money market rate higher to 15.25%, from less than 14% Thursday, as banks borrowed rupiah in the money market to back their dollar-long positions in the foreign exchange market. 

 The one-month swap premium increased to 25% from around 20% Thursday. 

 The rupiah's plunge also dragged Indonesian share prices 3.3% lower Friday. 

 The dollar's rise to above IDR10,000 is expected to trigger further dollar buying next week. 

 Dealers said the dollar's rise may incite panic dollar buying in the society like what happened in mid-1998, when many Indonesian bought dollars as the currency crisis was escalating into political crisis. "IDR10,000 is a very important psychological level," said a dealer. 

 Dealers expect the dollar to test the next resistance level of IDR10,500 Monday before rising to IDR11,000 if Bank Indonesia fails to increase its dollar selling.

title: Bk  Indonesia  Ready To  Intervene  To Help Rupiah -Governor
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's central bank governor said Friday the bank would continue to intervene to help the rupiah, but ruled out new measures to help the battered currency. 

 "We are always ready to intervene in the rupiah, but there is no new policy," Sjahril Sabirin told reporters. 

 Bank Indonesia's current policy is to intervene by selling dollars when the rupiah is weak, but it doesn't announce this intervention on a case-by-case basis. 

 Sjahril's comments suggest the bank won't consider other harsher measures - such as full capital controls - to restrict the rupiah's fall. 

 Earlier this year, the central bank banned offshore trading in rupiah, which has cut speculative activity, but it stopped short of banning the transfer of rupiah out of the country into dollars. 

 In afternoon trade, the dollar is at IDR10,050, much higher than IDR9,930 at Thursday's close in Asia. The rupiah is at its lowest levels since October 1998.

title: Bk  Indonesia  Gov: Will  Intervene  If IDR Below 10,000/Dlr

JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia drew a line of defense for the rupiah at IDR10,000 to the dollar, with the governor saying Tuesday the central bank would intervene to help the local unit above that level. 

 The central bank will also raise interest rates if necessary to help the rupiah, which is currently at over two-year lows of at IDR9,880 to the dollar, central bank governor Sjahril Sabirin told reporters. 

 "Bank Indonesia will take action if the rupiah breaches IDR10,000 to the dollar support," Sjahril said. 

Indonesia's central bank has a policy of intervening to support the rupiah through selling dollars, but it doesn't announce action on a daily basis. 

 Rates on the bank's one-month paper are currently at 14.79%, having risen sharply toward the end of last year to help the rupiah. 

 The rupiah is low as political tensions and security concerns continue to deter foreign investors. 

 Critics say higher rates are unlikely to bring back foreign investors to rupiah assets, but are necessary to keep imported inflation in check. 

 They also question Bank Indonesia's ability to intervene, given its lack of foreign reserves for a sustained defense of the currency. Foreign reserves are currently around $29 billion on a gross basis.

title: Emerging  FX  - Clouded by yen, Greenspan eyed.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 28 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies retreated in late trade on Wednesday as the dollar rose after the Bank of Japan cut interest rates. 

 The BOJ trimmed the overnight call rate and official discount rate by 10 basis points to 0.15 percent and 0.25 percent respectively, citing slowing overseas growth and declining stock prices. 

 The news caused the yen to drop briefly to around 116.70 from about 116 before the announcement. 

 The overall mood was cautious after Tuesday's news of a sharp drop in U.S. consumer confidence and ahead of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's congressional testimony at 1430 GMT. 

 "I don't think Greenspan would want to sound unduly pessimistic, especially coming just 14 days after his recent testimony," said Lee Boon Keng, currency strategist at DBS. 

 "So, I think we will get another rate cut in the next meeting. Those who expect an inter-meeting cut might be in for disappointment," he said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah remained soggy despite support from state banks as local corporate demand for dollars lurked against the backdrop of political troubles and an unresolved row between the IMF and the government. 

 The Thai baht slipped as the market digested dismal trade numbers showing a deficit in January - the second in 40 months. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah managed to hold to a firmer footing as state banks sold dollars in its defense. 

 Bank Indonesia said on Tuesday it would keep intervening and and might hike interest rates to boost the rupiah. 

 The key one-month SBI rate edged up to 14.79 percent from 14.75 percent at last week's central bank auction, below the 10-15 basis point rise expected by analysts. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said state banks sold dollars around the day's high of 9,632. But the rupiah still faced the tricky mix of poor sentiment and local corporate demand for dollars. 

 Another potential prop for the rupiah was also removed, with the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency (IBRA) saying it was delaying the conversion of $500 million into rupiah "for various reasons". IBRA had previously said it planned to convert the money from mid-February in conjunction with the central bank. 

 The rupiah, which has weakened over two percent since the beginning of the year, slipped to a 29-month low of 9,910 on Tuesday as already depressed sentiment took a turn for the worse amid worsening ethnic violence in Borneo. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht hovered near 43.00, but was off its intraday low as late news of a current account surplus offered some relief after the disappointing trade data. 

 Dealers in Bangkok said some interbank players took profits on the dollar after the central bank released current account and foreign debt data. 

 The current account showed a $298 million surplus in January despite a trade deficit of $282 million in the same month. Total private sector foreign debt fell to $46.4 billion at end-December against $47.2 billion the previous month. 

 The market was cautious ahead of stricter foreign exchange disclosure rules to take effect on Thursday. 

 "It could affect trading volume in the market. But again, it might not be as bad as most people think it will be. We'll see," said a dealer at a local bank in Bangkok. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso was stuck at the weaker end of a narrow 48.20-48.335 range as the market unwound long peso positions following its failure to reach highs of 45-46 despite a better political scene. 

 Manila dealers said the market was reluctant to take new positions ahead of a pending Supreme Court decision on former President Joseph Estrada's petition to be declared the legitimate president. Court officials said on Tuesday the decision would be made in around 10 days. 

 Meanwhile, Bureau of Treasury officials said on Wednesday they would continue to offer some Treasury bonds over the counter to meet immediate funding needs. 

 The Treasury announced on Monday it would suspend auctions of new bond issues for at least a month to reduce borrowing costs. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar was unmoved on Wednesday, with the Taipei spot market closed for a national holiday and offshore dealers of non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) reluctant to make bids. 

 But NDF dealers in Singapore said they expected pressure on spot and forward rates when trading resumes on Thursday, citing a 4.36 percent fall in the Nasdaq overnight and a weaker yen after the BOJ's rate cut. 

 The Taiwan dollar is vulnerable to shifts in the tech-heavy Nasdaq through foreign investment in stocks, and to the yen's moves as Taiwan competes with Japan in key exports to the U.S.

 It ended at 1,250.8 per dollar, near its opening of 1,250.7. It had closed Tuesday at 1,246.5. 

 Trade was driven by position-squaring ahead of Greenspan's testimony and a Korean holiday on Thursday. 

 "For the time being, the dollar looks set to continue trading in a 1,245-1,255 range with a breakout most likely to come from further deteriorating U.S. data or from the falling Nasdaq," said a UBS Warburg report. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar was hovering near the weaker end of its subdued intra-day 1.7400-1.7430 range after spiking higher overnight on stop-loss dollar sales in thin London trade. 

 Dollar/Sing rose briefly to 1.7430 on Wednesday before profit-taking set in as the yen came off its initial rate cut-inspired lows. 

 "It was just the market getting spooked," said one dealer. 

 But other dealers said players were selling dollars in expectation of a cut before the Fed's next rate-setting meeting on March 20.

title: Emerging  FX  - Rangebound ahead of Greenspan.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 27 (Reuters) - Asian currencies dragged their feet in recent ranges on Tuesday with their downside supported by near-term uncertainty over the direction of the U.S. dollar. 

 Analysts said wariness ahead of crucial U.S. consumer confidence data due later in the day and Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony on Wednesday, deterred players from making any aggressive moves. 

 After a steadier start in Asia, the dollar gave in to both the yen and euro on Greenspan-related rumours and dollar selling by Japanese exporters. 

 Dealers said vague rumours Greenspan would resign were not taken seriously but were used as an excuse to liquidate long dollar positions ahead of the consumer confidence data. 

 However, the yen-sensitive North Asian currencies gave up most of their early gains as foreign investors in their stock markets were unimpressed by the Nasdaq's overnight gains and continued to trim recently built portfolios. 

 Most Southeast Asian markets had few leads to follow and moved within tight ranges in thin trade, with the exception of the Indonesian rupiah which witnessed another volatile day. 

 The rupiah swooned to a fresh 28-month low, marred by more than a week of ethnic slaughter in Central Kalimantan and on uncertainty over the resumption of IMF lending, before recovering some ground on aggressive central bank intervention. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah skidded to an early low of 9,910 as local banks and companies scrounged for dollars amid jitters about the unrest. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said state banks began selling dollars once the rupiah broke 9,900 - a level it last saw in October 1998. The central bank was believed to be behind the selling, with the amount sold estimated at around $80 million or more. 

 Average daily trading volume in the onshore market has been between $50-$100 million for the past few weeks, while offshore activity has dried up following the central bank's trading curbs. 

 Bank Indonesia said it was intervening to help the rupiah, and would hike interest rates to protect the battered currency. The one-month SBI rate now stands at 14.75 percent. 

 However, deputy central bank govenor Anwar Nasution reiterated that these moves would have a limited impact if Indonesia failed to get its house in order. 

 The rupiah's latest bout of weakness comes amid fears over security as ethnic Dayaks continue their murderous rampage against Madurese settlers in the remote province of Kalimantan. 

 Analysts said there were also concerns over Jakarta's failure to resolve certain issues with the IMF in order to secure the release of a $400 million loan disbursal. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht was testing 42.80 resistance as offshore players unwound long dollar positions ahead of the March 1 implementation of the Bank of Thailand's new disclosure rules on forex deals. 

 Dealers said foreign banks both offshore and onshore were selling dollars as well as local stocks and bonds to ensure they had access to the baht after the new rules took effect. 

 However, dealers in Singapore said it was merely a precaution rather than a sign of real concern over the possibility of further controls. 

 The dollar was expected to be well-supported around 42.75/80, levels which it has not seen since February 21, as local companies were expected to buy dollars there. 

 But dealers added a firm break of that level could trigger stop-loss dollar sales. 

 The central bank will issue January data on manufacturing output, exports, imports and the current account on Wednesday. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso was trapped in a narrow range with exporter inflows limiting the downside and foreign banks, usually active on behalf of the central bank, capping gains. 

 Some dealers in Manila suspected the central bank, encouraged by subdued corporate demand for dollars and a steady flow from exporters, was buying dollars for foreign debt repayments. 

 Dealers said the market was also nervous over the Supreme Court's closed-door hearing of a petition, filed by former president Joseph Estrada, challenging the legitimacy of President Gloria Macapagal Arroyo's administration. 

 Officials said the court was unlikely to rule on the petition on Tuesday. 

 Dealers said the peso was likely to come under more pressure from month-end position squaring on Wednesday. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar was virtually flat from Monday's close of 32.345 with the market reluctant to position itself ahead of Greenspan's testimony. 

 Dealers in Singapore said trading was quiet as players ignored another piece of data showing a limping economy. 

 Taiwan's top economic planning agency said the economy slowed in January, flashing its "blue" light for the second consecutive month. Its index of leading indicators, which forecasts peaks and troughs in the business cycle, fell 1.1 percent on month to 97.6. 

 It blamed the slowdown on fewer working days in January due to a week-long Lunar New Year holiday, and noted a plan to add T$111.5 billion to the 2001 budget for public infrastructure works to fuel growth. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar was marginally stronger, staying well within the trading territory of the past month. 

 "It's nothing more than position adjustment," said one trader of Tuesday's move to the firmer end of the 1.7420-1.7480 range. 

 Some dealers said the market was squaring positions on the firmer yen, but others said it lacked clear direction. 

 The Sing could get that direction later in the week from the rupiah, which is teetering near the psychological 10,000 support. 

 Dealers said a slide past 10,000 in the rupiah could weaken the Sing dollar, given Singapore's close investment ties with Indonesia. 

 KOREAN WON -2 The won gained from a firmer yen despite foreign outflows from Seoul's stock market, which ended 1.32 percent lower as foreign investors fled the futures market, leading a drop in the spot market. 

 But onshore currency volumes were light in advance of a domestic holiday on March 1. 

 "I think it's going to stay quiet until the end of the week," said one trader of won non-deliverable forwards in Singapore. 

 Dealers said the market was likely to be long of dollars over the week, striking fresh long positions at 1,240/1,242. 

 Near-term dollar resistance is seen at 1,250, a level it has stayed shy of since February 19.

title: Asia Markets - Stocks slack,  forex  barely brighter.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Asian shares turned in a 

 lacklustre performance on Monday with Wall Street and talk 

 about rate cuts playing minor roles. Most currencies were 

 steady. 

     Regional markets focused on growing speculation of a U.S. 

 rate cut before the Federal Reserve policy meeting on March 20 

 given feeble equity prices and consumer confidence. 

     The Bank of Japan was also the subject of speculation, with 

 dealers talking about the possibility of a return to zero 

 interest rates ahead of a BOJ policy meeting. 

     But investors were reluctant to take big positions ahead of 

 other key events scheduled for later in the week. The 

 Conference Board consumer confidence index is due out on 

 Tuesday, and Fed chief Alan Greenspan will testify before a 

 Congressional committee on Wednesday. 

     Investors also failed to find much inspiration from either 

 the Nasdaq's slight bounce nor a small dip in U.S. blue 

 chips on Friday. 


    However, Taiwan tech shares	   took a knock-on hit



from Motorola's profit warning on Friday, while Korean



shares rose slightly on the back of the rate cut



expectations.



    Shares in Tokyo	   ended the day mixed, with techs



slipping as banking shares jumping on hopes for a BOJ easing.



    Hong Kong's Hang Seng	  was barely in negative



territory, but property stocks were buoyant amid the rate cut



speculation.



    RUPIAH RUFFLED, BAHT BOUNCED



    Most regional currencies were little changed, except for



the Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah , which headed



for entirely different directions.



    The rupiah went south as Indonesia's many economic and



political problems took their toll on local financial markets.



At the local opening, the currency quickly broke the 9,800



level to lows not seen since October 1998 amid worsening ethnic



violence in Central Kalimantan.



Dealers said onshore trading volume was slightly higher



than normal as the country's political and security picture



deteriorated.



Bank Indonesia said later in the day it was intervening to



help the battered rupiah. Senior deputy governor Anwar Nasution



blamed the rupiah's recent bout of weakness mainly on the



bloodshed in the remote Central Kalimantan province, which has



left up to 400 people dead in the past week.



But he also added the rupiah's woes were due to a "mix of



everything", including Jakarta's deadlock with its chief donor,



the International Monetary Fund.



The Fund delayed a $400 million loan disbursement to



Indonesia because of concerns over the new regional autonomy



laws and central bank independence. Talks between the IMF and



Indonesia proved fruitless, with a new round of talks yet to be



scheduled.



In contrast, the baht took cheer from new Prime



Minister Thaksin Shinawatra's plan to spend his way towards



economic growth.



Thaksin presented his controversial policies to parliament



on Monday, laying out nine top priorities to encourage economic



growth that focus on consumption.



Thai markets were particularly pleased with the



government's commitment to set up a national asset management



company to tackle bad debts in the system. Analysts too



approved of the plan.



"We think this is structurally positive to the market and



bank shares...we are more positive on the decisiveness of the



government in tackling the country's NPL problem because the



government could initiate other key policies," said Merrill



Lynch in a research note.



PHILIPPINES SUSPENDS BONDS



The Philippine Bureau of Treasury said on Friday it would



temporarily stop offering seven and 10-year Treasury bonds,



starting this week, to bring down the government's borrowing



costs.



Both longer-dated bonds were fetching yields significantly



higher than short-dated paper, with the seven-year at 16.0



percent and the 10-year at 17.4 percent against 10.456 percent



for 91-day paper and 11.783 percent for 182-day paper.



"I think they are just looking to fund themselves in an



area of the curve, which is probably around the 2-5 year which



has a lower risk premium, to reduce their costs," Adam Le



Mesurier, regional economist at Goldman Sachs, told Reuters



Television.



However, Standard Chartered Bank said the Treasury can help



prop up prices in longer-dated bonds and bring yields down only



if the central bank is steadfast in maintaining low interest



rates.



"It is easy to see why local bond market players demanded a



higher risk-premium on their investments...The BSP has a



penchant for jacking up domestic interest rates whenever the


currency comes under pressure," it said in a research note.

title: UPDATE 1-Bank  Indonesia  says  intervening  to help rupiah.
text:
JAKARTA, Feb 26 (Reuters) - Bank Indonesia said on Monday it was intervening to help the beleaguered rupiah and hoped to stop it breaching 10,000 against the U.S. dollar as ethnic violence in Borneo and soured relations with the IMF hit the unit. 

 "We will continue to intervene in the market but we should also address the main problems, the unrest and political problems," senior deputy governor Anwar Nasution told Reuters. 

 "Of course we hope we can stabilise the rupiah below 10,000." 

 By the latest trade, the currency was being quoted at 9,840/9,860 against the dollar, lows not seen since October 1998. It closed at 9,610 on Friday. 

 Lingering political and economic problems and sporadic bouts of violence have eaten away at the rupiah in the past year, wiping off some 25 percent of its value against the dollar. 

 Nasution blamed its recent woes on a "mix of everything", but mainly bloodshed around the town of Sampit in Central Kalimantan province that has killed up to 400 people in the past week. 

 "During the past two years we have been killing each other here and now look at the Sampit issue," he said. 

 A spat with the IMF was also a problem, he said. 

 "This is also having some affect. We need a new letter of intent for restructuring external debt of the public sector under the Paris Club agreement." 

 Indonesia has been at loggerheads with the International Monetary Fund over a $400 million loan delayed since December due to a number of missed economic reform targets and proposed central bank law reforms. 

 Financial markets had been looking for a concrete outcome from high-level talks between Indonesia and the Fund in Washington last week but there were no breakthroughs. 

 The IMF on Friday described the meeting as productive, saying both sides agreed to intensify discussions but there was no hint of a fresh mission or when the loan would be released. 

 The currency has been relatively steady in the past month, coping well with parliament's censure of President Abdurrahman Wahid over two financial scandals and subsequent demonstrations. 

 Nasution said foreign exchange curbs announced on January 15 remained effective but the currency was still exposed to the offshore rupiah non-deliverable forward (NDF) market. 

 "The rules are still effective but again that is only a very limited objective - a non underlying transaction of the rupiah, that's about it." 

 "We cannot ban the foreign banks in the Asian market in Singapore from doing their business. I don't even think the monetary authority in Singapore can control the foreign institutions in Asian currency units," he said. 

 The forex rules introduced last month include a ban on rupiah transfers to non-residents and a lower ceiling of $3 million on cumulative forward deals onshore banks can conduct with non-residents with no underlying investment purpose.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Dn Late On Corp Dlr Demand, World Bk
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah fell 2% to its lowest level since October 1998 on strong dollar demand by corporates and banks, as international lending agencies tightened the screws on the government, dealers said. 

 Worsening ethnic violence in Central Kalimantan province, on the island of Borneo, had also cast a shadow on the rupiah, dealers said. 

 Around 0900 GMT, the dollar was quoted at 9,830 rupiah, its highest level since October 1998, when Indonesia was mired in a financial crisis. Late Friday the dollar traded at IDR9,685. 

 The rupiah had dropped to as low as IDR9,865 earlier Monday, but found temporary respite when state banks sold dollars, probably on behalf of the central bank, and as commercial banks locked in profits, dealers said. 

 Corporates needing to repay their foreign debts scrambled for dollars amid expectations the rupiah could weaken further, after the World Bank warned last Friday it would cease all new lending to the government if the country slips into another crisis, and amid concerns the ethnic clashes in Borneo could spread further, dealers said. 

 Participants were also wondering about the outcome of Chief Economics Minister Rizal Ramli's meeting with the International Monetary Fund last week, dealers said. There are worries about the status of the International Monetary Fund's disbursement of a $400 million loan tranche, which has been suspended since December last year, as the government and the lending agency tried to iron out differences over issues of fiscal decentralization, a controversial amendment of a central bank law, and a delayed sale of the government's stakes in two local banks. 

 Genuine corporate demand early in the day emerged around IDR9,725 to IDR9,775, prompting other participants to cover their short dollar positions, dealers said. This triggered stop-loss dollar buying around IDR9,800, which pushed the dollar to as high as IDR9,865, they added. 

 "It's an accumulation of all the bad news," said a dealer at a European bank. "Today was the turning point when everybody decided to cover their short dollar positions." 

 The rupiah's fall Monday was its largest since the central bank imposed in mid-January its controversial foreign exchange regulations, which have effectively smothered offshore trading in the currency. 

Currency watchers said the restrictions have only served to slow down the rupiah's descent - and not halt it - since onshore dollar demand remains strong. 

 "Although Bank Indonesia's restrictions have given the rupiah near-term stability, this shows the problem is not coming from the offshore market, but rather onshore," said Mansoor Mohi-uddin, a regional currency strategist at UBS Warburg. "BI's (Bank Indonesia) restrictions haven't helped the currency because it's aiming at the wrong target." 

 Deutsche Bank has advised Indonesian corporates and investors to hedge their long rupiah positions before the dollar strengthens further, said strategist Peter Redward. 

 As long as Indonesia's problems aren't resolved, currency watchers said they expect the rupiah to slide further, citing the IDR10,000 as a major psychological support level. 

 "For the rest of this week, we'll see some pressure still on the rupiah," said the European bank dealer. "If the dollar goes to IDR10,000, it will spark panic again among the local corporate and retail players." 

 The rupiah's fall will likely be at a more gradual pace in the short term, as participants are wary of testing the central bank's resolve, dealers said. 

 Following the rupiah's fall, senior central bank officials warned Monday that it was prepared to defend the currency through a possible hike in the benchmark one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia rate and intervention in the foreign exchange market. 

 Dealers said Bank Indonesia's intervention Monday was modest, as it failed to counter the strong dollar demand, they added.

text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia Governor Sjahril Sabirin said Monday the central bank will intervene to support the rupiah if necessary. 

 "If needed, we will intervene in the market," Sjahril told reporters. 

 Sjahril's comments come after the currency dropped below 9,800 rupiah against the dollar earlier Monday on local corporate dollar demand. IDR9,800 is the dollar's highest level since October 1998. 

 Sjahril said it wasn't clear whether the current weakness in the rupiah was temporary or will persist and require intervention. He didn't offer any levels when the central bank will intervene. 

 Although he made the statement, dealers believe the central bank sold dollars through state banks earlier Monday. However, the amount was insignificant and failed to arrest the dollar's rise. 

 Concerns that the rupiah could weaken further, as international lenders toughen their stance on the Indonesian government, has fueled keen local corporate demand for dollars, dealers said. 

 The World Bank warned Friday that it would cease all new lending to the government if the country's problems escalate into a political or economic crisis. 

 Market participants are also worried about the status of the International Monetary Fund's disbursement of a delayed $400 million loan tranche, as the government and the lending agency try to iron out differences over issues of fiscal decentralization and the controversial amendment of a central bank law, which could undermine Bank Indonesia's independence.

title: Emerging  FX  - Domestic leads dominate as BOJ eases.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 9 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were steady to firmer late on Friday on the back of domestic leads such as asset sales and central bank intervention. 

 In terms of external factors, all eyes were on the Bank of Japan's policy board meeting which stretched late into the day, intensifying speculation of an easing, especially after a local television station reported the BOJ would cut its discount rate. 

 This was later borne out when the central bank said its policy board decided to cut the official discount rate to 0.350 percent from 0.50 percent, effective from February 13. 

 It was the first time the BOJ had cut the largely symbolic rate since September 1995. It also decided by a majority decision to keep the key overnight call rate at 0.25 percent. 

 The yen fell to its lowest in nearly two weeks against the dollar after the discount rate cut, which the government welcomed as a move that would help boost the economy. 

 "The yen remained weak but regional currencies did not pay as much attention to its level as what could happen if the BOJ decides to take a decisive step to reverse this clear downtrend in the economy," said a dealer at an Asian bank in Singapore. 

 "I guess people don't want to be caught too long on dollars when they return to the market on Monday. Local factors are also major drivers today," he said. 

 The ailing Indonesian rupiah recouped some lost ground following state bank dollar sales above 9,600, believed to be on the central bank's behalf. Bank Indonesia said it had intervened over the past several days to prop up the currency. The Korean won ended firmer in anticipation of capital inflows after Korea Exchange Bank (KEB) announced it would soon sell its credit card unit to a foreign firm. The sale could fetch around $700 million. 

 Next week, investors are likely to closely watch U.S. January retail sale numbers on Tuesday and Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's bi-annual testimony before Congress on monetary policy on the same day. 

 The market is keen to hear the Fed chief's opinions on the economy after he told lawmakers a few weeks ago that economic growth right now was probably "close to zero." 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso ended the week on a slightly stronger note, but failed to hold onto its intraday high of 47.945 as dollar sales from exporters and overseas workers lost steam. 

 Dealers in Manila said exporters emerged in early trading to sell dollars that they had held since the political crisis involving former president Joseph Estrada. 

 They added the current stable political situation has also induced more overseas workers to repatriate their earnings. 

 However, the peso slipped as those sales slowed, and then dipped in reaction to the central bank's decision to cut rates by 50 basis points, even though the decision was widely expected. 

 The central bank's cut on Friday completed the unwinding of a 400 basis point hike in October to defend the peso. The overnight borrowing and lending rates will be 11 percent and 13.25 percent, respectively, from Monday. 

Central bank governor Rafael Buenaventura said the bank did not expect much downside for the peso after the cuts given the calmer political situation. 

 However, analysts said higher inflation may curb the bank's ability to ease interest rates further. January inflation rose 6.9 percent on year - the highest rate in 22 months. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won ended higher on inflow hopes after KEB said it would soon sell its credit card unit to a foreign company. 

 Local media said DBS Group Holdings Ltd , Citibank Corp and Standard Chartered Plc were vying for a stake in KEB Credit Card. 

 But the won's upside was capped by the yen's weakness, net stock sales by foreign investors, and near-term technical resistance around 1,260, the 62.8 percent retracement of the dollar/won's January 4-January 18 upmove. 

 On the macro front, Finance Minister Jin Nyum said Korea's growth would be reduced to below four percent in 2001 if the U.S. economy experiences a hard landing. 

 The Bank of Korea has forecast that growth of 5.3 percent this year. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah edged slightly higher in thin trading, helped by state banks' dollar selling believed to be on behalf of the central bank. 

 Bank Indonesia said earlier in the day it had intervened in the market over the past several days to help the rupiah. 

 Violent demonstrations in East Java, the support base for beleaguered President Abdurrahman Wahid, had upset financial markets in Jakarta and placed pressure on the rupiah. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said local demand for dollars was sluggish, though it was expected to pick up if the rupiah strengthened past 9,580. 

 On the political front, Wahid delivered a fiery speech against his critics on Friday in front of his supporters in East Java. The ailing leader, who was censured by parliment over two financial scandals, was in the province to ease mounting political tensions and violence. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar nudged higher in line with other regional currencies in trade dominated by position squaring activities ahead of the weekend. 

 "There have been lots of two-way bets on the currency this week and people are squaring those positions because they don't know what will happen to the yen on Monday," said a dealer at a European bank. 

 "Also, the market will be closely watching Greenspan on Tuesday. No one wants to be caught on the wrong side," he said. Separately, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) said on Friday it did not know exactly when it would make the monetary policy statement which is eagerly awaited by the market. 

 The MAS said last month it was reviewing its 2001 inflation and growth forecasts given the negative external environment. 

 The market is divided on which way the MAS will lean. Some analysts say the top priority should be boosting growth, while others point to the need to pre-empt imported inflation. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar ended slightly higher in sluggish trade as the market continued to unwind long U.S. dollar positions. 

 Dealers in Taipei said last minute buying of U.S. dollars by the central bank slowed the local dollar's appreciation. 

 It has failed to convincingly test the 32.20 mark as the central bank has been consistently buying U.S. dollars throughout the week. 

 Analysts said the bank is seeking to maintain the competitveness of Taiwan's exports, especially given the softer outlook for the yen. 

 The cross rate between the Taiwan dollar and yen was at 3.6140 at 0852 GMT, which some analysts said may be too high for the bank's comfort. 

 Meanwhile, though local stocks managed to gain ground on Friday on hopes over banking sector reforms, another top computer company, Acer Inc. , reported disappointing sales for January. 

 Earlier in the week, heavyweight Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. issued a profit warning for the first quarter of the year, underscoring the downturn in the electronics cycle. 

 Analysts have said Taiwan is especially vulnerable to this downturn as it depends heavily on its high-tech exports. 

 THAI BAHT 

 Onshore baht trading was light and rangebound as the market awaited key cabinet appointments from newly named Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra. 

 The tycoon-turned-politician, who won a January 6 election and was formally named premier on Monday, has yet to name a finance minister. 

 "We're still waiting to see who will be finance minister," one Bangkok baht dealer said."Right now it's tough to break through 42.30 on the downside and 42.70 on the topside." 

 Thaksin said the cabinet list would be finalised by February 12, but added that the finance portfolio had yet to be decided. 

 The dealer said the baht remained in a tight range above 42.50 for most of the morning, but that some local banks and corporates had U.S. dollar sell stops above 42.60. 

 "If something smells bad on Monday, we could decide to break 42.70 or even 43.00," the dealer said.

title: B. Indonesia  says may still  intervene  to help rph.
text:
JAKARTA, Jan 19 (Reuters) - Bank Indonesia governor Sjahril Sabirin said on Friday the bank might continue to intervene in the foreign exchange market to give additional support to the rupiah, despite new curbs on foreign exchange trading. 

 Sabirin said the new rules, aimed at stamping out rupiah speculation, had helped stabilise the unit, but admitted the country's unstable political and security situation remained a factor. 

 "Regarding intervention, we can do it anytime," Sabirin said when asked whether central bank intervention was still needed. 

 When asked about the effectiveness of the new rules, Sabirin said: "The rules have helped stabilise the rupiah, even though this has not been achieved completely because of other factors influencing it, such as politics and security."

title: Emerging  FX  - Firmer, but pitfalls remain.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 7 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were generally a touch firmer late Thursday but analysts warn the slight gains may be deceptive with many risks still lurking. 

 Slower U.S. growth, political uncertainty, and stalled corporate and economic reform are all affecting regional markets. 

 The impeachment trial of President Joseph Estrada began late Thursday in Manila, where the markets have buckled under the recent political uncertainty and signs of a flagging economy. 

 Thailand will hold a general election on January 6, and doubts persist over the future of Indonesia's president. 

 For the time being, central bank intervention or unwinding of long dollar positions ahead of the year-end in illiquid markets will give regional currencies a temporary boost. 

 The firmer yen and stronger euro also gave regional currencies a lift. 

 Looking ahead, the market will be closely monitoring U.S. jobs data and a speech by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan on Friday. Greenspan hinted at an end of monetary tightening cycle earlier in the week. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar spiked up to post a high of 1.7340 in late trade on what dealers said was dollar/Sing selling by some American banks. 

 But strong demand for the U.S. dollars from local corporates below the 1.7350 mark pulled the Sing back to around 1.7360-70, still better than its day's low of 1.7430. 

 Some dealers attributed the sharp move to unwinding of long U.S. dollar positions in response to Wednesday's measures by Monetary Authority of Singapore to encourage foreign investors to invest or issue debt in local fixed income market. 

 The MAS said banks could now lend to non-residents for investment in the country, saying the move would help broaden investor base for Sing dollar assets. 

 It also allowed banks to make transactions in Singapore dollar currency options with other banks and financial institutions in Singapore. 

 "Sell on rumours and buy on news, that is how the market played the MAS announcement but some players might have been caught long or short," chief dealer of a European bank said. 

 He said the MAS announcement has disappointed those who were betting on broader liberalisation of Singapore's exchange rate policy. 

 Singapore manages the exchange rate against an undisclosed trade-weighted currency basket and in the past several months has repeatedly indicated its desire of an appreciation of the Sing against that basket. 

 But dealers said realisation in the market was growing that the measures were positive in the long-run. 

 Other dealers said low trading volumes exaggerated the move. 

 "Remember half of the market participants are on year-end holidays so the volume is thin and that exaggerates any move," a dealer said. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won strengthened on exporters' dollar-selling in otherwise thin, dull trade. 

 Dealers said moves in the currency are often exaggerated in illiquid markets, and there has been little interest in the won market with the lack of fresh incentives and year-end approaching. 

 As expected, the Bank of Korea kept its key overnight rate at 5.25 percent. Central bank governor Chon Chol-hwan said it would consider cutting interest rates when inflationary pressures ease and financial markets stabilise. 

 Chon also warned of an economic slowdown given shrinking exports earnings. According to Rebecca Patterson, a currency strategist at JP Morgan, that isn't the end of the challenges Korea faces. 

 "The market has priced in to a degree slowdowns in both Korea and the U.S. But we have more room to go. This isn't over, in Korea we're going to get more restructuring hiccups, more labour union strikes, and confidence, if you look at consumer or business surveys, is tanking," she said. 

 JP Morgan recently revised its won forecast to 1,270 by the end of the first quarter next year. 

 Patterson also noted that given a more competitve export sector, Korean authorities are also keeping a close eye on the yen/won cross-rate, seeking a range of 10.25-11.50. It stood at 10.81 late Thursday. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar was steady in late trade despite a rash of bad news for the island's economy. 

 Dealers said foreign-equity related inflows and exporters boosted the local dollar. But analysts have said the currency will weaken as economic growth slows. 

 Taiwan's November trade surplus came in far below expectations, falling 45.6 percent on year to US$774.6 million. The Ministry of Finance later said it expected full year 2000 exports to grow slower than previously expected due to a global economic slowdown. 

 The data comes on the heels of a revision of Standard & Poor's outlook for Taiwan to negative from stable because of delayed economic reforms as the political impasse between the president and legislature drags on. 

 Meanwhile, the central bank said its foreign exchange reserves dipped in November to US$108.231 billion due to an increase in private foreign currency deposits. Analysts said bank's defence of the local dollar might also have had something to do with the fall. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht shuffled towards the higher end of a narrow 43.49-43.65 range in line with firmer regionals. 

 But dealers in Bangkok said volumes were negligible, with only a few local corporates and banks in the market. Offshore players continue to shy away from the baht market following the central bank's clampdown on speculation. 

 However, analysts expect the baht to see further weakness in the run-up to the election and in its aftermath. 

 "The new government will likely be even weaker than the current. You have an economy that is slowing, reforms that are going slowly, and yields which are still low," JP Morgan's Patterson said. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah was helped up, after it hit a day low of 9,635, by state-run banks which dealers said were active on behalf of the central bank. 

 "It was basically the state banks...yes they were selling dollars on behalf of the central bank. They were selling dollars all along from 9,620 to 9,570," said chief dealer of a U.S. bank in Jakarta. 

 He said some dollar supply, close to rupiah's lows, was also seen coming from exporters. 

 Talk of central bank intervention sent Jakarta-based foreign banks and Singapore-based players scrambling to unwind their long dollar positions. 

 But dealers said importers and local corporates took advantage of the easing dollar and came in to support the dollar at around 9,550 level. 

 Dealers said as soon as the market senses lack of state banks' support, the rupiah would be back beyond the 9,600 level. 

 Dealers said the market was closely watching developments surrounding the controversial revamping of the central bank. 

 They said the Parliament that would go into recess from Saturday has yet to approve proposed changes in central bank laws aimed at making the bank more accountable and empower government to sack the institution's top officials. 

 The proposed changes have come under criticism as an attempt to bring under government control an institution that is guaranteed wide-ranging independence under existing laws. 

 The central bank governor on Wednesday resumed control of his office after nearly six months detention on charges of corruption. 

 Sjahril Sabirin's release from house arrest and his return to the central bank has raised fears of fresh rift between President Addurrahman Wahid and the bank. 

 Indonesia's chief economics minister Rizal Ramli said on Thursday changes to the central bank laws are expected to be approved by the parliament in January or February. 

 He also said all members of the board of governors should resign when the changes stand approved. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso edged down in late trade but moved in a tight range through most of the day with most players stayed away from the market as the impeachment trial against President Joseph Estrada began. 

 Dealers said the other factor that kept players cautious was Friday's weekly meeting of the central bank's monetary board. 

 The central bank has hinted earlier in the week of a cut in excessively high key domestic interest rates to help boost weakening economic growth. 

 Dealers said a cut in rates was widely expected, after a 50 basis point cut earlier in the week. 

 "But the uncertainty is on how deep the cut will be. So people are taking a cautious view," a dealer at a European bank in Manila said. 

 Some dealers said the central bank taking advantage of a relatively quite day was buying dollars to replenish its reserves.

title: Indonesia  Rupiah Ends Higher On  Central Bank Intervention
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah closed slightly higher Friday after a central bank intervention, but dollar demand remains healthy, dealers said. 

 The dollar nudged to IDR9,565 in intraday trade, just short of its year-high of IDR9,580, but Bank Indonesia's intervention pushed it lower. 

 The dollar closed at IDR9,520, down from IDR9,535 late Thursday in Asia. 

 Dealers said dollar-demand is still strong as corporates seek the U.S. currency to service yearend debts. 

 New figures showing Indonesia's November consumer price index was higher than expected, up 9.12% on-year and 1.32% on-month due to higher food prices, didn't impact the currency. 

 The rupiah was also unmoved by data showing imports rising 68.3% on-year in October, causing the trade surplus to decrease to $2.03 billion. 

 Traders said market players are still worried about the International Monetary Fund's concerns over the economy. 

 In a strongly worded letter dated Nov. 8, Anoop Singh, the Fund's Washington-based deputy director for Asia and the Pacific, demanded Jakarta move swiftly to reduce risks in its fiscal decentralization plan, use higher oil revenues to repay government debt and set a firm timetable for asset sales. 

 Failure to do so by early December, the letter suggests, could stop the IMF's board from approving fresh loans to the country under its $5 billion bailout program. 

 Indonesia's interbank overnight rate continued to hover around 10.75% to 10.85% - little changed from the previous day - as liquidity in the system remains sufficient.

title: Jakarta says  central bank  can still support rupiah.
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Indonesia's chief economics minister Rizal Ramli said on Tuesday Bank Indonesia can still intervene in the foreign exchange market to help the ailing rupiah despite the resignations from its board of governors. 

 Asked if the central bank could still intervene, Ramli said: "They remain active until new members (are appointed). They still have the right to make decisions." 

 The rupiah was trading at 9,450/9,470 against the dollar at 0455 GMT. It has lost more than 20 percent against the dollar this year, making it one of Asia's worst performers. 

 On Friday, the central bank said its acting chief and the six other deputy governors would quit to make way for a management reshuffle and a recapitalisation. 

 But the future of two deputy governors who did not sign the resignation letter and a third who did but was not included in the government's formal notification to parliament remains unclear. 

 Announcing the resignations, Bank Indonesia said the officials would continue their duties until replacements are named.
