title: Bk  Indonesia  Gov: Will Keep  Intervening  To Help Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's acting central bank governor said Friday the bank will continue to intervene in the foreign exchange market to help the rupiah. 

 When asked how much the central bank plans to use for intervention, Anwar Nasution said, "It's a secret." 

 Bank Indonesia has maintained a policy of selling U.S. dollar reserves to help the rupiah during periods of weakness. 

 Traders say the central bank has been active in the market since the rupiah fell through support at 9,000 rupiah to the dollar a few weeks ago. 

 The rupiah was slightly higher at IDR9,230 to the dollar after Nasution's comments versus IDR9,250 before. 

 Corporate debt repayments before the year-end continue to put the dollar on a bullish trend, but threat of intervention has pushed many players to cut long-dollar positions.

title: Emerging  FX  - Mixed on U.S. unease, steady euro.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a mixed 

 bag late Friday as uncertainty on the U.S. elections dragged on 

 and lack of fresh leads on local factors kept market activity 

 subdued. 


    Euro's	  Wednesday gains against the dollar helped by



European Central Bank intervention and U.S. election turmoil,



also made players cautious on their long dollar positions



against some of the regional currencies.



    Most regionals moved in a tight range and some were helped



by authorities or by the fear of their action.



    Reluctance on part of players to hold on to long dollar



positions through the weekend given lack of fresh leads



signalling direction of the markets or mood of the authorities,



also helped.



The peso, however, lived up to its reputation of being



relatively the most volatile currency in the region and amid



talk of intervention, moved both ways.



The Korean won and the Taiwan dollar were seen more



disturbed by the second day of losses on the tech-heavy Nasdaq



but unabated foreign fund inflows into equity markets helped



keep sentiment positive.



The euro in early European trade held close to its day's



peak around $0.8685 on intervention wariness, while the yen



came under pressure after downgrade of official estimates of



the Japan's economy for the first time in two years.



THAI BAHT



The baht rose to a high of 43.36 in low volume trade amid



what dealers said was a lull in demand for dollars from



corporates and on lack of activity by offshore players.



    Dealers said upticks in the Sing, rupiah and peso also



helped sentiment.



    "Most orders placed in the past week or ten days have been



filled. So there is not much demand for the dollars in the



market and the regionals are also doing fine today," a dealer



at a European bank in Bangkok said.



The dealer said baht was also supported by a steadier local



equity market that had seen foreign fund inflows earlier in the



week.



Dealers said dollar/baht was seen supported at around



43.15-43.20 levels, from where the dollar had rebounded last



week and in mid-October.



SINGAPORE DOLLAR



The Sing dollar clung to a tight range, with few factors



pushing it either way.



A dealer at a European bank said there was some local



corporate demand for U.S. dollars around 1.7350 and 1.7380. He



added that those companies were probably hoping to buy U.S.



dollar during the Sing dollar's recent run-up, and missed out



on those lower rates.



A stronger yen and euro is keeping the Sing dollar away



from falling much past 1.7400. The local dollar is managed



against a trade-weighted basket of currencies.



Looking ahead, dealers said third-quarter economic growth



data due out next Friday was not likely to influence the local



dollar's direction. However, the European bank dealer added he



expected the Sing dollar to fall past the 1.7500 level if the



data proves to be very strong, but still fails to boost the



Sing dollar.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah moved in a narrow range and was close to its day



high of 9,210 in late trade helped by central bank intervention


and on lack of fresh leads.



Bank Indonesia acting governor Anwar Nasution confirmed the


central bank was intervening to boost the troubled currency and



said it will continue to do so.



   The battered rupiah has lost over 20 percent this year,



making it one of Asia's worst performers.



    "It seems the central bank wants to hold the 9,200-9,250



range and it has been able to do that in the past couple of



days because there is very little demand from the corporates or



from offshore players," a dealer at a U.S. bank in Jakarta



said.



    Positive movement of the Sing and the baht also helped



sentiment, the dealer said.



    Dealers said a relatively calmer political front has also



cooled down the volatile forex market.



    KOREAN WON	   -2



    The won crept towards the lower end of the day's range with



caution dominating trade.



    Korea's corporate reforms had cheered the market, pushing



the won to around 1,131 won. But dollar-buying by a state bank



triggered fears that the central bank was intervening to curb



volatility.



While foreign equity-related inflows have lifted the won in



recent sessions, analysts are still pointing to souring



external factors as dimming the outlook for the won. Lower chip



prices and a slowdown in the U.S. economy will hurt Korea's



export-dependent economy, and some analysts forecast the won



weakening towards the 1,150 level.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar eased back towards Thursday's closing



levels after a hectic day of trading.



After propelling past the 32 level thanks to leftover



equity-related inflows, the Taiwan dollar then lost ground on



fund outflows.



Dealers said they suspected the central bank intervened to



help the Taiwan dollar, and that it also bought U.S. dollars



earlier to cap the Taiwan dollar's rise.



Morgan Stanley Capital International's re-weighting of



Taiwan's stocks has helped fuel the Taiwan dollar's gains in



recent sessions. However, analysts are divided on whether the



effect of the re-weighting significantly changes the outlook



for the local dollar.



    Some argue that the re-weighting signals massive foreign



inflows and will power the Taiwan dollar higher.



    Others, such as UBS Warburg, argue Taiwan's fundamentals



are weakening, and that the central bank is concerned about



slower economic growth in Taiwan as well as the entire region.



It said in a research note that only if the Taiwan dollar



breaks 31.50 would it change its view that the bank is willing



to allow a weaker Taiwan dollar.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso slipped in late trade, after touching a day high



of 49.25, on rumours amid vague concerns that the banking



industry may be in trouble.



The rumours were later denied by central bank governor



Rafael Buenaventura who said the country's banking sector was



healthy.



The governor also said he received text messages on his



mobile phone about two Philippine banks encountering financial



difficulties.



"It's not true," he said.



The onshore market closed at 50.20 to the dollar, from



Thursday's close of 49.95.



The peso stayed up for most of the day on talk of central



bank presence in the market and on inflow of some remittances



from overseas workers.



"There were rumours about some local banks ...and that



pulled down the peso very sharply," a dealer at a European bank



in Manila said.



The dealer said the market jittered by the continuing



political struggle between President Joseph Estrada and



opposition has turned very volatile and susceptible to rumours.



Estrada is facing growing pressure to step down amid an



impeachment trial on allegations he accepted bribes from



gambling syndicates.



Dealers said central bank pumped in at least $15 million in



morning session and a couple of banks offloaded remittance



inflows estimated at around $20 million.

million on Thursday.

title: Bk  Indonesia  To Use Rate Hike,  Intervention  To Help IDR
text:
- - 07/11/04-59G



0459GMT

 0507GMT 

 JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia acting governor Anwar Nasution repeated Tuesday that the nation's central bank will continue raising interest rates and sell the dollar in the currency market to help the sagging rupiah. 

 "We will utilize all mechanisms including interest rate hike, intervention, and stepping up on-site inspection on banks (dollar-rupiah transactions)," Nasution told reporters. 

 He expects that the moves will bring the dollar down to IDR8,500 at the end of the month. 

 The dollar was trading at 9.215 rupiah at 0527 GMT. 

 Nasution reiterated that Bank Indonesia hasn't made any decision whether it will lower the maximum amount, from its current $5 million, of rupiah that banks can sell to non-Indonesian residents in forward transactions. 

 "We have to study the advantages and disadvantages of such policy," he said. 

 He added that cutting down the limit may hurt banks in Singapore, which are active participants of the dollar-rupiah trading. 

 This is something that Indonesia doesn't want as "Singaporean banks contribute a lot to the Indonesian economy," he said. 

 Nasution also brushed aside a suggestion to make exporters compulsorily repatriate their dollar revenues to Indonesia to help the rupiah. 


-By Farida Husna;Dow Jones Newswires;62-21 3983 1277
-0- 07/11/00 05-42G



Meanwhile, the International Monetary Fund's deputy director for Asia
and Pacific, Anoop Singh, said that any change that Bank Indonesia may
consider will be "consistent with the current exchange rate system."



He didn't comment on whether the IMF will approve the move to cut the
forward limit.



The government adopts a floating exchange rate system and an open
capital account regime, which doesn't place any restriction on the
transfer of funds in and out of the country. All fund flows, however,
must be reported to bank Indonesia.



Singh added that the rupiah's current weakness is beyond economic
fundamentals.

title: Peso slips past 49/dlr, rupiah droops.
text:
0700 GMT - The Philippine peso trickled past the key 49 level as the euphoria from Monday's session faded, and the prospect of a long, drawn-out impeachment trial set in. 

 - Philippine central bank said it did not intervene in market on Tuesday, but some dealers in Manila said central bank spotted selling small amounts of dollars around 48.95 pesos. 

 - Dealers added local banks holding onto long dollar positions as hopes for quick exit by President Joseph Estrada recede. Volume now at $104 million. 

 - Estrada's National Security Adviser said president will not resign, and critics calling for his resignation should await verdict from impeachment trial. 

 - Central bank also said market not yet stable and still too early to lower key interest rates. 

 - Indonesian rupiah slid past 9,200 per dollar on local corporate demand from Jakarta but state banks spotted selling dollars again in early afternoon at 9,220 and 9,225. 

 - Dealers in Jakarta express worry over apparently conflicting statements from IMF and Bank Indonesia. 

 - Bank Indonesia said earlier in day it was using intervention, rates, and foreign exchange monitoring to help rupiah, spurring fears of further regulations. 

 - But IMF said Bank Indonesia committed to current exchange rate policy, and was discussing fine tuning it. 

 - "We'll just have to wait and see what they do," said a dealer at U.S. bank in Jakarta. Offshore and onshore volume estimated at $400 million.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Slightly Down Late; Set For More Weakness
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah weakened slightly late Thursday, barely reacting to a slew of news throughout the day as it showed signs of resuming its downward trend following a strong rebound over the past two days, dealers said. 

 The market reacted with indifference to the potential arrest of former President Suharto's youngest son, after he defied a summons by prosecutors to begin serving his prison term for corruption. 

 Even the looming threat of intervention by Bank Indonesia, after the acting governor, Anwar Nasution, said the central bank would continue to defend the currency, failed to lift the rupiah. 

 The dollar was wedged within a tight range of 9,135 to 9,175 rupiah all day. 

 Around 0900 GMT (4:00 a.m. EST), the dollar was at IDR9,170, up from IDR9,130 late Wednesday. 

 The rupiah resisted the upward pressure from the Singapore dollar and the Thai baht, which extended their recent recoveries as market participants unwound long dollar positions, dealers said. 

 In the case of the Indonesian currency, dollar demand from local corporates and offshore participants around IDR9,130 to IDR9,140 provided a floor for the U.S. currency, which had reversed sharply after it failed to break above the pscyhologically sensitive IDR9,500 resistance level Tuesday. 

 "I would expect (the dollar's) support around IDR9,300 to IDR9,120 to hold," said a European bank dealer in Singapore. "We'll probably move higher, maybe back up to around IDR9,200 to IDR9,210."

title: Indonesia  says to continue rupiah  intervention .
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 2 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank said on Thursday it would keep intervening in the foreign exchange market to support the embattled rupiah and that recent interest rate hikes were not sufficient to help. 

 Asked by reporters whether the bank had intervened and would continue to do so, acting central bank governor Anwar Nasution said: "This week, last week, next week." 

 He said increases of several basis points in the central bank's benchmark SBI rates - which has been the trend in recent weeks - was not enough to support the rupiah. 

 "Several basis points are not yet big enough," Nasution said on the sidelines of a debt conference. 

 Nasution added that he firmly believed the rupiah should be stronger than 9,000 to the dollar. At 0300 GMT the rupiah was quoted at 9,138/9,158. It has come under fresh pressure in the past few days.

title: Indonesia Grain-Arrivals peaking ahead of year-end.
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 2 (Reuters) - At least 150,000 tonnes of U.S soybean and 200,000 tonnes of soymeal will arrive in Indonesia in November and December as traders and feedmillers stock up ahead of long holidays at the year-end, traders said on Thursday. 

 Indonesians celebrate Christmas and the Moslem Eid el-Fitr in December. 

 "One handymax ship and two Panamax will arrive in November to bring in 150,000 tonnes of U.S soybean. Around 120,000 tonnes of U.S soymeal will also come in November-December," said one trader in Jakarta. 

 Another Jakarta trader said at least four vessels bringing in 100,000 tonnes of Indian soymeal were also expected to arrive in December. 

 "Everyone wants their goods to arrive here by mid-December at the latest. They want to avoid long holidays because there will be a shortage of workers and they will have to spend more money," said the second trader. 

 Indonesian workers normally go back to their hometowns to celebrate religious festivities. 

 But one trader in Surabaya said some of the Indian soymeal might not be able to reach Indonesia by mid-December because the Indian exporters were facing difficulties meeting the deadline. 

 "I think half of the amount will be delivered in January. The importers do not want the soymeal to come after mid-December, so they will delay the shipments," said the Surabaya trader. 

 Weak rupiah and rising demand ahead of year-end religious festivities have boosted local prices of soybean, soymeal and corn, traders said. 

 Corn rose to 975-1,050 rupiah/kg in Jakarta against last week's 925 rupiah/kg. Soymeal rose to 2,150-2,200 rupiah/kg. 

 The rupiah was quoted at 9,150/9,165 rupiah against the dollar by 0420 GMT. The battered currency has come under pressure in the past few days on worries over the country's political stability. 

 Bank Indonesia, the central bank, said on Thursday it would keep intervening in the foreign exchange market to support the rupiah. 

 Traders said rice supplies were abundant in Indonesia and saw no signs of fresh imports at least until January, although some rice from old contracts had yet to arrive. 

 "I don't see private traders signing new contracts since August. Bulog's warehouses are full of rice," said the first Jakarta trader, referring to state commodity regulator Bulog. 

 Bulog had earlier said it would not sign any more rice import contracts due to a glut in domestic supply.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Higher On Nasdaq Boost
text:
Of DOW JONES NEWSWIRES 


   TOKYO -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies closed stronger in Asia
Wednesday, after an overnight rebound in the Nasdaq dispelled some of
the gloom plaguing the region while signs emerged that South Korea
might be making progress in restructuring its economy.


 The New Taiwan dollar, however, ended lower Wednesday amid outflows of foreign equity funds from the local market, traders noted. 

 A holiday in the Philippines - where political turmoil has hurt sentiment in the region as a whole in recent weeks - also contributed to the respite in markets Wednesday. 

 The South Korean won was swept higher as stock prices in Seoul soared in response to the Nasdaq's 5.6% overnight jump and signs that the government might be getting out of the business of propping up teetering companies - which could be a positive development for the economy in the long run. 

 The Indonesian rupiah also got a break from its recent battering amid signs of easing pressure on the embattled President Abdurrahman Wahid. The U.S. dollar slid to 9,150 rupiah Wednesday, down from a three-month high of IDR9,490 earlier in the week. 

 But bargain hunters, betting that lingering political uncertainty in Indonesia will continue to plague its currency, helped to put a floor under the U.S. dollar, dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar and the Thai baht were lifted in part by buoyant rupiah and won. However, a new rule in Thailand that kicked in Wednesday requiring traders to report the purpose of each foreign exchange transaction stifled trading in the baht, dealers said. 

 Late Wednesday, the U.S. dollar at S$1.7498, easing from S$1.7563 late Tuesday. The U.S. currency was quoted at 43.630 baht, down from THB43.885 Tuesday. 

 Foreign investors piled into Korean shares Wednesday - boosting the won in the process - on reports that the government and creditors of Hyundai Engineering & Construction Co., one of the country's biggest construction companies, are considering the option of court receivership for the troubled construction company. 

 Market players took that to be a clear sign that the government won't try to prop up the troubled company - an indication that progress might be made in stripping the excess from South Korea's economy. 

 Hyundai Engineering narrowly avoided bankruptcy Tuesday following a debt default Monday. It faces more default risks because it's still having difficulty in securing loan extensions. 

 Late Wednesday, the U.S. dollar was at 1136.0 won, down from KRW1139.70 late Tuesday. 

 "The won got a boost from the stock market," said Steve Brice, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 However, Brice said that while the many people rejoiced at signs that South Korea is moving ahead with restructuring, the market still has to take account of the fallout from such moves - higher unemployment and other negatives that could weigh on the economy going forward. 


"The cyclical element will still have to be priced in," Brice said.
- - 01/11/00 09-18G



The Taiwan dollar bucked the general trend Wednesday, falling against
its U.S. counterpart. Intervention by the central bank supported the
Taiwan dollar during thin early trading, but the currency eventually
succumbed to weakness in local stock prices.



Taiwan's main stock index Wednesday closed down 119.16 points at
5425.02.



In addition to restructuring hopes, the won also found support from
data showing South Korea recorded a wider-than-expected trade surplus in
October, dealers said. The surplus stood at $1.4 billion in October,
wider than a consensus estimate of $1.2 billion.



Insofar as the Nasdaq's rally overnight helped to precipitate a
rebound in Asian currencies, the region remains vulnerable to another
shock from U.S. stock markets, traders said.



That is because not much has changed in terms of politics - the major
factor recently driving down most regional markets and currencies.



The Nasdaq's rise is "positive in the short-term, but it's clear that
a lot of issues remain as far as domestic politics are concerned,"
Standard Chartered Bank's Brice said.



Traders said political turmoil in the Philippines is far from over.
And that spells bad news for the peso, they said.



The peso could come under renewed downward pressure if the central
bank doesn't take remedial measures at its Monetary Board meeting this
Friday, a dealer said.



In Indonesia, Vice President Megawati Sukarnoputri's call Tuesday for
Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle members to stand behind Wahid
helped bandage market sentiment.



That helped drag the U.S. dollar down against the rupiah and has some
traders pondering whether the dollar will fall back below IDR9,000. The
dollar had traded in a tight IDR8,800-IDR8,980 range for more than a
month until this week.



Indonesian officials were quick to play up the rupiah's rally, telling
the market that easing political tensions - not the central bank - were
behind the move.



"There was no government intervention behind the rupiah's rebound
today," Indonesia's Senior Economics Minister Rizal Ramli said. He
attributed the rupiah's strength to Megawati's decision to increase
support for Wahid.



Still, traders said the political situation in Indonesia remains
precarious and tensions could flare up again if a serious candidate for
president emerges to challenge Wahid.



That has some people thinking that the rupiah might not have far to go
before it slides again.



"The rupiah's rally looks pretty much exhausted," Brice said, adding
he expects support to emerge around IDR9,050-IDR9,100.



-By Arran Scott, Dow Jones Newswires; 813-5255-2929;
arran.scott@dowjones.com

title: Indonesia 's Ramli denies rupiah  intervention .
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 1 (Reuters) - Indonesia's chief economics minister Rizal Ramli on Wednesday denied saying the central bank had intervened in the foreign exchange market last week to prop up the battered rupiah. 

 Ramli also said the rupiah's gains earlier on Wednesday were due to a better political climate after comments from some politicians that they supported embattled President Abdurrahman Wahid. 

 On Tuesday, Ramli told reporters the central bank had intervened in the foreign exchange market last week to help the currency. 

 "There was no intervention," Ramli said on Wednesday, when asked to reconfirm that the central bank had spent $10 million last week to intervene. Some analysts had said the amount was too small to affect the market. 

 Ramli on Tuesday blamed the rupiah's sharp fall the previous day on politicians who had demanded Wahid step down. 

Foreign exchange dealers say Bank Indonesia usually spends between $5-10 million daily in what central bank officials say is aimed at smoothing fluctuations in the foreign exchange market. 

 The rupiah was quoted at 9,145/9,165 against the dollar in afternoon trade on Wednesday compared with 9,330/9,380 in late trade on Tuesday. 

 Average daily turnover on the dollar/rupiah market is about $200 million, far lower than the more than $1 billion daily before the Asian financial meltdown hit in mid-1997.

title: Bk Indonesia Spent $10 Million Last Wk To Stabilize Rupiah -Min
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia spent $10 million last week to stabilize the rupiah, Senior Economics Minister Rizal Ramli said Tuesday. 

 "Last week almost $10 million was the cost for stabilizing the currency," Rizal told reporters, adding that the central bank will spend more this week to help the local currency. 

 Rizal's comments come after President Abdurrahman Wahid said Monday he was concerned by rupiah weakness, but didn't think the government would intervene. 

 The rupiah fell to a low of IDR9,490 Tuesday after Wahid's remarks, which confused the market. The central bank has recently followed a policy of intervening to help the rupiah when it drops through IDR9,000. 

 Players moved to sell dollars on Rizal's comments, pushing the pair to IDR9,350, down from 9,400 before the news. 

 Rizal didn't specify how the central bank had intervened to stabilize the rupiah, but Bank Indonesia normally uses a combination of selling dollars through state banks, and drawing down its supply of foreign reserves.

title: Indonesia  President: No  Intervention  to Help Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid said Monday the government wouldn't intervene in the foreign exchange market to help the ailing rupiah. 

 "We are very concerned about the weakening rupiah but the government has no plans to intervene in the market," spokesman Wimar Witoelar quoted the president as saying, without elaborating. 

 Last week, the central bank said it would intervene in the market through selling dollars if necessary, but didn't say whether it had actively sold foreign reserves recently. 

 The rupiah is off 30% since the start of the year amid a disappointing economic recovery and increasing calls for Wahid to step down.

title: Bank  Indonesia  to  intervene  if will have impact.
text:
JAKARTA, Oct 27 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank said on Friday it would intervene to prop up the battered rupiah, which broke the 9,000 psychological barrier the previous day, only if the move would have an impact. 

 "If needed, we will do it but we have to look at the factors (affecting the rupiah). If (the impact) is positive, we'll do it," central bank deputy governor Achjar Iljas told reporters. 

 "If not, why should we waste our dollars." 

 The rupiah, one of the world's worst performing currencies this year, has fallen by around 23 percent since the start of 2000. It was quoted at around 9,070/9,100 against the dollar in early afternoon trade on Friday.

title: Emerging  FX  - Regionals drift within weak ranges.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 25 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were a mixed 

 bag late on Wednesday, mostly holding their ground within 

 recent weak trading ranges. 

     Dealers said fear of intervention in Thailand and Korea and 

 a holiday in Indonesia and an off-day in Singapore on Thursday 

 kept activity and movement in the region's foreign exchange

 markets subdued. 

 But the peso plumbed a new all-time low as the political 

 turmoil amid impeachment proceedings against President Joseph 

 Estrada kept sentiment bearish. 

 Analysts said lingering worries about U.S. tech stocks, an 

 expected slow down in global growth and high oil prices were 

 likely to keep regionals under pressure. 

 "Even if there is a soft landing in the U.S. and the Fed 

 keeps interest rates unchanged till the end of the year, there 

 will be problems," a currency analyst at a European bank said. 

 He said global growth was likely to peak, Japan's growth 

 was likely to remain positive but weak and Europe was likely to 

 raise interest rates to stem inflation and defend the euro. 

     He said oil prices would eventually come down but not 

 before the middle of next year. 

     "The scenario represents a bearish outlook for growth and 

 exports and further easing of most of the currencies in the 

 region," he said. 


    The euro	  fell to a record low against the dollar as



the market overcame its fears of intervention in the absence



of



supportive statements from the Group of 20 meeting in Canada.



The yen slipped after a firm Tokyo start on a



statement from U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers



reiterating long-standing U.S. support for a strong dollar.



Oil prices were firmly entrenched above $33 a barrel as key



U.S. oil data increased the fear of a crunch in winter heating



oil supplies.



THAI BAHT



The baht see-sawed as the market was caught in a tug of war



between Bangkok-based players taking profit on the dollar's



recent gains and Singapore-based dealers squaring their



positions before a holiday on Thursday.



A dealer at a local bank in Singapore said there was heavy



dollar-selling at the beginning of the session, but that turned



around when the dollar was deemed as being oversold. "We still



prefer to go long on dollars," he said.



Dealers in Bangkok said the market generally ignored



comments by the Thai Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai and local



banks were spotted taking profit on the dollar around 43.70.



The prime minister told Reuters earlier the level of the



baht should be determined by the market. Separately, he said he



wasn't too concerned with the recent baht weakness and still



expected strong exports growth.



     Analysts say the economy may actually benefit from a



weaker baht as it is a boon for exports.



    While the dollar has been finding it difficult to



convincingly break the 44 baht level - a technically



significant level - many analysts and dealers expect it to hit



44.50 in the next month. Investors view the baht as a proxy for



the less liquid rupiah and peso. Moreover, the low interest



rates in Thailand make the baht an attractive funding play for



offshore investors.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah barely budged as markets in Jakarta were closed



due to a public holiday.



Given Indonesia's changeable politics, local companies have



been dominating that market, as offshore players with little



appetite for risk continue to avoid it.



Volumes in both the offshore and onshore markets have been



razor-thin and with little bullish news coming out of



Indonesia, most analysts forecast further downside for the



rupiah.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso slipped to a record low of 49.80 to the dollar as



political uncertainty surrounding the impeachment proceedings



against Estrada kept sentiments bearish.


Central bank governor, Rafael Buenaventura, confirmed the



bank intervened to support the currency, but he declined to



provide details.



    Dealers said the central bank started selling dollars soon



after the peso slipped in early trade.



    A currency analyst said Buenaventura's statement on Tuesday



that the central bank did not plan a rate hike for now could



have contributed to the early fall.



    KOREAN WON	   -2



    The won traded within a tight range in thin trading on the



back of remarks by Finance Minister Jin Nyum that the



government would limit the downside of the currency.



    But dealers said the impact of the central bank's verbal


intervention to smooth the won's slide would not work for long.



    They said worries about the Nasdaq coming off, fears of



escalation in the Middle East tension pushing up oil prices and



the outflow of foreign funds from equities was likely to hamper



the recovery of the won.



    The benchmark KOSPI	   closed 0.50 percent lower at



542.33.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR	



    The Taiwan dollar was softer against the dollar, as the



U.S. currency found favour in the spot and non deliverable



forward (NDF) market.



    Mohktar Hassan, a currency analyst at research house IFR



Asian Eye said the Taiwan dollar's trading trend has been to



open strong and end soft against the dollar with opening levels



supported by central bank selling of dollars.



    A 1.78-percent rise in the key Taiwan stock index on



Wednesday did little to support the Taiwan dollar.



    Instead, active buying of the U.S. dollar in the NDF market



and demand for the U.S. dollar for debt repayments pushed the



Taiwan dollar lower.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The baht stole the limelight away from the Singapore



dollar, which shuffled along a narrow range in quiet trading,



dealers said.



    A dealer at a European bank noted that activity only picked



up in the afternoon, when London-based players bought U.S.



dollars around S$1.7525/30.



    The Sing dollar has followed regional currencies lower in

    Moreover, the Sing dollar is managed in a trade-weighted



basket so it is affected by weakness in the euro and yen, which



carry greater weightage in that basket.



    Dealers also said weakness in the euro would drag down the

title: Asian  Currencies  Lower Late; Peso Again Leads Falls
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Friday the 13th lived up to its reputation. 

 An escalation of violence in the Middle East rocked global equity markets, ignited a savage oil price rally, and drove all Asian currencies lower. Faced with severe downward pressure, most regional central banks either intervened, or threatened to step into the market to support their local currencies. 

 The Philippine peso led the decliners again, falling for a fifth straight session on a deepening political scandal surrounding allegations President Joseph Estrada received millions of dollars in payoffs from illegal gambling operators. 

 Political instability has triggered capital flight this week from the Philippines, prompting the central bank Thursday to increase its overnight interest rates four percentage points, lifting the headline rate to 15%. 

 Although the peso ended the week at Thursday's all-time intraday low against the dollar of PHP48.500, the rate hike has at least stabilized the currency, which has fallen 6% during the past four weeks, and 17% so far this year. 

 Rising crude prices also hurt the peso. 

 The Philippines like most Asian economies - including South Korea, Thailand and India - is heavily dependent on oil imports for its energy needs. 

 So a surge in oil prices on fears supplies might be interrupted if violence in the Middle East escalates into an all-out war between Jews and Arabs is particularly damaging for the currency. 

 An apparent bombing of the U.K. embassy in Yemen early Friday crystallized those concerns, and some analysts said this could be a precursor to concerted attacks on Western interests. 

 The dollar ended at PHP48.500, up from PHP47.700 at Thursday's close. 

 The Singapore dollar was weaker despite apparent intervention early in the day by the Monetary Authority of Singapore to support the local dollar. 

 Traders said the MAS bought Singapore dollars against its U.S. counterpart through a number of local banks at around S$1.7570, pushing the local currency up to around S$1.7520. But the effect was short-lived as weakness in the peso and rupiah, and a 2.7% fall in the benchmark Straits Times Index of local stock prices knocked the Singapore dollar from its intraday highs. 

 A dealer at the European bank said: "The Sing dollar is surrounded by bad news. No matter what authorities do, sentiment is still weak and won't just change overnight." The MAS intervened a number of times above S$1.7500 in recent months to curb weakness in the local currency, which was inspired at that time by falls in the rupiah due to political problems in Indonesia. 

 The U.S. dollar late was at S$1.7550, up from S$1.7523 a day earlier. 

 In neighboring Indonesia, the central bank said it is considering whether to intervene in the market to support the rupiah, which hit a 10-week low early in the day of IDR9,030 against the dollar. 

 "We will need to evaluate what caused the rupiah weakness before we make a direct move in the market," said Bank Indonesia senior official Achjar Ilyas. 

 Bank Indonesia Acting Governor Anwar Nasution has previously said the central bank would defend the rupiah at IDR9,000, arguing that beyond this level it is grossly undervalued compared to economic fundamentals. 

 The dollar was at IDR8,955, up from IDR8,940 late Thursday. 

 Meanwhile, Bank of Thailand acknowledged for the first time there are signs of speculation against the baht in the foreign exchange market, activity that as a general rule might prompt a central bank to intervene. 

 Chetthavee Charoenpitaks, assistant central bank governor, told reporters the Bank is closely monitoring movements in the market, but declined to comment on whether the central bank plans to intervene to support the baht. 

 The baht hit a 28-month low Friday of THB43.68 against the dollar, and late in the session was at THB43.580, down from THB43.295. 

 In North Asia, the Korean won sank as local stock prices slumped 1.9%. 

 The dollar ended trade in Seoul at KRW1,128.5, up from KRW1,122.10 late Thursday. While in Taipei, the New Taiwan dollar dropped sharply to finish the week at NT$31.650 against the U.S. currency, down from NT$31.300 a day earlier.

title: Central Bk Watch: Bk Indonesia Helped By Politics
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column 

 JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's cloudy political picture ironically offers the country's central bank a window of opportunity to support the rupiah more effectively than it has been able to do in past, some economists say. 

 On Tuesday, a relatively peaceful meeting of coalition leaders in Yogyakarta, central Java, helped to ease fears that President Abdurrahman Wahid could be impeached by a meeting of the nation's highest legislative body next week. 

 But the gathering failed to reassure investors that Wahid's political opponents won't make such a move later this year, ensuring that political concerns will linger over Jakarta for months to come. 

 While damaging for investor confidence, the lack of clarity also discourages players from taking large positions for or against the rupiah in the forward market. And with fewer players in the market, Bank Indonesia should be better able to prop up the ailing rupiah by selling dollars to prevent any sharp moves. 


"The central bank can intervene with some effectiveness at the moment
given that the market is so thin," says Simon Flint, senior currency
strategist at Bank of America in Singapore.
-
        Intervention After 21-Month Dlr High
-



After rising to a 21-month high against the rupiah in mid-July, the
dollar has fallen back following central bank intervention.



Acting central bank governor, Anwar Nasution, has also backed up the
dollar selling with comments that Bank Indonesia is acting in tandem
with Singapore and other foreign monetary authorities to curb
speculation.



Apart from the fear of getting caught long dollars in such an illiquid
market, foreign banks are also being very careful not to anger the
central bank.



Bank Indonesia has put officials in many of the foreign dealing rooms,
ostensibly to check banks are keeping to regulations governing maximum
forward positions, but also to apply moral pressure not to speculate.



The central bank resorted to this kind of moral persuasion without
success last month, after a series of interest rate hikes were unable to
stem a hemorrhage of foreign capital from Indonesia due to political
concerns.



Rate hikes to 13.53% on the one-month note at last week's auction did
little to help the rupiah amid growing opposition to Wahid's
ten-month-old administration, and the arrest of central bank governor,
Sjahril Sabirin, amid allegations of corruption.



In such an environment, direct intervention, backed up by Indonesia's
relatively small $27 billion gross foreign reserves, was ineffective.



But with thinner market conditions prevailing now, dollar selling from
state banks is having an impact, pushing some foreign exchange
strategists to advise investors to get rid of any outstanding
long-dollar positions on spikes in the U.S. currency.



"Bank Indonesia will intervene again to keep the rupiah stable in the
run up to the MPR," says UBS Warburg Asian currency strategist Mansoor
Mohi-uddin.



"Thus with the offshore market still long dollar and Bank Indonesia
holding approximately $7 billion worth of forex reserves, the dollar
should be sold on rallies above IDR9,000 as we head toward the MPR," he
adds.
-
        Political Pressure Not Over
-



Longer term, strategists' views on the rupiah depends on how they see
the political situation unfolding.



Many analysts, including Bank of America's Flint, see the rupiah
moving back through IDR8,500 to the dollar if Wahid survives the MPR,
from IDR8,933 at Tuesday's close of Asian trading.



But Flint points out that the Yogyakarta meeting, although positive,
won't stop Wahid's political opponents from piling on the pressure later
this year.



Any concerted political effort against Wahid could easily change
investor sentiment, and make central intervention less effective.



"If there is a major shift in political risk, then it won't be
effective," he said.



UBS Warburg's Mohi-uddin is also targeting IDR8,500 in the short-term
on the likelihood of central bank intervention.



But like Flint, he points out that politicians such as Amien Rais,
head of the MPR, have said Wahid could face impeachment later in the
year, which would hurt rupiah sentiment, and leave the central bank
helpless.



Although the MPR has no constitutional power to impeach Wahid at this
month's meeting, the 700-member body will consider legislation that
could allow them to call the president to a special session later this
year.



That session would have the power to impeach the president.



"This could make markets worry about impeachment even if Wahid
survives this month," Mohi-uddin said.



Added to creeping U.S. interest rates, rupiah gains might only be
short-lived, he adds.

title: INTERVIEW:Bk Indonesia Says No Plan For Capital Controls
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's central bank doesn't have any plan to introduce any capital controls or any other form of curbs on trading in the rupiah, acting governor Anwar Nasution said Thursday. 

 "We're not going to introduce capital controls," Nasution said in an interview with Dow Jones Newswires. "We are quite allergic to the currency board system." 

 Instead, the central bank will strictly monitor banks' compliance with existing rules and regulations, Nasution said. 

 Bank Indonesia has recently actively monitored activities of commercial banks' dealing rooms in Jakarta to ensure that the rules are complied with, but this, Nasution said, wasn't a precursor to capital controls. "We are more serious in implementing the existing rules and regulations," Nasution said. 

 Visits by central bank officials to dealing rooms had made currency traders more cautious, helping to slow down the pace of the rupiah's slide. 

 Nasution also said the dollar should trade at 7,000 to 8,000 rupiah, adding that the country's improved economic fundamentals don't warrant a weakening rupiah. He said the dollar's current rate of around IDR9,000 was "ridiculous." 

 "All indicators point that we have made a lot of improvement," Nasution said. "There's no reason for the weakening of the rupiah." 

 Nasution said that even if Bank Indonesia intervenes in the market to support the rupiah, the intervention will be "very limited." 

 Separately, Nasution confirmed that the government will sign a letter of intent with the International Monetary Fund on Monday, which would pave the way for a $400 million disbursement of the next tranche of the IMF's loan package to Indonesia. 

 Nasution is in Singapore to attend a two-day regional central banking conference, which will end Friday.

title: MAS offers no comment on Bank Indonesia support.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 21 (Reuters) - The Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) declined comment on Friday on whether Indonesia's central bank had asked it to help stop offshore speculation in the rupiah. 

 MAS said it was Bank Indonesia's decision whether to intervene to stabilise its currency. 

 "It is Bank Indonesia's decision whether to stabilise the rupiah or take appropriate actions, including inspecting foreign banks in Indonesia," a MAS spokesman said in a written reply to Reuters queries. 

 MAS said it was official policy not to comment on its dealings with other central banks, other banks' actions or their exchange rates. 

 Indonesia's acting central bank governor, Anwar Nasution, said earlier on Friday the bank had asked neighbouring countries, such as Singapore, to help stop offshore speculation in the rupiah in a bid to stabilise the currency. 

 "They also see the need for the rupiah to stabilise because of their huge interest in Indonesia," Nasution said. 

 Indonesia's central bank also confirmed it had sent inspectors to monitor local banks' trading of the rupiah and said it had the right to continue such inspections in the future. 

 The move had been seen as an attempt by Bank Indonesia to curb speculation in the rupiah. 

 The dollar lost almost six percent against the rupiah during the week amid the moves by Bank Indonesia.

title: ANALYSIS-Southeast Asia's  FX  woes, 1997 and all that.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 14 (Reuters) - The gloom shrouding Southeast Asia's currencies in the wake of the rupiah's steep drop has spurred talk in the markets of a contagion effect, but analysts are quick to dismiss the notion. 

 This is not 1997, there is no balance of payments crisis and investors are not embarking on a 'sell-Asia' spree. 

 The rupiah's descent to 16-month lows last week amid mounting worries about Indonesia's political and security situation did spur some weakness in the Philippine peso, Thai baht and even the stalwart Singapore dollar. 

 But analysts note these declines are very much more tied to domestic ills or, in the case of Singapore, its trade-weighted currency basket. 

 "Simply viewing the recent weakness in Asian currencies as contagion is missing the fact that the recent trends in the baht and peso were merely continuations of primary trends of weakness," said Desmond Supple, economist at Barclays Capital. 

 "While sentiment in Asia inevitably suffers from political instability in Indonesia, the actual impact on the regional business cycle is minimal," he said. 

 With healthy current account surpluses, floating exchange rates and debt restructuring efforts, there is little risk of the herd-like sell-off that characterised the Asian crisis, resulting in forced devaluations and near economic collapse. 

 Analysts said governments had clearly learned the lesson of '97 and were opting to let currencies take the strain, avoiding expensive intervention or economically-damaging rate hikes. 

 NOT 1997 

 "The main point here is event risk has fallen in the region because all these economies have moved from fixed to floating exchange rates," said Vincent Low, strategist at Merrill Lynch. 

 "So moving from 37 to 40 (baht to the dollar) is very far removed from the days of the crisis when the Bank of Thailand's hand was forced and it had to go from 25 to 56 in a few months." 

 Low noted that Asia's macroeconomic profile was also much improved from before the crisis. 

 "We're talking about current account surpluses, companies that are less leveraged, short-term forex exposure has declined, easy monetary conditions". 

 Analysts said investors were, if anything, tending to differentiate more among individual economies in Asia, as evidenced by continuing portfolio inflows to Hong Kong, South Korea and Taiwan. 

 Even the Singapore dollar's fall to 16-month lows this week has more to do with the authorities condoning a mild depreciation as the currencies of its neighbours and export rivals slide. 

 In any case, the Sing dollar's 4.4 percent drop against the U.S. dollar since the start of the year is far removed from the peso's 10 percent loss and the rupiah's 27 percent slump. 

 REAL PROBLEMS 

 None of this detracts from the fact that Indonesia and the Philippines do face a very real threat unless they are somehow able to restore political and economic stability. 

 Both countries have been hard hit by doubts about their leadership, which have increasingly undermined their markets and economies, giving investor confidence a further jolt. 

 Thailand has also suffered a bit as opposition efforts to push for an early election spark worries about a delay to the national budget, but analysts say the risks are more contained. 

 The Philippine central bank, like the Bank of Thailand, has opted for a hands-off approach, which analysts see as appropriate given still subdued inflation and efforts to manage foreign debt. 

 Bank Indonesia has also ruled out forex intervention, but it has repeatedly hiked rates since May, pushing one-month central bank certificates to 13.1 percent from 10.9 percent on May 10. 

 Unfortunately, that hasn't really helped the rupiah. 

 "Once everybody starts selling the currency, the loss in confidence is much more overwhelming than anything that interest rates could do," said Mangal Goswami, regional economist at ABN-Amro Bank. 

 "Something has got to be resolved on the political front." 

 For Bank Indonesia, whose chief is himself embroiled in a political scandal, the options are less clear cut. 

 A sustained rupiah depreciation would inflate food prices, potentially sparking the kind of social unrest that led to former president Suharto being ousted in 1998. 

 At the same time, higher rates would magnify the cost of recapitalising the banking sector, already estimated at over 40 percent of gross domestic product. 

 "Higher interest rates are clearly an imperfect and incomplete solution to Indonesia's woes," said Steve Brice, treasury economist at Standard Chartered, in a research note. 

 "But those looking for perfect solutions will likely be disappointed."

title: UPDATE 4-Bombs rattle rupiah, threaten Indonesia economy.
text:
JAKARTA, July 5 (Reuters) - Indonesia's increasingly hostile political atmosphere rained further damage on the frail economy on Wednesday as the rupiah was swept to 16-month lows on fears of worsening instability and interest rates were hiked to defend it. 

 A bomb blast at the attorney-general's office late on Tuesday shattered windows and blew doors off their hinges. The damage done to Indonesia's hopes of economic recovery was worse. 

 The blast spurred jittery offshore players to mark down the rupiah, kicking the currency through technical support at 8,970 to the dollar and psychological support at 9,000, and sparking a clamour for dollars from panicked local corporates. 

 The discovery of more explosives at the attorney-general's offices on Wednesday dealt another blow to the currency, sending it to 9,305/9,335 to the dollar by 0845 GMT. 

 The rupiah is now at its weakest levels since March 1999, when fears were rife that upcoming parliamentary and presidential elections would descend into mass bloodshed and instability. 

 When Abdurrahman Wahid became president in October after a remarkably peaceful transition to democracy, it was hailed as a milestone on Indonesia's road to recovery. The fact that the currency market now judges political risk to be as severe as in the uncertain days of early 1999 shows how badly things have gone wrong. 

 POLITICAL UNCERTAINTY, ECONOMIC PAIN 

 The explosion at the attorney-general's office came amid swirling controversy over reports that several legislators would be questioned for stirring up trouble in the unruly country. 

 Wahid also faces a showdown with parliament next week, after legislators exercised their right to summon him for the first time ever, to explain the controversial sacking of two ministers. 

 The president must also navigate a meeting of the country's highest legislative body, the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR), in August. The MPR has the power to remove him, although analysts believe this is unlikely and his main potential rivals have said they will continue to give him their support. 

 But while Wahid is unlikely to be toppled, his grip on power looks increasingly tenuous, and with political risk rising most foreign investors are simply turning their back on the country. 

 The floundering rupiah, moreover, threatens to snuff out one of Indonesia's few bright spots - a relatively strong consumer-led economic recovery after two years of pain. 

 A weaker rupiah makes the debt burden crushing both the government and private sector even heavier. It threatens to re-ignite inflation. And by forcing interest rates up, it makes the huge bill of bank recapitalisation even higher. 

 "It's fair to say the rupiah is the foundation for everything," said the head of treasury at a European bank in Jakarta. "If it goes, everything else starts to go." 

 The rupiah is now trading far from the level of 7,000 to the dollar assumed in Indonesia's current budget. 

INTERVENTION LITTLE USE 

 Reports that Bank Indonesia was intervening gave the rupiah some respite on Wednesday, but dealers said intervention would not work for long, something the central bank also conceded. 

 "About intervention, we will not sell dollars because it will not help... At the moment, the problem is different, therefore monetary policy needs to be implemented consistently," Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Miranda Goeltom told reporters. 

 Bank Indonesia's weekly auction raised the benchmark SBI one-month interest rate to 12.69 percent from 12.33, the ninth consecutive rise in the rate, which now stands at its highest levels since December, further burdening businesses and pushing up government interest payments on bank recapitalisation bonds. 

 Analysts say that if interest rates stay this high for much longer, the cost of bank recapitalisation will start biting even harder into the government's budget. 

 Traders said there was a pattern to the action in the rupiah, with onshore corporates which need dollars for debt repayments and imports holding off, hoping for better levels to buy. But when key levels are broken, they panic and pile in. 

 "Generally volumes are still very low, you just get bursts of activity and that's what happened this morning," said Steve Brice, treasury economist at Standard Chartered in Singapore.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends At 16-Mo Low After Tue Bomb Blast
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah ended at a 16-month low Wednesday amid continuing jitters after a bomb blast ripped through the Attorney General's office late Tuesday. 

 After rising to an intraday high of IDR9,445, the dollar closed Wednesday at IDR9,395, up from IDR8,956 late Tuesday in Asia. 

 Dealers said the explosion at the Attorney General's office late Tuesday sparked a surge in dollar buying. Pressure on the rupiah could lift the dollar as high as IDR9,600 Thursday, one foreign dealer said. 

 The bomb exploded just after investigators had finished questioning former President Suharto's youngest son Hutomo "Tommy" Mandala Putra over alleged corruption. 

 The currency was further hurt Wednesday after police found another unexploded bomb at the Attorney General's office. The state prosecutor's complex was evacuated and cordoned off by police as a bomb squad removed the device. 

 A dealer with a foreign bank said Bank Indonesia must intervene to support the rupiah to bring the currency under control. 

 The central bank Wednesday raised interest rates on one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia notes for the ninth consecutive week, but this move has previously failed to stop the rupiah's slide. 

 "They have been raised a few times already and it's not helping at all," the dealer said. 

 He said some state banks were buying rupiah to try and support the currency but it was ineffective. 

 "The demand for dollars was just too overwhelming," he said. 

 Dealers expect a range of IDR9,300-9,600 Thursday.

title: Bk  Indonesia  To  Intervene  Selectively To Stabilise IDR
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia said Wednesday it will maintain the free float system for the rupiah while continuing to intervene selectively on a limited basis to maintain the currency's stability. 

 The rupiah exchange rate will be left to the market, it said in a statement. 

 The central bank statement said efforts will be taken "to maintain the rupiah's stability...in the foreign-currency market in a limited and selective manner." 

 The statement said the central bank will continue to maintain its net international reserves in line with the government's target. 

 Political friction between President Abdurrahman Wahid and the parliament fueled by conflicting comments by Wahid on police investigations into suspected corruption and riot-inciting by lawmakers has sent the rupiah crashing 7% since Friday. 

 At 1019 GMT, the dollar was trading at IDR9,395, up from IDR8,975 late Tuesday. 

 Confusion over the central bank's strategy to defend the rupiah also weighed on the currency Wednesday. 

 In its statement, Bank Indonesia said it expects the Indonesian economy to grow by between 3% and 4% during the third quarter of 2000.

title: Bk  Indonesia  Deputy Gov:Won't  Intervene  To Help Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia's Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom said Wednesday that the nation's central bank won't intervene in the currency market to help the rupiah as such a move won't help the ailing local unit. 

 "We are not going to intervene," Miranda told journalists on a sidelines of a seminar. 

 "We still see that the rupiah's weakness is only temporary," she added 

 Miranda's statement contradicts acting governor Anwar Nasution's statement Tuesday that Bank Indonesia had intervened to help the rupiah and "the central bank won't give up in helping the rupiah." 

 Dealers said earlier Wednesday that Bank Indonesia was heard selling the dollar through state banks to defend the rupiah. 

 (Corrected 0939GMT) 

 The rupiah has lost 5.4% of its value over the last three days on concerns about mounting political tension in the run-up of the August parliamentary session. 

 The dollar was trading at IDR9,195 at 0735 GMT, up from IDR8,960 late Tuesday in Asia. 

 Bank Indonesia has allowed the rate of it's one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia notes to rise over the last seven weeks due to the persistent rupiah's weakness. 

 The average rate of the note was 12.33% after a weekly auction last week. 

 Miranda said she expects banks won't demand a sharp increase in the SBI rate through a weekly auction, as a sharp increase on the benchmark rate will push other domestic interest rates up sharply. 

 "(A) sharp rise on domestic interest rates will hurt (the) economic recovery," Miranda said. 

 She added that the rupiah current weakness was due to political uncertainties. 

 "(The) domestic political situation is getting more and more uncertain," she said. "Under such circumstances the rupiah will be affected (weaken)." 

 She added that the rupiah weakness will boost inflationary pressures.

title: Rupiah off lows as Wahid tries to defuse tension.
text:
JAKARTA, July 4 (Reuters) - The battered Indonesian rupiah was off its day lows on Tuesday as worries over political uncertainty eased after President Abdurrahman Wahid attempted to defuse a potential showdown with parliament. 

 The rupiah has flirted with 9,000 to the U.S. dollar in the past two days on concerns over Indonesia's political stability. 

 By 0845 GMT it was being quoted at 8,948/8,963, after earlier coming close to 9,000, hitting its lowest levels since March 1999. It was quoted at 8,910/8,930 in late local trade on Monday. 

 "Some liquidation of long dollar positions following Wahid's remarks capped the rupiah's fall and provided it with solid support at around 8,960, but the outlook remains fragile," one foreign bank dealer said. 

 The rupiah was likely to be well supported at around 8,975 and immediate resistance was seen at around 8,900. Dealers said the central bank, Bank Indonesia, was likely to continue intervening into the market, albeit in small amounts, to prop up the currency. 

 The central bank engaged in minor intervention in the foreign exchange market to support the battered rupiah, acting Bank Indonesia head Anwar Nasution said on Tuesday. 

 Nasution repeated comments he made last week that the rupiah would become more stable after a key meeting in August of the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR), which will hear an account of President Abdurrahman Wahid's first turbulent year in office. 

 Offshore players, particularly European and British players, had bought dollars at around 8,900 earlier in the day but liquidated their long dollar positions in late trade, one bank dealer said. 

 Wahid denied on Tuesday saying parliamentarians were "culprits" behind violence in the country, and he lashed out at unnamed parties for playing political games. 

 In comments that appear to be an attempt to defuse a potential showdown with parliament, Wahid told a news conference that some legislators would only be questioned as witnesses over the country's troubles. 

 Finance Minister Bambang Sudibyo said on Tuesday the rupiah's fair value against the dollar, based on the country's economic fundamentals, was between 6,500 to 7,500. ((Jakarta newsroom +62 21 384 6364, Fax +62 21 344 8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Central Bank  Watch: Indonesia's Interest Rate Dilemma
text:
A Dow Jones Newswires Column 

 JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia's move to guide interest rates higher will raise the burden on the government of bank recapitalization, but is unlikely to lift the rupiah for long. 

 That makes one wonder why they bother at all. 

 The central bank has raised the rate on its benchmark one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia, or SBI, notes over the past five weeks in a bid to help the ailing rupiah amid climbing U.S. rates and a barrage of concerns about Indonesia's political and economic stability. 

 But so far, the hikes have failed to bolster the currency, which remains dogged by a number of political scandals, among them the high-profile row between Bank Indonesia Governor Sjahril Sabirin and President Abdurrahman Wahid amid allegations that the former was involved in a damaging banking scandal last year. 

 The rupiah closed Tuesday at 8,585 to the dollar, down 18% from 7,050 at the start of the year. 

 Bank Indonesia would need to hike interest rates much faster if it wants to persuade foreign capital to buy local assets and end the rupiah's 18% slide this year, economists say. 

 But bigger interest rate increases would also bring a fatter bill for funding the financial sector rescue, which the government has paid for by issuing bonds to help recapitalize banks since the 1997 financial system crash. 

 "The rate hikes at the moment are really not to strengthen the rupiah," said Pardy Kendi, a director at Bank Buana Indonesia. "I would prefer to call it a smoothing operation" in reaction to U.S. rate hikes, he added. 

 The one-month SBI rate stood at 11.13% last Wednesday, increasing by only a few basis points at weekly auctions since hitting a low of 10.88% April 26. 

 If the upward trend continues however, it would have a ripple effect on the budget, which already allocates a whopping 6.5% of gross domestic product to finance bank recapitalization. 


"I think they still have a small margin for increases of about 1 to
1.5 percentage points, but if the SBI goes higher than that, it would
affect the budget," said Martin Panggabean, an economist at PT Bank
Mandiri in Jakarta.
-
              Budget Concern
-



As of June 12, the government had issued 321.4 trillion rupiah
($1=IDR8,580) in recapitalization bonds and plans to issue another
IDR105 trillion sometime this month.



Of the total, around two-fifths of the bonds pay interest linked to
the SBI rates, or have floating rates, while the remainder carry a fixed
coupon of 14%.



Larger increases in interest rates would stretch government coffers,
which are already relying on multilateral credit lines to fund this
year's forecast budget deficit at 5% of gross domestic product.



"With increased interest rates, of course it would put more pressure
on the government," said Pardy at Bank Buana.



But the government is downplaying the fact its hands are tied when it
comes to financing a defense of the rupiah, and the central bank this
week appeared to signal to the market that it's comfortable with rising
rates, despite the budget impact.



Sjahril said Monday that the central bank will intervene to boost the
rupiah "every day." Although he gave few details, he said the SBI notes
were the only real tool to stabilize the currency, raising speculation
that he was indicating rates would continue to creep up.



On Tuesday, senior economics minister Kwik Kian Gie lent some support
to that view, arguing that rising rates would stem capital outflows and
help the rupiah.



"The interest rate increase is positive," Kwik told reporters. "People
will put their money offshore if we don't increase rates domestically."



Such comments mark a departure from the central bank's position last
month that it would only intervene in the market if it felt its actions
would have a positive effect on the rupiah. As the rupiah was sliding in
May, market participants took the central bank signals at the time to
mean that Bank Indonesia wouldn't seek to intervene in a foreign
exchange market intent on pushing the rupiah down.



While Sjahril's harder line signals Monday did lend some brief support
to the rupiah - as well as the myriad fundamental reasons for rupiah
weakness - most economists are taking the central bank jawboning with a
pinch of salt.



"The rupiah is driven by something else, not interest rates,"
Panggabean said, referring to negative foreign investor sentiment toward
Indonesia.
-
           Systemwide Rate Hike Unlikely
-



The upward trend in rates hasn't yet hurt Indonesia's fragile
recovery, but it could if it continues.



Interest rate hikes have failed to have a knock-on effect across the
financial system, as bank lending and deposit rates are higher than Bank
Indonesia rates.



"The current increase on SBI rates won't necessarily lead to an
increase in deposit and lending rates," Miranda Gultom, central bank
deputy governor, told reporters this week.



"It will drive these rates up only if the increase is drastic to an
extent that banks have to compete with SBI to attract depositors," she
said.



Currently, fixed deposit rates are between 12% and 14%, above the SBI
rates. As depositors have to pay banks a fixed charge to invest in SBI
notes, the spread is even higher than this.



But larger SBI rate hikes could start to attract depositors away from
the banks, forcing upward deposit and lending rate adjustments.



With low rates crucial to help Indonesia's corporate debt
restructuring efforts, the central bank has been keen to show it doesn't
want to force such a situation.



"We will try to minimize the costs of interest rate hikes," Achjar
Iljas, another deputy central bank governor, said this week, adding that
other factors apart from rates were behind the rupiah's fall.

 If the upward trend continues however, it would have a ripple effect on the budget, which already allocates a whopping 6.5% of gross domestic product to finance bank recapitalization. 


"I think they still have a small margin for increases of about 1 to
1.5 percentage points, but if the SBI goes higher than that, it would
affect the budget," said Martin Panggabean, an economist at PT Bank
Mandiri in Jakarta.
-
              Budget Concern
-



As of June 12, the government had issued 321.4 trillion rupiah
($1=IDR8,580) in recapitalization bonds and plans to issue another
IDR105 trillion sometime this month.



Of the total, around two-fifths of the bonds pay interest linked to
the SBI rates, or have floating rates, while the remainder carry a fixed
coupon of 14%.



Larger increases in interest rates would stretch government coffers,
which are already relying on multilateral credit lines to fund this
year's forecast budget deficit at 5% of gross domestic product.



"With increased interest rates, of course it would put more pressure
on the government," said Pardy at Bank Buana.



But the government is downplaying the fact its hands are tied when it
comes to financing a defense of the rupiah, and the central bank this
week appeared to signal to the market that it's comfortable with rising
rates, despite the budget impact.



Sjahril said Monday that the central bank will intervene to boost the
rupiah "every day." Although he gave few details, he said the SBI notes
were the only real tool to stabilize the currency, raising speculation
that he was indicating rates would continue to creep up.



On Tuesday, senior economics minister Kwik Kian Gie lent some support
to that view, arguing that rising rates would stem capital outflows and
help the rupiah.



"The interest rate increase is positive," Kwik told reporters. "People
will put their money offshore if we don't increase rates domestically."



Such comments mark a departure from the central bank's position last
month that it would only intervene in the market if it felt its actions
would have a positive effect on the rupiah. As the rupiah was sliding in
May, market participants took the central bank signals at the time to
mean that Bank Indonesia wouldn't seek to intervene in a foreign
exchange market intent on pushing the rupiah down.



While Sjahril's harder line signals Monday did lend some brief support
to the rupiah - as well as the myriad fundamental reasons for rupiah
weakness - most economists are taking the central bank jawboning with a
pinch of salt.



"The rupiah is driven by something else, not interest rates,"
Panggabean said, referring to negative foreign investor sentiment toward
Indonesia.
-
           Systemwide Rate Hike Unlikely
-



The upward trend in rates hasn't yet hurt Indonesia's fragile
recovery, but it could if it continues.



Interest rate hikes have failed to have a knock-on effect across the
financial system, as bank lending and deposit rates are higher than Bank
Indonesia rates.



"The current increase on SBI rates won't necessarily lead to an
increase in deposit and lending rates," Miranda Gultom, central bank
deputy governor, told reporters this week.



"It will drive these rates up only if the increase is drastic to an
extent that banks have to compete with SBI to attract depositors," she
said.



Currently, fixed deposit rates are between 12% and 14%, above the SBI
rates. As depositors have to pay banks a fixed charge to invest in SBI
notes, the spread is even higher than this.



But larger SBI rate hikes could start to attract depositors away from
the banks, forcing upward deposit and lending rate adjustments.



With low rates crucial to help Indonesia's corporate debt
restructuring efforts, the central bank has been keen to show it doesn't
want to force such a situation.



"We will try to minimize the costs of interest rate hikes," Achjar
Iljas, another deputy central bank governor, said this week, adding that
other factors apart from rates were behind the rupiah's fall.

title: Emerging  FX -Dozing ahead of US data, rupiah firms.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 13 (Reuters) - Asian regional currencies

 drifted higher in late trade on Tuesday as players took 

 advantage of the dollar's recent gains. 

     The rupiah was bolstered by talk Bank Indonesia was 

 prepared to intervene to shore up the ailing currency. 

     But trade was sluggish as investors lacked confidence and 

 willpower to chase the currencies vigorously either way ahead 

 of U.S. data and Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's 

 speech. 

 The U.S. is due to publish May retail sales data on Tuesday 

 and consumer price data on Wednesday. Greenspan is scheduled to 

 speak on business data analysis at 1710 GMT. 

 Investors are eyeing these events for clues on the Fed's 

 likely move on interest rates later this month. U.S. economists 

 polled by Reuters predicted on average the May retail sales 

 would be unchanged after a 0.2 percent decline in April. 

     A growing number of analysts now reckon Fed policymakers 

 are more likely to keep rates unchanged at the June meeting. 

     "Although many in the market do expect the dollar to lose 

 steam a bit in the medium-term, the rebound we see today is 

 just technical and linked to profit taking," said a senior 

 dealer at a major European bank. 

     "I don't think the dollar's bullish trend is reversing. 

 Buying dollars on dips is still the order of the day," he said. 


    The dollar retreated against the yen	  due to sporadic



selling interest from Japanese exporters at levels above 107.00



yen. However, players lacked enough confidence in Japan's



economic recovery to sell the dollar aggressively.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah strengthened as offshore players liquidated long



dollar positions but it failed to break key resistance at 8,550



as corporate dollar demand capped the upside.



Comments by chief economics minister Kwik Kian Gie



supporting a rise in interest rates to halt an outflow of



capital from the country failed to boost the rupiah.



    Bank Indonesia has recently increased the key interest rate



on its one-month SBI certificates to prop up the ailing rupiah.



    But the market remained sceptical about the central bank's



capacity to shield the currency via higher interest rates or



dollar buying intervention in the face of persistent worries



about the political outlook.



A continuing feud between central bank governor Sjahril



Sabirin and President Abdurrahman Wahid was also keeping



investors edgy.



KOREAN WON -2

consolidation provided little impetus to buy the currency.



    But despite its losses, it remained at the upper end of its



recent range.



    At 1,114.00, the dollar is already very close to oversold

strength index. A reading of 30 or below would indicate that it



is oversold.

brief rebound caused by dollar profit taking in early trade.



    Dealers said some players were cutting long dollar/peso



positions in the non-deliverable forward market.



    However, with the one-month premium dropping to around 68



centavos, a further sell-off is unlikely in the near-term, a



dealer at a U.S. bank said.



    On the political front, President Joseph Estrada was found



to be in good health except for mildly high cholestoral levels



and pre-existing gallstones.



    Estrada, 63, underwent medical tests after he was seen



grimacing in pain nd holding his right side during Independence



Day celebrations on Monday.

lately, gained some ground in sympathy with a rise in its



Indonesian counterpart.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mixed Early; Market Awaits US Econ Data
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies are mixed early Tuesday in cautious trade as market participants await the release of key U.S. economic data and the Federal Reserve chairman's assessment of the economy, dealers said. 

 Further signs of a slowdown in the U.S. economy could weigh on the dollar as it may prompt the Fed to be less aggressive in raising interest rates this year, they added. 

 Wednesday, U.S. consumer price index data for May will be issued. 

 Market participants will also be seeking more clues on the U.S. economy and where rates are headed when Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan speaks later Tuesday at a business economics conference. 

 The South Korean won has taken centerstage in the Asian market, as a 1.6% slide in the Seoul stock market damps the currency, dealers said. 

 The won is also coming under pressure on newspaper reports suggesting that international ratings agencies are unlikely to upgrade South Korea's ratings after the summit between North and South Korea, which starts Tuesday. Many had hoped for an upgrade as a successful summit would eventually reduce South Korea's country risk, market watchers said. 

 At 0135 GMT (9:35 p.m. EDT Monday), the dollar is at 1,114.40 won, up from Monday's close of KRW1,113.40. 

 The dollar has fallen to 42.38 pesos, from Friday's close of PHP42.465 as banks unwind their long dollar positions, dealers said. The Philippine market was closed Monday for a national holiday. 

Currency dealers are unruffled by President Joseph Estrada's illness, which isn't expected to be serious. 

 Estrada is expected to continue undergoing medical tests after suffering considerable pain on his right side Monday. 

 Elsewhere, the Indonesia rupiah was slightly stronger amid fears of intervention by the central bank. Bank Indonesia Governor Sjahril Sabirin said Monday the central bank would intervene in the market "every day" to support the rupiah, which authorities have repeatedly stressed in recent weeks is undervalued given the improving economy. 

 Bank Indonesia is expected to sell dollars in small amounts near 8,650 rupiah via state banks, dealers said. 

 The dollar has slipped to IDR8,575 from IDR8,608 late Monday. 

 Corporate demand for dollars is expected to keep the dollar supported around IDR8,550 to IDR8,600, while long liquidation from offshore participants in the U.S. currency will cap Tuesday's range around IDR8,670, dealers said. 

 The market will be awaiting news on the International Monetary Fund's latest review of Indonesia progress in implementing reform pledges. 

 In Thailand, the dollar is at 38.965 baht, down from THB39.065 late Monday. The dollar will remain capped around THB39.10 on long liquidation in the U.S. currency by offshore players, dealers said. Local corporate demand for dollars will support the dollar around THB38.80, they added. 

 Against its Singapore counterpart, the dollar is at S$1.7220, down slightly from S$1.7235 late Monday. The pair will likely remained confined within its recent range of S$1.7200 to S$1.7250, dealers said. 

 In Taiwan, the dollar is at NT$30.805, little changed from NT$30.802 late Monday.
