title: UPDATE 2-Indonesian rupiah hits 11,000/dlr.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 6 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah slipped past the 11,000 to the dollar mark on Tuesday for the first time since July 23 on corporate dollar demand as investors stayed pessimistic about Indonesia's economy, dealers in Jakarta said. 

 At 0548 GMT, the currency was quoted at 10,820/10,850, compared with 10,860 late on Monday. It touched the 11,000 mark earlier in the day, though profit-taking on the dollar and intervention by Bank Indonesia rescued it from further losses. 

 The central bank was spotted selling dollars aggressively in the market during the morning session, catching the market long on dollar, dealers said. A dealer at a foreign bank in Jakarta estimated the bank sold around $20 million, which he said was an unusually large amount. 

 Still, the dollar was well-supported around these levels, with local corporates including investment houses looking to buy it on dips. 

 Daily charts showed the dollar/rupiah was still overbought, though less so than it was this morning. The pair now has a 14-day relative strength index reading of 86, compared with 94 earlier in the day. 

 However, given Indonesia's poor economic fundamentals and the dearth of fresh dollar inflows, the rupiah is unlikely to enjoy a long-lasting rebound, no matter how overbought the dollar may appear. 

 GOOD NEWS FOR INDONESIA 

 Some dealers said players were hoping to reach the 11,500 to the dollar mark before taking profit on the dollar. 

 However, there was a rare bit of good news for Indonesia. The IMF said it would work as quickly as possible to sign a new pact with Jakarta. The country's IMF representative David Nellor said the Fund was impressed by the progress in some reforms. 

 But the market shrugged off the comments, with players more concerned about the immediate dearth of dollar inflows. 

 A team from the International Monetary Fund will also arrive this week to review current reforms, and begin talks on a new letter of intent under its $5 billion loan programme. 

 The chronically ailing rupiah has been falling steadily since mid-August, when optimism over President Megawati Sukarnoputri's new government began to fade. It has given up nearly all its gains from July 23-August 14, when it rallied from 11,125 to 8,200 against the dollar. 

 Dealers said the market was upset by signs of further trouble with the country's donors and lenders, with whom Jakarta needs good relations to help keep the struggling economy afloat. 

 The market was particularly perturbed by a critical report from the World Bank issued on Monday and by Standard and Poor's decision over the weekend to downgrade Indonesia's sovereign ratings to CCC from CCC-Plus, with a negative outlook. 

 PARIS CLUB MEET 

 Both reports came just ahead of key meetings between Jakarta and its donor and lenders. Jakarta will hold talks with its Consultative Group of donors on Wednesday and Thursday, during which the government is expected to ask for $3 billion to $4 billion in aid. 

 Next week, Indonesia will meet with its Paris Club of official lenders, and is expected to seek a restructuring of some $6 billion in debt. 

 The World Bank report said it expected the government to still "muddle through" the country's economic woes, adding that it needed to move more quickly to ensure fiscal sustainability and improve the investment climate. 

 Japan, the country's biggest creditor nation, has added its voice to the growing criticism over Jakarta's foot-dragging on reforms. The Japanese government said on Monday it wanted to see an improvement in reform efforts before disbursing fresh loans and grants. 

 Few expect Indonesia's donors and lenders to turn their backs on the country given its geo-political importance in the region's stability and the fact that it is the world's most populous Muslim nation. 

 Still, patience has been wearing thin over the snail-like pace on reform. 

 Analysts say the focal point of the meetings will be Jakarta's fumbling of asset sales and the privatisation process. 

 SEMEN GRESIK 

 The recent takeover by the West Sumatra provincial government of a unit of cement company PT Semen Gresik to prevent its sale to Mexico-based Cemex highlights the government's failure to raise revenues through asset sales to help fund the budget. 

 Though the government has yet to raise one cent towards its 2001 target of 6.5 trillion rupiah in asset sales, it has not revised its target yet. 

 State Enterprises Minister Laksama Sukardi recently conceded the government may have to re-think the timetable for its target after persistently sticking by it, saying the government had little choice given the budget deficit.

title: Emerging  FX -Steady on yen, but rupiah upset.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies drew 

 some strength from a steadier yen on Monday, but there 

 was no stopping for the Indonesian rupiah, which slid to fresh 

 three-month lows. 

     Despite dollar sales by the central bank, the rupiah 

 fumbled as the World Bank expressed disappointment with 

 Jakarta's progress on reforms in a report ahead of a donors' 

 meeting later in the week. 

     Gains in most regionals were also limited as a grim 

 economic outlook for the region attracted dollar bids at dips. 

     The Singapore dollar, after its sharp rebound from almost 

 four-month lows beyond 1.8350, met dollar demand from local 

 companies just below the 1.8100 level. 

     Equity-linked inflows helped the Korean won and Taiwan 

 dollar hold steady, but both were locked in recent narrow 

 ranges as the market waited for the policy-setting meeting of 

 the Federal Reserve due Tuesday. 

 With the Fed widely expected to slash its 2.50 percent key 

 fund rate by an aggressive 50 basis points, regional players 

 preferred to wait and watch for a response from local 

 authorities. 

 Withering hopes of a rate cut by the European Central Bank

 this week and a report indicating European governments could be 

 masking the true extent of their budget deficits pulled down 

 the euro to one-week lows against the dollar and the 

 yen. 

 The dollar managed to regain some ground against the yen 

 but struggled to make headway as players doubted a rate cut, 

 the tenth this year, would have a near-term impact on the 

 gloomy economic situation. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 Active intervention by Bank Indonesia helped slow the 

 losses, but failed to halt the ailing currency's decline. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said the central bank was in the market 

 to sell U.S. dollars at 10,650 and 10,800. The intervention was 

 countered by strong corporate dollar demand, however. 

 Bank Indonesia said it would keep intervening in the 

foreign exchange market to smooth sharp fluctuations in the 

 local currency. 

 However, it said it had no immediate target for the rupiah, 

 which lost almost two percent on Monday, adding its foreign 

 reserves could not be used excessively. 

 The rupiah was hit by a slew of negative news ranging from 

 a rating downgrade to concerns over huge debt loads. Standard 

 and Poor's on Friday cut Indonesia's long-term sovereign debt 

 rating to 'CCC' from 'CCC Plus' and also revised down its 

 outlook to negative from stable. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar was off its intraday high after players 

 took advantage of the U.S. dollar's pullback and bought the 

 U.S. currency on dips. 

 Some dealers suspected the Monetary Authority of Singapore 

 (MAS) might have had a hand in propping up the Sing dollar on 

 Friday night to keep it steady amid M&A talk and ahead of 

 elections. 

 "We would buy U.S. dollar/Sing dollar at 1.8129-1.8170, 

 stop out at 1.8070, with a target of 1.8350," the Bank of 

 America said in a daily note. 

 Dealers said the market was now focused on a new cabinet 

 lineup. Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, whose People's Action 

 Party enjoys a strong mandate, is expected to announce the new 

 cabinet on November 23. 

 In the money market, flush liquidity and deepening economic 

 gloom has kept short-dated SIBORs low. However, since they have 

 adjusted down quite substantially recently, their downside 

 should be limited from here. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht was trapped in a narrow range of 44.63 to 44.73, 

 with corporate dollar demand countered by dollar offers from 

 exporters. 

     The currency was underpinned by high baht funding costs in 

 the offshore market caused by a recent liquidity squeeze. 

     The one-month forward rate was quoted at 12/17 satang per 

 dollar and the 12-month rate at 140/170 satang. 

     Bank of Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula reiterated 

 on Monday that current interest rates were at appropriate 

 levels, indicating the central bank might not ease policy in 

 case of a further rate reduction by the Fed on Tuesday. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso notched slightly higher in thin trade thanks to a 

 trickle of dollar inflows from local banks. 

 Dealers in Manila said the currency usually enjoys gains 

 ahead of Christmas because Filipino overseas workers remit 

 their earnings home. 

 "If you want to buy dollars, do it at lower levels because 

 the peso should strengthen ahead of Christmas," said a local 

 bank dealer in Manila. 

     Still, they said the country's poor fundamentals continued 

 to nag the peso, limiting the currency's upside. 

     Moreover, the market was keenly watching the Fed's meeting 

 on Tuesday because it feels the Fed's decision may influence 

 whether the Philippine central bank cuts rates. 

     The central bank said earlier in the day better than 

 expected inflation in October, coupled with a Fed rate cut, may 

 give it room to slash its overnight borrowing and lending 

 rates, which now stand at 8.75 percent and 11.0 percent. 

     It will hold its weekly monetary board meeting on Thursday. 


    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won slipped slightly in a thin market with most players



sticking to the sidelines ahead of the FOMC.



    The Bank of Korea was scheduled to have its monthly



monetary board meeting on Thursday, and analysts were divided



as to whether it will cut its overnight call rate. While the



government is eager to boost growth, it is also mindful of



inflation. Still, inflation fell 0.4 percent in October on the



month, giving the central bank some room to ease.



    Foreign equity flows and a stable yen helped the won resist



further falls.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR



    The Taiwan dollar remained true to its recent range of



around 34.52, with already slow market activity moving at an



even more sluggish pace.



    Interest in the Taiwan dollar has dwindled in recent weeks



given the central bank's near daily, and formidable, presence



in the market.



    Balancing the need for a competitive exchange rate and



domestic confidence, the central bank has trained the Taiwan



dollar to stick within a very tight range.



    Even in the offshore non-deliverable forward market,



activity was at best subdued, dealers in Singapore said.

title: UPDATE1-Bank Indonesia says no immediate target for rupiah.
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank said on Monday it would keep intervening in the foreign exchange market to smooth out sharp fluctuations in the rupiah but said it had no immediate target for the brittle currency. 

 Buffeted by a spate of recent poor economic news, the rupiah weakened further on Monday, approaching 11,000 to the dollar, having lost nearly all its gains since the day President Megawati Sukarnoputri took power in late July. 

 Senior deputy bank governor Anwar Nasution said the country's foreign exchange reserves could not be used excessively to support the unit. By 0640 GMT it was being quoted at 10,850/10,900 to the dollar. 

 "(We) will keep doing it (intervention) but cannot use foreign exchange reserves excessively," Nasution told Reuters. 

 When asked if there was any plan to prevent the rupiah from hitting 11,000, Nasution added: "There is no such target. The intervention that we do is aimed at preventing drastic fluctuations. That's it." 

 Nasution said any measure to strengthen the rupiah would not just depend on intervention but also needed government action on economic reforms such as privatisation along with asset sales by the bank restructuring agency (IBRA). 

 "(Investors) are worried about whether we are serious in our privatisation programme and in the sale of IBRA assets," he said. 

 Dealers in Jakarta said problems with the government's privatisation and restructuring plans was dampening sentiment. Not a cent has been raised from privatisation this year. 

 In a blow for that programme, West Sumatra province last week unilaterally took over a unit of state-run Semen Gresik to stop its acquisition by Mexican cement giant Cemex. Cemex is trying to buying a majority stake in Gresik. 

 In addition, the World Bank on Monday expressed disappointment with Jakarta's progress on it latest pact of reforms with the International Monetary Fund. 

Foreign exchange dealers said the rupiah's fall on Monday was also partly due to a Standard & Poor's credit rating downgrade. 

 S&P on Friday cut Indonesia's long term sovereign debt rating to 'CCC' from 'CCC Plus' and also revised down the outlook to negative from stable.

title: Emerging  FX -Weak, but soft dollar caps downside.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies stayed 

 in narrow ranges on Friday though not far from recent lows, 

 aided by a retreating dollar and squaring of long dollar 

 positions ahead of the weekend. 

     That pushed the Singapore dollar off its three-month low 

 and kept the Thai baht off 10-week lows hit on Thursday. 

     The Korean won and the Taiwan dollar continued to benefit 

 from equity-related inflows and dollar sales by exporters for 

 month-end requirements of local currencies. 

     But none of that kept the Indonesian rupiah and the 

 Philippine peso from probing weaker levels. Only the fear of, 

 or actual central bank intervention, capped their downsides. 

     Data from the region showed further economic deterioration. 

 Singapore reported September manufacturing data, Thailand had 

 its trade numbers upto last month and a poll in Korea showed 

 economists expect industrial output to fall. 

 The dollar struggled in early European trade at its lowest 

 for the day against both the yen and the euro amid a 

 lack of fresh impetus to extend recent gains. 

 The dollar had set 2-= month highs against the yen on 

 Thursday and near seven-week highs versus the euro earlier this 

 week, cheered by growing resilience in the U.S. stock markets 

 to a seemingly-unending flow of bad news. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar failed to hold onto its overnight 

 gains, slipping close to levels of around 1.8275 seen late on 

 Thursday. 

 After enjoying a brief respite overnight in New York trade, 

 the Sing dollar found itself once again assailed by U.S. dollar 

 bids at the start of Asian trade. 

 Sentiment towards the Sing dollar was still negative, 

 dealers said, given the city-state's bleak economic 

 fundamentals. 

 Some in the market were convinced there was still further 

 downside for the currency after the Monetary Authority of 

 Singapore's decision to widen its neutral policy band on the 

 trade-weighted Sing dollar. 

 Singapore's economy is open, so the government uses the 

 trade-weighted exchange rate as its main policy tool, and its 

 current neutral stance means it seeks zero appreciation of the 

currency. 

 However, spurred by the struggling economy, the MAS 

 recently decided to widen its trading band, which the market 

 understood as tacit acceptance of a weaker currency. 

     On the macro front, Singapore reported that manufacturing 

 output fell by 22.3 percent in September on the year. 


    PHILIPPINE PESO



    The peso touched a new 11-week low amid a lack of dollar



supply and worries over deteriorating economic fundamentals



with fresh lending data reflecting a drop in borrowing by



manufacturers.



Dealers in Manila said most players were reluctant to take



aggressive positions on fears of central bank intervention.



That reluctance was reflected in a sharp drop of trading



volume, down to only $38 million, versus $100 million on



Thursday.



A central bank statement showed commercial bank lending had



shrunk 0.3 percent in August from a year ago due to a slowdown



in business activity, particularly in manufacturing.



THAI BAHT



The baht loitered in a tight range just shy of lows around



44.90 hit on Thursday supported by fears of central bank

intervention and month-end sale of dollars from exporters.



Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra reinforced those fears



saying the government would aim to boost exports but would also



seek to keep the baht stable.



    He, however, added that the recent weakness of the baht was



in line with other regional currencies.



    The commerce ministry said exports declined 9.95 percent in



September on the year while imports slipped 6.19 percent. For



the years first nine months, exports were down 3.97 percent



while imports rose 4.31 percent.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah found itself in trouble again, falling to 10,300



before the threat of intervention rescued it.



Bank Indonesia said it was intervening in the market to



protect the rupiah after the currency succumbed to mounting



dollar bids.



But dealers were divided whether the bank was in the



market, with some saying they spotted the bank selling dollars



around 10,270/80, and others saying the bank was not in the



market.



The currency has been on a steady downtrend since



mid-August, depressed by the troubled economy and the lack of



inflows. Dealers in Jakarta said the market was distressed over



news the Indonesian government had missed a deadline in selling



a majority stake of state-run cement firm Semen Gresik to



Mexico's Cemex.



KOREAN WON -2



The won squeezed out more gains, helped in large part by



equity-linked dollar inflows from foreign investors.



For the past few weeks, the won has been caught between the



downward force of a weaker yen and upward pressure from foreign



investors' net buying of local stocks.



Foreign investment has overridden a weaker yen for now but



analysts say the won could fall further if the yen continues to



flag against the dollar.



JP Morgan Chase said in a recent note the cross rate



between the yen and won has fallen, which could



cause the concern of the Korean authorities.



The government is believed to be keen on maintaining a



competitive exchange rate given the huge downturn in export



demand. Japan and Korea do compete on a number of key

title: Indonesia 's c.bank says  intervening  to help rupiah.
text:
JAKARTA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank said on Friday it was intervening in the foreign exchange market to help prop up the sagging rupiah currency, which earlier tested 10,300 against the dollar. 

 By 0638 GMT the rupiah was quoted at 10,250/10,270 against the dollar. 

 When asked if the central bank was still intervening, Governor Sjahril Sabirin said: "Yes, we keep doing it." 

 He did not say when the bank intervened or how much was spent. 

 The rupiah has been hit by anti-American sentiment in the world's largest Muslim country following U.S.-led strikes on Afghanistan earlier this month, but strong local corporate dollar demand is also keeping it under pressure.

title: Indonesian Rupiah Ends Up On Alleged Ctrl Bk Dollar Sales
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah recovered its early losses to end slightly up in thin trade Wednesday, due to alleged dollar selling by the central bank toward the session's close. 

 The dollar finished at 9,980 rupiah, down from Tuesday's close of IDR10,010. 

 The U.S. currency hit the day's high of IDR10,088 in early trading. State-owned oil and gas company Pertamina was said to have been buying dollars to finance fuel imports. 

 But Bank Indonesia, the central bank, later stepped in to sell the U.S. unit to push it below the psychologically important level of IDR10,000, dealers said. 

 Bank Indonesia officials couldn't be reached to confirm the rumored intervention. 

 "Bank Indonesia seemed very serious in its efforts to drive the dollar below IDR10,000," said a dealer with a foreign bank. 

 Dealers added that the players were also less jittery about the ongoing anti-U.S. protests in Indonesia as they have been largely kept under control. 

 Police Wednesday fired tear gas to stop Muslim student protesters from entering the parliament complex in Jakarta. They were demanding the government to cut ties with the U.S. following its airstrikes on Afghanistan. 

 Small-scale protests also took place in some Indonesian cities Wednesday, but they were peaceful. 

 Defense Minister Matori Abdul Djalil was quoted by the official Antara news agency as saying that the security forces won't hesitate to take stern action against any violent anti-U.S. protests. 

 Dealers expect the dollar to fall to IDR9,900 Thursday with its upside potential capped at IDR10,100.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Sharply Lower On US Attacks
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The rupiah took a beating in volatile trade Monday on market concerns that the U.S.-led air strike against Afghanistan will provoke violent anti-U.S. protests in Indonesia. 

 The dollar jumped at its open to its intraday high of 10,500 rupiah, a new ten-week high. 

 Profit-taking and alleged Bank Indonesia intervention drove the dollar lower to close at IDR10,163, 3.3% above its IDR9,825 close on Friday. 

 The militant Islamic Defenders Front has repeatedly threatened to attack U.S. citizens and interests in Indonesia if there are military strikes against Afghanistan. 

 The group has also threatened to assassinate U.S. Ambassador Robert Gelbard. 

 However, as of late Monday only around 600 students were reported to have staged a peaceful protest outside Gelbard's residence. They earlier protested outside the U.S. and U.K. embassies. 

 Police deployed dozens of armored vehicles and hundreds of personnel to prevent violent street protests. The U.S. embassy told its citizens living in Indonesia to stay at home in case of violent protests. Other western embassies gave similar advice to their citizens. 

 Investors are worried that the Indonesian government may need to crackdown on unruly radical Muslim groups, which could escalate into wider opposition if such a crackdown turns bloody. 

 "Things will become more complicated if the government mishandles the radical Muslim problem," said a dealer with a foreign bank. 

 The government has urged Indonesians not to overreact to the attacks on Afghanistan. 

 Still, the market is worried that more anti-U.S. protests may take place in coming days and the concern remains that these will turn violent, dealers added. 

 In a move to calm the market, Bank Indonesia Governor Sjahrir Sabirin reiterated Monday that the central bank will continue to sell dollars to defend the rupiah. 

 He said the central bank has sold dollars recently, but he declined say if it had intervened Monday. 

 Dealers said they believed the central bank sold between $10 million and $15 million in the local currency market Monday. 

 Dealers expect the dollar to test IDR10,500 again Tuesday as they expect the anti-U.S. protests to grow.

title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Down Late, Rupiah Leads Fall
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies were lower Monday, with the rupiah diving amid concerns that a series of air strikes against military installations in Afghanistan could spark further anti-U.S. protests in Indonesia, the world's most populous Muslim nation. 

 Elsewhere in the region, the reaction in foreign exchange markets was somewhat subdued, as a holiday in Tokyo sapped volume. Bucking the trend, the New Taiwan dollar and the South Korean won ended slightly higher as local players reduced their positions in the U.S. currency. 

 Thio Chin Loo, a regional currency strategist with BNP Paribas, noted that the dollar performed better Monday than in the immediate aftermath of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks in the U.S. She said this was partly because the U.S. and its allies had been telegraphing the retaliatory strikes for weeks, giving investors a chance to adjust positions. 

 "Prior to the (Sept. 11) event, the market was overall very bullish on the dollar, and post that event, the market has scaled back on their long dollar positions," she said. 

 Late Sunday, U.S. and U.K. forces began a series of bombing assaults on terrorist bases and other military sites in Afghanistan in an effort to destroy the terrorist organization run by Osama bin Laden, who is thought to have masterminded the Sept. 11 attacks. 

 Fears that the conflict could escalate prompted a wave of safe-haven flows into the Swiss franc Monday - and a flight out of currencies seen most vulnerable to heightened tension, such as the rupiah. 

 Highlighting the risks in Jakarta, one hardline group, the Islamic Defenders Front, responded to the bombing raids by publicly threatening to round up and expel U.S. citizens and other foreigners if Indonesia doesn't break diplomatic ties with Washington. 

 "We will destroy American assets and attack the U.S. Embassy," said Al Habib Muhammad Riziq Syihab, who heads the small but vocal anti-U.S. group. 

 At one point Monday, concerns about the potential for instability in Indonesia drove the rupiah down by 6% against the dollar, pushing the U.S. currency above IDR10,500. Intervention by the central bank helped put a floor under the local currency, and the dollar closed at IDR10,160, up from IDR9,830 late Friday. Dealers said they believed Bank Indonesia sold $5 million to stem losses in the local currency. 

 Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom said the volatility in the rupiah was temporary and that the central bank will continue to sell dollars as needed. However, traders pointed out that the central bank has limited reserves to prop up the rupiah. 

 UBS Warburg's foreign exchange strategist for Asia, Mansoor Mohi-uddin, expects the dollar to trade in a range of IDR9,500 to IDR10,500 during the next few days. 

 Elsewhere, the U.S. currency finished higher against the Singapore dollar, rising to S$1.7939 from S$1.7838 late Friday. The dollar rose as high as S$1.7960, a two-month high, before drifting back down. 

 Dealers said a large local bank was among the big dollar buyers - apparently for commercial purposes. Also, a U.S. investment house was reportedly buying Australian dollars and selling Singapore dollars, possibly in anticipation of Singapore Airlines Ltd. (P.SAL) making a bid for Ansett, the failed Australian airline company. 

 In the next few sessions, the U.S. currency will likely be supported at S$1.7880 and face key resistance at S$1.8000, traders said. 

 In the Philippines, the peso closed slightly lower in range-bound trade, with the dollar closing at its intraday high of PHP51.600, compared with PHP51.565 Friday. 

 After the close of trading, the central bank governor, Rafael Buenaventura, denied rumors in the market that the bank had intervened in support of the peso. Buenaventura also expressed hope that the peso wouldn't be hurt by news of several bombings in the southern part of the country early Monday. 

 Members of the extremist Muslim group Abu Sayyaf, which has ties to Osama bin Laden, are suspected of carrying out a series of bombings in three hotels in the province of Zamboanga in southern Philippines, a police official said. 

 Buenaventura downplayed the impact of the domestic attacks on peso sentiment, saying, "The market is taking it in stride." 

 In Bangkok, the dollar was at THB44.800 late Monday, up from THB44.705, buoyed by its gains against other regional currencies. Traders said resistance was pegged at THB44.850. 

 The New Taiwan dollar ended slightly higher at NT$34.557 to the dollar, compared with NT$34.559, in light trade, as many players retreated to the sidelines due to increased uncertainty. 

 In contrast to Indonesia, the Taiwanese central bank had to intervene Monday to prevent the local currency from strengthening too quickly, purchasing around US$100 million in exchange for New Taiwan dollars, traders said. 

 Mohi-uddin from UBS Warburg said the central bank was controlling the market very closely. "If you look at the September foreign exchange numbers - at an all time high in September - it shows how much the central bank has been buying." He added this will likely continue in October. 

 Monetary officials said Monday that Taiwan's foreign exchange reserves rose to a record US$115.20 billion at the end of September from US$114.14 billion in August. 

 Meantime, the South Korean won finished slightly stronger, as the dollar dipped to KRW1,311.6 from KRW1,312.2.

title: Indonesia  Fin Min: Intervention , Rate Hike Won't Help IDR
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesian Finance Minister Boediono said Monday that raising interest rates or intervening in the foreign currency market won't help the rupiah. 

 He said such moves would have little effect in the current circumstances. "The best thing we can do is maintain the domestic situation so it remains cool and calm," he said. 

 "It's something that we have to face as a reality, that raising interest rates or intervention won't be effective to help the rupiah," Boediono told reporters. 

 The dollar rose to an intraday high of IDR10,500 Monday from its close Friday at IDR9,825 on concerns the U.S. military strikes on Afghanistan will spark further anti-U.S. protests in Jakarta. 

 Boediono's comments come after Bank Indonesia's Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom earlier Monday said the central bank will continue to sell dollars cautiously to help the local unit. 

 While raising interest rates is unlikely to help ease the local currrency's slide, rates may still rise as a result of the rupiah's renewed weakness. 

 The weighted average interest rate on one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia notes rose slightly at last week's auction to 17.59% from 17.57% a week earlier. 

 Bank Indonesia had been expected to lower the SBI rate if the dollar didn't rise above IDR10,000. 

 The central bank can't afford to keep interest rates high because higher rates will jack up the costs of recapitalizing local banks.

title: Emerging  FX -Rocked by attacks, c.banks lend a hand.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were cowering 

 late Monday following the U.S.-led strikes in Afghanistan, the 

 first step of what may be a lengthy military response to the 

 September 11 attacks on the World Trade Center and the 

 Pentagon. 

     Among the big losers, the Indonesian rupiah hit 10-week 

 lows while the Singapore dollar was only just behind at a 

 nine-week trough. 

  A few of the currencies avoided steep losses as the threat of 

 official intervention hung over the markets and many players 

 opted for the sidelines until it became clearer how long the 

 conflict will last. 

     The news on that front left little hope for a quick 

 resolution, with U.S. Defence Secretary Donald Rumsfeld warning 

 there was no magic bullet in the operation, called 'Enduring 

 Freedom' and the U.S. government's arch-enemy, Osama bin Laden, 

 vowing no peace for America. 

     Among the regional currencies, the Indonesian rupiah 

 suffered the most as local banks and corporates rushed to buy 

 dollars amid growing fears that Muslim extremists would act on 

 their threats to expel foreigners in Indonesia. 

     The rupiah's troubles also dogged the Singapore dollar as 

 the city-state is viewed as being vulnerable to unrest in 

 Indonesia given its physical proximity. The Sing dollar also 

 has the misfortune of being a proxy for other Southeast Asian 

currencies as its market is the most liquid in the region. 


    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah shed over a 1,000 rupiah to the dollar at one



stage to lows around 10,550 as local players rushed to buy



dollars amid growing fears that Muslim radicals will carry out



their threat to drive out foreigners.



    Since the September 11 attacks, a small but strident



minority of Muslim extremists have threatened to kick out



foreigners if the U.S. struck Afghanistan.



    With the U.S.-led military operation now underway, the



market was skittish that these fringe groups may act, providing



another excuse for foreign investors to avoid Indonesia.



    Dealers in Jakarta said the scramble for dollars



steamrolled over Bank Indonesia's attempts to break the



rupiah's fall. The bank was spotted selling $2-3 million around



10,300/350. Later, the rupiah was pulled off its lows thanks to



profit-taking on the dollar, which had risen by as much as six



percent during the day.



    Bank Indonesia vowed to protect the rupiah, saying it would


intervene in the market. But the bank's governor added it did



not have immediate plans to hike interest rates, which are



already at two-year highs.



    The country's Finance Minister said intervention and higher



interest rates were unlikely to help, and stressed the need to



maintain domestic stability.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Singapore dollar stumbled to a near nine-week low of



1.7965 as the troubles in Indonesia rattled investors.



    The main cause for alarm was fears that any unrest in



Indonesia following the U.S. military strikes in Afghanistan



could spill over into Singapore. Dealers said commercial demand



for dollars also drove the Sing dollar down, with stop-loss



dollar buy orders triggered when it skidded past the 1.79 mark.



    Others, however, said the dollar's run against the Sing was



an overreaction as Singapore, a small city-state, is not an



obvious target even though it is surrounded by predominantly



Muslim countries.



    "It's really not too clever to buy dollar/Sing right now



because if you step back you would realise how expensive it



is," said a U.S. bank dealer.



    Indeed, charts showed the dollar/Sing was in overbought



territory, suggesting there was room for the dollar to correct



in the next few sessions. By late Monday, it had a 14-day



relative strength index reading of around 85.



    THAI BAHT



    The baht weakened against the dollar as U.S. names and



other onshore players were heard building long dollar positions



in the absence of fundamentals that argue for a stronger local


currency.



    Dealers said the weaker baht was likely to reduce the



chances of the central bank cutting interest rates. Bank of



Thailand Governor Pridiyathorn Devakula said on Monday he saw



no need for Thailand to cut rates.



    "No need to cut rates because Libor (the one-month London



interbank offered rate) is still higher than 2.5 percent. There



is no point of cutting rates," he said.



    Libor is a benchmark rate for the eurodollar and currently



stands at about 2.56 percent. Thailand's benchmark 14-day repo



rate currently stands at 2.5 percent.



    The Thai government has expressed concerns that lower rates



could trigger capital outflows and destabilise the currency and



the economy.



    KOREAN WON         -2



    The won piggybacked on a firmer yen and rose a notch to



1,311.6 from Friday's close of 1,312.2.



    Trading was light and orderly, with players showing little



reaction to the U.S.-led military operations in Afghanistan.



    Dealers also said players were probably on their best



behaviour after the government said before the market's open it



would intervene if it spotted volatility in the exchange rate.



    PHILIPPINE PESO



    The peso trailed lower after the other regional currencies,



though the central bank kept it from falling past 51.60.



    Dealers in Manila said the bank offered around $5-10



million when the currency slipped to 51.60 - a level where



most in the market expected intervention. With turnover of only



$48 million, the bank was able to stave off further losses for



the peso.



The peso was also aided by the fact that corporate dollar



demand was muted, partly because many local corporates had



already hedged their dollar needs. Dealers added the U.S.-led



strike was long expected.



Sentiment towards the peso, however, continued to sag given



the country's dismal economic outlook and expectations of a



U.S. recession.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar closed at 34.557, little moved from



Friday's close of 34.559 as players barely blinked at events on



the global and domestic fronts.



"Volumes are pitiful. My feeling is that the market has



already digested the bad news from home, and are just happy



sitting on their dollar longs," said a European bank forwards



dealer in Singapore.



The Ministry of Finance said the island's exports fell by a



massive 42.5 percent in September from the same period a year



ago, against expectations of a 36.8 percent fall. Imports also



suffered, dropping by 40.4 percent year-on-year.



The ministry added exports were unlikly to post growth



until the third quarter of 2002. Taiwan's economy has been



badly hit by the electronics downturn and a powerful typhoon.

title: Asia Markets -  Currencies , stocks easier on air strikes.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Asian currencies and stocks 

 eased on Monday following the overnight air strikes against 

 Afghanistan by the United States and Britain in retaliation for 

 the September 11 attacks on New York and Washington. 

     The bombing and missile strikes, which may mark the 

 begining of a long military campaign, were well-anticipated but 

 still raised concerns over economic and political implications 

 and fallout. 

     The markets slipped amid those concerns but as the strikes 

 lacked a shock element and Tokyo was closed for a national 

 holiday, the downside was limited. 

     "The fact that the military response has started was not a 

 major surprise and then Tokyo is out....the markets are much 

 quieter," said David Simmonds, Salmon Smith Barney's regional 

currency strategist. 

     The yen traded in a narrow range around the 120 mark as 

 players marked the dollar down, reflecting their reluctance to 

 take positions amid the uncertainty. 

     Major Asian equity markets dipped with Hong Kong's Heng 

 Seng down 2.7 percent by midday, Seoul's KOSPI ending off 1.15 

 percent and Taiwan's TAIEX down 1.82 percent. 

     AUTHORITIES ON ALERT 

     Even more cautious than the market players were the 

 region's central banks, some of whom announced their intention 

 to step into the market to quell any panic. 

     The Bank of Korea was the first to issue a warning it would 

intervene to stem excessive volatility in the currency  market. 

 Taiwan's cabinet pledged support to its stock market through 

 its stabilisation funds. 

     But while the North Asian central banks were more concerned 

 about the economic implications, analysts said authorities in 

 Indonesia and the Philippines may be more concerned about the 

 political fall out of the U.S.-led operation "Enduring 

 Freedom". 

     The Indonesian rupiah fell through the 10,000 mark to a 

 10-week low of 10,550 as radical Islamic groups in Jakarta 

 threatened to hunt foreigners and destroy foreign targets. 

     Bank Indonesia said it planned to intervene in the foreign 

 exchange market but would avoid hiking interest rates to prop 

 up the rupiah. 

     Dealers in Jakarta earlier said Bank Indonesia sold around 

 $2-3 million through brokers at the 10,300/10,350 level. 

     VULNERABLE CURRENCIES

     Analysts said similar worries would dominate trade in the 

 Philippines. The peso fell just shy of the 51.60 per dollar 

 level where the central bank was expected to intervene. 

Currency vulnerability for both Indonesia and Philippines 

 will make the much-needed lowering of key interest rates 

 difficult. 

     The Philippines had cut its key overnight rate by 25 

 basis-points only last week hoping for inflationary pressure to 

 ease and the peso to stabilise around 50-51 range by the end of 

 the year. 

 The key overnight borrowing rate now stands at 8.75 percent 

 and lending rate at 11 percent.

title: UPDATE 1-Indonesian  central bank  says to prop up rupiah.
text:
JAKARTA, Oct 8 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank said on Monday it planned to intervene in the foreign exchange market to defend the ailing rupiah, which hit a 10-week low of 10,550 per dollar in early trade over fears of rising anti-U.S. sentiment. 

 Radical Islamic groups in Indonesia have threatened to expel foreigners and destroy foreign targets following American-led attacks against Afghanistan which began on Sunday, and any unrest could unsettle foreign investors and weaken markets. 

 "We'll try with intervention... hopefully this will work," central bank governor Sjahril Sabirin told reporters, adding the currency's fall was temporary. 

 By 0455 GMT the rupiah was quoted at 10,200/10,250 against the dollar. 

 Dealers in Jakarta earlier said Bank Indonesia sold around $2-3 million through brokers at the 10,300/10,350 level. 

 Sabirin also said the Bank had no immediate plans to hike interest rates beyond their more than two-year highs to help defend the currency. 

 But Indonesia's Finance Minister Boediono said intervention would not help the beleaguered rupiah, trailing the 2001 state budget target of 9,600. 

 "...interest rate hikes and intervention won't work - the best (for the rupiah) is to maintain domestic conditions and to stay calm," Boediono told reporters. 

 "If the war is over the rupiah will strengthen," he added. 

 Jakarta stocks were also hit by market jitters that the attacks against Afghanistan could spark violence in the world's largest Muslim country. 

 By 0455 GMT GMT the benchmark composite index was down 3.57 percent at 367.78 after earlier falling five percent.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Higher;Corporate Dlr Demand Fizzles
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah ended higher Thursday as market participants unwound long dollar positions after the U.S. currency failed to sustain gains above the 9,900 rupiah level, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 9,738 rupiah, down from its close at IDR9,915 Wednesday. 

 The dollar fell below IDR9,900 in early morning trade and, although it briefly recovered to touch that level midday, failed to sustain its gains as fears of intervention by Bank Indonesia pushed the U.S. unit lower, dealers said. 

 But by Thursday dollar demand from local companies evaporated whenever the dollar rose past IDR9,850, dealers said. 

 "We reversed our positions as dollar demand fizzled above IDR9,850," said a dealer with a foreign bank. 

 Bank Indonesia has repeatedly said it will intervene to help the rupiah, although hasn't provided a target level for the local unit. 

 The rupiah had weakened beyond the psychologically important IDR10,000 level Tuesday to hit a three-month low against the dollar, although it regained some ground Wednesday on suspected central bank intervention. 

 A dealer with a state-owned bank said market participants saw the interest rate differential as another reason to unload dollars. "It's really costly to maintain long positions in the dollar with the (one-month) rupiah interest rate at around 17.8%, compared to the dollar interest rate at 2.5%," he said. 

 News that the International Monetary Fund doesn't object to the government's plan to sell a 51% stake in PT Bank Central Asia in tranches further helped dissipate bearish sentiment on the rupiah. 

 The Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency said Tuesday that it would sell a 30% stake in BCA before year-end, while the remaining 21% will be sold later. Analysts said that appeared to break a key agreement with the IMF to sell the entire 51% stake before the end of 2001. 

 However the IMF's senior representative in Indonesia, David Nellor, told Dow Jones Newswires: "at this stage they (the Indonesian government) have the discretion to sell 51% and will make a judgment at the appropriate time on commercial considerations, and what's best for the country." 

 Still, dealers said the rupiah is susceptible to weakness if bad news catches the market by surprise. 

 They expect the dollar to trade between IDR9,675 and IDR9,850 Friday.

title: Emerging  FX  - Get by with a little help from yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 4 (Reuters) - Asian currencies stood their 

 ground against the dollar late on Thursday, backed up by the 

 steady yen and, in some cases, their central banks. 

     The market, however, was increasingly divided as to whether 

 the regionals were going to suffer another bout of weakness or 

 manage to hold onto their newfound stability. 

     One group notes that risk aversion after the September 11 

 attacks struck the dollar and boosted the yen, which helped 

 most regionals, and this aversion could easily return depending 

 on how the U.S. chooses to retaliate. 

     They add the region's still healthy current account 

 surpluses should save the currencies from further falls. 

     Others who argue that the Asian currencies will head south 

 point towards the region's shaky growth outlook. They say risk 

 aversion, ultimately, would send investors packing out of Asia, 

 which is not good news in a region parched of foreign inflows. 

 "Emerging Asian FX should get some support from their 

 current account surpluses and the relatively stronger yen. 

 Beyond these assumptions, however, we believe risk aversion 

 will have other, even greater negative implications for 

 regional FX in the months ahead," said JP Morgan Chase in a 

 recent report. 

 Whatever the forex scenario, regional central banks are 

 showing a willingness to ease monetary policy to help cushion 

 their economies. The Philippines central bank joined the ranks 

 of Hong Kong and Taiwan on Thursday when it cut rates by a 

 quarter percentage point. 

 INDONESIAN RUPIAH 

 The rupiah crawled back to the right side of 9,700 as talk 

 of Bank Indonesia intervention sparked rounds of dollar 

 unwinding from corporates and interbank players. 

     The central bank was heard selling up to $50 million to 

 drag the local currency back from 9,900. 

     The rupiah was also supported by news that Indonesian Bank 

 Restructuring Agency (IBRA) would stick with its plan to sell 

 51 percent of the country's largest retail bank, Bank Central 

 Asia. 

 On the investment front, foreign investment approvals in 

 Indonesia from January to August fell to $5.75 billion from 

 $7.25 billion in the same period last year, according to data 

 from the Investment Coordinating Board. 

 Investors have reduced their Indonesian exposure since the 

 country plunged into political and economic turmoil in the late 

 1990s and have remained wary ever since. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar hovered near the day's trough around 1.7790 

 as the market remained concerned over the country's economic 

 outlook. 

 Economists polled by Reuters expected Singapore's economy 

 to contract 1.7 percent this year compared with 3.6 percent 

 growth they saw in a June survey. 

 The market is focused on preliminary numbers for third 

 quarter GDP expected on October 7. The market widely 

 anticipates an official downward revision of the forecast. 

 Charts show 1.7842 is a tough barrier for the U.S. 

 dollar/Sing dollar for now as it represents the 50 percent 

 retracement of the July 16-September 17 U.S. dollar downmove. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won was down but off early lows of 1,316 rescued by 

 export-related dollar inflows. Gains in local stock market also 

 helped cap the downside. 

 Dealers in Singapore said offshore players led the dollar 

 buying in both the spot and non-deliverable forward markets 

 after the three-day Chusok holidays. 

 They reported speculation the central bank, if it decided 

 not to follow others in the region by cutting interest rates, 

 may allow a weaker currency instead. 

 The central bank's monetary policy board held a meeting 

 early Thursday but a spokesman said any decision on further 

 rate cuts was unlikely until next week. 

 The short-term call rate is now at a record low of 4.00 

 percent after a 50 basis point cut in September, the fourth cut 

 this year. 

 PHILIPPINE PESO 

 The peso was off its session low of 51.61 helped by talk 

 the central bank had intervention in aid of the currency after 

 its monetary board decided to cut key overnight rates by 25 

 basis points. 

     Effective Friday the overnight borrowing rate would be 

 lowered to 8.75 percent and lending to 11 percent. 

     Dealers in Manila said they believed the central bank sold 

 dollars in both the non-deliverable and spot markets through 

 two foreign banks. 

     Others said subdued volume of $98.70 million suggested the 

central bank was not behind the move. The total turnover on 

 Wednesday was $95.60 million. 

     Keeping the upside limited was August export data that 

 showed a decline of 25.73 percent from August last year. The 

 decline was the sharpest drop in 21 years. 

     THAI BAHT 

     The baht lingered around 44.60 weighed down by dollar 

 demand from local corporates and oil companies, after dollar 

 sales by Singapore and Hong Kong names helped it off a low of 

 44.67. 

 Singapore dealers said uncertainty over the central bank's 

 interest rate policy was also prompting offshore players to 

 square out of their long dollar positions. 

 The government has repeatedly said it would not cut the 

 benchmark 2.5 percent 14-day repo rate but players believe 

 that, with most regional central banks following in the steps 

 of the Fed, the Bank of Thailand may yet succumb to the siren 

 call. 

 TAIWAN DOLLAR 

 The Taiwan dollar stayed in its comfort zone just above 

 34.60 despite another rate cut from the central bank. 

 However, Singapore dealers said trading in the 

 non-deliverable forward market was active, with dollar-buying 

 particularly strong in the one-month tenor. 

 They said the market was betting that the island's powerful 

central bank would soon let its currency weaken, at least 

 towards 35. 

     The one-month forward was quoted at 0.105/.125 in late 

 trade compared to 0.085/0.095 earlier in the day. 

     The central bank cut its key rates by 0.25 percentage 

 point. It also slashed its reserve requirement ratios to five 

 percent from 6.22 percent and its reserve requirement ratio on 

foreign exchange reserves to five percent from 10 percent. 

 All the moves were aimed at boosting the local economy, 

 which the government expects to contract by 0.37 percent this 

 year - Taiwan's first ever full-year contraction. 

 "They're basically saying they want banks to hold onto U.S. 

 dollars. So there's really no other direction for the Taiwan 

currency but down," said a U.S. bank dealer.

title: Emerging  FX  - Firm as dollar wilts against yen.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 4 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies took 

 heart early on Thursday as the yen resisted the dollar's 

 advances despite suprisingly upbeat U.S. services data. 

     While the Singapore dollar and Thai baht trotted after the 

 yen, vigilant central banks in Indonesian and the Philippines 

 were also keeping dollar bulls at bay. 

     Still, dealers said little has changed in sentiment towards 

 the rupiah and peso, which are expected to slowly sink under 

 the weight of sober economic outlooks for those countries. 

     Curiously, the currencies usually closely tied to the yen 

 -- the North Asians -- were coming under attack as players 

 focused on their domestic economic fundamentals. 

     The National Association of Purchasing Management's index 

 of U.S. non-manufacturing activity rose to 50.2 in September 

 from August's 45.5. Wall Street used that bit of news, hopes 

 for a huge stimulus package and a solid earnings outlook from 

 technology heavyweight Cisco to muster a rally. 

 Still, players in the foreign exchange market were less 

 sanguine, with many suspecting the services data may not fully 

 reflect the damage done by the September 11 attacks. 

     The dollar touched a high of around 121.48 yen in overnight 

 trade, before profit-takers chased it below the 121 level. 

     Dealers said with players continuing to book profits from 

 the dollar's two-week rise, most Asian currencies should enjoy 

 a temporary respite before the region's shaky fundamentals come 

 into view again. 

 With that in mind, more and more Asian central banks have 

 hopped on the rate-cutting bandwagon, with Taiwan's bank 

 cutting interest rates by a quarter percentage point Wednesday. 

 The Philippine central bank will meet later in the day and says 

 a rate cut is up for discussion. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Sing dollar hovered in a 1.7733-1.7776 range, with a 

 steadier yen providing some support. 

 Charts show 1.7842 is a tough barrier for the U.S. 

 dollar/Sing dollar for now as it represents the 50 percent 

 retracement of the July 16-September 17 U.S. dollar downmove. 

 The market is focused on preliminary figures for third 

 quarter GDP expected on October 7. The market widely expects an 

 official downward revision of the forecast. 

 Some analyst reckoned this might provide a good opportunity 

 for the central bank to shift policy to a loosening bias, so 

 implying a weaker Sing$. 

 THAI BAHT 

 Dollar profit-taking from both offshore and onshore parties 

 helped lift the baht from its overnight trough of 44.82. 

 "The dollar/yen direction remains the key factor. Once the 

 yen rebounded against the dollar, players also pared their long 

 dollar/baht positions," said a dealer in Bangkok. 

 Another dealer said 44.82 was still a good support for the 

 baht. Charts show a dollar break above that level will complete 

 a double bottom and could lead the dollar/baht much higher. 

     The tom/next rate was quoted at -0.5/-0.3 satang per dollar 

 offshore and -0.10/-0.04 satang onshore. 


     INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah held above 9,900 as those with exceedingly long



positions unwound the dollar after rumours that Bank Indonesia

intervened on Wednesday.



    "The stop was triggered at 9,950 yesterday and players are



wary of the central bank. Also, the fact that the market is



still very long of dollars underpins the rupiah," said a dealer



at a European bank in Jakarta.



But the upside for the rupiah should be capped by lingering



fears of escalation in anti-U.S. protests and concerns over



possible damage to foreign investor perception of the country's



judiciary after the acquittal of Tommy Suharto.



KOREAN WON -2



The won was knocked past Friday's closing level of 1,309.6



as markets re-opened in Seoul.



Singapore dealers said dollar buying interest in the



non-deliverable forward market spilled into the spot market.



One-month won NDFs rose to as high as 1,320/22 to the dollar



before easing to current levels around 1,316/18.



However, the currency's losses were capped by early gains



in the local stock market. The benchmark Korean Composite Stock



Price Index was up by over three percent, taking its cue from



the Nasdaq's overnight rise.



The Bank of Korea said its monetary policy board would meet



later in the day, but that a decision on rates would likely



come next week. Many analysts believe the central bank will



lower its short term call rate, which now stands at 4.00



percent, following the Federal Reserve's latest easing.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar slipped in early active trade to around



34.585 following the central bank's decision to slash rates



late on Wednesday.



Singapore dealers said the market was abuzz as to whether



the bank was going to match the latest rate cut with a



tolerance for a weaker exchange rate. The Taiwan central bank


has been actively intervening in the market to defend the local



dollar.



    But it has been known to drop its defence in the past to



help the island maintain its export competitiveness.



    Dollar-buying interest was the strongest in the one-month



non-deliverable forward, which was quoted at 0.085/0.095.



Dealers said offshore players were banking on the local


currency hitting 35 to the dollar soon.



The central bank lowered rates by a quarter percentage



point on Wednesday, stepping up its easing campaign as Taiwan



braces for an expected full-year contraction for 2001 - its



first ever.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso moved languidly around 51.57 as the market puzzled



over the central bank's next act.



Dealers in Manila said the central bank had been actively


intervening in the market to defend the frail peso, making most



players wary of being caught too long on dollar.



The market was also paying close attention to the bank's



monetary board meeting, scheduled for later in the day. Though



the bank has kept rates steady for months, many in the market



have been wondering if the latest Fed cut may inspire the bank



to also ease its key overnight rates.



With one government official predicting a rate cut, the


central bank has remained coy as to which way it might swing at



this week's meeting. The Philippine central bank governor has



said a rate cut may be up for discussion, but that the board



has to consider inflation and the exchange rate. CURRENCIES VS

title: Indonesia  Rupiah Ends Up;Ctrl Bank  Intervention  Suspected
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah ended higher Wednesday on what dealers suspect was intervention by Bank Indonesia in a market that was already long in dollars. 

 The dollar closed at 9,915 rupiah, down from its close Tuesday at IDR10,025. 

 Dealers believe that Bank Indonesia persistently sold the dollar above IDR10,000 to help the local unit, although Bank Indonesia wouldn't confirm any intervention in the market. 

 However, Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom said Wednesday that the central bank would keep intervening in the market to help the local unit. 

 The market was skeptical about the threat as Bank Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves aren't considered substantial. Its gross foreign exchange reserves amounted to $28.96 billion as of Sept. 28, down $44.5 million from a week earlier. 

 Gultom also said Bank Indonesia has enough foreign exchange reserves to defend the rupiah. 

 Dealers estimated that the central bank sold around $30 million Wednesday. Dealers also believe that the central bank sold that amount Tuesday. 

 Despite the rupiah's gains, a dealer with a foreign bank said "underlying sentiment is still bullish on the dollar." 

 He said the market is still concerned that there will be anti-U.S. protests in Jakarta if the U.S. attacks targets in Afghanistan to retaliate against the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks. 

 The U.S. State Department has warned U.S. citizens not to travel to Indonesia and has pulled nonessential embassy personnel out of the country. 

 The rupiah's recent weakness prompted Bank Indonesia to raise the weighted average rate on its one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia notes to 17.59% in a weekly auction late Wednesday, from 17.57% last week. 

 Dealers, however, said the rate hike won't significantly help sentiment towards the rupiah as the market is preoccupied with the possibility of domestic unrest. 

 They expect the dollar to trade between IDR9,850 and IDR10,050 Thursday.

title: Bk Indonesia Says Foreign Reserves Enough To Aid Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia said Wednesday that it has sufficient foreign reserves to support the rupiah, which sank to three-month lows against the U.S. dollar Tuesday. 

 "We have enough dollars to sell in order to make the market calm," Bank Indonesia deputy governor Miranda Gultom told reporters. 

 Indonesia's foreign reserves as of Sept. 28 stood at $28.966 billion, which analysts say will likely be inadequate to defend the rupiah in the longer term given huge foreign debt repayment needs. 

 The central bank's governor, Sjahril Sabirin, also repeated Bank Indonesia's regular stance that it is ready to intervene in the foreign exchange market to help the local currency. 

 The rupiah ended at a three-month low of IDR10,025 per dollar Tuesday as the Supreme Court's decision to acquit Tutomo "Tommy" Mandala Putra, the son of former dictator Suharto, of fraud hurt sentiment. The rupiah was also hammered by rising anti-U.S. protests in Indonesia. 

 The dollar was trading around IDR10,003 early Wednesday. 

 Bank Indonesia sold more than $30 million in the market Tuesday, but this failed to help the rupiah because demand for dollars was too strong, traders said. 

 -By Farida Husna, Dow Jones Newswires; 62 21 3983 1277; farida.husna@dowjones.com

title: Emerging  FX -Yen dampens spirits in thin holiday trade.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 1 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were on the 

 defensive early on Monday as the yen stumbled a bit after the 

 release of a dismal Japanese corporate sentiment survey. 

     Trading in the region was light as markets in Hong Kong, 

 Taipei, and Seoul were closed for public holidays, which may 

 help regionals stand their ground as trading interest was 

 modest. 

 The Bank of Japan's (BOJ) 'tankan' quarterly survey for 

 September showed sentiment from large manufacturers soured from 

 June, with the big manufacturers' diffusion index coming in at 

 minus 33 against minus 16 in June. 

 Still, the market did expect the grim news and was paying 

 more attention as to whether the BOJ would stop intervening now 

 that half-year bookclosing was over in Japan. 

 First impressiones were that it would continue to sell yen 

 when needed with Senior Japanese Finance Minsitry official 

 Zembei Mizoguchi saying on Monday the ministry would intervene

 in the foreign exchange market at appropriate times. 

 With recession looming over the region's biggest trading 

 partner, the United States, and its largest economy, Japan, 

 analysts say Asian countries were bracing for a protracted 

 slowdown, if not worse. 

 Looking ahead, the Federal Reserve's policy-setting 

 committee will meet on Tuesday, and is widely expected to cut 

 rates to help steady badly shaken sentiment. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar was dragged lower by the yen and the 

 city-state's own troubled economic outlook to hover aorund 

 1.7660. 

 Dealers said players were looking to stack up their long 

 U.S. dollar positions as the yen was seen as weakening past 120 

 again. Even more timid players were seeking to buy U.S. dollar 

 on dips. 

 Singapore will issue a revised 2001 gross domestic product 

 forecast on Sunday. The market has been chattering as to 

 whether the government will also shift its monetary policy 

 stance to loose from neutral because the economy, which is 

 already in a recession, is expected to see tougher times. 

     Still, the U.S. dollar could run aground at 1.7700, where 

 profit-taking was expected to emerge. 


    THAI BAHT



    The baht hovered near 44.50 in sympathy with a weaker yen,



with activity subdued ahead of the Fed meeting on Tuesday.



    But analysts say it is unlikely the Bank of Thailand will



cut its already very low benchmark rate in the near-term even



if the Fed cuts as expected.



    The market shrugged aside better than expected trade data



released on Friday as it is more focused on the ramifications



of the September 11 attacks on the Thai economy.



    The Commerce Ministry is expected to release September



consumer prices later in the day.



       INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah was weighed by corporate dollar demand and



concerns over potential violence caused by anti-U.S.



protesters.



    Hardline groups in Indonesia have warned of a jihad, or



holy war, if Afghanistan is hit while some have signed up to



fight for Afghanistan.



    Although the size of the anti-U.S. rallies have been pretty



small, some investors have taken such developments seriously,



dealers in Jakarta said.



    But fears of intervention by Bank Indonesia, which was



rumoured to have been in the market on Friday, should help



limit losses, dealers said.



    Charts show the dollar/rupiah is still trapped in the



uptrend channel dating back to August 14, indicating further



gains are likely for the U.S. currency.



    TAIWAN DOLLAR



    The Taiwan dollar barely moved in offshore trade as Taipei



markets were closed for the Mid Autumn Festival. They will



re-open on Tuesday.



    Singapore dealers said there was little trading interest in



the non-deliverable forward market. But they added the Taiwan



dollar was likely to be hurt by the yen's losses and the



island's economic malaise.



KOREAN WON -2



The won was barely traded in the offshore non-deliverable



forward market due to a long holiday onshore.



    Korea's financial markets are closed October 1-3 for the



Chusok or thanksgiving holiday.



    They will resume trading on Thursday.



    PHILIPPINE PESO



    The peso is expected to be kept in its recent range, with



51.40 seen as a good support. It opened at 51.35 compared with



51.32 at the close on Friday.



    The central bank said on Sunday it expected dollar



remittances from overseas workers to reach $5.5 to 6 billion



this year, around the same level as a year ago.



    Remittances from an estimated seven million Filipinos



living or working aboard contribute a vital chunk of the



country's gross national product.



    Meanwhile, the country's external debt rose to $50.89



billion at the end of June, up 1.9 percent from $49.94 billion



at the end of the first quarter. CURRENCIES VS U.S. DOLLAR

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Lower As Japanese Cos Buy Dollars
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah closed lower Wednesday as locally based Japanese companies bought dollars to finance imports, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 9,630 rupiah, up from IDR9,510 at the close Tuesday. 

 "We saw many Japanese companies buying dollars Wednesday to finance their imports," said a dealer with a foreign bank in Jakarta. 

 Dealers said the market was also nervous about a call by Indonesian Islamic groups for a holy war against the U.S. should it attack Afghanistan. 

 Dealers expect the dollar to trade between IDR9,575 and IDR9,675 Thursday if Bank Indonesia doesn't intervene to support the local currency. 

 Separately, the weighted average rate on one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia notes fell to 17.57% at Wednesday's weekly auction from 17.66% last week. 

 The drop in the rate - the first in several months - followed a fall in Indonesia's base money supply, which includes currency in circulation and banks' reserves with Bank Indonesia, to IDR110.91 trillion as of Sept. 21. 

 The central bank's target for the base money supply is IDR110.5 trillion. Dealers said they believed the benchmark interest rate fell because it's now unlikely that the central bank will try to drain more liquidity from the market.

title: Emerging  FX -Ride yen's coat tails, retaliation feared.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were choppy 

 on Friday with trade dominated by action in the yen 

 where the Bank of Japan intervened repeatedly to sell the 

currency. 

     Finance Minister Masajuro Shiokawa confirmed the Bank of 

 Japan had intervened, the third day this week the bank has 

 acted to curb the yen's appreciation. 

     The yen had hit 7-month highs on the dollar around 115.85 

 late Thursday following steep losses on Wall Street and 

 mounting concerns that last week's assault on the U.S. would 

 push the global economy into recession. 

     President George W. Bush's defiant speech to Congress on 

 Friday also fanned fears that the war against terrorism could 

 be a lengthy one, deepening uncertainties over global markets. 

     Analysts said the stronger yen and current account 

 surpluses in Asia should continue to support regional 

currencies in the short run, although rising risk aversion 

 would eventually have negative implications for offshore 

 investment in the region. 

     Trading was subdued as investors were reluctant to take new 

 positions aggressively ahead of a fresh batch of data to be 

 released by the U.S. and the region next week. 

     U.S. consumer confidence data, a key leading indicator of 

 economic growth, are out on Tuesday. 


    SINGAPORE DOLLAR



    The Sing dollar was lower at 1.7420 as gains from U.S.



dollar sales by a large U.S. name was erased by U.S. dollar



buying from a few local banks.



    Dealers said the Monetary Authority of Singapore was



unlikely to be behind the dollar purchases as the Sing dollar



at the current level was not out of sync with other regional


currencies.



Despite the currency's recent gains, JP Morgan Chase



continued to suggest that clients short the Sing dollar in



one-month forwards against the basket or the euro.



It said the Sing dollar had scope to drop to 1.7800 by the



end of October as Singapore's rapidly slowing economy could



prompt the MAS to guide it lower.



THAI BAHT



The baht drifted in a tight range of 44.14-44.25 as the



market lacked the resolve to push it out of this band.



"The market is rangebound. Players looked to buy the dollar



on dips toward 44.10, but a drop below 44.25 was met promptly



by profit-taking," said a Bangkok dealer.



On the domestic front, there was no shortage of bad news.



Finance Minister Somkid Jatusripitak said on Friday the



government would announce a revised 2002 gross domestic product



forecast early next week.



The Bangkok Post newspaper quoted Somkid as saying GDP in



2002 might be cut by one or two percentage points from the



current target of four to six percent growth.



INDONESIAN RUPIAH



The rupiah tracked the regionals higher as those who



overbought the U.S. dollar squared positions ahead of the



weekend.



Fears of intervention from the central bank, which has been



actively in the market lately, also gave the local currency


some support, dealers said.



In the money market, Bank Indonesia kept its intervention


rates unchanged at 15.125 percent for the overnight rate and



15.875 percent for the 7-day rate.



    The intervention rates are among the central bank's tools



to affect liquidity in the market.



    PHILIPPINE PESO

standstill, with a mere $19.50 million transacted compared with



average normal daily turnover of $80-100 million.



    The currency was trapped in a narrow 51.29-51.40 range.



    Dealers in Manila said the market was pretty squarish and



players were reluctant to take fresh positions amid fears the



U.S. might strike back as early as this weekend.

dollar purchases from importers and local stock sales by



foreign equity investors.



    Foreign investors sold a net of 50.3 billion won worth of



local shares on Friday, extending their net selling to five



days.



    But the won's downside in the near-term is likely to be



limited by seasonal dollar sales by exporters toward the end of



the month, dealers said.

title: Emerging  FX -Jolted by BOJ, Bush speech digested.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Asian currencies see-saw 

 once again as the yen first rises only to fall in the face of 

 apparent intervention from the Bank of Japan. 

     Yen had hit 7-month highs on the dollar around 115.85 

 following steep losses on Wall Street and mounting concerns 

 that the September 11 assault on the U.S. would push the global 

 economy into recession. 

 But the yen - tracked closely by regional currencies - pared 

 gains in early trade due to fears of potential BOJ 

intervention. And they did not have long to wait with the 

 dollar jumping to 116.87 yen on what dealers assumed was BOJ 

 buying. 

 If so this would be the third session this week that the 

 Jaspanese have intervened to try and limit the yen's gains, 

 though with limited success given the dollar started the week 

 around 118.00. 

 Activity was subdued overall in Asia as players watched 

 President George W. Bush giving a keynote speech to a joint 

 session of Congress, hoping for clues on what the U.S. will do 

 to punish the perpetrators. 

 Many also opted to take a wait-and-see stance ahead of a 

 fresh batch of data to be released by the U.S. and the region 

 next week. 

 U.S. consumer confidence data - a key leading indicator of 

 economic growth - are out on Tuesday. This will be the first 

 survey after the aerial attacks on the U.S. 

 The Bank of Thailand will release its key monthly economic 

 data including trade, balance of payment and industrial output 

 on September 28. 

 SINGAPORE DOLLAR 

 The Singapore dollar was trapped in a tight range early, 

 having rallied to 1.7375 from intraday low of around 1.7460 per 

 dollar hit the previous day. 

 But the Sing was barely changed compared to levels seen 

 late on Thursday when heavy U.S. dollar sales by at least one 

 U.S. name lifted the local currency of its lows. 

 One dealer from a European bank said the market was still 

 intent on offloading U.S. dollars, with the main market focus 

 centred on movements in dollar/yen. 

 But dealers expected potential gains on the Sing dollar to 

 be limited given the BOJ intervention and the possibility the 

Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) might enter the market to 

 limit volatility. 

 There has been talk that the MAS may have made efforts to 

 guide the Sing lower this week following credit easing by many 

 central banks in response to last week's attacks on the United 

 States. 

 The Sing dollar, believed to have been trading at the 

 extreme strong end of its supposed trading range of late, is 

 one of Singapore's main monetary policy tools. 

 KOREAN WON -2 

 The won came off overnight highs around 1,288 to stand at 

 1,295 in line with the yen with the upside was seen limited by 

 declines in domestic stocks. 

 By 0106 GMT, the benchmark KOSPI stock index was 

 down 2.74 percent at 467 points following continued falls on 

 Wall Street in the wake of last week's attacks. 

 Won sentiment was slightly boosted by expected month-end 

 dollar sales by exporters and confirmation that General Motors 

  would buy troubled Daewoo Motor. 

 General Motors said it would sign an MOU this morning to 

 take over two Daewoo Motor plants in South Korea with a final 

 deal expected by year's end. 

 On the non-deliverable forward market, the one-month won at 

 1,298.2/99.2 per dollar against 1,299.3/1,300.3 late on 

 Thursday. The six-month won was quoted at 1,302.0/03.0 against 

 1,308.5/09.5. 

 THAI BAHT 

 The baht retained its firm tone at 44.15 but the market 

 found few incentives to push it above 44.00 amid wariness of 

 BOJ intervention to curb the yen's appreciation. 

 In the money market, baht funding costs remained largely 

 steady in both offshore and onshore markets because there was 

 not much activity going on. 

 Meanwhile, the Tourism Authority of Thailand (TAT) said it 

 had lowered the visitor arrival forecast to 9.68 million from 

 10.3 million in the wake of attacks in the U.S. 

     Revenues from tourists made a substantial contribution to 

 Thailand's foreign exchange incomes. 


    PHILIPPINE PESO



    The peso barely traded early around 51.24 as players were



glued to TV sets, listening to what President George Bush has



to say to a joint session of Congress.



    "The market is watching for clues on what he is going to do



as far as military retaliation is concerned," said a Manila



dealer.



    Bush said the evidence the U.S. has gathered all points to



Osama bin Laden's militant group and made a list of demands of



Afghanistan's ruling Taliban.



    The peso closed at 51.29 in on Thursday.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH



    The rupiah was marked up in thin early trade to 9,440 due



to a combination of firmer regionals and fears of local central



bank dollar-selling intervention.



    Bank Indonesia was rumoured to have sold the dollar at



around 9,550-9,600 on Thursday to shore up the rupiah.



    But its gains should be capped by persistent dollar demand



from onshore companies and lingering concerns over the fate of



$8.8 billion debt talk with Paris Club of creditors which has



been stalled since the attacks on the U.S.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Down As Debt Problems Weigh
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah ended down Wednesday on corporate demand for dollars, but off its day lows as the central bank apparently sold dollars to help the local currency. 

 The dollar was quoted between 9,590 rupiah and IDR9,640 late Wednesday, much higher than IDR9,520 to IDR9,560 Tuesday. 

 The U.S. currency touched an intraday high of IDR9,760 as local companies bought dollars to repay debt or fund imports. 

 Bank Indonesia stepped in during thin afternoon trading to sell about $20 million through brokers, Jakarta-based bankers said. 

 "We will intervene in the market if necessary," Bank Indonesia Governor Sjahril Sabirin told reporters Wednesday. The bank's policy is to intervene, but not to comment on any particular action. 

 Still, the intervention is unlikely to help in the long term, with the rupiah remaining under pressure from debt repayment, traders said. Public debt alone is equal to a year's gross domestic product. 

 The rupiah is also facing pressure from fears any retaliation by the U.S. for last week's terrorist attacks could incite further unrest in Indonesia, the world's most populous Muslim nation. 

 The central bank's one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia, or SBI, note yielded 17.66% at Wednesday's auction, unchanged from a week earlier. 

 Governor Sjahril said Wednesday the bank won't raise rates further, but at the same time added that Indonesia was unlikely to follow the U.S. Federal Reserve's 50-basis-point rate cut to 3% earlier this week. 

 Indonesia is trying to cut rates to help ease the pressure of funding its budget deficit from domestic bonds. 

 Still, the central bank doesn't want to see the rate go too low as inflationary pressures remain in the economy. The rupiah currency is still relatively weak against the dollar, which makes imported goods more expensive. 

 The dollar is likely to trade in a range between IDR9,575 and IDR9,750 Thursday, traders said.
