title: Asian  Currencies  Mostly Lower Late; Rupiah Off 7-Mo Low
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Asian currencies were mostly lower late Tuesday in quiet trade ahead of an expected interest rate hike by the U.S. Federal Reserve. 

 The Indonesian rupiah was slightly weaker, but well above its intraday low. 

 Fears of intervention by Indonesia's central bank and state banks lifted the currency, which has plunged as much as 9% over the past week. 

 It rallied sharply from a near seven month-low after Indonesian President Abdurrahman Wahid urged the central bank and state-run banks to support the flagging local currency. 

 Syetarn Hansakul, an analyst with WestLB, said "Wahid's intervention comment today helped lend some support but may not be enough if U.S. FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee) impacts negatively tomorrow." 

 It is also unclear if Wahid could order the central bank, which in theory works independently from the president, to defend the local currency, analysts said. 

 Wahid also instructed Finance Minister Bambang Sudibyo to review the economic projections in this year's budget, which appear too optimistic. The government had based the budget on an exchange rate of 7,000 rupiah to a dollar. 

 The U.S. currency late in the local session was at 8,545 rupiah, marginally up from IDR8,541 late Monday, but well below its intraday high of IDR8,730. 

 The Thai baht, Philippine peso and New Taiwan dollar also drifted lower on expectations of an aggressive U.S. interest rate hike later Tuesday, while the South Korean won bucked the regional downtrend. 

 The FOMC is widely expected to raise short-term interest rates by half a percentage point in an effort to slow rapid U.S. economic growth to a more sustainable rate. 

 As the market has largely factored in a hike of this magnitude, some analysts say they expect a "relief rally" in Asian currencies in the short term if this occurs. 

 The extent of the rate hike is expected to be influenced by U.S. inflation data, to be released before the FOMC meets. 

 The looming U.S. rate hike and a domestic political crisis embattling Philippine President Joseph Estrada's administration dragged the Philippine peso to a 19-month low. 

 The Estrada administration has been widely criticized for its handling of the country's hostage crisis. 

 The dollar's gains were, however, capped at 41.640 pesos as banks that were long on dollars opted to take profit at this level before repurchasing the U.S. currency at a lower rate, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at PHP41.630 on the Philippine Dealing System, up from of PHP41.560 Monday. 

 Philippine central bank Governor Rafael Buenaventura said Tuesday that while the peso should strengthen after jitters over the Fed's rate decision subside, it will likely remain above PHP41 to a dollar in the near term. 

 Buenaventura reiterated that the central bank is prepared to provide dollar liquidity to the market if necessary, but this hasn't been needed yet. 

 The South Korean won ended little changed against the U.S. dollar as afternoon dollar selling by local banks offset earlier dollar buying by overseas players in the non-deliverable forward market, traders said. 

 The dollar finished at 1,114.60 won, barely changed from Monday's close at KRW1,114.70. 

 Bucking the regional weakness, the Singapore dollar was slightly stronger as participants locked in profits on some long U.S. dollar positions ahead of the FOMC's meeting, traders said. 

 Around 0950 GMT (5:50 a.m. EDT), the U.S. dollar was at S$1.7280, down from S$1.7296 late Monday in Asia. 

 A 50 basis-point U.S. rate increase will be neutral for the Singapore dollar, traders said, adding that they expected the U.S. unit to continue trading in a range of between S$1.7250 and S$1.7350. 

 However, the outlook for the likely level of the Singapore dollar has been clouded by the expectation that the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the de facto central bank, would intervene at the upper end of that range.

title: Bk  Indonesia  Deputy Gov: Pointless To  Intervene  In  Market
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia Deputy Governor Miranda Gultom said Monday it would be pointless for the central bank to support the Indonesian rupiah either by raising interest rates or direct dollar-selling in view of the current market panic. 

 She predicted that the central bank's one-month note yield would remain flat at Wednesday's auction, despite calls for action on interest rates to defend the currency. The Sertifikat Bank Indonesia note last week yielded 10.91%. 

 "Increasing the interest rate while the market panics is pointless," Miranda told reporters. 

 Non-monetary factors in Indonesia including political tension, coupled with expectations of a hike in U.S. interest rates, are driving the dollar upside, she said. 

 Miranda declined to forecast when the rupiah could recover from its current seven-month low. 

 The rupiah gained last Friday after President Abdurrahman Wahid said the government would act to boost the currency, sparking speculation among dealers that the government may introduce some form of capital controls. 

 But Wahid ruled out this option Monday and denied that he had called for specific action, saying only that he was watching the situation closely. 

 Bank Indonesia officials last week said they would intervene in the market to support the rupiah, but dealers say they have seen little sign of this. 

 In any case, few participants expect Bank Indonesia can halt the rupiah's decline, which has outstripped falls in most other regional currencies. 

 The dollar ended Asian trading at IDR8,540, up from IDR8,380 late Friday.

title: Asian  Currencies  Lower Early; Rupiah Sets Bearish Tone
text:
SINGAPORE -(Dow Jones)- Most Asian currencies are lower early Monday, pressured by persistent weakness in the Indonesian rupiah and the likelihood of higher U.S. interest rates. 

 The rupiah declined amid a continuing string of negative news coming out Jakarta, including a report that Indonesia's top economic minister threatened to resign over his frustration with the lack of progress on economic reforms. 

 Senior Economics Minister Kwik Kian Gie said bureaucratic red tape was hampering the country's efforts to comply with the reforms sought by the International Monetary Fund as part of its loan program with Indonesia, the Financial Times reported over the weekend. 

 Additionally, clashes between police and angry mobs of people in Jakarta's Chinatown Saturday dented sentiment in the rupiah, dealers said. The clashes began when officials tried to clear the sidewalks of the many vendors who gather there each day to sell items such as pirated video compact discs, police said. 

 At 0230 GMT (10:30 p.m. EDT Sunday), the dollar was quoted at 8,600 rupiah, up from IDR8,485 late Friday. 

 Dealers said the dollar could rise as high as IDR8,800 Monday if Bank Indonesia continues to refrain from intervening to support the rupiah. 

 The sinking rupiah, along with expectations that Federal Reserve policy makers will raise short-term rates by half a percentage point when they meet Tuesday, pushed the Singapore dollar lower. 

 The U.S. dollar was quoted at S$1.7273, up from S$1.7243 late Friday. Dealers said they expected the pair to test S$1.7300, but the threat of intervention by monetary authorities would prevent the U.S. dollar from going much above that. 

 Prospects for a widening interest rate differential with the U.S., the ongoing Mindanao hostage crisis and weak first-quarter agriculture production data are weighing on the Philippine peso. 

 The dollar was quoted at 41.575 pesos, up from PHP41.500 late Friday. Dealers said the pair could test PHP41.600, but the threat of central bank intervention should cap the dollar. 

 The U.S. dollar was well-bid against the New Taiwan dollar amid volatility in the local stock market. 

 The U.S. dollar was quoted at NT$30.758, up from NT$30.735 late Friday. Dealers said expect the pair to trade in narrow range of NT$30.700-NT$30.800 ahead of the May 20 presidential inauguration. 

 The Thai baht also was lower. The dollar was quoted at 38.975 baht, up from THB38.815 Friday. 

 The only currency to gain on the dollar was the South Korean won. The dollar was at 1,113.8 won, down from Friday's close of KRW1,114.50. 

 Dealers said they expect a range of KRW1,111-KRW1,116 Monday.

title: Battered rupiah cuts losses on Wahid comments.
text:
JAKARTA, May 12 (Reuters) - Indonesia's rupiah fell further on Friday on growing pessimism about the economy, but managed to claw back some ground late in the day after President Abdurrahman Wahid said the government may act to boost the currency. 

 The rupiah dived to a new seven-month low of 8,750 to the dollar during the day but was quoted at 8,460/8,510 by 0850 GMT, compared with 8,390/8,420 in late local trade on Thursday. 

 There was market talk that the central bank may intervene but dealers said there was little Bank Indonesia could do to boost the currency. 

Central bank governor Syahril Sabirin said Bank Indonesia would only intervene if such a move was considered effective. 

 The rupiah cut its losses after Wahid said the government would take action to lift the currency if it did not rebound by Monday. 

 "Wahid's comments prompted profit-taking (in the dollar) as the comments raised fresh fears the government might be tempted to apply a fixed foreign exchange rate regime, even though the possibility seems to be remote," one foreign bank dealer said. 

 Another dealer said she wondered what the government, in particular Wahid, had in mind to boost the rupiah. She cautioned that if Wahid did nothing to prop up the rupiah, the inaction would badly hurt the currency. 

 The president has taken over supervision of economic matters after the IMF delayed a loan disbursement due to slow progress on the economic front. 

 There have been worries about possible friction between the President and his economic czar, but Wahid again denied this on Friday saying his relations with the minister were still good. 

 Wahid said the rupiah's falls were due partly to fears of unrest to mark the second anniversary of riots in Jakarta on May 13 and 14, 1998. 

 But dealers said the weakness was more due to growing pessimism about the government's competence to turn the economy around. 

 They said the rupiah's falls were the result of an accummulation of disappointments over Wahid's handling of economic and political affairs. 

 Wahid's recent comment that an unidentified group was trying to topple him also rattled markets this week, dealers said. ((Jakarta newsroom +62 21 384 6364, Fax +62 21 344 8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Bank  Indonesia  says to  intervene  only if effective.
text:
JAKARTA, May 12 (Reuters) - Bank Indonesia said on Friday the central bank would intervene in the foreign exchange market only if this would be effective in bolstering the rupiah, which has dropped to seven-month lows. 

 Governor Syahril Sabirin said the bank had recently been intevening in the market, but declined to give any details of the amounts involved. 

 "If (intervention) is needed, Bank Indonesia will do it. If it is useful, BI will do it. If the move is considered to be useless, we will not do it," Sabirin told reporters. 

 Sabirin said he would wait for the outcome of the U.S. Federal Reserve meeting next week before deciding how the central bank should guide domestic interest rates. 

 By 0630 GMT the rupiah was quoted at 8,545/8,575 against the dollar compard with 8,390/8,420 in late trade on Thursday. 

 Dealers say intervention by the central bank is unlikely to have much of an impact on the rupiah's direction. ((Jakarta newsroom +6221 384-6364; Fax +6221 344-8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Central Bank  Watch: Bk Indonesia Rupiah Policy Paralysis
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- When Bank Indonesia obtained its independence from what it dubs "government meddling" in May last year, the main task entrusted to it was to protect the value of the rupiah. 

 The central bank's apparent fumbling this week, however, in reacting to the rupiah's slide to its lowest level in more than seven months, has highlighted the limited ammunition it has to safeguard the fragile currency and the weight of the economic and political factors that make it nearly impossible for Bank Indonesia to influence the rupiah. 

 After falling to a low of IDR8,768 per dollar - its lowest level since Sept. 23 - the rupiah recovered towards the end of the day to around IDR8,475, down from IDR8,370 late Thursday in Asia, helped partly by rupiah-supportive comments by President Abdurrahman Wahid, but not helped at all by the central bank, dealers say. 

 Part of Bank Indonesia's dilemma is that it doesn't have enough foreign exchange reserves to fund market intervention. But its hands are also tied as regards using other traditional methods to boost the currency, in particular its near inability to raise domestic interest rates to mitigate the impact of the upward trend in U.S. rates because of the damage this could do to the fragile economic recovery. 

 "There seem to be few options left for Bank Indonesia to reverse the rupiah's slide at the moment," said the treasury chief at a foreign bank in Jakarta. "Intervention will deplete its foreign exchange reserves easily." 

 Bank Indonesia officials have said repeatedly over recent days that the central bank would intervene and sell dollars to boost the rupiah in the foreign exchange markets and tighten rupiah supply in the money market, which could in turn push interest rates up. 


Officials - including governor Sjahril Sabirin and senior deputy
governor Anwar Nasution - said the nation has enough foreign exchange
reserves to allow Bank Indonesia to intervene in the currency markets.
Bk Indonesia Reluctant To Intervene


But, dealers thinks the bank's pockets aren't deep enough to fight the
dollar bulls.



"It's not easy for Bank Indonesia as market participants are more
powerful," said the head of the treasury department of an Asian bank in
Jakarta.



Indonesia's net foreign exchange reserves stood at $18.27 billion as
of May 5, and its gross foreign exchange reserves at $29.48 billion.



"Bank Indonesia is not capable of flexing strong muscle in the
market," said a dealer with a large European bank in Jakarta. "I don't
think it is at liberty to spend $100 million in one intervention."



This view was backed up by senior economics minister Kwik Kian Gie,
who told Dow Jones Newswires in an interview that battling psychological
factors in the market could lead swiftly to the depletion of the central
bank's reserves, as happened in late 1997 and early 1998.



The fact there has been no sign of intervention by Bank Indonesia
Friday - although the rupiah continued to hit fresh seven-month lows -
was taken by the market as evidence that Bank Indonesia's intervention
would be purely verbal.



Backing this up - and despite comments to the contrary on Wednesday
and Thursday - central bank governor Sjahril told journalists Friday
that Bank Indonesia will intervene only if it thinks the move will be
effective.



Sjahril's statement was taken as proof by the market that Bank
Indonesia recognizes that intervention wouldn't be effective now, given
the bullish trend of the dollar.



Still the central bank should be prepared to act to defend the rupiah
and should intervene "at least to tell the market that it's extremely
unhappy with the rupiah's level," said a chief of treasury at another
foreign bank.



The chief treasurer, like other many treasurers and dealers in
Jakarta, declined to comment on the rupiah or on the central bank's
policies on the record for this article, citing fears of intimidating
warning calls from Bank Indonesia.



In the money market meanwhile, Bank Indonesia's threat to tighten
liquidity, also proved baseless. On Thursday and Friday, the central
bank left all its money market intervention rates unchanged, another
sign that it remains reluctant to guide interest rates higher.



On Friday, it left the overnight rate unchanged at 9.125%, the rates
for the maturity of four and five days at 9.625% and the one-week rate
at 9.875%.



Upward Trend On U.S. Rates Imposes Tough Choice



"The market wants to see Bank Indonesia increasing interest rates to
make the rupiah more attractive," said another dealer. "But I guess,
they are worried that it will stifle economic growth, and will raise the
interest payment of the government bonds."



The government has issued a whopping IDR309 trillion worth of bonds as
of April to recapitalize 25 local banks and is expected to issue a
further IDR100 trillion of bonds to recapitalize several state and
private banks.



The bonds carry fixed rate and floating rates tied to the average
interest rates of Bank Indonesia's three-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia
notes, which currently stands at 10.91%.



The government calculates the cost to the budget this year of interest
payment on the bonds of 6.5% of Gross Domestic Product this year. As
well as increasing the pressure on Indonesia's recovering economy,
hiking rates now would jack up this already massive bond interest bill.



As evidence of the bank's policy paralysis, Sjahril said Friday that
Bank Indonesia won't guide interest rates up unless the U.S. Federal
Reserve raises rates by more than 50 basis points next week. Most
analysts don't expect the Fed to hike by more than that level.



Rising interest rate will also boost the interest burden Bank
Indonesia has to pay for its SBI notes. The outstanding amount SBI notes
was IDR91.8 trillion in March.



Treasury chiefs note that the upward trend in U.S. rates imposes a
tough choice for Indonesia and other countries in the region.



"Bank Indonesia will have to make a choice of prioritizing either the
currency, or economic growth," one of the chief treasurers said.
"Unfortunately it isn't an easy choice to make."



-By I Made Sentana; 62 21 3983 1277; imsentana@ap.org

title: Indonesia Govt Seems In Disarray Amid Market Slide
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- A barrage of confusing and contradictory remarks from top Indonesian policy makers have sent shivers through the nation's markets, as analysts worry that the government is in disarray and unable to tackle its formidable economic challenges. 

 Indonesian markets fell again Friday after the government and central bank sent conflicting signals about what, if anything, they plan to do about a sharp drop in the rupiah. 

 That followed an extraordinary warning Thursday from senior Indonesian economics minister Kwik Kian Gie about the risks of investing in the country, given its continuing political instability. 

 Kwik, in an interview with Dow Jones Newswires, also implicitly criticized his boss, President Abdurrahman Wahid, by saying he - unlike Wahid - would be ashamed to go on foreign trips to entice foreign investment into the country, given the risks involved. He also signaled that he was unhappy with the recent appointment by Wahid of some other economic advisers, prompting speculation that the minister's days in the cabinet are numbered. 

 Analysts say that the confusing comments, apparent bickering and market gyrations have sparked a sense of panic about the management of economic policy in Indonesia. 

 "I think this is another clear sign of a lack of unity in the cabinet," said Raden Pardede, chief economist at Danareksa Securities in Jakarta. 

 "If the government doesn't make some tough decisions now to regain confidence of the market, the rupiah could deteriorate further very quickly," he added. 


Along with the impact of the surging dollar, the comments sent the
rupiah sinking to IDR8,768 during Friday trade, its lowest level since
Sept. 23 and down 8% since Wednesday's close of Asian trade. Jakarta
stocks dipped 3.5% Thursday and a further 0.4% Friday.
-
Lack Of Clarity Hits Economic Progress
-



Although there are some signs of recovery in Indonesia - Kwik said
Thursday the economy grew 5% in the first two months of the year from a
year ago - Indonesia's multilateral lenders and private economists
reckon the economy won't recover in a sustainable way until Wahid's team
tackles deeply embedded structural issues such as the mountain of
private corporate debt and corruption at the courts.



But a lack of a clear, united approach to revamping the economy is
overriding any progress the government has already made.



For example, in a bid to stem the rupiah's hemorrhaging, Bank
Indonesia senior deputy governor Anwar Nasution said Wednesday that the
central bank was ready to step into the market to shore up the currency.



The next day, Kwik said that intervening would be fruitless, as
battling psychological factors in the market could swiftly lead to a
depletion of foreign exchange reserves. Another central bank deputy
governor then shot back later Thursday with a pledge that Bank Indonesia
would use "all possible means," to protect the currency.



But on Friday, central bank governor Sjahril Sabirin said Bank
Indonesia would only intervene "if it will be effective," backing up a
widely-held market view that the bank was hoping words would be
sufficient to talk the rupiah up, without having to resort to deeds.



Wahid himself has fueled the confusion. Earlier Friday, he said that
the government had no quick fix for the rupiah, saying it would wait a
week before deciding whether to intervene. But several hours later, he
said that the rupiah was sliding due to fears about unrest over the
weekend as protesters mark the second anniversary of riots that shook
Jakarta in May 1998.



If the rupiah remains weak on Monday, Wahid said the government would
act, although he didn't say in what manner.



"We will wait until May 15," he said. "If the dollar doesn't weaken,
then the government will take action"," he added, in comments that
helped give the rupiah a pre-weekend lift towards the close of trade
sending it to IDR8,300.
-
Growing Sense Of Panic
-



Many market participants believe Wahid is planning to further cull his
cabinet - in the wake of last month's firing of two economic ministers -
and Kwik is increasingly seen as next on the list. Wahid's recent
appointment of two controversial officials to monitor and supervise
Kwik's team has helped drive that speculation.



"One way or another, it looks like he is going to vacate his
portfolio," said Philip Wee, treasury economist at Standard Chartered in
Singapore.



This, political analysts say, could pile further pressure on Wahid's
coalition government and would make it increasingly difficult for the
Democratic Party of Struggle - in which Kwik is a senior member and of
which Vice-President Megawati Sukarnoputri is chairperson - to remain in
the cabinet.



But analysts also say Wahid needs to rein in his economic team, and if
he does replace Kwik he should do so swiftly, rather than waiting until
he delivers a key performance speech to parliament in August.



"Statements from politicians are confusing and marking the market
nervous," said Pande Raja Silalahi, an economist at the Center for
Strategic and International Studies in Jakarta.



"Now is the right time for the president to reorganize the
cabinet...so he can concentrate on economic issues and make a solid
team," he said. "He should not wait until August. Sacking Kwik may spark
some reaction on the market but it won't last long and it would be
better than all this uncertainty."

title: Indonesian Shares End Down As Rupiah Weakens Further
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesian shares ended lower Friday on fears the rupiah could weaken further and after Bank Indonesia warned of a possible interest rate hike. 

 The JSX Composite index ended down 0.4%, or 2.324 points at 526.877. Decliners led gainers 55 to 46, with 94 stocks unchanged. 

 Volume was 233 million shares valued at 494 billion rupiah (IDR). 

 The dollar was trading at IDR8,475, compared with IDR8,393 late Thursday. 

 A local dealer said many investors avoided the market due to the weakening rupiah, which touched a low of IDR8,775 against the greenback Friday - its lowest level since Sept. 23. 

 She said further rupiah instability could push the main index down to 500 points next week. 

 Another dealer with a foreign brokerage said market sentiment was further damped by comments by Bank Indonesia Governor Sjahril Sabirin, who said the central bank will intervene in currency trading only if it will be effective in boosting the rupiah. 

 His comment was interpreted by the market as a refusal by the central bank to help support the rupiah. 

 The dealer said the market was also concerned of a possible increase in domestic interest rates, which Sjahril said Bank Indonesia would do if the U.S. Federal Reserve raises the Federal fund rate by more than 50 basis points next week. 

 Blue chips were hardest hit by the rupiah's weakness, with market heavyweight Telkom losing IDR50, or 1.5%, to IDR3,275. 

 Cigarette producer Gudang Garam ended down IDR75, or 0.6%, at IDR12,500, while rival HM Sampoerna fell IDR50, or 0.4%, to IDR12,975. 

 International call operator Indosat was also hit - its shares ended down IDR100, or 0.9%, at IDR10,500. 

 But oil producer Medco Energi Corp. bucked the trend, with its shares ending up IDR125, or 3%, to IDR4,250 as the stronger dollar led to buying. All of Medco's profits are in U.S dollars.

title: Indonesia Wahid: IDR Weaker Due To May Riots Anniversary
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The current weakness of the rupiah is due to concerns about demonstrations to mark the second anniversary of the riots that shook Jakarta in May 1998, President Abdurrahman Wahid said Friday. 

 Speaking to reporters at his residence, Wahid said that "businessmen are buying dollars, because of concerns about the anniversary of the May riots," which is weighing on the rupiah. 

 He said the government would take action next week to shore up the rupiah - after the riots' anniversary - if necessary, although he didn't say what kind of action. 

 "We will wait until May 15," he said. "If the dollar doesn't weaken, then the government will take action." 

 Several groups of protestors are gathering in Jakarta, some to mark the anniversary of the killing of four students by police at Trisakti University in western Jakarta. 

 The four, who died May 12, 1998, were part of a massive swell of student-led protests and riots that year, which led to the downfall of former President Suharto on May 21. 

 Earlier Friday, Bank Indonesia Governor Sjahril Sabirin said the central bank will intervene only if the move will be effective in boosting the rupiah. 

 "I cannot say at what level we will intervene," he told journalists. "We will intervene if we think it will be effective." 

 Sjahril added that Bank Indonesia won't guide up local interest rates if the U.S. Federal Reserve raises the Federal funds rate by only 0.50 percentage point. 

 "We will follow suit only if the Fed raises interest rates above 0.50 percentage point," Sjahril said. 

 Dealers attributed the rupiah's slump to expectations of a 50-basis point increase in U.S. interest rates next week, combined with the general demand for dollars from local companies and domestic political uncertainties. 

 At 0739 GMT (3:39 a.m. EDT), the dollar was trading at IDR8,703, up from IDR8,393 late Thursday. The currency is off its session highs, but still is at its highest level since Sept. 23. 

 Wahid also said he won't sack Senior Economics Minister Kwik Kian Gie for remarks that Indonesia was too unstable for foreign investors. Wahid's comments helped quash speculation that such a move was imminent. 

 "I have no plans to replace Kwik Kian Gie," Wahid told reporters. "I have a very good relationship with him." 

 The president's expression of support comes after Kwik said that Indonesia isn't stable enough to attract foreign investors, comments that fueled a perception that the minister would be fired. 

 In a wide-ranging interview with Dow Jones Newswires Thursday, Kwik said the country still faced too much instability, sporadic anarchy, and social unrest to appeal to investors. 

 "I never talk about foreign investment and things like that because I'm realistic enough: if I were a foreign investor, I wouldn't come to Indonesia," he said. "The law enforcement is not there, but not only that, the whole thing is so confusing. How can you come here?" 

 But Kwik later played down the comments, saying he wasn't actually asking investors to avoid investing in Indonesia.

SINGAPORE, May 11 (Reuters) - Hefty losses in regional 

 stocks and the prospect of higher U.S. rates put Asian regional 

currencies on the defensive late on Thursday. 

     The fall was more pronounced in the rupiah and the baht 

 which hit their 2000 lows as flustered importers and corporate 

 players scurried to buy dollars. 

     Central banks in Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand were 

 heard intervening in the market to prop up their sliding 

currencies, but no official confirmation was available. 

     "Regional currency sales were broad-based. There's talk 

 that central banks were in the market today - Singapore, 

 Indonesia and Thailand," said Philip Wee, treasury economist at 

 Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. 

     "The dollar offers were mostly done through offshore banks. 

 But there's no confirmation on this," he said. 

     Analysts said Asian currencies would retain their weak tone 

 in the near-term against a backdrop of continued dollar 

 strength. 


    The dollar briefly rose above the 110 yen	  barrier as



a sharp fall in Tokyo shares overshadowed confidence in Japan's



economic recovery.



    The benchmark Nikkei	   closed 4.63 percent off on



Thursday, ending below 17,000 points for the first time since



September 27, 1999.



    INDONESIAN RUPIAH	



    A stream of dollar bids from offshore and corporate players



sent the rupiah reeling to 8,420 -- its lowest level since



September 29.



    Although talk of central bank intervention and sporadic



dollar profit-taking lifted the unit from its day low, market



sentiment remained glum.



    Dealers said any rebound could be temporary as corporate



dollar demand remained high and exporters were opting to park



their dollar receivables offshore amid political and economic



uncertainties.

The baht struggled to stand above the key 39.00 level where



the central bank was rumoured to have intervened.



Dealers said it was likely to slip back below the level



again soon due to sustained dollar demand from both offshore



and corporate players.



"If the central bank declares that it had indeed intervened


and that it hates to see the baht below 39, then market



participants might perhaps hold their baht sales for a while,"



said a dealer at a European bank.



    "But I don't think sellers would be deterred much by the



market talk," she said.



    SINGAPORE DOLLAR	



    The Singapore dollar staged a mild rebound amid market



rumours that the central bank had intervened to defend it after



it fell to 13-month lows against the U.S. dollar.



    Dealers said the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) was



spotted selling dollars fairly aggressively from the 1.7350



level downwards, pushing the Sing dollar back to the firm side



of 1.73.



There was also talk that the MAS had drained liquidity in



local money markets, pushing short-term interbank rates to



their highest since the last quarter of 1998 on Wednesday.



An MAS spokeswoman said the bank does not comment on its



actions in the market. The central bank has said in the past



that it intervenes in forex markets to smooth sharp moves in



the exchange rate.



PHILIPPINE PESO



The peso was at the lower end of its intra-day range,



offering few buying incentives as investors opted to wait for



the expected increase in U.S. interest rates next week.



The unresolved armed conflict in the southern Mindanao region



also weighed on sentiment, dealers said.



On the macro front, the country's gross international



reserves were $15.8 billion at the end of April, down from



$15.99 billion the previous month, a central bank official



said.



TAIWAN DOLLAR



The Taiwan dollar took its cue from the weaker yen and a



near 2.5 percent drop on the stock market, which pushed the



benchmark TAIEX to its lowest close in 2000.



Dealers said worries about the scale and impact of the next



Fed rate hike and hefty overnight losses on the Nasdaq



were depressing Taipei markets.



The Taiwan dollar's plight was worsened by the central



bank's failure to defend the T$30.72 level, where it has been



seen recently, though dealers said the bank was in the market



intermittently over the course of the day.



The central bank has been in the market of late and dealers



said its moves were aimed at eliminating market expectations of



a depreciation of the Taiwan dollar amid political



uncertainties.

The Korean won was quoted lower in thin offshore trade,



with local markets closed for Buddha's birthday.



    Finance Minister Lee Hun-Jai said Korea's GDP this year



would probably exceed an originally forecast six percent.



    He also said inflation this year would be within the



originally estimated three percent, while a strong export



performance would yield a continued trade surplus.



    Over the medium term, South Korea's GDP would be around six



percent and inflation below three percent, he added, without



specifying the time period.

title: Indonesia Kwik: Concerned About Weakness Of Rupiah
text:
- - 11/05/02-32G



0232GMT


 - - 11/05/02-32G 

 0233GMT 


- - 11/05/02-34G



0234GMT



JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian government is concerned about the
weakness of the rupiah and argues that the sliding currency doesn't
reflect economic fundamentals, Senior Economics Minister Kwik Kian Gie
said.



In an interview with Dow Jones Newswires, Kwik also said Indonesia's
ample foreign exchange reserves should be strengthening the rupiah.



"The rupiah's weakness is of course a concern," he said. "Economically
speaking, I don't understand why it is weakening."



The rupiah slid to a fresh seven-month low of 8,295 rupiah against the
greenback Thursday, hit by strong commercial dollar demand ahead of an
expected hike in U.S. interest rates and lingering uncertainty about
Indonesia's commitment to economic reforms.



The rupiah is also being hammered by the surging dollar. A series of
interest rate hikes by the U.S. Federal Reserve has made it much more
attractive to hold greenbacks. And market participants are expecting the
Federal Open Market Committee, the Fed's policy-making arm, to raise its
federal funds rate by at least 25 basis points.



Many market participants expect the local currency to weaken to
IDR8,500 to the greenback in the near term, and don't rule out a slide
to IDR9,000, well below the rupiah's level at the beginning of the year
of IDR7,000.



Kwik argued that growing foreign exchange reserves - Indonesia's net
reserves currently stand at $18.27 billion, well above the target of $14
billion agreed to with the International Monetary Fund - as well as
growth in exports and in the economy more broadly should lead to a much
stronger rupiah.



"In terms of foreign exchange reserves, in terms of growth, in terms
of growth in exports, in terms of everything we see, the economy is
really recovering," he said. "That's despite the fact that foreign
investment isn't coming back yet, that so many banks are still not
functioning, despite the fact that all conglomerates are still in (debt
restructuring) talks with the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency."



Kwik rejected suggestions that the economy's recovery in Indonesia is
too fragile to be sustainable, as it is led by consumer spending, rather
than investment and reforms.



"I don't understand why a recovery which is consumer-led is fragile,"
he said, arguing that the recovery doesn't need to be investment-led at
this stage, given excess capacity in the country.



Kwik said the appropriate level for the rupiah - based on the
economy's outlook - is stronger than IDR7,000, although he noted that
uncertainty about the government is having a psychological impact.



Despite concerns about the sliding currency, Kwik said it would be
pointless for the central bank to intervene.



"I don't think the central bank is going to do that," he said. "We
have experience that if things get out of hand psychologically in so
severe a manner, that forex reserves can be depleted in no time."



"I'm sure that Bank Indonesia knows about that and is not intervening
too much; that is the consequence of a free-float system."



Bank Indonesia Senior Deputy Governor Anwar Nasution said Wednesday
the central bank would intervene to shore up the flagging currency, but
traders say they haven't seen any evidence of this in Thursday trade.

title: Rupiah breaks 8,100/dlr on US rates, local nerves.
text:
JAKARTA, May 10 (Reuters) - Indonesia's rupiah fell through 8,100 for the first time since mid-October in early trade on Wednesday, hit by the prospect of higher U.S. rates and concerns over the country's political stability and economic progress. 

 By 0130 GMT the rupiah was quoted at 8,155/8,175 against the dollar compared with 8,060/8,080 in late local trade on Tuesday. 

 "Weak regional currencies due to speculation about higher U.S. interest rates dampened sentiment in the rupiah. The fears have prompted players to buy dollars now to repay or refinance foreign debt," one foreign bank dealer said. 

 Another bank dealer said most of the dollar buying orders in morning trading came from interbank players. He said local corporates were likely to follow suit later on Wednesday which could put further pressure on the rupiah. 

 There were no signs yet of Bank Indonesia intervening in the market to prop up the rupiah, but the central bank was likely to do so if the currency moved closer to 8,200, the dealer said. 

 He said the rupiah's fall to a low of 8,135 in New York trade overnight hurt sentiment on the currency in Asian morning trade on Wednesday. 

 A string of recent discouraging news on the domestic front also hit sentiment in the rupiah, dealers said. 

 President Abdurrahman Wahid said on Monday a "certain group" was trying to topple him before the upcoming meeting of Indonesia's highest legislative body in August. 

 Dealers said the government's slow progress in bank and corporate restructuring continued to dampen sentiment on the rupiah. ((Jakarta newsroom +62 21 384 6364, Fax +62 21 344 8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: REPEAT:Bank  Indonesia  To  Intervene  To Support IDR-Dep Gov
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia Senior Deputy Governor, Anwar Nasution said Wednesday that the central bank will intervene in the market to support the crumbling rupiah, which fell Wednesday to a seven-month low against the dollar. 

 "It's wrong to assume that BI isn't doing anything" to support the rupiah, he told reporters. "We will intervene." 

 Bank Indonesia rarely intervenes directly in the market, but does exchange dollars for rupiah, which amounts to a form of intervention. 

 The dollar ended Asian trading Wednesday at IDR8,205, up from IDR8,070 late Tuesday, as some dealers braced for a further rupiah depreciation. 

 Anwar said the rupiah should strengthen when Indonesia signs the next letter of intent with the International Monetary Fund, which is expected by early June. 

 This would support the rupiah in two ways: firstly, by paving the way for the release of blocked IMF loans; and secondly, by fulfilling Indonesia's pledge to the Paris Club of donor countries. 

 The Paris Club agreed last month to reschedule $5.8 billion in sovereign debt, pending a new IMF accord. 

 This rescheduling will reduce the amount of dollars that Indonesia needs to purchase in the market, Anwar said. 

 He declined to forecast a level for the rupiah after the letter of intent signing, and was similarly circumspect on how Bank Indonesia would intervene to support the currency.

title: Rupiah up ahead of president-parliament meeting.
text:
JAKARTA, April 27 (Reuters) - Indonesia's rupiah inched up early on Thursday as players sold dollars to take profits after the local currency fell through 8,000 to six-month lows on Wednesday. 

 Market sentiment, however, remained cautious as the market was awaiting President Abdurrahman Wahid's appearance before parliament later today where he will be quizzed on several controversial issues, including his plans to revoke a ban on communism. 

 By 0145 GMT the rupiah was quoted at 7,970/8,000 to the dollar compared with 8,020/8,050 in late local trade on Wednesday. 

 One U.S. bank dealer said immediate support for the rupiah was seen at 8,075 while resistance seen at 7,925. 

 "Most of those taking profits are interbank players. Players are now waiting for the outcome of the meeting between President Wahid and parliamentary members," the dealer said. 

 Monday's sacking of Investment and State Enterprises Minister Laksamana Sukardi and Trade Minister Yusuf Kalla is not on the agenda, but Wahid has been widely criticised over the move and it may well be raised during the meeting. 

 Another dealer said oral intervention by Bank Indonesia seemed to be effective this time. Players sold dollars to take profit after the central bank said on Wednesday it was ready to intervene into the market to prop up the rupiah. 

 The rupiah broke through 8,000 to the dollar on Wednesday, hit by doubts over the government's unity and economic competence following the sacking of two cabinet ministers earlier this week. 

 The sacking of the two ministers has sparked fears their parties could pull out of Indonesia ramshackle coalition and doubts over the ability of their replacements. 

 Wednesday's auction of one-month SBI certificates resulted in a weighted average interest rate of 10.88 percent, down from 10.92 percent last week. ((Gde Anugrah Arka, Jakarta newsroom +6221 384-6364; Fax +6221 344-8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Bk Indonesia Gov: Still Expects IDR To Move To 7,000/USD
text:
- - 26/04/02-50G



0250GMT


 JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Bank Indonesia will intervene if necessary to support the flagging rupiah, although it hasn't yet done so, central bank Governor Sjahril Sabirin said Wednesday. 

 Sjahril also said the central bank wouldn't seek to push up interest rates to boost the currency. 

 Asked whether Bank Indonesia would intervene in the market, Sjahril said: "Intervention, Yes." 

 He added that the central bank has ample foreign exchange reserves to do so, noting that they are at "an all-time high." 

 Market participants in Jakarta reckon Sjahril's comments were an effort to talk up the rupiah, with few expecting the central bank to actually step into the market. 

 Bank Indonesia rarely intervenes directly in the foreign exchange markets, but does change dollars for rupiah in the market as required. 

 Sjahril said Bank Indonesia is currently changing a modest amount of between $1.0 million to $5.0 million daily on the market. He said it would continue to supply dollars to "calm the market as required." 

 Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves as of April 20 stood at $18.19 billion, down from $18.31 billion the previous week. 

 The rupiah slid to a new six-month low of IDR8,070 early Wednesday, pushed down by commercial demand for dollars from Indonesian companies and political jitters in the fallout of the sacking of two ministers this week by President Abdurrahman Wahid. 

 The currency rebounded somewhat midmorning Wednesday on a bout of profit-taking, but at 0434 GMT (12:34 a.m. EDT), the currency was trading at IDR8,042 to the dollar, down from IDR7,935 late Tuesday. The rupiah is at its lowest level since Oct. 1. 

 Sjahril called the rupiah's weakness "temporary," noting that it was due to political factors. He maintained that the currency could still strengthen to IDR7,000 to the dollar, the level on which the 2000 budget is based. 

 The central bank governor said he expected interest rates to keep steady while the currency is weak, nothing that if there was any move upwards or downwards in rates, it would only be a slight one. 

 Interest rates on short-term central bank notes inched up last week to 10.92% from 10.92% previously. Bank Indonesia will auction IDR21.51 trillion of one-month notes later Wednesday. 

 Elsewhere, Sjahril said he doesn't expect the repayment of foreign debt by some local companies to have too much of an impact on the rupiah's level. 

 "Bank Indonesia has already taken into account the effect of the foreign debt repayments in our exchange rate calculations," Sjahril said. 

 Some local companies have been buying dollars to repay offshore debt, thus boosting the level of the greenback against the rupiah. 

 Sjahril said that with ample foreign exchange reserves - that are set to be buoyed further by healthy international oil prices - the rupiah could withstand the effects of the debt repayment.

title: Rupiah loses further ground after breaking 8,000.
text:
JAKARTA, April 26 (Reuters) - Indonesia's rupiah lost further ground early on Wednesday after falling through 8,000 to the dollar for the first time since the mid-October as the sacking of two ministers raised concerns over rifts in the government. 

 By 0240 GMT the currency was quoted at 8,040/8,060 against the dollar compared with 7,930/7,940 in late local trade on Tuesday. 

 "Our strategy is to remain long on dollars because of the political uncertainty. I see immediate support for the rupiah at 8,100 and resistance for the currency at 7,950," one European bank dealer said. 

 Another dealer said the market was already long on dollars but there were many players who were nervous because of rising political uncertainty. 

 Dealers said there were no signs yet that the central bank would intervene in the market to prop up the rupiah. 

 Bank Indonesia governor Syahril Sabirin said on Wednesday there was no need to intervene to strengthen the rupiah, saying the local unit could reach 7,000 to the dollar if there was no further political upheaval. 

 The rupiah had moved closer to 8,000 late last week but failed to break through the barrier due in part to support from local players, believed to be acting on behalf of the central bank, dealers said. 

 On Monday night, President Abdurrahman Wahid fired Investment and State Enterprises Minister Laksamana Sukardi and Trade Minister Yusuf Kalla, saying the country needed a united cabinet to deal with the battered economy. 

 But dealers said doubts surrounded Laksamana's replacement by a subordinate whose main qualification seems to be his closeness to Wahid. 

 Analysts say fighting among political parties for control of lucrative positions in government, state companies and the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency (IBRA) has hampered policy. The state enterprises ministry is seen as a key money spinner for the party that controls it. 

 The sackings came at the start of an IMF review into how closely Indonesia is sticking to its agreement on economic reforms in return for a $400 million loan payment, as well as substantial Paris Club debt rescheduling. 

 Acting IMF head Stanley Fischer said on Monday he hoped the delayed loan payment would finally be released by the end of May. It had originally been scheduled for early April but was put on hold because of government foot-dragging on implementing planned reforms. title: Emerging  FX  - Sick yen unnerves baht, Taiwan dlr.
text:

 at regional currencies late on Tuesday, with the Thai baht 

 leading the losers after shedding some 0.4 percent. 

     Only the Singapore dollar managed to tip-toe into positive 

 terrain following a slight bout of U.S. dollar profit-taking. 

     Options-related dollar sales triggered ahead of 112 yen 

  elbowed dollar/yen off six-month highs of 111.73 but yen 

 sentiment remained weak on worries over Japan's growth 

 prospects. 

 Japan's Economic Planning Minister Taichi Sakaiya said

title: Indonesian Money Market Rates Down As  Intervention  Rates Cut
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesian money market rates were mostly lower early Friday as Bank Indonesia cut its intervention rates by 50 basis points, dealers said. 

 Bank Indonesia cut its overnight rate to 10% from 10.50%; slashed the rates carrying maturities between two and six days to 10.50% from 11%; and the one-week rate was moved lower to 10.75% from 11.25%. 

 Bank Indonesia conducts a daily intervention to manage market liquidity. 

 The central bank also determines the interest rates based on liquidity conditions and on the weekly movements of the benchmark rate on its one-month SBI notes. 

 "It seems that Bank Indonesia is set to bring its overnight rate to pre-crisis level of 9% before the end of the year as its one-month SBI is declining ," said a dealer with a local bank. "Certainly, this is a good development for the economy. 

 Dealers, however, said that the impact of Bank Indonesia's rate cut on the money market rates was mitigated by an increase on liquidity demands Friday. 

 Liquidity demand increased as companies and banks paid need funds Thursday to pay their taxes, they said. 

 At 0202 GMT (9:02 p.m. EST Thursday), the overnight interbank rate - considered the benchmark rate - was between 10.25% and 10.75% for foreign and joint venture banks, down from between 10.75% and 10.875% Thursday. 

 Most local banks are paying overnight rates between 10.75% and 11.00%, down from between 11% and 11.50% Thursday. 

 At the same time in the foreign exchange market, the dollar was trading at IDR7,090, up a bit from IDR7,070 late Thursday in Asia.

title: Indonesian Money Market Rates Fall; Central Bk Cut Rates
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesian money market rates are down early Wednesday taking a cue from Bank Indonesia which lowers its intervention rates. 

 At 0330 GMT (10:30 p.m. EST), the overnight interbank rate - considered the benchmark rate - was at 10.75% for foreign banks down from 11% Tuesday and 11% for most local banks down from 11.25%. 

 Dealers said trading is quiet as most participants remain cautious in the wake of the liquidity problem at Bank Putera Multikarsa. 

 The bank, which is owned by the Texmaco Group, has been hit by a run on deposits since November, causing a liquidity problem. The central bank suspended its clearing activities Tuesday because it apparently failed to cover a negative balance with the central bank. 

 Most dealers said Bank Putera Multikarsa has little impact on the market because of the small size of the bank, but banks are still wary of lending to small banks. 

 The Texmaco Group has been embroiled in a scandal wherein it allegedly obtained hefty loans from state banks through high-level political influence. 

 Bank Indonesia signaled its intention to see lower rates by cutting the intervention rates by 25 basis points. 

 The central bank's overnight intervention rate is now down to 11% while two-day intervention rate is 11.5%. 

 Bank Indonesia intervenes daily in the money market to absorb excess liquidity. 

 The weekly auction of Bank Indonesia notes will likely lead to rates falling between 12.500% and 12.625%, slightly below last week's 12.860%. 

 The result of the auction will be known in the afternoon. 

 In the foreign exchange market, the dollar was trading at IDR7,210 rupiah, marginally changed from IDR7,215 traded late Tuesday.

title: Official Cites Web Of Corruption In Bank Negara Indonesia Lending
text:
JAKARTA, Indonesia -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's scandal-ridden banking sector was stung by fresh revelations of corruption Monday, this time by an allegation that the central bank and former President Suharto were involved in a conspiracy related to the handling of 9.65 trillion rupiah ($1.34 billion) in loans to the Texmaco Group, an influential conglomerate. 

 Laksamana Sukardi, the government's minister of investment and state enterprises, told Parliament that loans by PT Bank Negara Indonesia to the Texmaco Group involved "a ... high-level conspiracy." 

 The alleged conspiracy dated to late 1997, following the crash of Indonesia's currency, the rupiah, a tumble that impaired the financial positions of most Indonesian conglomerates. 

 Laksamana revealed that Bank Indonesia - the country's central bank - provided a total of $754.1 million plus 1.9 trillion rupiah in a preshipment trade-financing package to the Texmaco Group, contravening central-bank regulations that allowed only postshipment loans. 

 The group faced increasing financial strain as the rupiah depreciated, and had about $350 million in matured commercial paper and Yankee bonds that couldn't be rolled over. 

 Suharto intervened by instructing Bank Indonesia in writing to extend the facility and flout its own rules, Laksamana said, adding that the "preshipment facility was tailor-made for Texmaco and is a case of national-level collusion." 

 The Texmaco Group is controlled by Manimaren Sinivasan, who, according to the state-enterprises minister, is a close friend of Suharto. Manimaren's brother, Marimutu Manimaren, is a treasurer for former ruling party Golkar, and was named in the PricewaterhouseCoopers audit of the PT Bank Bali case. The Bank Bali scandal contributed to the downfall of B.J. Habibie, Suharto's successor. as president. 

 Further, Laksamana said Bank Indonesia tapped into the country's foreign-exchange reserves to provide the Texmaco Group with the loans, at a time when the rupiah faced heavy devaluation pressures. "Bank Indonesia used the country's foreign-exchange reserves to bail out a local company at a time when Indonesia (was) in dire need of foreign currencies," he said. 

 The amount of credit channeled through Bank Negara to Texmaco breached lending limits prescribed by the central bank, which stipulate that no bank can lend more than 20% of its capital to a single borrower, he said, without quantifying the percentage involved. However, the central bank waived this rule to allow the loans to the Texmaco Group. 

 Laksamana added that Suharto's interference in Bank Indonesia's operations was clear. 

 Even the ministry of trade and industry at that time turned a blind eye to the fact that only the Texmaco Group received preshipment loans, although the ministry had recommended two other business groups for such assistance. 

 The alleged collusion didn't stop after the loans were granted. A local media report disclosed and Bank Negara subsequently confirmed that it didn't report its loan exposure to the Texmaco Group to the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency, or IBRA, which was formed last year to reform the banking sector. Bank Negara is among the banks tagged for government recapitalization, to the tune of 52.8 trillion rupiah. 

 Under the recapitalization program, Bank Negara should have transferred the worst of its nonperforming loans to IBRA for recovery, since IBRA is empowered to tackle recalcitrant debtors. 

 Despite the Texmaco Group's failure to repay any of the loans that led Bank Negara to write off the debts completely last year, the bank didn't transfer the loans to IBRA. Most banking analysts say such loans should have been transferred to IBRA for more effective collection. 

 Pradjoto, a banking analyst who blew the whistle on the Bank Bali matter, said a big question is why Bank Negara didn't transfer the loans to IBRA. He suggested that the bank "is trying to avoid letting the powerful IBRA to be Texmaco's creditor." 

 If the loans were transferred, the Texmaco Group probably would be at or near the top of the list of IBRA's debtors in terms of the amount owed. 

 Bank Negara, which isn't related to Bank Negara, Malaysia's central bank, said earlier Monday that it is negotiating with the Texmaco Group on a debt-restructuring plan that would include a debt-to-equity conversion for part of the debt. 

 The bank's secretary, Sudirman, who like many Indonesians uses a single name, said the bank doesn't view the loans to the Texmaco Group as being so dire as to qualify for government recapitalization. The bank said the loans were classified as Category 4, meaning they were considered more likely to be repaid. In March, Bank Negara passed on the IBRA loans totaling 24.3 trillion rupiah. Those loans were rated as Category 5, meaning there was a very low chance of recovery. 

 Sudirman said Germany's Commerzbank AG is advising on the loan restructuring, but added that it is premature to state which of the Texmaco Group companies would be turned over to the bank. 

 The daily newspaper Harian Ekonomi Neraca said Monday that bank would gain control of five group companies and would seek a U.S. stock market listing for three of the units: PT Texmaco Perkasa Engineering, PT Perkasa Heavyndo Engineering and PT Multikarsa Investama. Of the three, only Texmaco Perkasa Engineering, which makes heavy equipment, is listed in Jakarta. 

 Multikarsa Investama has 4.08 trillion rupish of the total loan to the group, according to a statement released Friday by the Jakarta Stock Exchange. The second-largest debtor is the group's Polysindo Eka Perkasa unit with 1.45 trillion rupiah.

title: Indonesian Min: BNI Loans Reveals Top Level Corruption
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's scandal-ridden banking sector was hit Monday by revelations that the central bank and former President Suharto were involved in high-level corruption related to the handling of 9.65 trillion rupiah ($1=IDR7,310) in loans by a state bank to an influential conglomerate. 

 Laksamana Sukardi, Minister of investment and state-enterprises, told Parliament that the controversy surrounding PT Bank Negara Indonesia, or BNI's, hefty loans to the Texmaco Group was "a case of high-level conspiracy." 

 The so-called conspiracy dated back to late 1997 after the rupiah suffered from hefty depreciation and had seriously impaired the financial positions of most Indonesian conglomerates. 

 Laksamana revealed to parliament that Bank Indonesia - Indonesia's central bank - provided a total of $754.1 million plus IDR1.9 trillion in pre-shipment trade facility exclusively to diversified conglomerate Texmaco, contravening central bank regulations that only allow post-shipment facilities. 

 Texmaco faced increasing financial strain as the rupiah depreciated, and there were about $350 million in commercial papers and Yankee bonds that had matured at that time but couldn't be rolled over. 

 Then President Suharto even personally intervened to instruct Bank Indonesia through a letter to extend the facility and flout existing rules, Laksamana said. 

 The owner of Texmaco Group, Marimutu Sinivasan, is a close friend of Suharto. 

 "The pre-shipment facility was tailor-made for Texmaco and is a case of national-level collusion," Laksamana said. 

 Further, Laksamana said Bank Indonesia tapped into the country's foreign exchange reserves to provide Texmaco with the loan facilities, at a time when the currency was facing serious devaluation pressure. 

 "Bank Indonesia used the country's foreign exchange reserves to bail out a local company at a time when Indonesia is in dire need of foreign currencies," he said. 

 Also, the amount of credit facility channeled through BNI to Texmaco had also breached the legal lending limit prescribed by the central bank, which stipulates that no bank can lend more than 20% of its capital to a single business group, he said. 

 However, Bank Indonesia granted an exemption to this rule to allow the facility to go through to Texmaco. 

 Laksamana added that Suharto's interference in Bank Indonesia's operations was very clear. 

 Even the ministry of trade and industry at that time turned a blind eye to the fact that only Texmaco Group benefited from the pre-shipment facility, though the ministry had recommended two other business groups to be eligible for the facility. 

 The collusion trail didn't stop after the facilities were granted. A local media report disclosed and BNI subsequently confirmed that it didn't report its loan exposure to Texmaco Group to the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency, or IBRA. 

 IBRA was formed early last year to reform the shattered banking sector and BNI is one of the banks tagged for government recapitalization. 

 Under the recapitalization program, BNI should have transferred the worst portion of its non-performing loans to IBRA for recovery as IBRA has been given immense legal power to tackle recalcitrant debtors. 

 Despite Texmaco's failure to pay back any of the loans that led BNI to write off the loans completely last year, BNI didn't transfer the loans to IBRA and retain the loans on its books. 

 Most banking analysts reckon that such loans should have been transferred to IBRA for more effective collection. 

 "It's a big question mark as to why BNI didn't transfer the loan to IBRA, I think BNI is trying to avoid letting the powerful IBRA to be Texmaco's creditor," said Pradjoto, a banking analyst, and the whistle-blower of the on-going Bank Bali scandal. 

 If the loans were transferred, Texmaco Group would probably top the list as one of the largest debtors of IBRA, which has expressed determination to take stern steps against non-cooperative debtors. 

 BNI said in a press statement that it's negotiating with Texmaco on debt-restructuring proposal, which would include a debt-to-equity conversion. 

 The BNI scandal is the latest to hit the Indonesian banking sector. Since late July, the sector has been embroiled in the high-profiled Bank Bali scandal that involved the mis-use of funds under the government guarantee program, allegedly for political purposes. 

 And banking analysts say the BNI case is only one of possibly many collusion cases between state banks and powerful conglomerates

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Lower As Local Banks Buy Dlrs
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- The Indonesian rupiah closed lower against the U.S. dollar Friday as local banks bought the dollar for year-end needs, and due to the market's increasing nervousness over the separatist movement in the country's troubled province of Aceh. 

 After rising to an intraday high of 7,245 rupiah, the dollar closed at IDR7,205 in Asia, up slightly from IDR7,185 late Thursday. 

 Offshore market participants were seen trimming their rupiah exposure against feared Y2K-related problems, dealers said. 

 Market players are also getting more nervous over the Aceh crisis. The Acehnese have threatened to stage massive protests Dec. 4 in the province, on the northern tip of the island of Sumatra, to commemorate the 30th anniversary of their independence movement. 

 Dealers said Friday they didn't see any intervention from Indonesia's central bank. In fact, statebanks, which usually sell the dollar on behalf of the central bank, were seen buying the U.S. currency. 

 They said the replacement of Hamzah Haz as Coordinating Minister for Social Welfare and Poverty Eradication by Basri Hasanuddim didn't effect the market as the move was expected and his post isn't seen as important as other coordinating ministry portfolios such as social, politics and security, and economy. 

 The dollar is expected to rise Monday to test IDR7,275, with support seen at IDR7,100, dealers said.

title: Indonesia c.bank upbeat even if Habibie re-elected.
text:
JAKARTA, Oct 15 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank governor Syahril Sabirin said on Friday he expected the rupiah to strengthen to the 6,000 to 7,000 level against the dollar even if unpopular President B.J. Habibie is re-elected. 

 Sabirin said the central bank did not intervene in the foreign exchange market to prop the rupiah, which strengthened slightly on Friday. The currency had come under pressure this week on concerns that mass unrest would follow if Habibie won next week's presidential vote. 

 "The rupiah is expected to return to a realistic range of 6,000 to 7,000," Sabirin told reporters. 

 "Remain optimistic," Sabirin said when asked whether the expectation could be achieved if Habibie was re-elected. 

 Sabirin said the rupiah's slight rise on Friday was due to market psychology. 

 "It was because of psychological factors. BI (Bank Indonesia) did not intervene," he said. 

 The rupiah was quoted at 7,990/8,040 against the dollar by 1020 GMT compared with 8,110/8,130 in late local trade on Thursday. 

 Worries over Habibie's presidential re-election revived old anxieties. The rupiah plunged to an historic low of 17,000 in January 1998 when autocratic former president Suharto named Habibie as his vice-presidential candidate.

title: Indonesia Money Rates Flat Midday;Rupiah Up, Confuses Mkt
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesian money market rates remain flat Monday midday in thin trading as market participants are uncertain which direction rates will go. 

 At 0414 GMT (12:14 a.m. EDT), the overnight interbank rate - considered the benchmark rate - was at 11.75% for foreign banks, and between 12% and 12.25% for most local banks, unchanged from Friday's levels. 

 Dealers said the rupiah's rapid strengthening Monday has confused the market, which had anticipated some upward movement for interest rates. 

 The market took its cue from last week's auction of central bank notes, at which the one-month notes' average accepted rate was 13%, up from 12.97% a week earlier. 

 "So the market was of the view that the downward trend of interest rates is likely to stop," said a treasurer at a local bank. 

 However, the ascent of the rupiah Monday morning has quashed market talk of rising rates. 

 The market is now focusing on Wednesday's central bank notes auction, which is expected to give the market an indication of rate movement. 

 Bank Indonesia has maintained its intervention rates at 11.75% for overnight funds and 12.25% for two-day funds. 

 The rather lackluster money market was in stark contrast with the actively trading foreign exchange market. 

 The rupiah strengthened at a rapid pace to 7,605 rupiah at 0423 GMT, up from IDR7,970 late Friday, on continued expectations that an early presidential election will soon lead to political stability.

title: Thai c.bank watching baht, no reason to worry-PM.
text:
BANGKOK, Sept 17 (Reuters) - Thai Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai told reporters on Friday the central bank was closely watching the movement of the baht and there was no reason to worry about the currency. 

 "The baht at current levels is in line with expectations of most economists, who say that the baht at 36-40 to the dollar is not a cause of concern," Chuan said. 

 Chuan said the currency decline was in line with those of other regional units in Indonesia and the Philippines. 

 Asked if the government would intervene the foreign exchange market to shore up the currency, Chuan said the central bank was monitoring the situation. 

 Chuan said that although the weaker baht had caused a hike in domestic oil prices, it would benefit Thai exporters. 

 The baht remained at its lowest level since September 23 in early morning trade. It was trading at 40.05/40.10 to the doller against 40.00/40.05 late Thursday.

title: Key points of Indonesia bank scandal audit summary.
text:
JAKARTA, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Following are key points of a summary prepared by PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) of its audit of transactions in Indonesia's Bank Bali scandal. 

 The auditors produced a full report of more than 100 pages and a 36-page summary. The former has been kept confidential, but copies of the summary are circulating among legislators and financial officials in Jakarta and Reuters has obtained a copy. 

 In a letter accompanying the summary, PwC said it "does not include all of the facts uncovered by our investigation". In particular, it leaves out analysis of the flow of funds. 

 All those who have been named in connection with the Bank Bali affair have denied wrongdoing. The central bank says it regards the summary of the audit as unfair and speculative. 

 THE BANK BALI SCANDAL: The scandal concerns a payment of 546 billion rupiah ($68 million) by PT Bank Bali Tbk to PT Era Giat Prima (EGP) for the recovery of loans from the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency (IBRA). EGP is run by Setya Novanto, deputy treasurer of the ruling Golkar party. 

 The Bank Bali loans were made to banks which were later taken over or shut down by IBRA. Bank Bali tried to get the loans repaid for months under a government guarantee scheme, without success. But after Novanto's intervention, Bank Indonesia and IBRA authorised the payment of 904 billion rupiah to Bank Bali. 

 CONCLUSIONS: PwC says it "uncovered numerous indicators of fraud, noncompliance, irregularity, misappropriation, undue preferential treatment, concealment, bribery and corruption during the processing and payment of the Bank Bali claims". 

 It urges further investigation of the potential involvement of several people, including "ministers, senior government officials, members of parliament, political party officials and prominent members of the business community". 

 The audit concludes Bank Bali's claims for loan repayment were regarded as ineligible, but were nevertheless paid. 

 "Overwhelming amounts of evidence came to hand from Bank Indonesia and IBRA which evidenced their jointly held view that the Bank Bali claims were administratively ineligible," it says. 

 OPPORTUNITY FOR FRAUD: The audit says there was considerable uncertainty over whether Indonesia's government would pay interbank claims, and such knowledge therefore "would constitute extremely valuable insider information," allowing those in the know to buy interbank claims in the market at a large discount. 

 It says during the period when Bank Bali was approached, "a small circle of government officials was aware of international financial institution pressure to settle interbank claims and the Indonesian government's decision to make payments". 

 This small circle included the IBRA executive committee and Bank Indonesia's board of governors, the summary said. 

 THE BANK BALI TRANSACTION: The summary notes a "sudden reversal" in the handling of Bank Bali's claims by Bank Indonesia and IBRA. After originally saying the claims were ineligible, both institutions later paid them. 

 It names an individual at IBRA who personally sought to get the claims repaid, despite concerns of others in IBRA. It says Bank Indonesia also appeared to give the Bank Bali claims preferential treatment. 

 It notes reports of several meetings between Bank Bali and top financial and political officials. Some of these meetings have been confirmed by the participants, others denied. 

 Rudy Ramli, president director of Bank Bali when the deals were done, has produced a journal detailing various meetings with top officials and close associates of President B.J. Habibie. The audit says a confidential source has confirmed Ramli's account and its probe found nothing to dispute its substance. 

 The summary says that after the payment by Bank Indonesia of Bank Bali's 904 billion rupiah claim on June 1, there was an "immediate explosion of financial transactions...involving numerous individuals and entities". 

 "These transactions involve techniques commonly associated with money laundering, including currency swaps, foreign exchange transactions and cash withdrawals," it says. 

 LIMITS OF AUDIT: PwC was appointed to investigate the Bank Bali transactions after pressure from the International Monetary Fund and World Bank for a transparent, independent audit. 

 But the summary details several limitations. "PwC has not been afforded adequate time and sufficient access to information, and has been delayed from conducting an investigation which meets international standards and which ensures complete transparency and accountability to the public," it said. 

 "However, the restrictions that were placed on us were not so severe as to prevent us from reaching conclusions on key issues." 

 PwC says that at the request of the Supreme Audit Agency, its summary does not disclose the names of the ultimate recipients of the 546 billion rupiah commission paid by Bank Bali to EGP. 

 It says its investigations were hampered by the refusal of various parties to comply with requests for key documents and Bank Indonesia's refusal to allow access to some bank accounts. 

 It said there was an "overwhelming impression that certain parties were interested (whether from instruction or of their own volition) to ensure that our review did not determine the ultimate recipient of funds out of the claim payment". 

 DIVISIONS IN IBRA: The audit summary notes tensions between high-level officials in IBRA. It says these disputes led to a refusal to hire staff for certain divisions and raised concerns about the impact on IBRA's operations. 

 RISK OF RECURRENCE: The audit summary says "the current set up of the government guarantee scheme in IBRA and Bank Indonesia is not adequate to avoid a similar occurence". It recommends that IBRA develop a comprehensive fraud risk management programme. ((Andrew Marshall, Jakarta newsroom +62 21 384 6364, Fax +62 21 344 8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Indonesian Money Mkt Rates Steady;Ctrl Bk Keeps Rate Unch
text:

title: EMERGING MARKET  FX -Colombia peso at new depths.
text:
LONDON, Sept 8 (Reuters) - Colombia's crawling-peg currency system was looking shaky on Wednesday after the peso hit an all-time closing low against the dollar. 

 Emerging Asian currencies were dented again by Indonesia, where carnage in East Timor and a scandal at Bank Bali forced the rupiah through 8,500 to the dollar despite central bank intervention. 

 The Polish zloty sank deeper into the weak side of its broad trading band after a downward revision in the official growth forecast, and on continued concern that some privatisation inflows will be kept out of the foreign exchange market. 

 Speculation that Colombia will be forced to scrap its currency system and float the peso has escalated since Chile decided last week to do away with its own trading bands. 

 The Colombian currency slumped a further 1.2 percent on Tuesday to a record closing low of 1,981.5 to the dollar in Bogota, just 4.15 pesos above the floor of its daily band. 

 It was unmoved during the London morning, which generally sees very little Latin American currency trading, but was expected to come under further pressure later in the day. 

 Colombia needs to cut interest rates to stimulate the recession-hit economy, and analysts say it is only a matter of time before it ditches the band. 

 "If they have a further testing of the band and the markets know the political willpower is not there to raise interest rates, that could be the breaking point," said Neil Dougall, Latin America economist at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in London. 

 RUPIAH DIVES 

 The rupiah dived further amid fears the East Timor violence could affect much-needed loans from donors as the international community presses Indonesia to clamp down on anti-independence militias sowing terror in the territory. 

 The Bank Bali scandal also continued to rumble, with preliminary results from a probe into alleged insider trading due to be presented to parliament next week. 

 Bank Indonesia Governor Syahril Sabirin said the central bank was intervening to support the rupiah, but the action was having little effect. The government target for the rupiah was still in the range of 6,000 to 7,000 to the dollar, he added. 

 The rupiah's slide and this week's weaker yen tone continued to take their toll on other regional currencies. 

 The Thai baht dropped through 39 to the dollar on Tuesday, hitting an 11-month low of 39.40, and remained firmly on the weaker side of 39 on Wednesday. The Philippine peso also fell sharply, tumbling through 40 to the dollar to 10-month lows. 

 UNCERTAINTY INCREASES 

 Analysts said Indonesia's woes were an excuse to sell Asian currencies as uncertainty increased ahead of the year-end. 

 "There's no reason to think that what goes on in East Timor will affect the economies of Thailand or the Philippines, or to a certain extent even Singapore," Andrew Dermot-Fung, economist at Standard Chartered in Singapore, told Reuters Television. 

 "But in this kind of environment, with the Y2K issue, investments are just not really flowing into East Asia. Everyone wants to wait and see what's going to happen...(and) any excuse will be taken to sell off the region's currencies." 

 The zloty, which fell below its basket parity on Tuesday for the first time since March, weakened further to around 0.90 percent below the midpoint. 

 A revision of the Finance Ministry's GDP growth forecast to 5.2 percent from 5.6 percent in 2000 added to gloom over reduced prospects for capital flows into the market. 

 But most analysts said the zloty selloff was overdone, as a suggested debt buyback would use up only a small proportion of the large privatisation inflows expected later this year.

title: Indonesian rupiah touches 8,500 to dollar.
text:
JAKARTA, Sept 8 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah fell to 8,500 to the dollar on Wednesday amid concerns about the crisis in troubled East Timor. 

 The rupiah recovered slightly a few minutes later and was trading at 8,440/8,490 at around 0618 GMT. 

 "The rupiah broke the 8,500 level when most Indonesian forex dealers were having lunch. A player from Singapore bought a dollar offer at 8,500 probably from Indonesian players," a dealer with a foreign bank said. 

 The last time the currency was below 8,500 was on April 27. 

 Dealers expected further losses in the rupiah after overseas markets open. 

 Players took profits at around midday which brought the currency to the 8,300 level against the dollar but then it weakened again because sentiment was very weak, dealers said. 

 They said investors were concerned about international pressure on Indonesia's government due to the East Timor chaos and other domestic worries including the unresolved Bank Bali  scandal. 

 The IMF's statements that it is worried about Jakarta's economic program, the scandal over PT Bank Bali Tbk and the situation in East Timor caused players to release their rupiah holdings, dealers said. 

Indonesia's central bank said on Wednesday its intervention to support the sliding rupiah was having little impact. 

 The IMF said on Tuesday it is reviewing the situation in Indonesia and will shortly make a decision on whether to send a mission to Jakarta that was previously scheduled for mid-September. Bank Indonesia also said on Wednesday it would hold interest rates at current levels in the near future due to political and economic uncertainties. 

 Bank Indonesia is due to hold its regular auction of one and three month central bank SBI certificates on Wednesday. 

 Dealers said the possible further decline in the SBI rates would make the rupiah even less attractive. ((Moris Morissan, Jakarta newsroom +62 21 384-6364; Fax +6221 344-8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

 "The rupiah weakened as players wait for an overall solution over the bank controversy," one dealer with a foreign bank said.
