 The market was still very nervous about PT Bank Bali Tbk  and there seem to be few reasons to go long of rupiah while the situation remains so unclear, dealers said. 

 Dealers said there was no sign of state banks coming in early to support the rupiah. 

 A row over a large payment made by Bank Bali to have loans recovered from the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency (IBRA) has hurt the foreign exchange and stock markets, undermined confidence in IBRA and prompted Golkar dissidents to warn the party may drop Habibie as its presidential candidate. 

 The central bank has been trying to talk up the currency, and is selling around $5-10 million a day, although it insists this does not represent intervention. But despite Bank Indonesia's efforts, the rupiah has remained vulnerable. 

 "Until you get a clearer situation on what is going to happen with the banks and who is going to be blamed, the rupiah looks less attractive," a local dealer said.

title: Bank Indonesia Continues To Push Interest Rates Down

 JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--After running into some resistance to allowing interest rates to fall, Bank Indonesia has managed to convince foreign exchange and money markets that the decline can continue without harming the rupiah, market participants say. 

 Dealers say that by regularly intervening in the currency and money markets, the central bank has managed to signal that interest rates should continue to fall, without causing the rupiah to slip. 

 "The central bank is winning the battle against market sentiment," said Pardi Kendy, head of treasury at PT Bank Buana. "It intervened to keep the exchange rate below 7,000 (to the dollar) and it's managed to switch sentiment towards the rupiah back to neutral." 

 Short-term Sertificat Bank Indonesia interest rates have tumbled from around 35% at the beginning of the year to 13.13% at the weekly auction Wednesday. 

 The rate decline, which has been gradual and steady, has happened over the past few months largely without damaging the rupiah. This has been due to the central bank's successful efforts to decouple the exchange rate from interest rates. 

 In recent weeks, however, the decline in interest rates caused some jitters in the foreign exchange markets, prompting participants to sell rupiah, believing that the low rates render it unattractive to hold.

However, market watchers say the central bank has managed to convince
the market to adopt a more neutral stance toward the rupiah by using
state banks to aggressively sell dollars for rupiah and heave market
sentiment around. The fact that the pace of the interest rate decline
has slowed also has helped to limit any market panic.



"There are a lot of psychological factors involved in trading rupiah,
when somebody buys or sells in a big way, everybody follows suit," said
a dealer at Citibank in Jakarta.



"When state banks sell dollars aggressively like they have been doing,
this eliminates the panic effect and people start to ask whether it's
really worth it to buy dollars at these levels," he said.



Although Bank Indonesia doesn't unilaterally decide how much rates
should fall by - the market does - the central bank can greatly
influence the direction of yields by its presence in the market and by
guiding rates down.



Traders note that while the rupiah hasn't strengthened over recent
weeks due to a lack of major supporting factors, it hasn't really
weakened either. Repeated comments from government and central bank
officials indicating they're satisfied with the current rupiah level
have also helped to stop the currency from slipping.



The rupiah late Wednesday was quoted at IDR6,915, slightly lower than
IDR6,865 late Tuesday in Asia.



In the money markets, Bank Indonesia has helped guide rates close to
all-time lows while maintaining ample liquidity in the market, dealers
say.



"By edging down the overnight intervention rate gradually, Bank
Indonesia sends a psychological message to the market," said a money
market dealer at a U.S. bank in Jakarta.



"This indicates rates are going to come down again and limits market
concerns about sudden interest rate declines," the dealer said.



Bank Indonesia, which has been steadily cutting its overnight
intervention rate over recent months, Tuesday cut the rate at which it
offers to absorb liquidity from the market to 11.75% from 12% and
maintained that rate Wednesday ahead of the SBI rate cut.
-
                Interest Rate Declines Crucial
-



Pushing down interest rates has been a major focus of the central
bank. Under advice from the International Monetary Fund, interest rates
were jacked up last year at the height of Indonesia's financial crisis
to help prop up the then-plummeting rupiah.



The high rates - which rocketed to around 70% at one point -had a
drastic effect on much of Indonesia's real economy and its banks.
Lowering the rates is viewed as crucial to kickstarting the economy
again.



With inflation falling at a rapid pace, economists reckon Bank
Indonesia can continue to guide interest rates lower, although whether
they can fall to historic single-digit lows is viewed as unlikely.
(Indonesian interest rates have never been in single digits, the lowest
pre-crisis level was around 11.75% in 1987.)

title: WRAP: Indonesian Interest Rate Decline Spooks Rupiah
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's interest rate decline hit the rupiah Friday with the currency falling to its lowest level in a month, prompting market participants to talk of an end to its long bull run. 

 The rupiah's slide has also led to speculation that the downward trend in interest rates has come to an end. 

 With the Indonesian election commission expected to finally endorse the June poll results Monday and allocate parliamentary seats, concerns that Indonesia's political transition may not pass off peacefully are also weighing on the rupiah, analysts say. 

 Market participants continue to gamble that Megawati Sukarnopurti's Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle, or PDI-P, has the best chance of piecing together a coalition capable of winning the presidency later this year. 

 However, lingering signals that incumbent B.J. Habibie could also mount a challenge to retain the top job are causing some market jitters. 

 "People are a bit nervous," said Pardi Kendy, head of treasury at PT Bank Buana in Jakarta. "If PDI-P doesn't win, its supporters could go on the streets and create bloodshed." 

 The political concerns, coupled with external factors, including a general slump in currencies across the region and a hawkish interest rates stance by U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan, all combined to pile pressure on the rupiah. 


Having slipped slightly against the U.S. dollar over the past few
days, the currency hit an intraday low of IDR7,080 before ending Asian
trade at IDR6,860 to the dollar, down 1.3% from late Thursday and the
lowest level seen since June 22.
         Interest Rate Decline Main Factor



The Jakarta Stock Market was also hit by the weaker rupiah and fears
that the U.S. may raise rates at some point, sending the bellwether
index down 2.6%.



But the main factor weighing on the rupiah, analysts say, is the
decline in domestic short-term interest rates, which is causing the
local currency to lose its attraction to investors.



Short-term rates have tumbled from their lofty highs of 70% last
August to around 35% at the beginning of the year, and now stand at
14.5%. To a large extent, Bank Indonesia has managed to guide interest
rates down to ease pressure on the real economy while not harming the
rupiah, mainly by decoupling interest rates from the exchange rate.



That policy worked effectively as long as rates remained sufficiently
high by regional standards to still attract punters to the rupiah. Now,
that perception has changed, prompting many in the market to gamble that
the downward rate trend will stop at next week's central bank paper
auction.



"Bank Indonesia has to be very cautious in terms of lowering interest
rates further," said Ruth Setyabandi, treasury chief at Chase Manhattan
in Jakarta. "This is a very delicate balancing act for the central
bank."



The policy of allowing rates to fall at Bank Indonesia's weekly
Sertifikat Bank Indonesia auction has also been effective as other
positive factors were supporting the rupiah while rates were declining.
         Greenspan Factor Weighs On Market



Signs that the pickup in other Asian economies has abated though,
coupled with the tensions between China and Taiwan and the cloud of a
U.S. interest rate hike hanging over the region, means those supporting
factors are no longer there.



"The Greenspan and regional concerns are all fundamental reasons to
weaken the rupiah," said Kevin Ng, economist at ABN Amro in Singapore.



Money market participants in Jakarta say the rate decline already
prompted some to avoid buying central bank notes at the auctions over
the past couple of weeks and has led to large sales of SBI stocks in the
secondary market.



"Rates are going lower and lower and people fear they could fall to
single digits," said Pardi, at Bank Buana. "For those expecting high
yield from the rupiah, there's no reason to buy it."



Still, the government and the International Monetary Fund said Friday
that there was still room to "cautiously" let rates fall further. The
IMF has said interest rates could fall to historic single digit lows by
the end of the year, while Bank Indonesia says they would likely fall to
between 10-14%.



Given the regional downturn though, market participants doubt interest
rates can continue to fall for now, particularly while Indonesia's
political future remains uncertain.



Still, most dealers don't expect the rupiah to slide dramatically and
many bulls still expect the currency to strengthen back to IDR6,500 to
the greenback by the end of the year.



Pardi noted that the presence of the state banks in the market Friday
in bidding the rupiah back up was evidence that Bank Indonesia would
intervene to halt any marked weakening in the currency.



"I believe the market will try again to break the IDR7,000 level, but
the central bank and government will do its utmost to stop that," he
said.

title: FACTBOX - Chronology of financial crisis.
text:
LONDON, June 28 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of the financial crisis in emerging markets, first triggered by devaluation of the Thai baht two years ago. 

 1997 

 July 2 - After a failed defence of the Thai baht, Bangkok floats its currency and calls on the IMF for "technical assistance". The baht is effectively devalued by about 15-20 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah starts to crumble. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso slump as confidence in the region deteriorates. 

 August 11 - In Tokyo, the IMF unveils a rescue package for Thailand including loans of $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah plunges. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Oct 27 - Asian jitters spill over to world stock markets. The Dow plunges 554 points, its largest ever single-day point loss. 

 Oct 31 - IMF unveils Indonesia's $40 billion aid package, of which $23 billion is front-line defence. 

 Nov 17 - Korea abandons its defence of the won. 

 1998 

 Jan 12 - Peregrine, one of Asia's largest independent investment banks, collapses under a mountain of bad loans to Indonesian borrowers. 

 Jan 22 - The rupiah collapses. It is dealt at 17,000 to the dollar at one stage. Bank Indonesia intervenes and drives the currency back to end at 11,800. 

 March 23 - Indonesia nearly doubles interest rates to boost the rupiah and control inflation. 

 May 21 - President Suharto of Indonesia steps down under strong pressure and is succeeded by former deputy president B.J. Habibie. 

 June 5 - International lenders and Indonesian companies reach a deal to reschedule the country's massive corporate debt. 

 June 10 - China's central bank governor warns that the weak yen is having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade. 

 In Taiwan, the local dollar hits new 11-year lows and the Australian dollar plummets past 59 U.S. cents. 

 June 29 - South Korea closes banks for the first time, shutting five ailing operations in a major step towards meeting the mandate of the IMF rescue package. 

 July 13 - Japanese Prime Minister Hashimoto resigns. 

 August 17 - Russia sets a 90-day partial debt moratorium on foreign credits, says short-term rouble debt will be restructured. Government abandons floor value for rouble of 7.13 to the dollar, saying new lower limit is 9.5. 

 August 25 - Rouble suffers its worst one-day fall in nearly four years. Government announces rouble debt restructuring with terms which foreign investors say amount to default. 

 August 28 - Rouble trade is suspended indefinitely on the main Moscow Interbank Currency Exchange (MICEX). 

 August 31 - Wall Street suffers its second-largest points loss in history, plunging 6.37 percent and sparking another series of stock market routs in Asia. 

 September 2 - Russian Central bank abandons support for the rouble. 

 Malaysia announces that the ringgit will be fixed at 3.80 to the dollar indefinitely. 

 Wall Street stages its second-largest comeback in history, sparking a rally in Asian markets. 

 September 3 - Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is sacked. 

 September 9 - Russian Central bank chief Sergei Dubinin quits. 

 October 2 - Russian exporters start selling half of their hard currency revenues at MICEX under a central bank order aimed at supporting the rouble. Shares hit all-time lows. 

 October 28 - Brazil unveils a 28 billion reals ($23.5 billion) austerity plan of budget cuts and tax hikes to shore up the economy. 

 November 6 - The Russian government and foreign banks agree in general on terms to restructure short-term rouble debt. 

 November 13 - The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and rich nations announce a loan package totalling more than $41 billion for Brazil to avoid a financial meltdown in Latin America. 

 1999 

 January 13 - Brazil plunges deeper into crisis and sends world markets tumbling when it devalues the real. 

 June 15 - Mexico unveils a $23.7 billion financing programme designed to fireproof its economy. 

 March 10 - Brazil's lower house of parliament passes a bill raising a financial transaction tax, a key measure in its anti-crisis austerity plan. 

 April 28 - The IMF agrees to lend Russia $4.5 billion over 18 months but insists several reform proposals must be passed by its parliament before the money is released. 

 June 15 - Mexico unveils a $23.7 billion financing programme designed to fireproof its economy. 

 June 17 - Russia's State Duma votes against a petrol tax bill considered vital to win IMF cash promised in April. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1999.

title: Central bank  sees rupiah 7,500/dlr after election.
text:
JAKARTA, June 4 (Reuters) - Indonesian central bank governor Syahril Sabirin said on Friday he saw the rupiah firming to around 7,500 against the dollar after the Monday's parliamentary election. 

 "I feel after the election, the rupiah will strengthen probably to around 7,500 per dollar," Sabirin told reporters. 

 He said the fact that the campaign had been largely peaceful so far would also help the currency. 

 Sabirin said he expected security would be maintained after the election. 

 He said Bank Indonesia would not intervene to prop up the rupiah, but he added that the bank would convert dollars in small amounts from foreign loans to buy rupiah. 

 Sabirin said the strengthening rupiah would remain favourable for Indonesian exports. 

 "If the rupiah strengthened to around 7,000, we still can compete because that level is still competitive compared with other countries," he said. 

 Sabirin said he is optimistic that year-on-year inflation will be between 10-13 percent by end 1999, with the benchmark one-month central bank certificate (SBI) rate falling to 17-20 percent. 


The rupiah	  was quoted at 7,950/8,050 against the dollar at 0605 GMT, compared with 8,075/8,125 late on Thursday.



Wednesday's auction of one-month SBIs resulted in a weighted average interest rate of 24.65 percent against 26.12 percent a week earlier. ((Muklis Ali, Jakarta newsroom +62 21 384-6364; Fax +6221 344-8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Bank Indonesia/Rupiah -3: Could Move Quickly To IDR7,500
text:
"The rupiah would still be competitive at (IDR7,000 to the dollar), or even slightly lower than that maybe," Sjahril said. 

 He noted that Indonesia's currency had lost more of its value than other regional currencies, meaning it can still appreciate while maintaining its competitive edge. 

 At 0536 GMT (1:36 a.m. EDT), the rupiah was quoted at IDR8,065 to the dollar. Sjahril said the currency was stuck around that level now, as some doubts are lingering about how smoothly the elections will go. 

 He said he expects the currency could move to IDR7,500 to the dollar "quite easily," after the elections, though. The budget for fiscal year 2000, ending March 31, is based on an average rupiah/dollar level of IDR7,500. 

 Indonesia's election campaign winds down later Friday, bringing to an end three weeks of rallying by Indonesia's 48 political parties, which has been largely peaceful, even though the campaign has produced huge, euphoric crowds. 

 Many market-watchers are now betting that next week's elections leave a few parties with enough seats to form a strong coalition later this year, which in turn could lead to a rally in the rupiah, long considered a pariah currency in Asia. 

 A rupiah that is too strong, however, could raise some problems for the government in maintaining its export competitiveness, prompting speculation that the central bank might have to step into the market to depress the currency. 

 Sjahril said Friday, however, that the central bank will leave the rupiah's level to market forces, saying the central bank won't intervene. He said Bank Indonesia would continue to change foreign loans into rupiah on the market as required, though, which the central bank doesn't consider intervention per se.

 The firm rates were a result of foreign banks borrowing from the money market on the short-end to fund their purchase of the central bank's one-month notes. 

 Such strategy proves profitable as banks are expecting interest rates to come down. Banks buying the one-month notes can lock in the high interest rates while funding such purchases through the money market where rates are falling. 

 Dealers expect to see another 100- to 200-basis-point fall in the auction of one-month central bank notes later in the afternoon.

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Regionals buoyed by firmer yen.
text:
1010 GMT - Asian regional currencies were broadly firmer as 

 the yen strengthened on profit-taking by foreign funds which 

 had bought dollars on expectations of strong dollar demand. 

     Dealers said exporter offers were also depressing the 

 dollar. 

     But they said the dollar's downside was being supported so 

 far, as firm buying offers were said to be lined up at around 

 119.60-119.80 yen by Japanese investors. 

     *** Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara delivered a 

 cautiously upbeat outlook for 1999 in its annual report, 

 predicting the economy would recover modestly this year from 

 Asia's financial crisis. 

 Bank Negara said the country's gross domestic product was 

 expected to rise by one percent year-on-year in 1999 after 

 shrinking 6.7 percent the year before - its worst economic 

 performance since 1985. 

 It said the current account surplus was likely to shrink to 

 29.5 billion ringgit this year against 36.1 billion ringgit in 

 1998. 

     The Consumer Price Index is expected to be at four percent 

 against a 5.3 percent rise last year. 

     Bank Negara said interest rates would be maintained at 

 current levels if there were no inflationary pressures, which 

 it said was unlikely to be a serious risk. 

     *** The baht was again treading water after failing to 

 react to details of a $3.5 billion economic stimulus package, 

 unveiled by the government on Tuesday. 

     Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda said the package 

 should stimulate demand and help the economy grow between 0.4 

 percent and 1.4 percent, depending on exports. 

     Thailand officially signed sale contracts with eight 

 companies that won bids in the country's recent auction of loan 

 assets seized from defunct finance companies. 

     *** The Korean won slipped as state-run banks absorbed 

 dollar offers from exporters. 

     The government said consumer prices fell sharply in March, 

 as the more stable won kept a lid on price rises. 

     The CPI rose 0.5 percent year-on-year, down from a massive 

 9.0 percent rise a year earlier. The PPI fell 4.3 percent 

 year-on-year in March, against a 15.1 percent rise a year ago. 

     The government said the trade surplus was expected to reach 

 $2.2 billion in March, compared with a $3.68 billion surplus 

 last year. 

     *** The rupiah was on the right side of 9,000 per dollar 

 amid speculation Bank Indonesia had intervened aggressively to 

 prop it up ahead of the fiscal year-end today. 

     The market failed to react to Standard & Poor's reversal of 

 a move on Tuesday to downgrade Indonesia's long-term foreign 

currency rating. 

     S&P reset Indonesia's rating at triple-'C'-plus from SD 

 (selective default) and raised its outlook, ironically placing 

 Jakarta's rating higher than where it started the week. 

 It said the decision reflected Indonesia's rescheduling of 

 US$210 million worth of principal on a $350 million commercial 

 loan. 

 Indonesian central bank director Miranda Goeltom said there 

 was a high chance the country would achieve its March target of 

 zero percent month-on-month inflation. 

 Month-on-month inflation fell to 1.26 percent in February 

 from 2.97 percent a month ago. The February consumer price 

 index stood at 207.12, 53.39 percent higher than in February 

 1998.

 119.50 yen, while its advance would be limited to 121.50, where 

 exporter sales were expected. 

     They said Japanese banks were also expected to sell the yen 

 against other currencies like the euro and Australian dollar. 

     But the underlying trend of the euro remained bearish, 

 especially after the European Commission trimmed its 1999 

 growth forecast to 2.2 percent from 2.6 percent. 

     The continuing Kosovo crisis also added pressure on the 

 European currency. 

     *** The IMF approved a $4.9 billion payment for Brazil, the 

 second installment of a massive international rescue deal 

 agreed last year. 

     *** The baht was again treading water after failing to 

 react to details of a $3.5 billion economic stimulus package, 

 unveiled by the government on Tuesday. 

     The package aims to create almost half a million new jobs 

 through billions of baht in new government spending, tax breaks 

 for businesses and households and big cuts in energy prices. 

     Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda said the package 

 should stimulate demand and help the economy grow between 0.4 

 percent and 1.4 percent, depending on exports. 

     The IMF gave a thumbs-up to the package, saying it was an 

 important step towards recovery, with tax cuts carefully 

 designed to boost consumer spending and lower costs. 

     But analysts said the measures were only likely to produce 

 results around the last quarter of this year as the proposed 

 government expenditure filtered through the economy. 

     *** The Korean won was steady after gaining a bit of ground 

 on Tuesday as exporters flooded the market with dollars. 

     The government said foreign direct investment plans 

 totalled $620 million in March, against $243 million a year 

 ago. 

     Commerce Minister Park Tae-young said FDI plans received in 

 the first quarter of this year totalled $1.9 billion from $572 

 million the year before. 

     Park also said the government was considering easing the 

 strict 200 percent debt-to-equity ratio for major companies to 

 boost exports. 

     All companies are currently required to meet this target by 

 the end of the year. 

     *** The rupiah was holding up on the right side of 9,000 

 per dollar amid speculation Bank Indonesia had intervened

 aggressively to prop it up ahead of the fiscal year-end today. 

     Dealers said the move was expected to help companies book 

 improved first quarter financial results. 

     It also helped to counter the impact of a ratings downgrade 

 by Standard & Poor's. 

     The central bank said it regretted S&P's decision to slap 

 Indonesia with a "selective default" rating, noting that it had 

 never defaulted on commercial bank loans or bonds. 

     But an S&P official in New York said overnight that the 

 agency would probably remove the "selective default" foreign 

currency rating before too long. 

     He said Indonesia's weekend move to restructure some of its 

 debt could be seen as creditor positive in the larger scheme of 

 things.

title: Indonesian Rupiah Ends Higher After State Bank Dlr-Selling
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah closed higher in unusually active trading Tuesday as Bank Indonesia allegedly intervened via bank intermediaries in both offshore and domestic markets ahead the end of the fiscal year end. 

 The rupiah, however, gave up some of its gains in the afternoon session as local customers rushed to buy dollars, taking advantage of the sharp fall in the U.S. currency. 

 After jumping as high as 8,450 (IDR) to the dollar, the rupiah ended at IDR8,725 in the spot market in Asia, stronger from IDR8,850 late Monday. 

 "Bank Indonesia's intervention was likely tied up to a fiscal-year end window dressing," said a dealer with a local bank, noting that the dollar-selling took the market by surprise given that the central bank wasn't seen intervening indirectly in the market at the end of the calendar year. 

 There will be no trading Wednesday for fiscal-year book closing. 

 Dealers said the central bank acted via state banks and foreign banks. The bank rarely, if ever, intervenes directly. 

 Although dealers said Bank Indonesia ultimately failed to move the rupiah significantly, it mitigated the possible negative impact of a rating cut by Standard & Poor's Corp. Earlier Tuesday, the ratings agency cut Indonesia's long-term foreign currency credit rating to "selective default" from triple-C-plus. 

 Some dealers expect Bank Indonesia to intervene Thursday, marking the beginning of the new fiscal year, to bring the rupiah nearer to the bank's target of IDR7,500 to the dollar. 

 "If the rupiah continues to strengthen, the government will have more room to let interest rates fall," a dealer with a foreign bank said. 

 The average interest rate of Bank Indonesia's one-month note fell to 37.42% at the weekly auction Tuesday, marking the third consecutive weekly fall. 

 Other dealers, however, said Bank Indonesia's limited foreign exchange reserves limits its intervention capacity.

title: Rupiah strengthens ahead of fiscal year-end.
text:
JAKARTA, March 30 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah strengthened on Tuesday, with the central bank seen intervening in the market to prop up the currency ahead of fiscal year-end on Wednesday. 

 The rupiah ended at 8,740/8,750 against the dollar compared with 8,845/8,855 at the close of local trading on Monday. 

 "Bank Indonesia is likely to have agressively intervened into the market by selling dollars through Singapore, Hong Kong and Australian banks to prop up the rupiah ahead of fiscal year-end," one foreign bank dealer said. 

 The dealer said the move was expected to partly help corporates book improved first quarter financial results. 

 Dealers said news that Standard & Poor's on Tuesday lowered its long-term foreign currency sovereign credit rating on the Republic of Indonesia failed to weaken the rupiah, they said. 

 "The rating cut had largely been expected. It's not surprising," another dealer said. 

 Dealers said a slight fall in the key central bank certificates (SBIs) auction rates on Wednesday had largely been expected. 

 Bank Indonesia's weekly auction of one-month SBI certificates resulted in a weighted average interest rate of 37.42 percent against 37.48 percent last week. ((Jakarta newsroom +6221 384-6364; Fax +6221 344-8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Indonesian Money Mkt Rates Stable Early On Ample Liquidity
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesian money market rates were mostly steady early Wednesday as liquidity is ample in the market and banks are having no problem accessing funds. 

 Bank Indonesia injected 4.197 trillion rupiah (IDR) into the money market earlier in the day. The injection came from the maturity of rupiah Bank Indonesia absorbed during previous intervention, with maturities ranging from one to seven days. 

 At 0148 GMT (8:48 p.m. Tuesday EST), the overnight interbank rate - considered the benchmark rate - was between 33% and 34% for foreign and secured joint venture banks and between 34% and 35% for local banks. 

 Bank Indonesia is launching another intervention in the money market to absorb excess liquidity. It's offering an overnight rate at 33%, higher than its regular intervention rate at 30%. 

 Later in the day, the nation's central bank will hold auction of its one-month notes to absorb IDR12 trillion. 

 The note yield was 37.60% last week, down from 37.64% previously. 

 "We can easily get the same yield again," said a dealer with a local bank. 

 In the foreign exchange markets, the dollar was trading at IDR8,830, down from IDR8,910 late Tuesday in Asia.

title: Indonesian Money Market Rates Flat Ahead Of SBI Auction
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesian money-market interest rates were mostly unchanged Wednesday, with ample liquidity in the market ahead of the auction of one-month central bank notes later. 

 At around 0319 GMT (10:19 p.m. Tuesday EST), the overnight interbank rate - considered the benchmark rate - was between 33% and 34% for foreign and large joint-venture banks, and between 34% and 35% for better-quality local banks, both largely unchanged from Monday. 

 Dealers doubt Bank Indonesia will be able to guide interest rates lower at the auction of Sertifikat Bank Indonesia notes later in the session, despite comments by central bank Governor Sjahril Sabirin Tuesday indicating the bank would like to. 

 Bank Indonesia will seek to absorb 12.5 trillion rupiah (IDR) ($1=IDR8,900) at its weekly Wednesday central bank paper auction. 

 Bank Indonesia last week auctioned IDR9.983 trillion one-month SBI notes, at a weighted average interest rate of 37.64%. 

 The fact that the rupiah appears to have reversed its upward trend however, limits the central bank's options, said a treasury chief at a Jakarta bank. 

 "We don't expect much change in rates, considering the exchange rate hasn't recovered yet," he said. 

 In the foreign-exchange markets, the dollar was fetching IDR8,950, up from IDR8,855 late Tuesday in Asia. 

 Earlier, Bank Indonesia injected IDR4.422 trillion into the money market. 

 The injection represents the reversal of Bank Indonesia's daily intervention in the money market, which absorbs excess liquidity through borrowing from the market in maturities ranging from overnight to seven days.

title: Indonesian Money Mkt Rates Steady; No Bank-Deposit Runs Seen
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesian money-market rates were mostly steady midmorning Monday, as the market digested the government's major bank-reform plans unveiled this weekend. 

 Dealers said there was no evidence of deposit runs on banks in the wake of bank closures. 

 At 0320 GMT (10:20 p.m. Sunday EST), the overnight interbank rate - considered the benchmark rate - was between 32% and 33% for foreign and large joint-venture banks, unchanged from Friday. 

 "It's pretty much status quo in the money market," said the head of treasury at a foreign bank in Jakarta. 

 "You have to be positive," he said. "We've got through this weekend with a decent list of banks to close. It probably looked so bad two weeks ago, the market should be encouraged by this." 

 Indonesia closed 38 banks Saturday, took over seven others and said it would recapitalize an additional nine. The number of banks closed was at the top end of market expectations. 

 Treasury dealers said there was no evidence in the money market of deposit runs sparked by the closures - something which would become quickly evident from money-market liquidity movements. The treasury chief said this was because of the well-publicized fact that the government is guaranteeing all deposits. 

 Dealers said Bank Indonesia intervened early in the money market at a bidding rate of 33%, in a continued effort to drive the rupiah higher and absorb rupiah liquidity. 

 "Bank Indonesia's still intervening at 33%," said a treasury dealer at a U.S. bank. "This is a good move. The central bank wants to see the rupiah stronger and is trying to tighten rupiah liquidity." 

 Bank Indonesia's early - relatively high - intervention rate is unchanged from last week. The central bank injected IDR5.732 trillion into the money market early Monday, as a result of its intervention in the past week to absorb excess liquidity. 

 In the foreign-exchange markets meanwhile, the rupiah was quoted at IDR8,930, stronger than IDR9,150 late Friday, as the market welcomed the banking announcement.

title: Indonesian rupiah stable, testing 9,000.
text:
JAKARTA, March 8 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah was stable in early trade on Monday and was testing the 9,000 mark amid worries over weekend violence in the eastern island of Ambon, dealers said. 

 The rupiah was quoted at 8,900/8,920 against the dollar by 0220 GMT compared with 8,900/8,930 in late trading on Friday. 

 "The market has been testing the 9,000 mark for about a week. But the central bank, through state banks, has so far been able to keep the local currency mostly at the current levels," one foreign bank dealer said. 

 The central bank, Bank Indonesia, placed rupiah intervention rates on five tenors early on Monday. The central bank paid 30 percent for one-day, 33 percent for two, three and four-day money and 34 percent for seven-day money. 

 The intervention was seen as an effort to help tighten liquidity which would was expected to prevent the rupiah from breaking through 9,000, another dealer said. 

 Dealers, however, said rupiah liquidity remained largely sufficient for big banks. Bank Indonesia supplied some 3.5 trillion rupiah temporarily to the money market early on Monday. 

 More than 200 people have died in and around Ambon in two months in communal fighting between Christian Ambonese and Moslem migrants from elsewhere in the vast archipelago. ((Jakarta newsroom +6221 384-6364; Fax +6221 344-8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Indonesian Money Market Rates Up; Bk  Indonesia Intervenes
text:

title: Indonesia  Ginandjar says no CB  forex intervention .
text:
JAKARTA, May 1 (Reuters) - Indonesia's top economics minister Ginandjar Kartasasmita said on Friday the central bank would not intervene in the foreign exchange market and would allow the rupiah to float freely. 

 "(Central) Bank Indonesia will not risk its international reserves speculating in the foreign exchange market," he told Reuters in an interview. 

 "Accordingly, it will not intervene in the market, allowing the rupiah to float freely," he said. 

 Ginandjar, coordinating minister for economics and finance, also said an impartial central bank was essential to the country's reforms. 

 "One of the key elements of Indonesia's economic programme is to have an independent central bank that can restore the stability of the rupiah. 

 "The policies adopted to achieve the stability of the rupiah are fairly straightforward and simple and have been incorporated into the programme supported by the International Monetary Fund," he said. 

 The IMF's executive board is due to meet in Washington on Monday to review Indonesia's progress in economic reforms as well as to release $1.0 billion from the next $3.0 billion balance of payments loan, with the rest to be disbursed over the following two months. 

 Ginandjar, the guiding minister in the reform programme, also said Bank Indonesia would not create new rupiahs in net terms through its domestic operations. 

 "This policy implies that its net domestic credit expansion will be zero, maintaining the net domestic assets of its balance sheet at their end-March level," he said. 

 "Under this policy, any growth in liquidity credits will be offset by a corresponding increase in Bank Indonesia's open market operations," the minister added. 

 The central bank operates in the money market by issuing central bank certificates (SBIs) to drain excess liquidity, and buys short-term securities (SBPUs) to inject liquidity. 

 Ginandjar said the latest report from the central bank showed it had successfully implemented its policies since the beginning of April. 

 "The net international reserves of Bank Indonesia have increased by $1.1 billion since the end of March, thanks in part to the support from Bank Indonesia's foreign commercial bank correspondents. 

 "At the same time, its net domestic assets are below the end-March level, meaning that Bank Indonesia has had a contractionary stance in net terms. 

 "Continued action along these policies will restore the stability of the rupiah quickly," the minister said.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals off a bit as dollar rise.
text:
0500 GMT - Asian currencies slightly off their morning highs as the dollar extends its gains against the yen, but trading remains slow. 

 * The rupiah hovers around the 8,000 level but looks set for further weakness amid mounting social tension in Indonesia, where student protests demanding President Suharto's resignation are assuming a more menacing tone. 

 At least two students were injured at the weekend in clashes with police on the island of Sumatra. 

 * Indonesian rating agency PT Pefindo said problem loans may account for 60 percent of the banking industry's total loans by the end of this year if the country's private debt issue is not resolved. 

 It cut the ratings for seven Indonesian firms and lowered the outlook on all rated local banks, citing continued deterioration in asset quality and liquidity. 

 * Dealers say the rupiah's fall is currently being cushioned by dollar offers near 8,100 and the central bank's high interest rate policy. 

 * They say Bank Indonesia intervened in the money market this morning to drain excess liquidity and keep central bank deposit rates high. 

 * Elsewhere, Malaysia's continuing water shortage and fears the Rashid Hussain group's acquisition of troubled Sime Bank may dilute its earnings are casting a pall on Malaysian markets. 

 Trade Minister Rafidah Aziz said in weekend news reports that she has received letters from industrialists saying they may have to stop operating if the water problems persist. 

 * Kuala Lumpur shares are down nearly two percent but the ringgit appears to be holding up fairly well and dealers say 3.79 will be a tough barrier for the dollar. 

 * The Singapore dollar is being undermined by the yen's weakness and looks set to fall through 1.60 to the U.S. dollar. 

 * The Thai baht could continue to see some inflows from last week's Bangkok Bank share issue, but dollar demand from Hong Kong-based U.S. investment houses should cap its gains near 38.70 for the time being. 

 * Some dealers estimate that about three-quarters of the $1 billion raised by the share sale have already been through the market. 

 * The Philippine peso is weak but off its early lows, fuelled by banks buying dollars to cover forward contracts with multinational companies. 

 * Manila shares reached a seven-week closing low on worries about the presidential election in May and disappointing first quarter results. 

 * In South Korea, the finance ministry says direct foreign investment fell sharply to $572 million in the first quarter from $2.12 billion a year ago. 

 * This follows weekend news that the monthly jobless rate hit a 16-year high in March, with seasonally unadjusted unemployment soaring to 6.5 percent from 3.4 percent last March. 

 * But the won is up from its lows as traders bet on it climbing further on month-end exporter deals. 

 * The Taiwan dollar is back below the key T$33 level on the back of a sagging yen, but fears of the central bank will limit its decline.

title: Goldman Sachs Sees Stable Quarter For Most Southeast Asia  Currencies
text:
HONG KONG -(Dow Jones)- Southeast Asian currencies look set for a more stable second quarter, though for most, solid appreciation will have to wait until investors grow more confident in the battered region, Goldman Sachs said in a recent regional economic report. 

 The sole exception among traded Association of Southeast Asian Nation currencies is the Thai baht, which Goldman Sachs sees moving to 37.0 baht per dollar over the quarter and to 35.0 baht over the next six-to-12 months. 

 The strengthening will come as the country records a larger current-account surplus and more capital inflow, which will offset a deeper-than-expected downturn in Thailand's real economy this year, Goldman Sachs said in its latest Asian Economic Quarterly publication. 

 Indonesia's rupiah will stabilize between 7,000 and 7,500 to the U.S. dollar in the second quarter, due to the country's economic bailout and reform agreements with the International Monetary Fund, Goldman Sachs said. 

 Goldman Sachs indicated that the key risk to its Indonesia forecasts would be a slowdown or backsliding by the government on its economic reform and stabilization commitments to the IMF. 

 "Given the amount of depreciation of the currency, the state of the banking system, the external debt and the entrenched vested interests in the cabinet, the risks are high," Goldman Sachs said. 

 Without IMF intervention, Indonesia's economy would likely contract in both 1998 and 1999, Goldman Sachs said. As it is, Goldman Sachs is forecasting a 10% contraction of real gross domestic product and inflation of 50%. 

 The investment bank's figures for Thailand are only slightly better, with the economy seen contracting by 6.0% in 1998 and inflation running at about 13%. 

 In terms of Indonesia's currency stability, confidence will be an investor focus. Though the IMF agreement should stabilize the rupiah, "further appreciation is unlikely without...a clearer political picture and...settlement of the private sector's external claims," Goldman Sachs said. 

 Nominal interest rates are seen rising over the next three months, reflecting inflationary pressure, Goldman Sachs said. 

 Malaysia, whose economic growth is expected to slow to 2.5% in 1998, can expect to see the ringgit strengthen as regional sentiment improves, Goldman Sachs said. But as long as the country's top two leaders are differing on the treatment of bank shareholders during economic restructuring, capital inflows will be depressed and the ringgit's appreciation will be delayed, Goldman Sachs said. 

 The Singapore dollar moved generally in line with the rupiah and other regional currencies in the first quarter of the year, "as it has been buffeted by the contagion effects throughout the period," Goldman Sachs said. 

 The Monetary Authority of Singapore hasn't altered its monetary policy since reversing the currency's outright appreciation. To maintain price stability, the MAS continues to track the currency against a trade-weighted currency basket. That has resulted in a raising of interest rates in times of currency instability. The three-month rate, however, has eased from a peak of 12% to between 5.0% and 6.0% toward the end of the first quarter. 

 Singapore's growth this year is expected to hit 2.5% to 4.5%, according to government figures, and consumer prices should be only a touch higher.

title: Chronology of Indonesia's financial crisis.
text:
JAKARTA, April 8 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of Indonesia's financial crisis and political developments in the country the last eight months. 

 1997 

 July 8 - The rupiah starts to crumble. Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso all slump as confidence in the region fades. 

 August 14 - Jakarta abolishes managed exchange rate system. The rupiah sinks further. 

 October 6 - Rupiah hits a low of 3,845. 

 October 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the International Monetary Fund for financial assistance. 

 October 31 - Indonesia's IMF package unveiled. It provides more than $40 billion in aid, although front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 November 5 - IMF approves a $10-billion loan for Indonesia as part of the international package. 

 1998 

 January 6 - Indonesia unveils its 1998/99 budget projecting 32.1 percent growth in revenue and expenditure over current budget and four-percent economic growth. 

 The rupiah loses half its value against the dollar over five days, breaking through the 10,000 level before a slight recovery, on perceptions the budget would not meet IMF-mandated austerity measures and rumours Jakarta might declare a debt moratorium. 

 January 10 - Indonesia's President Suharto, under increasing international pressure to adhere to IMF conditions, announces the delay or review of 15 infrastructure projects. 

 January 11 - IMF first Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer in Jakarta for talks on the IMF's programme and how to proceed with it. 

 January 14 - IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus says in Jakarta the IMF is asking Indonesia to sign a new letter of intent committing itself to implementing further reforms. 

 January 15 - Camdessus and Suharto sign an agreement strengthening economic reforms. 

 January 16 - Camdessus says he expects Indonesian and Thai economies to recover within two years. 

 January 21 - The rupiah falls to a record low of 12,000 to the dollar as reports surface that corporates now paying dollar debts in rupiah. 

 January 22 - The rupiah collapses a week after the IMF package shows no signs of easing Indonesia's debt and confidence crisis, hitting a record low of 17,000 amid economic pessimism and hints Research and Technology Minister Jusuf Habibie may be the preferred vice-presidential candidate. Bank Indonesia intervenes and currency recovers to 11,800. 

 January 23 - Indonesia presents a revised budget sticking to IMF-agreed figures. The budget expects zero growth in fiscal 1998 and 20 percent inflation, but assumes the rupiah will be at 5,000 to the dollar. It ends the day at 12,000. 

 January 27 - Indonesia announces a temporary freeze on debt servicing but says it is not a moratorium as companies with dollars can pay creditors. It also announces banking reforms in which the government will guarantee the security of both depositors and creditors. 

 January 28 - Indonesia again stresses it has not sought a debt moratorium, saying a temporary freeze suggested on servicing corporate debts is voluntary. 

 Mobs attack shops owned by ethnic Chinese in Central Java over rising food prices. 

 February 3 - Singapore proposes a multilateral system of guarantees for Indonesian letters of credit. 

 February 4 - Indonesian government gives a lukewarm response to a proposal by U.S. economist Steve Hanke to set up a currency board, where the rupiah is pegged to another currency. 

 Suharto refuses to name a running mate in March election, saying this was the right of parliamentary groups. 

 February 6 - Thousands of troops and police in show of strength in practice sessions in Jakarta before the indirect presidential elections. Chief debt negotiator Radius Prawiro says Indonesia's total foreign debt is $137.424 billion. 

 February 9 - Growing unhappiness over Suharto's handling of the economic crisis leads to a signature campaign to replace him. 

 Suharto says he will announce new steps on the rupiah exchange rate, the first hint a fixed currency system might be implemented. Curfew is imposed in an eastern Indonesian town after more riots. 

 February 10 - Bank Indonesia Governor Soedradjad Djiwandono tells parliament the government is weighing the merits of a currency board system. 

 February 11 - Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad says the government is preparing for a currency board system. The rupiah rises to 7,200 to the dollar. 

 Suharto accuses unnamed parties of seeking to undermine the economy by driving the rupiah down. 

 Police detain 140 people after protests in Jakarta over rising food prices. 

 February 12 - The ruling Golkar party names Habibie and parliamentary speaker Harmoko as its vice presidential candidates. 

 February 13 - Suharto tells President Clinton the IMF is failing to stem Indonesia's financial crisis. Clinton objects to Jakarta's plans to fix the rupiah to the U.S. dollar through a currency board system. 

 The rupiah surges as high as 8,100 on signs the plan will proceed. 

 February 14 - The IMF threatens to halt the bail-out fund over Indonesia's plans to peg the rupiah. ASEAN central bankers discuss a proposal to use regional currencies for intra-regional trade. 

 Police detain 154 people in riots over rising prices that leave at least three dead, and Jakarta bans mass rallies during voting in March. Rioters torch shops owned by ethnic Chinese, churches and cars in three west Java towns. 

 Two rioters are shot dead in Praya town on Lombok island. 

 February 16 - Indonesian police warn they would shoot rioters on sight even as new military commander Wiranto played down the impact of the violence. 

 February 17 - President Suharto fires central bank governor Soedradjad Djiwandono for opposing the currency board proposal. Djiwandono is replaced by U.S.-trained economist Sjahril Sabirin. The sacking draws immediate attacks from global lenders as it is seen as a direct affront to their demands that Jakarta reform its economy. 

 February 18 - Habibie assured of the vice presidency after winning the backing of the powerful armed forces. 

 German Finance Minister Theo Waigel signs agreements to provide Indonesia with 375 million marks ($205.3 million) in financial aid to fight the economic crisis. 

 Thousands of students and labourers, angered by rising prices, stone dozens of shops and offices in the southeast Sulawesi capital. 

 February 19 - U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley and German Finance Minister Waigel insist Indonesia must follow IMF-prescribed economic reforms to get economy on track. 

 Chinese shopowners open a public relations drive in Java selling commodities at discounts to Javanese poor. 

 Singapore says it would make US$2 billion available if its plan for international guarantees for Indonesian letters of credit is implemented. 

 The IMF and United States, while stressing that the currency board scheme was premature, show flexibility by saying that the currency plan could be considered once banking reform, corporate debt and other economic issues had been addressed by Jakarta. 

 February 20 - Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad says Indonesia so far faced no problem in meeting state foreign debts, while telling parliament that the government wants to maintain good ties with the IMF. 

 Mar'ie says Suharto had instructed the finance ministry and the Central Bank to prepare for the introduction of a currency board by taking into consideration all views and development, locally and abroad. 

 February 26 - Indonesian companies hold their first formal meeting with a steering committee of lenders to find ways to resolve the country's $74 billion in private debt. 

 March 3 - U.S. special envoy Walter Mondale meets with Suharto, said by U.S. officials to be carrying a "blunt" message from President Clinton. 

 March 6 - IMF delays disbursement of second $3 billion tranche to Indonesia due on March 15, saying they will not discuss Indonesia's reform programme before April. 

 March 10 - Suharto re-elected President for a seventh five-year term by the 1,000 member People's Consultative Assembly (MPR), as thousands of students held protest rallies against the election. 

 March 11 - Suharto is sworn in. Habibie is elected vice-president. Markets are unmoved. 

 March 14 - Japanese prime minister Ryutaro Hashimoto arrives in Jakarta for talks with Suharto, the first G7 leader to do so. 

 March 16 - Suharto swears in 36 new cabinet ministers, including his daughter Siti Hardiyanti Rukmana and an old golfing buddy, as students and riot police clash at the National University in Jakarta. 

 March 18 - Indonesia's new top economic minister Ginandjar Kartasasmita meets with IMF Asia-Pacific head Hubert Neiss in a bid to review the country's reform process and get the delayed disbursement of $3 billion in aid back on track. 

 March 20 - Indonesia says decision has been made to drop for the time being the idea of implementing a currency board system. The government will however still look for a means to stabilise the battered rupiah. 

 Government proposes a five percent tax on foreign currency purchases. This idea was subsequently shelved. 

 March 24 - Indonesia consults Mexican officials on the "Ficorca" plan Mexico used to ease its debt crisis in 1983, sources said. 

 March 26 - The Jakarta post reports that unemployment has risen to about 8.7 million people, or 10 percent of the workforce. 

 March 27 - Indonesia proposes to the IMF a formula to resolve its huge private debt, drawing on the Ficorca model. 

 March 30 - Indonesia agrees to privatise 12 state-owned firms under the new reform agenda under discussion with the IMF. 

 March 31 - Indonesia's decision to freeze the minimum wage at 1997 levels is seen as effectively halving the real income of Indonesia's urban poor, due to 50 percent inflation expected in 1998. 

 April 2 - The IMF and Indonesia agree on new figures for the fiscal 1998/99 budget, including a decline of 5 percent in GDP, inflation rate of 45 percent and a budget deficit of 3.5 percent. 

 The IMF warns Suharto to show his commitment on tough reforms or lose IMF support. 

 IMF agrees to a gradual phasing-out of commodity subsidies in consideration of the increasingly troubled plight of poorer Indonesians. 

 April 3 - Singapore announces it will provide $3 billion in a bilateral trade finance scheme to enable Jakarta to pay for imports from Singapore. 

 April 4 - The government suspends the licences of seven banks under a bank reform scheme widely applauded by the IMF and the international financial community. Seven other banks were placed under the supervision of the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency. A few of Suharto's relatives and friends are known to control, or hold large equity stakes in, some of the banks. 

 April 6 - Finance Minster Faud Bawazier says the government will set up two state companies to handle the assets of liquidated banks and insure depositors. 

 April 7 - A committee of international bankers plan a meeting in New York later in April to discuss details of Indonesia's private debt restructuring. The meeting is to be attended by officials from the Indonesian central bank and the IMF. 

 The Export-Import Bank of Japan will extend $1 billion of an expected $3 billion loan to Jakarta. The loan will go to a trade-linked finance guarantee system, to aid in facilitating trade. 

 April 8 - Talks between Indonesia and the IMF are concluded. The IMF says a new agreement on economic reforms will be closely monitored and frequently reviewed to ensure Indonesia complies with its terms. Further loan disbursements are conditional on Indonesia's "substantive action" on reforms. 

 Indonesia revises its fiscal 1998/99 (April 1) economic growth expectation to minus four percent and its expected budget deficit to 3.2 percent of GDP. it also forecasts inflation for the fiscal year of 17 percent. 

 Indonesia also announces a gradual easing of subsidies on most commodities and the floating of seven state-owned companies. The government will also assist private firms in paying debt, and abolish the granting of monopoly privileges in basic commodities. 

 Japan says it will extend $2 billion in loans to Jakarta, out of $5 billion promised as part of the original IMF rescue package.

On the one hand, the IMF's apparent return to favor in Jakarta suggests its package of key reforms may yet go through. This is ultimately supportive of the rupiah over the long term and therefore may explain its recent stability, analysts said. 

 An alternative view is that some traders may simply be hanging onto positions in the currency in the hope of tidy profits if the fixed rate is indeed introduced. The argument follows that if those punters get a definitive 'no', they will dump the rupiah and send it sharply lower. 

 MFR's Koss describes three scenarios: 'You will have IDR15,000 in the short term if you don't have a currency board and you don't have an IMF plan and IDR5,000 if you just get a currency board - for a week, or as long as it would last. If you end up with an IMF package and no currency board, it might just hang in at these levels.' 

 Ironically, the frantic buying interest unleashed by the currency board issue may also have contributed to the rupiah's more stable performance of late. 

 'People were introduced to two-way markets again,' said Keith Woodfin, currency analyst at Foreign Exchange Analytics in Essex, Connecticut. 'People found some actual demand for the rupiah and that has given them a sense of caution' over holding short-rupiah positions. 

 Indeed, traders note that much of the rupiah's excessive volatility in January was due to a virtual drought of demand. Thin volumes produced precipitous downward slides and at the same time made it easier for Bank Indonesia, the central bank, to engineer rebounds through intervention. 

 But the signals coming out of Indonesia remain extremely discouraging, analysts say, and the possibility of massive flight from the rupiah remains high. 

 One crucial concern is the growing number of riots over rising prices across the country and the doubts over the security forces' ability to peacefully contain them.

title: Chronology of Indonesia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Feb 20 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of the financial crisis that has rocked Indonesia and the political developments in the country in the last eight months. 

 1997 

 July 8 -  The rupiah starts to crumble. Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso all slump as confidence in the region rapidly deteriorates. 

 August 14 - Jakarta abolishes system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah sinks further. 

 October 6 - Rupiah hits a low of 3,845. 

 October 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the International Monetary Fund (IMF) for financial assistance. 

 October 31 - Indonesia's IMF package unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 November 5 - IMF approves a $10-billion loan for Indonesia as part of the massive international package. 

 1998 

 January 6 - Indonesia unveils its 1998/99 budget projecting an increase of 32.1 percent growth in revenue and expenditure over the current budget and a four-percent economic growth rate. 

 The rupiah loses half its value against the dollar over five days, breaking through the 10,000 to the dollar level, before a slight recovery. 

 The freefall is triggered by perceptions that the budget was not tough enough to meet IMF-mandated austerity measures and by market talk that Jakarta might declare a debt moratorium. 

 January 10 - Indonesia's President Suharto comes under increasing international pressure to adhere to IMF conditions. He announces the delay or review of 15 big infrastructure projects. 

 January 11 - The IMF's first Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer arrives in Jakarta for talks about the IMF's programme and how to move ahead with it. 

 January 14 - IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus heads for Jakarta, saying the IMF was asking Indonesia to sign a new letter of intent committing itself to implementing further IMF reforms. 

 January 15 - Camdessus and President Suharto sign an agreement strengthening economic reforms. 

 January 16 - Camdessus says he expects the Indonesian and Thai economies to recover within two years. 

 January 21 - The rupiah falls to a record low of 12,000 to the dollar as reports surface that corporates were now paying their dollar debts off in rupiah. 

 January 22 - The rupiah collapses a week after the IMF package shows no signs of alleviating Indonesia's debt and confidence crisis. 

 The currency hits a record low of 17,000 amid economic pessimism and on hints that Research and Technology Minister Jusuf Habibie might be the preferred vice-presidential candidate. Bank Indonesia intervenes and pulls the currency back up to 11,800. 

 January 23 - Indonesia presents a revised budget sticking to figures agreed with the IMF. The budget expects zero growth in fiscal 1998 and inflation of 20 percent. But it also assumes the rupiah will be at a level of 5,000 to the dollar. It ends the day at 12,000. 

 January 27 - Indonesia announces a temporary freeze on debt servicing but says it is not a moratorium as companies with the dollars can pay their creditors. 

 It also announces banking reforms in which the government will guarantee the security of both depositors and creditors. 

 January 28 - Indonesia again stresses it has not sought a debt moratorium, saying a temporary freeze suggested on servicing corporate debts is entirely voluntary. 

 Mobs attack shops owned by ethnic Chinese in Central Java over rising food prices. 

 February 3 - Singapore proposes a multilateral system of guarantees for Indonesian letters of credit. 

 February 4 - Indonesian government gives a lukewarm response to a proposal by U.S. economist Steve Hanke to set up a currency board, where the rupiah is pegged to another currency, most likely the U.S. dollar. 

 Suharto refuses to name a running mate in March election, saying it was the right of parliamentary groups, not his right, to name the candidate. 

 February 6 - Thousands of troops and police put on a show of strength in practice sessions in Jakarta before the indirect presidential elections in early March. Chief debt negotiator Radius Prawiro says the country's total foreign debt was $137.424 billion. 

 February 9 - Growing unhappiness over Suharto's handling of the economic crisis leads to a signature campaign to replace him. 

 Suharto says he will announce new steps on the exchange rate of the rupiah, giving the first hint that the fixed currency system might be implemented. A curfew is imposed in an eastern Indonesian town after more riots. 

 February 10 - Bank Indonesia Governor Soedradjad Djiwandono tells parliament the government was weighing the merits of a currency board system. 

 Outgoing army chief Feisal Tanjung says recent riots were inflamed by people were trying to undermine national unity. Planning Minister Ginandjar Kartasasmita declines to be vice-president candidate, paving the way for Research and Technology Minister Jusuf Habibie. 

 February 11 - Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad tells parliament the government was preparing the groundwork for a currency board system. The rupiah rises to 7,200 to the dollar on Indonesia's plan to introduce a fixed-rate currency. 

 Suharto also accuses unnamed parties of seeking to undermine the economy by driving the rupiah down. 

 Police detain 140 people after protests in Jakarta over rising food prices. 

 February 12 - Suharto repeats warning of a plot to destabilise the government as hundreds riot in a West Java town. 

 Suharto also appoints a loyalist, General Wiranto, as new military chief. The ruling Golkar party names Habibie and parliamentary speaker Harmoko as its vice presidential candidates. 

 February 12 - The IMF insists Indonesia is not ready for a rigid currency regime. 

 February 13 - Suharto tells President Clinton the IMF was failing to stem his country's financial crisis. Clinton objects to Jakarta's plans to fix the rupiah to the U.S. dollar through a currency board system. 

 The rupiah surges to as high as 8,100 on signs the plan will proceed. 

 February 14 - The IMF threatens to cut off the bail-out fund for Indonesia over its plans to peg the rupiah. ASEAN central bankers discuss a proposal to promote the use of regional currencies for intra-regional trade. 

 Police detain 154 people in riots over rising prices which left at least three dead and Jakarta bans mass rallies during voting in March. Rioters had torched shops owned by ethnic Chinese, churches and cars in three west Java towns. 

 Two rioters are shot dead in Praya, a town in the holiday island of Lombok. 

 February 16 - Parliamentary speaker Harmoko withdraws from vice-presidential race in favour of Habibie, who was also endorsed by the Moslem-backed United Development Party. 

 As rioting over rising food prices worsens, Indonesian police warn they would shoot rioters on sight even as new military commander Wiranto played down the impact of the violence. 

 February 17 - President Suharto fires central bank governor Soedradjad Djiwandono for opposing the currency board proposal. 

 Djiwandono replaced by U.S.-trained economist Sjahril Sabirin. The sacking draws immediate attacks from global lenders as it is seen as a direct affront to their demands that Jakarta reform its economy. 

 February 18 - Habibie assured of the vice presidency after winning the backing of the powerful armed forces. 

 German Finance Minister Theo Waigel says President Suharto promised to rethink the currency board plan, throwing the markets into confusion about Jakarta's position on the scheme. 

 Waigel also signs agreements to provide Indonesia with 375 million marks ($205.3 million) in financial aid to fight the economic crisis. 

 Thousands of students and labourers, angered by rising prices, stone dozens of shops and offices in the southeast Sulawesi capital of Kendari, while a series of hoax bomb threats are received in Ujung Pandang in South Sulawesi. 

 February 19 - The country's currency crisis remains unresolved amid confusion over Jakarta's position on the currency board as rioting is reported in eastern Indonesia and West Java targeted at Chinese shopowners. The rupiah steady at 8,750/8,850. 

 U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley and German Finance Minister Waigel insist Indonesia must follow IMF-prescribed economic reforms to get economy on track. 

 Chinese shopowners open a public relations drive in  Java selling commodities at discounts to Javanese poor. China says it believed Indonesia could keep ethnic unity and deal with its economic crisis. 

 Singapore says it would make US$2 billion available if its plan for international guarantees for Indonesian letters of credit is implemented. 

 The IMF and United States, while stressing that the currency board scheme was premature, show flexibility by saying that the currency plan could be considered once banking reform, corporate debt and other economic issues had been addressed by Jakarta. 

 February 20 - Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad says Indonesia so far faced no problem in meeting state foreign debts, while telling parliament that the government wants to maintain good ties with the IMF. 

 Mar'ie says Suharto had instructed the finance ministry and the Central Bank to prepare for the introduction of a currency board by taking into consideration all views and development, locally and abroad. 

 Police brace for further unrest in Sulawesi island as no clear picture is seen on how the government would stabilise the rupiah.

title: Economist/ Currency  Boards/Asia-3: Assails IMF Crisis Mgmt
text:
Mexico in 1994 is a prime example of these events, as is Thailand, Indonesia and other countries with pegged exchange rates in Asia, according to Hanke. 

 Central banks 'have broad latitude to create base money,' Hanke notes, while 'Currency boards do not have this flexibility.' 

 'A currency board system required that domestic notes and coins, as well as deposit liabilities, be fully covered by foreign reserves denominated in foreign anchor currency, and that the domestic currency must trade, without restrictions, at an absolutely fixed exchange rate with the anchor currency,' he said. 

 He noted that currency boards 'run on automatic pilot' so that changes in the monetary base are 'determined solely by changes in the demand for domestic base money,' or what he defines as the balance of payments. 

 Hanke has long been critical of the IMF, partly because it played a role, in his view, in the demise of currency board arrangements that had been prevalent into the post-World War II period when the international monetary system shifted more toward central bank arrangements. 

 The IMF was created in the post-World War II period as a policeman of the global current account. And by Hanke's reckoning, it 'lent its weight and money to the establishment of new central banks' to create 'new clients and jobs for the boys,' he told the House Banking Committee. 

 Hanke is equally critical of the IMF in its handling of the Asia crisis. 

 'What the IMF has failed to realize is the fact that all of the countries in Asia where it intervened in 1997 - Thailand, Philippines, Indonesia and South Korea - had the same type of fatally flawed exchange-rate systems,' he stated. 

 'Although the dramatic events in Asia have generated a torrent of commentary about exchange rates, most of that commentary has either been half-baked or flat out wrong,' Hanke insists.

title: FOCUS-Indonesian markets finish higher on reforms.
text:
JAKARTA, Jan 27 (Reuters) - Indonesia's latest financial reform measures gave a boost to the embattled rupiah on Tuesday, with the stock market also edging up on improved sentiment. 

 Jakarta stocks closed up 0.55 percent at 476.31 points after a fall in state telecommunications company Telkom pulled the index off a high of 496.9 points. 

 The rupiah strengthened to 11,000/11,200 at the Jakarta close. It hit a low for the day of 14,000 against the U.S. dollar after opening at 14,000/14,500 in Singapore and 13,500/14,500 in Jakarta. 

Currency dealers said the central bank, Bank Indonesia, intervened in the market to give the rupiah a lift after the country unveiled new moves to reform the banking sector. 

 The bank sold dollars from the 13,500 to 11,200 levels, they said. 

 Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad announced the latest package of reforms, including government guarantees for depositors and creditors of the country's commercial banks. 

 Mar'ie also announced the creation of a new institution, the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency (IBRA), to ensure unsound banks were rehabilitated or merged with strong institutions. 

 The minister said the aim was to build a sound, modern and efficient banking system. 

 "With this guarantee in place, we expect that confidence in the banking system should soon begin to revive," a senior International Monetary Fund official said. 

 He said deposits should start to flow back into commercial banks and credit lines from foreign banks should be restored to allow trade to be financed. 

 Mar'ie said that in order to ensure adequate supplies of essential commodities, Bank Indonesia would provide a guarantee in foreign currency for imports of such goods. 

 The government-appointed debt negotiator, Radius Prawiro, announced a freeze on debt payments until a new framework was worked out between international lenders and Indonesian borrowers on how to tackle a crippling private sector foreign debt estimated at around $66 billion. 

 Prawiro also announced the setting up of a creditors' steering committee and borrowers' contact committee to manage the external debts of Indonesian corporations. 

 The central bank added further flavour to the day with a sharp interest rate hike in its short-term benchmark paper and a moderate increase in longer-term instruments to help restore confidence in the battered rupiah. 

 One currency analyst said this was aimed at giving rupiah investors a sufficient return while containing the risk of spiralling prices in basic commodities. 

 Although the government came out with a flurry of measures to get the crisis into control, market focus was on the private debt front, where the debate was whether the temporary freeze was a de facto moratorium or a respite to work out a new plan. 

 Mari Pangestu, economist at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said it was not a moratorium. 

 "I think it is temporary and not a moratorium," she said. "It is a temporary measure so that borrowers and lenders can sit together to discuss rescheduling, roll-overs or restructuring. A moratorium is only the last resort." 

 However, currency dealers said the full response from the market could only be seen next Monday when major financial centres reopened after Asia's extended long weekend. 

 They said central bank intervention had pointed to the possible direction, but a convinced market would pave the way for the rupiah to stage a full recovery despite nagging political questions on Indonesia's succession issue. 

 Dealers said spiralling prices also threatened social unrest that could further limit the rupiah's recovery.

title: FOCUS-Asia markets still jittery over Indonesia.
text:
HONG KONG, Jan 23 (Reuters) - Indonesia's revised budget did little to stabilise Asian markets on Friday, and some traded weaker on continued worries about the country's debt crisis. 

 Indonesian Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad raised revenue projections and expenditures in a new budget that appeared to closely track last week's deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 But traders said that in the absence of any big budget surprises, markets remained focused on the sliding rupiah and the nation's inability to pay its corporate debt. 

 "So what?" one Hong Kong trader said of the latest budget announcement. "There isn't a single solvent company in Indonesia with the rupiah so weak." 

 The central bank, Bank Indonesia, stepped in to support the rupiah on Friday morning. Dollar sales at the 14,000 level restored some short-term strength, but traders said the outlook was poor. 

 "This is not intervention designed to more permanently prop up the value of the rupiah...It is entirely centred on the spot, providing dollars to enable onshore Indonesian banks to repay their liabilities," Daniel Lian, head of markets research at ANZ in Singapore told Reuters Financial Television. 

 The rupiah interest rate is not high enough to compensate for uncertainty about the country's banking sector, private debt burden and political unease, he said. 

 "The rupiah rate doesn't offer compensation for investors for the risk premium, so there will not be support for the rupiah," Lian said, adding that he felt capital controls were inevitable. 

 The strongest stock market on Friday was Tokyo, which resumed its recent rally after Thursday's dip and closed up 2.34 percent at 16,789.11. 

 But the rupiah's freefall hurt parts of the region, even though many stock and currency markets managed to claw back some lost ground in late trading. 

 Hong Kong's Hang Seng index closed slightly stronger on Friday, reversing course in mid-afternoon as bargain-hunting surfaced. The index ended 36.47 points higher at 8,920.20 after a week-long battering triggered by the liquidation of brokerages Peregrine and C.A. Pacific Securities. 

 Dealers said the mood in Hong Kong remained grim, with the territory's confidence under siege just a few months after its July 1 return to Chinese sovereignty. 

 The overall tone in Asia was weak, with thin trading ahead of next week's Chinese New Year holiday exaggerating market movements. The rupiah's woes kept currencies soft while stock markets were mixed with sporadic signs of foreign interest. 

 Singapore's dollar was weaker at 1.7610 against 1.7565 on Thursday while its stock market dipped 0.76 percent to end at 1,259.83. 

 The Malaysian ringgit recovered from its low in the morning of 4.61 against the dollar, rising to 4.5280 in late trading. Dealers said ringgit investors took heart in the Indonesian central bank's rupiah intervention. 

 But longer-term concerns over Indonesia's currency pushed Malaysia's Composite Index of stocks down 2.89 percent to close at 558.57. 

 The Thai baht was virtually unchanged at 54.75 but stocks closed marginally higher, up 2.07 points, or 0.49 percent, at 422.87. 

 The Philippine peso recovered some ground to 43.80 after crashing through its third volatility band in early trade. But the unit's weakness in the absence of foreign buying helped to depress stocks by 0.21 percent to 1,704.07 points. 

 The Taiwan dollar quickly fell through the T$34 level, partly because of the weakness of the rupiah, but it recovered to close at T$33.925. The stock market was closed. 

 Jakarta stocks managed to gain ground throughout the day and closed 1.68 percent stronger at 450.98 on arbitrage with American Depositary Receipts, and domestic support, traders said. 

 Holiday cash demand lifted the South Korean won on Friday to 1,745.0 from 1,752.0 on Thursday while stocks made marginal gains to close at 486.86 points.
