title: FOCUS-Jakarta markets cool on budget, eye debt.
text:
JAKARTA, Jan 23 (Reuters) - Indonesia's financial markets reacted coolly to the government's 1998/99 revised budget on Friday as it contained no measures to solve the country's corporate debt mess, brokers and dealers said. 

 Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad's announcement of the budget before parliament had not been expected to address the looming debt nightmare, but analysts said the markets were growing restless and wanted to see quick action. 

 Senior government economic adviser Widjojo Nitisastro has said the government was working on the situation. 

 Vincent Low, fixed-income strategist at Merrill Lynch in Singapore, said all budget figures had been factored in because a fresh IMF-sponsored reform agreement had already shown revised growth, inflation and exchange rate assumptions. 

 "All this shows is that they (Indonesia) are becoming more realistic. But the immediate problem is still the corporate debt. It's not solved yet," said Low. 

 Mar'ie, formally presenting to the revised budget to parliament for the 1998/99 (April-March) fiscal year, confirmed figures announced last week of zero economic growth, an inflation rate of 20 percent and a rupiah level of 5,000 to the U.S. dollar. 

 Indonesia has total external debt of $140 billion, of which corporate debt is estimated at least at $66 billion. 

 The stock market struggled to rise after the budget announcement and was mainly helped by a climb in bellwether telecommunication shares. 

 The composite index of 287 companies edged up by 1.68 percent to end at 450.98 on Friday, with sentiment remaining shaky as the rupiah threatened to sink further. 

 However, the fragile rupiah calmed after the central bank intervened at the 14,000, 13,000 and 12,750 levels. 

 The rupiah ended in Jakarta at 13,000/13,500 after falling to a day low of 15,000 in the morning. 

 The rupiah crashed to a historic low of 17,000 on Thursday before rebounding to 12,000 on intervention. 

 Foreign currency dealers were seen holding back from attacks on the rupiah for now because of worries of renewed central bank intervention. 

 "The intervention programme of Bank Indonesia in the past three days is entirely centred on the spot and is essentially providing dollars to any onshore Indonesia banks to repay their liabilities," Daniel Lian, head of Asian markets research at ANZ Bank in Singapore, told Reuters Financial Television (RFTV). 

 "This is not an intervention that is designed to more permanently prop up the value of the rupiah. They are not in the position to do that," Lian said. 

 Jakarta dealers said rupiah settlement of maturing dollar contracts was among factors causing the currency to slide. 

Currency dealers said many domestic banks were hampered in mobilising sufficient dollar funds to meet maturing obligations after they had their credit lines cut. 

 Prolonged weakness in the rupiah has sparked fresh rumours of currency controls or even a debt moratorium, although the government has repeatedly said it was committed to repaying foreign debt. 

 Lian said investors were not getting enough return to get into the rupiah. 

 "The uncertainty about Indonesia's private currency debt and political uncertainty, compounded with heightened risk of social instability, is the risk premium that investors need to get in order to buy rupiah," Lian said. 

 "The rupiah interest rate at any measure doesn't offer to compensate investors the risk premium. There will be no support for the rupiah," Lian said. 

 "Obviously, Indonesian corporates have hoarded sizeable amounts of dollars overseas. When those dollars come back onshore, it could provide a lot of impetus to the rupiah, but we are not seeing it migrating back onshore," he said.

title: Asian  currencies  sag,  intervention  supports rupiah.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 23 (Reuters) - Depressed Asian currency markets largely ignored Indonesia's revised, IMF-endorsed 1998/99 budget, driving the rupiah to seek refuge in the arms of the central bank. 

 Dealers said the budget, which included a forecast of zero economic growth, inflation at 20 percent and a rupiah rate of 5,000 to the U.S. dollar, contained no surprises and left the market anxious about the unresolved issue of corporate debt. 

 "The market is not focusing so much on the budget revisions. It's just a theoretical exercise. What they want to see is how the government is going to cope with the debt restructuring," said the head of regional currencies trading at a European bank in Singapore. 

 "Up to now, they haven't offered anything and if nothing is done, the rupiah will not be able to stabilise at all," he said. 

 Dealers said intervention by Bank Indonesia in a very thin market, characterised by spreads as wide as 1,000 rupiah, was practically the only thing keeping the rupiah out of the depths. 

 The Indonesian central bank was believed to have sold dollars for rupiah at the 14,000 level and its repeated rate checking in Singapore and Jakarta kept traders on their toes. 

 "The market's very nervous of pushing dollar/rupiah higher. But if we don't see a retracement to 12,000 by Monday, there could be another sharp plunge in the rupiah," the dealer said. 

 "The demand for dollars from Jakarta is still very strong." 

 Banque Paribas said emergency Indonesian action to deal with the country's private sector debt crisis might be on the cards. 

 "What this implies for the currency market is that liquidity will likely dry up as the currency overshoots to unbelievable levels, and wide spreads could see offers reach 20,000," it said in a daily commentary. 

 Indonesia's troubles continued to weigh on other Asian markets, but the effect was more muted as activity wound down ahead of next week's holidays for the Lunar New Year and Islam's Eid al-Fitr. 

 Dealers began to view the rupiah more as an isolated disaster. 

 The Philippine peso, an island of relative calm in recent sessions, succumbed to mounting pressure from the region and fell far enough to trigger a market rule that effectively suspends trading for the day. 

 Manila traders said no central bank presence was detected and even foreign banks, which were actively selling dollars recently, had stopped doing so. 

 The Malaysian ringgit was weak at 4.5100 to the U.S. dollar, against 4.5325 late Thursday, but activity was confined to a subdued range with dollar bids around 4.45/50. 

 The Singapore dollar slipped to 1.7635 to the U.S. dollar, against Thursday's 1.7500, but dealers said it looked well supported around 1.7700 for the time being. 

 "There's ringgit/Sing selling from the 0.3900 level and also flight-to-quality buying (of the Singapore dollar) from Indonesia," a dealer said. 

 The Thai baht dipped to 54.65 to the dollar onshore from 54.45 on Thursday as the market awaited details of talks between Thai Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda and the IMF on a review of Bangkok's bailout package. 

 IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer said the talks, which features measures to accelerate Thailand's economic reforms, went well, but he gave no details. Tarrin said he would issue a statement on Friday. 

 In north Asia, the Seoul won outshone its regional counterparts, firming to 1,745 per dollar versus Thursday's 1,760 close on strong cash demand ahead of the Lunar new year festivities. 

 But dealers said its rise would be blocked by dollar demand from importers and banks with month-end debt servicing needs. 

 The Taiwan dollar sagged below the T$34.00 level from Thursday's 33.706 close as worries about the region triggered dollar demand from importers ahead of the new year break. 

 The Hong Kong dollar slipped to HK$7.7430 from a previous 7.7385 close as local interest rates eased. 

 The Australian dollar held above a support level of US$0.6560 but failed to make much headway due to fears about the rupiah. 

 The Indian rupee firmed to 38.65 per dollar as the impact of the central bank's measures to tighten liquidity overshadowed the potential contagion effect of other Asian currencies.

title: Indonesia's Rupiah Ends Lower Despite Central Bk Support
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's rupiah (IDR) closed sharply lower against the U.S. dollar in thin dealings Thursday - at one point hitting an all-time low of IDR16,500 against the U.S. dollar - despite reports of interventions from the nation's central bank, dealers said. 

 The rupiah closed at IDR12,250 for each dollar in Jakarta session, down 6% from its close Wednesday at IDR11,500. 

 Dealers said that the rupiah fell to an all-time low of IDR16,500 in Singapore dealings. But, the rate was quoted among brokers, while in the interbank system, the new all-time low for the rupiah was IDR14,600, they added. 

 Dealers stated that maturing debts of Indonesian companies pushed the currency to new lows. 

 'The dollar jumped up because demand for the currency was not fulfilled. Virtually there were no dollar sellers,' said Pardi Kendy, the head of the treasury department of PT Bank Buana Indonesia. 

 Dealers welcome Bank Indonesia's relatively active interventions Thursday to ease the downward pressure on the rupiah. 

 As reported earlier, Bank Indonesia was heard intervening first before lunch time, and then shortly before dealings ended. 

 Dealers said the interbank trading was almost non-existent Thursday as no banks were willing to quote prices at the current level, further exacerbating the dollar shortage. 

 'The risk and the reward are not justifiable at these levels. It's just not worth it,' said a dealer with a large foreign bank in Jakarta. 

 Dealers, however, noted that the dollar shortage happened partly because foreign banks are unwilling to lend their dollars out, or are only doing business with good local banks, because of the increasing risk of default. This created liquidity disparities, dealers said. 

 'The market is so segregated and there were no market benchmarks we can use,' a dealer with a local bank added. 

 Although debt-related concerns were cited as the primary factor behind the rupiah's fall, the uncertainty over presidential succession also weighed on the currency.

title: FOCUS-Indonesian rupiah sinks, debt crisis mounts.
text:
JAKARTA, Jan 22 (Reuters) - Indonesia's rupiah currency melted to fresh lows on Thursday as the government grappled with a foreign debt nightmare and the prospect of mass lay-offs. 

 Businessmen and analysts said the economy was grinding to a halt because of currency, liquidity and debt turmoil. 

 But they said the full impact of the crisis would not be felt until next month when many workers returned after a Moslem holiday period and found factories shut. 

 "At this (currency) level, if anything a company produces has even a bit of imported content, it is finished," said an executive at a textile firm. "We are talking about factories closing down and lay-offs." 

 The rupiah sank to 15,000 to the U.S. dollar in early thin Singapore trade -- down a massive 84 percent since it was at 2,400 last July before Asia's currency crisis swept the region. 

 The rupiah later recovered on concerted central bank intervention and was quoted at 12,000/12,500 by 0850 GMT. 

 But its plunge dragged the rest of Asia's financial markets into a downward spiral, trashing the immediate outlook for the once supremely confident region. 

 While Indonesia's capital Jakarta was calm on Thursday, a sense of despondency gripped residents as they watched their currency crumble in the country's worst economic crisis in decades. 

 Hotel lobbies are eerily quiet as foreign businessmen stay home, concerned about where Indonesia's plunge into economic disaster will lead. Rising food prices have already triggered looting in East Java and panic buying in Jakarta this month. 

 In a stark warning, officials said on Thursday at least one million people were expected to lose jobs this year. 

 "The present unemployment figure stands at 2.7 million as of January," Sutikno, a spokesman for the Manpower Ministry said. 

 "This is expected to increase this year because at least one million people will lose their jobs in the wake of the crisis," he said by telephone. 

 Mainly Moslem Indonesia and the IMF announced fresh reforms last week to stem blood-letting on financial markets. But the package, which superceded earlier measures agreed in return for a $43 billion bail-out, has failed to stop the haemorrhage. 

 Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad said late on Wednesday the government was working to resolve the corporate debt problem, but reiterated there would be no government bail-out. 

 Banking sources said the government and the International Monetary Fund were looking at ways to deal with private sector debt. 

 They said the talks were not formal negotiations, but both sides were trying to find some way of dealing with corporate foreign debt estimated at around $66 billion. 

 Indonesia has put its total foreign debt at $140 billion, and each drop in the rupiah squeezed indebted companies harder. 

 Jakarta stocks opened down and kept sliding on fears over the rupiah and the debt crisis. The composite index closed down 4.82 percent at 443.53 points. 

 Dealers said a number of factors had savaged the rupiah early on Thursday. 

 They said local players had difficulty meeting maturing dollar contracts and concerns lingered over the political outlook for Indonesia after hints Research and Technology Minister Jusuf Habibie may be President Suharto's preferred vice-presidential candidate in March presidential polls. 

 Markets have reacted with horror to the possible elevation of the profligate Habibie, which would make him potential successor to the 76-year-old Suharto. 

 Suharto, in power since 1965, said on Tuesday he was ready to stand for a seventh five-year term despite unprecedented calls for him to quit. 

 At least 200 students staged a fresh protest against Suharto on Thursday, urging the former army general to step down. 

 A senior government official said on Thursday Indonesia would step up forex intervention to defend the rupiah. 

 "The government of Indonesia will do its utmost to stabilise the rupiah's value against the dollar," he said. 

 But economists were mainly gloomy about the corporate sector, saying most listed companies were now technically bankrupt. 

 Tom Soulsby, head of research for ANZ Securities in Jakarta, said the economy was likely to shrink and a 10 percent contraction was not out of the question. 

 Analysts and businessmen said the full impact of the crisis was not visible yet because of the annual slowdown in production during the Islamic holy month of Ramadan. Ramadan ends with the Eid ul-Fitr festival on January 30-31. 

 "Most workers are on holiday already," said the textile executive. "I think when they return next month, many of them will find their factory gates locked."

title: FOCUS-Rupiah's slump knocks Jakarta stocks down.
text:
JAKARTA, Jan 22 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah slumped to a record low of 17,000 against the dollar on Thursday before central bank intervention helped save the battered currency from a total meltdown. 

 The market was battered by Indonesia's corporate debt, which has assumed nightmarish proportions, and hints that Research and Technology Minister Jusuf Habibie may be the running mate for President Suharto in March elections. 

 The stock market spinned down as the rupiah staged a free-fall to 17,000 from a nervous opening of 11,500/11,800 in Jakarta and 12,000/12,500 in Singapore after a steady close in New York at 11,200/11,700 overnight. 

 The rupiah stabilised at midday after the central bank stepped in, selling dollars for rupiah, and after a senior official said the government was committed to defending the rupiah with its existing stand-by facility. 

 The bank intervened again in the afternoon at the 12,000 and 11,500 levels, helping the rupiah stabilise at 12,000/12,500 at the close in Jakarta. 

 The stock market's composite index shed six percent in morning trade before ending down 4.82 percent at 443.53, ending five days of gains. 

 Vincent Low, fixed-income strategist at Merrill Lynch in Singapore, said the pressure on the rupiah started last week when one-month offshore swap rates collapsed. 

 "It made rupiah relatively cheap to borrow to fund a short spot position overnight. So I think that was the vulnerable point in the rupiah," Low said. 

 He said offshore forward rates had come up a little bit currently due to tightening rupiah liquidity. 

 "But the immediate pressure point remains the corporate debt. There are also reports that people are paying back their dollar-denominated debt in rupiah. This is going to put pressure on the rupiah," Low said. 

Currency dealers said many domestic banks were hampered in mobilising sufficient dollar funds to meet maturing obligations after they had their credit lines cut. 

 The foreign exchange and money markets in Jakarta have been fragmented in the wake of a deteriorating banking sector because of the prolonged currency crisis. 

 Dealers said local banks had offered to settle maturing payments to their counterparts in Jakarta and offshore with rupiah funds, forcing their counterparts to cover their own short dollar positions from the market. 

 Indonesia has total external debt of $140 billion, of which corporate debt is estimated at least at $66 billion. 

 Low said the problem was that reforms Jakarta has agreed with the IMF only tackled issues of a very long-term nature. 

 "The work-out process of the programme is very long. The corporate debt is a short-term problem which is not being solved by any of the measures," he said. 

 "You can reform, you can do a budget that convinces the market that you are serious to that reform. But in the mean time how does it help the corporate debt situation? It doesn't. 

 "That is the dilemma the authorities are in," Low said. 

 To counter the short-term problem and to buy some time, a senior government official said Indonesia will step up intervention in the foreign exchange market. 

 "The government of Indonesia will do its utmost to stabilise the rupiah's value against the dollar," the official told Reuters. 

 The senior official said Indonesia would soon draw on an existing $2 billion stand-by loan facility and partly use it to defend the currency. 

 "This fund has never been used although it's there." 

 He said Indonesia was negotiating to speed up the withdrawal of the second tranche of the $3 billion IMF facility after Indonesia finalised reform in the banking sector. 

 "It's not that we don't have enough reserves. With the increased reserves from these sources, we will have additional power to stabilise the currency," the official said. 

 Senior government economic adviser Widjojo Nitisastro said late on Wednesday that the government was aware of the country's private debt crisis and was working on the problem. 

 "We cannot inform you much about what we are doing but let me assure you we are aware of this problem and we are working on this problem," he told reporters. 

 "We have to be very careful, very systematic in our approach and we will have to come to effective answers to our challenges," said Widjojo.

title: FOCUS - Asian  currencies  shudder as rupiah succumbs.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 22 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah broke down on Thursday amid mounting jitters about the country's debt crisis, a mere week after a package of stiff new IMF-led reforms sparked hopes of real change. 

 It dived 20 percent to 15,000 per dollar within the first hour of Asian trade, casting a shadow over other Asian currency and stock markets. 

 Dealers said trading was extremely erratic, with bids from brokers at levels of 16,500 and 17,000. 

 In Jakarta, there were reports banks had cut their interbank lines because they did not want to trade in current market conditions, while Singapore dealers also complained of a dwindling interbank market. 

 "People just don't want to quote this currency any more. There's still a lot of (dollar) buying interest from U.S. funds, Jakarta centres, everywhere. And nobody has any dollars to offer," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The rupiah stood at 11,600/12,000 to the dollar at 0920 GMT after Bank Indonesia intervened repeatedly, selling dollars for rupiah at the 14,000 and 13,500 levels early and then at 12,500 in late trade. 

 A senior government official said Indonesia would step up intervention in the foreign exchange market and soon draw on an existing $2.0 billion stand-by loan to defend the rupiah. 

 But dealers said the market was still overwhelmingly in favour of the dollar following the government's failure to convincingly address the country's corporate debt, estimated at $65 billion, and growing bank liquidity problems. 

Central bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said on Wednesday the government would soon announce guidelines to resolve liquidity and solvency problems in the private banking sector. 

 The rupiah was also hit by political worries after hints Research and Technology Minister Jusuf Habibie, viewed negatively by the markets, may be President Suharto's preferred vice-presidential candidate in March polls. 

 Analysts said Indonesia urgently needed to find ways to reschedule or repackage its mountain of corporate debt. 

 "Everyone knows now that they're not paying up...Although they've said that they won't bail out the private sector debts, I think they'll have to do something," said Chia Woon Khien, head of Asian research at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken. 

 The rupiah's dizzying drop did not wreak the usual havoc in Asian currency markets as Indonesia's problems were increasingly being perceived as a domestic crisis, dealers and analysts said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit hit a morning low of 4.58 to the dollar, but then recovered to 4.4900/00 at 0920 GMT, still down from its late Wednesday levels of 4.4350/650. 

 The Singapore dollar recovered some of its early losses, to stand at 1.7585/1.7625 against the U.S. dollar from 1.7580/30 late on Wednesday. 

 The Thai baht fell to 54.20/40 to the dollar onshore against 53.70/53.75 late on Wednesday. Dealers said offshore baht hit an early low of 55.30 in a knee-jerk reaction to the rupiah's drop. It was at 53.20/70 at 0920 GMT. 

 "The baht would likely follow the rupiah's footsteps offshore. A limited local corporate demand for dollars to pay off foreign debt was offset by new inflow of foreign funds into the Thai stock market," a foreign bank dealer in Bangkok said. 

 The Philippine peso stumbled to 42.72/82 per dollar against its previous 41.90 close as the central bank kept out of the market after days of indirect intervention. 

Central bank deputy governor Alberto Reyes said the bank would open its one-month lending facility to banks which cut their dollar overbought positions and would buy bank treasury bill holdings at market rates to add liquidity to the system. 

 The South Korean won fell to 1,754/60 per dollar from Wednesday's 1,723 close as the rupiah's drop fanned speculative dollar purchases. 

 But traders said dollar sales by exporters and demand for the won before the Lunar New Year break would cushion its fall. 

 The Taiwan dollar surrendered its early gains drawn from the yen's rise and strong local cash demand ahead of the holidays, as players fretted about the rupiah. 

 The Australian dollar lost half a cent to $0.6578/85 on worries the rupiah's plunge would trigger another cycle of competitive devaluations. 

 The Indian rupee was at 38.725/755 to the dollar from a previous 38.75/80 close and dealers said it was likely to be rangebound as the market absorbed the central bank's measures to tighten liquidity.

title: FOCUS-Indonesian crisis seen halving corn imports.
text:
JAKARTA, Jan 22 (Reuters) - Indonesian imports of corn and soymeal, the main ingredients in animal feed, were set to plunge this year as the country's economic crisis squeezes meat and poultry consumption, industry sources said on Thursday. 

 They said the feedmeal sector, which has been growing by up to 15 percent a year during the last seven years on the back of rising incomes, could take as long to recover fully. 

 "There has been a significant fall in feedmeal production because of the country's economic crisis," Budiarto Soebijanto, chairman of the Federation of Feedmeal Producers, told Reuters. 

 He said soymeal imports were expected to fall by 50 percent to some 500,000 tonnes this year, while corn imports would range between zero and 500,000 tonnes, depending on local production. Indonesia imported about one million tonnes of corn last year. 

 Indonesia produced 10.3 million tonnes of corn in 1996, but output is estimated to have fallen by about 30 percent last year because of a drought linked to the El Nino weather pattern. 

 Industry sources said they expected output to increase by about 10 to 15 percent this year from the 1997 level, barring any recurrence of drought conditions in growing areas. 

 Indonesia is facing its worst economic crisis in decades, with the rupiah currency having lost some 80 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar since last July. 

 The government has projected zero growth and an inflation rate of 20 percent in fiscal 1998/99 (April-March), while one million workers are expected to lose their jobs this year. 

 "I think the industry will take six to seven years to recover fully," one industry source said. "We have to rebuilt the consumer base all over again." 

 "Workers in the lower income group are our main customers. They eat an egg a day, and least a (chicken) leg or wing. They now need income improvement and new jobs," he added. 

 He said the country would need to redevelop labour-intensive sectors such as the property and textile industries, which have been slowed considerably by the economic crisis. 

 Industry sources said the amount of feedmeal sold in the local market was expected to have declined by 25 percent in 1997 and another 25 percent this year from 3.5 million tonnes in 1996. 

 "Feed production costs have increased by more than three times because of the high cost of imported raw material coupled with operational costs," one source said. 

 He said the cost of imported raw materials, which constitute 80 percent of total raw material costs, have increased sharply because of the rupiah's fall against the dollar. 

 "Production costs have increased to 2,380 rupiah/kg from 700 rupiah last July at an exchange rate of 10,000 rupiah to the dollar and if based on July prices," he said. 

 The rupiah fell to a fresh low of 15,000 to the dollar on Thursday but regained some lost ground after central bank intervention. 

 The sources said many of the 40 feedmills in Indonesia had reduced production by between 30 and 40 percent, with some even cutting back output by more than 50 percent. 

 "Many feedmills are facing problems in opening LCs (letters of credits) while others are having cash flow problems. There is talk that some have completely halted production," one said. 

 He said export credit guarantees offered by the United States could be useful to some feedmills, but added that one constraint was that imports would have to be at least 30,000 tonnes. 

 "Under the current circumstances, 30,000 tonnes would be viewed as a giant shipment," he said.

title: Intervention  will help rupiah near-term - analysts.
text:
SINGAPORE, Jan 22 (Reuters) - Central bank intervention is the right step for Indonesia to take and will help halt the rupiah's slide, but only in the near-term, analysts said. 

Intervention has certainly come at the eleventh hour, given the rupiah's 60 percent slide since the turn of the year, but will help arrest the meltdown because volume in dollar/rupiah is so tiny at the moment. 

 "It's not a long-term answer, but with spreads as wide as we are seeing in dollar/rupiah, it won't take much to move it by 600 or 1,000," said Chiang Yao Chye, head of Asia Pacific Research at CIBC in Singapore. 

 Spreads in dollar/rupiah have been as wide as 1,000 rupiah when trading has become highly erratic. 

 On Thursday there were bids from brokers for rupiah at levels of 16,500 and 17,000 to the U.S. dollar, but it was unclear now much business was being done at these levels, dealers said. 

 The rupiah opened around 11,000 but quickly started to fall, and Singapore traders reported dollars going through at 15,000 in early business. 

 It was then Bank Indonesia entered the market, selling dollars at 13,500 rupiah, then again at 14,000. 

 Late in the day the central bank said it would step up forex intervention if need be and would soon draw on an existing $2.0 billion stand-by loan facility and partly use it to defend the currency. 

 "The government of Indonesia will do its utmost to stabilise the rupiah's value against the dollar," a senior government official said. 

 After that, the central bank was in again at 12,000 in late trading. 

 Dealers said with spreads so wide and trading volume so thin, any central bank buying of dollars would have a significant impact. 

 "Immediately the offer (on dollar/rupiah) gets hit, it jumps up by the spread," said one trader. "So with very little, they will be able to move it in 1,000 roop (rupiah) jumps. And that will continue to work as long as volume remains as tiny as it is." 

Intervention is certainly not the complete answer for Indonesia, but something has to be done to stop the rot in the rupiah and intervention is a way of buying time, analysts said. 

 "It won't provide long-term stability but they have to buy time given the extent of the rupiah's fall," CIBC's Yao Chye said. 

 "Long-term solutions have to be addressed and would have to include a debt restructuring programme." 

 Indonesia has around $140 billion total external debt, of which around $66 billion is in the hands of the private sector. 

 Dealers noted there had been talk in the market of dollar/rupiah going to 20,000 by the end of the week, but that looked highly unlikely if the central bank kept up its intervention.

title: Most Asian markets fall further; Seoul, Jakarta up.
text:
HONG KONG (Reuters) - Ignoring soothing words from U.S. officials in Jakarta that spurred some hope of a solution to the economic chaos in Indonesia, most Asian markets fell further Monday. 

 Stock markets in Hong Kong, Tokyo and Sydney were all weaker, while the yen fell against the U.S. dollar and the Thai baht resumed its slide, setting a record low. But the South Korean market strengthened. 

 In Hong Kong, the blue-chip Hang Seng index crashed through the key 8,000 barrier soon after the opening. 

 The index shed 11 percent before recovering to close 773 points, or 8.70 percent, weaker at 8,121 162, reflecting the possible liquidation of high-flying investment bank Peregrine Investment Holdings and rising interest rates. 

 Tokyo's Nikkei index sank 2.21 percent to 14,664, sparking renewed jitters about the health of its banking sector, while Australian shares were down 2.33 percent at 2,542. 

 But Jakarta bucked the regional trend on market hopes that renewed talks between senior officials from the United States and the International Monetary Fund could find a resolution to Indonesia's woes. 

 The outcome of talks between the IMF and President Suharto would not be made public until Thursday. 

 But IMF First Deputy Managing Director Stanley Fischer said the talks went well. "This was a very, very good meeting. We agreed on how to proceed," he told reporters. 

 Jakarta stocks were up 1.16 percent while the rupiah was slightly weaker at 8,600/9,000. 

 U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers was expected in Jakarta later Monday to follow up on Friday's intervention by President Clinton, who stressed the need for Indonesia to comply with economic reforms attached to an IMF aid package valued at $43 billion. 

 There was however mounting concern of an impending political crisis in Jakarta, with renewed calls for Suharto to step aside after ruling Indonesia with an iron fist for 32 years. 

 Two prominent Moslem leaders on Monday added their voices to weekend demands from Megawati Sukarnoputri, daughter of the man Suharto replaced in 1965, for him to step down. 

 The mood remained bleak elsewhere in the region. 

 Weaker markets in Hong Kong, Tokyo and Sydney prompted renewed fears of a spread of the Asian contagion to the region's healthiest economies. 

 The Hong Kong dollar peg to the U.S. dollar remained firm, but currency forwards widened and interest rates soared in another sign of the spread of the U.S. dollar hedging that has crushed currencies throughout the region. 

 Taipei fell victim to the trouble in Hong Kong, with the main stock index closing 4.68 percent weaker at 7,375.14, while the weaker yen helped to pummel the Taiwan dollar below a 10-year low at T$34.40 to the U.S. dollar. 

 Singapore stocks were also off by more than 10 percent at 1,050.88 while the Singapore dollar continued to fall, reaching 1.7940/90 against 1.7690/7740 late Friday. 

 The Thai baht hit fresh record lows of 56.50 to the U.S. dollar, with players unimpressed by central bank measures to curb speculation. The Malaysian ringgit was also weaker, helping to depress the main stock index by around 3 percent. 

 South Korean stocks were up 3.50 percent at 456.20. Dealers said the opening of the Seoul stock market to 100 percent foreign interest had forced a change in weightings in key benchmark indices, forcing investors with long-term positions to raise their weightings. 

 The interest helped the Korean won to firm, although regional woes capped the upside.

title: G7 seen unlikely to support sick Asian  currencies .
text:
LONDON, Jan 9 (Reuters) - Direct intervention to support ailing Asian currencies by the central banks' from the major industrialised nations is unlikely without supportive domestic policy changes, analysts said. 

 Despite rumours this week, analysts said they were highly sceptical whether such central bank action had taken place. 

 "You can only build confidence in exchange rates for five minutes if you intervene and do nothing else," said Joe Prendergast, head of global currency strategy at CSFB in London. 

 "That would only work in tandem with the desired policy reforms being put in place in these countries. The lack of these reforms is the nub of the problem in the first place." 

 There was speculation late on Thursday that the U.S. Federal Reserve was checking commercial bank dealing rates for Asian currencies, with a view to possible dollar sales. The Fed declined to comment. 

 The dollar's relentless rise against Asian currencies since mid-1997 has accelerated during the first full trading week of this year. 

 The Indonesian rupiah, hit by concern about debt defaults across the country and rising political risks, plummeted from 5,400 per dollar on December 31 to as high as 10,700 on Thursday. 

 The Malaysian ringgit, the Thai baht, Taiwan and Singapore dollars all plunged too. Only the Korean won, which collapsed late last year, held its own this week as private foreign banks agreed to roll over its maturing debts. 

 While foreign exchange analysts said Fed action on the dollar/yen rate was possible, they argued that moves to shore up other regional Asian currencies would be both difficult to organise and risky. 

 The U.S. Congress is already uncomfortable with the amount of money the U.S. has contributed to the International Monetary Fund's bail-out packages for Thailand, Indonesia and South Korea, analysts said. 

 The U.S. has made clear this week that Indonesia's 1998/99 budget is well short of IMF guidelines and further aid may be dependent on correcting it. 

 In a 25-minute telephone conversation early Friday, U.S. President Bill Clinton told Suharto that Indonesia had to follow through with the economic reforms laid out in the $40 billion IMF package. 

 U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers visits Indonesia and other Asian nations from Saturday. IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus and his First Deputy Stanley Fischer visit Indonesia on Sunday. 

 "I don't think direct intervention is on the agenda. They will probably continue to use verbal support and insist on reforms in return for aid," said Sara Zervos, emerging markets economist at BZW in London. 

 European enthusiasm for any participation is also seen to be lukewarm at best. 

 Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer has sounded a cautionary note in recent months about financial aid to Asia's troubled economies, warning that the provision of funds must be tied to strict conditions imposing structural reforms. 

 Bank of Korea governor Lee Kyung-shick met officials from the Bundesbank on Friday to discuss Korea's economic crisis and ensure German backing for international financial support. 

 Lee, who has already held talks in London and Paris, will go on to Basle on Monday for a regular meeting of Group of 10 central bankers at the headquarters of the Bank for International Settlements. 

 British Prime Minister Tony Blair, currently the European Union president, said on his arrival in Tokyo on Friday that Asia needed to make "hard choices" to restore confidence in the region's tumbling economies. 

 Blair is also the incoming chair of the "Group of Eight" industrialised nations, the traditional G7 plus Russia. Finance ministers from the G7 meet in London on February 21.

title: FOCUS - Asian  currencies  idle on New Year's eve.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 31 (Reuters) - Asian currency traders sat on their hands on Wednesday as holidays in several centres, including Tokyo, severely inhibited trade on New Year's Eve. 

 The South Korean won remained prey to year-end dollar demand from importers and companies scrambling to meet debt payments. It ended at 1,695 to the dollar against Tuesday's 1,590 close. 

 But dealers said sentiment was boosted by news the International Monetary Fund (IMF) had approved payment of $2 billion to Seoul under an accelerated schedule to ease South Korea's credit crunch. 

 Foreign commercial and investment banks also pledged on Tuesday to roll over billions of dollars of short-term debt, giving South Korean banks an extra month's breathing space. 

 The won's weakness was limited to the 1,800 level against the dollar as a result of all the good news, but there was no consensus among dealers over the won's longer-term prospects. 

 "If more foreign lenders roll over loans to Korean companies and provide fresh loans, the currency market could improve quite quickly in January," said a foreign bank dealer in Seoul. 

 Selling orders were also placed around 1,800 won for three-month non-deliverable forwards in overseas markets. 

 But some dealers remained pessimistic. 

 "Right now things look slightly better for Korea. But there's still a lot of bad news that's not filtered through. I think the won will be in worse trouble next year," said a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore. 

 The Taiwan dollar shed its early gains and slipped to T$32.638/698 to the U.S. dollar at 0800 GMT from Tuesday's T$32.600 close as exporter sales of the U.S. dollar were offset by importer demand in an otherwise slow year-end market. 

 Taiwan central bank governor Sheu Yuan-dong said Asia's financial turmoil would affect Taiwan in 1998, but the government would press forward with financial reforms. 

 He told an annual year-end news conference the central bank would keep its target zone for the overnight interbank rate at 6.5-7.0 percent and would only intervene in the foreign exchange market in the face of abnormal or speculative factors. 

 The Hong Kong dollar edged up to 7.7472/82 against the U.S. dollar from Tuesday's 7.7493/03 close. 

 Elsewhere, the Indonesian rupiah remained soft, hitting lows of around 5,800 to the dollar in subdued offshore trade with Jakarta foreign exchange markets closed for book squaring. 

 Singapore dealers said Jakarta banks were updating screen prices at lower levels than the actual traded rates in an effort to suppress the rupiah's decline. 

 "They're trying to window-dress the rate down. We even saw a quote of 4,800/6,000 for $10 (million). But there's nearly no market here," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 Dealers said they had not seen any sign of actual intervention by Bank Indonesia in Singapore markets and the rupiah would struggle to rise above the 5,000 level after Tuesday's interventions failed to boost it. 

 An Indonesian court's decision to postpone the liquidation of Bank Jakarta, one of 16 banks ordered closed by the government in November as part of economic reforms, was expected to be poorly received by the market once trading resumed. 

 The bank is part-owned by Probosutedjo, President Suharto's half brother. 

 The Thai baht was very thinly traded as many participants were out after the government changed the New Year's market holiday to January 2 from December 31. 

 The baht slid to 47.60/48.20 to the dollar onshore against 47.05/15 late on Tuesday. The offshore rate was at 46.80/47.30 against 46.20/46.70. 

 The Bank of Thailand projected the government would post a current account deficit of $4 billion, or 2.4 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), for 1997, a government spokesman said. 

 Akapol Sorasuchart also said Thailand's GDP was expected to grow at 0.3 percent in 1997 and contract by 0.7 percent in 1998.

title: FOCUS - Asia  currencies  hit by seasonal dollar demand.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 30 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies yielded to commercial demand for dollars in otherwise uninspired trade on Tuesday as activity wound down for the end of the year. 

 The South Korean won shed early gains and fell sharply on dollar demand from importers and for year-end interest payments on foreign debts. 

 Dealers said news that major U.S., European and Japanese lenders were planning to roll over loans to South Korean banks had been largely priced in by the market. 

 "All the good news is already factored in. And there's still a lot of corporate demand for dollars," said a Japanese bank dealer in Singapore. 

 Even intervention by the central bank and reports that banks in the U.S., Europe and Japan were considering extending new credit to Seoul of as much as $10 billion failed to lift the won in late trade. 

 "What we want to see and hear more than anything else is an immediate inflow of real foreign hard currency into the market," a local bank dealer in Seoul said. "If not, all news will be just an empty announcement." 

 Seoul traders said the Bank of Korea sold dollars at 1,640 won in a clear attempt to cap the dollar's surge. 

 But the won closed weak at 1,590 to the dollar against its opening 1,220 and Monday's 1,395 close. 

 It had opened sharply higher as some local banks tried to push the dollar down in an attempt to reduce their foreign currency losses before book closing. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended higher at T$32.600 to the U.S. dollar against Monday's T$32.686 close, boosted by bargain-hunting interest in an otherwise slow market. 

 The Hong Kong dollar ended near its day low on consistent year-end demand for the U.S. dollar while forwards remained firm in line with higher domestic interbank rates. 

 In Southeast Asia, the Indonesian rupiah stayed soft but was off its lows against the dollar amid fears of central bank intervention. 

 "Dollar/rupiah is the most well bid of all the dollar/regionals. But the market is on the defensive because of Bank Indonesia. There's talk they'll intervene today or tomorrow," the Japanese bank dealer said. 

 The central bank sold dollars for rupiah at the 5,300 level late on Monday. 

 Dealers said companies had placed dollar buying orders at various levels on expectations the central bank would intervene again to boost the rupiah for the year end. 

 They said short-dated swaps recovered above par as operators began boosting their rupiah reserves. 

 The Indonesian forex market will be closed on Wednesday for book-closing and on Thursday for the New Year holiday. Trading will resume on Friday. 

 The Thai baht was little changed at 47.15/40 to the dollar onshore at 0930 GMT against 46.85/47.05 late on Monday in listless trade. 

 The market appeared to shrug off a slew of economic data including an increase in Thailand's current account surplus to a preliminary 26.3 billion baht in October from a revised 2.9 billion baht surplus in September. 

 The trade surplus also widened to 23.3 billion baht in October from 7.9 billion baht in September, but Thailand's balance of payments fell into a 185 billion baht deficit in November from a 58.3 billion baht surplus in October. 

 The Malaysian ringgit remained under pressure from commercial dollar demand, but dealers did not expect it to weaken beyond 3.93 to the dollar for the time being. 

 The Singapore dollar slithered through the 1.67 level to the U.S. dollar in dull trade. 

 Philippine markets are closed for holidays until January 2.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Dives Amid Debt, Policy Worries: Amplifier
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah plunged to a new record low Wednesday, as domestic demand for dollars again reached panic levels after reports that the country's short-term debt burden is higher than previously thought. 

 After falling as far as 6,300 rupiah to the dollar from a Tuesday closing of 5,450 rupiah, the currency bounced back after reports of late afternoon intervention by Bank Indonesia, the nation's central bank, trading late Wednesday in Asia around 5,750 rupiah versus the dollar. But analysts said the currency may head still lower in coming days. 

 As well as worries about the short-term debt burden faced by Indonesian companies, sentiment has been hurt by the recent downgrades of Indonesian debt by major ratings agencies, which have heightened fears international banks will be unwilling to roll-over their loans to the corporate sector. 

 Earlier this week, Moody's Investor Service lowered its rating for Indonesia to Ba1, a 'junk' bond rating. 

 What is needed, analysts say, is more evidence that the government is prepared to take serious steps to control the crisis - such as measures to create more competition in the financial sector and open up the property market to foreigner investment. Little new has emerged since Indonesia implemented some reforms after turning to the International Monetary Fund in October for a near $40 billion bailout. Thailand and Malaysia, meanwhile, now appear to be taking the need for reform seriously, analysts say. 

 As a result, a cabinet meeting headed by President Suharto Wednesday proved a disappointment for the markets - yielding little more than a request for Indonesians to refrain from buying imported items.

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  take heart as yen surges.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 17 (Reuters) - Asian currencies calmed down a bit on Wednesday as the dollar dropped dramatically against the yen following the Bank of Japan's unexpected -- and repeated -- interventions and news of a massive Japanese income tax cut. 

 The dollar lost what had looked like a firm grip above the 131 yen level and fell as low as 125.85 yen in Tokyo trade. 

 But no one was prepared to predict the end of its reign over Asian currencies just yet. 

 "Overall, sentiment in the whole of Asia is still very fragile so what we're seeing today may just be a technical rebound. I think the dollar demand is very real," said Jacqueline Ong, regional economist at I.D.E.A. 

Currencies in Southeast Asia, where the region's economic crisis had its beginning, had a much better day. 

 The Philippine peso reversed course, the Singapore dollar recovered from a heavy fall, the Malaysian ringgit moved higher and the Indonesian rupiah stopped falling. 

 The peso bounced to 39.904/937 to the U.S. dollar at 0530 GMT after hitting an all-time low of 41.60 earlier. 

 Manila traders said the central bank was seen selling dollars heavily at various levels in an effort to counter dollar demand amid shrinking supply. 

 News the Bankers Association of the Philippines (BAP) and the central bank had agreed to set up a dollar pool to cover the requirements of oil companies and other corporations helped boost the peso, they said. 

Central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the bank had also agreed to enter into non-deliverable forward contracts with dollar borrowers to ease demand in the spot market. 

 The Singapore dollar also staged a recovery as talk of intervention in overnight trade and possibly early on Wednesday by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the de facto central bank, spooked the market. 

 It was quoted at 1.6885/915 to the U.S. dollar at 0530 GMT after firming through the 1.6800 level against a morning low of 1.7010. 

 "The MAS was in in London last night. When dollar/Sing got to a high of 1.7175, they were in selling," a senior regional currencies trader said. 

 "I heard they were in again through some local banks this morning. But then again, other local banks were bidding on the other side," he said. 

 The Singapore dollar caved in to mounting pressure and dived through the key 1.70 level in thin London trade on Tuesday, reaching lows not seen in over six years. 

 The sharp drop meant the once static currency had lost nearly seven percent in three trading days as poor year-end liquidity exaggerated movements. 

 Dealers and analysts said it remained in a downtrend but the market was likely to avoid the 1.70 level for the time being. 

 "They (the MAS) don't mind a weaker Sing. In fact, they'd welcome it for now, but not too fast," the dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit also pulled back from its lows on the yen's rebound and on talk of foreign inflows to the stock market. It was at 3.8300/400 to the dollar against 3.8825/925 late on Tuesday. 

 Dealers said the thin market was keeping the ringgit volatile, with small volumes causing wild gyrations. 

 The Indonesian rupiah hovered between 5,450 and 5,600 to the dollar all morning as spreads narrowed to 50/100 points amid dwindling interest. 

 Dealers said the dollar maintained a firm undertone against the rupiah, which gained little mileage from news that President Suharto would attend a public function on Thursday. 

 Worries about his health have sent the rupiah spiralling to new lows in the past week. 

 The Thai baht was little changed at 47.80/48.00 to the dollar onshore against 47.60/48.10 late on Tuesday. The offshore rate stood at 46.65/85 against 46.90/47.20. 

 Dealers said they expected the baht to have a steadier day as regional currencies should gain from the yen's rise. 

 In north Asia, the South Korean won slipped for the first time this week due to dollar buying for importer settlements due early next week. 

 The won was at 1,505/10 to the dollar against Tuesday's 1,425 close, but dealers said its decline would be limited by fears of central bank intervention. 

 The Taiwan dollar continued to be driven by external factors, firming to T$32.644/669 against Tuesday's T$32.820 close as traders watched the yen rebound. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was protected from weakening through the 7.75 level to the U.S. dollar by thin year-end conditions and the yen's rise. 

 Dealers said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority did not appear to have intervened in the foreign exchange market, but it was seen offering three-month money in early trade. 

 A European bank dealer in Singapore said the ringgit's ability to hold above the 3.93 per dollar level for the second time on Tuesday suggested i 

 The Philippine peso and the Singapore dollar had the most volatile morning, both rebounding sharply against the U.S. dollar 

 Asian currencies posted fresh losses on Tuesday as persistent dollar demand and dwindling trading volumes sparked fresh carnage in foreign exchange markets. 

 Only the South Korean won defied logic, surging nearly 16 percent to highs of 1,350 against the dollar after the central bank decided late on Monday to scrap its 10 percent trading band. It ended at 1,425.0 against Monday's 1,563.9 close. 

 Dealers said the won was benefitting from expectations of heavy dollar inflows under the IMF's $57 billion bailout scheme for South Korea, which had moved players to unwind long dollar positions built during the won's near 50 percent drop last week. 

 The government's decision to float the won, as requested by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), sell off one or two troubled banks and push forward with a $10 billion sovereign bond issue boosted Korean financial markets on Tuesday. 

 But dealers said sentiment could quickly turn negative if more of the pledged IMF loans were not disbursed soon. 

 The won was also expected to face selling pressure from importers seeking dollars towards the weekend. 

 Its improved fortunes gave the Taiwan dollar an opening boost, but it soon shed the gains in the face of strong U.S. dollar demand from importers. 

 Taipei traders said there was also concern about the previously sturdy Singapore dollar's sharp falls, which triggered renewed fears of a competitive depreciation in the Taiwan dollar. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended at T$32.820 to the U.S. dollar, its lowest close since November 1987, against Monday's T$32.746 close. It hit a low of T$32.950. 

 Dealers said the central bank appeared to have intervened in the last minute of trade in a bid to keep its dollar above the psychological T$33 level. 

 The Hong Kong dollar remained on the cusp of the key 7.75 level to the U.S. dollar, but forwards eased in the wake of the won's rebound. 

 Dealers said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority was heard buying the local dollar via a major commercial bank to limit the U.S. dollar's rise. 

 Southeast Asian currencies were off their lows but remained weak and weary as companies scrambled to buy dollars to meet loan payments amid shrinking liquidity and widening spreads. 

 "There's just a lack of liquidity in the market. There are very few interbank players around so if you're buying, the whole world knows you're buying," said Jimmy Koh, regional economist at I.D.E.A. in Singapore. 

 "Given the widening spreads, the pace of depreciation is much faster. People are just extremely bearish on the region," he added. 

 Dealers said transaction volumes had fallen sharply as players sought to limit their exposure to growing market volatility towards the year end. 

 "In the middle of the year, people would trade something like 20 to 50 (million) dollars. But lately because of the volatility and the fact that the big figure changes so fast ... positions have been reduced to one to two (million) dollars," said a European bank dealer in Singapore. 

 The Indonesian rupiah recovered in late trade as attempts to test the 6,000 level failed, causing a pullback in the currency which was reinforced by central bank intervention. 

 It was at 5,500/600 to the dollar at 1020 GMT after Bank Indonesia sold dollars at 5,700, dealers said. The rupiah hit an early record low of 5,980 to the dollar. 

 Dealers said it remained fragile on lingering worries about President Suharto's health despite clear signs he was gradually resuming work after a period of rest and corporate difficulties in meeting debt payments. 

 They said liquidity had practically dried up and spreads of 200 or 300 points were exacerbating the rupiah's moves. 

 The Thai baht's abrupt recovery from a record low of 49.35 against the dollar sparked speculation of central bank support. 

 Bangkok dealers said exporters sold dollars around the 48 baht level, but the Thai unit remained weak at 47.50/48.00 to the dollar against 47.30/90 late on Monday. 

 Offshore baht was at 46.90/47.20 against 46.90/47.40. 

 Finance Minister Tarrin Nimmanahaeminda appealed to Thais to refrain from speculating against the baht and said the government would use the limited resources at hand to defend it. 

 The Philippine peso ended at a record low of 40.214 to the dollar against a previous 38.853 close despite intervention by the central bank. Further falls were only prevented by the activation of volatility bands. 

 Poor market liquidity -- total turnover was a mere $9.5 million -- did little for the peso's condition and dealers expected more declines. 

Central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the peso would only recover if people stopped speculating against it. 

 Dealers attributed the peso's steep drop to panic buying of dollars by firms with dollar exposures and importers hedging future dollar requirements. 

 A slowdown in remittances from overseas contract workers was also contributing to the shortage of dollars. 

 The Singapore dollar fell within a hair's breadth of the key 1.70 level to the U.S. dollar, but fears of central bank intervention pulled it back from the edge, dealers said. 

 It was at its weakest in more than six years at 1.6935/55 to the U.S. dollar at 1020 GMT after hitting a low of 1.6995. Late on Monday it was at 1.6835/65. 

 There was no consensus among dealers about the likelihood of the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) selling U.S. dollars above the 1.70 level, or over whether it was behind a spurt of dollar sales that pushed the Singapore dollar up to an early high of 1.6660. 

 "I think they were in at least once or twice this morning, but it didn't really help because dollar/Sing is still biddish," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 I.D.E.A.'s Koh was skeptical about the MAS intervening given the sharp falls in other regional currencies. 

 "The authorities have affirmed again and again that they look at the Singapore dollar, not just against the U.S. dollar, but on a trade-weighted basis," he said. 

 The MAS declined to confirm rumours about an intervention. 

 The Malaysian ringgit recovered as players took profit on the dollar's gains after the rupiah rose on Bank Indonesia's intervention. 

 It firmed to 3.8825/925 to the dollar against 3.9025/125 late on Monday.

title: Ringgit recovers on Indonesian  intervention .
text:
KUALA LUMPUR, Dec 16 (Reuters) - The ringgit recovered on profit-taking triggered by the Indonesian central bank's intervention to defend the rupiah on Tuesday afternoon, foreign exchange dealers said. 

 The ringgit moved up to 3.8700/8900 to the dollar against a low of 3.9130 a few hours earlier. 

 "The intervention was not big, but it had a psychological impact on the market," said Ishak Ismail, market intelligence analyst with I.D.E.A. in Singapore. 

 He said the intervention by Bank Indonesia was not big, just a few million dollars. 

 Dealers said ringgit was expected to stay below 3.85 to the dollar in the near-term. 

 They said the Indonesian intervention, coming on the heels of similar action by the South Korean central bank and the Korean government's decision to ease trading band restrictions on the won, had a deep impact on the market. 

 South Korea on Monday floated the won by abolishing the fluctuation band. 

 "Because the market is so thin, small amounts can look very big and move the currencies through big figures," said a dealer with a Malaysian bank. 

 Dealers said the ringgit, like other currencies, was becoming a victim of a liquidity crunch. The lack of liquidity was exaggerating the movement of the currency. 

 "That is why spreads are getting wider," the Singapore-based analyst said. 

 Dealers said there was little impact from the statement by leaders of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) on the currency issue. The leaders are meeting in Kuala Lumpur. 

 "They are just reiterating what they have said before," said a dealer.

title: FOCUS - Korean malaise stalks Asian  currencies .
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 10 (Reuters) - Asian currencies were shrouded in gloom on Wednesday as the South Korean won sank to new lows despite government efforts to calm shaky markets. 

 The won hit its daily lower limit of 1,565.9 to the dollar within the first half hour of trade, down almost seven percent from Tuesday's 1,460 close. Trading was suspended for the rest of the day. 

 A Finance Ministry suspension of business at five merchant banks and worries about Seoul's ability to redeem short-term foreign debt obligations precipitated the won's descent. 

 Dealers scoffed at Finance Minister Lim Chang-yuel's package of measures to stabilise the markets and draw in foreign funds, focusing instead on the suspension of the banks after last week's closure of nine merchant banks. 

 "The measure is just a peanut. Foreign investors are not fools," said a foreign bank dealer in Seoul. 

 The central Bank of Korea sold dollars in value-today and value-tomorrow transactions in a desperate bid to prevent corporate defaults. 

 But there was little sign of respite for the won. 

 "Without dollar supplies from the outside, the upbeat pressure for the greenback will not be easily changed," said Lee Chang-sun, senior analyst at LG Economic Research Institute. 

 North Asian currencies were worst hit by the won's woes. 

 The Taiwan dollar fell through the T$32 support level to the U.S. dollar, ending at T$32.229 from Tuesday's T$31.963 close. 

 Taipei dealers attributed the drop partly to active non-delivery forward buying of U.S. dollars by foreign fund managers following the Taiwan dollar's recent failure to extend its gains significantly. 

 But exporter U.S. dollar sales and fund inflows to the stock market were expected to contain the Taiwan dollar's decline. 

 The Hong Kong dollar hit a six-week low of 7.7450/60 to the U.S. dollar and forwards rose sharply in the face of short-selling by overseas players. 

 "We're hearing there are a lot of European funds trying to get out of the stock markets in Korea and Hong Kong," a said U.S. bank dealer in Singapore. 

 The blue chip Hang Seng Index ended 4.08 percent lower at 11,022.41, its low for the day. 

 In Southeast Asia, the Indonesian rupiah remained in the hotseat as players swooped on any mention of President Suharto's health in thin, easily-spooked year-end markets. 

 State Secretary Murdiono's announcement that Suharto would attend an informal summit of the nine-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Kuala Lumpur next week gave some respite to the rupiah. 

 But it failed to sustain gains above the 4,400 level. 

 "There's still a lot of corporate dollar demand for year-end interest payments in U.S. dollars, or for hedging," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The rupiah tumbled to a historic low of 4,600 to the dollar on Tuesday before Murdiono denied rumours that Suharto had been taken to hospital. 

 Dealers said Bank Indonesia was seen intervening in the spot market and squeezing short-dated liquidity to prop up the rupiah, but had limited impact. 

 The Malaysian ringgit fluctuated in a wide range but remained largely depressed by the plight of the won and rupiah. 

 Talk of large dollar offers from agents of Bank Negara Malaysia above the 3.6850/6900 levels cushioned the ringgit's falls, but dealers said there was dollar buying interest around 3.6400. 

 The Singapore dollar looked soft in the face of strong local and offshore bids for the U.S. dollar below the 1.62 level. 

 "Technically, the market is looking at 1.63. The Singapore dollar still has a long way to go compared with the others, especially the ringgit," said Ishak Ismail, market intelligence analyst at I.D.E.A. 

 The Thai baht hovered around 42.10/25 to the dollar in thin offshore markets for most of the day. The onshore market was closed for the Constitution Day holiday. 

 Dealers shrugged off comments by Deputy Prime Minister Supachai Panitchpakdi that Thailand may consider lowering interest rates after the first quarter of 1998. 

 The Philippine peso finished soft at 35.24 to the dollar against a previous 35.105 after the central bank cut its overnight borrowing rate to 11 percent from 12 percent.

title: Indonesia: Officials Investigate Cause Of Office Block Fire
text:
JAKARTA (AP-Dow Jones)--Firefighters were investigating whether sparks from a welding torch started a massive blaze in a newly built high-rise office block in which 15 people died, newspapers reported Tuesday. 

 Earlier speculation had that Monday's blaze, which gutted the three top floors of the Bank Indonesia tower on Jakarta's main street, might have been caused by an electrical fault. 

 However, the newspaper Kompas quoted Jakarta fire chief Suharso as saying this was unlikely because mains power had not been connected to the affected floors. 

 'Maybe the fire was caused by another factor, such as people welding,' Suharso reportedly said. 

 He was not immediately available for further comment Tuesday. 

 Nine of the 15 dead perished after they were trapped in a smoke-filled elevator. 

 The newspaper Republika reported that four badly burned bodies had not been identified. 

 Five survivors were hospitalized with burns and smoke inhalation. 

 The damaged building was one of two brand new 25-story towers where workmen had been carrying out finishing touches to several executive suites and meeting rooms. 

 About 200 people who had been working in offices on lower floors were evacuated. Four workmen escaped the flames and were lifted to safety by a helicopter. 

 Another helicopter repeatedly emptied a large water bucket on the fire that burned for more than five hours. 

 The fire was another crisis for Bank Indonesia, the nation's central bank, which is trying to prop up Indonesia's ailing currency. 

 Despite the bank's intervention and a $40 billion rescue plan, led by the International Monetary Fund, the value of the rupiah has slid dramatically over many weeks. 

 After morning trading Tuesday, the rupiah dived to around 4,575 rupiah to the U.S. dollar.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Dn 9% At New Low On Suharto Worries
text:
JAKARTA (AP-Dow Jones)--Indonesia's rupiah plunged more than 9% to an all-time low of 4,575 against the U.S. dollar Tuesday on fears that President Suharto had taken seriously ill. 

 And while the government officially denied these rumors, dealers say that jittery markets, skepticism, and continued demand for dollars will prevent a sharp rebound for the rupiah anytime soon. Many suspect the currency will weaken even further. 

 'You just have to look at the spot rate to see that few people have much confidence in the political situation in Indonesia right now,' said a foreign exchange dealer in Singapore. 'I don't see any rebound in the market.' 

 The rupiah's fall Tuesday was fast and furious and went unchallenged by Bank Indonesia, the nation's central bank, which has been intervening in the spot market in recent days. 

 After opening at 4,155 rupiah, the dollar continued a rapid climb through one important psychological level after another. Rumors centered on Suharto being seriously ill to him even being dead. Denials from palace officials and Suharto's personal spokesman couldn't damp the sell-off. 

 The dollar eventually closed Asian trading at 4,565 rupiah, down slightly from the day's high. 

 Looking ahead dealers say the market will take some time to steady from Tuesday's shock. They look, in particular, to public appearances by Suharto to stymie the rupiah's plunge, but even that they say may only slightly damp dollar demand. 

 'You must remember that Indonesian companies still need billions of dollars to satisfy their dollar positions, and this will keep pressure on the currency,' another Singapore-based trader said.

title: Indonesia's Military Signals Worries Over Socio-Political Stability
text:
JAKARTA, Indonesia -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia's top military leader, Feisal Tanjung, said Monday that the current monetary crisis could threaten the nation's political stability, the state news agency Antara reported. 

 The general's comments during a hearing in parliament came as the country's battered currency, the rupiah, continued its tailspin, falling to an all-time low of 4,175 against the dollar amidst concerns about the health of President Suharto. Helping to drive the rupiah down was local corporate demand for dollars, currency dealers said. 

 Monday's steep 3.6% plunge occurred despite intervention by Bank Indonesia, the nation's central bank, to support the rupiah. The size of the central bank's purchases, however, was viewed by analysts as too small to cause any significant moves in the market. 

 Tanjung, meanwhile, told parliament that the military is "intensifying activities that will create more conducive socio-political conditions and maintain peace and order." He added that the armed forces "will continue to be vigilant against possible upheavals." The general said that measures have already been taken to foil any attempts to disturb the operations of Indonesia's largest legislative body, the People's Consultative Assembly. 

 Analysts have raised concerns that the current monetary crisis will give way to social unrest as layoffs increase and disposable income diminishes. 

 The general, however, was confident that the armed forces has "done its best to maintain the nation's stability to ensure unity and cohesiveness." 

 The People's Consultative Assembly is scheduled to convene in March to elect the next president and vice president. 

 Meanwhile, in the currency market, the dollar was trading at 4,165 rupiah late in Asian dealings, up, sharply from its close Friday at 4,025 rupiah. The dollar hit its all-time high of 4,175 rupiah shortly before the end of Asian trading but was brought down by central bankintervention. 

 Concerns over President Suharto's health surfaced Friday when the 76-year-old leader failed to attend a government function. Late Friday, however, the government said that President Suharto would be taking a 10-day rest to recuperate from an overseas trip. 

 Mounting worries about Suharto, combined with massive local demand for dollars, are expected to exert more downward pressure on the rupiah, and traders said they expect a test of 4,200 on Tuesday. 

 Dealers noted that a fire at the central bank Monday that killed at least 14 people did little to build confidence in the rupiah. The fire was in a new central-bank building directly adjacent to Central Bank Gov. Soedradjad Djiwandono's office. Damage caused by the blaze is expected to cause delays in clearing transactions with the central bank Tuesday. 

 Despite the slump in the currency, Indonesian share prices closed higher Monday on trading by foreign investors aimed at year-end window dressing and in line with the rebound of some major regional markets. The Jakarta Stock Exchange index closed up 2%, or 8.835 points, to 423.613 points. Trading volume was 412 million shares with total turnover valued at 430 billion rupiah, according to a local securities house. Gainers outpaced losers by 70 to 45, with 85 shares finishing even, and 68 stocks untraded. 

 An analyst with a European brokerage firm said rumors that state-owned companies will spend 1% of their total capital reserves to buy shares and mutual funds to support the country's slumping market prompted investors to take buying positions. 

 Dealers also suspected the day's gain was due to the government propping up some state-owned big-capitalization issues through state-owned brokerages.

title: FOCUS - Rupiah, won reel to lows but ringgit buoyed.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 8 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah and South Korean won plumbed new depths on Monday but elsewhere on the Asian currency scene the Malaysian ringgit managed a solid gain, analysts said. 

 The rupiah's recent dire performance continued with a  vengeance and intervention by Bank Indonesia failed to stop the rot. 

 Reports that President Suharto had been advised to take a 10-day rest unsettled the market but the underlying worries about the scale of private sector debt is the main driving force. 

 Analysts reckon Indonesian firms have run up around $65 billion in overseas debt and about half of it remains unhedged. 

 This obviously bodes ill for the rupiah and is raising fears of a swathe of corporate defaults. 

 "It really is a bad situation and the unhedged debt is substantial," said a Singapore-based analyst who recently returned from a trip to Indonesia. "Against this background investor confidence will remain weak and it is hard to call a bottom for the rupiah." 

 In late business the rupiah was trading around the day's low of 4,145 per dollar, nearly 3.5 percent down on Friday's close. 

 In South Korea, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) loan honeymoon appeared to be over. The won dived to close at a historic low of 1,342.40 per dollar. 

 The central bank stepped in to sell dollars at 1,340 won but traders said it was like standing in front of a train. 

 The unrelenting fall of the won came amid fears that more banks and finance companies face bankruptcy in the wake of the IMF's $57 billion bail-out package last week. 

 The collapse of South Korea's 12th largest industrial conglomerate, Halla Group, on Saturday after defaulting on loan payments triggered a rush into dollars by exporters and by importers for future payments. 

 South Koreans vote in presidential elections on December 18 and the impression was that some IMF conditions to overhaul the financial system could be renegotiated by the new government, analysts said. 

 "The market is still a little nervous of that as well and generally the behaviour by exporters in Korea is to hold on to dollars as long as they can," said Kobus van der Wath, chief treasury economist with Standard Chartered Bank in Singapore. 

 "The market fully realises that with the Halla Group becoming another casualty on Friday there is a lot of debt that will become more difficult to service." 

 The Malaysian ringgit had a brighter day with a rise to 3.6600 per dollar from 3.7180 late on Friday. 

 It firmed in reaction to a package of economic measures put in place by Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim last week aimed at calming the overheating economy. 

 "The measures were pretty well received. It was one sign the government recognised the problems," said a dealer with a Japanese bank. 

 A surge on the Kuala Lumpur stock market, up 14 percent at one stage in reaction to the package, helped push up the ringgit. 

 Thailand's baht ended steady after an initial slide, finding support from news that only two of 58 finance companies would be allowed to reopen. 

 The market had expected more of the firms to be allowed to resume trading and were pleasantly surprised by the government's tough stance. 

 The baht was at 41.850/000 per dollar onshore against 41.75/41.85 late Friday. 

 The offshore rate was 41.200/300 against 41.60/41.70. 

 The Singapore dollar dipped in choppy activity on the won's losses and in response to Trade and Industry Minister Lee Yock Suan's comments on Sunday the government would review its three-week-old 1998 economic growth forecast of five to seven percent. 

 Dollar/sing was quoted at 1.6175/90 against an early 1.6215, after profit-taking on dollar positions. 

 Taiwan's dollar also slipped in sympathy with the won to T$31.900/909 per dollar compared with Saturday's T$31.775 close.

title: Indonesian rupiah recovers after  intervention .
text:
JAKARTA, Dec 8 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah recovered from a historic low of 4,090 against the dollar in Jakarta and 4,085 in Singapore following central bank intervention. 

 Dealers said Bank Indonesia came in at the 4,070 level and helped calm a market hit by early regional weakness and by news that President Suharto had been advised to take 10 days rest. 

 They said the limited intervention provided some support for the rupiah. However, the currency failed to mirror a recovery in the ringgit, which bounced ahead of Malaysian Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim's speech in parliament. 

 Spot rupiah was at 4,065/75 at 0330 GMT, compared with an opening of 4,010/30. 

 Dealers said the market was weighed down mainly by Friday's news that Suharto was hit by fatigue and had cancelled a trip to Iran. 

 But the news hit a market already long on dollar positions, helping limit the rupiah decline, they said. 

 One foreign bank dealer said Suharto's health factor seemed to have also prevented the rupiah from recovering along with the ringgit. Instead, the rupiah absorbed weaknesses in the won and the baht. 

 State Secretary Murdiono announced last Friday that Suharto had cancelled a planned trip to Iran after being advised to take 10 days rest because of fatigue. 

 He said Suharto's doctors had opined that the president's health was good. Suharto returned to Jakarta last week from a strenuous 12-day trip that took him to Namibia, South Africa, Canada and Saudi Arabia. 

 The rupiah fell to a historic low of 4,090 in the morning on selling by both off- and onshore operators before profit-taking emerged and intervention by the central bank provided some stability in the currency. 

 The rupiah also withstood pressure in New York on Friday as the thin market there had established long positions on dollars. 

 Dealers said the rupiah remained vulnerable and the underlying tone was still weak. However, one Singapore-based dealer said the rupiah was likely to creep higher to the 4,000 level because a further recovery in ringgit later in the day would trigger more profit-taking in dollars against the rupiah. 

 Short-end swaps remained flush with ample offshore cash-flows, driving them further down into negative territory and forcing the central bank to absorb overnight liquidity. 

 Dealers said Bank Indonesia was seen bidding for overnight money at around 17 percent in the morning. They said offshore swap selling also pushed domestic rates down. 

 But they could not explain the persistent rich supplies of rupiah in Singapore market which aided long dollar holdings. 

 One U.S. bank dealer said cheap short-front swaps had also triggered some selling at the longer-end, up to six months.
