title: FOCUS-Southeast Asia  currencies  brief rises dashed.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 5 (Reuters) - The party to celebrate the International Monetary Fund (IMF) rescue package for South Korea turned sour on Friday as some Southeast Asian currencies reeled to new lows, prompting repeated central bank intervention. 

 A fresh bout of selling from overseas operators drove the Malaysian ringgit and Indonesian rupiah to record lows. 

Currency experts said the market was generally positive over South Korea's $57 billion rescue package, but was worried about how strictly the IMF terms would be implemented. 

 "On currencies, it's sell on the facts. People are just taking profit. There's clearly uncertainty for the economy," said David Cohen, senior economist with Standard & Poors/MMS. 

 South Korea's won dropped to 1,220/1,240 at midday compared with Thursday's close of 1,170.00, spurred by merchant banks conducting dollar short covering. 

 Dealers said tight liquidity ahead of the IMF's fund injection of a first payment of $5.6 billion and a second portion of $3.6 billion triggered dollar purchases. 

 But it was Southeast Asia's currencies which changed direction more sharply after gaining on Thursday. 

 The rupiah collapsed past the psychological 4,000 per dollar barrier despite intervention by the Bank of Indonesia. 

 "People are still hoarding dollars. Mmost of it is commercial buying for loan repayments," a local brokerage dealer said. 

 He said speculation was a smaller factor in the slide as this were dwindling toward the year end. 

 The Malaysian ringgit skidded to new low of 3.8065 from Thursday's 3.7050 on follow-through sales. 

 Dealers said the market was jittery over overseas selling ahead of a news conference called by Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim later on Friday. 

 "The market is worried about what will come out of the conference, if there will be capital controls," a dealer with a U.S. investment house said. 

 The Singapore dollar sank in tandem to breach a new low of 1.6200 at 0440 GMT, before paring losses. 

 Trade in the Sing dollar was mostly thin and choppy, and seemed to be tracking the activity in the ringgit and rupiah, dealers said. 

 Activity in the Thai baht was thinned by a public holiday in Thailand celebrating the King's birthday. 

 Offshore rates slipped to 41.750/41.800 in mid-afternoon against 41.60/41.70 in late Thursday trade. 

 Dealers said Monday's expected decision over the future of Thailand suspended finance firms lent some support. 

 The Philippine peso was a shade weaker at 35.070/120 versus 35.055 on Thursday, with a lack of dollar demand prevailing. 

 Taiwan's dollar continued to hold firm, aided by rises in the stock market and the more positive outlook after the IMF bail-out for South Korea. 

 The Taiwan dollar was quoted at T$31.86 per dollar against a finish of T$31.90 on Thursday. 

 In Hong Kong, the local dollar inched up to 7.7355/7.7365 against the U.S. dollar compared with 7.7372/7.7382 late on Thursday.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Ends Dn But Rebounds From All-Time Low
text:
JAKARTA (AP-Dow Jones)--Indonesia's rupiah closed slightly lower against the U.S. dollar Friday after hitting its all-time low, but rebounded later on the back of interventions by Bank Indonesia, the nation's central bank, and the unwinding of long dollar positions, dealers said. 

 Selling pressure on the rupiah stemmed from an overall bearish sentiment towards Asian currencies and was led by a sell-off by domestic interests. Bank Indonesia interventions and a well-received reform package announced by Malaysia late Friday, however, supported the rupiah late in the day. 

 The dollar closed Asian trading at 3,965 rupiah, slightly higher than its Thursday close of 3,955. The dollar traded at an all-time high of 4,020 rupiah at 0630 GMT (1:30 a.m., EST) as regional currencies fell, but weakened gradually as Bank Indonesia came into the market. 

 Bank Indonesia appeared to have lost its attempts to keep the rupiah under the 4,000 level but was aided by Malaysia's package and an unwinding of long-dollar positions. Dealers say the rupiah's fate next week depends on whether positive sentiment stemming from Malaysia's move carries through. 

 'Let's just hope that the good reaction to the Malaysia package can last longer than initial reactions to the Thai and Indonesian reform packages,' said one Indonesia analysts in Jakarta.

title: FOCUS-Rupiah, ringgit catch cold after Korea deal.
text:
SINGAPORE, Dec 4 (Reuters) - Joy was only fleeting for some Asian currencies on Thursday after they were heartened by the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) expanded aid package of $57 billion to South Korea, dealers said. 

 A fresh bout of selling from overseas operators drove the Malaysian ringgit and Indonesian rupiah back down the slippery slope in late trade, after they had risen in early trade. 

 The early mood was mildly euphoric after the aid package boosted confidence in the South Korean won, but even then market participants said they expected more blood-letting from corporate failures and downgrading. 

 "There was some pull back and consolidation but the bias is still against Asia," a dealer with a Japanese bank said. 

 He said the ringgit was sold down after Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said a $3.0 billion bridge project with Indonesia would go ahead despite the shelving of other mega projects due to the sharp fall in the ringgit. 

 In late trade, the ringgit hit an all-time low of 3.7150/7250 per dollar compared with 3.6500/6600 mid-morning. 

 The assault on the ringgit had ripple effects, bruising Indonesia's vulnerable rupiah most sharply. 

Indonesia's central bank intervened to prop up the currency by selectively selling the U.S. dollar from the 3,955 level to the 3,945 level. At 1040 GMT, it stood at 3,940. 

 Dealers said they anticipated more central bank action to halt further losses if the rupiah drifted to 4,000 per dollar. 

 A report from research house I.D.E.A. said eyes were focused on the 4,000 level with targets gapping to 4,100 thereafter. 

 "The idea of a joint intervention 'shelved' till markets calmed down now removes only credible threat against a big figure move on the rupiah," it said. 

 Early gains in Asian currencies were attributed to profit taking by those who had gone long on dollars in recent days. 

 The easing of South Korea's foreign exchange shortages with the IMF aid package would cap dollar gains against the won, and therefore, other regional currencies, some dealers said. 

 "The increased dollar supply before the end of the year will help the won, but I can see the strength being short lived," a dealer with a U.S. brokerage said. 

 The won/dollar rate perked up to 1,130 before sliding back to 1,163 in late action against 1,196.00 on Wednesday. 

 While the inflow of billions of dollars for South Korea begins this week, loan defaults and other financial crises could limit a recovery and lead the won back to 1,300, dealers said. 

 The Thai baht continued to gain on South Korea's loan deal and its central bank's defence of the currency on Wednesday. 

 "The baht has recovered from lows and is experiencing good activity, gaining also from profit taking in dollar longs," said Alison Seng, economist with Standard & Poors/MMS. 

 She said assurance from the Bank of Thailand that half the US$6 billion in foreign debt maturing in December would be rolled over could underpin the baht. 

 Technical support in the short term was pegged at 40.80 per dollar with traders also likely to buy dollar/baht on dips. 

 Dollar/baht was quoted at 41.650/850 per dollar onshore at 1045 GMT against 42.85/42.68 on Wednesday. 

 The Singapore dollar held steady despite renewed weakness in other regional currencies. It came close to striking 52-month lows at 1.6160 against the dollar, but the trend was not sustained. The currency was at 1.6100/1.6120 at 1050 GMT. 

 There was no impact on the Sing dollar from an announcement by de facto central bank, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), that it was unlikely to take part in Seoul's aid package. But dealers said the market was mixed over whether the Sing remained a safe haven currency or if it would decline to stay competitive with the other Southeast Asian currencies. 

 The Philippine peso eased a notch to 35.150/300 compared with 35.25 previously, but its upside remained limited. The rise was based on a lack of demand for dollars, dealers said. 

 Taiwan's dollar recovered sharply on the back of the won and Taipei's stronger stock market. The Taiwan dollar was quoted at T$31.866 per U.S. dollar against Wednesday's T$32.201 close. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was rangebound in late trade at 7.7370/7.7380 against 7.7385/7.7395 on Wednesday.

title: FOCUS-Indonesian markets dive to record lows.
text:
JAKARTA, Dec 3 (Reuters) - Indonesia's rupiah plunged to a historic low on Wednesday and the stock market closed at its lowest level in more than four years. 

 The markets also ignored comments from U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan that the world economy would emerge stronger once Asia's financial problems have been resolved. 

 The rupiah plunged to a record low of 3,985 against the dollar before settling at 3,955/65 at the close in Jakarta. 

 The currency has fallen slowly but steadily since July, with a brief respite in early November after the International Monetary Fund (IMF) set up a reform-cum-aid package for the country. 

 Under the package, Indonesia cut back on several big-ticket infrastructure projects and closed down 16 well-connected banks. 

 But the continued slide of the rupiah and the stock market, along with other regional markets, suggested confidence had not returned, raising calls for a repeat of October's concerted intervention in currency markets by the monetary authorities of Indonesia, Singapore and Japan. 

 However, Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad said in Malaysia on Tuesday that concerted central bank intervention had been put on hold because the entire region was in a slump. 

 The Jakarta composite index of 279 companies ended at a 51-month low of 389.68 points, down 1.17 percent on the day. But analysts said the bottom was not in sight although the market was cheap now. 

 They said expectations of poor corporate earnings until next year continued to contribute to the gloomy outlook for the market, with the upcoming presidential election next March also undermining sentiment. 

 "The rupiah is not unique. You got the baht at 43 and the ringgit at 3.66. These are all record lows. It's just amazing," said Vincent Low, fixed-income strategist with Merrill Lynch. 

 The market appeared to shrug off positive data which was announced during the day, including a healthy trade surplus of $1,246.6 million in September. 

 However, inflation data also announced on Wednesday was seen as somewhat worrisome, with consumer prices rising 1.65 percent in November, putting the year-on-year figure at 9.56 percent. 

 "This is a danger that Indonesia is facing now," Low said, adding stagflation might become a reality, with the economy slowing down while inflation was on the rise. 

 But he said a weaker currency always led to higher inflation in an open economy, adding that the El Nino weather phenomenon, which has led to a crippling drought in Indonesia, had also contributed to the woes. 

 President Suharto also warned of the dangers of the prolonged economic crisis and said the Indonesian people needed to be united at such a critical juncture. 

 "Let us take a lesson from this bitter ordeal to enable us to continue our national development process," Suharto was quoted by local newspapers as saying on Tuesday. 

 "Let us boost our national efficiency...because only with such strength will we able to enter a more free and open world trade and economy," he said. 

 Suharto said the government would not hesitate to take all necessary measures to find the best way out of the financial upheaval. 

 Greenspan said a slowdown in Asian growth was inevitable, but that this could be temporary.

title: IMF Camdessus/Mahathir/Amplifier -3: New IMF Facility
text:
The continuing confusion over the status of the negotiations caused more selling in Asia's financial markets Tuesday, with the South Korean won plunging to new record lows and Southeast Asian currencies dragged lower in its wake. Indonesian Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad added to the selling pressure in the rupiah by telling reporters in Kuala Lumpur that Bank Indonesia wouldn't intervene to prop up the Indonesian currency while markets were so volatile. 

 What may be more optimistic for South Korea were the signs at the Kuala Lumpur meeting that it could be the first country to benefit from a new short-term funding mechanism that is being developed by the IMF as part of the Manila framework. 

 The idea is for the IMF to advance big short-term loans to nations struggling to restore confidence so that they can cover their foreign-currency obligations. That would back up a broader long-term IMF program that also involves needed economic reforms. 

 An official from Japan's Ministry of Finance said in Kuala Lumpur that South Korea could benefit from this new lending, which would be at market rates and repayable over six months to a year. The idea is to show the markets that the funding is there - and hopefully the money might never need to be drawn, the official said. 

 The Kuala Lumpur meeting was attended by finance ministers of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) and senior financial officials from the U.S., South Korea, Japan, China, Hong Kong and Australia. Camdessus attended some of the session. 

 Asean groups Brunei, Burma, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam. 

 Camdessus said he expects the structure of the eventual South Korean bailout will be similar to Indonesia's, which is seen as a sort of prototype for the principles of the Manila Framework. Indonesia received $18 billion in assistance from the IMF and other multilateral donors. But 'second line' commitments from Japan, Singapore, the U.S. and other countries brought the total to nearly $40 billion. 

 Under the Manila framework, the main funding is supposed to come from the multilaterals, while extra funding can be lined up by donor countries if required. 

 Camdessus said the IMF had received positive answers from potential donors to the South Korea bailout.

title: Indonesia  says to  intervene  in  forex  if needed.
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 24 (Reuters) - Indonesia's central bank will intervene in foreign exchange markets if needed, either alone or in concert with the Bank of Japan and the Monetary Authority of Singapore, bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said on Monday. 

 He also told a parliamentary commission hearing that he hoped the Indonesian economy would begin to recover in the second-half of next year. 

 "In the short-term, economic activity is expected to slow down, especially this year until the middle of next year, as a result of adjustments in the economy and response to policies which were needed in the public and private sector to strengthen economic fundamentals," he said. 

 Djiwandono said there was a trend that economic expansion in the second half of this year might slow down and that economic growth as a whole in 1997 would decline compared to 1996. 

 He said inflation was expected to increase while consumption and domestic investment would soften. But he said non-oil exports were expected to improve, while imports were showing signs of slowing down. 

 "...we hope the current account deficit will decline," he said. 

 Djiwandono said it would take time fia to restore confidence in the economy following recent developments in the economy and monetary sector. 

 "The combination of these two phenomena has brought a broad impact to the economy and is difficult contain in the short term," he said. 

 He said the disruption in investor confidence in regional economies, including Indonesia, had caused capital inflows into the local economy to dry up. 

 "We are even seeing signs of a reverse to capital inflows which we have used to finance our development," he said. 

 "The crisis has caused a flight from rupiah to currencies which are considered strong, and there are also flights to physical assets, especially cash, and a switch to low-risk investments," he said.

title: FOCUS-Indonesian markets take hit from the won.
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 21 (Reuters) - Indonesia's financial markets ended the week sharply lower, hit by concern over the South Korean won and a general lack of investor confidence in the region, economic analysts said on Friday. 

 "The continued share fall in the Jakarta market on Friday was a result of the steep fall of the South Korean Won, which also depressed the rupiah," said Anna Martiana, an analyst with PT BNI Securities. 

 The composite stock index fell 1.23 percent to 391.26 points on Friday, down 10 percent on the week. Friday's levels were a far cry from a record 742.95 on July 9 before the financial crisis in Thailand sent shock waves through the region. 

 The rupiah ended the day in Jakarta at 3,615 against the dollar after touching a low of 3,635 before the central bank, Bank Indonesia, intervened. It opened on Friday at 3,545/55 

 An analyst said the continued fall of the rupiah and the Jakarta stock index along with most other Southeast Asian markets indicated an erosion in investor confidence in the region. 

 "Most foreign institutional investors have shifted their focus away from this region following the currency turmoil," said Jordan Zulkarnaen, an analyst at brokerage Pentasena Arthasentosa. 

 Some analysts said they expected further losses in the Jakarta market by the end of the year due to the economic crisis. 

 "I expect the composite index to hover between 325 to 350 points by the year-end," Zulkarnaen said. 

 He added, however, he expected a recovery by next March. 

 Martiana predicted the composite index would not fall much below its current level by the end of December. 

 She said the Jakarta market was currently experiencing one of its worst-ever periods with investors no longer looking at corporate fundamentals. They just wanted to sell, she added. 

 "I noticed that even stocks without foreign debts and which export most of their products are also under selling pressure," she said. 

 "This is not a question of a company's fundamental basis anymore, but a poor global outlook," she added. 

 Another analyst said poor sentiment towards local companies hit by large private dollar-denominated loans and foreign exchange losses was also expected to depress the market. 

 But most brokers welcomed remarks by Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad that private debt was an issue between private firms and their lenders, and the government had no plans to intervene.

title: Key dates in Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 21 (Reuters) - South Korea said on Friday it was talking to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) about emergency loans. 

 This was the latest development in a string of financial crises across Asia. 

 The following are key dates: 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency is hit by a massive attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thailand's finance minister. 

 July 2 - The Bank of Thailand announces a managed float of the baht and calls on the International Monetary Fund for "technical assistance". 

 The announcement effectively devalues the baht by 15-20 percent. It ends at a record low of 28.80 to the dollar. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. The intervention works and the currency hits a high of 2.5100/10 after a low of 2.5240/50. 

 July 11 - The Philippine central bank says in a statement it will allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is starting to be affected. In a surprise move, Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Currency meltdown. 

 The ringgit hits a 38-month low of 2.6530 to the dollar. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad launches bitter attack on "rogue speculators". 

 The Hong Kong dollar remains steady, but territory later reveals US$1 billion was spent on intervention during a period of two hours on an unspecified day in July. 

 August 5 - Thailand unveils an austerity plan and complete revamp of its finance sector as part of IMF-suggested policies for a rescue package. 

 August 11 - The IMF unveils in Tokyo a rescue package for Thailand including loans totalling $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 13 - The rupiah begins to come under severe pressure. It hits an historic low of 2,682 to the dollar before ending at 2,655. The central bank actively intervenes in its defence. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of a band. The rupiah plunges to 2,755. 

 August 19 - The South Korean won hits an all time low of 901 to the dollar. The currency has been sliding gradually during the year. On January 1 it stood at 842. 

 August 20 - The IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. The package now totals $16.7 billion. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bailout package, bringing it to a total of $17.2 billion. 

 Oct 2 - Won slips to 913.50 on news Ssangbang Wool faces a debt default. Corporate defaults have been one of the reasons for the won's fall. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 28 - The won's fall accelerates. It ends at 953 despite central bank intervention. 

 Oct 30 - The won -- which has a 2.25 percent daily trading band -- hits its lowest permitted level of 984.70. 

 Oct 31 - The IMF package for Indonesia is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - The won will "never, never, never" breach the psychologically important 1000 barrier a Korean central bank official says. 

 Nov 2 - Indonesia announces the liquidation of 16 unhealthy banks under the IMF economic reform programme. 

 Nov 4 - Thailand's government collapses as Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh resigns. The baht rises to 38.75 from 40.95 on the unpopular premier's departure. 

 Nov 7 - The markets are now openly speculating Seoul will have to go to the IMF to help defend the won. The won ends at 979.90 and traders are targetting the 1000 barrier. 

 In Thailand, opposition Democrat leader Chuan Leekpai says he will form the new government. 

 Nov 9 - Chuan is appointed new Thai premier. 

 Nov 10 - The won closes at 999.00 to the dollar. 

 Nov 17 - South Korea cracks. The central bank announces it will no longer defend the 986 level to the dollar. The won immediately falls its daily limit down to 1008.60. 

 Nov 18 - The Korean central bank suggests to the finance ministry that Korea should seek an IMF bailout loan. The won is at its 1012.80 daily limit low. 

 Nov 19 - Korean finance minister Kang Kyong-shik resigns to take responsibility for the financial turmoil. South Korea also widens its daily band limit on the won to 10 percent. 

 Nov 21 - Finance ministry official announces that Seoul is discussing details of a bailout package with the IMF. 

 (c) Reuters Limited 1997

title: FOCUS - Won hits Asian  currencies , more downside seen.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Bears dominated trading in most Asian currencies on Tuesday after the South Korean won sank to a new low against the U.S. dollar, prompting one central bank -- Indonesia's -- to intervene, forex dealers said. 

 They said further weakness in regional currencies was expected unless the respective authorities intervene. 

 The bearish sentiment was heightened by a seven percent plunge in the Malaysian stock market. 

 "Korean won and the sharp drop in Malaysia's stock market were the two main factors today. We are looking at the return of competitive devaluations in the region," said a dealer with a European institution in Singapore. 

 The won hit an all time low of 1,012.80 even as its finance ministry denied having totally abandoned its defence. 

 "The market was unimpressed. The concern now is Korea is in a real mess and there is a very good chance it will need aid from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). Despite its denials, the market perception is that it will need help," said a dealer with a local bank. 

 Asked about the outlook for the won, he said: "There is no target, no such thing as a stop since it hinges on sentiment and sentiment is very poor." 

 The dealer, however, said 1,200 could be "the magical resistance" for the won at year-end. 

 Fears of a contagion effect from the ailing won sent the Malaysian ringgit reeling to a low of 3.4000 per dollar on late Tuesday and dealers said it could test 3.5000 easily. 

 The ringgit was further depressed by its stock market collapse on news infrastructure firm United Engineerings (Malaysia) Bhd (UEM) had bought a big stake in Renong Bhd, a move seen negative for UEM. 

 "Stops were triggered as U.S. and offshore funds bought dollar/ringgit from around 3.38," said a dealer with a European bank in Kuala Lumpur. 

 Selling of the ringgit against the Singapore dollar weighed on the ringgit. 

 "We might see the ringgit/Sing retesting its low of 45 in the coming weeks," said the dealer with a European institution in Singapore. 

 The Singapore dollar too sank to a low along with the won. Singapore dealers said 1.5910 was traded in the morning. 

 "In the medium term, the Singapore dollar could test 1.62 easily if the Korean won weakens further and the ringgit problem worsens," said a local dealer. 

 Dealers were awaiting details of measures to shore up Singapore's ailing property sector announced by the government. 

 "I think at 1.6000, the authorities will be watching very closely. It would be a strong short-term resistance with possible interventions and corporate selling (of dollars)," said the local dealer. 

 The Thai baht too succumbed to the ailing won, testing the 40.00 level per dollar. 

 The baht was at 39.80/90 per dollar compared to 39.35/45 in the morning. 

 "The europhia over the new government is over. People are watching real issues like financial reforms, debt roll-over for clearer directions," the local dealer said. 

Interventions by the central bank throughout Tuesday kept the rupiah unscathed from the contagion effect, dealers siad. 

 The rupiah rose to 3,440 from 3,465 earlier. 

 "But the rupiah's strength is likely to be temporary. What is unique is the BI (Bank of Indonesia) intervened on its won this time. We want to see if the other central banks will intervene," said the local dealer. 

 Dealers said it was difficult for the central bank to support the rupiah because of the general weakness in the region. 

 Elsewhere in North Asia, the Taiwan dollar hit a 10 year low and ended at 31.770 to the dollar. 

 "The Taiwan dollar has to fall in tandem because Korea is its main competitor," said the Singapore-based dealer with a European institution.

title: FOCUS - Asian  currencies  lose grip as won slips.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Fears of a contagion effect from the ailing South Korean won sent shivers throughout Asian currencies, especially after the Bank of Korea asked its finance ministry to consider a bailout aid package from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), forex dealers said. 

 "This might trigger the next shockwave throughout Asia. The worst is not over if the won continues to erode daily," said a dealer with Singapore bank. 

 A central bank official in Seoul told Reuters it had suggested the finance ministry seek IMF aid "as a last resort to overcome the currency troubles". 

 Dealers said said the won's near-term target could be around 1,025/30 per dollar. 

 The won hit a new low and daily limit of 1,012.8 even as authorities said they had "never totally abandoned" the won defence and continued to watch the situation to counter its drop. 

 "We have never totally abandoned the defence and yesterday, an unexpectedly big (dollar) demand forced us to temporarily retreat," Kim Suk-dong, chief of the ministry's foreign funds department, said in a telephone interview. 

 "We simply thought it would be helpful to accommodate the downward pressure on the won," Kim said. 

 The Taiwan dollar sank to its lowest level in 10 years at 31.800, compared to 31.366 on Monday. 

 Dealers said the Taiwan dollar could test 32.00 if the central bank does not intervene but profit-taking on the greenback could cushion the fall. 

 The Malaysian rinngit also took a beating, falling to around 3.3750/00, compared to 3.3220/320 on Monday. 

 Dealers said the 6.22 percent drop in Malaysia's main composite stock index to 625.77 also depressed sentiment. 

 "U.S. funds were seen selling the ringgit/Sing and dollar/ringgit firmed," said the dealer with a Singapore bank. 

 He said the ringgit could test 3.4000 later in the week. 

 The Thai baht dipped further on continued dollar demand from corporates and foreign stock investors, dealers said. 

 It eased to 39.550/650 per dollar onshore compared with 39.10/39.20 late on Monday. 

 In the offshore market, it dipped to 39.100/200 to the dollar against 38.60/38.90 late on Monday. 

 Dealers said corporates continued to buy dollars to repay or hedge their dollar-denominated debts. 

 Thai corporates' disastrous third quarter results also added pressure on the baht. 

 "The poor result and distressing outlook provided incentives for foreign investors to cut losses and repatriate the money," said another dealer. 

 After succumbing to lower levels on the won's woes, the Indonesian rupiah rebounded against the dollar after intervention from the central bank, dealers said. 

 They said Bank Indonesia stepped in when the rupiah fell to an early low of 3,525 from an opening of 3,470/90. 

 Dealers said the central bank came in sporadically and managed to push the rupiah up to a high of 3,485 before the market settled at around 3,435.00/5.00 at 0445 GMT. 

 They said the central bank wanted to signal to the market that it was guarding the rupiah at the 3,500 level. 

 Dealers said the intervention in the spot market was expected, but the central bank also stepped into the swap market by buying tom/next swaps to absorb excess liquidity. 

 "The intervention is not surprising. But the central bank also moved into the tom/next market in the early morning," one European bank dealer said. 

 "This suggests that the central bank is trying to absorb excess rupiah from the market to maintain rupiah stability." 

 Dealers said the central bank was trying to keep tom/next swap around par despite ample liquidity. 

 But they were uncertain how long the central bank would try to keep the rupiah above the 3,500 level as overall regional currencies were relatively weak. 

 The Singapore dollar too headed south after Senior Minster Lee Kuan Yew said the level of the local currency was a matter for the market to decide. 

 After hitting a low of 1.5910, the Singapore dollar was quoted around 1.5872/82 at 0445 GMT. 

 Dealers said the Singapore dollar could next test 1.5960 to the greenback before heading down further to 1.6000.

title: FOCUS-Asian  currencies  muffled by weekend lethargy.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 14 (Reuters) - Asian currencies shuffled in listless ranges on Friday as the absence of fresh leads reinforced the market's pre-weekend lethargy. 

 Dealers said trading interest was dwindling as banks and investment houses squared their books for the end of the year. 

 "Time is passing a bit slower. It's just the usual year-end phenomenon. People who've made enough money are just trying to protect their positions," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah, on soft ground for much of the day, slid to a low of 3,460 to the dollar on late afternoon rumours concerning Indonesia's PT Bank Central Asia (BCA). 

 The bank's parent Salim Group denied the rumours, which included speculation over the closure of BCA's offices in Singapore, Malaysia and Hong Kong, a clearing deficit in Medan, and the health of the group's co-founder Sudono Salim. 

 Dealers treated the rumours with some skepticism as they occured in thin, easily manipulated Friday afternoon markets. 

 "I wouldn't be surprised if they're unfounded -- just somebody trying to make extra bucks," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The rupiah settled down to 3,435/45 to the dollar by 1030 GMT, little changed from its earlier levels, after the rumours were denied and on talk the Indonesian central bank had checked rates or even intervened. 

 "There were some rumours Bank Indonesia came in to check rates but the market didn't really sell the dollar down. It's been supported around 3,425/35 all day," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 Dealers said the rupiah remained under pressure from dollar demand from domestic companies and Japanese and Hong Kong parties. 

 But players remained cautious about buying the dollar aggressively due to fears of central bank intervention. Bank Indonesia was believed to have sold dollars above the 3,400 rupiah level early on Thursday. 

 Corporate dollar demand also kept the Thai baht weak at 38.85/95 to the dollar onshore against 38.70/38.80 late on Thursday. The offshore rate was at 38.30/40 against 38.30/31. 

 Dealers said the initial euphoria over the appointment of Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai had worn off and players were now keenly seeking signs the new government would be committed to economic reform. 

 IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus, in Bangkok as part of a Southeast Asia tour, said Thailand had not sought changes to the terms of its $17.2 billion bailout package. 

 He also said he believed most of Thailand's 58 suspended finance firms were insolvent and should be closed permanently. 

 The market shrugged off his comments and news Thai foreign reserves had risen at end October due mostly to loan drawdowns from the IMF package. 

 In Malaysia, the ringgit remained sandwiched between corporate dollar demand at 3.30 ringgit and dollar offers from agents of Bank Negara at 3.33. 

 Across the border, the Singapore dollar was steady but still weak at 1.5810/25 to the U.S. dollar from 1.5790/00 on Thursday. 

 "I'd expect dollar/Sing to move higher to 1.5850. There's buying interest from local banks at the lower end and there's still room for competitive depreciation in the Singapore dollar," a Singapore-based analyst said. 

 The Philippine peso ended lower at 33.99 to the dollar from a previous 33.93 close. Manila traders said it would have weakened further if the central bank had not stood firm selling dollars at the 33.98 level. 

 In north Asia, the central Bank of Korea stuck to its defence of the won, selling dollars at 987.0 won in opening trade and then at 986.00 won in the afternoon. 

 The won ended at 986.30 to the dollar against Thursday's 986.70 close. 

 Dealers said the won would not breach the key 1,000 level for now but it remained vulnerable to further depreciation. 

 "The central bank doesn't have inexhaustible dollar reserves to pour into the market. The won's recent strength is a temporary phenomenon," a foreign bank dealer in Seoul said. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended lower at T$31.240 to the dollar from Thursday's T$31.105 close as investors kept a wary eye on the apparent recovery of the yen and won. 

 Dealers said there was strong speculative pressure on the currency in the form of non-deliverable forward buying but its falls were cushioned by exporter sales of the U.S. dollar. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was at 7.7300/20 per U.S. dollar against Thursday's 7.7320/40 close. 

 Interbank rates remained soft as liquidity eased after the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's clarification of rules on borrowing from its discount window. 

 Hong Kong Secretary for Trade and Industry Denise Yue said she expected the impact of regional market turmoil on Hong Kong to be short-lived.

title: Indonesian rupiah rebounds on  intervention .

 They said Bank Indonesia stepped in as the rupiah fell to touch the day's low of 3,450 in the afternoon following market rumours concerning PT Bank Central Asia (BCA) after a run on deposits at the bank's offices in Medan, north Sumatra. 

 The executive director of Indonesia's Salim Group said on Friday there was no basis for market rumours concerning the group's bank. 

 "The rumours are baseless," group executive director and bank commissioner Benny Santoso told Reuters. 

 The rumours ranged from the closure of BCA's offices in Singapore, Malaysia, Hong Kong, to a clearing deficit in Medan, to the death of Salim Group's founder Sudono Salim, one of Indonesia's richest men. 

 However, the Salim Group and PT Bank Danamon later said they had agreed on a partnership, and Credit Suisse First Boston was evaluating a significant equity investment in Bank Danamon, the second largest private bank in Indonesia.

 Santoso said Sudono was in good health and was due take part in an event organised by the PT Indomobil, an automotive company owned by the Salim group, on Friday evening. 

 He said BCA had a representative office in Singapore which was operating as usual. 

 "BCA has only a branch in New York and an affiliate in Hong Kong. Both are also operating as usual," Santoso said. 

 He said it was not true that BCA had suffered a deficit at Friday's clearing in Medan, north Sumatra.

title: APEC/Focus On  Currencies  -4:  Intervention  'Model' For Fund
text:
Some Southeast Asian countries may resist an Asia Fund that falls wholly under the control of the IMF. And the idea of including the U.S. in a regional surveillance body, when the Clinton administration is having trouble providing any money for the Asian countries in trouble, could be controversial. 

 Officials at Japan's Finance Ministry say they've scaled back some of their earlier plans for the Asia Fund in the face of resistance from the U.S. 

 Instead of a permanent fund, they may propose that Asian countries should pledge their willingness to provide emergency credit lines, similar to the IMF's facilities, in the event of a crisis. The credits would be subject to the IMF's conditions on fiscal and monetary reform - effectively acting as a supplement to the IMF's own lending. Alternatively, strong Asian countries could set up direct credit lines with the weaker economies. 

 But Japanese officials say even these ideas, which they may put forward at the Manila meeting, may not be acceptable to the U.S. 

 Japanese vice minister of finance for international affairs Eisuke Sakakibara, a key player in the Asia Fund planning, is scheduled to attend the Manila meeting, as well as U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers. Deputy finance ministers and central bank officials from Australia, Brunei, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand will also attend, as well as representatives of the IMF, World Bank and ADB. 

 Even if Japan is modifying its plans, Southeast Asian countries still seem intent on creating a proper fund, with Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad stressing this week that plans for such a facility are still intact. 

 And Philippine president Fidel Ramos has repeatedly talked about an Asia fund in the context of both APEC and ASEAN, describing it as something that 'would assure participating economies of the availability of funds and that reforms and adjustment measures are pursued.' 

 Dalla said recent intervention in the currency markets by the central banks of Japan and Singapore could provide a model for how an Asia fund might work. When the Bank of Japan and Monetary Authority of Singapore joined Bank Indonesia in buying rupiah on the foreign exchange market this month, they weren't just trying to halt a slide in the rupiah, but trying to build confidence around Indonesia's newly-agreed IMF program. 

 That kind of market intervention, sewn right onto the side of an IMF package, goes to the heart of what an Asia fund might be, said Dalla. 'It will be for forex operations,' with the IMF-imposed controls acting as a 'safety net,' he said.

title: FOCUS - Asian  currencies  tread water as won recovers.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 11 (Reuters) - Most Asian currencies remained in well-worn territory on Tuesday as the stricken Korean won managed to stave off further attacks with the help of its central bank. 

 Dealers said the Bank of Korea stepped in to rescue the won from the brink of the psychological 1,000-to-the-dollar level in opening trade and later lowered its intervention level. 

 The won ended at 989.90 to the dollar after the central bank sold dollars aggressively at 999.90 won and then at 989.00 won. 

 The Bank of Korea backed its action with strong verbal support, discouraging heavy won sales for the time being. 

 A central bank official said the bank would strenuously support the won's "Maginot Line" of 1,000. 

 "We will absolutely defend the 1,000 won level to the dollar," a central bank official said. "To this end, we will implement stronger measures." 

 Singapore dealers said the central bank's efforts had caused won non-deliverable forwards to come off their highs as well. 

 "The reason the forwards are moving to the left is because people are probably saying that the spot Korean won is not going to pass 1,000 anytime soon. They think the central bank is not going to let it," said one dealer. 

 But not everyone was convinced. 

 "Any strengthening in the won would be a correction. I don't foresee any help for the won in the short term," a senior regional currencies dealer in Singapore said. 

 Korea's overnight call loan rate shot to a yearly high of 14.50 percent as merchant banks, saddled with bad debts following major bankruptcies, sought hard cash to buy dollars. 

 The government said it would soon announce a financial stabilisation package, including relief for the troubled banks. 

 Elsewhere in north Asia, the Taiwan dollar ended weak but off its lows on the won's recovery and speculation the central bank had intervened to defend the Taiwan dollar at the T$31 level to the U.S. dollar. 

 It ended at T$30.992 against Monday's T$30.985. 

 Dealers said the Taiwan dollar's direction would continue to be driven by the won's moves due to intense competition between the two territories in key export markets. 

 "The only reason for the Taiwan dollar to cross 31.00 is if the won goes past 1,000," a Singapore dealer said. 

 The Hong Kong dollar eased to 7.7315/45 to the U.S. dollar from 7.7295/10 at Monday's close, but dealers said there was little impact on the interbank market from Monday's run on International Bank of Asia. 

 However, some dealers said they expected borrowing costs of smaller banks to rise after the incident. Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said Hong Kong authorities would help International Bank of Asia meet its obligations. 

 In Southeast Asia, the Thai baht slid to 37.90/38.10 to the dollar onshore from 37.10/37.30 late on Monday as initial euphoria over the appointment of new Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai faded. 

 Dealers said the market was awaiting details of Chuan's new cabinet and concrete steps to rehabilitate the financial sector. 

 Chuan was quoted in an interview with a Thai newspaper as saying he expected to be able to revitalise confidence in the immediate term to halt capital flight from Thailand and solve liquidity problems. 

 "People are just waiting to see what the new man is going to do and how the government is going to shape up," said one dealer. 

 Dealers said the baht's direction would also hinge on the ability of the government and private sector to persuade foreign creditors to roll over $21-$30 billion of short-term debt due by the end of this year. 

 The offshore baht rate eased to 37.84/94 to the dollar from Monday's 37.20/35 as unwinding of long dollar forward positions abated. 

 But dealers said the baht could head higher as the remainder of the positions, established when the baht came under speculative attack six months ago, matured by the end of the week. 

 The Philippine peso rose to close at 33.82 to the dollar from a previous 34.27, after breaching its first volatility band at 34.74 and hitting a high of 34.48. 

 Manila traders said the peso was boosted by large inflows from overseas contract workers repatriating their wages and talk a Hong Kong firm might have moved some funds to Philippine-based banks to buy shares in a local beer and food conglomerate. 

 After the market close, central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the peso's depreciation had been "over-exaggerated" and it was likely to correct in line with economic fundamentals. 

 The Indonesian rupiah hovered between 3,310 and 3,330 to the dollar, trapped between corporate dollar demand and fears of concerted central bank intervention. 

 Dealers said the government's pledge on Monday to close 16 unhealthy banks despite potential political fallout had boosted support for the rupiah. 

 Joint interventions by the central banks of Japan, Singapore and Indonesia to buy the rupiah last week had also helped stabilise the currency for the time being. 

 The Malaysian ringgit edged up to 3.2960/60 to the dollar from Monday's 3.3150/250, but activity was confined to a very narrow range, dealers said. 

 A Standard & Poor's report saying it did not see Malaysia facing the same problems as Indonesia and Thailand helped prop up the ringgit, dealers said.

 But dealers said the baht could head higher as the remainder of the positions, established when the baht came under speculative attack six months ago, matured by the end of the week. 

 The Indonesian rupiah hovered between 3,310 and 3,330 to the dollar, trapped between corporate dollar demand and fears of concerted central bank intervention. 

 Dealers said the government's pledge on Monday to close 16 unhealthy banks despite potential political fallout had boosted support for the rupiah. 

 Joint interventions by the central banks of Japan, Singapore and Indonesia to buy the rupiah last week had also helped stabilise the currency for the time being. 

 "The 3,350 level is very well resisted and also well monitored at the moment," the Singapore dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit edged up to 3.3035/135 to the dollar from Monday's 3.3150/250, but activity was confined to a very narrow range, dealers said. 

 A Standard & Poor's report saying it did not see Malaysia facing the same problems as Indonesia and Thailand helped prop up the ringgit, dealers said. 

 "The S&P report had an impact though not very much. It pushed dollar/ringgit down to 3.30 from around 3.32," another European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 The Philippine peso firmed to 33.60/99 to the dollar from Monday's 34.27 close on easing corporate dollar demand and expectations of fund inflows from overseas contract workers. 

 Sentiment was also helped by the government's decision to appeal for a reconsideration of last week's Supreme Court decision declaring oil deregulation unconstitutional. 

 In North Asia, the Taiwan dollar continued to mirror the won's moves on expectations it would have to undergo a competitive depreciation if the won fell further. 

 The Taiwan dollar firmed to T$30.957/999 after slipping to T$31.010/030 against Monday's T$30.985 close. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was steady at 7.7290/00 to the U.S. dollar while interbank rates remained firm.

title: Indonesian rupiah steady in slow late trading.
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 7 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah was steady against the dollar in slow late trading on Friday as swap rates edged up slightly, dealers said. 

 They said the central bank stepped in briefly, selling dollars from 3,308 to 3,302 level, but met support from Jakarta and offshore fund managers. 

 Spot rupiah was at 3,290/3,300 at 0900 GMT, compared with an opening of 3,265/95. Dealers said the rupiah was mainly in a range trading between 3,290 and 3,330 on Friday. 

 One local bank dealer said dollar buying interest from Jakarta was still unabated, aided by relatively ample rupiah. 

 One Singapore-based dealer said there was some dollar buying from fund managers, but the upside was capped by operators in Singapore caught with long dollar positions looking to square their positions ahead of the weekend. 

 He said the arrival of Jakarta players, combined with fund managers buying of dollars, kept the rupiah trading in a narrow range throughout the day. 

 The dealer said fund managers were financing their purchases with funding from the swap market, driving overall swap rates to increase across the curve. 

 In Jakarta, swap rates were driven higher due to increases in Singapore market, defying declines in interbank rates. 

 Overnight rupiah was at 14.0/14.5 percent, with operators still looking for buyers in late afternoon. Tom/next swap was last quoted at 2.25/2.75, one-week at 10/15, one-month at 50/60, two at 75/100, three at 100/130, six at 230/280 and one-year at 430/480 points. 

 In Singapore, tom/next swap was at 2.5/3.5, one-week at 35/60, one-month at 115/140, two at 185/215, three at 230/250, six at 330/350 and one-year at 535/565 points. 

 Dealers said the market was indirectly affected by declines of the Korean Won and the new Taiwan dollars. 

 "It has no direct implication on the Southeast Asian currencies. But people are generally concerned with the on-going crisis over there," one foreign bank dealer said. 

 Dealers said the market was also cautious after another round of concerted intervention from three central banks on Thursday following the first one on Monday. 

 "Some also tried to short the dollar in expectation of the appearance of one of the central banks," one said. 

 The central banks, the Monetary Authority of Singapore, the Bank of Japan and Bank Indonesia, had said earlier they would continue to intervene to stabilise the rupiah. 

 Meanwhile, the market was so far unaffected by a bid by Bank Andromeda, part-owned by President Suharto's second son Bambang Trihatmodjo to have a government closure order revoked. 

 Trihatmodjo filed a lawsuit on Wednesday and was followed on Friday by Suharto's half-brother Probosutedjo, whose partly-owned Bank Jakarta was also among the 16 banks shut down.

title: FOCUS - Korean won woes weigh on Asian  currencies .
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 6 (Reuters) - Worries about a possible devaluation of the Korean won, Thailand's political troubles and the illness of its king and Indonesia's long road to economic recovery depressed Asian currency markets on Thursday. 

 The U.S. dollar's rise to six-month highs against the yen worsened the plight of regional currencies, but dealers said there was no sign of panic selling and many institutions were winding down for the year-end. 

 The South Korean won fell through the 970 level to the dollar, previously a trigger-point for central bank support, sparking rumours overseas of an impending devaluation. 

 But a Bank of Korea official said the central bank had no plans to devalue the won or widen its 2.25 percent trading band. "Our will to stabilise the foreign exchange market is as firm as ever," the official said. 

 The central bank intervened to sell dollars at 975 won, cushioning further declines in the won for the time being. 

 "The dollar will trade mostly under 975 won level, but if the central bank doesn't intervene, the dollar could rise to 980 won," a dealer in Seoul said. The won was at 975.30/5.30 at 0445 GMT against Wednesday's close at 969.70. 

 The central bank official said the bank did not concentrate exclusively on maintaining one level for its interventions. "Watching the dollar/yen movement and adjusting our markets accordingly is important for stability as well." 

 Korea's dwindling foreign reserves and stricken financial sector have triggered growing speculation it might need to seek help from the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 In Thailand, the baht lost its footing as the market awaited the outcome of talks between political parties to choose a successor to outgoing Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh. 

 Former prime ministers Chuan Leekpai and Chatichai Choonhavan are touted as front-runners for the post, but conflicting Thai media reports left the market reluctant to act. 

 "At the moment, nobody even knows who the actual prime minister is," the head of regional currencies at a European bank in Singapore said. 

 Bangkok dealers said the baht was receiving some support from exporters on a belief that it would strengthen if Chuan, leader of the Democrat Party, became prime minister. 

 The baht was at 39.10/20 to the dollar onshore against 38.90/39.20 late on Wednesday. Offshore baht was at 39.20/40 against 39.00/25. 

 Dealers said the health of 69-year-old King Bhumibol Adulyadej also remained a source of concern. 

 "If something happens to the King, that will undermine investor confidence again. He's the only one who can have some impact on the political scene," the Singapore dealer said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah slipped to 3,330/40 to the dollar from 3,300/10 late on Wednesday, but dealers said activity was confined to a narrow range between dollar demand and fears of aggressive central bank intervention. 

 "The market seems stuck with short-covering at the 3,330 level from Singapore and selling interest from Jakarta at the 3,340 level," a U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said. 

 Singapore dealers said players were having trouble pushing the dollar above the 3,400 rupiah level due to fears of a repeat of Monday's coordinated intervention in forex markets by Japan, Singapore and Indonesia. 

 The IMF's approval of a $10 billion loan package as part of a massive international bailout for Indonesia had no impact. 

 IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus praised Jakarta's efforts to reform the economy, but said slower growth and higher inflation would be unavoidable over the next two years. 

 The Malaysian ringgit weakened to 3.3200/300 to the dollar from 3.2750/850 late Wednesday on news Kuala Lumpur had approved a start next year to work on a 10 billion ringgit landbridge with Thailand. 

 "The market is asking how serious is Malaysia in trying to cap its current account deficit. This kind of news certainly doesn't help," a dealer with a European bank in Singapore said. 

 The government recently announced a delay in several large infrastructure and construction projects in a move to slow down the economy and cut the current account deficit. 

 The Singapore dollar looked soft but was off its lows of 1.5795 to the U.S. dollar on a flight-to-quality from Thailand. 

 But dealers said it was likely to weaken again alongside its neighbours, with forwards seen moving to the right. 

 The Philippine peso recovered a bit after falling through the 35 to the dollar level in early trade, but dealers said sentiment remained poor after the Supreme Court's decision to declare oil deregulation unconstitutional. 

 The Hong Kong dollar firmed to 7.7300/20 from 7.7325/35 on Wednesday as the wide interest rate spread with the U.S. dollar attracted players seeking a higher yield. 

 Hong Kong Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa said he expected interest rates to fall once the government succeeded in defending the local dollar's peg to the U.S. dollar. 

 He said the government's policy of defending the peg "will never change". 

 Hong Kong interest rates have risen in recent months as investors positioned for a possible attack on the peg and the Hong Kong Monetary Authority moved to discourage speculation. 

 The Taiwan dollar eased to T$30.640/710 from Wednesday's T$30.451 close, under pressure from the U.S. dollar's overnight surge against the yen.

 The rupiah rallied on Monday as three central banks rode on momentum sparked by Jakarta's economic reform to support the rupiah. It rose eight percent due to the coordinated intervention by the Bank of Japan, the Monetary Authority of Singapore and Bank Indonesia.

title: Singapore Aid Policy -2: Singapore Dlr Affected
text:
Since the Thai baht was floated in July, the Singapore dollar has fallen 8.5%. 

 'No matter how good Singapore's policy making is, it will still be held hostage to the policy mistakes of neighboring countries,' said Malik. 'The currency crisis shows that Singapore is guilty by association'. 

 Singapore's Foreign Ministry didn't immediately respond to questions on the switch of policy on foreign aid. 

 But Singapore's politicians have admitted that, despite the country's huge foreign exchange reserves and healthy economy, that the city state hasn't been untouched by the regional crisis. 'Growth will be slightly slower, but nothing to be alarmed about,' Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong was quoted as saying last week. 

 Manmindar Singh, economist at Nomura Singapore, said financial aid from Singapore could help restore confidence to the southeast Asian region as a whole. 

 Indeed on Monday, the rupiah rallied strongly on news of details of the IMF package for Indonesia and after the Monetary Authority of Singapore joined the central banks of Japan and Indonesia in intervening to support the rupiah. 

 That boosted the Singapore dollar and the Singapore stock market as well. 

 This higher profile in the Southeast Asian rescue packages has been accompanied by a higher profile for Singapore internationally. Singapore agreed earlier this year to contribute about US$470 million to a new emergency IMF funding mechanism known as the 'New Arrangements To Borrow,' which is expected to total US$50 billion. 

 Impetus for the NAB came after the 1995 bailout for Mexico, which sparked concerns that the IMF might need to raise extra funding quickly, particularly in situations where the U.S. was less motivated to act separately. 

 The NAB will replace an old IMF emergency program that included contributions only from the Group of 10 (G-10) leading industrialized nations. 

 Singapore has also expressed interest in Japan's controversial idea of creating an 'Asia Fund,' though officials have stressed that the facility should be made subordinate to the IMF. 

 Singapore's Goh has also stressed bilateral aid for Indonesia will be contingent on the reform measures agreed with the IMF.

 Dealers said the central bank stepped in several times trying to keep the rupiah below the 3,250 level. 

 But swap rates increased in both domestic and offshore markets on fears of tight rupiah liquidity following concerted intervention from three central banks on Monday. 

 Spot rupiah was at 3,240/60 at 0950 GMT after hovering in the range between 3,205 and 3,265 throughout the day.

 Dealers said offshore swap rates surged across the curve as operators scrambled for rupiah financing as the intervention on Monday seemed to have drained rupiah liquidity from the market.

 Swap rates were reflecting Monday's heavy intervention, with rates accelerating upward in the Singapore market. 

 "The market here is feeling the effect now. People are rushing for rupiah liquidity," one Singapore-based dealer said. 

 "The two-tier swap market is showing its full effect. Rates offshore have soared," the dealer said, adding the shorter the tenor, the higher were the premiums.

title: FOCUS - Asian  currencies  gain as baht cheers up.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The Thai baht greeted Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh's promise to resign with gusto on Tuesday, bringing cheer to most Southeast Asian currencies. 

 The baht made a strong start after Chavalit's surprise announcement late on Monday, sparking predictions that the rally was overdone and would soon fizzle out. 

 But official assurances that political changes would not hurt implementation of IMF-backed economic reforms and news of government spending cuts kept the baht well bid through the day. It ended at its day high of 38.60/80 to the dollar onshore, more than five percent above late Monday levels of 40.90/41.00. The offshore rate was at 38.40/50 at 1040 GMT against 39.85/40.35 previously. 

 "It seems the market is quite receptive to Chavalit's resignation," a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 He said spirits were further lifted by announcements that the government would lop another 18 billion baht from 1997/98 spending, on top of a previous 100 billion baht cut. 

 Thai stocks also rallied with the composite SET index adding 6.9 percent to end at 478.33. But currency traders remained conservative about the baht's potential for more gains. 

 "I just can't see dollar/baht continuing to come off. I can't see the baht strengthening much further than 37.50/38.00," one said. 

 And while Chavalit's decision to resign removed some of the market's immediate gloom, Thailand still faced a long, arduous road in rehabilitating its economy, analysts said. 

 "A change of leadership obviously means something has to be done and decisions which have to be taken are not going to be popular," said Kim Teo, managing director of Nicholas-Applegate Capital Management Asia. 

 Teo said Southeast Asian markets were in for more pain in the next six to 12 months as Thailand and Indonesia moved to restructure their economies in line with IMF requirements. 

 "The reaction we are seeing in the markets is more a technical bounce from an oversold position," he said. "Currencies will remain weakish but certainly not at the near panic collapses we've seen," he added. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah continued to rise on appreciation of the government's efforts to reform the economy in response to a massive IMF-led international aid package. 

 Dealers said the scramble caused by tighter liquidity after three central banks intervened on Monday to buy the rupiah lifted forward rates in early trade. 

 The value of concerted dollar sales for rupiah in Singapore on Monday by the Bank of Japan (BOJ), the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and Bank Indonesia was estimated at $300 to $500 million, senior Japanese traders said. 

 Singapore dealers said Bank Indonesia had intervened again on Tuesday to sell dollars. 

 "They sold quite a few times even around the low of 3,210. I don't think it was really big amounts but they tried to cap (the dollar) above 3,270," the U.S. bank dealer said. 

 The rupiah was at 3,260/70 to the dollar against its New York close at 3,205, sharply up from its Monday Asian close at 3,300/10. 

 The Singapore dollar was at 1.5555/75 to the U.S. dollar, off its highs of 1.5450 after active U.S. dollar buying by local banks below the 1.5500 level. 

 Dealers said there were rumours the dollar purchases were on behalf of the MAS, which was believed to be buying back dollars after Monday's intervention to support the rupiah. 

 Malaysia's ringgit was at 3.2675/775 to the dollar against 3.2600/700 late on Monday. 

 Dealers said selling was expected after the ringgit's recent bounce, but they saw a further test of the 3.20 per dollar resistance. 

 The Philippine peso ended higher at 34.84 to the dollar from a previous 35.14 close. The central bank offered dollars at 34.85/90 pesos but found no takers. 

Central bank governor Gabriel Singson said the policy-making Monetary Board would discuss by how much to lower the overnight lending rate at a regular meeting on Wednesday. The rate is at 16.125 percent. 

 Even the Taiwan dollar and South Korean won perked up on Tuesday. The Taiwan dollar ended sharply up at T$30.730 against Monday's 10-year low of T$31.245. 

 Dealers said investors took profit on U.S. dollar gains after the central bank said on Monday the Taiwan dollar had lost too much value. 

 On Tuesday, the central bank said the Taiwan dollar's recent depreciation made Taiwan remained "extremely competitive" against South Korea and Singapore in global export markets. 

 The South Korean won ended at 961.00 against Monday's 969.90 close after the central bank poured an estimated $300 million into the market to support it. 

 Only the Hong Kong dollar slipped as traders unwound long positions on a belief that the premium of Hong Kong dollar interest rates over U.S. rates would wane. 

 Hong Kong Monetary Authority Chief Executive Joseph Yam said last week that domestic interest rates were likely to ease in the short term.

title: Concerted dlr sales for rupiah $300-500mln - traders.
text:
TOKYO, Nov 4 (Reuters) - The value of concerted dollar sales for the Indonesian rupiah in Singapore on Monday by the Bank of Japan (BOJ), the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and Bank Indonesia was estimated at $300 million to $500 million, senior traders said on Tuesday. 

 "It (the dollar-selling intervention) came in small lots at many commercial banks, and the total would be $300-$500 million," said a senior trader at a Japanese bank. 

 The amount, although it was clearly less than $1 billion, was considered to be substantial for the rupiah market, even though its turnover had recently been boosted by speculative demand, they said. 

 Traders said that the BOJ, the MAS and Bank Indonesia may intervene again should the rupiah weaken beyond 3,300 to the U.S. dollar. 

 Neither the BOJ nor the MAS used the so-called `dollar-repo` arrangements which enable Indonesia to borrow dollars for the short term from Japan and Singapore by selling from its holdings of U.S. Treasury securities with a promise to buy them back later. 

 A dollar repo pact was established in April 1996 and comprises nine Asian central banks, including those of Japan, Indonesia and Singapore. 

 The rupiah was quoted at 3,212.00/3,222.00 to the dollar at 0342 GMT, compared with the New York close of 3,205. 

 The rupiah rallied on Monday to a high of 3,255 to the dollar from the opening of around 3,540/55 due to concerted intervention by the BOJ, MAS and Bank Indonesia. 

 Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said in a statement on Monday that the three monetary authorities agreed they would be ready to act in the market as and when necessary in the future. 

 "Japan's participation in the intervention shows Japan's position to support Indonesia and we hope that it will bring about currency stability," Mitsuzuka said.

title: FOCUS-Indonesian markets mixed on reform package.
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 3 (Reuters) - The rupiah surged against the dollar on Monday in the wake of economic reforms planned by the government and coordinated intervention by monetary authorities in Indonesia, Japan and Singapore, analysts said. 

 But the Jakarta share market was lukewarm, rising initially in line with the rupiah, but falling back before ending slightly up in a volatile trading day, stockbrokers said. 

Currency dealers said the eight percent recovery in the rupiah against the dollar in a single day was also helped by the intervention from the Bank of Japan (BOJ), the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and Bank Indonesia. 

 "The intervention is riding on the positive momentum that was caused by the announcement of the reforms," said Vincent Low, fixed-income strategist of Merrill Lynch in Singapore. 

 However, the IMF-led economic package failed to ignite a sustainable rally in the stock market. The composite of 277 companies edged up 0.26 percent to close at 501.71 points. 

 The market opened with a jump of almost three percent on local-led speculative buying in banking shares, but failed to trigger a follow-through from offshore investors. 

 "There is no major response from investors although the package is positive in the long-run. I think people are still waiting for more details on the package," said Stephanus Partono, an analyst with Goldman Sachs in Singapore. 

 "We maintain a neutral weighting as we do not expect a major rally in the market. The regional markets are still weak and the Indonesian economy is likely to slow down," he said. 

 Partono said investors were also waiting to see whether the rupiah could hold on to newly gained territory against the dollar. "What the market needs is rupiah stability." 

 Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad said Bank Indonesia had acted in concert with Singapore and Japan on Monday to support the rupiah. The finance ministries of Singapore and Japan also said that they had intervened to show confidence in the macroeconomic policies of the Indonesian government. 

 The rupiah ended at 3,270/3,000 against the dollar in Jakarta, compared with an opening of 3,550. The rupiah fell to a historic low of 3,850 on October 6. 

 "Today's concerted effort was aimed at strengthening the rupiah to levels more appropriate with the fundamentals of the Indonesian economy," Mar'ie said. 

 "The three authorities also confirmed that they stand ready to take steps necessary in the future to maintain stability of the rupiah as a part of stabilising currencies in the region." 

 Mar'ie said this effort would contribute positively to the implementation of the assistance package supported by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank. 

 "In the eyes of the IMF and other nations, Indonesia is of very strategic importance to Asia, such a large economy with such a huge population. Indonesia ranks quite high in Asia. You can see the commitment by everybody in Asia," Low said. REUTERS

title: FOCUS-SE Asian  currencies  leap as optimism returns.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Southeast Asian currencies leapt on Monday as Indonesia's early efforts to reform its economy in response to a massive IMF-led aid package sparked hopes the region might be headed for a turnaround. 

 Asian stock markets, particularly Hong Kong and Singapore, also benefitted from the rosier mood, rising substantially. 

 The Indonesian rupiah led Asian currencies higher, shooting to a high of 3,240 to the dollar, a gain of more than nine percent from its opening around 3,540/55 after Japan and Singapore said they had intervened to support the rupiah. 

 In separate statements released in Singapore, the two Finance Ministries said the Bank of Japan (BOJ) and Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had intervened in Singapore foreign exchange markets with Bank Indonesia. 

 Singapore Finance Minister Richard Hu said in a statement the MAS bought Indonesian rupiah against the U.S. dollar in concert with the other authorities. 

 "Singapore's participation in this joint intervention reflects our confidence in the macroeconomic policies of the Indonesian government," it said. 

 Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said the operation was "aimed at correcting excessive depreciation of the Indonesian rupiah," and the three authorities would be ready to act again when necessary. 

 Dealers said the rupiah, which opened on an upbeat note, sharply extended its gains after the intervention was confirmed. 

 "The market was already very happy with the package...It was very timely to come in and strike while the iron was hot," said a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore. 

 She said Japan and Singapore had probably intervened in "token amounts" with Indonesia selling the bulk of dollars, but the move caught players off-guard in a market severely thinned by a Japanese holiday. 

 Singapore and Japan said on Saturday they were each ready to extend US$5.0 billion to Indonesia to supplement resources organised by the International Monetary Fund (IMF). 

 Indonesia could receive upto US$40 billion in financial aid from multilateral agencies and individual countries provided it meets strict IMF conditions to rehabilitate its economy. 

 Analysts saw Monday's joint intervention as aimed at curbing a further loss of confidence in Indonesia, especially in the face of Thailand's persistent woes. 

 "I guess regional central banks felt they could have done more in the case of Thailand. They didn't and things got worse, so if they didn't do anything aggressive now, they'd never turn it around," said Chia Woon Khien, head of Asian research at Skandinaviska Enskilda Banken in Singapore. 

 "Indonesia's case was also slightly less problematic so they were more willing to commit their money and the market was more willing to believe in their commitment," she added. 

 The Indonesian government liquidation of 16 unhealthy banks, some of them linked to President Suharto's family, was welcomed by currency and stock markets. 

 "Indonesia has helped a lot. They've taken firm actions, unlike the Thais," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 In August, the IMF organised $17.2 billion in aid for Thailand and on Monday the Thai baht was the only Southeast Asian currency to fall, plagued by political uncertainties and delays in implementing financial sector reforms. 

 The baht was at 40.90/41.000 to the dollar onshore at 1005 GMT, off a low of 41.00 against Friday's 40.70/41.00. It was firmer offshore at 40.20/40 against 40.60/90 previously. 

 Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh came under fresh pressure to resign on Monday as a key coalition partner, former prime minister Chatichai Choonhavan, quit his advisory post. 

 The market shrugged off expressions of confidence in the baht's long-term stability fromFinance Minister Kosit Panpiemras, whot urged Thais to refrain from buying foreign currencies unless absolutely necessary. 

 The Singapore dollar remained near its highs at 1.5525/55 to the U.S. dollar against an opening below 1.5740. Singapore's benchmark stock index ended the day with a hefty 7.83 percent rise to 1,703.95 points. 

 "It looks like dollar/Sing has seen a top at 1.5970. If it rallies to 1.5700/40 now, I'd favour a sell," another European bank dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit surged to a high of 3.2500 against 3.4070/180 late on Friday. 

 Comments by U.S. financier George Soros also fuelled buying of Southeast Asian currencies, dealers said. He told the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) he believed the world's financial turbulence was over and called for international regulatory coordination to head off further storms. 

 "What he says goes," said the U.S. bank dealer. 

 The Philippine peso ended up at 35.14 to the dollar against Friday's 35.42 close on gains in other regional currencies and the central bank's early interventions to sell $500,000. 

Central bank governor Gabriel Singson said he would meet commercial bank presidents to discuss ways to cut bank lending rates and reduce volatility in the peso. 

 The Taiwan dollar ploughed new depths, ending at T$31.245 to the U.S. dollar amid widespread expectations of long-term depreciation as the central bank remained out of view. 

 After the market closed, the central bank cited an external index showing the Taiwan dollar had lost too much value, but vowed to let the market determine its exchange rate. 

 The South Korean won ended weak at 969.9 to the dollar against 964.60 on Friday despite central bank interventions. 

 A Bank of Korea official told Reuters on Saturday the battered won would "never, never, never" breach the psychological 1,000 to the dollar level. 

 "That was a dangerous statement. It immediately made the won go to 970 today: never say never," said a Singapore dealer. 

 The Australian dollar received a boost from a firm set of retail sales data, swinging sentiment against a rate cut. It firmed to $0.7129/34 from an early $0.7007/12.
