title: FOCUS-SE Asian  currencies  surge on rupiah rally.
text:
SINGAPORE, Nov 3 (Reuters) - Most Southeast Asian currencies surged on Monday as Indonesia's early efforts to reform its economy in response to a massive IMF-led international aid package put a shine on the region. 

 A more upbeat mood on most Asian stock markets, particularly Hong Kong and Singapore, also boosted regional currencies, dealers said. 

 The Indonesian rupiah shot to a high of 3,255 to the dollar from an opening around 3,540/55 on talk of concerted intervention by foreign central banks. 

 Singapore dealers attributed the scale of the rupiah's rise to intervention by the Bank of Japan to sell dollars through the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS). 

 They said confirmation of the intervention by the Singapore and Japanese Finance Ministries gave the rupiah another push. 

 In separate statements released in Singapore, the ministries said the Bank of Japan (BOJ) and Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) had intervened in Singapore foreign exchange markets in concert with Bank Indonesia. 

 Singapore Finance Minister Richard Hu said in the statement the MAS bought Indonesian rupiah against the U.S. dollar in concert with the other authorities. 

 "Singapore's participation in this joint intervention reflects our confidence in the macroeconomic policies of the Indonesian government," it said. 

 Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said in a statement the operation was "aimed at correcting excessive depreciation of the Indonesian rupiah," and the three authorities would be ready to act again when necessary. 

 Dealers said the rupiah was also lifted by Indonesia's weekend move to liquidate 16 unhealthy banks, reflecting a keen desire to meet an IMF-backed programme to restore its economy. 

 "Indonesia has helped a lot. They've taken firm actions, unlike the Thais," a European bank dealer in Singapore said. 

 In August, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) organised $17.2 billion in aid for Thailand and on Monday the Thai baht was the only Southeast Asian currency to fall, plagued by political uncertainties and delays in implementing financial sector reforms. 

 The baht was at 41.050/180 to the dollar onshore against 40.70/41.00 late on Friday. But it firmed to 39.92/40.12 offshore against 40.60/90 previously. 

 "Corporates and importers bought actively as they are not sure where the baht would go given political uncertainties," a local bank dealer in Bangkok said. 

 "Moreover, once the baht hit the 40.00 level, it generated a lot of doubts over the government's ability to handle the economy," the dealer said. 

 Other dealers said the baht's drop reflected both genuine commercial dollar demand and speculative buying. 

 Finance Minister Kosit Panpiemras urged Thais to refrain from buying foreign currencies unless absolutely necessary. 

 He also said he was confident of the long-term stability of the baht, which has plunged to new lows in recent days, if IMF guidelines were followed. 

 The Singapore dollar was sharply higher at 1.5530/66 to the U.S. dollar at 0500 GMT against an opening below 1.5740. 

 Singapore's benchmark stock index ended the morning 5.84 percent higher at 1,678.72 points. 

 "It looks like dollar/Sing has seen a top at 1.5970. If it rallies to 1.5700/40 now, I'd favour a sell," another European bank dealer said. She said the U.S. dollar's breach of the 1.5740 technical support would limit its upside. 

 The Malaysian ringgit surged to 3.2550/650 to the dollar from 3.4070/180 late on Friday, as players focused on the rupiah's gains. A Singapore dealer said a large oil company was heard to be a big ringgit buyer. 

 Dealers said funds were likely to take profits on their long dollar positions after U.S. financier George Soros said there was a need for more market regulation, echoing Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's now familiar refrain. 

 Soros told the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) on Saturday that recent market turmoil showed the need for central banks and regulators to band together to rein in speculators. 

 Mahathir has repeatedly accused Soros of taking positions against the ringgit and intensifying its drop. 

 The Philippine peso was firm at 35.15/25 to the dollar against Friday's 35.42 close as the market took its cue from the central bank's offer price of 35.40 to 35.20 pesos. 

 In North Asia, the Taiwan dollar ploughed new depths of T$31.240 to the U.S. dollar amid widespread expectations of long-term depreciation as the central bank remained out of view. 

 The South Korean won remained depressed at 966.50/9.80 to the dollar despite the central bank's intervention to sell about $300 million at 965 won. The central bank stepped in again at the 970 won level. 

 A Bank of Korea official told Reuters on Saturday the battered won would "never, never, never" breach the psychological 1,000 to the dollar level. 

 "That was a dangerous statement. It immediately made the won go to 970 today: never say never," said a Singapore dealer. 

 The Hong Kong dollar was steady at 7.7325/45 to the U.S. dollar as forwards eased and interbank rates came off. Dealers said the Hong Kong Monetary Authority was not seen adding liquidity to the market after last week's operations. 

 The Australian dollar received a boost from a firm set of retail sales data, swinging sentiment against a rate cut. It firmed to $0.7125/35 from an early $0.7007/12.

title: Key dates in Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 24 (Reuters) - A dramatic week on the Hong Kong stock market, with a savage fall followed by a partial recovery, is the latest development in a string of financial crises across East Asia. 

 The following are key dates: 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency is hit by a massive attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate 1-3/4 percentage points to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thailand's finance minister. 

 The resignation has immediate financial impact in the Philippines, where the overnight rate rises to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - The Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yonchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - The Bank of Thailand announces a managed float of the baht and calls on the International Monetary Fund for "technical assistance". 

 The announcement effectively devalues the baht by about 15-20 percent. It ends at a record low of 28.80 to the dollar. 

 In Manila, the central bank is forced to intervene heavily to defend the peso. 

 July 3 - The Philippine central bank raises the overnight lending rate to 24 percent from 15 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. The intervention works and the currency hits a high of 2.5100/10 after a low of 2.5240/50. 

 July 11 - The Philippine central bank says in a statement it will allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is starting to be affected. In a surprise move, Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Currency meltdown. 

 The ringgit hits 38-month low of 2.6530 to the dollar. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad launches bitter attack on "rogue speculators". 

 The Hong Kong dollar remains steady, but territory later reveals US$1 billion was spent on intervention during a period of two hours on an unspecified day in July. 

 July 26 - Mahathir names hedge fund manager George Soros as the man responsible for the attack on the ringgit. He later brands Soros a "moron". 

 August 5 - Thailand unveils austerity plan and complete revamp of finance sector as part of IMF suggested policies for a rescue package. Central bank suspends 48 finance firms. 

 August 11 - The IMF unveils in Tokyo a rescue package for Thailand including loans totalling $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 13 - The rupiah begins to come under severe pressure. It hits a historic low of 2,682 to the dollar before ending at 2,655. The central bank actively intervenes in its defence. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of a band. The rupiah plunges to 2,755. 

 August 16 - An unnamed Beijing source tells a local Hong Kong newspaper that China is prepared to use US$50 billion to defend the Hong Kong dollar. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. The package now totals $16.7 billion. Brunei later adds $500 to the bailout package, bringing it to a total of $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 4 - Carnage in the Philippine peso continues. It falls to a record low of 32.43 to the dollar before central bank intervention helps it up slightly to end at 32.38. 

 Ringgit breaks through 3.0000 to the dollar barrier. 

 Mahathir delays several multi-billion dollar construction projects. 

 Sept 16 - Indonesia says it will postpone projects worth 39 trillion rupiah in an attempt to slash the budget shortfall. 

 Sept 20 - Mahathir tells delegates to the IMF/World Bank annual conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral and should be stopped. 

 Sept 21 - Soros says "Dr Mahathir is a menace to his own country". 

 Oct 1 - Mahathir repeats his siren call for tighter regulation, or a total ban, on forex trading. The currency falls four percent in less than two hours to a low of 3.4080. 

 Oct 6 - The rupiah hits a low of 3,845. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 14 - Vietnam, bowing to months of pressure on its dong currency, doubles the permitted trading range to 10 percent either side of the daily official rate. 

 Oct 17 - Malaysia presents a belt-tightening budget to try to stop the economy sliding into recession. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. The Hang Seng index plunges 23.34 percent to 10,426.30 by Thursday's close, after 13,601.01 the previous Friday. 

 The Hong Kong dollar is linked to the U.S. dollar at an official rate of 7.8 to one. After the turmoil in Southeast Asian markets, the heat is on the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Oct 24 - The Hong Kong stock market makes a partial recovery, climbing 6.89 percent to 11,144.34, but this still leaves the market 25 percent weaker than it was at the start of October.

title: Indonesian  central bank  steps in as rupiah falls.
text:
JAKARTA, Oct 16 (Reuters) - The Indonesian central bank stepped into the foreign exchange market as the rupiah fell through the 3,600 level against the dollar in early Thursday trading, dealers said.

title: Key dates in Southeast Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 8 (Reuter) - Indonesia's announcement on Wednesday that it will seek assistance from the International Monetary Fund was the latest development in Southeast Asia's financial crisis. 

 The following are key dates: 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency is hit by a massive attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate 1-3/4 percentage points to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 May 16 - Thailand says foreign speculators will have to "pay the price" for their attacks by buying back the baht from the more expensive swap market. 

 Again the Philippines is affected. The overnight rate is hiked seven percentage points to 20 percent and the central bank sells more dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thailand's finance minister. 

 The resignation has immediate impact in the Philippines. There, the central bank had cut the overnight rate in the morning to 12.75 percent from 13 percent. But after the resignation announcement it jacks it back up to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - The Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yonchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - The Bank of Thailand announces a managed float of the baht and calls on the International Monetary Fund for "technical assistance". 

 The announcement effectively devalues the baht by about 15-20 percent. It ends at a record low of 28.80 to the dollar. 

 In Manila, the central bank is forced to intervene heavily to defend the peso. 

 July 3 - The Philippine central bank raises the overnight lending rate to 24 percent from 15 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. The intervention works and the currency hits a high of 2.5100/10 after a low of 2.5240/50. 

 July 11 - The Philippine central bank says in a statement it will allow the peso to move in a wider range against the dollar. The IMF backs the move and Managing Director Camdessus says he would recommend the IMF board approve the Philippines' request for an extension of its Extended Fund Facility (EFF). 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah is starting to be affected. In a surprise move, Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support under fast-track regulations drawn up after the 1995 Mexican crisis. 

 July 24 - Currency meltdown. 

 The ringgit hits 38-month low of 2.6530 to the dollar. Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad launches bitter attack on "rogue speculators". 

 The Singapore dollar hits 32-month low of 1.4738 to the dollar. 

 The Hong Kong dollar remains steady, but territory later reveals US$1 billion was spent on intervention during a period of two hours on an unspecified day in July. 

 July 26 - Mahathir names hedge fund manager George Soros as the man responsible for the attack on the ringgit. He later brands Soros a "moron". 

 August 5 - Thailand unveils austerity plan and complete revamp of finance sector as part of IMF suggested policies for a rescue package. Central bank suspends 48 finance firms. 

 August 11 - The IMF unveils in Tokyo a rescue package for Thailand including loans totalling $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 13 - The rupiah begins to come under severe pressure. It hits a historic low of 2,682 to the dollar before ending at 2,655. The central bank actively intervenes in its defence. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of managing the exchange rate through the use of a band. The rupiah plunges to 2,755. 

 August 16 - An unnamed Beijing source tells a local Hong Kong newspaper that China is prepared to use US$50 billion to defend the Hong Kong dollar. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. The package now totals $16.7 billion. 

 August 27 - Brunei adds $500 million more to Thailand's bailout package, bringing it to a total of $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 2 - A falling equity market helps push the Philippine peso to a record low of 30.90 to the dollar. 

 In Jakarta, the rupiah ends at 3,045. 

 Sept 3 - Indonesia announces measures to revive investor confidence in the country, including scrapping a 49 percent limit on foreign purchases of shares at initial public offerings and a hike in luxury taxes. 

 The package has little impact on the rupiah. 

 Sept 4 - Carnage in the Philippine peso continues. It falls to a record low of 32.43 to the dollar before central bank intervention helps it up slightly to end at 32.38. 

 Ringgit breaks through 3.0000 to the dollar barrier. 

 Mahathir delays several multi-billion dollar construction projects. A controversial measure to ban short selling in 100 key stocks will also be withdrawn. 

 Sept 16 - Indonesia says it will postpone projects worth 39 trillion rupiah in an attempt to slash the budget shortfall. 

 Sept 20 - Mahathir tells delegates to the IMF/World Bank annual conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral and should be stopped. 

 Sept 21 - Soros says "Dr Mahathir is a menace to his own country". 

 Sept 22 - The forex market gives its answer to Mahathir. The ringgit tumbles more than two percent to end at 3.1220 to the dollar. 

 Sept 30 - Ringgit fall continues. Mahathir says in Chile that 1998 Malaysian economic growth would slow due to the falling ringgit. It hits a low of 3.2150. 

 Oct 1 - Mahathir repeats his siren call for tighter regulation, or a total ban, on forex trading. The currency falls four percent in less than two hours to a low of 3.4080. 

 Oct 6 - The rupiah hits a low of 3,845. Dealers are now talking of the possibility of Indonesia having to go to the IMF for help. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Regionals firm on  central bank  fea.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 7 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies regained their footing on Tuesday as traders turned cautious about buying the dollar too aggressively amid growing talk of central bank intervention in very thin markets. 

 Bank Indonesia, which stepped in to sell dollars when the rupiah slumped to an all-time low of 3,850 per dollar on Monday, was believed to have intervened again on Tuesday. 

 Dealers said the central bank had sold dollars in small amounts, pushing the rupiah to a high of 3,475 against its opening 3,600/50. 

 But persistent dollar demand from underhedged domestic companies and offshore funds jumping on the bandwagon pushed the rupiah back down to 3,640/50 by 0455 GMT. 

 The rupiah's overnight gains after State Secretary Murdiono said the government would take steps to stabilise the rupiah, while remaining committed to free foreign exchange flows, also helped sentiment. 

 The Philippine central bank also stepped in to prop up the peso as it fell prey to pent-up dollar demand from foreign banks, diving to a record low of 35.981 per dollar. 

 Manila traders said the central bank's dollar sales from the 35.85 peso level helped turn the tide, pushing the peso back up to 34.65/75 by 0455 GMT. 

 The reimposition of a volatility band added to the market mayhem as the peso twice breached its limits before the central bank intervention, leading to trade suspensions. 

 The Bankers Association of the Philippines, which operates the electronic forex dealing system, decided late on Monday to reintroduce the band due to the peso's recent volatility. 

 It calls for a 30-minute recess if the peso moves outside a two percent limit. Upon resumption of trading, the band is narrowed to one percent and trading can be suspended two more times before being stopped for the rest of the day. 

 Elsewhere, the Malaysian ringgit recovered sharply amid rumours in Singapore that the central Bank Negara Malaysia was intervening to support the unit. 

 But Malaysian dealers said they had not detected the central bank's presence and most attributed the ringgit's rise to commercial demand and buying of the unit against the Singapore dollar. 

 "U.S. names were said to be buying about $200-$300 million in ringgit/Sing," said one Singapore dealer. 

 Dealers said the market was also plagued by fears Malaysia might implement a two-tier market, similar to Thailand's system, after Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's repeated calls for further curbs on currency trading. 

 There was confusion on foreign exchange markets when the format on a Reuters currency quotation page was mistakenly changed early on Tuesday. The changes gave the impression a two-tier market had been created in the ringgit, rupiah and peso. 

 This mistake was subsequently corrected to reflect global consolidated contributions. 

 The Singapore dollar recovered from its lows around 1.5470 to the U.S. dollar in line with the ringgit's move, but its gains were capped by buying of the ringgit/Sing cross. 

 Dealers said the market was awaiting discussion in parliament, later in the day, about the impact of the Southeast Asian currency crisis on Singapore's economy and whether steps were being taken to address it. 

 The Thai baht showed a firm bias on growing optimism about the government's finance sector reform package, due to be announced on October 15. 

 "It is a very narrow bid and offer, I think people are looking into the future for October 15 and some people think the news will come out positively," a local bank dealer in Bangkok said. Onshore baht was at 36.60/65 to the dollar while the offshore rate was at 35.65/75.

title: ASIAN EXOTICS - Rupiah shaky despite BI move.
text:
SINGAPORE, Oct 6 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah remained badly shaken on Monday after its steep early drop drove the central bank to intervene and sell dollars for the first time in weeks, dealers said. 

 The rupiah dived to an all-time low of 3,845 to the dollar as domestic companies and offshore funds scrambled for dollars, bringing down other Southeast Asian currencies as well. 

 It was back at 3,800 at 0445 GMT after recovering to around 3,725 on Bank Indonesia's intervention, compared with an opening around 3,700/50. 

 Some dealers said the central bank did not sell a large amount of dollars, as the market was already very thin with deals of $1-$2 million triggering wild swings. 

 The unexpected intervention gave the rupiah some respite but dealers said its prospects remained grim, with seeing it headed for 4,000 to the dollar as Indonesian companies grappled with huge foreign debts. 

 "A lot of people don't see an end to this. It's now like a chicken and egg situation. Companies that were fine at 2,500 (rupiah to the dollar) are not at 3,800," said a U.S. bank dealer in Singapore. 

 She said there were growing rumours that Indonesian companies with large dollar call options were going to default on their positions. 

 "Many of them have written dollar calls and they're not professional option traders. So they've left them unhedged," she said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit succumbed to fresh selling as players quickly shrugged off news of a large trade surplus in August and looked for excuses to buy the dollar again. It was at 3.3730/800 to the dollar against an early high of 3.3580. 

 Malaysia announced an August trade surplus of 1.2 billion ringgit on Saturday, after deficits of 900 million ringgit in July and 2.8 billion ringgit in June. 

 Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's repeated calls for tight curbs on currency trading kept a lid on the ringgit, dealers said. 

 Mahathir told a news conference in Buenos Aires on Friday that current regulation was clearly insufficient. 

 "We have already set a limit to currency trading...but it is quite obvious that it is not effective," he said. 

 Dealers said they expected dollar/ringgit to stay firm but its rise could be limited by caution ahead of Malaysia's budget on October 17. 

 The Singapore dollar looked set to head for 1.55 to the U.S. dollar as buying of the ringgit from opening levels of 45.60/65 Singapore cents depressed the Singapore unit, dealers said. 

 The Singapore dollar was at 1.5485/95 against 1.5422/37 late on Friday. 

 The Thai baht weakened along with its neighbours as players turned to the dollar ahead of Thailand's eagerly awaited financial reform package, due on October 15. 

 News at the weekend that Thailand might need more than the $17.2 billion loan package arranged by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to pull out of its economic crisis also depressed the baht, dealers said. 

 It fell to 36.80/37.00 per dollar onshore against 36.40/36.50 late on Friday. It was at 36.30/45 offshore against 35.55/75. 

 Bank of Thailand Assistant Governor Siri Ganjarerndee told a conference in Bangkok that Thailand's original assumptions about the amount of short-term debt to be rolled over may have been overly optimistic. 

 In the Philippines, surging overnight money rates kept the peso somewhat protected from the region's woes, but dealers said it showed signs of weakness. 

 The interbank call loan rate hit a high of 105 percent, knocking the wind out of the stock market where the main index breached its 2,000 support to end down 3.37 percent at 1,961.24. 

 The peso was at 34.926 to the dollar against Friday's 34.91 close, reflecting last week's "gentlemen's agreement" among bankers not to trade the peso below 34.926 to the dollar and to limit over-the-counter dollar sales to the 35.275 rate.

 Officials at Bank Indonesia, however, refused to confirm or deny the intervention reports. 

 Because the volume of trading has been thin in the market in recent weeks, some optimists hold that pressure on the rupiah has been exaggerated. They also note that quarter-ending periods traditionally put added pressure on the Indonesian currency as companies move to square their dollar positions. 

 More bearish sentiment, however, focuses on monthly charges of between $5-$10 billion in dollar-denominated debt coming due. And with export-based companies apparently unwilling to let go of their dollars, there is the potential for continued downward pressure on the rupiah - and a growing number of loan defaults 

 With overnight lending rates still hovering well above 30%, there is concern that the health of Indonesia's overall financial system is facing a serious threat, adding credibility to the calls for IMF or World Bank assistance. 

 Bank Indonesia, for its part, does not have a strong record in regulating the nation's banking sector. The number of banks has grown to a dangerously high one of 239, and the central bank has been unable over the past two years to force a consolidation. 

 Critics point to the central bank's inability to liquidate institutions such as Bank Pacific and Bank Yama as examples. Both institutions have extremely high levels of non-performing loans but remain in operation; many critics point to the banks' politically well-connected owners.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Plunges Again; IMF Help May Be Needed
text:
JAKARTA (AP-Dow Jones)--Indonesia's rupiah plunged again Monday, prompting some economists to suggest the country may need to turn to the International Monetary Fund and World Bank to restore lasting stability and confidence to the country's financial markets. 

 The rupiah fell to another record low of 3,857.50 rupiah to the dollar Monday before before intervention by Bank Indonesia, the central bank, and a meeting of top economic officials hosted by President Suharto helped to reverse the slide somewhat. 

 Even so, the dollar was trading late Monday at 3,717.50 rupiah, up from 3,660 rupiah late Friday and 3,405 rupiah late on Thursday - losing 8.4% of its value in two trading sessions. The currency has dropped 37% since the beginning of the year. 

 The meeting at the presidential palace resulted in new measures to help domestic exporters get access to imports. And Coordinating Minister for Economy, Finance, and Development Supervision Saleh Afiff announced that the government is lobbying international creditors to roll over their lendings to Indonesian companies to ease the pressure on the rupiah. State Secretary Moerdiono issued a plea to local companies not to hoard their dollar holdings. 

 Some Indonesian companies have been struggling to repay dollar borrowings taken out before the recent collapse in the rupiah's value. 

 But several economists argue that domestic measures won't be enough. 

 'There's an enormous shortage of dollars (among Indonesian companies) but it's also a psychological problem - that is why the IMF or World Bank are needed,' said Kwik Kian Gie, a prominent Indonesian economist. 'No one believes that the government alone can solve the problem.'

title: Indonesian rupiah remains weak, but off low.
text:
JAKARTA, Sept 30 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah remained weak against the dollar in thin early trading on Tuesday after falling to a historic low of 3,290, dealers said. 

 They said continued high corporate demand for dollars, either for hedging or to repay maturing papers, appeared to be one reason for sustained pressure on the rupiah. 

 They said sufficient liquidity supply, coupled with the falling Malaysian ringgit, had added to rupiah woes. 

 Spot rupiah was at 3,267/77 at 0400 GMT, compared with an opening of 3,205/15 on Tuesday. Tomorrow and today rupiah were at 3,260.25/67.25 and 3,261.0/68.0, respectively. 

 Overnight rupiah was around 17/18 percent and overnight swap was at par/0.1 point. Tom/next was at 0.2/0.5. 

 Dealers said a shortage of dollar supply was another factor which boosted the U.S. currency. 

 One foreign bank dealer said some offshore dollar buying and continued domestic hedging in the spot market had weakened the rupiah further to new lows on Tuesday. 

 One chief dealer with a local bank said some corporates whose papers were maturing seemed to be borrowing from the interbank dollar market rather than buying spot dollars. 

 "Some seem to think it's too expensive to buy dollars from the spot market. So they just borrow short-term from the interbank market," he said, adding that this was reflected by rising overnight dollar rates to 25 percent. 

 Dealers said overnight dollar rose to as high as 40 percent on Monday, suggesting a short-term dollar liquidity problem. 

 "We also see some dollar purchases from some state banks. They won't buy it for speculation. This must be genuine dollar demand," the chief dealer said. 

 He viewed the current high dollar demand as a short-term liquidity problem which might be eased probably through some supply of dollar liquidity from the central bank. 

 "An intervention might not be helpful because it would reduce Indonesia's reserve. Besides, the region is not in a good shape yet," the dealer said. 

 "But a temporary dollar injection, sort of dollar lending to the interbank market, might help reduce the tightness in the market. This will not affect currency reserves," he added. 

 The dealer said the price for the on-going high corporate demand was reflected in higher interbank rates for dollars or exchange rates, meaning rising dollars. 

 "But an improved dollar liquidity may help reduce pressure in the interbank market and the positive impact could probably spill over to the spot market," the dealer said. 

 "This could be a short-term way out while in the longer term we have to resort to fundamentals," he added. 

 One Singapore-based dealer said rises of the dollar appeared to be more Jakarta-driven, helped by relatively good supply of domestic liquidity. 

 "But rates are exaggerated due to thin volumes," he said, adding the rupiah was moving in tandem with the ringgit. 

 He said from the offshore-point of view offshore players were still long in cash-flows. 

 "It shouldn't be any problem for offshore to sell rupiah and buy spot dollars because they are very well funded," the dealer said, adding they were also well prepared in ringgit. 

 One-week swap was at 3.5/6.5, one-month at 25/35, two at 55/70, three at 90/105, six at 180/200 and one-year at 350/380.

title: Thai baht drop depresses S.E.Asian  currencies .

SINGAPORE, Aug 22 (Reuter) - Southeast Asian currencies slid once more on Friday as the Thai baht fell to record lows, spurring fresh buying of the dollar across the board. 

 The baht hit a new record low of 34.10 to the dollar onshore in the afternoon after heavy commercial demand for dollars and nagging concerns about Thailand's economic and political outlook pushed the baht through the key 33 level in early trade. 

 "When the baht breached the 33 level, everyone lost confidence and wanted to unwind the baht as quickly as possible," a Bangkok dealer said. 

 The baht was quoted at 34.10/40 to the dollar at 0855 GMT against 33.13/32 five hours earlier. Offshore baht was at 33.65/80 against 32.70/32.80. 

 Concern that Thailand's shrinking foreign reserves would be affected by big forward swap contracts carried by the central bank also hurt sentiment for the baht, dealers said. 

 The central bank said on Thursday it had $23.4 billion in forward swap contracts that are due over the next 12 months, of which $8.6 billion are onshore and $14.8 billion offshore. 

 The forward contracts were taken to defend the baht during massive speculative attacks in May. 

 "With 33 being broken, the sky's the limit. It's in uncharted territory," the head of Asian currencies at a European bank in Singapore said. 

 He said the baht looked set to hit 35 to the dollar and the central bank was unlikely to intervene to stop the slide. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah recovered from its lows but remained weak as players covered short dollar positions ahead of the weekend and local companies sought to hedge their positions. 

 "The funds are buying the dollar again after liquidating their positions above the 2,900 level," the Singapore dealer said. Sentiment was also depressed by Standard and Poor's announcement on Thursday that it had revised the ratings outlook on Indonesian banks to negative from stable, he added. 

 Reports of a run on deposits at one of Indonesia's banks were also affecting the market, he said. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,700/10 after falling to a low of 2,755 against 2,675/75 late on Thursday. 

 A Japanese bank dealer in Jakarta said the rupiah could strengthen through the 2,700 level again as the outlook for liquidity remained tight. 

 "Liquidity is still the main concern. Operators are also preparing for Monday because the previous central bank forward intervention will mature," the dealer said. 

 The Malaysian ringgit surrendered early gains and fell sharply on spillover from the rupiah and baht, though thin volumes and wide spreads continued to exaggerate activity. 

 The ringgit was at 2.7685/715 to the dollar after reaching a high of 2.7430 earlier, against 2.7650/700 late on Thursday. 

 The Singapore dollar slid back through the 1.50 to the U.S. dollar level and was quoted at 1.5040/50 at 0855 GMT. 

 "But the pace will be slower as the market is looking more favourably at the Singapore dollar than the other regionals," a dealer said, citing strong Singapore export figures announced on Wednesday and an upward revision of its 1997 growth forecast. 

 The Philippine peso ended firmer on inflows of arbitrage money and as exporters and other companies converted foreign currency deposits to pesos following recent central bank moves to tighten liquidity. 

 The peso finished at 29.85 to the dollar against Thursday's close of 29.885. 

 In Taiwan, the central bank's prolonged defence of the T$28.727 level in the face of offshore speculative pressure finally dampened demand for U.S. dollars. 

 The Taiwan dollar ended virtually unchanged at T$28.725.

title: FOCUS- Indonesia  rupiah down again, no  intervention . [CORRECTED 12:20 GMT]
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 15 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah was hit again on Friday as investors panicked in the aftermath of its float and pushed the unit to yet another historic low against the dollar. 

 By the close of trading in Jakarta, the rupiah was at 2,880/2,910 against the dollar, which was about four percent weaker (corrects from "more than one percent weaker") than the 2,770/90 open but off a 2,960 low. 

 Dealers said they waited in vain for central bank intervention to restore confidence. 

 The central bank, Bank Indonesia, lifted the intervention band on Thursday, effectively floating the currency, but said it reserved the right to step into the market if deemed necessary. 

 Edwin Png, head of treasury for Bank of America in Jakarta, said the steep falls had made the market jittery. 

 "I have housewives calling me up to ask about the rate," he said in the early afternoon. "Bank Indonesia should intervene now or else I see the rate going up to 3,000 later in the day and 3,200 next week." 

 "They should do both. They should intervene and they should tighten liquidity." 

 In the event, the rate did not fall that far despite the lack of intervention. But dealers and analysts said the tone of the market was weak because many Indonesian companies were scrambling to hedge their dollar exposures. 

 They added that volumes were thin because most investors squared positions ahead of the weekend. 

 Most however said the panic in the rupiah would be short-lived and that the currency would soon trade at more realistic levels, perhaps some time next week. 

 "We'll see the bottom end of the rupiah start to appear fairly soon," said Kevin Evans, senior analyst at ANZ Securities in Jakarta. 

 "I'm looking for the rupiah to come in at the end of this year somewhere between 2,700 and 2,800. We'll see it recover somewhat and then see a stable cycle after that." 

 "There is some nervousness onshore because a lot of corporates had not fully hedged their dollar liability and thus we may indeed go to the 3,000 level before the rupiah begins to recover towards more sustainable levels in line with its basic fundamentals," Bill Belchere, the head of Asian fixed income research at Merrill Lynch, told Reuters Financial Television. 

 "We do believe the fundamentals are sound, Indonesia is not like Thailand in any way," he added. "However, it's a very nervous market, you cannot contain the effect of spillover in the medium-term. However, in the longer-term we are sure Indonesia has very fine economic prospects and we would see the rupiah somewhere between 2,600 and 2,700 to the dollar." 

 The prolonged spell of currency weakness which has hit Southeast Asia began in May with attacks on the Thai baht. Thailand was forced to devalue its currency in July and has said it has received pledges worth $17 billion from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and Asian nations. 

 The IMF has welcomed Indonesia's decision to allow its currency to float, saying the move would allow the country's economy to continue its recent impressive performance. 

 "In present circumstances, a floating exchange rate will enhance the effectiveness of macroeconomic policies aimed at sustaining high rates of growth with financial stability," said Stanley Fischer, acting managing director of the IMF, in a statement issued in Washington. 

 Fischer called Indonesia's decision timely and said it came partly in response to turbulence on regional currency markets. He said floating the rupiah was "in line with Bank Indonesia's steady progress toward greater exchange rate flexibility, particularly over the last two years".

title: FOCUS-Rupiah plunges,dealers look for  intervention .
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 15 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah plunged further on Friday, the day after it was floated, and dealers said they were looking to the central bank to intervene and restore market confidence. 

 The rupiah fell to a new record low of 2,915 to the dollar by early afternoon from its opening level of 2,770/90 after liquidity suddenly eased from a record overnight rate of 125 percent to about 30 percent. 

 The overnight rate determines whether it is profitable for investors to borrow rupiah to speculate in the foreign exchange market. 

 "At this rate, borrowing costs are just about five rupiah (per dollar). It's extremely profitable for people to speculate, since there are swings of about 100 rupiah in the spot rate," said one dealer. 

 Edwin Png, head of treasury for Bank of America in Jakarta, said the market was losing confidence. 

 "I have housewives calling me up to ask about the rate," he said. "Bank Indonesia should intervene now or else I see the rate going up to 3,000 later in the day and 3,200 next week. 

 "They should do both. They should intervene and they should tighten liquidity." 

 Other dealers said the easing in liquidity appeared to have come about after some state-owned banks offered money in the market and added that that implied the central bank was being inconsistent in its policy. 

 "They said yesterday that they would maintain tightness, but it doesn't look as if they are doing so," said one dealer. 

 The overnight rate shot up in the morning because of Bank Indonesia's intervention on Wednesday with about $500 million. The money became due on Friday. 

 Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad said on Thursday, less than an hour after the central bank removed its intervention band and effectively floated the rupiah, that tight monetary and fiscal policies were in place and any changes would depend on developments. 

Central Bank Governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said although the intervention band had been scrapped, authorities reserved the right to intervene if they deemed necessary. The band had determined at what levels the bank would step into the market. 

 "Of course Bank Indonesia would like to intervene to keep developments on course, to smooth the adaptment period," he said on Thursday. 

 But State Planning Minister Ginanjar Kartasasmita appeared to hint that authorities would allow the market to decide the level of the rupiah. 

 "If they (speculators) see the government will not intervene, we hope they will reduce their speculative activity," he told reporters on Friday. 

 "Our fundamental economy is sound. We are entering a new era of market principles. It is the correct time for the government to carry out such a policy," he said. 

 Earlier, the International Monetary Fund hailed the move to float the rupiah, saying it was good for the economy. 

 "In present circumstances, a floating exchange rate will enhance the effectiveness of macroeconomic policies aimed at sustaining high rates of growth with financial stability," said Stanley Fischer, acting managing director of the IMF, in a statement issued in Washington.

title: Indonesian rupiah stable, IMF welcomes BI move.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 15 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah was stable against the dollar in moderate early trading on Friday, a day after it was allowed to float, recovering from an overnight dip in London to 2,815, dealers said. 

 The International Monetary Fund (IMF) welcomed the float, saying the move would allow the country's economy to continue its recent impressive performance. 

 "In present circumstances, a floating exchange rate will enhance the effectiveness of macroeconomic policies aimed at sustaining high rates of growth with financial stability," said Stanley Fischer, acting managing director of the IMF. 

 Dealers said offshore sentiment appeared to be positive on the rupiah, with buying orders seen entering the market and capping the dollar at the 2,800 level. "But our main worry is local corporates who are eager to hedge now despite the tight rupiah conditions," one dealer said. 

 Spot rupiah was at 2,790/2,800 at 0235 GMT, compared with an opening of 2,770/90. The rupiah strengthened to a high of 2,770 but sustained local buying interest pushed the dollar up again. 

 Dealers said offshore operators were not as aggressive as before since there was no longer any speculative push to test the intervention band. 

 Bank Indonesia announced on Thursday it was immediately ending its system of managing exchange rates through the use of an intervention band, effectively floating the rupiah. 

 "Some offshores are trying to lock in the attractive yield. But nervous local corporates have dented any possible rupiah recovery," another said, adding that it would take some days for the market to fully digest the new exchange rate system. 

Central bank intervention on Wednesday of some $500 million, which was maturing on Friday, together with a tight short-term monetary policy, sent overnight rates to a record high of 125 percent before they eased slightly to 110 percent. 

 Swap rates were driven up by the tight liquidity in the money market, with overnight swap soaring to a high of 26/27 points, equivalent to 360 percent interest. 

 Dealers said the dollar was also supported by operators who were caught short on dollars on Thursday and were trying to square their positions on Friday. 

 Fischer called Indonesia's decision timely and said it came partly in response to turbulence on regional currency markets. 

 He said floating the rupiah was "in line with Bank Indonesia's steady progress toward greater exchange rate flexibility, particularly over the last two years." 

 "The floating of the rupiah, in combination with Indonesia's strong fundamentals, supported by prudent fiscal and monetary policies, will allow its economy to continue its impressive economic performance of the last several years," Fischer said in a statement.

title: FOCUS - Indonesian markets roiled by rupiah float.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 14 (Reuter) - Indonesia succumbed to speculative attacks and floated the rupiah on Thursday, triggering steep declines in the currency and stock prices. 

 Bank Indonesia, the central bank, announced it was immediately ending its system of managing exchange rates through the use of an intervention band -- the parameters under which the bank stepped into the foreign exchange market. 

 The move made Indonesia the latest southeast Asian nation to cave in to the currency pressures which have been afflicting the region since early July. 

 "Theoretically, it's a free float," bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono told Reuters Financial Television in an interview. 

 "But of course Bank Indonesia would like to intervene to keep developments on course, to smooth the adaptment period. 

 "You can also call it a managed float without a band." 

 The rupiah dove on the news, plunging about four percent or more than 100 points after opening at 2,648/58 against the dollar. In the mid-afternoon, it was trading at 2,750/60 and appeared to have temporarily stabilised, dealers said. 

 The bank had last fixed the intervention band at 2,378/2,682 on Wednesday. Under the previous system of exchange rate management, the rupiah was allowed to fluctuate within an intervention band whose mid-point was set on a daily basis by the central bank. 

 The rupiah has fallen about 17 percent in the year so far, compared with an unofficial government target of four-to-five percent annual depreciation. 

 On July 1, the rupiah was trading at around 2,430 against the dollar although subsequent pressures took it down to a record low of 2,665 on July 21 and then 2,682 on Wednesday. 

 Dealers said the market was still looking for a new equilibrium level and much could depend on how traders in London and New York reacted to the news. 

 Indonesian stocks, already suffering from the lingering problems in regional currency markets, were hammered by the news of the float, with the composite index diving 2.37 percent to a 13-week low of 643.01 points. 

 The index has dropped almost 80 points since the beginning of the month. 

 Djiwandono noted that the Thai baht and the Philippine peso had been floated since speculative attacks on regional currencies began, while the Malaysian ringgit and the Singapore dollar were being traded without any pre-announced limits. 

 "We are a regional market now. We are moving together," Djiwandono said. 

 "In the last few weeks Indonesia is the only one which had a band, it's the only one defending the rupiah," he said adding that maintaining that position would be more and more difficult. 

 "We are adjusting to the new realities," he said. "The new reality in the ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations) region is floating (currencies)." 

 Economists were confident that healthy economic fundamentals would help the currency recover. 

 "It's much more prudent than widening the band and giving the market a fresh target to aim at," said Desmond Supple, regional currencies specialist at BZW Asia in Singapore. 

 "Doggedly defending the band would whittle away at the country's reserves, raise interest rates and slow growth." 

 He said it was not surprising the rupiah had plunged on the announcement but said there was scope for recovery later. 

 "We are going to see substantial over-shooting," Supple said. "But it (the announcement) lays the conditions for reversal of the rupiah in the long-term and bring it back to a semblance of fair value." 

 Some market-watchers said it was possible that after abandoning the intervention band, Indonesia could introduce some form of mild capital controls to limit the scope for speculation. 

 Both Malaysia and Singapore have adopted systems which prevent sizeable non-trade forward transactions. 

 But Djiwandono said there would be no move to introduce exchange controls on the rupiah. 

 "Why should we control?" he said when asked if there was a possibility of any such move."

title: Indonesian rupiah dives, depressing others.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 14 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah's steep drop after Jakarta announced a more flexible exchange rate regime dragged down other Southeast Asian currencies on Thursday. 

 A central bank announcement that it would stop posting a daily dollar/rupiah intervention band, removing the parameters within which it steps into the foreign exchange market, sent the rupiah diving by over as five percent from its levels late on Wednesday. 

 The timing of the action by the Indonesian central bank came as a surprise a day after it raised rates and sold dollars to keep the rupiah within its intervention band. 

 "Theoretically, it's a free float," central bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono told Reuters Financial Television. 

 "But of course Bank Indonesia would like to intervene to keep developments on course," he said, in order to smooth the period of adapting to the move. 

 "You can also call it a managed float without a band." 

 The rupiah fell as low as 2,810 during the day against its opening around 2,648/58. It was quoted at 2,760/70 at 0925 GMT. 

 Dealers said the rupiah appeared to have stabilised temporarily, but the reaction of players in London and New York would shape its direction. 

 Analysts hailed the Indonesian move as a welcome response to currency and economic turmoil in the region, which has highlighted the need for greater exchange rate flexibility. 

 "It's much more prudent than widening the band and giving the market a fresh target to aim at," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian currency research at BZW Asia in Singapore. 

 "Doggedly defending the band would whittle away at the country's reserves, raise interest rates and slow growth." 

 Other Southeast Asian currencies, which started the day on relatively firm footing following the dollar's overnight drop against the majors, fell along with the rupiah. 

 Comments by Malaysian Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim exacerbated pressure on the ringgit. He said the government was concerned about the sharp rise in Malaysia's June trade deficit to 2.8 billion ringgit and it may use taxes or fiscal measures to cut imports and stimulate exports. 

 The ringgit fell from a high of 2.7530 to the dollar after the remarks. It was quoted at 2.7665/715 against 2.7815/45 late on Wednesday. 

 A government official denied later rumours that Malaysia planned to cut the statutory reserve requirement of banks. 

 The Singapore slipped back through the 1.51 level against the U.S. dollar and the Thai baht also came under pressure, partly from commercial dollar demand, but dealers said activity was muted. 

 The Philippine peso recovered from an early low of 29.620 to the dollar, but ended weak at 29.49 on concerns about regional currency volatility. 

 Manila traders said the central bank did not step in to defend the peso, but kept its offer rate for the dollar 10 centavos above the best offer. 

 They said the currency remained fragile after the central bank cut its overnight borrowing rate by four percentage points to 14 percent amid persistent demand for dollars. 

 The Taiwan dollar finished fractionally firmer at T$28.725 on suspected central bank intervention.

title: Indonesia adopts more flexible exchange rate.
text:
SINGAPORE, Aug 14 (Reuter) - Bank Indonesia kept the foreign exchange market on its toes on Thursday by announcing it would stop publishing formal intervention limits for the rupiah, sending the currency into uncharted territory. 

 While the move had been anticipated by many in the market, the timing came as a surprise given the Indonesian authorities on Wednesday raised interest rates and intervened in the foreign exchange market to stop the rupiah breaching the bottom of the now defunct band. 

 Analysts were positive about the move and, given the recent turmoil and period of economic and currency adjustment in the region, said it made perfect sense to allow more exchange rate flexibility. 

 Indonesian central bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said on Thursday the bank's decision was taken because other countries in the region had floated their currencies. 

 "Indonesia is the only one with a band," he said. "It's no longer an advantage." 

 Djiwandono said the lifting of the bank's intervention band implied a free float of the rupiah although it reserved the right to intervene if needed. 

 "Theoretically, it's a free float," he told Reuters Financial Television in an interview. "But of course Bank Indonesia would like to intervene to keep developments on course, to smooth the adaptment period." 

 However, analysts very much doubted that it signalled a pure free float and while Bank Indonesia may not publish levels, it almost certainly had them in mind. 

 "It doesn't mean the central bank is totally out of the market so it's not a real free float in that sense," said Chiang Yao Chye, Head of Asia Pacific Research at CIBC in Singapore. 

 "It's obviously some kind of managed float...it's very likely that they do have a band in mind but the big difference is that it's not going to be as transparent as before and set targets for speculators to aim at." 

 The rupiah finally settled just shy of the 2,800 level in late business on Thursday, about five percent down on the day. 

 A U.S. bank dealer in Jakarta said offshore players drove the action although overall volume was light. 

 In late trading on Wednesday the rupiah sparked central bank intervention by inching down to flirt with the old lower band limit of 2,682. 

 "I think to move to the current level is a bit difficult to explain on the basis of fundamentals but we haven't seen much of a focus on fundamentals in any of these markets in the past few weeks," said Kobus Van Der Wath, Regional Head of Treasury Economics at Standard Chartered Bank. 

 Lack of liquidity has had a lot to do with the sort of wild currency moves seen of late, analysts said. 

 The move would seem to be similar to that adopted by Thailand after the baht crisis. 

 The Thai central bank used to publish a daily rate for the baht against the dollar and it was kept within a four satang range around that level, in other words a band in which the baht would be kept. 

 After the crisis, the bank continued to publish a daily reference rate but did not have an official range. 

 "If there had been a band widening it would not have worked because...you are exposed in the light and the speculators are hidden in the dark," said the then Thai Central Bank Governor Rerngchai Marakanond. 

 Indonesia is thinking along the same lines and has simply stopped publishing the rates, although the move still signals a more flexible approach to exchange rates. 

 "Initially (after the baht crisis) central banks slowly tried to regain control but the thinking now appears to be embracing the concept of flexible exchange rates with the hope of deriving the benefits of lower interest rates and perhaps more relaxed forward curves," Standard Chartered's Van Der Wath said. 

 The question which was now being asked in the market was whether Indonesia would go the way of Malaysia and introduce some kind of mild capital controls as a partial counter to the more flexible system. 

 Malaysia recently adopted a system similar to that in Singapore which prevents sizeable non-trade forward trades. 

 By imposing these controls overseas players are limited in the amount of currency they can obtain, thereby limiting the scope for speculation. 

 "I don't think it's Bank Indonesia's style," said Van Der Wath. "It would take the edge off speculators' activities and is a possibility, but not really Bank Indonesia's style."

title: Weaker Indonesian rupiah both blight and blessing.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 14 (Reuter) - The sharp decline of the Indonesian rupiah against the U.S. dollar will be both a blessing and blight for the country's corporate sector, officials and analysts said on Thursday. 

 "There will be some positive effects and there will negative effects," Investment Minister Sanyoto Sastrowardoyo told reporters on the fringes of an international capital market conference. 

 "It will depend on whether their (companies') market is overseas or local. Whether their loans are from within the country or from overseas," he said after the conference was opened by President Suharto. "It cannot be generalised." 

 The rupiah plunged to a historic low against the dollar on Thursday after the government decided to scrap its intervention band, effectively floating the currency. 

 Sanyoto said the decline had yet to impact foreign investment in Indonesia, the world's fourth-most populous country with more than 200 million people. 

Central Bank governor Sudradjat Djiwandono told the conference the intervention band was no longer an advantage to Indonesia following similar moves by Thailand and the Philippines. 

 He said other countries in the region such as Malaysia and Singapore did not have intervention bands. 

 PT Tambang Timah, the world's largest integrated tin mining company, which is also listed on the London Stock Exchange, is one of the companies expected to benefit from the weak rupiah. 

 "It will not be a problem," Timah president-director Erry Riana told Reuters. "Our exports are denominated in U.S. dollars." 

 Erry said the company's second half net profit was expected to be better than its performance in the first six months of this year, when it posted a net profit of 57.30 billion rupiah ($20.8 million) against 70.58 billion rupiah in the year-ago period. 

 Astra International, Indonesia's largest automobile producer, said it would be hit by the rupiah's decline. 

 Astra Finance Director Rini Soewandi told a briefing that the company had a loan exposure of $1.6 billion as of end-July denominated in the U.S. currency. 

 "Astra has a 25 percent open position in July and this means a translation loss of 70 billion rupiah before taxes," she said. 

 She said, however, that improved performance in the first half of this year has led the company to revise its 1997 net profit forecast to 721 billion rupiah from 627 billion rupiah. 

 Soewandi said total revenue forecasts for the year had been revised to 16.3 trillion rupiah from 15.4 trillion. 

 Government-controlled PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia (Telkom), the biggest capitalised company on the Jakarta Stock Exchange, said it had total "two-step" loans of about 4.4 trillion rupiah. 

 Under the two-step loan system, financial institutions lend to the government, which in turn lends to state enterprises. 

 Telkom chief financial officer Harry Supangkat said only two of the latest two-step loans from the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank were in dollars, adding that they were "very small" and already hedged. 

 Jonathan Zax, corporate development and investor relations director of cigarette-maker PT Hanjaya Mandala Sampoerna, said the company had debts totalling $270 million. 

 "Our total debt is about $270 million and we are covered on about $225 million of it," he said, adding that the company had hedged at between 2,490-2,520 to the dollar.

title: FOCUS-Indonesia floats rupiah,  currency  plunges.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 14 (Reuter) - Indonesia floated the rupiah on Thursday, triggering a steep 100-point fall in the currency against the dollar and taking it deep into uncharted waters. 

 Bank Indonesia, the central bank, announced it was lifting the intervention band with immediate effect, abandoning the parameters under which the bank steps into the foreign exchange market. 

 "Theoretically, it's a free float," bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono told Reuters Financial Television in an interview. 

 "But of course Bank Indonesia would like to intervene to keep developments on course," he said, in order to smoothen the period of adapting to the new move. 

 "You can also call it a managed float without a band." 

 The rupiah dived on the news by more than 100 points from an opening of 2,648/58 against the dollar. 

 In mid-afternoon, it was trading at 2,750/60 and appeared to have temporarily stabilised, dealers said. 

 The bank had last fixed the intervention band at 2,378/2,682 on Wednesday. 

Indonesia becomes the latest Southeast Asian nation to succumb to the currency pressures which have been afflicting the region since early July. 

 On July 1, the rupiah was trading at around 2,430 per dollar although subsequent pressures pulled it to a record low of 2,665 on July 21 and to 2,682 on Wednesday. 

 Djiwandono said the Thai baht and the Philippine peso had been floated since speculative attacks on regional currencies began, while the Malaysian ringgit and the Singapore dollar were being traded without any pre-announced limits. 

 "We are a regional market now. We are moving together," Djiwandono said. 

 "In the last few weeks Indonesia is the only one which had a band. It's the only one defending the rupiah," he said, adding that maintaining that position would be increasingly difficult. 

 "We are adjusting to the new realities," he said. "The new reality in the ASEAN (Association of South East Asian Nations) region is floating (currencies)." 

 Economists said the move was a positive one. 

 "It's much more prudent than widening the band and giving the market a fresh target to aim at," said Desmond Supple, regional currencies specialist at BZW Asia in Singapore. 

 "Doggedly defending the band would whittle away at the country's reserves, raise interest rates and slow growth." 

 He said it was not surprising that the rupiah had plunged on the announcement but added that there was scope for recovery later. 

 "We are going to see substantial over-shooting," Supple said. "But it (the announcement) lays the conditions for reversal of the rupiah in the long-term and bring it back to a semblance of fair value." 

 Some market-watchers said it was possible that after abandoning the intervention band, Indonesia could introduce some form of mild capital controls to limit the scope for speculation. 

 Both Malaysia and Singapore have adopted systems which prevent sizeable non-trade forward transactions. 

 But Djiwandono said there would be no move to introduce exchange controls on the rupiah. 

 "Why should we control?" he said when asked if there was a possibility of any such move."

title: INDONESIA C.BANK GOVERNOR CALLS MOVE A FREE FLOAT.

title: Indonesian rupiah slumps, pulls down others.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 14 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah slumped and pulled down other Southeast Asian currencies on Thursday after Bank Indonesia (BI) scrapped the daily announcement of its intervention band. 

 The timing of the action by the Indonesian central bank, seen as amounting to a managed float of the currency, came as a surprise a day after it raised rates and sold dollars to keep the rupiah within its intervention band. 

 BI governor Sudradjad Djiwandono told a capital market conference the central bank's band move was only an adjustment to neighbouring countries. 

 The rupiah fell to a historic low of 2,765 after the announcement against its opening around 2,648/58. By 0430 GMT, it had stabilised around 2,750/80. 

 A state bank dealer in Jakarta said the statement did not imply the removal of the band, only its announcement. "This implies that the band will be invisible, allowing the central bank to intervene any time it wants," he said. 

 "Basically Bank Indonesia can intervene at any time. It's a good move," said Desmond Supple, head of Asian currency research at BZW Asia in Singapore. 

 "It's much more prudent than widening the band and giving the market a fresh target to aim at," he said. 

 "Doggedly defending the band would whittle away at the country's reserves, raise interest rates and slow growth." 

 He said it was not surprising that the rupiah had plunged on the announcement, but that there was scope for recovery later. 

 "We are going to see substantial over-shooting," Supple said. "But (the announcement) lays the conditions for reversal of the rupiah in the long-term and bring it back to a semblance of fair value." 

 Other Southeast Asian currencies, which started the day on relatively firm footing following the dollar's overnight drop against the majors, fell along with the rupiah. 

 "The rupiah's the mover and shaker today. If dollar/rupiah does settle down, the rest of the (dollar/)Asians should top out too," a U.S. bank dealer said. 

 Comments by Malaysian Finance Minister Anwar Ibrahim exacerbated pressure on the ringgit. He said the government was concerned about the sharp rise in Malaysia's June trade deficit to 2.8 billion ringgit and it may use taxes or fiscal measures to cut imports and stimulate exports. 

 But his remark that the government need not cancel major infrastructure projects caused confusion a day after Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad said plans for large projects would be reviewed following the ringgit's steep decline. 

 The ringgit fell from a high of 2.7530 to the dollar after the remarks. It was quoted at 2.7720/70 at 0430 GMT but dealers said it remained vulnerable to more weakness. 

 The Singapore dollar slipped back through the 1.51 level against the U.S. dollar and the Thai baht also came under pressure, partly from commercial dollar demand, but dealers said activity was muted. 

 The baht was at 31.50/31.60 to the dollar onshore against 31.43/31.55 late on Wednesday. It was at 31.25/35 offshore. 

 The Philippine peso recovered from an early low of 29.620 to the dollar, but remained fragile after the central bank cut its rates amid persistent demand for dollars. 

 The overnight borrowing rate was cut by four percentage points to 14 percent and liquidity reserves raised to five percent from four percent to moderate the impact on the peso. 

 The Taiwan dollar was largely steady on suspected intervention by the central bank to sell U.S. dollars at T$28.727. It was seen trading in a narrow T$28.70-75 range.

title: INDONESIA STRESSES NEED FOR INVESTOR CONFIDENCE.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 14 (Reuter) - Indonesia's President Suharto said on Thursday that financial market authorities must maintain investor confidence in the country or risk capital flight. 

 "I appeal to our capital market authorities to continue to maintain and enhance investor confidence," he said. 

 "Because once these investors lose confidence in our capital market, they will quickly and easily move their funds to capital markets in other countries." 

 Suharto made no mention of the weakness which has plagued Indonesia's foreign exchange and equity markets for several weeks. 

 The rupiah plunged to a historic low of 2,765 against the dollar on Thursday after the central Bank Indonesia said it would stop announcing its daily intervention and conversion bands with immediate effect. 

 The move was seen as amounting to free float of currency after the central bank hiked rates and sold dollars in a vain bid to protect the rupiah from heavy speculative attacks. 

 The stock market index has plunged about seven percent since the beginning of the month on the higher interest rates imposed by Bank Indonesia and a slew of rights issues. 

 They were sharply down in early trade on Thursday following the central bank rupiah announcement. 

 Suharto said Indonesia needed funds raised by the capital market to meet its development goals. He said the nation would require some 815 trillion rupiah ($307.5 billion) for its 1994-1999 development plan and about 77 percent of this was to come from the public. 

 "It is precisely through the capital market that the substantial investment target can hopefully be reached," he said. "A healthy capital market also reinforces the confidence of the international community that our economy is competitive to funnel funding resources more efficiently." 

 Suharto was speaking at the inauguration of a two-day conference being held to mark the 20th anniversary of Indonesia's Capital Market Supervisory Agency (Bapepam). 

 He noted also that domestic investment on Indonesia's stock market had increased in the past year, mainly through the rapid growth of local mutual funds. 

 "The launching of mutual funds has in fact increased the number of shares being traded by local investors to more than 56 percent of the daily transaction on the Jakarta Stock Exchange," he said. 

 "Furthermore, mutual funds have shown a rapid growth in terms of the number of institutions, investment managers and fund management." 

 Indonesia allowed the setting up of domestic mutual funds last year and 64 are now in operation. They now dominate transactions on the local bourse, where foreign investors until two years ago carried out about 70 percent of the daily trades.

title: Indonesia, Forced To Float Rupiah, Bracing For Corporate Impact
text:
JAKARTA -(Dow Jones)- Indonesia was finally forced by currency speculators Thursday to join several of its Southeast Asian neighbors and float its currency. 

 The central bank abolished the 12% dollar-rupiah trading band, and allowed the currency to float. The move - ending what has long been seen as Indonesia's "free lunch" - sent the rupiah plunging nearly 7%, and caused the Jakarta Stock Exchange to lose a further 16 points on the day. 

 From a pre-float level of 2,640 rupiah, the U.S. dollar shot up almost immediately to 2,755 rupiah. The dollar then traded slightly down, before ending Asian trading at 2,825 rupiah. 

 On Wednesday, currency speculators had fixed their sights on Indonesia, only to be stopped when the central bank apparently intervened - with massive trades to buy rupiah - to stabilize the currency. 

 On Thursday central Bank Indonesia Governor Soedradjad Djiwandono conceded Indonesia's previous "managed depreciation" policy become a liability amid the new era of liberalized currency regimes. 

 "Our managed band was once seen as liberal, and an advantage for Indonesia," Soedradjad said. "But with Thailand and the Philippines floating, it no longer is." 

 Central banks around the region have been signaling they aren't prepared to defend their currencies against a surging U.S. dollar; the Singapore dollar and Malaysian ringgit led regional currencies lower Tuesday on new indications of this policy, though both currencies were more stable Wednesday. 

 For years, the rupiah's high yields, combined with the predictability of the central bank's managed depreciation policy, offered incredibly high returns for investors - with little risk. 

 As a result, the currency remained strong despite numerous political and economic shocks within the county. 

 "I just think we couldn't believe this would ever end," said the president-director of a European brokerage house in Jakarta. "Obviously, we were wrong." 

 Economists and financial analysts lauded the Bank Indonesia's "prudent action," but there's a growing chorus of concern over issues ranging from the the impact of the free-float on Indonesian companies to the likelihood of increased inflation. 

 Significantly exposed to offshore debt - and believed to be insufficiently hedged against foreign exchange losses - commerical balance sheets are expected to suffer severe damage from the rupiah's current level. 

 "You hear many corporates saying they are properly hedged against the rupiah's plunge. You hear them say that their bottom lines aren't going to be affected," said Agnes Safford, president-director of ABN Amro Hoare Govett in Jakarta. "I wish it were true, but it is hard to fathom." 

 Pharmaceuticals, electronics, and electrical appliance companies are expected to particularly hard hit, analysts say, and large companies, such as HM Sampoerna, PT Bakrie & Brothers, and the Sinar Mas Group, will feel the impact. 

 With corporate earnings in serious doubt, the stock market forecast isn't particularly rosy. Analysts say foreign investors are hardly expected to jump back into the equities markets, although fixed-income investments will continue to look attractive with the Indonesian economy unsettled. Late Thursday, an overnight rupiah time deposit was yielding a heady 28%. 

 In just over a week, Jakarta's main equity index has dropped 10% to Thursday's close of 643.011. It's down 15% since hitting an all-time high of 740 on July 8. 

 Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad said Thursday that the liquidity squeeze is "only temporary" and market participants believe him. They also note, however, that with inflation expected to rise on the back of the rupiah's depreciation - and foreign inflows a must - the extent to which Bank Indonesia can reasonably cut rates is limited. The concern is that the current situation will expose greater cracks in the nation's financial system, than any previously expected. 

 Indonesian banks, for example, are not known for the quality of their assets. Any serious cash-flow problems experienced by a major Indonesian conglomerate could have a ripple effect throughout the economy. 

 "We think for the time being that the banking sector looks relatively okay," said an official at an international financial organization in Jakarta. "But it's in an environment like this one that you realize you have problems that you weren't aware of before."

title: Bank  Indonesia / Intervene /Sources: $100 Mln Said Spent

JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's central bank, Bank Indonesia, intervened in the spot market at around 0725 GMT, selling the U.S. dollar at around the 2,675 rupiah level, according to traders at three separate foreign exchange banks in Jakarta.

text:
SINGAPORE (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's key commodity markets were relatively undisturbed by the rupiah's break out of its trading band on continued selling pressure against the dollar Wednesday, traders from a variety of commodity market sectors said Wednesday.

title: Spotlight on the rupiah, Asian regionals pressured.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 13 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah took centre stage in a still nervous Asian foreign exchange market on Wednesday, plunging to a historic low and forcing a defensive interest rate rise and central bank intervention. 

 Bank Indonesia was forced to step in after the rupiah shrugged off the rate rise and dropped to the lower limit of its 12 percent trading band. 

 It fell to a low of 2,682 to the dollar in the afternoon before recovering on the intervention to 2,640/50. The bank's intervention band, the parameters outside of which it will enter the market, was last pegged at 2,378/2,682. 

 But intervention could well be a losing battle given the continuing weakness in all Southeast Asian currencies. 

 "It's useless for the central bank to intervene in a bearish market," said Jimmy Koh, regional economist for the I.D.E.A. research consultancy. He noted that the Malaysian central bank had spent some $8.8 billion in intervention measures when the ringgit was under attack earlier this month, but with little to show for its efforts. 

 The rate rise came as a bit of a surprise as the very rates which were cut last Friday by 50 basis points were raised 100 basis points, so on a net basis policy is tighter now. 

 "They are raising short-term rates but keeping the long-term rates, which determine lending and spending behaviour in the economy, at current levels," said Manu Bhaskaran, Group Head of Research at SocGen Crosby. 

 "The central bank has a clear strategy and I think they will use short-term rates where necessary to hold the currency." 

 Elsewhere, the Singapore dollar remained under pressure but recouped some of its losses on talk of possible central bank intervention near its low of 1.5175 to the U.S. dollar. 

 It was at a late 1.5100 where dealers said there are strong bids for U.S. dollars. 

 They said local banks were seen selling the U.S. dollar near its highs earlier, often an indication of the central bank's presence, but no confirmation was available. 

 A European bank dealer said the U.S. dollar would be bought on any dips to 1.5100 or 1.5050 for an eventual move up to 1.53. 

 The Malaysian ringgit moved narrowly but showed persistent signs of weakness and dealers said the market was likely to take a crack at the 2.80 level, a low not seen since the ringgit was officially floated in 1973. 

 "Dollar/ringgit could still reach 2.80 and probably go above that level," said a Malaysian bank dealer. "But I'm expecting some resistance at 2.7850." 

 The ringgit was quoted at 2.7775 to the dollar against 2.7645/75 at the close of Kuala Lumpur trade on Tuesday. 

 The Thai baht started easier but regained its composure to trade at a late 31.430 onshore and 31.350 offshore. 

 Dealers said there were some sales of dollars offshore ahead of the expected mid-August maturity of short baht forward positions, established when the Thai currency came under speculative attack three months ago. 

 The Philippine peso remained weak as banks bought up the dollar in volatile regional currency markets. 

 Corporate customers are also looking to buy dollars at the moment and that was keeping the pressure on the peso, dealers said. 

 The peso was at 28.85 against its previous close at 28.66. Manila traders said the central bank might have sold dollars at the 28.70/28.78 levels earlier but no confirmation was available. 

 The Taiwan dollar remained weak but fears of central bank intervention and tight liquidity in domestic money markets helped limit any decline. It was at a late 28.726 per U.S. dollar, little changed from Tuesday's close.
