title: Rupiah slips but clings to 8,000 level as '98 ends.
text:
JAKARTA, Dec 30 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah came under fresh pressure in the final hours of 1998 trade on Wednesday but clung to 8,000 to the dollar, boosted by a central bank pledge to defend the currency against further weakness, dealers said. 

 The rupiah was quoted in late Jakarta trade at 7,990/8,090 after trading in a range of 7,900 to 8,100 through the day - well above the January and June lows of 17,000 but still a long way from its 1997 close of 5,300. 

 Most dealers and analysts expect the currency to slide in the months ahead. 

 But central bank governor Sjahril Sabirin told reporters the monetary authorities would try to prevent the currency weakening below 8,000 to the dollar. 

 "The comments by the governor that they want to maintain the rupiah below 8,000 caused some dollar selling, but there was no follow-through from the central bank so people eventually recovered their positions again," said a dealer at a European bank in Jakarta. 

 The central bank has been converting $10-15 million a day in aid and loan dollars into rupiah in recent months, giving the beleaguered Indonesian currency a significant boost in the thin market conditions. 

 The central bank insists this does not constitute intervention. But dealers say Bank Indonesia has been intervening in the market to prop up the rupiah when it comes under pressure, sometimes selling large amounts of dollars. 

 Dealers said Sabirin's comments could signal a more openly pro-active stance on the part of the central bank to defend the rupiah. Officials have said the budget for Indonesia's 1999/2000 fiscal year assumes an exchange rate of 7,000 to 8,000. 

 Indonesia's top economics minister Ginandjar Kartasasmita said earlier this month that the rupiah could strengthen beyond 7,000 to the dollar once parliamentary elections scheduled for June are out of the way. 

 But many analysts believe the rupiah is headed lower, citing concern about unrest ahead of the elections and the possibility of a liquidity explosion as Indonesia struggles to pay for its budget commitments and fund an ambitious bank recapitalisation programme. 

 Chartists say the currency seems to be slipping out of its recent range of 7,500 to 8,000 rupiah and this could signal a slide towards 9,000. 

 "I think the market sentiment is that the rupiah will weaken again come next year," one dealer said. "But my view is that yes it will weaken but the central bank will be keeping an eye on it. I don't think that during the month of Ramadhan you will see major fluctuations." ((Andrew Marshall, Jakarta newsroom +6221 384-6364; Fax +6221 344-8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)). 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Indonesia c.bank says will try to halt rupiah fall.

 The rupiah has weakened to around 8,000 against the dollar in early trading on Wednesday from around 7,600 early last week. 

 Sabirin said the rupiah's weakness was temporary and largely due to year-end and Eid al-Fitr Moslem celebrations. 

 In recent months the central bank has been converting $10-15 million a day of aid and loan dollars into rupiah, giving the domestic currency a significant boost in thin market conditions. 

 Bank Indonesia insists the conversion should not be regarded as intervention. But some dealers and analysts say the central bank has been intervening, converting larger amounts of dollars to support the rupiah when it comes under pressure. title: Rupiah edges down, braced for fresh demonstrations.
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 20 (Reuters) - The rupiah edged lower on Friday with dealers saying the market was nervous about fresh protests in Jakarta a week after violent clashes in the capital left at least 14 dead and turned the business district into a battlezone. 

 By 0240 GMT the Indonesian currency was quoted at 7,525/7,625 compared with 7,425/7,525 at the close in Jakarta on Thursday. 

 Dealers said most players were expected to square their positions and shut up shop early to avoid expected protests in the business district around Atma Jaya university, where nine students died last week in clashes with the security forces. 

 "The market is cautious about students on the streets. Today is the seventh day after the students died and probably there will be crowds again in the Atma Jaya area," said one dealer at a U.S. bank in Jakarta. 

 The currency was largely unaffected by last week's unrest, and some dealers said they suspected Bank Indonesia had been converting an increased amount of aid and loan dollars into rupiah to prop it up. 

 Indonesia says it has been converting $5-15 million a day of aid and loan dollars into rupiah in recent months, giving the local currency a significant boost in a market where daily volume rarely exceeds $200 million. 

 Some dealers say the central bank changed up to $50 million a day last week to support the currency. But Bank Indonesia insists it is not intervening in the market and says its selling of dollars for rupiah is purely to meet budgetary needs and satisfy the market's dollar demand. 

 Dennis de Tray, the World Bank's country director for Indonesia, said on Thursday recent gains by the rupiah were "real" and not the result of central bank intervention. 

 "The important, underlined piece of information on the exchange rate...is that the recent strengthening of the rupiah, contrary to what you may have read, is not being driven by Bank Indonesia intervention," he told a conference in Jakarta. 

 He said the International Monetary Fund, which closely monitored such matters, had told him the currency had not been boosted by intervention. 

 "But also data on foreign reserves, published regularly, simply does not support the story of massive intervention by Bank Indonesia," he said. ((Andrew Marshall, Jakarta newsroom +6221 384 6364; Fax +6221 344 8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Intervention  not behind rupiah gains - World Bank.
text:

 "The important, underlined piece of information on the exchange rate...is that the recent strengthening of the rupiah, contrary to what you may have read, is not being driven by Bank Indonesia intervention," Dennis de Tray told a conference in Jakarta. 

 He said the International Monetary Fund, which closely monitored such matters, had told him the currency had not been boosted by intervention. 

 "But also data on foreign reserves, published regularly, simply does not support the story of massive intervention by Bank Indonesia," he said. 

 Bank Indonesia has said it is changing around $5 million to $15 million a day of foreign aid and loans into rupiah, a significant amount in a market where daily volume rarely reaches $200 million. The central bank insists the conversion should not be considered intervention. 

 The currency has climbed from a low of 17,000 per dollar in June to around 7,500 now, and held its ground over the last week despite violent clashes on the streets of Jakarta which left at least 14 dead. 

 Some analysts have said the rupiah's recent stability was due to Bank Indonesia converting an increased amount of dollars into rupiah. 

 De Tray said that after adjusting for inflation, the rupiah had depreciated by around 40 percent since July 1997, "comparable to the level of depreciation in December 1997, before Indonesia entered serious political crisis". This was a positive sign, he said. 

 But he warned that continued recovery required political stability. 

 "The economy is beginning to mend but it won't hold if the politics don't hold," he said. "Indonesia must decide whether it will hold together or fall apart." ((Andrew Marshall, Jakarta newsroom +6221 384 6364; Fax +6221 344 8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: FOCUS-Jakarta markets grind to a halt amid clashes.
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Indonesia's financial markets ground to a halt on Friday as violent clashes in the heart of Jakarta's business district left at least three people dead and virtually shut down trading in stocks and the rupiah. 

 Most bank offices were deserted as police and troops fired rubber bullets, tear gas and bursts from a water cannon to clear more than 10,000 protesters from the central business district. Elsewhere, at least two more people were killed in clashes. 

 The violence had little impact on Indonesia's currency and stock market but dealers said this was due to a dearth of trade rather than a sign of confidence in the country's fragile political stability. 

 The rupiah ended at 7,800/7,900 to the dollar in Jakarta compared with 7,750/7,850 the day before. The stock market slipped 0.7 percent to 355.54 points. 

 But both markets gained over the week, despite days of mounting tension and clashes as thousands took to the streets to protest against a special session of the country's highest legislative body, the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR).

 "Operators were unwilling to take any new positions. Many operators had already gone home before the market closed," one dealer at a foreign bank in Jakarta said. 

 The rupiah's strengthening in recent days surprised many operators, who had been long of dollars and were forced into stop-less selling as the week progressed.

 "It has all the hallmarks of intervention," said the head of treasury at a foreign bank. 

Indonesia has been converting $10-15 million a day of aid and loan dollars into rupiah in recent months, giving the local currency a significant boost in the thin market conditions. 

 Bank Indonesia insists it is not intervening in the market and says its selling of dollars for rupiah is purely to meet budgetary needs and satisfy the market's dollar demand.

title: Rupiah steady, keeps wary eye on assembly clashes.
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 12 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah was steady in early trade on Thursday, help up by more offshore dollar selling despite growing concerns about clashes on the streets of Jakarta, dealers said. 

 "The dollar selling started in Hong Kong early this week and was joined by Singapore yesterday and today," said the head of treasury at a foreign bank in Jakarta. "It has all the signs of being intervention but it's surprising it's coming from offshore." 

 By 0255 GMT the rupiah was quoted at 7,750/7,850 to the dollar compared with 7,700/7,800 late on Wednesday. 

 Dealers said many market players had been long of dollars ahead of this week's special session of Indonesia's highest legislative body, the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR). 

 The rupiah's gains this week took many by surprise and triggered stop-loss dollar selling. 

 "A lot of people in the market have been caught long and keep having to dump out all the time," the head of treasury said. 

 A dealer at a U.S. bank in Jakarta said dollar selling had failed to lift the rupiah on Thursday because of growing nervousness about unrest during the MPR assembly session. 

 On Wednesday, Indonesian troops fired into the air and baton-charged thousands of students protesting against the special session. 

 "The situation in Jakarta seems to be getting worse, slightly worse," the dealer said. "But the dollar selling has continued in Singapore, so the rupiah is fairly stable." 

 Indonesia has been converting $10-15 million a day of aid and loan dollars into rupiah in recent months, giving the local currency a significant boost in the thin market conditions - Merrill Lynch has estimated average daily turnover at just $70 million. 

 But Bank Indonesia insists it is not intervening in the market and says its selling of dollars for rupiah is purely to meet budgetary needs and satisfy the market's dollar demand. 

 Dealers disagree, however, and believe the central bank has had a hand in boosting the rupiah this week. 

 International Monetary Fund Asia Pacific Director Hubert Neiss, in Indonesia for a regular monthly review of the country's progress on economic reforms, said on Wednesday there was no reason the rupiah could not strengthen further. 

 Asked whether concerns about the political situation were affecting the market, he said: "Political conditions always affect confidence and confidence affects the market. We hope that confidence will further increase and the rupiah will further strengthen. There is no reason why it shouldn't strengthen." 

 Bank Indonesia's weekly auction of its one-month SBI certificates on Wednesday resulted in a weighted average interest rate of 51.16 percent against 53.66 percent last week. 

 The bank said the monthly auction of its three-month SBI paper resulted in a weigthed interest rate of 50.49 percent against 58.71 percent last month. 

 Dealers said the inverted yield curve showed the market expected interest rates to continue falling. ((Andrew Marshall, Jakarta newsroom +6221 384 6364; Fax +6221 344 8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Rupiah gains, breaks 8,000 on offshore dlr selling.
text:

 They said early dollar selling out of Singapore had bolstered the currency but could not say whether Bank Indonesia was behind the trades. 

 "There has been some selling this morning, so far just by Singapore players," said one dealer at a European bank in Jakarta. "We don't know whether BI is behind it." 

 By 0120 GMT the rupiah was quoted at 7,700/7,900 to the dollar, after closing at 8,100 in Jakarta on Wednesday.

 Indonesia's highest legislative body, the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR), is holding a four-day special session to ratify the country's election timetable and discuss laws which President B.J. Habibie says will promote democracy.

text:
Most market participants remain bullish on the peso, saying foreign direct investment and remittances from expatriate Filipinos will bolster the currency over the coming months. According to Basu at CSFB, however, that optimism may be sorely misplaced.

 Basu points to a current account that is barely in balance, the high level of banks' net foreign liabilities relative to the overall size of their balance sheets, and foreign reserves, which at $7.7 billion, he describes as "puny", compared with the Philippines' levels of short term debt.

title: Indonesia rupiah climbs despite assembly nerves.
text:
JAKARTA, Nov 10 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah gained ground in afternoon trade on Tuesday on dollar selling both offshore and in Jakarta, with some dealers saying they suspected the central bank had a hand in boosting the local currency. 

 By 0815 GMT the rupiah was quoted at 8,000/8,200 to the dollar, compared with 8,500/8,600 in early trade and 8,425/8,525 at the close of Jakarta dealings on Monday. 

 "We've seen dollar selling in Hong Kong, mainly through interbank players," said a dealer at a U.S. bank in Jakarta. 

 "Some suspect that some of the selling in Hong Kong is on behalf of Bank Indonesia." 

 Another dealer said there were rumours that Bank Indonesia had been selling more dollars than usual but this had not been confirmed. 

 "German names have been selling, but we don't know what's behind that," said the dealer at a European bank in Jakarta. "We don't know whether there is intervention, we still haven't been able to substantiate that." 

Indonesia's highest legislative body, the People's Consultative Assembly (MPR), began a four-day special session to ratify the country's eletion timetable and discuss laws which President B.J. Habibie has promised will make a more democratic Indonesia. 

 But markets are focused less on the political machinations inside Jakarta's parliament building than on events on the streets outside - where clashes are feared between pro-reform protesters spearheaded by students and Moslem groups armed with sticks who have vowed to protect the assembly. 

 Indonesia has been converting $10-15 million a day of aid and loan dollars into rupiah in recent months, giving the local currency a significant boost in the thin market conditions - Merrill Lynch has estimated average daily turnover in the rupiah at around just $70 million. 

 Dealers said earlier this week they expected the central bank to step up the amount of dollars being converted into rupiah if nervousness about the assembly meeting hit the local currency. 

 Indonesian state banks were aggressively bidding rupiah higher, as in recent days, dealers said. 

 The central bank insists it is not intervening in the market and says its selling of dollars for rupiah is purely to meet budgetary needs and satisfy the market's dollar demand. 

 The rupiah was also boosted on Tuesday by comments from International Monetary Fund first deputy managing director Stanley Fischer, who said in a speech in Australia there was no reason why the currency could not move back to 7,000 to the dollar. 

 "We guess that with the amount of inflation that has happened so far this year...if the currency were to stop in the 6,500-7,000 or so (range) you would find yourself with a devaluation in real terms roughly similar to that in the other crisis countries of somewhere between 25 and 35 percent," he said. 

 No major trouble was reported at the start of the assembly session, although thousands of government supporters, many with sharpened bamboo sticks, rallied near the parliament building, occasionally attacking passers-by. 

 They later moved off without any major incident. 

 Reuters reporters at the scene said government security forces had trouble keeping the demonstrators under control and that nearby roads were closed, including the toll road to the airport. 

 Thousands of students gathered at a central Jakarta university campus for a protest rally but said they had not yet decided whether to march on parliament because of the danger of clashes with government supporters. title: Indonesia rupiah edges higher, tone seen firm.
text:
JAKARTA, Oct 26 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah edged higher against the dollar on Monday and dealers said sentiment on the local currency was likely to remain firm on Tuesday. 

 The rupiah ended at 7,400/7,500 against the dollar compared with 7,800/7,900 in Friday's Jakarta trading. 

 Dealers said the rupiah's rise was partly due to overeas dollar selling amid a thin market and a local newspaper report that the central bank might reimpose an intervention band. 

 Miranda Goeltom, a director with Bank Indonesia, however, denied the report and said the bank did not have plans to impose the band. 

 Dealers said reimposing the band might not work best in the current volatile regional currency markets as players might be tempted to break the band which in turn could force the central bank to abandon it again. 

 Dealers, however, said expected further conversion of aid dollars into rupiah and a relatively stable political situation were likely to keep sentiment firm on the local currency. ((Jakarta newsroom +6221 384-6364; Fax +6221 344-8404, jakarta.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: ASIA  FOREX  - Rupiah and peso gain, others steady.
text:
0800 GMT - The regional currencies had a quietly steady day 

 as dollar/yen held in a narrow range, but the rupiah firmed as 

 aid dollars flowed across the foreign exchanges. 

      Dollar/yen was little changed from Friday's late Asian 

 level but it was up a little on Friday's New York close. 

     Japan's still acute banking sector problems will tend to 

 prevent the yen moving any higher but for now most traders do 

 not see it dipping below the 120 per dollar level. 

     The dollar did get some support from news that European 

 leaders believe the conditions are right for interest rate 

 cuts. 

     *** The rupiah stood out with another good gain but its 

 recent rally does seem to be slowing and many in the market do 

 not see it moving substantially higher from here. 

     The rupiah has rallied some 35 percent this month and has 

 more than doubled in value against the dollar since its June 

 low of around 17,000. 

     The move higher has been fuelled by the conversion of aid 

 dollars into rupiah and despite the apparently spectacular 

 rally it is still almost 70 percent down on levels seen before 

 the Asia crisis kicked-off in July 1997. 

Indonesia's central bank has no plans to intervene on the 

 rupiah in coming months but will aim to create conditions which 

 prevent excessive volatility. 

 "We will let the rupiah move in accordance with market 

 laws. Bank Indonesia will not intervene," Bank Indonesia

 director Achyar Iljas was quoted as saying by the official 

 Antara news agency. 

 The rupiah did gain some support from a local newspaper 

 report that the central bank might reimpose an intervention

 band. 

 *** In Malaysia trouble flared at the weekend with two 

 policemen and 12 protesters injured and 241 arrested as crowds 

 clashed with police. 

 Supporters of the detained former deputy prime minister 

 Anwar Ibrahim threw rocks and petrol bombs around a mosque in 

 the Moslem Kampong Bharu district. 

     Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad condemned his opponents 

 saying his government would not be intimidated. 

     Away from his political problems, Mahathir's budget on 

 Friday received only a lukewarm response from analysts. 

     There was some praise that it would help stimulate the 

 economy but there is concern over just how Malaysia would fund 

 its projected budget deficit of 6.1 percent of GDP in 1999. 

     Analysts say there is no way the funding for next year's 

 budget can come from domestic sources and foresee aid from 

 outside the country being necessary. 

     Mahathir proposed more than four billion ringgit ($1 

 billion) be spent on the transport sector and offered tax cuts 

 for exporters, local manufacturers of consumer durables and 

 investors in unit trusts. 

 Malaysia's Second Finance Minister Mustapa Mohamed said the 

 government will not have any problem funding a projected 1999 

 budget deficit. 

 He told Reuters Television that capital controls imposed in 

 September have been a success, and Malaysia would consider the 

 competitiveness of its neighbours' currencies before scrapping 

 the controls. 

 *** The peso was another bright spot on continued 

 speculation that dollars from direct investment will make their 

 way across the foreign exchanges. 

 Traders said there was talk that proceeds from the sale of 

 San Miguel Corporation's stake in Nestle Philippines Inc and 

 Coca-Cola Beverages were finding their way into the market. 

 San Miguel sold its 45 percent stake in Nestle last August 

 for about $695 million. In July, it sold its stake in Coca-Cola 

 for 339.6 million sterling or around 24 billion pesos. 

     The Philippine Lower House on Sunday approved a proposed 

 1999 national budget of 579.5 billion pesos ($13.8 billion). 

     The proposed appropriation is 9.7 percent higher than this 

 year's budget and targets a lower budget deficit of 17.9 

 billion pesos from this year's projected deficit of 40 billion 

 pesos. 

 The budget bill will go through a third reading for a final 

 vote when Congress reconvenes next month, although this is 

 considered a mere formality. 

 *** The Taiwan dollar closed at a seven-month high against 

 its U.S. counterpart amid U.S. dollar selling in form of 

 non-delivery forward and central bank selling. 

     *** The Korean won and the Singapore dollar both eased 

 slightly. 

     Singapore CPI fell 1.4% in September on a year-on-year 

 basis and was down 0.3% from August. This followed a 0.8%

title: Rupiah quiet after  currency  control denials.
text:
JAKARTA, Sept 16 (Reuters) - Indonesia's rupiah currency was stable in quiet early trade on Wednesday with dealers satisified that the country was not poised to abandon its free-floating exchange rate system and impose foreign exchange controls. 

 "Now the rumours about the foreign exchange controls have gone, the rupiah has stabilised," a dealer with a U.S. bank said. 

 The rupiah was quoted at 10,825/11,025 to the dollar at 0220 GMT on Wednesday, but did not trade through the 11,000 barrier. 

 On Tuesday, the unit made substantial gains against the dollar as traders bought rupiah, anxious to close out positions and limit exposure to outstanding rupiah positions they would be unable to cover if controls were introduced. 

 It closed at 11,000/11,100 to the dollar. 

 Bank Indonesia governor, Syahril Sabirin said there were no plans to abandon the free float, quashing the rumours. 

 "With no more rumours, there is no need to buy. I think we'll see the rupiah range-trading today and breaking 11,000 will be hard," a local dealer said. 

 Traders are also waiting for the results of the central bank's weekly auction of its one-month certificates. The bank aims to absorb about 11 trillion rupiah in the auction. 

 The auction will give a sign on the likely direction of interest rates. Most in the market expect the weighted average interest rate of the SBI to be lower than last week's 69.9 percent. 

 "If the interest rate comes down, it will be a good sign for the economy. The market is looking for a fall," a dealer said. 

 Bank Indonesia said earlier on Wednesday its intervention rates, which the central bank uses to fine tune short term monetary targets in daily operations, had been lowered across the board.

title: Bk  Indonesia /Cap Controls -3: Says Not  Intervening  In Mkt
text:
Since Malaysia implemented sweeping capital controls last week, market participants have speculated that Indonesia may follow suit with some form of controlled system, although the government and Bank Indonesia officials deny this. 

 Indonesia operated a form of foreign exchange control during the late 1960s and early 1970s. That system led to a black market in foreign currency and smuggling and the central bank eventually abandoned it. 

 Given the sprawling nature of the country and its myriad of islands, Indonesia isn't seen as being in a position to enforce capital controls in any case. 

 Bank Indonesia has said it would consider some form of managed exchange rate system for the rupiah, however, which many market operators say it will eventually have to do to better support the currency. 

 Elsehwere, Sjahril said the central bank was exchanging between $5 and $15 million a day for rupiah in the spot market. He said the funds were part of international lending to Indonesia. The governor said this wasn't market intervention, however. 

 "The bank is not intervening, just supplying money to the market for exports or imports," Sjahril said. He said the amount of dollars supplied to the market daily will depend on the amount of foreign aid released.

title: HK welcomes stable markets, but wants results.
text:
HONG KONG, Sept 8 (Reuters) - Hong Kong residents, shell shocked by deflated stock and property values, high interest rates and rising unemployment, on Tuesday welcomed the promise of relief from new government measures to stabilise local markets. 

 But political analysts warned that the territory's leaders will face mounting public pressure if the new regulations and a costly stock market intervention fail to produce results. 

 "Any kind of draconian measure will be accepted because Hong Kong people are infused with the desire to avoid an economic meltdown," said political observer Lau Siu-kai. 

 "But in the long-term, people will want results. How can you put in billions of dollars and not see results?" said Lau, who is also a sociology professor at the Chinese University. 

 Starting in mid-August, the government has spent more than HK$100 billion (US$12.9 billion) on stock and futures to foil market manipulators it accused of attacking the local dollar to drive interest rates up and stock prices down to take profits on short stock positions. 

 Since then, Hong Kong's struggle with economic recession has become intertwined with the government's fight against market speculators and its defence of the territory's U.S. dollar-linked exchange rate. 

 Local media have described the government's actions as a "war" with international hedge funds who are preying on Hong Kong's open economy and regional economic instability. 

 Editorial cartoons and even front-page newspaper graphics have depicted Hong Kong Monetary Authority boss Joseph Yam and other officials in sword fights with dark-suited figures labeled "speculators" in defence of the dollar peg. 

 Discussion of the government's measures and the strength of the dollar peg - viewed as unimpeachable just a few months ago - now dominate talk among business people and non-investors alike. 

 Residents have largely voiced support for the actions, saying they may prevent the territory from suffering the same type of economic meltdown plaguing neighbouring countries, such as Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia. 

 "Market intervention is necessary. Speculators who come here can create trouble," said retiree Lo Kam-seng, 55. "If the government doesn't intervene, the stock market will fall even more." 

 Lo added that during "normal times," intervention would not be good for the economy. 

 The HKMA announced over the weekend seven measures to strengthen the currency board and on Monday the government unveiled a 30-point plan to tighten rules and improve transparency in stock and futures markets. 

 But while many approved of the measures, the applause was muted as some wondered if Hong Kong, which has prided itself as one of the world's most open economies, might perhaps be paying too high a cost, both monetarily and in damage to its free-market reputation. 

 "The money would have been better spent on education, welfare or to lower the unemployment rate where more people would stand to gain," said Chris Chan, a working mother. 

 Political analyst Sonny Lo, an associate professor of politics at the University of Hong Kong, said there would be more domestic pressure on leader Tung Chee-hwa's administration after this spate with foreign speculators. 

 "This issue has polarised Hong Kong society, with some agreeing that fighting speculators is right and must cost money, while the other camp wants the government to concentrate on domestic issues, such as welfare," Lo said.

title: ASIA FOCUS - Chronology of Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 3 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of Asia's financial crisis. 

 1997 

 Jan 23 - Leading South Korean steel maker Hanbo Steel Corp defaults on loans, the first of a string of major corporate failures in 1997. 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency comes under attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thai finance minister. Resignation has immediate impact in the Philippines, where the overnight deposit rate rises to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - After a failed defence of the Thai baht, Bangkok floats its currency and calls on the IMF for "technical assistance". 

 The baht is effectively devalued by about 15-20 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah starts to crumble. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso slump as confidence in the region deteriorates. 

 August 11 - In Tokyo, the IMF unveils a rescue package for Thailand including loans of $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah plunges. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bail-out package, bringing it to $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 20 - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad tells delegates of IMF/World Bank conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Around this time the South Korean won also begins to slump in value. 

 Oct 27 - Asian jitters spill over on to world stock markets. The Dow plunges 554 points, its largest single-day point loss ever. 

 Oct 31 - Indonesia's IMF package is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - Indonesia shuts down 16 troubled banks. 

 Nov 5 - IMF approves a $10 billion loan for Indonesia as part of the massive international package. 

 Nov 17 - Korea abandons its defence of the won, which rapidly falls to 1,000 to the dollar. 

 Dec 4 - IMF approves a $21 billion loan for South Korea, part of a bail-out package that will total nearly $60 billion. 

 Dec 8 - Thailand closes 56 of 58 previously suspended finance companies. 

 1998 

 Jan 8 - Representatives of the IMF and South Korea agree to a 90-day rollover of short-term debt. 

 Jan 12 - Peregrine, one of Asia's largest independent investment banks, collapses under a mountain of bad loans to Indonesian borrowers. Shares fall sharply in Hong Kong, China and Singapore. 

 Jan 15 - IMF managing director Michel Camdessus and President Suharto sign an agreement strengthening economic reforms. 

 Jan 22 - The rupiah collapses. It is dealt at 17,000 to the dollar at one stage. Bank Indonesia intervenes and drives the currency back to end at 11,800. 

 Jan 27 - Indonesia announces a temporary freeze on debt servicing. 

 Jan 28 - International creditor banks and the South Korean government say they have agreed on a plan to exchange $24 billion of short-term debt for new loans maturing in one, two and three years. 

 Jan 30 - U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warns Asia's financial crisis could spread. 

 Feb 14 - The IMF threatens to cut off the bail-out fund for Indonesia over its plans to introduce a currency board. 

 Feb 26 - Indonesia's borrowers and lenders begin negotiations on rescheduling at least $70 billion in private off-shore debt. 

 March 1 - Indonesian President Suharto says reforms prescribed by the IMF have not worked. 

 March 4 - The IMF approves release of the third tranche payment from Thailand's package and commends the Thai government for its economic reforms. 

 March 6 - IMF says its board will not discuss Indonesia's economic reform programme before April, effectively delaying a $3 billion payment initially expected by March 15. 

 March 23 - Indonesia nearly doubles interest rates to boost the rupiah and control inflation. 

 April 1 - Japan begins steps aimed at liberalising its financial markets to make them "free, fair and global" by 2001. Tokyo share prices fall, the yen dips and Japan's central bank governor pronounces every economic indicator bad. 

 April 2 - The chairman of electronics giant Sony, Norio Ohga, says the Japanese economy is on the verge of collapse. 

 April 3 - U.S. ratings agency Moody's lowers its outlook on Japan's sovereign debt to negative from stable. Asian currencies fall sharply on the news. 

 May 7 - Fears that riots in the Indonesian city of Medan will spill over into a wider social crisis send regional stocks into retreat. 

 May 11 - India stuns the world with announcement of three underground nuclear tests. Pakistan stocks tumble 3.52 percent while India's National Stock Exchange index slides 2.55 percent. 

 May 13 - The United States imposes economic sanctions on India and Japan suspends some loans. 

 May 14 - Mobs rampage through Jakarta and students demand Suharto's resignation. Indonesia's worsening crisis takes centre-stage for Asian markets, several of which suffer sharp losses. 

 May 15 - Suharto returns home from a Group of 15 summit in Egypt amid signs he is losing his 32-year grip on power. 

 May 21 - Suharto steps down under strong pressure and is succeeded by former deputy president B.J. Habibie. Markets enjoy a limited rally. Jakarta stocks surge more than three percent. 

 May 25 - South Korean shares plummet 6.78 percent despite a lifting of foreign ownership limits on stocks. Most other Asian markets shrug off Seoul's fall. 

 May 26 - Seoul's KOSPI share index continues to dive, losing a further six percent, hurt by a looming recession and labour unrest. 

 May 27 - Asian markets are hammered as the yen falls against the dollar and amid mounting fears of economic recession. Hong Kong stocks plunge more than five percent after Chief Executive Tung Chee-hwa warns of possible recession. 

 May 28 - Pakistan conducts nuclear tests. 

 May 29 - The dollar rockets to a seven-year high of 139 yen on fears of a possible nuclear arms race in Asia and after news that Japan's unemployment rate hit 4.1 percent in April, its highest level since the end of World War Two. 

 Recession looms in much of Asia. Hong Kong reports that its gross domestic product contracted two percent in first quarter of 1998. About the same time Indonesia and Malaysia also report their economies contracted in the first quarter. 

 June 1 - Pakistani stocks plunge 12.38 percent as traders get their first chance to react to sanctions imposed after the country's nuclear tests. Asian markets are hit as nuclear tension adds to a cocktail of domestic problems. 

 June 5 - International lenders and Indonesian companies reach a deal to reschedule the country's massive corporate debt. 

 June 8 - The yen falls past 140 to the dollar, sending a shudder through Asian markets. Signs that Japan and other leading economies are unlikely to intervene to support the unit sap confidence further. 

 June 10 - China's central bank governor warns that the weak yen is having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade, raising fears that China may devalue its yuan currency. Markets across Asia tumble, led by a near five percent fall on Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index. 

 In Taiwan, the local dollar hits new 11-year lows and the Australian dollar plummets past 59 U.S. cents. 

 June 11 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin all but rules out the possibility of joint intervention by major industrial powers to bolster the yen. He says the weak yen reflects the state of the Japanese economy. 

 June 12 - Economic Planning Agency says Japan's gross domestic product fell by an annualised rate of 5.3 percent in the first quarter, signalling recession. The yen dives towards 145 to the dollar as hopes fade of official intervention. 

 June 17 - The U.S. joins Japan in selling the dollar in favour of the yen. 

 The action takes markets by surprise and the yen rises to a high of around 134 at one stage from a level of some 142.50 prior to the intervention. 

 June 19 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin tells Reuters he is not expecting high level meetings in Tokyo to produce specific new action plans on the economy. His statements put further pressure on the yen. 

 June 20 - Top finance officials from the Group of Seven meet in Tokyo and vow to cooperate as appropriate in the currency markets. 

 June 23 - IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus calls the yen fall a "crisis within the crisis". 

 June 25 - Indonesia and the IMF sign another letter of intent - the fourth. The letter says that Indonesian GDP is expected to contract by at least 10 percent in 1998 and says the rupiah will stabilise at around 10,000 by the last quarter of 1998. 

 June 26 - Malaysia cuts bank statutory reserve requirements to eight percent from 10 percent. 

 June 29 - For the first time, South Korea closes banks, shutting five ailing operations in a major step towards meeting the mandate of the massive IMF rescue package. 

 July 2 - World Bank approves $1 billion loan disbursement to Indonesia, another $6 billion to arrive from international donors. 

 Japan Prime Minister Hashimoto and the ruling Liberal Democratic Party agree to adopt bridge bank system to tackle the country's massive bad loans. 

 July 4 - Foreign Minister Keizo Obuchi hints at permanent tax cuts. 

 July 8 - Hashimoto vows to seek permanent tax cuts and an overhaul of the tax system, but reveals no details. 

 July 9 - South Korea announces its intention to double this year's budget deficit in a bid to stimulate the economy. 

 July 12 - The ruling LDP is trounced in Upper House elections, winning only 44 seats, well short of a majority and 17 less than the 61 it had held prior to the election. 

 South Korea's Financial Supervisory Commission imposes involuntary restructuring on conglomerates, or chaebols, directing eight banks to pick about 16 chaebols for the exercise. 

 July 13 - PM Hashimoto announces his resignation and cancels planned official visits to France and the United States. 

 July 14 - Tens of thousands of South Korean workers down tools to protest against wage cuts and layoffs, part of the massive corporate restructuring programme. 

 July 15 - IMF approves immediate $1 billion loan payment to Indonesia. 

 July 16 - Striking Korean workers return to work, but warn of further protests if necessary. 

 Indonesia revises 98/99 budget to reflect the deteriorating economy, assuming a rupiah/dlr rate of 10,600. 

 Foreign governments announce their agreement to reschedule the country's $54.4 billion in sovereign debt. 

 July 20 - Protests begin at Hyundai's factory in Ulsan, striking workers pitch tents. 

 July 23 - Record 7.0 percent unemployment in South Korea, with more than 1.5 million unemployed. 

 July 24 - Obuchi wins 225 votes out of 411 in LDP voting to become LDP president and, almost certainly, prime minister. 

 July 29 - Moody's Investors Service warned that it may downgrade credit ratings of Thai banks due to poor results. 

 July 30 - Parliament formally names Obuchi prime minister; he then announces his new cabinet. 

 August 3 - Thailand unveils 25 point plan to salvage its economy at the start of two weeks of talks with the IMF. The plan includes measures to create jobs and stimulate the economy, and is later endorsed by the IMF. 

 Indonesia launches debt rescheduling agency to aid the country's debt-ridden companies. 

 August 6 - New Japanese prime minister Obuchi announces a plan to vary tax cuts according to existing tax brackets, and says he will ask parliament to approve cuts worth more than six trillion yen ($41.3 billion). 

 August 14 - The Hong Kong government intervenes in the local stock market, buying stocks to squeeze out investors accused of playing the currency and interest rates against the stock market. The Hang Seng Index soars 8.47 percent. 

 August 17 - Russia effectively devalues the rouble and declares a 90-day moratorium on some foreign debt. The next day, Asian markets slide. 

 Thousands of Hyundai Motor workers rally near the South Korean company's main factory complex in Ulsan, suspending production in protest over layoffs. Police stand ready for action. 

 August 25 - Hyundai workers return to work after a union-brokered agreement to limit number of layoffs. 

 August 26 - IMF approves $1 billion loan to Indonesia. 

 August 31 - Wall Street suffers its second-largest point loss in history, plunging 6.37 percent and sparking another series of stock market routs in Asia. 

 IMF approves $900 million loan payment to South Korea. 

 Sept 1 - Malaysia imposes new foreign exchange controls to contain speculation and restrict capital flows. The IMF warns that the move may undermine investor confidence. 

 Sept 2 - Malaysia announces that the ringgit will be fixed at 3.80 to the dollar indefinitely. 

 Wall Street stages its second-largest comeback in history, sparking off a rally in Asian markets. 

 Deputy Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is sacked. Police state that Anwar is under investigation over allegations made in a banned book, "Fifty Reasons Why Anwar Cannot Become Prime Minister".

title: ASIA FOCUS - Chronology of Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, Sept 3 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of Asia's financial crisis. 

 1997 

 Jan 23 - Leading South Korean steel maker Hanbo Steel Corp defaults on loans, the first of a string of major corporate failures in 1997. 

 May 14-15 - Thailand's baht currency comes under attack by speculators who decided Thailand's slowing economy and political instability meant it was time to sell. Thailand and Singapore jointly intervene to defend the baht. 

 The Philippines is affected. The central bank raises the overnight rate 1-percentage points to 13 percent and dumps dollars. 

 June 19 - Amnuay Viravan, staunchly against devaluing the baht, resigns as Thai finance minister. Resignation has immediate impact in the Philippines, where the overnight deposit rate rises to 15 percent. 

 June 27 - Thai central bank suspends operations of 16 cash-strapped finance companies and orders them to submit merger or consolidation plans. 

 June 30 - Thai Prime Minister Chavalit Yongchaiyudh assures the nation in a televised address there will be no devaluation of the baht. 

 July 2 - After a failed defence of the Thai baht, Bangkok floats its currency and calls on the IMF for "technical assistance". 

 The baht is effectively devalued by about 15-20 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah starts to crumble. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso slump as confidence in the region deteriorates. 

 August 11 - In Tokyo, the IMF unveils a rescue package for Thailand including loans of $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah plunges. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bail-out package, bringing it to $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 20 - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad tells delegates of IMF/World Bank conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Around this time the South Korean won also begins to slump in value. 

 Oct 27 - Asian jitters spill over on to world stock markets. The Dow plunges 554 points, its largest single-day point loss ever. 

 Oct 31 - Indonesia's IMF package is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - Indonesia shuts down 16 troubled banks. 

 Nov 5 - IMF approves a $10 billion loan for Indonesia as part of the massive international package. 

 Nov 17 - Korea abandons its defence of the won, which rapidly falls to 1,000 to the dollar. 

 Dec 4 - IMF approves a $21 billion loan for South Korea, part of a bail-out package that will total nearly $60 billion. 

 Dec 8 - Thailand closes 56 of 58 previously suspended finance companies. 

 1998 

 Jan 8 - Representatives of the IMF and South Korea agree to a 90-day rollover of short-term debt. 

 Jan 12 - Peregrine, one of Asia's largest independent investment banks, collapses under a mountain of bad loans to Indonesian borrowers. Shares fall sharply in Hong Kong, China and Singapore. 

 Jan 15 - IMF managing director Michel Camdessus and President Suharto sign an agreement strengthening economic reforms. 

 Jan 22 - The rupiah collapses. It is dealt at 17,000 to the dollar at one stage. Bank Indonesia intervenes and drives the currency back to end at 11,800. 

 Jan 27 - Indonesia announces a temporary freeze on debt servicing. 

 Jan 28 - International creditor banks and the South Korean government say they have agreed on a plan to exchange $24 billion of short-term debt for new loans maturing in one, two and three years. 

 Jan 30 - U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warns Asia's financial crisis could spread. 

 Feb 14 - The IMF threatens to cut off the bail-out fund for Indonesia over its plans to introduce a currency board. 

 Feb 26 - Indonesia's borrowers and lenders begin negotiations on rescheduling at least $70 billion in private off-shore debt. 

 March 1 - Indonesian President Suharto says reforms prescribed by the IMF have not worked. 

 March 4 - The IMF approves release of the third tranche payment from Thailand's package and commends the Thai government for its economic reforms. 

 March 6 - IMF says its board will not discuss Indonesia's economic reform programme before April, effectively delaying a $3 billion payment initially expected by March 15. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: FOCUS-Indonesia wants sound banks by year-end.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Indonesian Finance Minister Bambang Subianto said on Tuesday he wanted a sound banking system in place in the country by the end of the year to bring interest and exchange rates under control and restore business confidence. 

 "We want the sector healthier by the year end to get them (the banks) supporting the economy for 1999," Subianto told a capital markets conference in Jakarta. 

 Restoring the health of the ailing banking sector is a pre-requisite if Indonesia was to restore its currency exchange rate to sensible, sustainable levels, bring down soaring interest and inflation rates and return liquidity to a cash-strangled economy. 

 "Our main objective is to have a banking system in place to be able to support the economy properly," Subianto said. 

 Bank reform is a key tenet of the $41.2 billion rescue package prescribed by the International Monetary Fund for Indonesia, which is in the throes of its worst economic crisis in more than 30 years, threatening massive social unrest in its wake. 

 Analysts say the perilous health of the banks has been the major factor behind the collapse in confidence in Indonesia, whose corporations are struggling to dig themselves out from under a foreign debt mountain of some $80 billion. 

 Subianto last week took serious steps on the road to reconstructing the sector, freezing, merging or nationalising 11 ailing banks. The minister said he intended to resolve the fate of 38 others under the watch of the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency (IBRA) in the very near future. 

 "In the coming months you will see decisions coming on the other 38," he told the conference. 

 Subianto's words provided fresh stimulus for the strengthening rupiah currency, which analysts say could be heading for the 10,000 level to the U.S. dollar by the year end. 

 It broke decisively through 12,000 a week ago and has tested 11,000 several times since. At 0831 GMT on Tuesday, the rupiah was quoted at 10,950/11,125 per dollar. It was around 2,500 to the dollar before the economic crisis hit in July last year. 

 Sjahril Sabirin, governor of the central bank, Bank Indonesia, told conference delegates: "This morning the rupiah strengthened above 11,000 to the dollar. We are winning!" 

 The market disagreed with him however. "The rupiah was bid below 11,000 yes, but it was only screen play. The best it has done was 11,250," a dealer with a U.S. bank told Reuters. 

 Another dealer said: "It was bid through 11,000, but nobody took it. The resistance seems to be at 11,200 at the moment." Technical factors point to a 10,000 level to the U.S. dollar by the year end, mainly as a result of some $10 billion of loans and aid due for injection in the country in the fiscal year ending in March 1999. 

 These dollars will be converted into rupiah for spending on infrastructure and other projects. 

 Stabilising the exchange rate would also be a big help in slashing choking interest rates, which Bank Indonesia set at a weighted average of 70.14 percent for its one month paper in auctions last week. 

Central bank managing director, Miranda Gultom said tackling interest and exchange rates were the priority to get business costs back under control, although there was no avoiding the short term pain of high rates. 

 "We have to stabilise the rupiah - there is no question about it," she told the conference, adding that tight monetary policy was still needed "even though high interest rates will hamper our effort to start on the road to recovery". 

 She said the return to a managed exchange rate system could also be on the agenda for the future. Indonesia had a system of managed exchange rates through an intervention band until last August when the rupiah was freed after the financial crisis hit the region. 

Currency traders in Jakarta said such a move would be welcome. 

 "It would be a good idea. We would be better able to plan our topside and our bottom and draw up stop loss programmes," said a dealer with a European bank. 

 Added impetus for the rupiah against the dollar should come if the government's reforms began to restore the confidence that has evaporated in the economy domestically and internationally. 

 Dennis de Tray, the World Bank's chief representative in Indonesia, said the best strategy to restore confidence was to set quick win reform targets that beat market expectations. 

 "Actions, not words, restore confidence. You can promise the moon, but you have to deliver it," he told delegates, adding that the government had tried to introduce reform measures in the past but they had failed live up to what was anticipated. 

 "You have to stay ahead of the expectation curve," he said. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Bank Indonesia not ruling out managed  forex  rate.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 25 (Reuters) - Bank Indonesia Managing Director Miranda Gultom said on Tuesday the central bank was not ruling out the eventual introduction of a managed exchange rate system. 

 "A fixed exchange rate may not be something that can be done now," Gultom told a capital markets conference in Jakarta. 

 "But we are not ruling out a moving intervention band or a crawling intervention band," she said. 

 Gultom said such a system would require strong discipline in monetary management. 

Indonesia had a system of managed exchange rates through an intervention band until last August, when the rupiah was freed after the financial crisis hit Southeast Asia.

title: Riot fears keep rupiah quiet in early trade.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 14 (Reuters) - The rupiah softened in early Friday trade with fears about possible weekend violence ahead of Indonesia's independence day keeping pressure on the currency, dealers said. 

 "The risk is on the top side and if the riots happen, the rupiah is going to be a victim too," a dealer with one U.S. bank said. 

 At 0220 GMT the rupiah was being traded around 13,000 against the dollar from an earlier high of 12,700, with dealers expecting a range of 12,900 to 13,100 to hold at least for the morning session. 

 "After lunch I'm not sure where we will go if the rumours about riots continue," a dealer with a local bank said. 

 Bank Indonesia's intervention in the market at about the 13,000 level was also cited as a factor causing the rupiah to weaken. 

 "When the central bank went in, traders sold," a dealer said. 

 On the positive side, foreign traders were responding more warmly to the news that the interbank exchange of debt offer was progressing, after initial fears that the deal meant more bad news for Indonesian banks. 

 About US$2.7 billion of eligible external interbank debt of Indonesian banks scheduled to mature in the fiscal year ending March 31, 1999 will be exchanged for an equal amount of new loans guaranteed by Bank Indonesia with one, two, three and four-year maturities. 

 "People initially read this as defaulting, but now they realise it has international blessing, they are more relaxed about it," a dealer with a European bank said. 

 But hesitancy would remain through the day, dealers said, with the market set to react sharply to any news of unrest.

title: Indonesia Rupiah Up Late -2: Pushes Through Key Level
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah bounced up late Friday on aggressive selling of U.S. dollars by state-owned banks which overwrote lingering market fears about potential unrest this long weekend. 

 At 0916 GMT (5:16 a.m. EDT), the rupiah was quoted at IDR12,750 per U.S. dollar, much stronger than IDR12,950 traded late Thursday. 

 Dealers reported heavy selling of U.S. dollars by state banks around the key level of IDR13,000.

 He estimated the state banks spent about $30 million-$50 million during the day to boost the currency.

title: Indonesian Rupiah Slightly Higher Late On Debt Reschedule
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--he Indonesian rupiah ended the Asian day slightly higher Wednesday, cheered by the government's confirmation that it isn't unilaterally missing payments on its principal sovereign debt. 

 The dollar was fetching 13,000 rupiah (IDR) at the end of Asian trade, weaker than IDR13,200 the same time Tuesday. The rupiah is also sharply higher than IDR13,550 in offshore trade Tuesday. 

 Market participants said trade remained thin, however. 

 "There's no demand really, the market's still very quiet," said the treasury chief with a local bank, adding that many investors were remaining clear of the currency ahead of Indonesian Independence day on Monday, fearing potential uprest. 

 The rupiah weakened sharply Tuesday on the back of reports that the country had missed sovereign debt payments. The currency rebounded, however, after Senior Economics Minister Ginandjar Kartasasmita said Indonesia had simply started to reschedule some of its debt in line with agreements with its major international lenders. 

 The Treasury Chief said state banks had offered to sell dollars at IDR13,100, but said Bank Indonesia itself hadn't been seen intervening in the market. 

 "We haven't detected anything from Bank Indonesia," he said. "We saw some selling from state banks but as usual aren't sure if they're acting for themselves or for Bank Indonesia." 

 The market also focused Wednesday on the central bank'sotes. 

 The bank raised IDR15.14 trillion rupiah at the third auction of its one-month Sertifikat Bank Indonesia, above its target of IDR13 trillion, a bank official said. 

 The auction of one-month notes raised IDR15.14 trillion at a weighted average rate of 69.5%, up from 68.3% last week. 

 The official said 95.1% of all bids were accepted.

title: Indonesian Rupiah Up Mid-Morning On Govt Debt Rescheduling
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah was slightly higher mid-morning Wednesday as the market welcomed the government's move to start rescheduling its sovereign debt in line with agreements with its major international lenders - and not unilaterally. 

 At 0315 GMT (11:15 p.m. EDT Tuesday), the rupiah was trading at 13,175 rupiah (IDR), up from IDR13,200 late Tuesday in Asian trading. The currency is stronger than IDR13,550 during London trade Tuesday. 

 "It has strengthened a lot compared to last night," said a dealer at a Japanese bank. 

 The rupiah weakened sharply Tuesday on the back of reports that the country had missed sovereign debt payments. The currency rebounded, however, after senior economics minister Ginandjar Kartasasmita said Indonesia had simply started to reschedule some of its debt in line with agrerments with the International Monetary Fund, the Group of Seven and the Paris Club of Creditor Nations. 

 He stressed that Indonesia would continue to pay interest on its debt, as agreed with its lenders. 

 The trader said Ginandjar's commments helped inject confidence in the market. 

 He added that the move by state-owned banks to offer to sell dollars was also keeping the currency stable. 

 "Earlier this morning, the state banks offered to sell U.S. dollars at IDR13,250 and then they offered to sell at IDR13,175," the dealer said. 

 He added that Bank Indonesia itself wasn't seen intervening in the market. Central bank governor Sjahril Sabirin said Tuesday the bank would intervene regularly and at the appropriate times to support the rupiah. 

 The central bank will offer to sell IDR13 trillion of one-month central bank notes later Wednesday with settlement Thursday. 

 "Banks don't want to hold short positions knowing that the rupiah will be tighter ahead of the auction," said a dealer at a Singaporean bank. 

 The rupiah is expected to trade within a tight range of IDR13,000 to IDR13,200 for the rest of the day.

title: Indonesian Rupiah Up Slightly Late On State Bk  Intervention
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--The Indonesian rupiah was up slightly late Tuesday despite sliding regional currencies, with intervention by state-owned banks lending support to the currency. 

 At 0851 GMT (4:51 a.m. EDT), the rupiah was quoted at 13,050 rupiah (IDR) to the dollar, slightly up from IDR13,100 late Monday. 

 Dealers said trading was thin, with concerns about further weakening of regional currencies in particular the yen and the possible devaluation of the Chinese yuan, keeping investors clear of the rupiah. 

 Dealers said the state-owned banks stepped into the market when the rupiah was at IDR13,100 and offered to sell the dollar at IDR13,050. 

 "The amount is quite small. I guess it's roughly US$15 million to US$25 million," said a dealer at a Japanese bank. 

 Bank Indonesia, the country's central bank, wasn't seen directly intervening in the market. 

Central bank governor Sjahril Sabirin said earlier Tuesday that the bank would intervene in the market regularly to boost the rupiah. He said the bank had intervened Monday. 

 Meanwhile, although there was little movement in the spot market, market players have been positioning themselves in the swap market ahead of the auction of central bank notes on Wednesday.

title: Bk  Indonesia /Regularly  Intervene  -3: Tight Monetary Policy
text:
Sjahril also reiterated the bank would maintain a tight monetary policy, also to boost the rupiah. 

 At 0508 GMT Tuesday, the dollar is fetching IDR12,975, down from IDR13,100 late Monday in Asia. 

 Under Indonesia's agreement with the International Monetary Fund, the central bank has pledged to keep interest rates high to support the currency. Its tight monetary policy has thus far failed to strengthen the rupiah significantly, however. 

 Sjahril said the full implementation of the Frankfurt agreement between Indonesian debtors and international banks to reschedule private sector debt was also crucial to lend support to the rupiah. 

 He said once the agreement is in place "offshore banks will reopen credit lines to Indonesia." 

 The Indonesian Debt Restructuring Agency - set up under the Frankfurt agreement - opened for business last week, although no Indonesian debtors have yet joined or even pledged to join. 

 The agency outlines a way to reschedule foreign private debt, thus offering some breathing space to the nation's cash-strapped companies and its shaky foreign-exchange market. 

 The pact offers a voluntary program to debt-laden companies under which their obligations will be extended by eight years and under which they will receive access to dollars at a locked-in rate - set last week at 13,233 rupiah to the dollar. 

 The continued free-fall of the rupiah against the dollar, however, has prompted many companies to question the merits of entering the agreement.

title: Rupiah ends lower on north Asian  currencies .
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 7 (Reuters) - The rupiah ended slightly lower against the dollar on Friday following jitters in the Japanese yen, Chinese yuan and the Hong Kong dollar, dealers said. 

 They said dollar short-covering ahead of a long weekend in Singapore also helped push the rupiah lower. 

 Spot rupiah ended at 12,850 after hovering between 12,650 and 13,000 through the day after opening at 12,675/12,775. The rupiah ended on Thursday at 12,650/12,750 in Jakarta and at 12,750/12,850 in New York. 

 The rupiah however ended the week higher compared with 13,125 last Friday on improved sentiment due to anticipation of inflows from international donors. 

 Dealers said sustained weakness in the yen had concerned the market over how long could the yuan withstand pressures. 

 Fears the yuan could be devalued and an attack on the Hong Kong dollar kept pressure on the regionals. 

 "Sentiment was rather mixed in the afternoon. I think it's mainly due to the yen, yuan and Hong Kong dollars," one said. 

 The American bank dealer said the central bank was seen selling small amounts of dollars, but that failed to prevent the rupiah inching closer to the 13,000 level. 

 Dealers said operators were also concerned over rumours of possible unrest in the run-up to the celebration of Indonesia's Independence Day on August 17. 

 "People are a bit worried about the rumours. I think some will take precautionary steps," one local bank dealer said. 

 Jakarta's police chief Nugroho Djajusman said security forces were on guard against any new unrest in the capital, amid rumours that fresh riots were being planned. 

 Nugroho said the city's residents should also organise their own security measures against crime and the threat of unrest. 

 But he said that rumours circulating in the city that there would be violence on August 17 were unfounded. 

 Dealers said the new letter of chief economics minister Ginandjar Kartasasmita to the IMF following recent review of the country's structural and adjustment programmes announced on Friday had no effect on the market. 

 They said the substantive points were in the banking sector, with the government specifying what actions were to be taken in the next few weeks. 

 "It has been long expected. There is no impact in the market," one chief treasurer with a local bank said. 

 Chief economics minister Ginandjar Kartasasmita has said Indonesia would use international aid in dollars to buy rupiah in the foreign exchange markets in the coming months. 

 Ginandjar said the ecomomy's main source of trouble was a lack of international confidence reflected in the level of the rupiah compared to the dollar. 

 He said the government aimed to raise the rupiah to about 10,000 to the dollar by the end of March 1999. 

 He said that in the course of the coming months there would be continuous purchases of the rupiah in the market, which was not the same as intervention but should help. 

 Dealers said liquidity eased in the afternoon after a tight start due to carry-forward effect from Wednesday. They said overnight money for state banks eased to 53 percent. 

 In the morning, overnight money for state and foreign banks hovered around 63 and 65 percent, for local banks around 70 to 75 percent and for banks under supervision around 100 percent. 

 Dealers said it might be due to carry-forward impact from a higher-than-expected allocation of central bank weekly auction 

 They said SBIs rates were much higher than interbank rates, allowing operators to arbitrage. 

 The banks' weekly auction of SBIs resulted in an absorption of 14,151 billion rupiah at a weighted average interest rate of 68.33 percent, accounting for 87 percent of the incoming bids. 

 The central bank had targeted mopping up 13 trillion rupiah for its 28-day paper or treasury bills. 

 Dealers said swap rates were little changed in the afternoon. In Singapore, spot/next swaps were at 17/19, one-week at 130/140, one-month at 600/620, two at 1,070/1,170, three at 1,550/1,650, six at 2,900/3,100, nine at 4,100/4,400 and one-year at 5,400/5,700 points. 

 Bank Indonesia on Friday added rupiah intervention rates for two more tenors in mid-morning, dealers said. 

 They said the central bank paid 51 percent for overnight money and 53 percent for four-and five-day money. The bank had earlier only set 53 percent for six-day money.

title: Rupiah slightly softer on weakening yen.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 7 (Reuters) - The rupiah was a shade softer against the dollar on Friday morning on continued weakness in the yen, dealers said. 

 Spot rupiah was last given at 12,775 at 0225 GMT after opening at 12,675/12,775. The rupiah ended on Thursday at 12,650/12,750 in Jakarta and at 12,750/12,850 in New York. 

 "Sentiment is not as strong as in the past few days. I think it might be linked to jitters in the region on continued weakness in the yen," one American bank dealer said. 

 Dealers said resistance at the 12,500 level remained strong, suggesting a possible range of 12,600 and 12,900 for the day. 

 They said only a few trades had gone through so far, but operators were cautious of central bank actions following its price checking on Thursday. Some said the bank had intervened in very small amounts, indicating possible capital inflows. 

 Chief economics minister Ginandjar Kartasasmita has said Indonesia would use international aid in dollars to buy rupiah in the foreign exchange markets in the coming months. 

 Ginandjar said the ecomomy's main source of trouble was a lack of international confidence reflected in the level of the rupiah compared to the dollar. 

 He said the government aimed to raise the rupiah to about 10,000 to the dollar by the end of March 1999. 

 He said that in the course of the coming months there would be continuous purchases of the rupiah in the market, which was not the same as intervention but should help. 

 Dealers said the market remained cautious on fears of unrest as the government has not got prices under control. 

 Meanwhile, a group of 15 prominent Indonesian economists issued a declaration on Thursday warning that the country's very existence was threatened unless the government changed its economic course. 

 The declaration said if there was no prompt action, the situation would move towards a total destruction of the economy, bringing along the collapse of the social and political life of the people and the existence of Indonesia. 

 It said economic policies under President B.J. Habibie had not shown an improvement compared with the government of former president Suharto, and the government's lack of political legitimacy was impeding economic recovery. 

 Dealers said liquidity was tighter in the morning, with overnight money for state and foreign banks hovering around 63 and 65 percent, for local banks at around 70 to 75 percent and for banks under supervision around 100 percent. 

 They said it might be due to carry-forward impact from a higher-than-expected allocation of central bank weekly auction. 

 "I think it's due to the Wednesday effect. Many have gone short to arbitrage with the interbank market. They are now covering back," one local bank dealer said.

title: Indonesian rupiah holds on gains as yen recovers.
text:
JAKARTA, Aug 5 (Reuters) - The rupiah held on to its gains against the dollar in late trading on Wednesday on the back of a recovering yen, dealers said. 

 They said the rupiah could renew its test on the 12,500 resistance level if the yen sustained its recovery. Some dealers were sceptical because of the gloomy economic outlook. 

 Spot rupiah ended in Jakarta at 12,750 after hovering between 12,650 and 12,900 through the day. The rupiah ended on Tuesday at 12,950 in Jakarta. 

 "Sentiment is still strong on the rupiah. But a lot depends on the yen," one European bank dealer said. 

 Dealers said the yen seemed to given a firmer tone to regional currencies following the steep sell-off in U.S. stocks overnight, dragging stock markets lower across the region. 

 "I think the U.S. economy is not immune to troubles in Asia. How do you want to sell if we can't absorb their goods? People are looking at the mark and sterling now," one American bank dealer said. 

 Meanwhile, Deputy U.S. Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers set a bearish tone for Asian markets by saying the financial troubles in the region might be far from over. 

 "I would say we have a long way to go in working through these problems," Summers told the National Governors' Association, when asked about Asia's financial crisis. 

 "But I think with a strong response, and particularly if the Japanese take what I think are crucial steps for them, I think this can remain very much a contained situation, and that there is no inherent reason why it needs...to pose a threat to the basic momentum of an American economic expansion." 

 He said the economies of South Korea and Thailand were under more control, but the situation in Indonesia was more serious. 

 "Relative to six months ago, I think that there is a sense of the situation coming under more control in Korea and in Thailand, relative to what most observers would have expected six months ago," Summers said. 

 "I think that largely for political rather than economic reasons, the situation in Indonesia is more serious than it appeared six months ago," Summers added. 

 Dealers said the yield curve remained on an inverted trend, with supports in shorter-dates below one-month for arbitrage and funding purposes while the longer-end tended to soften. 

 One foreign bank dealer said an easing trend in longer-term rates suggested improved rupiah expectations.

 The central bank had targeted mopping up 13 trillion rupiah for its 28-day paper or treasury bills. 

 Dealers said the higher than expected rupiah contraction allowed the central bank to relax its intervention policy.

 The dealer however said the new system could endanger small banks' balance sheets because depositors could switch deposits to risk-free treasury bills with high returns.

title: Indonesian rupiah holds on above the 13,000 level.
text:

 "I believe Japan's experienced cabinet will be able to overcome its economic problems," he said. 

 Ginandjar said he hoped the rupiah would also strengthen by the end of the year without giving a target figure. The IMF has said a target of 10,000 to the dollar by the end of the current fiscal year next March still appeared attainable.

title: Rupiah extends gains, rises above 13,500 on CGI.
text:
JAKARTA, July 29 (Reuters) - The rupiah extended its two-day gains against the dollar on Wednesday morning, breaking a strong resistance level at the 13,500 level. 

 Dealers said the rupiah's upward momentum continued to benefit from the on-going donors' meeting in Paris which was expected to yield another $7-$8 billion aid for Indonesia. 

 Spot rupiah rose to a high of 13,400 in the morning before settling at around 13,350/13,450 at 0215 GMT. The rupiah was last traded above the 13,350 level in early June before it was pushed down to comply with Frankfurt debt restructuring scheme. 

 "It's the Paris meeting which seems to feed the market with optimistic sentiment," one Western bank dealer said. 

 The Consultative Group for Indonesia (CGI) meeting in Paris on July 28 and 29 will decide on the amount of money pledged for the country's development projects. 

 Vikram Nehru, the World Bank's economist for Indonesia, said the bank was hoping donors would agree to disburse $7-$8 billion in aid to Jakarta in the year to March 1999. 

 World Bank officials called the meeting crucial and said the amount of money made available to Jakarta in the coming year would help determine the speed of economic recovery. 

 Dealers said there was a chance for the rupiah to test the next resistance level of 13,000 if regional currencies could maintain their stability and the yen's slide was halted. 

 But some said there were worries that operators could take profits once the confirmation of CGI aid came through. 

 Others said another factor which could weigh on the market was the new auction system with quantitative targets, allowing interest rates to be fully determined by the market. 

 They said operators welcomed the tender system but the worries were rates could ease before it was actually allowed to reward investors with the country's high risk profile. 

 "I don't see the scope for lower interest rates currently. Unlike Thailand and South Korea, Indonesia's economy has not bottomed out yet," one currency analyst said. 

 Bank Indonesia on Tuesday set its first indicative target for its new auction system amounting to 13 trillion rupiah for 28-day paper, with settlement on July 30. Banks could submit bids on Wednesday between 8 a.m. and 2 p.m. (0100-0700 GMT), with the minimum bid set at 500 million rupiah. 

 Dealers said expectation of a possible easing in interest rates with the new quantitative target also drove short-end swaps lower, dragging other tenors to follow. 

 They said offshore operators were cutting down their overborrowed rupiah cash flows as local players removed their recent supports in tom/next swaps. 

 "People are selling now to lock in lower rates," one said.

title: Rupiah steady amid focus on riot anniversary.
text:
JAKARTA, July 27 (Reuters) - The rupiah was steady against the dollar on Monday morning amid plans to mark the second anniversary of riots in Jakarta following the takeover of the headquarters of the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) following the ousting of Megawati Sukarnoputri as party leader. 

Currency dealers said the rupiah had held on well despite fears of possible unrest connected with the anniversary. 

 Serious riots had followed the takeover of the PDI offices in central Jakarta in July 1996 by a government-backed faction that had deposed Megawati as PDI chief.

 Dealers said the rupiah was largely neglected as offshore operators focused on gloomy economic outlook in the region. 

 "There was not much going on in the rupiah. We see instead some pressure in the ringgit and the Singapore dollars," one Western bank dealer said. 

 He said the market was waiting for the outcome of the country's donors meeting July 28 and 29 in Paris. 

 The Consultative Group for Indonesia (CGI) meeting would decide on the amount of loans to the country. Planning Minister Boediono said donors are likely to pledge a larger amount of loans, compared with the $5.3 billion in 1997.
