title: Rupiah strengthens, shrugs off riot anniversary.
text:
JAKARTA, July 27 (Reuters) - The rupiah strengthened against the dollar on Monday, shrugging off the anniversary of 1996 riots in Jakarta that went off peacefully, dealers said. 

 They said the rupiah instead was given a boost by optimistic expectations of a meeting of donor countries on Indonesia in Paris this week. 

 Spot rupiah crossed the 14,000 resistance level to a high of 13,800 before ending in Jakarta at 13,950 after hovering between 14,050 and 14,300 last week. 

 Some dealers linked the rise to anticipation of increased loans from the Paris meeting to help cover the budget deficit. 

 Dealers said stop-loss dollar selling was triggered after the rupiah touched the 14,000 level. The rupiah was hovering around 14,200 level in the morning. 

 "We see some dollar selling from a European name. We don't know what was the reason. That helped boost the rupiah in a thin market," an American bank dealer said. 

 The Consultative Group for Indonesia (CGI) meeting in Paris on Tuesday and Wednesday will decide on the amount of loans to the country. Planning Minister Boediono said amount was likely to be over the 1997 figure of $5.3 billion. 

 The government has said it had already secured $6.2 billion in budget support from donor countries. 

 Meanwhile, a spokeswoman of the Development Cooperation Ministry said on Sunday that the Dutch government had replied positively to a request by President B.J. Habibie to resume development funding for Indonesia. 

 Dealers said the market was calm despite initial jitters over plans to mark the second anniversary of riots in Jakarta following the takeover of the headquarters of the Indonesian Democratic Party (PDI) after the ousting of Megawati Sukarnoputri as party leader. 

Currency dealers said the rupiah had held up well despite fears of possible unrest connected with the anniversary. 

 Serious riots had followed the takeover of the PDI offices in central Jakarta in July 1996 by a government-backed faction that had deposed Megawati as PDI chief. 

 However, the anniversary passed peacefully. 

 Thousands of troops and police had been placed on alert across Jakarta after authorities banned a rally in the city centre fearing outbreaks of violence. 

 Dealers said operators were also looking forward for the implementation on Wednesday of a new auction system. 

 The central bank plans to start with the auction of one-month paper on Wednesday and later expand to a full range of maturities as agreed with the International Monetary Fund. 

Currency analysts said the move would be the first step by the central bank in switching to an open auction system after almost two decades of setting interest rates administratively. 

 In the afternoon, Bank Indonesia added intervention in overnight money into its monetary programme, dealers said. 

 They said the central bank offered to buy overnight money at 48 percent, apparently to meet its monetary target. They said the central bank in the morning was only offering three tenors in its intervention activity. 

 The bank paid 53 percent for three-day money, 60 percent for 10-day and 61 percent for 17-day. 

 Dealers said operators were seen unloading forwards after spot rupiah staged a recovery in the afternoon.

title: ASIA FOCUS - Chronology of Asia's financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, July 2 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of Asia's financial crisis. 

 1997 

 July 2 - After a failed defence of the Thai baht, Bangkok floats its currency and calls on the IMF for "technical assistance". 

 The baht is effectively devalued by about 15-20 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah starts to crumble. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso slump as confidence in the region deteriorates. 

 August 11 - In Tokyo, the IMF unveils a rescue package for Thailand including loans of $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah plunges. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bail-out package, bringing it to $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 20 - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad tells delegates of IMF/World Bank conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Around this time the South Korean won also begins to slump in value. 

 Oct 27 - Asian jitters spill over on to world stock markets. The Dow plunges 554 points, its largest single-day point loss ever. 

 Oct 31 - Indonesia's IMF package is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - Indonesia shuts down 16 troubled banks. 

 Nov 5 - IMF approves a $10 billion loan for Indonesia as part of the massive international package. 

 Nov 17 - Korea abandons its defence of the won, which rapidly falls to 1,000 to the dollar. 

 Dec 4 - IMF approves a $21 billion loan for South Korea, part of a bail-out package that will total nearly $60 billion. 

 Dec 8 - Thailand closes 56 of 58 previously suspended finance companies. 

 1998 

 Jan 8 - Representatives of the IMF and South Korea agree to a 90-day rollover of short-term debt. 

 Jan 12 - Peregrine, one of Asia's largest independent investment banks, collapses under a mountain of bad loans to Indonesian borrowers. Shares fall sharply in Hong Kong, China and Singapore. 

 Jan 15 - IMF managing director Michel Camdessus and President Suharto sign an agreement strengthening economic reforms. 

 Jan 22 - The rupiah collapses. It is dealt at 17,000 to the dollar at one stage. Bank Indonesia intervenes and drives the currency back to end at 11,800. 

 Jan 27 - Indonesia announces a temporary freeze on debt servicing. 

 Jan 28 - International creditor banks and the South Korean government say they have agreed on a plan to exchange $24 billion of short-term debt for new loans maturing in one, two and three years. 

 Jan 30 - U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warns Asia's financial crisis could spread. 

 Feb 14 - The IMF threatens to cut off the bail-out fund for Indonesia over its plans to introduce a currency board. 

 Feb 26 - Indonesia's borrowers and lenders begin negotiations on rescheduling at least $70 billion in private off-shore debt. 

 March 1 - Suharto says reforms prescribed by the IMF have not worked. 

 March 4 - The IMF approves release of the third tranche payment from Thailand's package and commends the Thai government for its economic reforms. 

 March 6 - IMF says its board will not discuss Indonesia's economic reform programme before April, effectively delaying a $3 billion payment initially expected by March 15. 

 March 23 - Indonesia nearly doubles interest rates to boost the rupiah and control inflation. 

 April 1 - Japan begins steps aimed at liberalising its financial markets to make them "free, fair and global" by 2001. Tokyo share prices fall, the yen dips and Japan's central bank governor pronounces every economic indicator bad. 

 April 2 - The chairman of electronics giant Sony, Norio Ohga, says the Japanese economy is on the verge of collapse. 

 April 3 - U.S. ratings agency Moody's lowers its outlook on Japan's sovereign debt to negative from stable. Asian currencies fall sharply on the news. 

 May 7 - Fears that riots in the Indonesian city of Medan will spill over into a wider social crisis send regional stocks into retreat. 

 May 11 - India stuns the world with announcement of three underground nuclear tests. Pakistan stocks tumble 3.52 percent while India's National Stock Exchange index slides 2.55 percent. 

 May 13 - The United States imposes economic sanctions on India and Japan suspends some loans. 

 May 14 - Mobs rampage through Jakarta and students demand Suharto's resignation. Indonesia's worsening crisis takes centre-stage for Asian markets, several of which suffer sharp losses. 

 May 15 - Suharto returns home from Egypt amid signs he is losing his 32-year grip on power. 

 May 21 - Suharto steps down and is succeeded by former deputy president B.J. Habibie. Markets enjoy a limited rally. Jakarta stocks surge more than three percent. 

 May 25 - South Korean shares plummet 6.78 percent despite a lifting of foreign ownership limits on stocks. Most other Asian markets shrug off Seoul's fall. 

 May 26 - Seoul's KOSPI share index continues to dive, losing a further six percent, hurt by a looming recession and labour unrest. 

 May 27 - Asian markets are hammered as the yen falls against the dollar and amid mounting fears of economic recession. Hong Kong stocks plunge more than five percent after Chief Executive Tung Chee Hwa warns of possible recession. 

 May 28 - Pakistan conducts nuclear tests. 

 May 29 - The dollar rockets to a seven-year high of 139 yen on fears of a possible nuclear arms race in Asia and after news that Japan's unemployment rate hit 4.1 percent in April, its highest level since the end of World War Two. 

 Recession looms in much of Asia. Hong Kong reports that its gross domestic product contracted two percent in first quarter of 1998. About the same time Indonesia and Malaysia also report their economies contracted in the first quarter. 

 June 1 - Pakistani stocks plunge 12.38 percent as traders get their first chance to react to sanctions imposed after the country's nuclear tests. Asian markets are hit as nuclear tension adds to a cocktail of domestic problems. 

 June 5 - International lenders and Indonesian companies reach a deal to reschedule the country's massive corporate debt. 

 June 8 - The yen falls past 140 to the dollar, sending a shudder through Asian markets. Signs that Japan and other leading economies are unlikely to intervene to support the unit sap confidence further. 

 June 10 - China's central bank governor warns that the weak yen is having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade, raising fears that China may devalue its yuan currency. Markets across Asia tumble, led by a near five percent fall on Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index. 

 In Taiwan, the local dollar hits new 11-year lows and the Australian dollar plummets past 59 U.S. cents. 

 June 11 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin all but rules out the possibility of joint intervention by major industrial powers to bolster the yen. He says the weak yen reflects the state of the Japanese economy. 

 June 12 - Economic Planning Agency says Japan's gross domestic product fell by an annualised rate of 5.3 percent in the first quarter, signalling recession. The yen dives towards 145 to the dollar as hopes fade of official intervention. 

 June 17 - The U.S. joins Japan in selling the dollar in favour of the yen. 

 The action takes markets by surprise and the yen rises to a high of around 134 at one stage from a level of some 142.50 prior to the intervention. 

 June 19 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin tells Reuters he is not expecting high level meetings in Tokyo to produce specific new action plans on the economy. His statements puts further pressure on the yen. 

 June 20 - Top finance officials from the Group of Seven meet in Tokyo and vow to cooperate as appropriate in the currency markets. 

 June 23 - Michel Camdessus calls the yen fall a "crisis within the crisis". 

 June 25 - Indonesia and the IMF sign another letter of intent - the fourth. The letter says that Indonesian GDP is expected to contract by at least 10 percent in 1998 and says the rupiah will stabilise at around 10,000 by the last quarter of 1998. 

 June 26 - Malaysia cuts bank statutory reserve requirements to eight percent from 10 percent. 

 June 29 - For the first time, South Korea closes banks, shutting five ailing operations in a major step towards meeting the mandate of the massive IMF rescue package. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Chronology of Indonesia's financial crisis.
text:
JAKARTA, June 25 (Reuters) - A chronology of Indonesia's financial crisis. 

 1997 

 Jul 8 - The rupiah starts to crumble. Jakarta widens its rupiah trading band to 12 from eight percent. 

 Aug 14 - Jakarta abolishes managed exchange rate system. The rupiah sinks further. 

 Oct 6 - Rupiah hits a low of 3,845. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the International Monetary Fund for assistance. 

 Oct 31 - IMF package unveiled with more than $40 billion in aid. 

 1998 

 Jan 6 - Indonesia unveils its 1998/99 budget projecting four percent economic growth. The rupiah loses half its value against the dollar over five days, breaking through 10,000. 

 Jan 10 - President Suharto announces the delay or review of 15 infrastructure projects. 

 Jan 14 - IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus says the IMF is asking Indonesia to sign a new letter of intent. 

 Jan 15 - Camdessus and Suharto sign an agreement strengthening economic reforms. 

 Jan 22 - The rupiah hits a low of 17,000. Bank Indonesia intervenes and it recovers to 11,800. 

 Jan 23 - Indonesia presents a revised budget expecting zero growth in fiscal 1998 and 20 percent inflation, but which assumes the rupiah will be at 5,000 to the dollar. 

 Jan 27 - Indonesia announces a temporary freeze on debt servicing. 

 Jan 28 - Mobs attack shops owned by ethnic Chinese in Central Java over rising food prices. 

 Feb 4 - Indonesian government gives a lukewarm response to a proposal by U.S. economist Steve Hanke to peg the rupiah under a currency board system. 

 Feb 6 - Chief debt negotiator Radius Prawiro says Indonesia's total foreign debt is $137.424 billion. 

 Feb 9 - Signature campaign to replace Suharto begins. 

 Feb 11 - Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad says government is preparing for a currency board. The rupiah rises to 7,200 to the dollar. Police detain 140 people after protests in Jakarta. 

 Feb 12 - Ruling Golkar party names Research and Technology Minister B.J. Habibie as one of its vice presidential candidates. 

 Feb 13 - Suharto tells President Clinton the IMF is failing to stem Indonesia's financial crisis. Clinton objects to Jakarta's currency board plans. 

 Feb 14 - IMF threatens to halt its bail-out fund. Police detain 154 people in riots over rising prices that leave at least three dead. 

 Feb 17 - Suharto fires central bank governor Soedradjad Djiwandono for opposing currency board. Djiwandono is replaced by U.S.-trained economist Sjahril Sabirin. 

 Feb 18 - Habibie wins armed forces' backing for vice-presidency. 

 Feb 19 - U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley and German Finance Minister Waigel insist Indonesia must follow IMF-prescribed reforms. 

 Feb 20 - Finance Minister Mar'ie Muhammad says Indonesia so far faced no problem in meeting state foreign debts. 

 Feb 26 - Indonesian companies hold their first formal meeting with a steering committee of lenders to resolve the country's estimated $74 billion in private debt. 

 Mar 6 - IMF delays disbursement of second $3 billion tranche to Indonesia due March 15. 

 Mar 10 - Suharto re-elected president for a seventh five-year term by the 1,000 member People's Consultative Assembly (MPR), as thousands of students hold protest rallies. 

 Mar 11 - Suharto sworn in. Habibie elected vice-president. 

 Mar 16 - Suharto swears in 36 new cabinet ministers, including daughter Siti Hardiyanti Rukmana and a golfing buddy, as students and riot police clash at the National University in Jakarta. 

 Mar 20 - Indonesia says decision has been made to drop the idea of a currency board for the time being. 

 Mar 26 - The Jakarta post reports that unemployment has risen to about 8.7 million people, or 10 percent of the workforce. 

 Mar 27 - Indonesia proposes to the IMF a formula to resolve its huge private debt, drawing on the Mexican "Ficorca" model. 

 Apr 2 - IMF and Indonesia agree new figures for the fiscal 1998/99 budget, including a decline of five percent in GDP, inflation of 45 percent and a budget deficit of 3.5 percent. IMF warns Suharto to show commitment on tough reforms or lose its support. 

 Apr 4 - Government suspends licences of seven banks. Seven other banks placed under the supervision of the Indonesian Bank Restructuring Agency. Suharto relatives and friends are known to control some of them, or hold large equity stakes. 

 Apr 6 - Finance Minster Faud Bawazier says the government will set up two state companies to handle the assets of liquidated banks and insure depositors. 

 Apr 8 - The IMF says a new agreement on economic reforms will be closely monitored. Indonesia revises its fiscal 1998/99 (April 1) economic growth expectation to minus four percent and its expected budget deficit to 3.2 percent of GDP. It forecasts inflation for the fiscal year of 17 percent. 

 Apr 16 - Indonesia reaches a framework agreement with banks over corporate debts. 

 Apr 22 - Indonesia announces it has met all reform deadlines agreed with the IMF. The rupiah rises to 7,800. 

 May 4 - IMF resumes its stalled lending programme to Indonesia with payment of a $1 billion instalment. 

 May 5 - Riots break out in the Sumatran city of Medan. The violence over several days results in at least six deaths. 

 May 13 - Riots spread to Jakarta and the shooting of at least four student protesters there pushes the rupiah to around 10,000. 

 May 14 - Savage rioting engulfs Jakarta. Suharto cuts short a state visit to Egypt. Later estimates put the total dead at around 1,200. 

 May 16 - Suharto announces plans to reshuffle cabinet. 

 May 18 - Rupiah trading resumes, quoted at 12,600. 

 May 19 - Thousands of students occupy parliament. Suharto says he will step down after seeing through constitutional reforms. 

 May 20 - The IMF says it will not be paying its next $1 billion instalment on June 4. 

 May 21 - President Suharto resigns after 32 years in power. Vice President Habibie sworn in as president. 

 May 30 - IMF's Hubert Neiss concludes four days of talks with Indonesian officials. Neiss says he has no reason to doubt economists' forecasts the Indonesian economy could contract by 10 percent or more in 1998. 

 Jun 4 - International banks agree to reschedule Indonesia's corporate debt mountain of some $80 billion. 

 June 15 - The rupiah trades at around 14,700. Neiss says the target of 6,000 will be reset. 

 June 23 - Bank Indonesia says that in the third week of June it had continued to meet IMF performance criteria.

title: Bk Indonesia To Provide Dlrs For Trade Financing Arrears
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's central bank will provide U.S. dollars to Indonesian banks, who will settle their trade financing arrears this month in order to mitigate the upward pressure on the dollar, Bank Indonesia Syahril Sabirin said Wednesday. 

 Syahril made the statement to answer a question if Bank Indonesia will intervene to boost the plummeting rupiah. 

 The rupiah has been falling more than 16% since Tuesday as local banks have to pay their interbank debt and trade financing arrears by a new June 26 deadline. The arrears amounted to an estimated $800 million. 

 "As long as the dollar is needed for trade financing, the central bank will provide the currency to the banks," said Syahril. "That is how we intervene in the market." 

 He, however, did not elaborate how Bank Indonesia will provide the dollars to banks. 

 Bankers have suggested that Bank Indonesia provide the dollars through swap facilities. 

 Bank Indonesia has said earlier that it will take over the payment of the arrears if banks are unable to do so.

title: Chronology of the Asian financial crisis.
text:
SINGAPORE, June 12 (Reuters) - The following is a chronology of Asia's financial crisis. 

 1997 

 July 2 - After a failed defence of the Thai baht, Bangkok floats its currency and calls on the IMF for "technical assistance". 

 The baht is effectively devalued by about 15-20 percent. 

 July 8 - Malaysia's central Bank Negara has to intervene aggressively to defend the ringgit. 

 In Indonesia, the rupiah starts to crumble. 

 July 11 - Philippine peso effectively devalued. 

 July 14 - The IMF offers the Philippines almost $1.1 billion in financial support. 

 July 24 - Asian currency meltdown. The rupiah, baht, ringgit and peso slump as confidence in the region deteriorates. 

 August 11 - In Tokyo, the IMF unveils a rescue package for Thailand including loans of $16 billion from the IMF and Asian nations. 

 August 14 - Indonesia abolishes its system of a managed exchange rate. The rupiah plunges. 

 August 20 - IMF approves a $3.9 billion credit for Thailand. Brunei later adds $500 million to the bail-out package, bringing it to $17.2 billion. 

 Sept 20 - Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad tells delegates of IMF/World Bank conference in Hong Kong that currency trading is immoral. 

 Oct 8 - Indonesia says it will ask the IMF for financial assistance. 

 Oct 20-23 - The Hong Kong stock market suffers its heaviest drubbing ever, shedding nearly a quarter of its value in four days on uncertainty over the Hong Kong dollar. 

 Around this time the South Korean won also begins to slump in value. 

 Oct 27 - Asian jitters spill over on to world stock markets. The Dow plunges 554 points, its largest single-day point loss ever. 

 Oct 31 - Indonesia's IMF package is unveiled. It provides for as much as $40 billion in aid, although the front-line defence is $23 billion. 

 Nov 1 - Indonesia shuts down 16 troubled banks. 

 Nov 5 - IMF approves a $10 billion loan for Indonesia as part of the massive international package. 

 Nov 17 - Korea abandons its defence of the won, which rapidly falls to 1,000 to the dollar. 

 Dec 4 - IMF approves a $21 billion loan for South Korea, part of a bail-out package that will total nearly $60 billion. 

 Dec 8 - Thailand closes 56 of 58 previously suspended finance companies. 

 1998 

 Jan 8 - Representatives of the IMF and South Korea agree to a 90-day rollover of short-term debt. 

 Jan 12 - Peregrine, one of Asia's largest independent investment banks, collapses under a mountain of bad loans to Indonesian borrowers. Shares fall sharply in Hong Kong, China and Singapore. 

 Jan 15 - IMF managing director Michel Camdessus and President Suharto sign an agreement strengthening economic reforms. 

 Jan 22 - The rupiah collapses. It is dealt at 17,000 to the dollar at one stage. Bank Indonesia intervenes and drives the currency back to end at 11,800. 

 Jan 27 - Indonesia announces a temporary freeze on debt servicing. 

 Jan 28 - International creditor banks and the South Korean government say they have agreed on a plan to exchange $24 billion of short-term debt for new loans maturing in one, two and three years. 

 Jan 30 - U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan warns Asia's financial crisis could spread. 

 Feb 14 - The IMF threatens to cut off the bail-out fund for Indonesia over its plans to introduce a currency board. 

 Feb 26 - Indonesia's borrowers and lenders begin negotiations on rescheduling at least $70 billion in private off-shore debt. 

 March 1 - Suharto says reforms prescribed by the IMF have not worked. 

 March 4 - The IMF approves release of the third tranche payment from Thailand's package and commends the Thai government for its economic reforms. 

 March 6 - IMF says its board will not discuss Indonesia's economic reform programme before April, effectively delaying a $3 billion payment initially expected by March 15. 

 March 23 - Indonesia nearly doubles interest rates to boost the rupiah and control inflation. 

 April 1 - Japan begins steps aimed at liberalising its financial markets to make them "free, fair and global" by 2001. Tokyo share prices fall, the yen dips and Japan's central bank governor pronounces every economic indicator bad. 

 April 2 - The chairman of electronics giant Sony, Norio Ohga, says the Japanese economy is on the verge of collapse. 

 April 3 - U.S. ratings agency Moody's lowers its outlook on Japan's sovereign debt to negative from stable. Asian currencies fall sharply on the news. 

 May 7 - Fears that riots in the Indonesian city of Medan will spill over into a wider social crisis send regional stocks into retreat. 

 May 11 - India stuns the world with announcement of three underground nuclear tests. Pakistan stocks tumble 3.52 percent while India's National Stock Exchange index slides 2.55 percent. 

 May 13 - The United States imposes economic sanctions on India and Japan suspends some loans. 

 May 14 - Mobs rampage through Jakarta and students demand Suharto's resignation. Indonesia's worsening crisis takes centre-stage for Asian markets, several of which suffer sharp losses. 

 May 15 - Suharto returns home from Egypt amid signs he is losing his 32-year grip on power. 

 May 21 - Suharto steps down and is succeeded by former deputy president B.J. Habibie. Markets enjoy a limited rally. Jakarta stocks surge more than three percent. 

 May 25 - South Korean shares plummet 6.78 percent despite a lifting of foreign ownership limits on stocks. Most other Asian markets shrug off Seoul's fall. 

 May 26 - Seoul's KOSPI share index continues to dive, losing a further six percent, hurt by a looming recession and labour unrest. 

 May 27 - Asian markets are hammered as the yen falls against the dollar and amid mounting fears of economic recession. Hong Kong stocks plunge more than five percent after Chief Executive Tung Chee Hwa warns of possible recession. 

 May 28 - Pakistan conducts nuclear tests. 

 May 29 - The dollar rockets to a seven-year high of 139 yen on fears of a possible nuclear arms race in Asia and after news that Japan's unemployment rate hit 4.1 percent in April, its highest level since the end of World War Two. 

 Recession looms in much of Asia. Hong Kong reports that its gross domestic product contracted two percent in first quarter of 1998. About the same time Indonesia and Malaysia also report their economies contracted in the first quarter. 

 June 1 - Pakistani stocks plunge 12.38 percent as traders get their first chance to react to sanctions imposed after the country's nuclear tests. Asian markets are hit as nuclear tension adds to a cocktail of domestic problems. 

 June 5 - International lenders and Indonesian companies reach a deal to reschedule the country's massive corporate debt. 

 June 8 - The yen falls past 140 to the dollar, sending a shudder through Asian markets. Signs that Japan and other leading economies are unlikely to intervene to support the unit sap confidence further. 

 June 10 - China's central bank governor warns that the weak yen is having a severe impact on Beijing's foreign trade, raising fears that China may devalue its yuan currency. Markets across Asia tumble, led by a near five percent fall on Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index. 

 In Taiwan, the local dollar hits new 11-year lows and the Australian dollar plummets past 59 U.S. cents. 

 June 11 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin all but rules out the possibility of joint intervention by major industrial powers to bolster the yen. He says the weak yen reflects the state of the Japanese economy. 

 June 12 - Economic Planning Agency says Japan's gross domestic product fell by an annualised rate of 5.3 percent in the first quarter, signalling recession. The yen dives towards 145 to the dollar as hopes fade of official intervention. 

 (C) Reuters Limited 1998.

title: Japan reserve policy won't soon be altered by euro.
text:
TOKYO, May 11 (Reuters) - Despite euphoria at the impending birth of the euro, Japan's monetary authorities say they do not intend to jump at the chance to boost holdings of the new European currency soon after its debut in January 1999. 

 Japan, holder of the world's largest foreign reserves, is cautious about making snap decisions to reshuffle components of its reserves, now denominated in U.S. dollars. 

 "The euro will be officially launched with 11 European nations. However, there's much uncertainty along the way as to how the euro will fare, what character it will possess and how the unified European financial market will look," said a senior official at the Ministry of Finance. 

 "Japan will take steps after all these factors become clearer," he said. 

 The European Union (EU) held a landmark summit on May 1 and 2 in Brussels, agreeing to launch the single currency in January 1999 with 11 members, and appointing the first president of the European Central Bank (ECB). 

 One monetary source said sound macroeconomic policy in European nations would be in the interests of the Japanese government, while integrated European financial markets free from currency risks could benefit Japanese firms operating there. 

 But he and analysts said there was uncertainty over whether tight monetary and fiscal policy by European nations would be maintained in concert after the euro was introduced. 

 Germany and the Netherlands could favor tight monetary policies, while Spain and Italy may not accept them, depending on the economic situation. 

 Still, some foreign central banks already see the euro in a positive light. Taiwan's central bank said last week it would shift one billion marks into euro holdings immediately after it was launched. 

 Japanese private investors have been shifting some investment into European bonds and equities in the belief that the euro will have a smooth launch, while trying to avoid excessive exposure to U.S. asset markets, currency dealers said. 

 Regarding the possibility of Japanese authorities' increasing euro holdings, however, Taisuke Tanaka, strategist of global foreign exchange at Credit Suisse said: "In the short-term period it isn't possible. But on a long-term horizon it is." 

 Some monetary sources agreed. 

 "If Japan comes to realise that stabilising the euro is important to the stability of the yen, Japan would hold it or increase euro holdings to prepare for cases of concerted currency intervention," said the monetary source. 

 Analysts estimated over 90 percent of Japan's $205.758 billion reserves outstanding was denominated in U.S. dollars, and the rest was in European currencies such as the mark and sterling. 

 Japan also began holding the Indonesia rupiah last November as a result of concerted intervention with the Monetary Authority of Singapore and Bank Indonesia. 

 The action, aimed at propping up the value of the rupiah against the dollar, was based on Japanese authorities' judgment that Asian currency stability would be important to Japan's economy and firms operating there, monetary officials said. 

 Some analysts said European currency holdings by the Finance Ministry were likely to be converted into the euro automatically after 1999. 

 But most said no shift to the euro at the expense of the dollar would take place because of wider economic and political relations with the United States. 

 Credit Suisse's Tanaka said: "Besides economic relations with the United States, political incentives could influence Japan to hold the bulk of reserves in the dollar." ((Tokyo Treasury Desk +81-3 3432 1396 tokyo.newsroom@reuters.com)).

title: Indonesia Boosts Interest Rates, But  Currency  Continues To Plunge
text:
JAKARTA, Indonesia -(Dow Jones)- Bank Indonesia Governor Sjahril Sabirin announced an across-the-board increase in interest rates Thursday to boost the nation's currency, but the rupiah failed to respond amid a wave of selling prompted by fears of escalating social unrest. 

 Sabirin said the rate increase was meant "to support the rupiah and to curb inflation, which remains high." Following the announcement, overnight lending rates were increased to 48% from 44%; two-day rates to 49% from 45%; and three-to-six-day rates to 50% from 46%. 

 The move came in the face of massive unrest over government-mandated price increases as part of an International Monetary Fund bailout of the Indonesian economy. Fears that rioting that resulted in six deaths in the city of Medan Wednesday would worsen were mostly to blame for a plunge in the rupiah to 9,620 rupiah to the dollar Thursday from Wednesday's close of 9,050. 

 The IMF, which is overseeing a vital bailout package for Indonesia, forced the government to slash generous subsidies on food, fuel and other necessities that have aided poor Indonesians for years. Thousands of people protested by burning cars, tossing rocks at police and attacking hundreds of Chinese-owned stores. 

 Stocks, meanwhile, climbed 5.3% on the Jakarta Stock Exchange following their 4.7% plunge Wednesday. Analysts attributed the increase to arbitrage buying in telecommunications stocks. 

 The IMF disbursed $1 billion in aid to the Indonesian government Monday. Originally, the agency had planned to disburse $3 billion in aid in mid-March but suspended the program during a protracted fight with Indonesian authorities. Now, the remaining $2 billion will be disbursed over the next two months if Indonesia demonstrates its will to comply with the program. 

 The IMF program will free up other loans for the battered Indonesian economy, which began to unravel with the collapse of the rupiah last August. The World Bank and Asian Development Bank are each expected to approve loans of about $500 million over the next few weeks. 

 Sjahril said the central bank currently believes high interest rates are more effective in stabilizing the rupiah than market intervention. He wouldn't, however, rule out intervening in the market in the future. 

 Bank Indonesia's director Miranda Gultom added that despite of criticisms on the effectiveness of the rate rise to support the rupiah, the last rate rise in April enticed capital inflows. It showed by the fact that that the value of government securities purchased by foreigners rose to 14.3 trillion rupiah as of April 30 compared to only 1.9 trillion rupiah April 1, Miranda added. 

 Meanwhile, the country's military commander said his troops are forming a team to assist in the advancement of the International Monetary Fund-backed economic program, although he stated that any reforms would be implemented "gradually and constitutionally." The army also sent reinforcements to the riot-torn city of Medan, and offered an olive branch to protesting Indonesian students. 

 Armed Forces General Commander Wiranto stated that the head of the military's faction in parliament, Syarwan Hamid, will be appointed to lead the team which that will be charged with advancing reforms. He also said that the body will include the military's general chief of staff, Fachrul Razi. 

 Meanwhile, Wiranto urged student activists to desist from taking protests off campus for fear of "hurting national stability." He instead invited the students serve as a moral and intellectual force in support of reform. 

 The commander also said the military would establish a framework to put economic and political reforms on the national agenda, an apparent concession to student groups that have been calling for political change.

title: Emerging market  forex -Rupiah dives, zloty in check.
text:
LONDON, May 6 (Reuters) - The Indonesian rupiah continued its tumble to a six-week low in European trade on Wednesday while analysts looked to possible central bank action as the unit approached 9,000 on the dollar. 

 Alarm at increased rioting in the northern Sumatran city of Medan wiped out earlier optimism about the country following International Monetary Fund approval of a $1.0 billion loan earlier in the week. 

 "Unless the civil violence dies down the rupiah could go back to 10,000," said Roger Francis, senior analyst emerging markets at IBJ International. 

 "But I think the situation may be better than the currency markets suggest...People are worried that it will snowball but there's a better than even chance that it won't." 

 Mitul Kotecha, treasury economist at Standard Chartered, said the market was eyeing the 9,000 level in the short term. 

 "I think 9,000 is a key level at which you would expect some kind of resistance from the central bank," he said. 

 "The focus is still to use monetary policy so if you would probably see rates firm up to defend the rupiah rather than any intervention through the foreign exchange market." 

 Shockwaves from Indonesia took their toll on other regional currencies with Malaysia's ringgit a notable casualty, further weakened by comments from Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad on a possible cut in rates. 

 South Korea's won was also punished as stocks tumbled amid threats of an all-out strike by the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions late in May or early in June unless the government guaranteed job security. 

 Analysts said the downside for the won appeared limited given the strong turnaround in South Korea's external position. 

 In Eastern Europe, the authorities struggled once again to cap a rampant zloty, intervening to buy both dollars and marks. 

 "The authorities don't want the zloty to appreciate too fast but I still think it is going to push higher eventually, especially after those comments yesterday by Dabrowski, though I doubt everyone on the board shares his very strong views," said Jesper Dannesboe, currency trader at ABN AMRO in London. 

 Marek Dabrowski, a member of the central bank's 10-member decision-making monetary council, said on Tuesday the zloty's crawling peg devaluation rate was too fast to reach this year's inflation target. 

 "Our strategy is still to buy the zloty on any dips, based on the very strong fundamentals and the fact that the council is still focusing on inflation." 

 The Czech crown was weaker as foreigners lightened exposure, wary of central bank intervention following comments from Finance Minister Ivan Pilip on Tuesday that the current level of the unit did not reflect the economic situation.

title: Indonesia Min-2: No Net Rupiah Creation Via Domestic Ops
text:
JAKARTA (Dow Jones)--Indonesia's top economics minister pledged that the country's central bank won't intervene in the market to support the rupiah. 

 Ginanadjar Kartasasmita, coordinating minister for the economy, finance and industry, told Dow Jones Newswrires Friday that Bank Indonesia 'will not risk its international reserves speculating in the foreign exchange market.' 

 The minister, who negotiating Indonesia's latest agreement with the International Monetary Fund, said that last year 'we bled ourselves of $10 billion (in reserves) to intervene, without any success.' 

 Ginandjar said the rupiah has strengthened considerably since early March 'without any central bank intervention', which he says reflects better sentiment about Indonesia and belief it will seriously undertake reform. Many bankers, however, say they believe it's Indonesia's high interest rates that have contributed the most to strengthening the rupiah from around IDR10,000 in early March. 

 He also said the central bank won't 'create new rupiah' in net terms through its domestic operations. Many bankers have expressed concern that Bank Indonesia has pumped tens of trillions of rupiah into Indonesian banks since last year to support the country's battered banking sector.

title: Indonesia says reserves not hurt by rupiah fall.
text:
JAKARTA, July 9 (Reuter) - Indonesia's central bank governor said on Tuesday that the country's foreign exchange reserves were not hurt by last week's fall in the rupiah on concerns over President Suharto's health. 

 "The recent speculation has not had any impact on our foreign exchange reserves. Total trading last Thursday was relatively small," Governor Sudradjad Djiwandono told reporters. 

 The rupiah plunged to a year-low of 2,349 to the dollar on Thursday following unfounded rumours that Suharto had suffered a heart attack. 

 It has since stabilised and was trading at 2,339.00 on Tuesday afternoon. The government has said Suharto is in good health but is currently in Germany for three days of medical checks which are slated to begin today. 

 The central bank did not intervene in the market despite the fall, because even after the drop the rupiah was well within the bank's intervention band, Sudradjad said. 

 He added that Bank Indonesia will continue its prudent policies to maintain the confidence of foreign investors in the country's economy. 

 Official sources said last week Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves had risen to $16.483 billion in June from $15.914 billion in May. 

 "What Bank Indonesia can do is continuously show our macro- economic consistency. We will continue our prudent monetary policy, including controlling inflation and the dollar-rupiah exchange rate," Sudradjad said. 

 He said those steps in addition to a prudent loan policy and foreign exchange reserve management would lead to a healthy current account. 

 Sudradjad also said Bank Indonesia has taken steps to curb fluctuations in the exchange rate, including maintaining relatively large reserves and coordinating action with other central banks. 

 Earlier, speaking at the opening of an international seminar on the 50th anniversary of Bank BNI 1946, Sudradjad said restructuring the banking industry was a high priority of the central bank. 

 "We will continue to encourage banks to merge as a part of restructuring. The mergers between banks are likely to increase their competitiveness," he said.

JAKARTA (AP-Dow Jones)--Indonesia's rupiah is flat versus the U.S. dollar in extremely slow trading early Tuesday as the market waits for market-moving news in an amply liquid market, dealers said. 

 Analysts also say that the market has accommodated itself to the new currency trading band unveiled Thursday by Bank Indonesia, the central bank. The intervention band was widened to 118 rupiah from 66 rupiah, and its conversion band was widened to 46 rupiah from 44. 

 The U.S. dollar is being bought at 2,322.37 rupiah in the spot market at 0319 GMT Tuesday after starting the day at 2,322.50 rupiah. 

 'It is a very dull in the market today, with nothing moving the spot or forward markets either way,' said a dealer at a foreign bank. 'Yesterday's liquidity was tight, so the dollar has moved up a bit on improved conditions, but outside of that there's nothing.' 

 Because of this languid environment, traders see the dollar trading in an extremely tight range of between 2,322 rupiah and 2,323 rupiah Tuesday. 

 Dealers say, however, that the dollar should move up a bit later in the week as people seek dollar-funding to pay off overseas obligations.

title: Indonesia moves to curb capital inflow.
text:
JAKARTA, June 14 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah surged against the U.S. currency after the central bank widened its dollar-rupiah trading band in an attempt to stem the inflow of speculative funds, currency dealers said on Friday. 

 But they were unsure whether the move was potent enough because highly attractive domestic interest rates could continue to be a magnet for foreign funds. 

 Bank Indonesia on Thursday widened its dollar-rupiah intervention band to 118 rupiah or five percent at 2,315/2,433 rupiah to the dollar from 66 rupiah or three percent. 

 The central bank intervenes in the foreign exchange market when the exchange rate goes outside the parameters. 

 "The central bank is wise to widen it now. It shows the rupiah market is getting more and more mature, which allows the market to decide the exchange rate," Edwin Png, chief treasurer of Bank of America in Jakarta told Reuters. 

 The move took the market by surprise and sent the dollar tumbling even though the broadening had been long-expected by players because of bullish sentiment on the rupiah. 

 "The market has become more mature as of yesterday. There was some support (for the dollar) and operators did not sell the dollar down to central bank's base rate," Png said. 

 "The market forces somehow determined what is the best exchange rate. That is a good sign," he added. 

 Bank Indonesia said the move was aimed at curbing the inflow of speculative funds and increasing its monetary control. 

 The central bank was forced to absorb dollars, estimated at a total of some $800 million, from the market three times in the past two weeks after the dollar hit its floor rate. 

 Economists said the absorption induced fresh rupiah supply which threatened the central bank's broad M2 money supply aggregate, which is targeted to grow 17 percent for 1996/97 (April-March) fiscal year. 

 M2 year-on-year growth in April was 30 percent. 

Currency dealers were unsure whether the band move would help reduce short-term inflows as interest rate differentials between the dollar and the rupiah were in favour of the local currency. 

 Pardy Kendy, chief treasurer of PT Bank Buana Indonesia, said the central bank was caught in the dilemma of controlling money supply growth while narrowing interest rate differentials. 

Currency dealers said the rupiah offered some 2.5 percent gains for investors, assuming the interest rate differential of the rupiah to the dollar at about eight percent and a rupiah depreciation of around 5.5 percent annually. 

 "It's a fantastic amount," Kendy said. 

 He said interest rate cuts to narrow the difference would be difficult because it would trigger another round of credit growth which the bank was now trying to control. 

 "It's a difficult dilemma. The central bank has to reduce short-term capital inflows while bringing the money supply down to an acceptable level," Kendy said. 

 Economists had suggested the possibility of a hike in the reserve requirement rate to curb money supply growth. 

 But Kendy said a hike in the reserve rate would invite further capital inflows because of higher interest rates, although it may help tighten credit growth. 

 "It's not an easy job. It's not to be envied," one said.

title: Bank Indonesia widens dollar-rupiah trading band.
text:
JAKARTA, June 13 (Reuter) - Indonesia's central bank, Bank Indonesia, said on Thursday it had widened the dollar-rupiah intervention band to 118 rupiah, or five percent, from 66 rupiah or three percent previously. 

 The central bank said the conversion band remained unchanged at two percent, or 46 rupiah. 

 "To increase the effectivity of monetary management and to maintain foreign exchange rate due to rising capital flows it is necessary to proceed with the policy," the bank said in a statement. 

 It said the domestic foreign exchange market should be able to accomodate supply and demand from local and overseas. 

 "This should reduce pressure on the country's foreign exchange reserves and should help increase monetary stability and foreign reserves," the bank said. 

 The new intervention band was at 2,315/2,433 rupiah to the dollar, and the conversion band was fixed at 2,315.0/2,361.0. 

 The central bank intervenes in foreign exchange markets if the exchange rate goes outside the perimeters. 

 The central bank said the managed floating rate of the rupiah through a basket of currencies will be maintained. 

 The rupiah rose sharply against the dollar after the central bank broadened its intervention band. 

 Dealers said the rupiah touched a high of 2,320.0 from 2,336.0 before the dollar managed to rebound to 2,327.5/28.0 late in the afternoon. 

 One U.S. bank dealer said the move had surprised the market although it had been widely anticipated. 

 "There was no quote immediately after the widening. The dollar suddenly tumbled to 2,330 and fell all the way down to a low 2,320.0," one European bank dealer said. 

 "Operators keep saying 'yours' all the time whatever price you quoted. It'a a bit drastic," he added. 

 However, he said the dollar rebounded gradually and could stabilise at around the 2,327/28.0 level. 

 One U.S. bank dealer said it was not clear where the rate would head on Friday, but the liquidity condition could become the factor to look at in the short-term. 

 The fall of the dollar after the broadening of the band was in line with market expectations because the market was bullish on the rupiah before the long-anticipated move was realised.

title: Indonesian economy seen gaining confidence.
text:
JAKARTA, June 4 (Reuter) - Indonesian money supply has risen above the central bank's target, while inflation remains under control, indicating increased confidence in the fast-developing economy, economists said on Tuesday. 

 But they said an overshooting of money aggregates might strengthen market speculation of an imminent central bank move to widen its dollar-rupiah intervention band. 

 Economists said foreign investors were pouring money into the country, which expects economic growth of around seven percent this year, against 8.07 percent in 1995. 

 "It comes as no surprise to us. It's an unwritten approval that investors have confidence in the economy," JP Morgan economist Vincent Low told Reuters. 

 Indonesia's consumer price index for May was expected to rise by between 0.05 and 0.07 percent, against 0.78 percent in April, banking sources told Reuters. 

 Year-on-year inflation in April was 7.95 percent, against 8.86 percent in March 1996, and 10.02 percent in April 1995. 

 Economists attributed the decrease to an easing in prices of key consumer goods, after the first quarter index was hit by a rise in public transport fares in March and the Moslem Eid al-Fitr and Chinese Lunar new year holidays in February. 

 They said that year-on-year growth of the broad money aggregate, M2, was 30 percent in April, against 28 percent in March. 

Central bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said last month that M2 growth needed to be curbed. Indonesia aims for M2 growth of 17 percent for 1996/97 (April-March). 

 "I think it's suggesting that our economy is growing at a fast pace, reflected by rising M2. It seems other indicators are under control," Pardi Kendy, chief treasurer of PT Bank Buana Indonesia, told Reuters. 

 "I believe the money supplies were being driven by two sources, official foreign reserves and loans growth," JP Morgan's Low said. 

 Economists said rising foreign capital inflow, both short and longer-term, seemed to have helped boost reserves. 

 Short-term inflow was driven by an attractive interest rate differential offered by the rupiah, while the longer-term inflow came from soaring foreign investments as confidence in the economy continued to grow. 

 "Official foreign reserves have been rising quite quickly. It's a pretty rapid reserve accumulation," Low said. 

 Indonesia's foreign exchange reserves rose steadily to $15.961 billion in April from $14.789 billion in January. 

 "What you see in the reserve figure is also being reflected in the strength of the rupiah. It's trading at a very strong end of the central bank's (intervention) band," Low said. 

 One senior economist suggested the central bank might again widen the intervention band for dollar-rupiah trading, having broadened it to three percent last December. 

 The rupiah was quoted at 2,332.75 to the dollar on Tuesday. 

 The World Bank said in its latest report on Indonesia that higher reserve requirements and a wider intervention band could increase the effectiveness of monetary policy. 

 The intervention band allows the central bank to intervene in the foreign exchange market if market rates move out of the range. 

 One currency dealer said the central bank might have to widen the band. Otherwise, it would have to absorb dollars from the market, which would in turn induce fresh inflows.

title: Indonesia seen squeezing money supply growth.
text:
JAKARTA, May 30 (Reuter) - Indonesia's central bank may broaden its dollar-rupiah intervention band and raise reserve requirements for banks to clamp down on money supply growth, economists said on Thursday. 

 One economist said Bank Indonesia, the central bank, might move again to widen the intervention band for dollar-rupiah trading after broadening it to three percent, or 66 points (rupiah to the dollar), last December. 

 The bank can intervene in the foreign exchange market when market rates move out of the range the bank fixes on a daily basis. 

 The economist said the central bank might also consider raising the reserve requirement, last raised in February to three percent from two percent, to curtail new loans. 

 JP Morgan said in its May report that Bank Indonesia would probably attempt to restrict credit through regulatory measures and a further increase in the reserve requirement. 

 "I think the central bank may have to take action on the band again. But I don't know when," the economist said. There was no official comment from the bank. 

 "There is a distinct possibility the band will be widened. It will be good for the central bank to take some steam off the market," said Winston Koh, of JP Morgan in Singapore. 

 Koh said a wider band was in line with Bank Indonesia's policy that the dollar-rupiah rate moved toward a free-float within the band itself. 

Central bank governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said last week that the growth of M2 money supply needed to be curbed. 

 Djiwandono said that although growth in M1 showed indications of slowing since the third quarter of 1995, broad M2 money supply remained high. M2 growth was 26.79 percent in the year to February 1996, compared with 28.04 percent in the year to November 1995. 

 The 1996/97 (April-March) state budget set an M2 growth target of 17 percent. 

 Djiwandono said strong credit demand was responsible for high M2 growth. 

 Dealers said high domestic interest rates had attracted capital inflow, which had complicated monetary management and kept the dollar under pressure for several months. 

 "The central bank may have to widen the band because otherwise it has to absorb dollars from the market, which could undermine its money supply target. Dollar-buying will induce fresh funds in the market," one dealer said. 

 He said the band might be broadened before a rise in the reserve rate because Bank Indonesia might wait to see the full impact of February's reserve increase. 

 Dealers said speculation about a possible change in the band would put the dollar under further pressure in anticipation that the U.S. currency might continue easing within a broader band. 

 They said the dollar had softened in response to past widenings of the band. 

 "It's just a question of time when the central bank will be forced to absorb dollars from the market, because sentiment on the rupiah has been strong. It could be the right timing again," one dealer said. 

 The central bank's intervention band on Thursday was fixed at 2,331.0/2,397 and the conversion rate at 2,331.0/2,375.0.

 Late Monday Bank Indonesia raised its intervention band by one rupiah and became 2,330 rupiah - 2,396 rupiah. Banks can sell the dollar to Bank Indonesia if it touches 2,330 rupiah. It usually happens if banks desperately need the local currency. 

 Yayang Wijaya at PT Bank Mitsubishi Buana, however, sees no urgency for banks at the moment to sell the dollar to Bank Indonesia as in fact rupiah supply early Tuesday was still sufficient. 

 Because of those two reasons, the dollar is seen trapped Tuesday between support level of 2,330.50 rupiah and resistance level of 2,332 rupiah.

title: Rupiah edges down on ample Jakarta money market.
text:

 They said operators were well prepared to face the last trading days before heading for a long weekend and the first day of the new reserve requirement rate. 

 "The market was flooded with rupiah while lacking dollars, causing the value of today dollars to jump," one European bank dealer said, adding that light panic was seen after opening. 

 He said Singapore players were seen buying today dollars up to a high of 2,299.0 before they settled at 2,296.50/97.25. 

 Dealers attributed the excess rupiah supply to the maturing central bank securities (SBIs) and at least $500 million of maturing spot dollars sold to the central bank last Wednesday.

 "You can see how liquid is the market now," he said. 

 However, operators shortage of dollars could not utilise the incredibly low swap premiums and were hit by relatively expensive overnight rate in the money market, he said.

title: Indonesia  sets  intervention  band for  forex  trading.
text:
JAKARTA, Dec 29 (Reuter) - Indonesia's central bank announced a new intervention band for dollar-rupiah trading on Friday aimed at increasing the effectiveness of monetary controls and maintaining a stable exchange rate. 

 Bank Indonesia set a new band of three percent or 66 points (rupiah to the dollar) which would allow it to intervene in the foreign exchange market when the market rate moves 1.5 percent up or down. 

 "To improve the effectiveness of monetary control and the stability of the exchange rate in order to anticipate future growth of capital flow, we see the need to further develop the foreign exchange market," Paul Soetopo, managing director of Bank Indonesia, told a news conference. 

 Soetopo said the move was also aimed at reducing pressure on the government's foreign exchange reserves. The rupiah strengthened to 2,284.0/89.0 to the dollar from Thursday's closing at 2,291.50/92.0 in the Singapore market, currency dealers said. 

 "The managed floating system which is based on a basket of currencies and has become the central mechanism to calculate the exchange rate of the rupiah will be maintained," he said. 

 He said the conversion rate band of two percent - one percent up or down - or 44 points, fixed by Bank Indonesia on a daily basis, remained unchanged. 

 The central bank's dollar conversion rate on Friday was fixed at 2,286/2,330 to the rupiah. 

 A Bank Indonesia official told Reuters the new intervention band would be the range which allows banks to buy or sell dollars with the central bank. 

 But the central bank has the authority to intervene in the foreign exchange market at any time, even when the dollar-rupiah rate was within the intervention band. 

 The conversion rate is the rate for export drafts and other transactions with government bodies. 

 The official said the central bank would consider on a case-by-case basis when commercial banks wanted to buy/sell dollars with Bank Indonesia when the market rate was within the zone between the conversion and intervention bands. 

 Bank Indonesia said it will announce the conversion and the intervention rates at 3.00 p.m. (0800 GMT) every trading day. 

 Soetopo also announced on Friday a set of measures to regulate derivatives trading. Soetopo said the rules, effective from Friday, permit banks to carry out derivatives transactions related only to foreign exchange and interest rates. 

 "Derivatives transactions in shares would be approved by the central bank on a case-by-case basis," he said. 

 He said derivatives trading should be based on healthy and prudent principles and such trades must be approved by banks' board of commissioners and directors. 

 Soetopo said maximum loss exposure should not exceed 10 percent of a bank's capital while derivatives trading resulting from a customer's order could cover up to 10 times his margin deposits placed with a bank. 

 He said banks are also obliged to give a detailed explanation of the risks involved in derivatives trading. 

 The central bank had widened the spread of dollar buying/selling four times since 1992. 

 It said the moves had helped develop the domestic foreign exchange market and reduced the dependency on the central bank. 

 The central bank said foreign exchange trading volume has risen to $4.6 billion a day in 1995, compared with $2.7 billion daily in 1992 while transactions with Bank Indonesia declined to $24 million a day from $37 million in the same period.

If Bank Indonesia continues to weaken the rupiah through its fixing, but the rupiah remains strong in the spot market in November and December, the dollar could fall through the bottom of the trading band and prompt Bank Indonesia to intervene, dealers say, as it has in the past. In December 1994, Bank Indonesia entered the currency market and bought dollars to accelerate the rupiah depreciation. 

 The question being asked in foreign exchange desks in Jakarta and the region is: will currency markets go along with the depreciation of the rupiah? And if monetary authorities want a weaker rupiah, when will they start to push down the rupiah fixing? 

 Daniel Lian, a regional economist with NatWest Markets in Singapore, believes currency players have no choice but to go along with a central-bank induced depreciation. Bank Indonesia will get its way and depreciate the rupiah versus the dollar by 5% this year, Lian said. 

 'If Bank Indonesia raises the (dollar) fixing, I don't think people will bet on the rupiah and try to get in the way of depreciation,' Lian said. 

 However, other currency market players believe the market won't see the rupiah depreciate that much without a fight.

The yen's recent appreciation has been bearish for the rupiah because 40% of Indonesia's $88 billion in total foreign debt is denominated in yen. The markets are afraid Indonesia could be crushed by this burden if the yen rises too much. 

 However, Bank Indonesia sent a message to foreign exchange markets and offshore banks Tuesday it won't allow rumors and speculators to abuse its currency without penalty. 

 It was a marked turnaround from the past three trading days, when Bank Indonesia uncharacteristically ignored the dollar's rise beyond the upper limits of the trading band, which stands between 2,204 rupiah and 2,234 rupiah. The limits are respectively the dollar-selling and dollar-buying rates. 

 Part of the surprise Tuesday was that the central bank chose to pounce on a day when the dollar only touched the top of the range, but didn't break it.

title: Indonesia raises key rate to defend rupiah.
text:
JAKARTA, Jan 16 (Reuter) - Indonesia's central bank, in fresh action following major market intervention last week, hiked key discount rates on Monday to boost the rupiah after earlier fears of a possible Mexican-style devaluation. 

 "We have raised the interest rates of SBPUs for all maturities by half a percentage point," an official told Reuters. 

Currency dealers, who said the move would help support the rupiah, said it was also aimed at stopping players from taking advantage of interest rate differentials. 

 "The move was aimed at preventing banks from taking advantage of the short-term securities (SBPUs) to buy the U.S. currency," one chief dealer with a foreign bank said. 

 One-week money was raised to 15.0 percent from 14.5 percent, two-week money to 15.25 percent from 14.75 percent, and one, three, six and 12-month money to 15.75 from 15.25 percent. 

 Surat Berharga Pasar Uang (SBPUs) are short-term securities bought by the central bank to inject additional liquidity into the banking system. 

 But one money market dealer said the hike was not enough to reduce short-term interest rate differentials between the key discount rates and forward premiums. 

 Value spot dollars were quoted around 2,211.00/12.50 in midday compared with an early high of 2,220 rupiah, but they appeared to be moving in a safe area far below Bank Indonesia's Friday ceiling of 2,188/2,218 rupiah. 

 "The move was positive but players can still utilise central bank facilities to buy dollars because of attractive margins on forward premiums," he said. 

 One-month forward premiums were at 11.5 percent, which if added to the revenue from dollar-deposits at 7.25 percent, were comparable to SBPUs of the same maturity at 15.75 percent, he said. 

 "The central bank could intervene again in the forward market to minimise arbitrage possibilities," he added. 

 The foreign exchange market appeared to have stabilised after Bank Indonesia's strong intervention in the market last week totalling $500 million. This followed earlier strong statements that ruled out any possible devaluation. 

 Bank Indonesia Governor Sudradjad Djiwandono said on Saturday foreign fund managers did not understand the fundamental strength of Indonesia's economy. 

 Their concerns over Indonesia's foreign debt of almost $100 billion also triggered a week-long dumping of the currency. 

 But economists and analysts have said any comparisons with Mexico's current financial crisis are unfair and irrational. 

 Dennis de Tray, director of the World Bank in Jakarta, told Reuters on Saturday that with Indonesia's small current account deficit relative to gross domestic product and with non-oil exports expected to top 15 percent growth this year, the country faced no real challenge in its debt management. 

 The foreign bank chief dealer said there was not much buying interest in dollars on Monday but that a higher closing in New York overnight appeared to have left the market nervous. 

 "The market still has not indicated in which direction the dollar is heading. But at the level people in London and the U.S. are buying I do not mind selling to them," he said. 

 "Volume was thin. We did some (dollar) selling this morning and then the dollar market collapsed," he said. 

 Value spot dollars were quoted around 2,211.00/12.50 at midday compared with an early high of 2,220 rupiah.

title: Indonesia says no plan to reschedule foreign debt.
text:
JAKARTA, Jan 16 (Reuter) - Indonesian President Suharto on Monday said the country has no plan to reschedule its foreign debt, which has hit almost $100 billion and triggered fears of a Mexican-style financial crisis. 

 "We have never thought to reschedule our foreign debt and there is no reason to reschedule it. Our foreign debt is in a safe position," State Secretary Murdiono quoted Suharto as saying when he meet with reporters at the Presidential palace. 

 "Our foreign debt is being handled well," Suharto said. 

 The comments from Suharto, an ex-army general credited with helping rescue Indonesia from near economic chaos after he took over in the late 1960s, coincided with moves by the central bank to hike key discount rates on Monday to boost the rupiah. 

 Indonesia's foreign exchange and stock markets were hit last week by investor nervousness that Indonesia's foreign debt level could trigger a Mexican-style devaluation. 

 The foreign exchange market earlier on Monday appeared to have stabilised after Bank Indonesia's strong intervention in the market last week totalling $500 million. This followed earlier strong statements that ruled out any devaluation. 

 Economists, including the World Bank, believe foreign speculators have ignored the fundamental strength of Indonesia's booming economy. 

 Bankers have said Indonesia's total foreign debt, with less than 50 percent held by the private sector, currently stands at around $95 billion. 

 About 40 percent of the debt is denominated in Japanese yen. Indonesia has never defaulted on or rescheduled its debt payments. 

 Murdiono said Suharto -- believed to pay special attention to Indonesia's foreign debt and inflation rate -- always watched economic developments closely . 

 Murdiono also joined the country's top economic ministers in stressing that Indonesia, Asia's only member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), would not devalue the rupiah. 

 "The government does not see any reason for it (a devaluation). The situation in 1986 is very different. The oil price dropped sharply to below $10 a barrel from $30 at that time. But now it is different," he said. 

 Dealers have said the foreign financial community has painful memories of Indonesia's two devaluations in the 1980s; in 1983 and 1986. 

 Murdiono also said the government was committed to maintaining its free foreign exchange system, which he said was vital to attract badly needed foreign investment. 

 "This has been our policy since the beginning of development. The government is convinced that this is the correct step," he added. 

 Bank Indonesia, the central bank, raised by half a percentage point the interest rate on short-term securities (SBPUs) of all maturities on Monday. 

Currency dealers, who said the move would help support the rupiah, said it was also aimed at stopping players from taking advantage of interest rate differentials. 

 Surat Berharga Pasar Uang (SBPUs) are short-term securities bought by the central bank to inject additional liquidity into the banking system. 

 But one money market dealer said the hike was not enough to reduce short-term interest rate differentials between the key discount rates and forward premiums. 

 "The move was positive but players can still utilise central bank facilities to buy dollars because of attractive margins on forward premiums," he said.

title: Indonesian rupiah withstands foreign pressure.
text:
JAKARTA, Jan 13 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah stabilised against the dollar following concerted central bank action to support the currency on Friday after a week-long attack by offshore banks, dealers said. 

 They said the intervention by Bank Indonesia seemed to have calmed down nervous trading conditions, at least temporarily. 

 "It was a good move from the central bank. Finally it has shown its teeth," one private bank dealer said. 

 The central bank sold spot dollars, outrights and swaps in the market to kill devaluation rumours, dealers said. 

 They said the intervention pulled the dollar down to stabilise at around 2,219/19 rupiah from a day's high of 2,235 rupiah. 

 "The central bank move was quite positive. They want to show foreign speculators that they want to maintain that exchange rate," said an economist who asked not to be named. 

 Other analysts said the week-long dumping of the rupiah was an overreaction which had not been backed by fundamentals. 

 Indonesia's coordinating minister for the economy Saleh Afiff said on Thursday that the rupiah was competitive and ruled out any devaluation. 

 "Foreign fund managers view Asian and Latin American countries together as emerging markets," the economist, who works with a U.S. investment house, told Reuters. 

 "In fact Asia is very different from Latin America. Asia is politically more stable and economic fundamentals are much sounder," he said. 

 "Why compare the two together?" he asked. 

 Other analysts added that Indonesia's current account deficit accounts for only two percent of the gross domestic product. They said the huge debt is not viewed as a problem as long as non-oil exports continue to grow, and provided there are no external shocks. 

 The attack on the rupiah started last Friday in the United States on fears over Indonesia's large foreign debt, but the intensity rose on Wednesday. 

 "The inflow of foreign exchange earnings should be able to repay the debt obligation of interest and principal," the economist said. 

 Dealers who had been waiting for the central bank to move after the dollar rose above the bank's band, welcomed the move saying it would help stabilise the market.

title: FOCUS-Rupiah seen weakening further in short term.
text:
JAKARTA, July 24 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah, which has been volatile after plunging to a record low against the dollar on Monday, is likely to weaken in the short-term despite the country's strong economic fundamentals, economists said on Thursday. 

 They said problems in rolling over corporate debt and contagion from weakness in several regional currencies should push the rupiah toward the lower end of the central bank's intervention band. 

 "I still think we are still firmly in an environment of dollar strength against the regionals," said Desmond Supple, regional currency specialist at BZW Asia in Singapore. 

 "Over the short-term, I would expect to see convergence of spot rupiah and the weaker end of the intervention band. While fundamentally this weakness is not justified, this contagion continues to ensure that the perceptions of fundamentals are more important than the fundamentals themselves." 

 The rupiah opened in Jakarta at 2,575/85 against the dollar on Thursday and by late evening was trading at 2,613 in the spot market. The central bank posted its intervention band at 2,378/2,682. 

 It crashed to a historic low of 2,665 against the dollar on Monday after becoming the latest currency to fall victim to speculative attacks which have plagued the region. 

Central bank intervention brought about a partial recovery on that day, but the currency has been extremely volatile with swings between 2,530 and 2,625 since then. 

 Traders say although the rate has not fallen out of the band, Bank Indonesia, the central bank, has pumped some $700 million into the market. 

 But they add that regional fallout, especially from the Thai baht, has made those efforts apparently futile. 

 UBS Research said in a report that markets would take some time to assess the differences between the fundamentals of the Indonesian and Thai economies. 

 "The baht was attacked because of the perception that the rigid exchange rate regime was inconsistent with sharply dropping economic activity and high domestic interest rates," it said. 

 "Conditions are different in Indonesia, which has a much more flexible foreign exchange system, robust economic activity and ample liquidity in the financial system." 

 But the report cautioned that rupiah weakness would persist for the next three to six months, at least partly because of problems in Indonesian corporate debt. 

 "There is evidence that more Indonesian corporates are facing difficulties in rolling over their maturing foreign liabilities," UBS said, pointing to higher risk premiums and possibly lower credit limits because of falling investor confidence in nations with large current account deficits. 

 "As a result, more Indonesian corporates will have to buy rupiah and convert into foreign currency domestically," it said. "Unless supported by strong intervention from Bank Indonesia, this will add pressure to the rupiah." 

 Over the longer-term, analysts and dealers said 2,550 was fair value for the rupiah. 

 "At the 2,550 level, that's really comfortable," said an analyst with a U.S. bank in Singapore, adding that many fund managers were looking to sell dollars above the 2,600 level. 

 Others said the longer-term view was that strong exports in the second half of the year should bolster the currency, which would then recover to a four-to-five percent guided depreciation trend.

title: Rupiah may weaken on corporate debt problems - UBS.
text:
JAKARTA, July 24 (Reuter) - The Indonesian rupiah, which fell to a historic low against the dollar earlier this week, is likely to come under further pressure as the corporate sector is facing debt problems, UBS Research said on Thursday. 

 "There is evidence that more Indonesian corporates are facing difficulties in rolling over their maturing foreign liabilities," the group said in a report, pointing to higher risk premiums and possibly lower credit limits because of falling investor confidence in nations with large current account deficits. 

 "As a result, more Indonesian corporates will have to buy rupiah and convert into foreign currency domestically," it said. 

 "Unless supported by strong intervention from Bank Indonesia, this will add pressure to the rupiah." 

 The rupiah was volatile on Thursday on a spillover of regional currency weakness. 

 It opened at 2,575/85 to the dollar, plunged to a low of 2,625 and was trading at 2,586 in the late afternoon. 

 On Monday, the rupiah plunged to a historic low of 2,665 to the dollar after a fierce speculative attack but recovered marginally on central bank intervention. 

 UBS said further weakness in the rupiah was likely to continue for the next three to six months. 

 Noting that the weakness was triggered by contagion from the Thai baht, it said: "Markets will take time to correctly assess the fundamental differences between the Indonesian and Thai economies." 

 "The baht was attacked because of the perception that the rigid exchange rate regime was inconsistent with sharply dropping economic activity and high domestic interest rates," UBS said. 

 "Conditions are different in Indonesia, which has a much more flexible foreign exchange system, robust economic activity and ample liquidity in the financial system."

title: Indonesia's Rupiah Lower Late On Regional Bearishness
text:
JAKARTA (AP-Dow Jones)--Indonesia's rupiah closed lower against the U.S. dollar in volatile dealings late Thursday on bearish sentiment over regional currencies, dealers said. 

 The dollar closed at 2,615 rupiah in the spot market, up from Wednesday close at 2,591.50 rupiah. The dollar hit an intraday high of 2,625 rupiah. 

 'The rupiah gained some of its lost ground during the Asian trading session, especially after the Thai baht recovered against the dollar on Bank of Thailand's intervention. But, the rupiah had to give it up when London-based participants entered the market,' said a dealer with a local bank. 

 Some dealers said Bank Indonesia intervened by selling the dollar again Thursday, which helped prop the rupiah up to 2,582.50 rupiah in the spot market. But many dealers did not hear of Bank Indonesia's intervention. 

 'It's probably only a (psychological) war launched to help the rupiah,' a dealer commented. 

 Bank Indonesia refused to comment on its actions. 

 The central bank, however, did openly intervene through the money market by draining 2.1 trillion rupiah out of the system. This was done by selling Sertifikat Bank Indonesia notes. Bank Indonesia also suspended the purchase of Surat Berharga Pasar Uang - money-market notes. 

 As activity was still focused on the spot market, trading on the swap market was quiet Thursday, with swap rates remaining relatively stable, dealers said. 

 Bank Indonesia left the dollar-rupiah trading band unchanged Thursday at 2,378 rupiah-2,682 rupiah.

title: Indonesia: Suharto Urges Banks To Deal With Bad Loans
text:
JAKARTA (AP-Dow Jones)--President Suharto urged Indonesian banks Thursday to overcome a growing problem of bad loans. 

 'I want to draw your attention to the issue of bad debt, although progress has been made in general to cope with the problem,' he said when opening a conference of bank executives. 

 According to Bank Indonesia, the country's central bank, bad loans amounted to 10.2 trillion rupiahs ($3.9 billion) or 2.93% of bank credits in April 1997. The percentage rose from 2.58% in December 1996 after a sharp fall from 3.29% in December 1995. 

 State-owned banks recorded 6.7 trillion rupiah ($2.6 billion) in bad loans. 

 Bank Indonesia Governor Soedradjad Djiwandono said the country's currency was now on an improving trend after a 5.4% drop against the U.S. dollar earlier this week. 

 Djiwandono said intervention by Bank Indonesia has headed off speculative attacks that had weakened the currency.
